Not a day slid by over Christendom, with its courts and cloisters, its tolling bells and market cries, but some unchronicled soul did a deed that would have sounded heroic had it been spoken from a pulpit in sonorous Latin. Yet the great books of the age—those crabbed, worm-scented registers the learned loved—tended to file such lives away like dry herbs between pages: labeled, flattened, and robbed of their living savour.

There exists, indeed, a mouldy chronicle, writ in Latin that clanks like chain-mail. In it a certain chapter is nothing but short, hard sentences—each a fact, each a stone. Beneath those stones, if one stoops and listens, there is warmth: two hearts beating; bread cut; tears swallowed; a young man with ink on his fingers and hunger in his belly; a girl with a father’s weight upon her hand. They lived without trumpets and died without songs, more than four hundred years ago, and lie still in that stern page as unpitied as fossils in rock. If their story be made to breathe again for an hour, it may be that the indifference of centuries will seem a little shameful.

It was past the middle of the fifteenth century. Louis XI wore France like a cunning glove; Edward IV sat wrongful in England; and Philip the Good, who had pushed aside his cousin Jacqueline and broken her heart, reigned in Holland with a magnificence that fed on rarity. Our tale begins in that Holland, in the little town of Tergou, with the low songs of wind in the reeds, the slap of canal-water against timber, and the morning bell that measured labour better than any clock.

Elias the cloth-merchant lived there with Catherine his wife. He dealt wholesale and retail in cloth and silk and brown holland; but, above all, in curried leather—tough, well-fed hide, worked with oil and tannin till it shone and would take twenty years’ wear. Such leather was prized by the middling folk, for it turned a common knife; and knives were free that century, too free—men being apt, even at dinner, to lay down their meat and carve their neighbour upon a moderate difference of opinion.

They were well to do, and might have been easy in their burgher’s prosperity but for the nine children Heaven had sent them, one almost every year, as steadily as harvest. When the first came, and the next, and the next, they had thanked the saints loudly and never asked why; babies then were like bright toys placed in busy hands for evening solace. But olive-branches do not stay green shoots. They rise into saplings, and saplings into hungry young trees; and as Elias and Catherine’s hair threaded with grey, the fate of large families looked them in the face whenever supper was laid.

Holland was a provident land. Reckless parents were as rare there as disobedient children. So when the huge brown loaf—dark, sour-sweet with rye, its crust thick as a rampart—came in on its great trencher, looking like a fortress in a moat, and then, after one solemn circuit of the table, seemed to have melted away into nine mouths, Elias and Catherine would exchange a glance over the crumbs and say, low enough that the youngsters should not hear and yet often enough that they did: “Who is to find bread for them all when we are gone?”

To the little ones, dinner and supper came by nature like sunrise and sunset. They thought the brown loaf must for ever go round their family circle, set in their stomachs, and rise again from the family oven with the morning’s crackle. Yet that repeated sentence awakened the elder boys’ Dutch thoughtfulness. Some began to think good thoughts—of work, and thrift, and apprenticeship. Some thought ill thoughts—of waiting, and grasping, and play.

One day Elias, measuring the lengthening elbows and broadening shoulders around his board, said, “Kate, the children grow so, this table will soon be too small.”

“We cannot afford it, Eli,” Catherine replied, answering not his words but the worry beneath them, as women do.

At times their anxiety sharpened into a pride that stung them more than fear. Free burghers had their dignity as well as nobles; and Catherine could not bear the thought that any of her blood should sink down among the beggars when she and Elias were in the ground.

So they did what Holland taught: they denied themselves. They clothed the small bodies, fed the great mouths, and still put by a hoard—coin by coin, like ants making a hill. In the steel-banded coffer with its florid key, every spare stiver went in; and as the little treasure grew, a secret pleasure grew with it—one the miser hoarding for himself never knows, because this was hoarded against the day their children would not be children.

Then, like a knife slid quietly into bread, the first severing came.

Richart, the eldest but one, nineteen and steady-faced—one of those youths whose calm outside makes strangers mistake the iron within—came to his mother and begged her, with composed speech and a moist eye, to intercede with his father: he wished to go to Amsterdam and be placed with a merchant.

“It is the life that likes me,” he said. “Merchants are wealthy. I am good at numbers. Prithee, good mother, take my part; and I shall ever be, as I am now, your debtor.”

Catherine lifted both hands as if warding off a blow.

“What! leave Tergou!”

“What is one street to me more than another? If I can leave the folk of Tergou, I can surely leave the stones.”

“What! quit your poor father now he is no longer young?”

“Mother, if I can leave you, I can leave—”

“What! leave your poor brothers and sisters, that love you so dear?”

“There are enough in the house without me.”

At that Catherine’s heart turned over. “What mean you, Richart? Who is more thought of than you? Stay—have I spoken sharp to you? Have I been unkind to you?”

“Never that I know of,” he said gravely, the tear swelling clear. “And if you had, you should never hear of it from me. Mother—it all lies in a word, and nothing can change my mind. There will be one mouth less for you to feed.”

“There now—see what my tongue has done,” Catherine cried, and her tears came fast. She saw her first bird on the edge of the nest, testing his wings against the wind. Richart had a will that did not waste words.

So it ended as such talk must. Richart went to Amsterdam with a face so long and sorrowful as Tergou had never seen on him, and a heart like granite.

That afternoon at supper there was one mouth less. The brown loaf came in—its warm scent of rye and sour leaven rising like comfort—and Catherine looked at Richart’s chair and wept bitterly. Elias, to cover his own pain with roughness, shouted at the children, “Sit wider, can’t ye: sit wider!” and then turned his head away over the back of his seat and sat silent, listening to the domestic sounds—chewing, swallowing, the fire’s soft hiss—made suddenly strange by absence.

To fit Richart out and place him with Vander Stegen the merchant took all the hoard but one gold crown. They began again, gathering like ants, coin by coin, while the oven breathed twice a day and the wind worried the shutters.

Two years passed. Richart found a niche for his brother Jacob, and Jacob left Tergou directly after dinner, which was at eleven of the forenoon. Elias remembered that former supper, and when the family gathered again and the loaf came round, he whispered this time, “Sit wider, dears!”—as if loudness could summon grief.

Till that instant Catherine would not see the gap. Her daughter Catherine had begged her: do not grieve to-night, mother; and she had promised, because the children’s hearts were tender to her sorrow. But when Elias whispered “Sit wider,” the promise broke like thin crust.

“Ay,” she said, forcing calm, “the table will soon be too big for the children, and you thought it would be too small.” Then her apron went up and she wept sore. “’Tis the best that leave us,” she sobbed; “that is the cruel part.”

“Nay! nay!” Elias said. “Our children are good children, and all are dear alike. Heed her not! What God takes from us still seems better than what He spares to us; that is to say, men are by nature unthankful—and women silly.”

“And I say Richart and Jacob were the flower of the flock,” Catherine answered through tears.

Again the coffer stood empty. Again they filled it the slow, sure way. In those days speculation ran mostly to cards and dice; Elias knew no road to wealth but the road of saving. “A penny saved is a penny gained,” was his creed. All not needed for trade and bare living went into the steel-banded box. They denied themselves, not by grand gestures but by the humble luxuries—an extra pinch of spice, a bit of smoked eel, a cup more of small beer—each giving up in turn, then catching one another’s looks and smiling, because the joy of forgoing for one’s own blood has a sweetness no indulgence buys.

In three years more they had gleaned enough to set up their fourth son as a master-tailor and their eldest daughter as a robemaker in Tergou—two more mouths turned into hands. Their trade would throw work their way. Yet again the coffer was drained to the dregs, and the shop too bled a little, in goods if not in coin.

And still there remained four at home: two unable to win bread, and two unwilling.

The unable were Giles, a dwarf of the wrong sort—half stupidity, half malice, all head and claws and voice—run from by dogs and frank women, but championed through thick and thin by his mother; and little Catherine, who could move only on crutches. She lived in pain, but smiled through it, with a marble face, violet eyes, and long silky lashes; no fretful or repining word ever slipped from her lips.

The unwilling were Sybrandt, the youngest, too much in love with play to work; and Cornelis, the eldest, who had made calculations and stuck to the hearth, waiting for dead men’s shoes.

Worn by repeated efforts—and, more, dispirited by the moral and bodily infirmities of those now left on hand—Elias and Catherine often said, with the loaf dwindling and the fire dropping, “What will become of all these when we shall be no longer here to take care of them?”

But after they had said it many times, the domestic horizon cleared of a sudden; and though the words stayed by habit, they were said now half mechanically, and then Catherine would brighten, as if the very syllables tasted different: “But thanks to St. Bavon and all the saints, there’s Gerard.”

Gerard was for years a son apart. He was meant for the Church, and the Church in those days could always feed her children—by hook or by crook. No great hopes were built on him; his family had no influence to win benefices, and his own habits were frivolous—habits Elias would not have borne in any other than a clerk destined for a cowl.

His frivolities were reading and penmanship. He loved ink as some boys love dice. He could scarce be dragged from his desk to his meals; and the day was never long enough for him. He carried a tinder-box and brimstone matches everywhere, begged ends of candles from neighbours, and lit them at unreasonable hours—aye, even at eight o’clock at night in winter, when the very burgomaster was abed and decent folk listened to the honest quiet of the town: the faint creak of a sign-board in wind, the distant churn of a mill, the canal’s lap, and, in a good house, the low domestic sounds of knife on crust and pot-lid on stew.

Endured at home, his practices were encouraged by the monks of a neighbouring convent. They had taught him penmanship and continued to teach him until one day, in the middle of a lesson, they discovered he was teaching them. They pointed it out merrily. Gerard hung his head and blushed; he had suspected as much, but mistrusted his own judgement in so delicate a matter.

“But, my son,” said an elderly monk, peering kindly, “how is it that you, to whom God has given an eye so true, a hand so subtle yet firm, and a heart to love these beautiful crafts—how is it you do not colour as well as write? A scroll looks but barren unless a border of fruit and leaves and rich arabesques surround the good words and charm the sense as those do the soul and understanding; to say nothing of pictures of holy men and women departed, with which the several chapters should be adorned—so that not alone the eye is soothed with brave, sweetly blended colours, but the heart lifted by effigies of saints in glory. Answer me, my son.”

Gerard, confused, muttered he had tried illuminating but had not succeeded well; and thus it rested.

Soon after, a fellow-enthusiast appeared—in the unwonted form of an old lady. Margaret, sister and survivor of the brothers Van Eyck, had left Flanders and come to end her days in her native country. She bought a small house near Tergou. In time she heard of Gerard and saw some of his handiwork. It pleased her so well she sent her woman Reicht Heynes to ask him to come.

Acquaintance followed, as it must, for little Tergou had never held two zealots of this sort at once. At first the old lady damped Gerard’s courage terribly. At each visit she fished out from holes and corners drawings and paintings—some by her own hand—that seemed to him unapproachable. But if the artist overpowered him, the woman kept his heart up. She and Reicht turned him inside out like a glove. From him they drew, too, what the good monks had missed: the true reason he did not illuminate. He could not afford the gold, the blue, the red—only cheap earths. He was afraid to ask his mother for the dear colours; and he was sure she would refuse.

Then Margaret Van Eyck gave him a little brush—gold, vermilion, and ultramarine—and a piece of good vellum to lay them on. He almost adored her. As he left her house Reicht ran after him with a candle and two quarters; in his gratitude he quite kissed her. Better even than gold and lapis was the sympathy offered to an isolated enthusiast. It was always ready; and as he returned it, an affection sprang up between the old painter and the young caligrapher, characteristic of an age when fine arts and higher mechanical arts were not sharply divided and artists sought out and loved one another.

Backed by a friendship so venerable and strengthened by women’s sympathy, Gerard advanced in skill. His spirits rose visibly. He still looked behind him when he was dragged to dinner in the middle of an initial G; but once seated he showed great social qualities and a gay humour that had before only peeped out. Often he set the table in a roar, sometimes with his own wit, sometimes with jests glossy-new to his family because drawn from antiquity, those dead tongues whose words, when brought into Dutch mouths, never sounded quite the same—like spices that change in the grinding.

In return for what he owed the monks, he made them exquisite copies from two of their choicest manuscripts: the life of their founder and their Comedies of Terence, the monastery finding the vellum.

Now Philip the Good—Duke of Burgundy, Luxemburg, and Brabant; Earl of Holland and Zealand; Lord of Friesland; Count of Flanders, Artois, and Hainault; Lord of Salins and Macklyn—was a versatile prince.

He could fight as well as any king going; and he could lie as well as any, save the King of France. He hunted mightily and could read and write. He loved jewels like a woman, and gorgeous apparel. He loved maids of honour, and paintings generally—witness his ennobling of Jan Van Eyck. He had a rage for giants, dwarfs, and Turks: turbaned men blazing with jewels stood planted about him. His agents inveigled them from Istamboul with fair promises; then, once caught, he baptized them by brute force in a tub, and after that let them squat facing Mecca and invoke Mahound as much as they pleased, laughing in his sleeve at their simplicity in fancying they were still infidels. He kept lions in cages and fleet leopards trained by Orientals to run down hare and deer.

In short, he relished all rarities except humdrum virtues. Anything singularly pretty, or diabolically ugly—this was your customer. The best of him was his open hand to the poor; the next best, that he fostered the arts in earnest. Of this he now gave a signal proof: he offered prizes for the best specimens of orfevrerie, religious and secular; for the best paintings in white of egg, oils, and tempera, on panel, silk, or metal; for the best transparent painting on glass; for the best illuminating and border-painting on vellum; and for the fairest writing on vellum. Burgomasters of the towns were commanded to aid poorer competitors by receiving their work and sending it to Rotterdam at the town’s expense.

When this was cried by the bellman through the streets of Tergou—his voice beating against gables and slipping along the canal—thousand mouths opened, but one heart truly beat hard: Gerard’s.

He told his family timidly he should try for two prizes. They stared in silence; his audacity blew the breath out of them. Then one horrid laugh exploded on the floor like a petard. Gerard looked down. It was Giles the dwarf, slit and fanged from ear to ear at Gerard’s expense, laughing like a lion.

Nature, relenting at making Giles so small, had given him the biggest voice on record. His whisper was a bassoon. He was like those stunted, wide-mouthed pieces of ordnance on fortifications—more like a flower-pot than a cannon; but, heaven help the tympans, how he bellowed.

Gerard turned red with anger, the more because the others began to titter. Little Catherine saw; a pink tinge came to her cheek, and she spoke softly, with her quiet courage.

“Why do you laugh? Is it because he is our brother you think he cannot be capable? Yes, Gerard, try with the rest. Many say you are skilful; and mother and I will pray the Virgin to guide your hand.”

“Thank you, little Kate,” Gerard said, his heat cooling. “You shall pray to our Lady—and our mother shall buy me vellum and the colours to illuminate with.”

“What will they cost, my lad?” Catherine asked, already suspecting pain.

“Two gold crowns.”

“What!” screamed the housewife. “When the bushel of rye costs but a groat! What—me spend a month’s meal and meat and fire on such vanity as that? The lightning from Heaven would fall on me, and my children would all be beggars.”

“Mother,” sighed little Catherine, imploring.

“Oh, it is in vain, Kate,” Gerard said, with a sigh that tasted of disappointment like cold ashes. “I shall have to give it up, or ask the dame Van Eyck. She would give it me, but I think shame to be for ever taking from her.”

“It is not her affair,” Catherine snapped, sudden and sharp, jealousy flaring that another woman’s kindness should come between her and her son. “What has she to do coming between me and my son?” And she left the room red-faced.

Little Catherine smiled, patient as ever. Presently the housewife returned with a gracious, affectionate air and two little gold pieces in her hand.

“There, sweetheart,” she said. “You won’t have to trouble dame or demoiselle for two paltry crowns.”

Gerard’s gratitude rose, then turned at once into thought: how to spare that purse that was the family’s hearth. “One will do, mother,” he said. “I will ask the good monks to let me send my copy of their Terence. It is on snowy vellum, and I can write no better. Then I shall only need six sheets for my borders and miniatures, and gold for my ground, and prime colours—one crown will do.”

“Never tyne the ship for want of a bit of tar, Gerard,” said his changeable mother; yet she added, half laughing, half wincing, “Well—there. I will put the crown in my pocket. That won’t be like putting it back in the box. Going to the box to take out instead of putting in is like going to my heart with a knife for so many drops of blood. You will be sure to want it, Gerard. The house is never built for less than the builder counted on.”

And indeed, when the time came, Gerard longed not only to compete but to go to Rotterdam and see the Duke, and, more than that, to see the work of his rivals—so as to learn even from defeat. The crown came out of Catherine’s pocket with good grace. Gerard would soon be a priest; it seemed hard if he might not enjoy the world a little before separating from it for life.

The night before he went, Margaret Van Eyck asked him to carry a letter for her. When he looked at it, to his surprise it was addressed to the Princess Marie at the Stadthouse in Rotterdam.

The day before the prizes were to be distributed Gerard started in his holiday suit: a doublet of silver-grey cloth with sleeves; over it a jerkin of the same, sleeveless; tight-fitting buckskin hose from waist to heel, fastened by points to the doublet; shoes pointed in moderation and held by a strap under the hollow of the foot. His flowing hair lay on head and neck, and his hat was pinned between his shoulders, further secured by a purple silk ribbon little Kate had passed round it and knotted neatly on his breast. Below the hat, attached to the upper rim of his broad waist-belt, hung his leathern wallet.

The road’s sound accompanied him: larks flinging bright notes above the fields, the hush of wind through reeds, the distant creak of cart-wheels, and now and then, near a farm, the steady clop of a flail or the lowing of cattle. Such sounds were as much a part of the day’s health as bread in the belly; they soothed him as he walked, and the thought of Rotterdam—with its crowding cries and clang of trade—rose before him like a different music.

Within a league of the city he was tired; but soon he fell in with a pair more tired than he. An old man sat by the roadside quite worn out, and a comely young woman stood holding his hand, her face brimful of concern. Country folk trudged by, noticing nothing amiss; but Gerard, trained by his craft to read the tale in surfaces, read it in their dress.

The old man wore a gown, a fur tippet, and a velvet cap—signs of dignity; yet the triangular purse at his girdle was lean, the gown rusty, the fur worn—signs of poverty. The young woman was in plain russet; but snow-white lawn covered the part of her neck the gown left visible and ended half-way up her white throat in a little band of gold embroidery. Her head-dress was new to Gerard: instead of hiding her hair in piled linen, she wore an open network of silver cord with silver spangles at the interstices. In it her glossy auburn hair rolled in front into two solid waves and was supported behind in a luxurious, shapely mass. He saw also the old man’s pallor and the tears in the young woman’s eyes.

He passed them a few yards, drew his conclusions, then turned back and came towards them bashfully.

“Father,” he said, “I fear you are tired.”

“Indeed, my son, I am,” the old man replied, “and faint for lack of food.”

Gerard’s address pleased the old man more than the girl. She coloured as if caught in need and, with reserve, said it was her fault: she had underrated the distance and imprudently let her father start too late.

“No, no,” said the old man. “It is not the distance, it is the want of nourishment.”

The girl put her arms round his neck with tender concern; but under that cover she whispered, warning and shame together, “Father—a stranger—a young man!”

Too late. Gerard, simple as breathing and taking charity as a matter of course, fell to gathering sticks with great expedition. He took down his wallet. Out came a manchet of bread and the iron flask his careful mother had put up; out came his everlasting tinder-box. He struck brimstone, lit a match, then a candle-end, then the sticks. The first faint smell of singed wood rose. He set the iron flask on the little blaze and dropped on his stomach to blow, cheeks puffing, breath making the coals glow.

When he looked up, he saw the girl’s face had thawed. She watched his briskness with a demure smile that was half gratitude and half amusement.

He laughed back. “Mind the pot,” he said, nodding at the flask, “and don’t let it spill, for Heaven’s sake: there’s a cleft stick to hold it safe with.” And with that he set off running towards a corn-field at some distance.

“The soup is hot,” said Gerard.

“But how are we to get it to our mouths?” asked the elder, staring at the little flask as though it were a brazier from some desert tale.

“Father, the young man has brought us straws,” said Margaret; and there was a sly kindness in her smile, as if she took pleasure in small domestic miracles.

“Ay, ay,” grumbled the old scholar; “but my poor bones are stiff; and, by St. John, the fire is too fierce for a body to kneel over with these short reeds. Yet—by all the saints—the young man is adroit!”

Gerard did not answer; he acted. The knot at his breast came undone under his fingers as if it had been waiting for him all day. He snatched off his hat, dropped a stone into each corner to weight it, wrapped his hand in the tail of his jerkin against the heat, whisked the flask from the coals, wedged it safe between the stones, and slid the hat—now a rude tray—beneath Peter’s nose with a cheerful look.

The air that rose from the broth was a whole kitchen’s comfort: wine warmed to sweetness, bread softened into it till it yielded without losing its heart, and a savour of herbs and browned crust that clung to the nostril like a remembered hearth. Peter’s trembling hand guided the rye-straw to his lips; he drew, cautiously at first; then with a longer pull. His face, a moment ago pinched and colourless, began to kindle—as if the heat went not only into his mouth but down into his very will.

“Hippocrates and Galen!” he cried, sucking again as if he would drink youth through a reed. “’Tis soupe au vin—the restorative of restoratives. Blessed be the nation that invented it, and the woman that made it, and the young man that brings it to fainting folk. Here, child—sip while I enlighten our host as to the history and virtues of this sovereign compound.”

Margaret took her turn obediently, but her eyes danced at Gerard over the straw, amused in advance; for she knew the moment that glint came into her father’s eye he was off like a cart with the brake loosed.

“This corroborative, young sir,” Peter began, swelling with his own learning as with the wine, “was unknown to the ancients. We find it neither in their treatises, nor in those popular narratives that betray, by accident, many a remedy both in chirurgery and physic proper. Hector, in the Ilias, if my memory—”

“Alas! he’s off,” murmured Margaret; yet not unlovingly, for she had lived with this torrent of words as with weather.

“—was invited by one of the ladies to drink wine,” Peter continued, as if no mortal had interrupted him. “He declined, pleading he was going into battle and must not weaken his powers. Now if soupe au vin had been known in Troy, he would have added—in the hexameter, mark you—‘But a soupe au vin, madam, I will degust, and gratefully.’ Not only from civility—no perfect commander lacks that virtue—but from prudence. Men going to blows need sustenance; and generals that bring hungry soldiers against fed ones are defeated in all ages by inferior numbers. The Romans lost a great battle in the north of Italy to Hannibal by this neglect alone. Yet this divine elixir gives force to the limbs and ardour to the spirits in one moment. Observe: I was faint and heart-sick a minute ago—now I suck this celestial cordial and behold me brave as Achilles and strong as an eagle!”

“Oh, father—now? An eagle, alack!” Margaret’s laugh was half protest, half delight.

“Girl, I defy thee and all the world. Ready—like a foaming charger—to devour the space between this and Rotterdam, and strong to combat the ills of life, even poverty and old age; which last philosophers call the summum malum. Negatur—unless the man’s life hath been ill-spent, which, by the bye, it generally hath. Now for the moderns!”

“Father! dear father!”

“Fear me not, child; I will be brief—unreasonably brief. The soupe au vin occurs not in modern science; but that is only proof—if proof were needed—that for these few hundred years physicians have been idiots, with their chicken-broth and their decoctions of gold; attributing the highest qualities to that meat which has the least juice of any meat, and to that metal which has less chemical virtue than any metal. Mountebanks! dunces! homicides! Since from these no light is to be gathered, go we to chroniclers. First: Duguesclin, a French knight, being about to join battle with the English—masters then of half France, sturdy strikers by sea and land—drank not one but three soupes au vin in honour of the Blessed Trinity. This done, he charged; and, as might have been foretold, killed a multitude and drove the rest into the sea. And he is but the first of a long list of holy and hard-hitting ones sustentated, fortified, corroborated, and consoled—”

“Dear father,” Margaret interrupted, holding up the hat with both hands, pleading as if she begged a child to sleep, “prithee add thyself to that venerable company ere the soup cools.”

Peter, thus coaxed, put the straw back between his lips; and the reed made a faint whispering sound as he drew—one of those little intimate noises that belong to hunger turning into ease.

It spared them the “modern instances,” and gave Gerard a moment to say, with honest warmth, how proud his mother would be that her simple broth had profited a man of learning.

“Ay,” said Margaret, “but she would like it ill to see her son give all and take none himself. Why brought you but two straws?”

“Fair mistress,” said Gerard, his youth getting the better of his prudence, “I hoped you would let me put my lips to your straw, there being but two.”

She smiled—and blushed, as if the heat from the fire had suddenly leapt to her cheeks. “Never beg that you may command,” she answered. “The straw is not mine; ’tis yours. You cut it in yonder field.”

“I cut it, and that made it mine,” said he, watching her mouth as much as the reed. “But after that, your lip touched it—and that made it yours.”

“Did it? Then I will lend it you. There—now it is yours again; your lip has touched it.”

“No,” he said softly. “It belongs to us both now. Let us divide it.”

“By all means; you have a knife.”

“No; I will not cut it—that would be unlucky. I’ll bite it. There. I shall keep my half: you will burn yours once you get home, I doubt.”

“You know me not. I waste nothing,” she said with quick pride. “It is odds but I make a hairpin of it, or something.”

That thrift—so like a house’s good order—did not tease him as she meant it to; it sobered him, dashed his little triumph, and set him striving for other words. But none came; and soon the bread and soup were done.

Then the old scholar rose to go on; and there came a small difficulty: Gerard the adroit could not tie again the ribbon at his breast as Catherine had tied it. He fumbled; he reddened. Margaret, after watching him sidelong with mischief and pity blended—offered her help; for at her age a girl’s tenderness and sauciness change places like hands in a dance, and she had seen she had put him out of countenance.

She bent her head—fair and stately—so that the auburn hair, glossed and warmed, shone through its silver net as if the day itself had tangled in it. Her fingers—white, supple, careful—played upon the stubborn ribbon. She coaxed it into obedience, drawing the ends, easing them, flattening the knot with touches that were light as flour-dust on a baker’s palm. Then, when the bow was made, she pressed the centre with her convexed hand in a final little pat—a woman’s sure seal upon the work: Now keep.

Gerard felt that gentle pressure not on the ribbon but on his heart. Something opened in him—like a door on a room he had not known existed—full of strange light and trembling sweetness.

“There,” said Margaret, drawing back to take one sharp survey of her handiwork; and, lifting her eyes for the simplest approval, met instead the full, yearning gaze of his adoration. The blood flew to her face. She dropped her lashes as if they were curtains she could pull against daylight. A tremor went through her; she retreated with cheeks that betrayed her more than tears would have done, and took her father’s arm on the far side.

Gerard, ashamed that his eyes had frightened her, took the other arm. So the two young creatures went downcast and conscious, propping along the old man—who, restored by wine-soup and vanity, moved with a defiant spring and the self-belief of his own “eagle.”

They entered Rotterdam by the Schiedamze Poort. Gerard knew nothing of the town; Peter directed him toward the Hooch Straet where the Stadthouse stood. He himself, with Margaret, meant to go to a cousin in the Ooster-Waagen Straet. So, almost as soon as they were inside the gate, their roads must part.

They bade each other friendly farewell; and Gerard plunged into the great town.

At once a deep loneliness fell on him—one of those hushes that can live inside a crowd. The streets were thick with folk, yet he felt as if a door had shut behind him and left him outside all warmth. Then he cursed himself that, out of delicacy, he had not asked his late companions who they were or where they lived.

“Beshrew my shamefacedness!” he muttered. “Their words and their breeding were above their means; and something whispered me they would not be known. I shall never see her more. Oh weary world—I hate you and your ways. To think I must meet beauty and goodness and learning—three pearls of price—and never see them more!”

He walked as his feet chose, his mind elsewhere, and so lost his way. Presently he found himself in a stream of people all moving one way; he joined them, reasoning they must be bound for the Stadthouse. But the current of bodies carried him out upon a wide meadow by the Maas; and there the pull that drew them became plain.

Games were in full cry: wrestling with the thud and grunt of bodies; the sharp clap of palm-play; the ring of archery; the laughter at tumblers—men and, to his astonishment, women—whose feet beat the earth like quick drum-taps. There was legerdemain, and a trained bear that stood on his head, marched upright, and bowed with prodigious gravity; a hare beat a drum; a cock strutted on little stilts with the disdain of a tiny tyrant.

All these things wrung a laugh from Gerard now and then; yet the gay din could not tune his heart. He heard, above the muddle of voices, one young man telling another the Duke had been in the meadow, but was gone to the Stadthouse to entertain the burgomasters and aldermen, the competitors for the prizes, and their friends. Hunger—plain, bodily hunger, that had been forgotten in longing—rose up in Gerard at the thought of a prince’s supper. He left the riverside and found, this time, the Hooch Straet; and it led him straight to the Stadthouse.

But at one door he was refused, and at another; and at last he came to the great gate of the courtyard. Soldiers kept it; and over them presided a major-domo, pompous as a painted saint: embroidered collar, gold chain, white staff tipped with a golden knob. A crowd pressed there, each trying to soften that official rock. They surged up like waves and fell back like foam.

Gerard struggled nearer—and when he was within four heads of the gate his heart gave a leap: Peter was there, Margaret on his arm, begging humbly for entrance.

“My cousin the alderman is not at home; they say he is here.”

“What is that to me, old man?” said the major-domo.

“If you will not let us pass in to him, at least take this leaf from my tablet to my cousin. See, I have written his name; he will come out to us.”

“For what do you take me? I carry no messages; I keep the gate.”

Then he bawled, inexorable, so that his voice cracked like a whip:

“No strangers enter here, but the competitors and their companies!”

“Come, old man,” cried a voice in the crowd, “you have gotten your answer; make way.”

Margaret turned half round, her face eager, her voice clear with distress. “Good people, we are come from far, and my father is old; and my cousin has a new servant that knows us not, and would not let us sit in our cousin’s house.”

At that the crowd laughed—coarse, careless. Margaret shrank as if struck. At that instant a hand closed over hers—warm, sure, sudden as a bell-note in a storm. It was Gerard. The touch steadied her like a hand at the small of the back when one stumbles on a step. A little cry of joy and appeal broke from her; and the tears, that had been held back by pride, came now, prettily, despite her.

The jostling, the fear, the mortification—that her cousin had not even warned his servant, and that caution, however faithful, had turned them into beggars at a stranger’s gate—had all worked upon her; and then this familiar face, this kind grasp, arrived as if Providence itself had elbowed through the crowd.

“All is well now,” remarked a coarse humourist. “She hath gotten her sweetheart.”

“Haw! haw! haw!” went the laughter again.

Margaret dropped Gerard’s hand instantly; and turned, eyes flashing through wet lashes. “I have no sweetheart, you rude men. But I am friendless in your boorish town, and this is a friend; and one who knows—what you know not—how to treat the aged and the weak.”

The crowd fell dead silent. They had been thoughtless, not malignant; and her rebuke, sharp as it was, struck true.

In the sudden quiet Gerard addressed the porter. “I am a competitor, sir.”

“What is your name?” The major-domo eyed him as if weighing a coin.

“Gerard, the son of Elias.”

The man took a slip of parchment and peered. “Gerard Eliassoen can enter.”

“With my company—these two.”

“Nay; those are not your company. They came before you.”

“What matter? They are my friends, and without them I go not in.”

“Stay without, then.”

“That will I not.”

“That we shall see.”

“We will—and speedily.” And Gerard, driven by something fiercer than hunger, raised a voice of such startling power that it struck the street like a trumpet and sent its echo clattering among the stones. “Ho! PHILIP, EARL OF HOLLAND!”

“Are you mad?” cried the porter, turning pale.

“HERE IS ONE OF YOUR VARLETS DEFIES YOU—”

“Hush, hush!”

“—AND WILL NOT LET YOUR GUESTS PASS IN!”

“Hush! murder! The Duke’s there. I’m dead,” whimpered the major-domo; and then, trying to drown Gerard’s thunder, he roared with all his lungs:

“OPEN THE GATE, YE KNAVES! WAY THERE FOR GERARD ELIASSOEN AND HIS COMPANY! (The fiends go with him!)”

The gate swung wide as if on enchanted hinges. Eight soldiers lowered their pikes halfway, making an arch; and under that bristling honour Gerard marched, with Margaret and Peter, triumphant. The moment they passed, the pikes clashed together to bar the gap, almost pinning a citizen who tried to wedge in after them.

A few steps beyond the guarded portal and the world changed, as if they had crossed from street-dust into a tale. The courtyard was laid with tables loaded with rich meats and piled with gorgeous plate. Above, a leafy canopy of fresh-cut branches—plane and lime—was fastened with taste to cords of gold, silver, and blue silk that traversed the space. Fruits of many hues hung among the green; some were no fruit at all but wonders in gold, silver, and wax, peeping like bright eyes through leaves.

The Duke’s minstrels touched their lutes now and then; and the sound—fine, plucked, and quick—ran between laughter and talk like a brook through stones. A fountain played red Burgundy in six jets that met and fought in the air. The evening sun struck through those purple spouts, turning them into molten rubies; and the light, stained with the grape’s blood, flung crimson glories on fair faces, snowy beards, velvet and satin, jewelled hilts, gold that glowed, silver that gleamed, and glass that flashed.

Gerard and his friends stood dazzled, spell-bound; and even the old scholar’s tongue stilled, as if the sight had taken his breath.

A whisper ran: “Salute the Duke! Salute the Duke!” They looked up. Under a dais sat their sovereign, high and easy in his state, bidding them welcome with a kindly wave. The men bowed low; Margaret curtsied with deep grace. The Duke turned his hand again and pointed the newcomers out to a knot of valets.

Instantly seven of his people sprang forward, seated the three at a table, and set before them fifteen many-coloured soups in little silver bowls, and as many wines in crystal vases.

“Nay, father,” said Margaret—only now recovering her manners amid the bustle—“let us not eat till we have thanked our good friend.”

“Girl, he is our guardian angel,” said Peter, his eyes shining.

Gerard, overwhelmed in a different way, hid his face in his hands a moment. “Tell me when you have done,” said he, “and I will reappear and have my supper, for I am hungry. I know which of us three is the happiest at meeting again.”

“Me?” asked Margaret.

“No. Guess again.”

“Father?”

“No.”

“Then I have no guess which it can be,” she said; and gave a little crow of happiness that made even Peter smile.

They tasted soup; and the bowls began to empty as hands moved briskly—bread dipped, spoon lifted, lips warmed. Fish followed in a dozen fashions; patties where lobster and almonds met in strange richness; others of almonds and cream; then little brouets and crisp rissoles, each with its own scent rising—pepper here, saffron there, vinegar sharpened, butter mellowed. Then came a wild boar that smelled divine—fat and spice and the dark sweetness of roasted flesh.

Margaret shrieked twice and sprang back, pinching Gerard in her fright.

Why? The Duke’s cook had been too clever. He had given the dish not only savour but semblance: by burnt sugar and edible colours he had restored to the beast the very hair and bristles taken off by fire and water. The great tusks were set in place; the mouth wore that grim “smile” that tusk lends; and two eyes of coloured sugar glowed in the head.

St. Argus—what eyes! Bright, bloodshot, threatening—eyes that seemed to follow each motion of knife and spoon. And there, on the far side, two gilt valets set the monster down before them with smiling, benevolent pride; old Peter clasped his hands in pious admiration; Margaret wheeled away, horror-struck, fingers still biting Gerard’s arm; Gerard, foolishly delighted at the pinch; and all around, guests grinning at the comedy.

“What’s to do?” shouted the Duke, hearing the signals of female distress. Seven attendants sprang and told him. He laughed. “Give her of the beef-stuffing, then, and bring me Sir Boar.”

Benevolent monarch: the beef-stuffing was his own dish. On these days an ox was roasted whole and reserved for the poor; but this wise prince had discovered that whatever venison, hare, lamb, poultry, and the like you skewered into that beef cavern cooked to perfection—keeping its own juices and taking in the rich breath of the ox. At his word the valets drove silver tridents into the steaming cave at random and speared forth a kid, a cygnet, and a handful of wildfowl. These smoked before Gerard and company; and Peter’s face, which had clouded at the loss of the boar, expanded and shone again, as if the meat itself had smoothed his temper.

Afterwards came tarts—twenty kinds—fruits and herbs, sweet and sharp mingled; and last, confectionery on a scale that mocked church and castle: cathedrals of sugar gilt and painted in the hollows of their carvings; castles with moats and ditches made to the life; elephants and camels and toads; knights on horseback jousting; kings and princesses looking on; trumpeters blowing; all these figures edible, their veins filled with scented sweetness. Art made to be destroyed: guests breached bastions, crunched crusaders, cracked bishops cope and crosier, as remorselessly as children crack comfits; sipping hippocras and spiced drinks, Greek and Corsican wines. And now and then little Turkish boys—turbaned, spangled, jewelled, gilded—came offering on bended knee golden troughs of rose-water and orange-water to cool and perfume the guests’ hands.

Yet long before this final marvel, appetite had yielded. Gerard suddenly remembered the letter he bore to the Princess Marie, and, leaning to a servant, asked in an undertone if he would deliver it. The man took it with deep obeisance: he could not carry it himself, but would place it instantly in the hands of one of the Princess’s suite, several of whom were near.

Peter and Margaret had come not to dine but to find their cousin; yet the old gentleman ate heartily, and being worn with travel and revived by wine-soup and rich meat, he dropped asleep where he sat and forgot his errand. Margaret did not wake him, nor remind him; and we shall hear why.

Meanwhile that cousin—an alderman—sat within a few feet of them, just behind, and had spied them when Margaret screamed at the boar. But he forbore to speak, for municipal reasons. Margaret was plainly dressed, and Peter inclined to threadbare. So the alderman said to himself: It will be time enough to claim them when the sun sets and folk disperse. Then I will take my poor relations home, and none will be the wiser.

Half the courses were lost on Gerard and Margaret. They were no great eaters; and besides, they were feeding on sweet thoughts that steal the edge from hunger. Yet there is another delicacy of sense besides taste—the delight of colour, music, and perfume—and those pleasures worked on them perhaps more strongly than on any pair there. The lute-strings’ clear notes laid a net over the courtyard’s murmur; the fountain’s splash was a cool, continual singing; and above both drifted the smells of roasted meat, crushed herbs, spiced wine, and the green breath of broken branches.

Margaret leaned back, half closing her eyes, and murmured to Gerard, as if the sound of her own words might shatter the spell. “What a lovely scene! The warm sun, the green shade, the rich dresses, the bright music of the lutes and the cool music of the fountain—and all faces so happy and gay! And then—it is to you we owe it.”

Gerard answered only with his eyes; and she, seeing them, said in a languid whisper, “Now, speak not to me. Let me listen to the fountain. What are you a competitor for?”

He told her.

“Very well. You will gain one prize, at least.”

“Which? which? Have you seen any of my work?”

“I? no. But you will gain a prize.”

“I hope so; but what makes you think so?”

“Because you were so good to my father.”

He smiled at the logic, and bent his head at the praise, and again was silent.

“Speak not,” she murmured. “They say this is a world of sin and misery. Can that be? What is your opinion?”

“No,” said Gerard, with the confident rebellion of youth. “That is but a silly old song our elders keep repeating out of custom. It is not true.”

“How can you know?” she asked, suddenly grave beneath her sweetness. “You are but a child.”

“Why, only look round!” he cried, and his voice, for once, had no thunder in it—only wonder. “And then—I thought I had lost you for ever; and you are by my side; and now the minstrels are going to play again. Sin and misery? Stuff and nonsense!”

The lutes burst out afresh; delicate harmony ran through the leafy canopy like wind through grain.

“What do you admire most of all these beautiful things, Gerard?” she asked.

“You know my name?” he said, startled. “How is that?”

“White magic. I am a—witch,” she answered, teasingly.

“Angels are never witches,” said he. “But I can’t think how you—”

“Foolish boy! Was it not cried at the gate loud enough to deave one?”

“So it was. Where is my head?” He drew breath, and looked at her as if all the painted sugar castles and ruby wine-jets were nothing beside the living miracle next to him. “What do I admire most? If you will sit a little more that way, I’ll tell you.”

“This way?”

“Yes—so that the light may fall on you. There.” His voice softened, thickened, as if the words must wade through his own heart. “I see many fair things here, fairer than I could have conceived; but the fairest of all, to my eye, is your lovely hair in its silver frame, and the setting sun kissing it. It minds me of what the Vulgate praises for beauty—‘an apple of gold in a network of silver.’ And oh, what a pity I did not know you before I sent in my poor endeavours at illuminating! I could illuminate so much better now. I could do everything better. There—now the sun is full on it—it is like an aureole. So our Lady looked, and none since her until to-day.”

“Oh, fie!” cried Margaret, shrinking and colouring. “It is wicked to talk so. Compare a poor, coarse-favoured girl like me with the Queen of Heaven? Oh, Gerard! I thought you were a good young man.”

Gerard tried to gather himself, to explain, but his senses were too full—light, music, perfume, the nearness of her—his words came out like bread too quickly baked.

“I am no worse than the rest,” he stammered; “but how can I help having eyes—and a heart? Margaret!”

“Gerard!”

“Be not angry now!”

“Now, is it likely?”

“I love you.”

“Oh, for shame! You must not say that to me,” she whispered, and the blush that flooded her face was fiercer than her rebuke.

“I can’t help it,” said Gerard, low and obstinate as a vow. “I love you. I love you.”

A grave, white-haired seneschal approached their board with a softness of step that seemed to hush the very air around him. Over the clatter of trenchers and the thin music of knives on pewter, he asked, courteous as a priest at the altar, whether Gerard Eliassoen sat among them.

“I am he,” said Gerard; and the seneschal inclined his head.

“The Princess Marie would confer with you, young sir. I am charged to conduct you.”

At that, every face within earshot swung round as if tugged by one string—eyes sharp with curiosity, and sharper with envy—fastening on the young man who was to be summoned like a dish from the common table to a princess’s private board. Gerard rose at once.

“I wager we shall not see you again,” said Margaret, very calm; but the colour crept, despite herself, into her cheek.

“That you will,” he answered; and then, bending to her ear where the warm smell of bread and spiced wine hung about her hair, he whispered, “This is my good princess; but you are my queen.” Aloud he added, “Wait for me, I pray you. I will presently return.”

“Ay, ay!” said Peter, waking and speaking in the same breath, as if the words had knocked him awake.

Gerard went with the seneschal, and, the instant he was gone, those two—plain in dress, strangers in a rich hall—found themselves stared at as though their homely wool had suddenly turned to cloth of gold merely by sitting near the man a princess had sent for.

William Johnson, seeing the eyes, seized his moment. He came forward, put on surprise as one puts on a cloak, and claimed them loudly for kin.

“And to think there was I at your backs, and you saw me not!”

“Nay, cousin Johnson,” said Margaret, chill as well-water drawn, “I saw you long syne.”

“You saw me, and spoke not?”

“Cousin, it was for you to welcome us to Rotterdam, as it is for us to welcome you at Sevenbergen. Your servant denied us a seat in your house.”

“The idiot!”

“And I had a mind to see whether it was ‘like maid like master;’ for there is sooth in bywords.”

The blood rushed to William Johnson’s face so quickly it was as if a hot kettle had been clapped upon it. He read something in her keen steadiness that made him wary of defending himself in words; so he took the wiser road and tried deeds instead. He insisted they must come home with him at once—home, where bread was cut under his own roof and a welcome could be proved by fire on the hearth and honest ale in the jug.

“Who doubts it, cousin? Who doubts it?” said the scholar, smoothing the thing with scholarship as one smooths a rough crust with a knife.

Margaret thanked him with due grace, yet would not rise. She said she wished to hear the minstrels again; and indeed the strains—thin as threads of silver—were winding through the hall, sliding between laughter and talk like smoke.

A quarter of an hour passed. Many guests had left; the din had loosened a little, like a market when the best buyers are gone. Johnson renewed his urging, and then Margaret’s true reason came out, the way the heart’s truth will show itself even when wrapped in manners.

“It were ill manners to our friend; and he will lose us. He knows not where we lodge in Rotterdam, and the city is large, and we have parted company once already.”

“Oh!” said Johnson, quick as a man finding an easy stitch for a tear he feared. “We will provide for that. My young man— ahem! I mean my secretary—shall sit here and wait, and bring him on to my house. He shall lodge with me and with no other.”

“Cousin, we shall be too burdensome.”

“Nay, nay. You shall see whether you are welcome or not, you and your friends, and your friends’ friends, if need be; and I shall hear what the Princess would with him.”

At the word lodge—under the same roof—joy leapt in Margaret so suddenly she felt it in her throat; then a small misgiving pricked, like a bone hidden in stew.

“But if your young man should be thoughtless, and go play, and Gerard miss him?”

“He go play? He leave that spot where I put him, and bid him stay?” Johnson’s voice rose with injured certainty. “Ho! Stand forth, Hans Cloterman!”

A figure in black serge and dark violet hose rose as if drawn up by a cord. He took two steps and halted before them. Not a muscle twitched. His face was long and solemn, his bearing starched to the very soul, as if duty had been baked into him like salt into cured meat. Seeing him, Margaret—being very happy and therefore dangerously near laughter—could hardly keep her countenance.

She leaned and whispered to Johnson, “I would put my hand in the fire for him.”

“We are at your command, cousin,” she added, “as soon as you have given him his orders.”

Hans was instructed to sit at the table, wait for Gerard, and conduct him to Ooster-Waagen Straet. He answered not with words, but by calmly taking the seat indicated, as though the chair itself were a post of honour. Then Margaret, Peter, and William Johnson went away.

“And, indeed, it is time you were abed, father, after all your travel,” said Margaret; for that had been simmering in her mind all along, like broth kept for the weak.

Hans Cloterman sat. The minutes ran past him like water past a mill-stone, and stirred no impatience in that perfect image of propriety. Johnson had laughed to scorn the thought of his secretary forsaking duty for sport. Yet the eye that enforces steadiness was gone now; and time, like a sly cook, began to add an ingredient no one had ordered.

Hans, solemn and businesslike, improved the waiting by quaffing—gravely, silently, and at short but accurately measured intervals—goblets of Corsican wine. It was strong; so was his head. But after Gerard had been absent near an hour, the model secretary, still maintaining a face as rigid as a chapel door, conceived that Creation itself expected Hans Cloterman to drink the health of all good fellows, and by name of the Duke of Burgundy there present. With this lofty purpose he filled bumper nine, rose gingerly, and, having attained his full height, instantly rolled upon the grass with the goblet still in hand. The cold liquor spilled over more than one ankle; their owners frisked and cursed; but Hans, in the total eclipse of reason, never disturbed one solemn muscle.

Meanwhile the seneschal had led Gerard through passages where torchlight wavered like flame seen through wine. They came to the pavilion-door. There sat certain young noblemen—embroidered, feathered—keeping watch on the heir-apparent and playing cards by the red glare of torches held by servants whose arms must have ached with the stillness.

A whisper from the seneschal; one of the nobles rose as though forced, stared at Gerard with haughty surprise, and disappeared within. He returned and beckoned; and so, through another passage or two, they were brought to an antechamber where three more young gentlemen sat—furred, feathered, glittering like bright birds—deep in dice as though salvation depended on pips.

“You can’t see the Princess—it is too late,” said one, without lifting much more than his eyelids.

“She passed this way but now with her nurse,” said another. “Gone to bed, doll and all. Deuce—ace again!”

Gerard, crestfallen, prepared to retire. But the seneschal, with an incredulous smile, replied, “The young man is here by the Countess’s orders; be so good as conduct him to her ladies.”

A superb Adonis rose with the injured air of one made to wait upon a commoner, and led Gerard into a room where eleven ladies sat or lolled, chattering like magpies. Two, more industrious than the rest, played cat’s-cradle; their fingers moved as deftly as their tongues. At sight of a stranger, all tongues stopped at once, as if a single peg had been pulled from a mechanism; and all eyes turned, simultaneously, to fix him like pins.

Gerard had been ill at ease before; but this sudden battery of eyes drove his gaze to the ground. The ladies, finding there was a creature they could startle, giggled—delighted with their own power, as children delight in making a timid dog shrink. Then a duenna said severely, “Mesdames!” and the giggling died as if modesty were a cord drawn tight.

This same duenna took Gerard and marched before him in solemn silence. His heart sank; for a moment he half longed to bolt like a hare.

“What must princes be,” he thought, “when their courtiers are so freezing? Doubtless they take their breeding from him they serve.”

These thoughts were cut short: the duenna opened into another room. Three ladies sat working, the quick whisper of thread through cloth making its small, domestic music amid all this grandeur; and a pretty little girl was tuning a lute, testing each string until it sat true, like a cook tasting broth until the salt is right.

The ladies were richly but not showily dressed. The duenna went to one who was hemming a kerchief, spoke low; and that lady turned with a smile and beckoned Gerard near. She did not rise, yet the very motion of laying aside her work was full of ease and grace, the sort that makes ceremony feel like kindness.

“Margaret Van Eyck is an old friend of mine, sir,” she said at once, “and I am right glad to have a letter from her hand, and thankful to you for bringing it safely. Marie, my love, this is the gentleman who brought you that pretty miniature.”

“I thank you a thousand times,” said the young Princess with eager warmth.

“I am glad you feel her debtor, sweetheart,” said the Countess of Charolois, “for our friend would have us do him a little service in return.”

“I will do anything on earth for him,” the girl burst out.

“Anything on earth is nothing in the world,” replied her mother quietly—soft, yet with a weight beneath, as if she knew what “anything” can cost. Then to Gerard: “Well, then—what would you have me to do, sir?”

Gerard understood now what company he stood in; the air itself seemed finer, like flour sifted twice. He spoke gently, a little tremulous.

“My sovereign demoiselle—where there have been no pains, there needs no reward.”

“But we must obey mamma,” said the Princess, quick as a bird. “All the world must obey.”

“That is true,” said Gerard; and then, finding courage in a request that harmed no one, “Then reward me, if you will, by letting me hear the stave you were going to sing and I did interrupt it.”

“What! you love music, sir?” the Princess cried.

“I adore it.”

She glanced to her mother, who smiled assent. Then the child took her lute and sang a romaunt of the day. She was but twelve, yet well taught and painstaking. Her small hand swept the chords with courage and precision; the notes of the arpeggio came clear and bright as if someone had scattered little stars over dark water. But the chief charm was her voice: not mighty, but round and ringing, clear as a bell heard across a frosty field. There was modest eloquence in her singing; she knew none of the tricks by which older throats counterfeit feeling. She was too young to be theatrical, even to be sentimental; so nothing was forced. It all seemed to gush, as if the song had been stored in her like scent in a bruised herb.

When she ceased, and the clink of glasses in far rooms resumed, Gerard’s eyes were wet. The Countess watched him; it was common to applaud a princess loudly, but not to be moved in cheek and eye.

When the last vibration of the lute died, she asked demurely, “Was he content?”

Gerard started; speech broke the spell like a hand clapped on water.

“Oh, madam,” he cried, “surely it is thus that cherubs and seraphs sing, and charm the saints in heaven.”

“I am somewhat of your opinion, my young friend,” said the Countess, with emotion; and she looked on her child with love and gentle pride, the kind of look that seems to acknowledge both the sweetness and the briefness of youth.

Then she resumed, business returning as softly as a lid set on a pot.

“My old friend requests me to be serviceable to you. It is the first favour she has done us the honour of asking, and the request is sacred. You are in holy orders, sir?”

Gerard bowed.

“I fear you are not a priest—you look too young.”

“Oh no, madam. I am not even a sub-deacon. I am only a lector; but next month I shall be an exorcist, and before long an acolyte.”

“Well, Monsieur Gerard, with your accomplishments you can soon pass through the inferior orders. And let me beg you to do so. For the day after you have said your first mass I shall have the pleasure of appointing you to a benefice.”

“Oh, madam—”

“And, Marie, remember I make this promise in your name as well as my own.”

“Fear not, mamma. I will not forget,” cried the Princess; then, with a rush of bright fancy, “But if he will take my advice, what he will be is Bishop of Liège. The Bishop of Liège is a beautiful bishop. What! do you not remember him, mamma, that day we were at Liège? He was braver than grandpapa himself. He had on a crown—a high one—and it was cut in the middle, and it was full of such beautiful jewels; and his gown stiff with gold; and his mantle too; and it had a broad border, all pictures; but above all, his gloves—you have no such gloves, mamma. They were embroidered and covered with jewels, and scented with such lovely scent; I smelt them all the time he was giving me his blessing on my head with them. Dear old man! I dare say he will die soon—most old people do—and then, sir, you can be bishop, you know, and wear—”

“Gently, Marie, gently,” said her mother. “Bishoprics are for old gentlemen; and this is a young gentleman.”

“Mamma! he is not so very young.”

“Not compared with you, Marie, eh?”

“He is of good birth, dear mamma; and I am sure he is good enough for a bishop.”

“Alas! mademoiselle, you are mistaken,” said Gerard, low.

“I know not that, Monsieur Gerard,” said the Countess, and there was a mild amusement in her gaze. “But I am a little puzzled to know on what grounds mademoiselle pronounces your character so boldly.”

“Alas! mamma,” said the Princess, lifting her brows as if the question were wilful blindness, “you have not looked at his face, then.”

“I beg your pardon,” said the Countess. “I have. Well, sir, if I cannot go quite so fast as my daughter, attribute it to my age, not to want of interest in your welfare. A benefice will do to begin your career with; and I must take care it is not too far from—what call you the place?”

“Tergou, madam.”

“A priest gives up much,” the Countess continued; “often, I fear, he learns too late how much.” And her woman’s eye rested a moment on Gerard with a pity that surprised him, as if she looked past his cassock-to-be and saw, beneath, the ordinary human hungers and the domestic joys he would be asked to renounce. “At least you shall be near your friends. Have you a mother?”

“Yes, madam, thanks be to God!”

“Good. You shall have a church near Tergou. She will thank me. And now, sir, we must not detain you too long from those who have a better claim on your society than we have. Duchess, oblige me by bidding one of the pages conduct him to the hall of banquet; the way is hard to find.”

Gerard bowed low, and backed towards the door.

“I hope it will be a nice benefice,” the Princess called after him with a pretty smile; then shook her head with a solemn little doubt, as if prophesying weather: “but you had better have been Bishop of Liège.”

He followed his conductor, heart warm with gratitude. Yet before he reached the banqueting hall a chill stole over him, the way cool air creeps under a door when the fire has been high. A mind bred to quiet days cannot hold contrary feelings evenly; it is seized by each in turn. With the Countess, novelty and honour had filled him—this promise, this royal favour, the pride it would bring at home. But now passion found its voice again.

Give up Margaret—whose soft hand still seemed to lie in his palm, whose deep eyes had lodged in his breast like a relic? Resign her, and that whole world of joy she had opened upon him this day, for a benefice and a priest’s lonely title?

The revulsion came so strong he resolved, hastily and fiercely, to say nothing at home of the offered living.

“The Countess is so good,” he told himself, clinging to hope as a hungry man clings to crust. “She has a hundred ways to aid a young man’s fortune. She will not compel me to be a priest when she learns I love one of her sex. One would almost think she knows it; she cast a strange look, and said, ‘A priest gives up much, too much.’ She will give me a place about the palace.”

That thought eased him. He reached the banqueting hall, thanked his guide, and ran with bright, eager eyes to Margaret.

He came in sight of the table.

She was gone.

Peter was gone too.

No one of their party remained—only a citizen in sober garments had just tumbled beneath the board, dead drunk, and several were hauling him up to carry him off, his limp weight sliding like a sack of wet grain. Gerard never guessed how important that solemn drunkard was to him. He looked only for Beauty, and let the Beast lie.

He ran wildly through the hall, now grown emptier; the laughter thinned, the air stale with spilled wine and trampled rushes. She was not there. He left the palace, and outside found a crowd gaping at two great fan-lights newly kindled over the gate—two bright openings of flame that made the night seem almost a cheated thing.

He asked, urgent, whether they had seen an old man in a gown, and a lovely girl, pass out.

They laughed. They were staring at those new lights that turned night into day; they would not trouble their heads about old men and young wenches—everyday sights.

From another knot he learned a Mystery was being played under canvas hard by, and half Rotterdam had gone to see it. That lifted his hopes; he hurried there, listening for any voice he knew amid the murmuring, the fife’s thin cry, the thud of feet on turf.

The Mystery was in full course. Holy and unholy alike were dragged into the same rude daylight: divine personages—too sacred to name with ease—came clumsily down from heaven to bandy sophistry with the cardinal Virtues, the nine Muses, and the seven deadly sins, all in human shape and, to Gerard’s eye, too much alike in their painted solemnity. To hearten the weary matter in rattled the Prince of the power of the air, and an imp kept molesting him, buffeting him with a bladder; at each thwack the crowd roared as if the sound itself were their supper.

When the Vices had delivered a good store of obscenity and the Virtues had answered with twaddle, the celestials—Muses included—went gingerly back to heaven one by one; for there was but one cloud, and two artisans worked it up with its supernatural freight, then worked it down with a winch, all in full sight. When that was done, the bottomless pit opened and flamed in the centre of the stage; carpenters and Virtues shoved the Vices in, and then the Virtues, and Beelzebub, and his tormentor danced merrily round the place of eternal torture to fife and tabor, as if damnation were a harvest-home.

This entertainment had been writ by the Bishop of Ghent to diffuse religious sentiment by the aid of the senses—eyes to see, ears to be struck, bodies to jolt with laughter. Yet Gerard, whose ear had lately been filled with a child’s pure singing, found no comfort in this harsh din, no health in this riot of noise. The crowd’s merriment beat against him like a smith’s hammer; it seemed to drive his own thoughts into a smaller, darker corner. He watched faces lit by flare and torch, and could not find the one face he sought. He could not even stay to the end. He went away in the second act, in the midst of a much-admired passage wherein Justice out-quibbled Satan, and walked street after street, listening for the particular cadence of Margaret’s speech, the country turn of her words that carried home in them like the taste of milk in fresh bread.

But Rotterdam was wide, and the night had many mouths and none spoke her name.

At last, worn quite out, he went to a hostelry and slept till daybreak. All that day, heavy and heartsick, he sought her again—market, quay, church-porch, lanes where fish-smell and peat-smoke clung together, broader streets where hoofbeats rang and voices clattered like loose pans—yet he could never fall in with her nor her father, nor obtain the slightest clue.

Then suspicion, like sourness in milk, began to rise. He told himself she was false, or had changed her mind. Irritation joined sorrow; and the good fortune that had fallen on him—the angels in his purse, the medal on his breast, the Countess’s promise—seemed now only to mock him, like rich sauce set before a man who cannot swallow.

On the third day, after he had once more gone through every street he could think of, he stopped as if struck by a sudden certainty.

“She is not in the town,” he said aloud, “and I shall never see her again. I will go home.”

So he started for Tergou with royal favour promised, with fifteen golden angels in his purse, a golden medal on his bosom, and a heart heavy as lead.

Near on four of the afternoon, when the day has begun to cool and even the road-dust lies down a little, Eli was in his shop with the shutters half-open to the street, weighing hose and measuring cloth as steadily as a man counts beads. The eldest and the youngest were abroad. Catherine and her little crippled maid had been so long strained upon Gerard’s absence that they had limped and hurried a little way down the road to peer for him, as if sight could conjure him nearer. So it fell out that Giles, whom the neighbours called Sampsonet in mockery and in awe, had the sitting-room to himself.

It was a room that told you, before a word was spoken, what sort of folk dwelt there. The very floor confessed a creed. Dutch tiles, blue and white and bright as a rinsed dish, lay underfoot—so glazed and so often washed that you could have set a trencher down and eaten without fear of taint. The house smelt not of stale rushes and old bones, but of lye-soap, clean water, and a faint ghost of yesterday’s broth lingering in the oak. From the shop came the mild rasp of shears, the soft thump of folded stockings, and the street’s harmless music: a cart-wheel grumbling in sand, a child’s call, a distant bell knitting the air together. The quiet was not emptiness but order; each sound had its place, and so did each object.

One large window looked to the road. Its stone cross-work, heavy and square, stood proud in the middle like a true cross to the eye, and had been stared at in prayer so often that the very light seemed to fall more devoutly through it. The panes were small, lozenge-shaped, and tied together with lead, each diamond holding a little slice of afternoon. The chairs were rude things, stout and plain, all but the great arm-chair of oak, carved at the crown and so high-backed that a man’s head, sitting, stopped two feet short of the top. On the wall hung the copper pail for holy water, narrowed at the waist like a woman’s body, with a little besom beside it to scatter blessing in a fine spray. A long narrow table of massive oak ran the length of the room—the sort of table that has received prayers, loaves, quarrels, and christening-cakes, and keeps them all in its grain.

And at the table’s rim, as if he were some grotesque carving come alive, clung Giles.

Nature had made him with lavish care—head and shoulders strong, the chest full and corded—then, as though interrupted by a call, had finished the rest in haste. He was all wedge: broad above, dwindled below, an inverted cone set upon legs too slight for such a furnace of arms. His very imbalance had become his craft. There was little weight to drag his limbs downward; his hands were like grapnels. He could shin up a pole as quick as a squirrel, and hang from a bough by one fist till others’ wrists burned at the thought. It pleased him—insanely, childishly—to make a playground of the household’s honesty: to grip the dinner-table with both hands and swing, and then, crowning joy, to seize the very rim with his teeth and let go with his hands, holding on by those great ivories as if he were a beast of the woods.

There he was now: teeth sunk in the oak, eyes bright and wild, claws of hands lifted as if to pounce—like some imp nailed to decent furniture.

Little Kate came in on her crutches and stopped short. The room’s cleanliness, the long table’s smooth edge, the order of things—these struck her before Giles’s bravado did. She had her mother’s heart for what fed and sheltered them, for the good oak that had borne their bowls and bread.

“Oh, Giles! how can you?” she cried, more fear than anger in her voice. “Mother is at hand. It dents the table.”

“Go and tell her, little tale-bearer,” snarled Giles, and his words were as sharp as a knife on a platter. “You are the one for making mischief.”

“Am I?” said Kate, steady as a cook with a hot pot. “That is news to me.”

“The biggest in Tergou,” growled Giles, and fastened on again with spiteful relish.

“Oh, indeed!” said Kate, and the dryness of it was new in her mouth, like vinegar tasted by a child. She had scarce flung that small dart before her eyes filled. She lowered herself as best she could, sat, and cried quietly, as if tears were another kind of washing.

Catherine came in almost upon the sound—her step quick, her hearing sharpened by care. The house’s hush broke a little: the crutch tips on tile, the mother’s skirt whispering, Giles’s breath under the table as he dropped and crouched there, glaring from the shadows.

“What is to do now?” said Catherine sharply, the way a woman speaks when her pot is in danger of boiling over and her child is missing besides. Her eyes, experienced as hands, went from Kate’s wet cheeks to Giles’s guilty posture and the way his mouth had been. Her palm itched.

“Nay, mother,” Kate said, wiping her face with the back of her hand. “It was but a foolish word Giles spoke. I had not noticed it at another time; but I was tired and in care for Gerard, you know.”

At that, a voice—faint, as if the road had taken it toll and left only breath—came from the door.

“Let no one be in care for me.”

Gerard stood there—pale, dusted with travel, the very lines of his face drawn thin by haste and disappointment and hope. He tottered in, and the room’s ordered sounds—shop-noises, street-bell, the small domestic hush—were drowned in a rising burst: Catherine’s cry, Kate’s sob turned to laughter, questions tumbling like apples into a basket. And Gerard, knocked up by beating Rotterdam like a covert for Margaret and then the long journey home, dropped exhausted into the nearest chair—the tall one, which made his tiredness look smaller by its height.

Yet youth is elastic. Give it a chair, a swallow of small beer, the sight of loving faces, and it springs back. In a handful of breaths he was no longer a ghost at the threshold but the bright centre of a ring.

“Now then,” said Eli’s wife, hands hovering as if to feel him safe and whole, “the prizes—tell us the prizes.”

Gerard’s eyes lit, and with the light came a new music in his speech, quick and eager as a spoon on a bowl.

“I was admitted,” he said, “to see the competitors’ works, all laid out in an enormous hall before the judges pronounced.”

His hands moved as if laying out pages, arranging colours, weighing gold.

“Oh, mother! oh, Kate! when I saw the goldsmiths’ work, I had liked to have fallen on the floor. I thought not all the goldsmiths on earth had so much gold, silver, jewels, and craft of design and facture. But in sooth, all the arts are divine.”

To please the women, and because he himself had been dazzled as any hungry man is by a rich board, he described the church treasures as if reciting a feast: reliquaries like small bright houses, feretories, calices with rims as clean as a well, crosiers curling like pastry hooks, crosses, pyxes, monstrances—each thing wrought so cunningly that you could almost taste the patient hours in the metal. Then the worldly splendours: goblets, hanaps, watches and clocks, chains and brooches, all shining, all exact. He spoke of them until their mouths did what mouths will do at the thought of plenty: they watered. For in every age, hunger and desire are cousins; the tongue knows.

“But, Kate,” he went on, and now his voice softened like butter melting, “when I came to the illuminated work from Ghent and Bruges, my heart sank. Mine was dirt by the side of it. For the first minute I could almost have cried; but I prayed for a better spirit, and presently I was able to enjoy them, and thank God for those lovely works, and for those skilful, patient craftsmen, whom I own my masters.”

He told how the coloured pages—greens like crushed herbs, reds like wine, blues deep as the canal at dusk—had been so beautiful he forgot his own black and white. “But next day,” he said, “when all the other prizes had been given, they came to the writing, and whose name think you was called first?”

“Yours,” said Kate simply, as if naming the next dish she knew must come.

The others laughed her down. Kate, who had learned to hear tones as much as words—who knew how joy sounds before it shows—only looked at Gerard.

“You may well laugh,” said Gerard, and his cheeks flushed as if heat had been brought near. “But for all that, Gerard Eliassoen of Tergou was the name the herald shouted.”

He described it so plainly it became present: the herald’s voice ringing in the high hall; Gerard standing stupid, shoved forward by hands he scarcely felt; the air swimming; himself on his knees on a cushion at the Duke’s feet, like a child at a great table. The Duke spoke; Gerard, fluttered like a caught bird, could not answer. And then—no glaive to cut off his dull head, as his fear had half-invented—but a gold medal laid into his hand.

“And there it is,” he said, and drew it out.

There was a yell and almost a scramble—human voices breaking into a small riot, the room suddenly full of edges and breath and reaching fingers.

“And then,” said Gerard, savoring the moment as one savors a good bite, “he gave me fifteen great bright golden angels. I had seen one before, but I never handled one. Here they are.”

He poured them out, and the gold rang softly as it struck apron and palm: a little rain of metal, a sound that changes a room. It made the tile-floor seem whiter, the oak table older, the air sharper. Even the street noises beyond the window seemed to lean in and listen.

“Oh, Gerard! oh, Gerard!”

He began to portion them with a tenderness that was like carving meat fairly, giving each his share not by greed but by story.
