“There is one for you, our eldest; and one for you, Sybrandt, and for you, Little Mischief; and two for thee, Little Lily, because God hath afflicted thee; and one for myself, to buy colours and vellum; and nine for her that nursed us all, and risked the two crowns upon poor Gerard’s hand.”

The gold drew out what lay in each heart as fire brings out smell from spice. Cornelis and Sybrandt clutched their coins and stared—one glare of greed, another of envy toward Kate who had got two. Giles seized his and rolled it along the clean tiles, and went gambolling after it, his laughter a cracked little trumpet against the room’s quiet decency. Little Lily, with her crutches beside her, sat down as if her strength had been replaced by something gentler, and held out her arms to Gerard with a gesture so full of love it hushed even Giles for a blink. Catherine, at first benumbed by the shower of gold that had fallen on her apron like a sudden harvest, broke into tears.

“Leave kissing him, Kate,” she cried, half laughing, half sobbing, the old maternal jealousy rising like yeast. “He is my son, not yours. Ah, Gerard! my boy! I have not loved you as you deserved.”

Gerard slid from his chair and threw himself on his knees beside her as if the floor were a chapel. She flung her arms round him, weeping for joy and pride upon his neck; and the sound of her crying was not sorrowful but rich—like a pot boiling over because it is full.

“Good lad! good lad!” cried Eli from the doorway of the shop, drawn in by the commotion, his voice thickened with feeling he tried to keep stern. “I must go and tell the neighbours. Lend me the medal, Gerard; I’ll show it my good friend Peter Buyskens; he is ever regaling me with how his son Jorian won the tin mug a shooting at the butts.”

“Ay, do, my man,” Catherine said, wiping her cheeks and suddenly proud as if she had baked the bread that fed the whole street. “And show Peter Buyskens one of the angels. Tell him there are fourteen more where that came from. Mind you bring it me back!”

“Stay a minute, father,” said Gerard, and his joy deepened, for there was yet something beneath it like a sweeter seasoning. “There is better news behind.”

“Better! better than this?” Eli stared, as a man stares who thinks his table already groans with food and is told there is another course.

Then Gerard told them of his interview with the Countess, and the house rang with joy—joy that was not only loud but echoing, as if it bounced off the clean tiles and came back larger. To Catherine it sounded like the end of fear.

“Now God bless the good lady,” she cried, “and bless the dame Van Eyck! A benefice? our son! My cares are at an end. Eli, my good friend and master, now we two can die happy whenever our time comes. This dear boy will take our place, and none of these loved ones will want a home or a friend.”

From that hour the family’s speech changed, as a kitchen changes when a new spice is brought in: everything is flavored by it. Gerard was looked on as the stay of the house. He was a son apart—beloved, leaned upon, indulged. What had been shared before now began to be measured: what was “for Gerard,” what suited “his future.” Cornelis and Sybrandt, hearing that new tone, grew jealous; their faces tightened when his name was praised, and in their hearts they longed for the day he should go to his benefice—get rid of the favourite, and have his reverence’s purse open to them. With those views, Gerard himself unconsciously worked; for love, which had once made his blood leap, now throbbed dully like a bruise that heals but remembers.

He thought more highly of himself, as youths do when the world has clapped them on the back; and he resented with more spirit Margaret’s ingratitude and discourtesy. Yet the memory of her had power to chill him toward the rest of her sex; a wound, even when it closes, teaches the skin. For every reason—hurt pride, new ambition, the comfort of being needed—he wished to be ordained priest as soon as he could pass the intermediate orders.

He knew the Vulgate already better than most clergy about that country, and he studied the rubric and the dogmas with his friends the monks. Their Latin, their church-words, their solemn phrases came to him like a borrowed tongue—useful, authoritative, and yet, when he lay awake, not quite fitting the innermost parts of his thought the way his own dialect did. Certain feelings—shame, longing, the taste of his mother’s stew, the sound of Kate’s crutch on tile—would not translate cleanly into the Church’s dominant speech. But he pushed that unease down, as one pushes down a stubborn loaf, because the form must be made.

The first time the bishop came that way, Gerard applied to be admitted exorcist, the third step in holy orders. The bishop questioned him and ordained him at once. Gerard had to kneel; after a short prayer the bishop delivered to him a little manuscript full of exorcisms—compact as a spice-box, potent by reputation—and said, “Take this, Gerard, and have power to lay hands on the possessed, whether baptized or catechumens!”

Gerard took it reverently. The words rang in his ears on the walk home, mixing with the village’s familiar sounds—the lowing of cattle, the clack of a distant mallet, a lark falling through the air like a thread of song. The world was the same world of bread and tiles and neighbours’ gossip; yet now, by the Church’s utterance, he was invested with power to cast out demons. The thought sat oddly beside the homely: a holy book tucked under his arm, the smell of boiled onions from some doorway, his own hunger returning after excitement as hunger always returns.

As he came near his home, little Kate met him on her crutches, breathless with news. Her face shone, and the crutches clicked on the tiles within hearing, a small steady rhythm like a spoon against a bowl.

“Oh, Gerard!” she cried. “Who, think you, hath sent to our house seeking you?—the burgomaster himself.”

“Ghysbrecht Van Swieten!” Gerard stopped short. The name did not sound like joy; it sounded like iron laid down on wood. “What would he with me?”

“Nay, Gerard, I know not. But he seems urgent to see you. You are to go to his house on the instant.”

“Well,” said Gerard, and drew a breath as if bracing against wind, “he is the burgomaster: I will go; but it likes me not. Kate, I have seen him cast such a look on me as no friend casts. No matter; such looks forewarn the wise. To be sure, he knows.”

“Knows what, Gerard?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

“Kate,” he said, and though his voice was steady, something in it tightened like a cord, “I’ll go.”

Ghysbrecht van Swieten had the sort of craft that did not announce itself with trumpets. It came softly, like a knife slid under a crust to test whether the loaf had taken the bake: no flourish, only certainty. He began, as a man begins who means to smell a secret before he tastes it.

“The town records,” said he, turning a stiff page as if it were a dried rind, “are crabbedly written, and the ink is rusty with age. They need a fair hand to make them readable again.”

Outside, the town’s day went on in its own key: wheels worrying the stones, a far hammer counting time on iron, a gull’s harsh cry over the river wind. Within, the room held its own quieter acoustics—paper whispering, a pen’s imagined scratch, and the burgomaster’s voice placed carefully, as one places salt.

He offered Gerard the honor of transcribing them.

Gerard, who had learned what steady work costs in hours and in the ache of the wrist, asked at once what he would be paid.

Ghysbrecht named a sum that would scarce have bought the tools: quills, ink, parchment—the bare victuals of the craft, leaving the worker to starve on gratitude.

“But, burgomaster,” said Gerard, “my labour? Here is a year’s work.”

“Your labour?” Ghysbrecht let the words fall as if they were chaff. “Call you marking parchment labour? Little sweat goes to that, I trow.”

“’Tis labour,” Gerard answered, and his voice held, like a well-made broth, both heat and restraint, “and skilled labour to boot; and that is better paid in all crafts than rude labour, sweat or no sweat. Besides, there’s my time.”

“Your time?” The burgomaster’s eyes narrowed, keen as a cook’s when a boy swears the oven was hot enough. “Why, what is time to you, at two-and-twenty?”

Then, fixing his gaze on Gerard, to watch what the words would draw out as surely as warm fat draws scent from herbs, he said, lightly and yet with a hook in it:

“Say, rather, you are idle grown. You are in love. Your body is with these chanting monks, but your heart is with Peter Brandt and his red-haired girl.”

The name, spoken into the room, changed its sound. It was like dropping a pebble into a cistern and waiting for the return. Even the street-noise seemed to pause, as if listening.

“I know no Peter Brandt,” said Gerard.

That denial, too neat, was a lid clapped on a pot too fast; it made Ghysbrecht surer there was something boiling underneath.

“Ye lie!” he shouted, and the word cracked in the air like a board snapped across a knee. “Did I not find you at her elbow on the road to Rotterdam?”

“Ah!”

“Ah!” Ghysbrecht pressed, savoring the small exclamation the way a man savors the first yielding of meat to the tooth. “And you were seen at Sevenbergen but t’other day.”

“Was I?”

“Ah—and at Peter’s house.”

“At Sevenbergen?” The question sprang from Gerard before he could bridle it, sharp and naked, betraying itself the way a tongue betrays a man’s birthplace on a single vowel.

“Ay, at Sevenbergen,” said Ghysbrecht, and the triumph in him was quiet, not unlike the satisfaction of a trap that has felt the brush of fur. It was a guess flung out boldly as fact—a draw, a baited line meant to make the fish show itself.

Yet the effect was not what the crafty man had expected.

Gerard started up as if a sudden sound had struck him from behind. His breath came quick; his fingers trembled, and in his eyes there was a bright, nervous sparkle—fear, yes, but not of the burgomaster’s anger. It was fear with direction, as if it heard a call only it could understand.

“Burgomaster,” he said, and his voice shook despite his effort to keep it steady, “I have not been at Sevenbergen these three years, and I know not the name of those you saw me with, nor where they dwelt; but, as my time is precious, though you value it not, give you good day.”

The words were plain, but they carried the stubborn weight of a man who knows his own measure, as a baker knows the weight of flour by the pull on his arms. And with that he darted out, leaving behind him only the hush after a door, and the street’s rougher music rushing in to fill the place.

Ghysbrecht sprang up in huge ire—his temper rising like scum in an ill-watched pot—yet he checked himself and sank back into his chair, thinking harder than he had spoken.

“He fears me not,” he muttered. “He knows something, if not all.”

The room’s quiet returned, but it was no longer restful. The sounds from outside—cartwheels, voices, the constant grind of the town—seemed suddenly like accomplices, able to hide a man’s passage in their common clamor.

He called hastily to his trusty servant and almost dragged him to the window.

“See you yon man?” he cried. “Haste! follow him! But let him not see you. He is young, but old in craft. Keep him in sight all day. Let me know whither he goes, and what he does.”

The servant went.

All day the town’s noises thickened and thinned: the midday bell, the chatter at stalls where salted fish and brown bread changed hands, the sharp rattle of shutters, the evening’s softer tread. Ghysbrecht waited through it as a man waits through a long cooking, smelling for change, listening for the first telltale bubble.

It was night when the servant returned.

“Well? well?” cried Van Swieten eagerly, the impatience in him like hunger.

“Master,” said the servant, and his breath still carried the day’s dust and the damp of roads, “the young man went from you to Sevenbergen.”

Ghysbrecht groaned, as if the sound had struck him in the belly. The name lay on his tongue with the weight of old stories, of dialects spoken low and differently beyond the town’s gates, where a man’s words could be as telling as his face.

“To the house,” the servant added, “of Peter the Magician.”

And Ghysbrecht, in the darkening room where the city’s din faded into a night’s thinner sound, felt the circle close.

“Look into your own heart and write!” cried Herr Cant; and all the earth’s cuckoos took up the note, thin and tireless, as if a single call could make a man truthful. Look into the Rhine where it runs darkest, and the Thames where it runs thickest, and swear you have painted the bottom. Drop a bucket into a well of self-deceit, and because the water comes up cold and shining, call it immortal truth.

Yet no child of Adam reads his own heart plain, not at first. He must learn the alphabet of feeling by poring over other hearts—listening to their confessions as one listens to a market square at dawn, when every sound has its place: the clop of hooves, the hush of a broom, the soft chime of a spoon against a bowl. Only then, with borrowed light, can he spell out his own desires; and even then he stumbles over the words.

Halfway to Sevenbergen Gerard tried it. The road had its own music: larks above the wet fields; a cart far off, squealing in its axle like a bad fiddle; the steady, comforting crunch of his soles on grit. He asked his heart why he was going.

It answered him at once, bold as a drummer.

“We go out of curiosity—to learn why she jilted us; to show her it has not broken our hearts; to prove we are content with our honours and our benefice in prospectu; and we want neither her nor any ally of her fickle sex.”

That was what it said. Gerard almost believed it, because pride makes a tidy story, like a loaf squared off to seem larger than it is. But another truth ran beneath, as water runs under ice.

He found Peter Brandt’s cottage without much asking. The place sat low and honest to the earth, thatch smelling of sun-warmed straw and last week’s smoke. In the doorway a girl sat sewing. The click of the needle through linen was small, exact—one of those domestic sounds that can quiet a mind or unhinge it, depending on what the mind has lost. A stalwart figure leaned beside her with a longbow, talking in the plain, unhurried way of a man who has stood in ranks and learned to waste no breath.

At the sight of that man, a sharp, unreasonable pang went through Gerard, as if a string inside him had been plucked too hard. Then the fellow turned his head; the face was weathered, the hair grizzled, the shoulders still broad though the years were past fifty. An old soldier. Gerard knew him—Martin, who had shot at the butts with such clean force that even boys stopped their boasting to watch.

Another moment, and Gerard stood before them.

Margaret looked up. Her work fell in her lap. A faint cry escaped her, almost swallowed at once; and her face went white and then red, as if blood and breath were arguing over who owned her. The show of it was swift; she put it away too quickly, and her manner turned cool—cooler than it would have been if she had felt nothing.

“What! is it you, Master Gerard?” she said, as though the name had no taste in her mouth. “What on earth brings you here, I wonder?”

“I was passing by and saw you,” said he. “So I thought I would give you good day, and ask after your father.”

“My father is well. He will be here anon.”

“Then I may as well stay till he comes.”

“As you will.” Her fingers gathered up the fallen sewing, too composed, too careful. Then, without looking at him, she spoke to the bowman. “Good Martin, step into the village and tell my father here is a friend of his.”

“And not of yours?” Gerard’s words slipped out before he could catch them.

She lifted her eyes then, and they were steady. “My father’s friends are mine.”

“That is doubtful,” said Gerard, bitterness rising like over-salted broth. “It was not like a friend to promise to wait for me, and then make off the moment my back was turned. Cruel Margaret, you little know how I searched the town for you; how, for want of you, nothing was pleasant to me.”

She held her needle still. The air between them had changed; even the cottage seemed to listen. “These are idle words,” she answered. “If you had desired my father’s company—or mine—you would have come back. There I had a bed laid for you, sir, at my cousin’s, and he would have made much of you; and, who knows, I might have made much of you too. I was in the humour that day.” Her lip trembled, and she punished it into stillness. “You will not catch me in the same mind again—neither you nor any young man, I warrant me.”

“Margaret,” cried Gerard, “I came back the moment the Countess let me go; but you were not there.”

“Nay, you did not, or you had seen Hans Cloterman at our table; we left him to bring you on.”

“I saw no one there,” said Gerard, baffled, “but only a drunken man, that had just tumbled down.”

“At our table?” She leaned forward a little, the way a cook leans to judge whether the scent is true or deceptive. “How was he clad?”

“Nay, I took little heed,” said Gerard; “in sad-coloured garb.”

At that, warmth began to creep back into her face, as if some buried ember had been found. Yet she would not surrender at once; she put on incredulity like a stiff cap and pinned it tight. Question after question she asked, sharp and shrewd—where he had stood, what he had seen, how long he had waited, who had spoken. Gerard answered each as loyally as if he were under oath. He had no art in lying, and no desire to learn it now.

Slowly the cloud thinned. Their two accounts fitted together at last, not like rival tales but like two halves of a broken platter: a misunderstanding, simple as spilt ale on a crowded bench, yet bitter enough to sour two hearts for months. Hans Cloterman. A drunken stranger. A moment’s absence and a wrong face, and all their hopes had been driven off like geese.

When they both saw it, silence fell—a silence with its own sound, louder than speech: the breath they took at the same time; the tiny rustle of linen in Margaret’s lap; a distant cock crowing as if it were any morning in the world.

Then came the revulsion—tenderness surging back all the more fiercely because they had wounded each other. And after tenderness, more perilous still, came confession: neither had been happy since; neither had found the days sweet; and without this chance meeting, neither believed they ever would.

Gerard, seeking shelter from the sudden blaze of feeling, let his eyes rove—only to fasten on a treasure that lay open on the table: a manuscript Vulgate. The sight of it struck him like the smell of fresh bread to a hungry man. Manuscripts were his delight; he moved toward it as a hawk drops to prey.

But before his fingers could touch the page, two white hands fell flat upon it, swift as wings. Above them bent Margaret’s face, and it was red now for shame and for laughter half-choked.

“Nay,” said Gerard softly, the heat of joy in his voice, “take away your hands, Margaret, that I may see where you are reading; and I will read there too at home. So shall my soul meet yours in the sacred page.”

She shook her head, stubborn and smiling, guarding it like a pot on the hearth no one must taste yet.

“You will not?” said he. “Nay, then I must kiss them away.”

And he did—once, and again, and again—until the very persistence of his kisses made her fingers retreat in surrender, for sheer shame. The book lay open, and the words showed clear:

“An apple of gold in a network of silver.”

“There, now,” she cried, half laughing, half vexed with herself, “I had been hunting for it ever so long, and found it but even now—and to be caught!” And, inconsistent as a girl can be when her heart is too full to keep its own rules, she pointed it out with her white finger, as proud as if she had cooked a perfect dish and been teased at the first bite.

“Ay,” said Gerard, eyes on her more than on the Latin, “but to-day it is all hidden in that great cap.”

“It is a comely cap,” she retorted, quick as a sparrow, “I’m told by some.”

“Maybe; but what it hides is beautiful.”

“It is not,” she said, turning her head away though the corner of her mouth betrayed her. “It is hideous.”

“Well, it was beautiful at Rotterdam.”

“Ay,” she breathed, and the sigh carried more truth than her sharpness had done. “Everything was beautiful that day.”

At that moment the latch lifted and Peter Brandt came in with the smell of outdoors on him—damp earth, wind, and the faint tang of stable. His entrance broke the spell without destroying it, the way a spoon breaks the skin on warm milk without cooling it. He welcomed Gerard with a hearty face and a good grip, and would have him stay supper.

Margaret vanished at once, as if a daughter’s duty had been waiting just behind the door. Gerard sat with Peter and talked learnedly—of books, of letters, of the old tongues that carry a people’s memory like seed in a pouch. Words in one mouth, he found, did not always mean the same thing in another; a phrase could be harmless in a city and an insult in a village. Even the way men named bread and barley, ale and cheese, marked who they were and what they held sacred. Gerard listened, and in the background he heard the cottage’s homely orchestra: the scrape of a pot, the rinse of water, the soft thud of a loaf set down, and the steady crackle of the hearth that made all speech gentler.

Then Margaret returned.

Her hair was no longer hidden; it lay gathered in a silver net that caught the lamplight like dew in a spider’s web. She shot Gerard a glance—half arch, half coy—and went about the board with a light step, setting things down with that quiet authority women have when they feed a house. The scent of supper rose: warm bread, a simple fare honestly cooked, and something green and sharp that cleared the head. She moved between father and guest, beaming now with gaiety and happiness as if the day had been remade.

When the meal was done and the evening cooled, Gerard coaxed her out. She objected—and came. He coaxed her down the road toward Tergou; she declined—and came. The air held the day’s last sweetness; hedges murmured with hidden life; somewhere a stream talked to itself over stones, and the far-off village carried its small sounds as a shell carries the sea.

They strolled up and down, hand in hand, as if the simple act could mend what had been torn. And when at last he must go, they pledged each other never to quarrel nor misunderstand again. The promise was earnest as prayer and as fragile as a thin wafer.

They sealed it with a long, loving kiss.

Gerard went home on wings, the road’s noises turned to music under his feet.

From that day he spent most evenings with Margaret, and their attachment deepened and deepened on both sides, until the hours they spent together were the hours they lived; the rest they counted and underwent. At the outset all went smoothly. Obstacles there were, but they seemed distant and small to the eyes of hope, youth, and love. The feelings and passions of so many persons—whom this attachment would thwart—gave no warning smoke to show their volcanic nature and power. The course of true love ran smoothly, placidly, until it had drawn these two young hearts into its current for ever.

And then—

The morning broke as if some lord had spilled a casket of bright stuffs across the street: velvet that drank the sun and gave it back softened, plumes that nodded like wheat heads in a light wind, and horses going by in such sleek order that even their hoofs seemed to flash in time. Tergou ran to its windows and balconies the way a kitchen runs to its door when a new scent comes up the lane—curiosity first, then appetite.

The French ambassador rode through to hunt in the neighbouring forest, with his own train and, for Burgundy’s honour, a borrowed handful of the Duke’s servants. Before them all went the Duke’s tumbler—solemn as a church beadle one moment, rolling off his horse the next with such artless ignominy that the gravest faces cracked. He would spill himself into the dust, legs and arms all askew, then climb back up by the beast’s tail as if it were the most natural stirrup in Christendom. The crowd’s laughter followed him like a ripple follows a dropped pebble.

But the eye was drawn, too, to the leopard.

A huntsman sat a Flemish horse of giant build—broad as a threshing-board, muscles shifting beneath its hide with every step. Strapped to the rider’s loins was a long wooden box, contrived like a traveling bench, and upon it crouched the leopard: bright, glossy, dappled with ink-dark rosettes, her body coiled as if she could spring clean through the air and land on the far side of the street. A chain lay along her foreleg to the huntsman’s hand.

People pressed near. One or two, emboldened by the morning’s gaiety, stretched fingers as if the spotted coat were some rare fur at market.

The huntsman’s shout cracked across the lane like a cleaver on a block. “Beware! At Antwerp one did but fling a handful of dust at her, and the Duke made dust of him.”

“Gramercy!” someone breathed.

“I speak sooth. The good Duke shut him in a cell under ground, and the rats cleaned the flesh off his bones in a night. Served him right, for molesting the poor thing.”

Fear ran through the crowd and cooled their hands. It was as if the street’s music changed key: less laughter, more murmuring; the very clop of the hooves sounded sharper now that men had been reminded what power could do when it chose to be offended.

Then came a sound to mend their spirits: a thin, fluty voice, piping from a body that should have thundered.

The Duke’s giant brought up the rear—a Hungarian seven feet four, a wall of a man on long legs, yet speaking as if a bird had learned words and could not quite push them out. He was vain, and so unaware of his own absurdity that he fed on it. His sharp little voice travelled up, and caught Giles—Giles the dwarf—perched atop a balcony like a watchful cat.

“Hallo, brother!” squeaked the giant. “I had nearly passed without seeing thee.”

Giles answered from his small chest with a great bell of a bellow. “You are plain enough to see.”

“Come on my shoulder, brother,” piped Titan, offering an arm the size of a hunk of mutton, fist like a mallet.

“If I do I’ll cuff your ears,” roared Giles, and the town burst into such laughter that it seemed the street itself had learned to sing.

Yet the laughter was not for wit alone. It was for that mad duet the air carried: the mountain giving birth to a squeak, the mole-hill belching thunder. In a world where the ear reads a man before the eye has finished its glance, the voices made a farce of nature’s expectations. Even the horses’ snorts and the jangling harness seemed to join in, each sound finding its place in the morning’s rough music.

The giant, thinking himself applauded for cleverness, played on Giles the more—until Giles, who had little fear and less patience, lost the last thread of command.

Like a stone dropped from a roof, the dwarf let himself fall upon the giant’s neck. One hand knotted in the man’s hair, the other drummed blows upon his head with astonishing quickness. At first the giant laughed, his fluty he-he rising. Then the weight and the stinging rain of punches changed laughter to yelps.

“He! he! Ah! ha!—hallo!—oh! oh! Holy saints! Help, or I must throttle the imp. I can’t—I'll split your skull against the—”

In blind fury he ran backward, aiming to dash Giles against the balcony. Giles felt the danger as a cook feels the first curl of smoke from a neglected pan: in an instant, without pausing to wonder, he seized the balcony rail with both hands and whipped himself over, just as the giant’s head struck the wood with a stunning crack.

The crowd roared—relief, triumph, and that hungry delight people take in any nimble escape. Giles had become, in a blink, their champion, their own small thunder resisting ducal bulk.

The giant, crimson with rage, grabbed two of the laughers. He knocked them together like dumb-bells, shook them as if to beat sense into their bones, and flung them down. Catherine shrieked and threw her apron over Giles as if cloth could ward off wrath. The giant strode away after the party, still boiling, his thin voice squealing curses that sounded the more impotent for his vastness.

No one in that moment guessed what a seed had been dropped into the day—how a small scene, all noise and sport, might sprout consequences later. For now the effect was immediate and, to Giles, profitable. Tergou swelled with pride in him; their smiles softened. When he went begging parchment for Gerard, they were more affable than before. He drove a steady trade: begged the scraps and leaves gratis, and Gerard paid him coppers for each—because ink and prayer and learning must have something to bite on, even when money is thin.

That afternoon, inside the little house where leather and glue and family breath mingled, Catherine and her daughter sat and spoke of what warmed them most: Gerard—his goodness, his benefice, and the brightened prospects that now seemed, like a well-risen loaf, to promise substance and comfort.

“He will marry Cornelis and Sybrandt,” Catherine said, counting practical joys as women do while their hands keep busy in thought. “They can wed, good housewives, now if they will. Gerard will take care of you and Giles when we are gone.”

“Yes, mother—and we can confess to him instead of to a stranger,” said Kate.

“Ay, girl! and he can give the sacred oil to your father and me, and close our eyes when our time comes.”

“Oh, mother, not for many, many years,” Kate pleaded. “Pray speak not of that; it always makes me sad. I hope to go before you, mother dear. No; let us be gay to-day. I am out of pain, mother—quite out of all pain. It seems so strange; and I feel so bright and happy that—mother, can you keep a secret?”

“Nobody better, child. Why, you know I can.”

“Then I will show you something so beautiful. You never saw the like, I trow. Only Gerard must never know; for sure he means to surprise us with it. He covers it up so, and sometimes he carries it away altogether.”

Kate took her crutches and moved slowly away. Her mother watched, curiosity rising like yeast. She returned with something wrapped in cloth. When she uncovered it, a presence seemed to enter the room: a painted Virgin, with her insignia, her tiara, and a wealth of hair flowing loose over her shoulders—gold like sunlit flax, set down in strokes that held light.

Catherine drew in her breath as if incense had been lit. “It is herself,” she whispered. “It is the Queen of Heaven. I never saw one like her to my mind before.”

“And her eyes, mother—lifted to the sky as if they belonged there and not to a mortal creature. And her beautiful hair of burning gold.”

“And to think I have a son that can make the saints live again upon a piece of wood!”

“The reason is, he is a young saint himself, mother. He is too good for this world; he is here to portray the blessed, and then to go away and be with them for ever.”

They had not half exhausted their wonder when a voice—unwelcome as a cold draught across a hearth—sounded at the door. By one of those quick, silent instincts, they hid the picture again, though no one yet had asked to see it.

The man who entered had not crossed their threshold in ten years: Ghysbrecht Van Swieten.

He came in casting his eyes around, not openly, but with a furtive measuring. The two women stared—at him, then at each other—as if some old wound had walked back into the room. “The burgomaster,” they said, and in their tone lay memory enough to make a man defensive.

“Yes,” he answered, stiff. “I own the last time I came here was not on a friendly errand. Men love their own interest—Eli’s and mine were contrary. Well, let this visit atone the last. To-day I come on your business and none of mine.”

Catherine and Kate exchanged a glance of contempt that was swift as a knife’s flash.

“It is about your son Gerard.”

“Ay, ay,” Catherine snapped, “you want him to work for the town all for nothing. He told us.”

“I come on no such errand,” said Ghysbrecht, too quickly. “It is to let you know he has fallen into bad hands.”

“Now Heaven and the saints forbid!” Catherine cried, and the mother in her rose like a flame. “Man, torture not a mother. Speak out—and quickly. Speak ere you have time to coin falsehood: we know thee.”

The burgomaster’s face paled at the affront, and spite came and sat beside whatever other motives had brought him.

“Thus it is, then,” he said, teeth grinding as the words ran fast. “Your son Gerard is more like to be father of a family than a priest. He is for ever with Margaret—Peter Brandt’s red-haired girl—and loves her like a cow her calf.”

Mother and daughter both burst out laughing.

Ghysbrecht stared, thrown off balance as a man is when his expected chord is met with a different tune. “What! you knew it?”

“Carry this tale to those who know not my son, Gerard,” Catherine said. “Women are nought to him.”

“Other women, mayhap. But this one is the apple of his eye, or will be, if you part them not, and soon. Come, dame—make me not waste time and friendly counsel. My servant has seen them together a score times, handed, and reading babies in one another’s eyes like—you know, dame—you have been young, too.”

Catherine’s laughter died. Her hand went to her breast as if he had struck there. “Girl, I am ill at ease. Yea, I have been young, and know how blind and foolish the young are. My heart—he has turned me sick in a moment. Kate, if it should be true—”

“Nay, nay!” Kate cried, quick as a pan snatched from the fire. “Gerard might love a young woman; all young men do. I can’t find what they see in them to love so; but if he did, he would let us know. He would not deceive us. You wicked man! No, dear mother, look not so. Gerard is too good to love a creature of earth. His love is for our Lady and the saints. Ah! I will show you the picture—if his heart was earthly, could he paint the Queen of Heaven like that? Look! look!”

She whipped the cloth away and thrust the panel forward. In that moment Kate herself, lit from within by certainty, seemed to outshine the painted face—so that Ghysbrecht, confronted by two sorts of fervour, stood with mouth and eyes open, turning as if on a pivot between the women and the picture.

“Why,” he gasped, “it is herself.”

“Isn’t it!” Kate cried, and for the first time her hostility softened. “You admire it? I forgive you for frightening us.”

“Am I in a mad-house?” said Ghysbrecht, bewildered into bluntness. “You show me a picture of the girl, and you say he painted it, and that is a proof he cannot love her. Why, they all paint their sweethearts, painters do.”

“A picture of the girl?” Kate echoed, shocked as if he had spat on the floor. “Fie! this is no girl. This is our blessed Lady.”

“No, no. It is Margaret Brandt.”

“Oh blind! It is the Queen of Heaven.”

“No; only of Sevenbergen village.”

“Profane man! behold her crown!”

“Silly child—look at her red hair! Would the Virgin be seen in red hair? She who had the pick of all the colours ten thousand years before the world began.”

Their voices rose; the house filled with quarrel the way a larder fills with sharp smells when something has turned. And as loud words carry farther than gentle ones, an anxious face appeared at the edge of the open door: their neighbour Peter Buyskens, drawn by the clamour as surely as a man is drawn by the sound of a market bell.

“What is to do?” he asked in a cautious whisper. “We can hear you all across the street. What on earth is to do?”

“Oh, neighbour,” Catherine cried, “what is to do? Why, here is the burgomaster blackening our Gerard.”

“Stop!” Ghysbrecht snapped, pouncing on Peter as on a witness. “Peter Buyskens is come in the nick of time. He knows father and daughter both. They cast their glamour on him.”

“What! is she a witch too?” asked Peter, half in jest, half uneasy at the burgomaster’s heat.

“Else the egg takes not after the bird. Why is her father called the magician? I tell you they bewitched this very Peter; they cast unholy spells on him, and cured him of the colic. Now, Peter—look, and tell me who is that? And you be silent, women, for a moment, if you can. Who is it, Peter?”

Peter’s eye went to the picture and stayed there, caught as if by a hook. “Well, to be sure!” he said slowly.

“Who is it?” Ghysbrecht repeated, stamping impatience into the floor.

Peter smiled, faintly. “Why, you know as well as I do. But what have they put a crown on her for? I never saw her in a crown, for my part.”

“Man alive!” the burgomaster burst out. “Can’t you open your great jaws and speak a wench’s name plain out to oblige three people?”

“I’d do a great deal more to oblige one of you than that, burgomaster,” Peter retorted, nettled. “If it isn’t as natural as life!”

“Curse the man! he won’t, he won’t—curse him!”

“Why, what have I done now?”

Kate, turning pale, leaned forward on her crutches as if her very bones needed the answer. “Oh, sir—for pity’s sake tell us. Are these the features of a living woman, of—of—Margaret Brandt?”

“A mirror is not truer, my little maid.”

“But is it she, sir, for very certain?”

“Why, who else should it be?”

“Now, why couldn’t you say so at once?” Ghysbrecht snarled, triumphant.

“I did say so, as plain as I could speak,” Peter snapped back.

They bristled at each other over this small bone of contention, so taken with their own disputing that they did not see Catherine and Kate had drawn their aprons over their heads and begun to rock to and fro, stricken as if a blow had fallen.

Then Elias came in from the shop, drawn by the raised voices the way a man is drawn by the wrong sound in his own house—like a kettle screaming when it ought to be singing low.

He stood aghast. Though Catherine’s face was covered, she knew his footstep, the weight and rhythm of it learned over years like the sound of one’s own hearth-lid. “That is my poor man,” she sobbed. “Tell him, good Peter Buyskens, for I have not the courage.”

Elias went pale. The burgomaster’s presence after so many years, and the women’s distress, made his mind leap to calamity.

“Richart! Jacob!” he gasped—naming their sons as if death must have chosen one.

“No, no,” Ghysbrecht said. “It is nearer home, and nobody is dead or dying, old friend.”

“God bless you, burgomaster!” Elias breathed, as if a band had been cut from his chest. “Ah! something has gone off my breast that was like to choke me. Now, what is the matter?”

Ghysbrecht told him all, and set the picture forward as proof. Elias looked, listened, and then—strangely—his first feeling was relief, rough and practical.

“Is that all?” he said. “What are ye roaring and bellowing for? It is vexing—it is angering, but it is not like death, not even sickness. Boys will be boys. He will outgrow that disease: ’tis but skin-deep.”

But when Ghysbrecht added that Margaret was a girl of good character, and no such intimacy was likely unless marriage had been spoken of, Elias’s brow darkened, and the easy tolerance baked into hardness.

“Marriage! that shall never be,” he said, stern as a man laying down a rule at the table. “I’ll stay that—ay, by force, if need be—as I would his hand lifted to cut his throat. I’d do what old John Koestein did t’other day.”

“And what is that, in Heaven’s name?” Catherine cried, snatching her apron away so her face showed, wet and shaken.

It was the burgomaster who answered, almost with satisfaction, for the law gives some men a relish as salt gives broth. “He made me shut young Albert Koestein up in the prison of the Stadthouse till he knocked under. It was not long. Forty-eight hours all alone, on bread and water, cooled his hot stomach. ‘Tell my father I am his humble servant,’ says he, ‘and let me into the sun once more—the sun is worth all the wenches in the world.’”

“Oh, the cruelty of men!” Catherine sighed.

“As to that,” Elias returned, “the burgomaster has no choice: it is the law. And if a father says, ‘Burgomaster, lock up my son,’ he must do it. A fine thing it would be if a father might not lock up his own son.”

“Well, well! it won’t come to that with me and my son. He never disobeyed me in his life; he never shall. Where is he? It is past supper-time. Where is he, Kate?”

“Alas! I know not, father.”

“I know,” said Ghysbrecht. “He is at Sevenbergen. My servant met him on the road.”

Supper was set and eaten without comfort. The familiar sounds of the house—bowls touched, bread broken, a cup set down—came muffled, as if grief had padded the room. Evening deepened, and still no Gerard. Eight o’clock came—no Gerard. At last Elias sent all to bed but Catherine.

“You and I will walk abroad, wife, and talk over this new care.”

“Abroad, my man, at this time? Whither?”

“Why, on the road to Sevenbergen.”

“Oh no,” Kate had cried earlier. “No hasty words, father. Poor Gerard! he never vexed you before.”

“Fear me not,” Elias had answered. “But it must end; and I am not one that trusts to-morrow with to-day’s work.”

So the old pair went out hand in hand, not with elbows linked—folk had not yet learned that fashion—but with fingers twined in the older way, as if the hand were the true rope between two lives. They walked in silence awhile. The night was clear and balmy, and it had its own hush: the soft lay of air on leaves, the far-off bark of a dog, a cart somewhere creaking like an old song. In such quiet, memory rises readily, as stew rises when the pot has been left undisturbed and the flavours have had time to marry.

“It is a many years since we walked so late, my man,” Catherine said softly.

“Ay, sweetheart—more than we shall see again,” Elias murmured, and then, like a thorn, “Is he never coming, I wonder?”

“Not since our courting days, Eli.”

“No. Ay, you were a buxom lass then.”

“And you were a comely lad, as ever a girl’s eye stole a look at. I do suppose Gerard is with her now, as you used to be with me. Nature is strong, and the same in all our generations.”

“Nay, I hope he has left her by now—confound her—or we shall be here all night.”

“Eli!”

“Well, Kate?”

“I have been happy with you, sweetheart, for all our rubs—much happier, I trow, than if I had—been—a—a—nun. You won’t speak harshly to the poor child? One can be firm without being harsh.”

“Surely.”

“Have you been happy with me, my poor Eli?”

“Why, you know I have. Friends I have known, but none like thee. Buss me, wife!”

“A heart to share joy and grief with is a great comfort to man or woman. Isn’t it, Eli?”

“It is so, my lass. ‘It doth joy double, and halveth trouble,’ runs the byword. And so I have found it, sweetheart. Ah! here comes the young fool.”

Catherine’s fingers tightened on his hand. They were in the shadow of trees, though the moon rode bright; and their son did not see them. Gerard came down the road singing in the moonlight, his face shining as if the night itself had seasoned him with happiness.

While the burgomaster in far Tergou was busy unmasking Gerard, another kind of calamity gathered in Sevenbergen, and it began, as so many storms in human houses do, with an empty shelf and a hungry heart.

Margaret came to old Martin Wittenhaagen with tears that seemed to have salt in them like the brine of a winter ham. “Martin,” she said, “there is nothing in the house. Nothing. And Gerard is coming; and he is so thoughtless—he forgets to sup at home. When he gives over work he runs to me straight, poor soul, and often he comes quite faint. And to think I have nothing to set before my servant that loves me so dear.”

Her distress was the housewife’s distress, yet deeper than a bare stomach: it was the dread of failing in that ancient covenant between hearth and wanderer—the one language that needs no grammar, only fire, knife, and bread.

Martin scratched his grey head, as if counsel might be found under the scalp. “What can I do?”

“It is Thursday,” said she, and wiped her eyes with the back of her hand, already smelling of soot and yesterday’s onions. “It is your day to shoot. Sooth to say, I counted on you to-day.”

“Nay,” said Martin, with the stubbornness of a man who has learned obedience by pain. “I may not shoot when the Duke or his friends are at the chase. Read else. I am no scholar.” And from his pouch he drew a parchment, stiff with age, fat with the Duke’s seal.

Margaret bent, and though she could not read the words, she read the power in the wax. Martin, with soldierly patience, spelled the sense: Philip of Burgundy granted him four merks yearly, and licence to shoot three arrows once a week—on Thursday, and on no other day—in any of the Duke’s forests in Holland, at any game save a buck of seven years or a doe with fawn; and even then not if the Duke hunted, nor any friend of his. If so, Martin must not disturb the woods, on peril of salary and head, and a fine of one penny—set down with a cruelty almost comic beside the loss of life.

Margaret sighed. The house was empty; the forest was full; and between them lay a strip of law as sharp as a carving-knife.

“Come, cheer up, mistress,” said Martin at last, his old scarred face softening for her. “For your sake I’ll peril my carcass; I have done that for many a one not worth your forefinger. It is no such mighty risk either. I’ll but step into the skirts of the forest here. It is odds but they drive a hare or a fawn within reach of my arrow.”

“If I let you go,” she said quickly, “you must promise me not to go far, and not to be seen. Far better Gerard went supperless than ill should come to you, faithful Martin.”

He promised; and she watched him take his bow and three arrows as a woman watches the last loaf go out of doors. He stole off, cautious as a thief, into the wood scarce a furlong away.

The forest already held the day’s music. Far off, horns sounded thin and ghostly, as if blown through old linen. There was the low stir of frightened life—the tick and hush of leaves, the sudden percussion of hooves, the quick snapping of twigs. All game was afoot. Even the air had that raw green smell that rises when something large has just passed: bruised fern, torn moss, sap bleeding in silence.

“Come,” thought Martin, “I shall soon fill the pot, and no one be the wiser.”

He took his stand behind a thick oak that commanded an open glade. He strung his bow—no toy, but a true engine of war: English yew, six feet and more, thick-limbed, with a string that, when it sang, sang clean as a harp. Martin’s chest was broad, his arms corded like ropes; he could draw a three-foot arrow to the head, and when it flew, the eye could scarce keep pace with it. This bow had once sent its message through mail and leather in the old quarrels of Hoeks and Kabeljauws, when men fought near enough to hear each other breathe, and death came with a visible flight, not hidden in smoke.

A hare came cantering into view, then sat sprightly, her ears making a neat V against the grass. Martin raised the great bow; he was thinking of the pot, of the comfort of broth, of the smell of fat hissing on coals, and he hurried. The string twanged; the arrow went like a needle of light—so near it seemed to strike her—yet it kissed the earth, flashed under her belly, hissed along the short grass, and was gone.

The hare sprang three feet straight up as if the ground had bit her, and then fled at full speed.

“Bungler!” said Martin, and the word was honest: he blamed himself, not the beast.

He had scarce fitted another arrow when a wood-pigeon settled on the very tree beneath which he stood, plump and grey, thinking itself safe in a soldier’s shadow.

“Aha,” thought he, “you are small, but dainty.”

This time he took pains. He drew smoothly, loosed without snatch. The shaft struck; feathers flew up like dust in sun. Yet it had torn, not fairly pierced. The bird fluttered away, breast ragged, and by a great effort rose above the branches, flew fifty yards, and died somewhere in the thick green where a man could not follow without betraying himself.

“Luck is against me,” he muttered, and his mouth tasted bitter as burnt crust.

He nocked the third arrow and watched the glade with a hunger that was half his own, half Margaret’s. Then came a bustle behind him—leaves torn in haste, the ground drummed—he turned just in time to see a noble buck cross the open, too late for a shot. Rage seized him; he dashed his bow down with an imprecation.

At that very moment a long spotted thing slid swift as poured oil across the grass after the deer, belly near the earth, shoulders rolling. Martin knew her: the Duke’s leopard.

“The hunters will not be far,” he thought, cold sweat pricking him. “And I must not be seen. Gerard must go supperless this night.”

He plunged into the wood, for that was his way home—following the buck and the leopard by instinct more than choice. He had not gone far when an unusual sound met him: leaves rustling violently, the harsh trampling of a great struggle.

He hurried, and came upon a sight to turn a man’s stomach and sharpen it too. The leopard was on the buck’s back, tearing with tooth and claw, and the buck ran in a broken circle, bounding as if the earth itself were flinging him. Blood poured down his hide in dark ropes, and the air stank of iron and warm life.

Then in Martin rose a desperate resolve—not the thought of profit, but of Margaret’s bare table, the empty pot, and Gerard coming in with that faint look. Venison was not merely meat; it was a feast, a kind of mercy. He drew his arrow to the head and drove it home into the deer. Even with the brute on his back the buck bounded high, as though trying once more to escape the world, and fell dead.

The leopard went on tearing as if nothing had happened.

Martin waited, hoping she would gorge and leave him the carcass. The minutes crawled; the forest’s sounds seemed suddenly too loud: far horns, near crows, the constant whisper of leaves like talk in a tongue older than men. At last he walked up and laid his hand on the buck’s leg.

The leopard gave a growl that shook the air. She ceased sucking, lifted her head, and fixed on Martin a look like green fire under water—sulky, suspicious, and wholly without law.

What was to be done? Martin had heard it said that wild creatures cannot stand the human eye. He stood erect and stared her down.

She stared back—and then, brutally ignorant of all that men tell each other in taverns, she sprang.

There was barely time. Martin caught her by the throat before her teeth could crush his face. One claw seized his shoulder and rent it; the other, aimed at his cheek, would have ended him, but Martin wore no hat—only a scapulary of tough leather like his jerkin, and he had drawn it over his head like a hood; the claw caught in that loose leather and tore at it, snarled, and slipped.

He kept her jaws from him with great difficulty, his fingers sunk into her throat as if he would strangle the life itself. She kept rending his shoulder. It was like blunt reaping-hooks grinding and tearing through flesh. Pain like hot iron ran along his arm and down his side; yet instead of cowing him it raised his blood. He gnashed his teeth, rage answering rage, and squeezed her neck with a force that had once drawn bows and hauled men from ditches.

Their eyes flared at one another. Now the man’s were near as furious as the brute’s.

She felt the throttling and made a wild effort to free herself. In the struggle she dragged his leather hood across his face and blinded him, and tore her claw out of his shoulder—flesh and all. But still he throttled, hand and arm like iron.

Presently her long tail, that had lashed the air high and proud, sank.

“Aha!” cried Martin, joyfully, and gripped her like death. Her body lost its spring; in his hands she became a choked, powerless thing. He held on till all motion ceased, then dashed her to the earth. Panting, he threw back his hood.

The leopard lay mute at his feet, tongue out, paw bloody.

And then, for the first time, terror fell on Martin—not the fear of teeth, but of men. “I am a dead man,” he whispered. “I have slain the Duke’s leopard.”

He snatched handfuls of leaves and flung them over her in a foolish, desperate attempt to hide what could not be hidden. Then he shouldered the buck—warm, heavy, a whole feast across his back—and staggered away, leaving a trail of blood all the way: his own mixed with the deer’s, both darkening the moss.

He burst into Peter’s house a horrible figure, bleeding and bloodstained, and flung the carcass down so that it thudded on the floor like a delivered sentence.

“There—no questions,” he gasped. “But broil me a steak on’t, for I am faint.”

Margaret did not see he was wounded; she thought the blood was all from the deer. Her hands flew at once to the work as if work were prayer. She set the fire to a fiercer heat, raked embers, laid iron to glow. The smell of fresh venison rose—sweet and wild, with that clean woodland tang. She cut thick steaks across the grain, seasoned simply as poor folk do when the meat itself is rare: a little salt, perhaps a pinch of dried herb saved from summer. Fat hissed as it touched the hot iron; smoke curled, smelling of pine and flesh; the sound of sizzling was like comfort spoken aloud.

Apart, the stout soldier stanching and binding his own wound, bit on a strip of leather, tied tight with practised fingers, and said nothing. Soon Gerard came, and the three of them supped royally—broiled venison hot from the fire, juices running, crust browned, the hearth giving its red light to their faces. Gerard, with a wonderful thoughtfulness, had brought a flask of Schiedam; the sharp spirit cut the richness, warmed Martin’s blood, and made the room for a moment seem like the safest place on earth.

Under that warmth Martin revived enough to tell them how the venison was got; and they made merry over it, laughing as if laughter could salt the meat against tomorrow. Their voices mingled with the household sounds—the crack of firewood, the scrape of knife on trencher, the swallow of drink. Outside, the wind moved in the trees like distant surf.

Their mirth was broken as suddenly as a bone snaps.

Margaret’s eye fixed and would not move. The color left her cheek. She tried to speak and could not; only lifted a trembling finger toward the window.

They followed her pointing, and there, in the twilight, crouched a dark form, low and patient, with eyes like glowworms—green fire in a living face.

It was the leopard.

They stood petrified, held by those eyes as by a spell. Then from the wood came a single deep bay—one note, heavy as doom.

Martin trembled at it. “They have lost her,” he whispered, “and laid muzzled bloodhounds on her scent. They will find her here—and the venison. Good-bye, friends. Martin Wittenhaagen ends here.”

Gerard snatched up the bow and thrust it into the soldier’s hands. “Be a man,” he cried. “Shoot her, and fling her into the wood ere they come up. Who will know?”

More voices of hounds broke out—nearer, many-throated. The air seemed to fill with sound, a hunting music that was not music to the hunted: baying, yelping, men shouting, feet crashing through underbrush. It pressed on the little house like water rising.

“Curse her!” cried Martin. “I spared her once; now she must die, or I—or both more likely.” He reared the bow and drew an arrow to the head.

“Nay! nay!” cried Margaret, and seized the arrow with both hands.

It broke in half. The pieces fell on either side of the bow.

At that same instant the hounds’ tongues burst all about the house: they were hot upon the scent. Men’s voices rang close; the yard seemed suddenly full.

“What have you done, wench?” Martin cried, hoarse with panic and pain. “You have put the halter round my throat.”

“No!” Margaret flung back. “I have saved you. Stand back from the window, both! Your knife—quick!”

And before either could hinder her, she seized Martin’s long-pointed knife—almost tore it from his girdle—and darted out of the room.

Outside, the house was now ringed with baying dogs and shouting men. And still the glowworm eyes at the window did not move.

Margaret tore a great gobbet from the venison—still steaming where the knife had opened it, the browned edge sweating salt and rosemary—and ran straight to the casement. She flung it outward as one tosses a crust to a barn-cat; only these were no barn-cats.

Two green points, like coals blown alive in a dark hearth, slid forward from the hedge. The beast sprang, and the night answered with a savage, tearing snarl; bone grated, sinew cracked; there came that sickening, busy crunching a kitchen hears when a cleaver finds cartilage—only this cleaver had fangs.

At that same instant a hound gave tongue so near and so huge that it seemed the very boards of the house bayed with it. The sound rolled through the rooms, ricocheting from rafter to rafter; and all three at the window shrank together, as folk do when thunder breaks too close for comfort. Gerard felt Margaret’s shoulder against him, and even Martin, who would face a fair fight, drew back at the violence of the noise: there is a kind of sound that makes the heart believe in claws.

The leopard, fearing for her supper, gathered the meat and glided away—not a rush, but a smooth, stealthy withdrawal, as if the darkness itself had learned to walk. The crunching receded toward the woods.

Then, almost before the last snarl died, the chase burst past the window—horses, men, and dogs in a mad, clattering ribbon. Hooves struck flint from the hard road, harness jingled, men shouted, and the pack’s full cry poured after the vanished quarry like wind through winter branches. The house stood still again, but the night kept the echo; even after the riders had gone, the air seemed to throb where their noise had been.

Martin and his companions breathed at last. The leopard was swift, and the pack would not have her within a league of their hearth. Hands met—rough palm to rough palm—and for a moment the very act of gripping one another was like setting a potlid hard upon boiling fear.

Margaret seized her respite to cry, as women do when the danger has passed and the body remembers it has a throat. Gerard kissed the tears away, tasting salt, and, with it, a tenderness sharper than any spice.

They went back to table. The venison, though diminished, still sent up its rich, forest smell—blood tamed by fire, fat rendered to sweetness. Gerard lifted his cup and drank to woman’s wit.

“’Tis stronger than man’s force,” said he.

“Ay,” said Margaret, wiping her cheek and forcing a steadier breath, “when those she loves are in danger; not else.”

That night he stayed later than his custom. When at last he went out, the air smelt of damp earth and the cold green of leaf-shadow. Behind him, through the shutters, he could still hear domestic sounds—the settle creaking, a ladle rinsed, a foot on stone—small, homely noises that made the late uproar seem a nightmare a man wakes from into the comfort of his own bed.

He had not gone far when two figures rose out of the black under some trees and almost barred his way. The starlight caught their faces: his father and his mother.

So late. So set. Something in their stillness turned the night chill.

He stopped. They stood grim and silent, like folk at a graveside who have resolved their grief into judgment.

He stammered some question.

“Why ask?” said his father. “You know why we are here.”

“Oh, Gerard!” said his mother; and in that one sound reproach and love lay twisted together like two strands in a cord.

Gerard’s heart quaked. He could not find speech that did not sound guilty, nor silence that did not sound defiant, and so he stood dumb.

His father, seeing his confusion, softened only enough to sting.

“Nay, you need not hang your head. You are not the first young fool that has been caught by a red cheek and a pair of blue eyes.”

“Nay, nay!” put in Catherine. “It was witchcraft; Peter the Magician is well known for that.”

“Come, Sir Priest,” resumed his father, “you know you must not meddle with women folk. But give us your promise to go no more to Sevenbergen, and here all ends: we won’t be hard on you for one fault.”

“I cannot promise that, father.”

“Not promise it, you young hypocrite!”

“Nay, father, miscall me not.” Gerard’s voice shook, but not with fear alone; something in him was weary of swallowing words. “I lacked courage to tell you what I knew would vex you; and right grateful am I to that good friend, whoever he be, that has let you wot. ’Tis a load off my mind. Yes, father, I love Margaret; and call me not a priest, for a priest I will never be. I will die sooner.”

“That we shall see, young man. Come, gainsay me no more; you will learn what ’tis to disrespect a father.”

Gerard held his peace. The three walked home under the trees, their footsteps muffled by last year’s leaves, silence thickening between them. Only now and then Catherine’s deep sigh broke it, like a kettle letting out its grief.

From that hour the little house at Tergou was no longer the abode of peace.

Next day they took Gerard to task before the whole family, as if he had spilled sour ale into the bread-dough and must answer for the waste. Every voice was loud against him, except little Kate’s—and the dwarf’s, who took his cue from her as naturally as a dog looks to a child that feeds it. Cornelis and Sybrandt were bitterer than their father; there is a spite in brothers that takes the form of righteousness.

Gerard, who had been yesterday the universal pet, stood dismayed in the storm of tongues. His eyes went wistfully to his little sister: her lashes were wet, and the corners of her mouth trembled at the harsh words flung upon him. Yet she gave him no comfort. She turned her head away as if looking at him made the pain sharper, and said, piously and cruelly at once, as youth can:

“Dear, dear Gerard, pray to Heaven to cure you of this folly!”

“What, are you against me too?” said Gerard, softly; and something seemed to give way in him, not with a crack, but with a slow, aching tear.

He rose with a deep sigh and left the house, and went to Sevenbergen.

At the beginning of such quarrels—where affection binds those whose interests and convictions clash—the wrong is not always plain. Both can be honest at the outset, and then a calm friend who sees two sides is a gift rarer than fine pepper in a poor pantry. But let dissension simmer; let it be stirred each day by temper and pride, and it thickens. Human nature, like a pot neglected, burns at the bottom for want of patience, and at last both parties are in the wrong.

The combatants were unequally matched. Elias was angry; Cornelis and Sybrandt spiteful; but Gerard, having a larger and more cultivated mind, saw both sides where they saw but one. His trouble did not sharpen into wrath; it sank into unhappiness. He was lonely in it too. He could open his heart to no one.

Margaret Brandt was high-spirited. He dared not tell her all he endured at home; she was capable—so clean was her pride—of siding with his people by resigning him, though it would cut her own heart to do it. As for Margaret Van Eyck, she had once been a great comfort to him; but now he shrank from making her his confidant. Her story was common talk: in early life she had many offers of marriage and refused them, choosing art—an art that a wife’s and mother’s duties so often smother. Thus she remained single and painted with her brothers. How could he tell her that he meant to decline the benefice she had won him, and for the sake of the very thing she had once sacrificed with so steady a hand?

Gerard, at this time, bade fair to succumb.

But his adversaries had a strange ally—Catherine senior.

Good-hearted, uneducated, she could not, like her daughter, act quietly and firmly; still less could she act upon a plan. At times she irritated Gerard and so—oddly—helped him; for anger, like strong broth, sustains when appetite fails. At other times she whirled round and fell upon her own side like a hen pecking her own chicks.

Once, when they were all together, Cornelis said with a sneer, “Our Gerard wed Margaret Brandt? Why, it is hunger marrying thirst.”

“And what will it be when you marry?” cried Catherine in a flash. “Gerard can paint, Gerard can write, but what can you do to keep a woman, ye lazy loon? Nought but wait for your father’s shoon. Oh, we can see why you and Sybrandt would not have the poor boy to marry. You are afraid he will come to us for a share of our substance. And say that he does, and say that we give it him, it isn’t yourn we part from, and mayhap never will be.”

On such days Gerard smiled to himself, sly and grateful, and took heart. Temporary confusion fell on Catherine’s allies, as when a cook’s sharp answer silences grumblers round the board.

But after more than six months of fretting came the climax. Elias told his son, before the whole household, that he had ordered the burgomaster to imprison him in the Stadthouse rather than let him marry Margaret.

Gerard turned pale; anger drained the colour from him as if he had been bled. Yet by a great effort he held his peace.

His father went on, relentless. “And a priest you shall be before the year is out, nilly-willy.”

“Is it so?” cried Gerard; and now the restraint broke like a cord. “Then hear me, all. By God and St. Bavon I swear I will never be a priest while Margaret lives. Since force is to decide it, and not love and duty, try force, father; but force shall not serve you, for the day I see the burgomaster come for me, I leave Tergou for ever, and Holland too, and my father’s house, where it seems I have been valued all these years, not for myself, but for what is to be got out of me.”

He flung out of the room, white with anger and desperation.

“There!” cried Catherine. “That comes of driving young folks too hard. But men are crueller than tigers, even to their own flesh and blood. Now, Heaven forbid he should ever leave us, married or single.”

Outside, the air hit Gerard like cold water on a fevered brow. His heart panted; his cheeks were bloodless. At the threshold he met Reicht Heynes, who had been watching for him with that look servants get when they bring urgent news and hope it will not be blamed on them.

She had a message: Mistress Margaret Van Eyck desired to see him.

He went, and found the old lady seated grim as a judge, as if her very chair were a tribunal. She wasted no time in soft words.

She inquired coldly why he had not visited her of late. Before he could answer, she said, with a dry sting, “I thought we had been friends, young sir.”

Gerard stood the picture of doubt and consternation, like a boy caught with honey on his fingers.

“It is because you never told her you were in love,” said Reicht, pitying his distress.

“Silence, wench!” cried Margaret Van Eyck. “Why should he tell us his affairs? We are not his friends: we have not deserved his confidence.”

“Alas! my second mother,” said Gerard, “I did not dare to tell you my folly.”

“What folly? Is it folly to love?”

“I am told so every day of my life.”

“You need not have been afraid to tell my mistress; she is always kind to true lovers.”

“Madam—Reicht—I was afraid because I was told…”

“Well, you were told—?”

“That in your youth you scorned love, preferring art.”

“I did, boy; and what is the end of it?” The old woman’s voice changed; it took on a rough sincerity that rasped like a knife on a whetstone. “Behold me here a barren stock, while the women of my youth have a troop of children at their side, and grandchildren at their knee. I gave up the sweet joys of wifehood and motherhood for what? For my dear brothers. They have gone and left me long ago. For my art. It has all but left me too. I have the knowledge still, but what avails that when the hand trembles?

“No, Gerard; I look on you as my son. You are good, you are handsome, you are a painter—though not like some I have known. I will not let you throw your youth away as I did mine: you shall marry this Margaret. I have inquired, and she is a good daughter. Reicht here is a gossip. She has told me all about it. But that need not hinder you to tell me.”

Joy went through him like warm wine. To be permitted—almost commanded—to speak Margaret’s name aloud with praise, and to one who could comprehend what he loved in her, was like being allowed to open a shutter in a close room.

Soon two pairs of eyes were wet over his story; and when he saw that, his own blurred too. Reicht sniffed and wiped her nose with her apron, as if tears were only another kitchen inconvenience.

Women, when they love, have a courage that is their own kind: not the brute, solitary daring that struts and strikes, but a vicarious hardihood that sends others forth and will not let them falter. Under the quiet of that room Gerard felt it press upon him—steady as kneading-hands working stubborn dough into obedience.

Mistress Van Eyck and Reicht agreed: a man should take the bull by the horns. Gerard’s course was to marry Margaret Brandt off-hand; the old folk would come to after a while, once the deed was beyond recall. Whereas, the longer things stood as they were, the more each day would season bitterness into habit.

“See how pale and thin they have made him amongst them,” said Mistress Van Eyck.

“Indeed you are, Master Gerard,” said Reicht. “It makes a body sad to see a young man so wasted and worn. Mistress, when I met him in the street to-day, I had liked to have burst out crying: he was so changed.”

“And I’ll be bound the others keep their colour; ah, Reicht? such as it is.”

“Oh, I see no odds in them.”

“Of course not. We painters are no match for boors. We are glass; they are stone. We can’t stand the worry, worry, worry of little minds; and it is not for the good of mankind we should be exposed to it. It is hard enough, Heaven knows, to design and paint a masterpiece, without having gnats and flies stinging us to death into the bargain.”

Exasperated as Gerard was by his father’s threat, he listened to these friendly voices urging rebellion. Yet his heart resisted.

“I do not fear my father’s violence,” he said, “but I do fear his anger. When it came to the point he would not imprison me. I would marry Margaret to-morrow if that was my only fear. No; he would disown me. I should take Margaret from her father and give her a poor husband, who would never thrive, weighed down by his parent’s curse.

“Madam! I sometimes think if I could marry her secretly, and then take her away to some country where my craft is better paid than in this; and after a year or two, when the storm had blown over, you know, could come back with money in my purse, and say, ‘My dear parents, we do not seek your substance, we but ask you to love us once more as you used, and as we have never ceased to love you’—but, alas! I shall be told these are the dreams of an inexperienced young man.”

The old lady’s eyes sparkled, and not with mockery.

“It is no dream,” said she, “but a piece of wonderful common-sense in a boy; it remains to be seen whether you have spirit to carry out your own thought. There is a country, Gerard, where certain fortune awaits you at this moment. Here the arts freeze, but there they flourish, as they never yet flourished in any age or land.”

“It is Italy!” cried Gerard, as if a bell had been struck inside him. “It is Italy!”

“Ay, Italy! where painters are honoured like princes, and scribes are paid three hundred crowns for copying a single manuscript. Know you not that his Holiness the Pope has written to every land for skilful scribes to copy the hundreds of precious manuscripts that are pouring into that favoured land from Constantinople, whence learning and learned men are driven by the barbarian Turks?”

“Nay, I know not that,” said Gerard; “but it has been the dream and hope of my life to visit Italy, the queen of all the arts; oh, madam! But the journey—and we are all so poor.”

“Find you the heart to go, I’ll find the means. I know where to lay my hand on ten golden angels: they will take you to Rome—and the girl with you, if she loves you as she ought.”

They sat till midnight over this, as if planning a household’s provisions for a long winter: what could be carried, what must be bought on the road, what dangers must be accounted for. Outside, the world had its own acoustics—far dogs, a late cart, the wind in bare branches—and the quiet between those sounds seemed full of possibility, as if silence itself were a map with roads drawn in it.

After that day Gerard’s spirits lifted, and he moved through the gibes and harsh words at home as if he wore a secret charm under his shirt. And Mistress Van Eyck gave him not only money, but money’s worth.

“I will tell you secrets,” said she, leaning toward him with eyes that lit as a fire lights when fat drips upon it, “secrets I learned from masters that are gone from me and have left no fellow behind. Even the Italians know them not; and what I tell you now in Tergou you shall sell there in Florence.

“Note my brother Jan’s pictures: time, which fades all other paintings, leaves his colours bright as the day they left the easel. The reason is, he did nothing blindly, in a hurry. He trusted to no hireling to grind his colours; he did it himself, or saw it done. His panel was prepared and prepared again—I will show you how—a year before he laid his colour on. Most men are content to have their work sucked up and lost, sooner than not be in a hurry. Bad painters are always in a hurry.

“Above all, Gerard, I warn you: use but little oil, and never boil it. Boiling melts that vegetable dross into its heart which it is our business to clear away; for impure oil is death to colour. No; take your oil and pour it into a bottle with water. In a day or two the water will turn muddy: that is muck from the oil. Pour the dirty water carefully away and add fresh. When that is poured away, you will fancy the oil is clear. You’re mistaken.”

“Reicht,” she called, without turning her head, “fetch me that!”

Reicht brought a glass trough with a glass lid that fitted tight.

“When your oil has been washed in bottle, put it into this trough with water, and put the trough in the sun all day. You will soon see the water turbid again. But mark: you must not carry this game too far, or the sun will turn your oil to varnish. When it is as clear as crystal, not too luscious, drain carefully, and cork it up tight.

“Grind your own prime colours, and lay them on with this oil, and they shall live. Hubert would put sand or salt in the water to clear the oil quicker. But Jan used to say, ‘Water will do it best; give water time.’ Jan Van Eyck was never in a hurry, and that is why the world will not forget him in a hurry.”

To Gerard these “receipts” were not dry counsel but a kind of inheritance. He took them as a cook takes a mother’s knowledge—how much salt to pinch, when to lift the lid, what heat will coax and what heat will ruin. There are arts that enter through the senses first, and only afterward through the mind.

Thus furnished with means and craft, Gerard decided to marry and fly with his wife to Italy.

Now nothing remained but to tell Margaret Brandt his resolution, and to publish the banns as quietly as might be. He went to Sevenbergen earlier than his wont, his heart beating like a pestle in a mortar.

He began with Margaret—told her of Mistress Van Eyck’s goodness, of Italy, of the plan made with such grave hope. He asked her to stand with him in it.

She refused him flat.

“No, Gerard. You and I have never spoken of your family; but when you come to marriage—” She stopped, as if the word itself had pricked her pride. Then she began again, more steadily. “I do think your father has no ill-will to me more than to another. He told Peter Buyskens as much, and Peter told me. But so long as he is bent on your being a priest—you ought have told me this instead of I you—I could not marry you, Gerard, dearly as I love you.”

He strove to shake her. He argued; he pleaded; he promised. He could make her cry easily—her tears came as readily as clear whey from pressed curds—but he could not make her yield.

Then impatience and hurt made him unjust.

“Very well!” he cried. “Then you are on their side, and you will drive me to be a priest, for this must end one way or another. My parents hate me in earnest, but my lover only loves me in jest.”

And with that wild bitter speech he flung away home again, leaving Margaret weeping.

Yet when a man misbehaves, the effect on a girl who truly loves is strange: it makes her pity him. Not because she finds the fault sweet, but because she hears the misery behind it. “How unhappy, how vexed, how poor he must be to misbehave,” her heart reasons. “Poor thing.”

Margaret was full of that womanly pity when—scarce an hour and a half after he left—Gerard came running back again, panting with anger and grief. In his hands he carried the torn fragments of a picture.

“There, Margaret! see! see! the wretches! Look at their spite! They have cut your portrait to pieces.”

She looked. Some malicious hand had indeed sliced the painted panel into five parts, as one quarters a loaf with rage rather than hunger. A cut went straight through the very face—the face he had laboured over as carefully as a baker scores a crust for beauty and for rise. Six months’ patient work—layer upon layer, colour coaxed and dried, glazes laid like thin honey—now hacked and ruined.

Margaret was good, but she was not ice. Blood rushed to her forehead; shame and anger and a fierce tenderness all at once.

“Who did it?”

“Nay, I know not,” he cried. “I dared not ask; for I should hate the hand that did it, ay, till my dying day. My poor Margaret! The butchers, the ruffians! Six months’ work cut out of my life, and nothing to show for it now. See, they have hacked through your very face—the sweet face that every one loves who knows it. Oh, heartless, merciless vipers!”

“Never mind, Gerard,” said Margaret, breathing fast, her hands clenched as if she could knead the world into fairness. “Since this is how they treat you for my sake—Ye rob him of my portrait, do ye? Well, then, he shall have the face itself, such as it is.”

“Oh, Margaret!”

“Yes, Gerard. Since they are so cruel, I will be the kinder. Forgive me for refusing you. I will be your wife—to-morrow, if it is your pleasure.”

He kissed her hands with rapture—kissed them as if they were the very means of his salvation—and then her lips. In a tumult of joy he ran for Peter and Martin.

They came and witnessed the betrothal; and in those days a betrothal was no light, whispered thing, but a solemn act—bread and salt to it in spirit, as binding as any oath, and for more than a century later so held, though now the world has grown clever at unbinding what once held fast.

The banns had to be called thrice, as folk do still, yet here the old rule bent easily in a little country church. The curate at Sevenbergen was new in his cure, and youth pleading with eyes is a language no priest is proof against. So on Monday, at matins and again at vespers, he cried Gerard and Margaret—swift, hushed, and with no gaping Tergou faces to carry the news home like chaff on the wind. They went out into the sharp, clean air with hearts that beat as if each rib were a drum.
