At dawn next day they stole in again, warm from walking fast, smelling of dew and lane-dust, their hands cold but their hopes hot. The church had that homely scent of damp stone, old wood, and yesterday’s incense clinging like smoke in a cookhouse beam. The curate began—

—and a stranger rose.

“ I forbid the banns.”

The word fell like a cleaver on a board. He spoke of age, of parents, of consent. Margaret’s breath stopped; Gerard went white as flour.

Outside, by the church-door where lichens mottled the stone, they clung together and argued in broken whispers, as if speech itself might be overheard and twisted into evidence. They had scarce decided anything when the very man who had done the mischief came sidling up with the air of a tradesman offering wares.

He was sorry—so sorry. In truth, he loved to further young happiness; only his living lay in forbidding banns. Yet there was a remedy, simple as salting a pot: “The young people give me a crown, and I undo my work handsomely. I tell the cure I was misinformed, and all goes smoothly.”

“A crown?” Gerard burst out. “I will give you a golden angel.”

The fellow’s eyes brightened as if a lamp had been lit behind them. He took Gerard by the sleeve, went in, and with oily humility confessed his “ridiculous mistake,” swearing that one look at the parties had corrected him. The curate, relieved to have the knot cut, promised to marry them next day at ten.

Thus the knave walked off with an angel in his purse and mischief in his throat. Like many a sharp rogue, he was a fool in drink. He went straight to a hostelry at Tergou by the green where men practised archery and played at their rude sports, and there he drank his angel away as if it were ale, bragging between gulps of how he had barred and unbarred a marriage with the same easy hand.

Sybrandt was there—Sybrandt who haunted such places as flies haunt a larder. He drank in every word, not missing a syllable, for inheritance had made his ears keen. He ran home, found his father gone to Rotterdam to buy cloth, caught Cornelis’s eye, drew him out, and spilled the tale.

In most great households some sheep go black. These two were Gerard’s. Idleness had soured them; waiting on a death they ought to fear as sin soured them more. Their mother’s thrift, which in her and her husband was joined with labour and meant provision for children, had turned in these two into a dry, hungry avarice. It made them cruel in fancy first, then in counsel, and counsel is often the first kneading of a crime.

They agreed to keep their mother in ignorance—her heart blew hot and cold—then went to the burgomaster. They had sense enough to know Ghysbrecht Van Swieten disliked this match, though they could not tell why.

The burgomaster saw through them as one sees through thin beer. Yet he did not let them see through him. He put on magistrate’s coldness as a cook puts a lid on a pot, hiding the simmer beneath.

“Since the father of the family is not here,” said he, “his duty falleth on me, who am the father of the town. I know your father’s mind; leave all to me; and, above all, tell not a woman a word of this—least of all the women that are in your own house: for chattering tongues mar wisest counsels.”

He dismissed them with a touch of contempt; he was ashamed of the company he must use.

They went home, and there sat Gerard, low on a stool at his mother’s knee. She was smoothing his hair with the same hand that had kneaded bread for him when he was little; her voice had the softened sound of milk poured into a pot.

She promised to stand by him with his father, to thwart him no more.

Her change was born, not of argument, but of that quick remorse which sometimes follows a woman’s quick wrath. In a moment of sharp irritation she had cut Margaret’s picture to pieces. She had watched Gerard gather the fragments with hands that trembled as if handling sacred wafer; she had seen him turn as pale as death and sit motionless, staring till tears came and blinded him. Terror at what she had done struck her; then grief; then a wordless resolve—she would never confess, but she would make it up. So now her tenderness flowed back to her son like warm broth into a chilled belly.

Gerard, knowing nothing of the cause, felt shame for his own dark suspicion. In his inexperience of women’s winding ways, her kindness seemed proof. He kissed her again and again, and went to bed with a heart lifted, thinking his mother was his mother at the very hinge of his fate.

At ten next morning, Gerard and Margaret stood in Sevenbergen church. He was bright with joy; she was all blush and trembling courage. Peter was there, and Martin Wittenhaagen—no more. Secrecy was their only shield.

Margaret had refused Italy. She could not leave her father—so learned, so helpless in the world’s plain dealings, as a scholar may be helpless before a boiling pot. It was settled they should slip into Flanders for a few weeks till the storm in Tergou spent itself.

The curate came quickly. It seemed an age. He stood at the altar and called them forward. They went hand in hand, the happiest two in Holland. The book opened.

But ere one word of the rite could pass his lips, a harsh voice struck the air.

“Forbear!”

Constables from Tergou came up the aisle and laid hands on Gerard in the name of the law. Martin’s long knife flashed out, quick as a cook’s blade at a table.

“Forbear, man!” cried the priest. “What! draw your weapon in a church? And ye who interrupt this holy sacrament—what means this impiety?”

“There is no impiety, father,” said the burgomaster’s servant, respectful as a man who carries authority. “This young man would marry against his father’s will, and his father hath prayed our burgomaster to deal with him according to the law. Let him deny it if he can.”

“Is this so, young man?”

Gerard hung his head. He could not lie in God’s house.

“We take him to Rotterdam to abide the sentence of the Duke.”

Margaret’s cry burst out as if torn from her throat. The two, who a heartbeat ago had been poised on heaven’s edge, fell to sobbing in each other’s arms so bitterly that even the men who seized him drew back, ashamed. One of them, good-natured, came close under colour of parting them and whispered to Margaret, “Rotterdam? It is a lie. We but take him to our Stadthouse.”

They dragged Gerard out, set him on horseback, and took the road toward Rotterdam—then halted, turned, made sly detours as if stirring a pot to hide what lies at the bottom, and by evening carried him to Tergou. Outside the town a rude covered cart waited, canvas drawn. They thrust him in, and about five o’clock smuggled him into the Stadthouse prison.

Up flights of stairs they drove him, then into a small room with only a slit of window crossed by a single vertical iron bar. The place smelled of old damp and human fear. The only furniture was a huge oak chest, black with age and rubbed smooth at the edges like a kneading-trough that has served generations.

Imprisonment then was a road toward death. Cold, solitude, hunger, torture—often poison. Gerard felt himself in an enemy’s hands.

“Oh, the look that man gave me on the road,” he thought. “There is more here than my father’s wrath. I doubt I shall see no more the light of day.”

He knelt and commended his soul to God.

Then he sprang up and flung himself at the iron bar, clutched it, braced his knees against the wall, and peered out. For a bare minute he saw what only a captive values beyond measure: Martin Wittenhaagen’s back.

Martin sat below by the brook near the Stadthouse, fishing—quiet as if nothing in the world mattered but the bite of a fish, though his stillness was watchfulness. Gerard whistled. Martin’s head snapped round; he saw Gerard’s face in the slit, made a signal, gathered his line and bow, and went swiftly away.

Gerard held on a moment longer, hungry for that comfort of a friendly sight. Falling back heavily, he wrenched the rusty bar loose from the stonework—it gave with a groan like a nail in rotten plank—just as Ghysbrecht Van Swieten slipped in behind him.

The burgomaster’s eye flicked to the iron, then to the window. He said nothing. The slit was a hundred feet above the ground; if Gerard chose to jump, let him.

He set down a brown loaf and a pitcher of water on the chest in solemn silence. The loaf’s smell rose—coarse rye, honest and sour—yet Gerard’s stomach, that had been gnawing him, turned wary. Poison was a cook’s fear too: a little bitterness hidden in sweetness, a death folded into food.

His first impulse was to brain Ghysbrecht with the iron and rush out; but the burgomaster coughed softly, and three stout fellows showed at the door, armed.

“My orders are to keep you thus,” said Ghysbrecht, “until you shall bind yourself by an oath to leave Margaret Brandt, and return to the Church, to which you have belonged from your cradle.”

“Death sooner.”

“With all my heart.”

The burgomaster withdrew.

Martin sped back to Sevenbergen. There he found Margaret pale, shaken, yet like a woman whose hands, once set to kneading, will not stop till the bread is made. She was finishing a letter to the Countess Charolois, appealing against Ghysbrecht’s violence and treachery.

“Courage!” Martin cried. “I have found him. He is in the haunted tower, right at the top of it. Ay, I know the place: many a poor fellow hath gone up there straight, and come down feet foremost.”

He told how he had looked up and seen Gerard’s face at a window like a slit in a wall.

“Oh, Martin—how did he look?”

“He looked like Gerard Eliassoen.”

“But was he pale?”

“A little.”

“Looked he anxious? Like one doomed?”

“Nay, nay; as bright as a pewter pot.”

“You mock me. Stay—then that must have been at sight of you. He counts on us. Oh, what shall we do? Martin, good friend, take this at once to Rotterdam.”

Martin held out his hand for the letter. Peter had sat silent, strangely attentive, his scholar’s brow folded as if he were reading a page none else could see.

“Put not your trust in princes,” said he.

“Alas!” Margaret answered. “What else have we to trust in?”

“Knowledge.”

“Your learning will not serve us here,” she cried, the words sharp with despair.

“How know you that?” Peter returned, kindling. “Wit hath been too strong for iron bars ere to-day.”

“Ay,” said Martin, “but nature is stronger than wit, and she is against us. Think of the height! No ladder in Holland might reach him.”

“I need no ladder,” said Peter. “What I need is a gold crown.”

“I have money,” said Margaret quickly. “I have nine angels. Gerard gave them me to keep; but what do they avail? The burgomaster will not be bribed to let Gerard free.”

“What do they avail?” Peter leaned forward, the old man’s eyes bright. “Give me but one crown, and the young man shall sup with us this night.”

His certainty startled them. For an instant hope rose in Margaret—then she caught Martin’s look: benevolent contempt, as for a learned man speaking of fieldwork he has never done.

“It passes the powers of man’s invention,” she sighed.

“Invention!” cried Peter. “A fig for invention. What need we invention at this time of day? Everything hath been said that is to be said, and done that ever will be done. I shall tell you how a Florentine knight was shut up in a tower higher than Gerard’s; yet did his faithful squire stand at the tower foot and get him out, with no other engine than that in your hand, Martin, and certain kickshaws I shall buy for a crown.”

Martin turned his bow over in his hands, as if interrogating the wood and horn. His doubt stayed. Then Peter told his tale—how the squire at Brescia sent up fine thread, drew up stronger cord by it, then a rope, simple as drawing a thick line through a needle’s eye by first passing silk. Like the best craft—like good cookery, too—the science was plain when once shown. Their wonder changed: how had they called impossible what was not even difficult?

The letter never went to Rotterdam. They trusted to Peter’s learning and their own hands.

It was nine o’clock, clear moon, the kind of night where every sound carries—the brook’s whisper, a late footstep, the dry clack of a shutter in wind. Gerard senior was still away; the rest of the household had long been abed.

In the Eliassoen house, a white figure stood by the dwarf’s bed, moonlight glancing off it. With an unearthly noise between yell and snarl, Giles rolled off his bed and under it in one unbroken movement, as quick and smooth as a cat.

A soft voice followed him.

“Why, Giles, are you afeard of me?”

His head rose cautiously. It was only his sister Kate. She put her finger to her lips.

“Hush! lest the wicked Cornelis or the wicked Sybrandt hear us.”

Giles’s hooked hands seized the bed; with one gymnastic motion he was back atop it.

Kate whispered what she had learned. All day Gerard had not come home; fear drove her to listen at Cornelis and Sybrandt’s door. She had heard Gerard’s name and a discovery that chilled her: Gerard was in prison, in the haunted tower of the Stadthouse—there by their father’s authority, they said. Yet their father was in Rotterdam. Treachery lay in it, plain as mould in a loaf.

She begged Giles to go with her to the tower foot, to give poor Gerard a word of comfort and tell him their father was absent and would surely release him when he returned.

“Dear Giles, I would go alone, but I am afeard of the spirits men say do haunt the tower; but with you I shall not be afeard.”

“Nor I with you,” said Giles stoutly. “I don’t believe there are any spirits in Tergou. I never saw one. This last was the likest one ever I saw; and it was but you, Kate, after all.”

Within half an hour they slipped out, Kate making Giles carry a lantern though the night was bright.

“The lantern gives me more courage against evil spirits,” she whispered.

Up in the tower, the first day of solitude broke Gerard as hunger breaks the stubborn. As the sun fell, his heart sank with it. He was faint; he had feared the loaf and water and had scarcely tasted them. The cell grew colder; the damp seemed to crawl into his bones. He sat on the chest, head bowed, arms hanging, his whole body a picture of despondency.

Then something struck the wall beyond him with a sharp tap and rattled to the floor at his feet.

An arrow.

He saw the white feather and shrank, a chill sliding over him—assassination, then, from outside. He crouched and waited for the next. None came.

He crept forward and took up the arrow. It had no head. Hope leapt in him, sudden and fierce. He felt along it with trembling fingers and found something soft bound to it. One of his odd habits—keeping tinder close—served him now like a blessing. He struck a light.

By the little flame he saw a skein of silk tied to the shaft, and words written on the wood.

Well beloved, make fast the silk to thy knife and lower to us: but hold thine end fast: then count an hundred and draw up.

His eyes devoured the words. He seized the oak chest and dragged it to the window with strength that would not have come to him a moment before. He climbed atop, peered down, and saw figures at the tower foot—so dim they seemed one great shape.

He waved his bonnet. Then he unwound the silk carefully and tied it to his knife, lowered the knife till the thread slackened, held fast, and counted a hundred with lips moving soundlessly.

He drew up. The silk came heavier. At a knot, stout whipcord replaced it. He hauled again, and another knot: now a thicker cord. He began to pull, and the weight grew heavy.

Suddenly he understood. He pulled with all his might until sweat ran down him, and below in the moonlight a great shape rose out of the tower’s shadow like a snake: rope, rope, rope, coming up as bread dough rises under a cloth. With a last heave the rope’s end reached his hand.

He dragged it into the cell, passed it through both handles of the chest, and knotted it fast. Then he sat a moment, chest heaving, to gather breath and courage.

He must be sure the chest would bear him. He jumped on it. Once—twice—at the third jump the side burst open and a host of parchments scuttled out like pale rats. After the first fear, he saw it had opened, not broken—some secret spring loosed. Yet it shook his trust in the chest’s strength. He made it safer: he took the iron bar he had torn from the window and lashed it across the rope and the window with the small cord, to help bear strain.

Then he climbed up again, put a foot through the slit, and sat half in, half out, one hand on the rope within. The night was very still; he could hear his own heart as if it were a drum in a hollow room. Free air touched his face, and that touch gave him courage to risk what all must lose one day, but not yet—for liberty.

The worst was the first move onto the rope outside. He set himself like a swimmer: body to the waist still in the cell, legs out. Holding the inside rope with both hands, he felt with his feet for the rope outside, pinched it between the soles, made it fast, murmured a short prayer, then wriggled out.

For one dreadful moment he hung outside from the iron bar by one hand while the other searched for the rope; it lay tight against the wall, hard to grasp. At last his fingers closed on it. He let go the bar, caught the rope with both hands—but his body dropped a yard.

A stifled cry rose from below.

He clenched his teeth, nipped the rope with his feet, and began to descend, hand over hand. Rough stones slid past his cheek. One was green with moss. He glanced up—his window already far—and once down: the figures below seemed terribly small. Dizziness swam in him. He fixed his eyes on the wall close by and went down, down, down, past a rusty slimy streak ten feet long. The rope burned his hands as if he were pulling hot pots from a fire.

He looked up again. The slit was distant now. He dared look down: thirty feet below, Margaret and Martin stood with arms outstretched, their eyes and teeth shining in the moon as they breathed hard.

“Take care, Gerard—oh, take care! Look not down,” Margaret whispered.

“Fear me not,” he cried, and came faster, joy lending speed.

In a minute his feet reached their hands. They seized him before he touched ground, and all three clung together, silent, trembling with relief.

“Hush,” breathed Margaret. “Away in silence, dear one.”

They stole along the wall’s shadow. They had not gone many yards when a stream of light shot from an angle and lay across their path like a barrier of fire, and whispers and footsteps sounded close.

“Back!” hissed Martin. “Keep in the shade.”

They hurried back, passed the dangling rope, and made for a little square projecting tower. They had barely rounded it when the light went trembling past them and flickered away.

“A lantern,” groaned Martin. “They are after us.”

“Give me my knife,” whispered Gerard. “I’ll never be taken alive.”

“No, no,” murmured Margaret. “Is there no way out where we are?”

“None,” Martin whispered. “None. But I carry six lives at my shoulder.” He strung his bow, set an arrow. “In war never wait to be struck. I will kill one or two ere they shall know whence their death comes.”

He motioned them still and glided to the corner, bow half drawn, ready to loose the moment a man offered his chest to the moon.

Gerard and Margaret held their breath, sick with the thought. They had never seen a man die. And Gerard, in that tight silence, felt a wild hope—half shameful—that the pursuer might be Ghysbrecht himself. A soldier would send an arrow through a burgher as through a boar.

But the future, though a footstep away, stays unknown.

Martin’s bow did not steady. It wavered—shook violently. The stout man staggered back, knees knocking, cheeks blanched. The arrow fell from his fingers. He clutched Gerard’s shoulder as if to prove he touched life.

“Let me feel flesh and blood,” he gasped. “The haunted tower! the haunted tower!”

His terror leaped to them like fire to dry straw. They could scarce speak for fear.

“Hush!” he panted. “It will hear you up the wall! It is going up the wall! Its head is on fire. Up the wall, as mortal creatures walk upon green sward. If you know a prayer, say it—for hell is loose to-night.”

“I have power to exorcise spirits,” Gerard whispered, trembling. “I will venture forth.”

“Go alone then,” said Martin hoarsely. “I have looked on’t once, and live.”

The burgomaster’s look had been like a blade turned in the light—one flash, and Gerard understood it meant to cut him from the world. Imprisonment sealed the lesson: Ghysbrecht was no magistrate to him now, but an enemy with patience enough to wait for dark. So when he slipped along the angle of the tower, he did not truly expect spirits. He expected cord, knife, and treachery—some contrivance set for a man whose escape could scarcely be guessed.

A soft, brave hand slid into his.

Margaret was at his side. Not to counsel him from peril, but to step into it with him, as if danger were a hearth they must both tend.

They had only to clear the last shadow to see the tower itself—and then their steps stopped of their own accord, as if the stones had grown a voice and said, Be still.

Halfway up the wall, something climbed.

It was no man. Its head burned—steady, intent—like an enormous glowworm, a fistful of fire in the night air. The body behind that light was dark, yet its outline could be read in the red spill cast over the masonry: long, nearly four feet, moving with a purpose that made the skin tighten. At the foot of the tower stood another thing: white, upright, the exact semblance of a woman, motionless as a candle set before an altar.

Gerard’s breath rasped. Margaret’s fingers clenched his.

“The rope,” Gerard whispered, and the whisper sounded too loud in the meadow’s hush. “The rope—look—’tis going up the rope.”

Now he saw it: a new rope, running from the window of his late cell down to the grass, taut as a drawn bowstring. The fiery-headed creature climbed by it, and, reaching the window, vanished inward; at once the cell was lit from within, the little square reddening as if a forge had been kindled where his chains had been.

The white figure below did not move.

Awe has its own cold. It benumbs the knees and makes the heart beat against the ribs like a fist on a door. And then—stranger still—terror will sometimes turn into a wild desire to rush upon the very thing that should not be touched, as if the mind would end the suspense by ending itself.

That impulse took Margaret.

She loosened Gerard’s hand as quietly as if she had only set down a cup. Her face was bewildered; then, with a cry that tore through the night like cloth, she darted toward the white shape.

To Gerard it was plain as scripture: the evil one was drawing her to perdition.

He dropped to his knees on the damp grass. The earth smelled of crushed stalks and cold stone, and somewhere, beyond the tower’s bulk, a night-bird clicked and paused, as if listening too.

“Exorcizo vos,” he cried, voice breaking on the Latin he had learned with such care. “In nomine beatae Mariae, exorcizo vos!”

The words came in a rush, less prayer than weapon. And—mercifully—he heard, not a hellish laugh, but a feeble cry: fear, unmistakable, human in its thinness.

Hell, it seemed, had its little weaknesses.

He redoubled his exorcisms; and when he dared look up, he saw the white shape on its knees at Margaret’s, hands lifted not to seize but to plead, and he heard it praying—piteously—for mercy.

Footsteps came—hasty, uneven—Kate and Giles, drawn by dread and loyalty. Their lantern made a small trembling sun, and its flame shook in the night wind as though the air itself were disturbed by what it carried.

They halted, astonished, at the sight of the rope dangling from the prisoner’s window.

“I see how ’tis,” said Giles at once, his mind taking facts as they landed. “Our Gerard hath come down this rope. He is clear. Up I go and see.”

“No, Giles—no!” Kate clutched at him, her voice full of that quick, frightened wisdom that sees a snare everywhere once it has been bitten by one. “Seest thou not ’tis glamour? This rope is a line the evil one casts out to wile thee to destruction. He knows the weakness of each heart. He hath seen how fond thou art of going up things. Where should our Gerard come by a rope? And how fasten it in the sky like this? ’Tis not in nature. Holy saints protect us, for hell is abroad.”

“Stuff,” said the dwarf, with the plain logic of a body made for climbing. “The way to hell is down, and this rope leads up. I never had the luck to go up such a long rope. It may be years ere I fall in with so long a rope all ready for me. As well be knocked on the head at once as never know happiness.”

And he sprang to it with a little cry of delight, as a cat will leap to a board where fish lie cooling—smell and promise in one. His huge arms took hold; his legs, light as feathers, began to work; and up he went so fast it seemed the rope itself drew him.

Kate’s fear fought her love. She could win only one concession.

“Stay—let me fasten the lantern on thy neck.” Her hands shook, but her knot was sure. “A light scares ill spirits.”

So the lantern hung at the nape of Giles’s neck, and he became, in the night’s eye, the very glowworm they had seen: a moving head of fire climbing the tower.

Kate watched him, trembling so that even her crutches quivered under her. Then, suddenly, the white figure did what stone cannot do: it seemed to start from the solid masonry itself and flew at her with more than mortal speed.

Kate’s cry was small, strangled by terror; her tongue clove to her palate. She dropped her crutches. Down she sank on her knees, hiding her face, moaning as if bargaining with the dark.

“Take my body,” she sobbed, “but spare my soul!”

Margaret, panting from her rush and her fear, stopped short.

“Why—it is a woman!”

Kate, peering through her fingers, voice quivering with the same astonishment: “Why—it is a woman!”

“How you scared me!” Margaret gasped, and her hand went to her breast as if to keep her heart from leaping out.

“I am scared enough myself,” Kate answered, tears breaking loose. “Oh! oh! oh!”

The two stood close in the lantern’s weak circle, women made suddenly sisters by fright. Above them the rope creaked softly, and the tower’s stones drank the light without giving any back. Far off, a dog barked once and was silent; the night seemed to measure every sound as carefully as a cook measures salt, for too much would spoil the whole.

“This is strange,” Kate whispered, forcing her mind to order the pieces. “But the fiery-headed thing? Yet it was with you, and you are harmless! Why are you here at this time o’ night?”

“Nay—why are you?” Margaret returned, and then, as the answer shaped itself, her eyes widened. “Perhaps we are on the same errand. Ah—you are his good sister, Kate.”

“And you are Margaret Brandt.”

“Yes.”

“All the better,” Kate breathed, relief and fear mingled. “You love him. You are here. Then Giles was right. He has won free.”

Gerard stepped forward then, his very presence like a door opened onto certainty. The sight of him drew a sound from Kate that was half sob, half laugh strangled in her throat. For an instant the tower and its trickery—if trickery it was—fell away, and there was only family, only the sudden hunger of the heart satisfied by the plain fact of a loved one breathing in front of you.

But the night had not done with them.

From above came a noise that made the hair lift at the nape: hollow and unearthly, like a voice thrown up out of a grave, a sepulchre made ventriloquist.

“PARCHMENT!—PARCHMENT!—PARCHMENT!”

Each time it was louder, as if the tower itself learned the word and enjoyed it.

They stared upward, and there was Giles at the window, both hands crammed with rolled skins, his face lit from below by the lantern at his neck. The light turned him into a little demon in a glass shrine—lurid, transparent at the edges, his grin too wide for any saint’s carving.

With a shout of “PARCHMENT!” he hurled the first bundle down.

They came like wounded wild-ducks: some dropping in a dead collapse, others fluttering and catching air, others spreading and wheeling slowly, pale as bleached bones as they spiraled toward the grass. They slapped down, one upon another, whitening the dark ground.

Again: “PARCHMENT—PARCHMENT!”

Another flock fell. Then another. The meadow filled with records and skins—things that had once lain in quiet chests, smelling of calf and smoke and old ink, the slow labor of scribes and clerks turned suddenly into a storm.

At last Giles slid down the rope like a falling star, his light racing after him, and landed with the briskness of one who has done a night’s work and is hungry for his pay. Business before sentiment, his concave claw went out.

“Settle,” he said, eyes bright, “for the merchandise I delivered.”

“Hush,” Gerard snapped, listening to the night as if it were an enemy with ears. “Thou speakest too loud. Gather them up, and follow us to a safer place than this.”

Kate, still kneeling, lifted her face. “Wilt thou come home with me, Gerard?”

“I have no home.”

“You shall not say so,” she pleaded, pain and devotion in her voice. “Who is more welcome than thou wilt be, after this cruel wrong, to thy father’s house?”

“Father!” Gerard answered, and the word came out like a bitter herb crushed between the teeth. “I have no father. He that was my father is turned my gaoler. I have escaped from his hands; I will never come within their reach again.”

“An enemy did this,” Kate insisted, “and not our father.” And in a rush she told him what she had overheard Cornelis and Sybrandt say—how those two had put their tongues to the burgomaster’s ear and their malice into the town’s law.

But the wound was too fresh. Gerard’s indignation, long held like a simmering pot, boiled over at last.

“Cornelis and Sybrandt are ill curs,” he said, voice low and fierce, “that have shown me their teeth this long while. But they could do no more. My father it is that gave the burgomaster authority, or he durst not have laid a finger on me, that am a free burgher of this town. So be it, then. I was his son. I am his prisoner. He hath played his part; I shall play mine. Farewell the burgh where I was born and lived honestly and was put in prison. While there is another town left in creation, I’ll never trouble you again, Tergou.”

“Gerard—Gerard,” Kate sobbed, reaching toward him and finding only air.

Margaret leaned close to Kate, whispering with the quick, practical tenderness of a woman who knows when words will scald. “Do not gainsay him now. Give his choler time to cool.”

Kate turned, searching Margaret’s face as though reading a recipe by poor light—looking for the true measure of her. “Let me look at thee.”

Whatever she found there eased her; she whispered, “’Tis a comely face—and no mischief-maker’s.”

“Fear me not,” Margaret murmured back. “I could not be happy without your love, as well as Gerard’s.”

“These are comfortable words,” Kate said, and the sob in them was softer now. Then, with a sudden honesty that made Margaret’s throat tighten, she said, “I little thought to like thee so well. My heart is willing, but my infirmity will not let me embrace thee.”

At that, Margaret went to her and wound her arms gently round the slight, hampered body, and kissed her with the warmth of a promise. “Often he hath spoken of thee to me, Kate; and often I longed for this.”

“You, too, Gerard,” Kate said, turning her cheek to him. “Kiss me ere you go; for my heart lies heavy at parting with you this night.”

Gerard bent and kissed her—briefly, as men do when they are trying not to feel too much—and Kate took up her crutches again. She went homeward, tapping softly into the dark; the last thing they heard of her was a little patient sigh, as if the night itself had exhaled through her.

Then tears stood thick in Margaret’s eyes. She watched the black lane swallow Kate’s small figure. Gerard, already facing the road to Sevenbergen, did not notice the sigh; the noise of his own anger filled his ears.

They turned to go. Behind them, Giles nudged Gerard with his bundle of parchments and held out his claw again, greedy as hunger.

Margaret caught Gerard’s sleeve. “Nay—why take what is not ours?”

“Oh, spoil an enemy how thou canst.”

“But may they not make it a handle for fresh violence?”

“How can they?” Gerard said harshly. “Thinkest thou I shall stay in Tergou after this? The burgomaster robbed me of my liberty. I doubt I should take his life for it, if I could.”

“Oh, fie, Gerard.”

“What!” he flung back. “Is life worth more than liberty? Well—I can’t take his life, so I take the first thing that comes to hand.”

He tossed Giles a few small coins. The urchin’s face lit as if the lantern had been moved into it; he clutched the money, then his parchments, and shuffled away after his sister, the tower’s shadow swallowing his small, eager shape.

Martin joined them as they made for Sevenbergen, stepping into their company like a stitch drawn through cloth—quiet, firm, binding their flight together. And away they went, leaving the haunted tower behind them with its rope and its pale papers strewn like spilled flour on the grass, while the night’s sounds closed in again: the whisper of leaves, the far-off bark, the thin creak of wood, and the steady, living music of the road under their feet.

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten carried the key of Gerard’s chamber in the greasy warmth of his pouch, as a man carries a bone meant for a dog he dislikes. He would not go early. “A little hunger does good,” he told himself, and, as if hunger were a spice he could measure with two fingers, he let the morning simmer.

Below, the town had its usual broth of sounds: the thin clack of wooden pattens on damp stone; the cough of a cartwheel; a smith’s far hammer answering another hammer as though the streets had learned a trade-song. From a baker’s door drifted the round, honest scent of rye crust and hot yeast, and it made Ghysbrecht’s malice feel the more unnatural—like vinegar poured into milk. Even so, he waited until ten of the clock.

Then he climbed, one stair at a time, with a loaf under his arm and a pitcher in his hand, and behind him his servant Dierich went close, trusty, well-armed, boots making a dull, disciplined thud against the boards. At the prison door Ghysbrecht paused and listened. No shuffling. No groan. No beggar’s prayer. Only the house’s own small noises—timber settling, a faint draft humming as it worried at a crack.

A grim smile gathered on him. “By this time he will be as down-hearted as Albert Koestein was,” he thought, tasting the thought as one tastes a bitter herb and likes it.

He lifted the latch and pushed.

The cell stood empty.

For a breath he did not understand what his eyes told him. His body stiffened in a queer, arrested way—as if the sinews that moved him had been cut. Then the strength went out of him all at once; he trembled so that the loaf slipped in his grasp. Dierich, seeing his master’s back go rigid and then shake, crept nearer and peered over his shoulder.

There was the rope. There the iron bar drawn out. The blank pallet. The open space where a young man should have been.

Dierich let out a loud cry of wonder. But his surprise doubled when Ghysbrecht, disregarding rope and bar and everything that spoke of escape, flung himself down before the chest that stood in the cell—an old, blunt-nosed coffer—and began to feel it all over with quivering hands, patting and pawing it as if the wood might still be warm with what it had held. He bent his face into it and stared, not at the chamber, not at the means of flight, but into that hollow belly.

Dierich stared at him as at a man suddenly struck by some planet. “Why, master—what is the matter?”

Ghysbrecht’s pale lips worked and made no sound. His hands fell. He kept staring into the chest, as if by staring he could make parchment grow again as dough rises under a cloth.

“Why, master,” said Dierich, bewildered, “what avails glaring into that empty box? The lad is not there. See here—note the cunning of the young rogue; he hath taken out the bar, and—”

“GONE! GONE! GONE!” screamed Ghysbrecht, and the word was not for Gerard alone.

“Gone!” echoed Dierich. “What is gone, Holy saints! he is planet-struck!”

“STOP THIEF!” shrieked Ghysbrecht. He whirled on Dierich and clutched him by the collar, shaking him with such fury that the servant’s teeth clicked. “D’ye stand there, knave, and see your master robbed? Run! fly! A hundred crowns to him that finds it me again. No—no! ’tis in vain. Oh, fool! fool! to leave that in the same room with him. But none ever found the secret spring before. None ever would but he. It was to be. It is to be. Lost! lost!”

The burst burned out as suddenly as it flared. His years and his ailments took him by the shoulders and sat him down. He sank against the chest, muttering like a man repeating a charm that has failed him. “Lost… lost…”

“What is lost, master?” Dierich asked, and in his voice there was a rough kindness, the way a man speaks to a pot that has boiled over—half pity, half impatience.

“House and lands and good name,” groaned Ghysbrecht, and wrung his hands feebly.

“WHAT?” Dierich’s one word rang out with such sharp curiosity that it pricked Ghysbrecht back into craft, like a pin into a bladder.

Ghysbrecht blinked, gathered himself, and let cunning smooth his face. “I have lost the town records,” he stammered; and he looked askant at Dierich like a fox caught too near a hen-roost.

“Oh—is that all?”

“Is’t not enough?” Ghysbrecht seized on the safer grievance at once. “What will the burghers say to me? What will the burghs do?” Then, with a new urgency: “A hundred crowns to him who shall recover them; all, mind, all that were in this box. If one be missing, I give nothing.”

“’Tis a bargain, master,” said Dierich promptly. “The hundred crowns are in my pouch already—if I find the skins. See you not that where Gerard Eliassoen is, there are the pieces of sheepskin you rate so high?”

“That is true; that is true, good Dierich—good faithful Dierich. All, mind—all that were in the chest.”

“Master, I will take the constables to Gerard’s house, and seize him for the theft.”

“The theft?” Ghysbrecht caught at the word as if it were a handle. “Ay! good; very good. It is theft. I forgot that.” Then the malice in him leaned down into its own shadow. “So, as he is a thief now, we will put him in the dungeons below, where the toads are and the rats. Dierich, that man must never see daylight again. ’Tis his own fault; he must be prying. Quick, quick! ere he has time to talk—you know, time to talk.”

In less than half an hour Dierich Brower and four constables stood in the hosier’s house, their boots bringing in the street’s damp and their iron clinking softly—a hard little music that turned the domestic air sour. Catherine, pale with that dread which comes of loving an impulsive boy, faced them with floury hands as if she had been interrupted at kneading.

They demanded young Gerard.

“Alas! what has he done now?” she cried. “That boy will break my heart.”

“Nay, dame, but a trick of youth,” said Dierich smoothly; his voice was like oil on a pan—quieting, slippery. “He hath but made off with certain skins of parchment, in a frolic doubtless; but the burgomaster is answerable to the burgh for their safe keeping, so he is in care about them. As for the youth, he will doubtless be quit for a reprimand.”

The gentleness of the words, and the familiarity of the house, imposed on Catherine’s honest fear; she clutched at the hope of “a reprimand” as a poor cook clutches at a crust. But her daughter Kate, who listened with a sharper hunger and a finer ear, heard the strain beneath the smoothness. And when it appeared Gerard was not at home—had not been at home that night—Dierich’s mask slipped. His disappointment came out of him in a harshness too big for “a frolic.”

“Come away then,” said he roughly to the constables. “We are wasting time.” And, with a vehemence that betrayed a private stake: “I’ll find him if he is above ground.”

As he turned to go, Kate made him a small signal. He bade his men move on, and waited outside the door where the air sounded wider—the street murmuring, a child’s cry, the soft slap of water in a gutter. Kate joined him quickly.

“Hush!” she said. “My mother knows not. Gerard has left Tergou.”

Dierich’s eyes sharpened. “How?”

“I saw him last night.”

“Ay! Where?” The eagerness jumped in him.

“At the foot of the haunted tower.”

“At the foot—” Dierich’s mind ran at once to rope and bar. “How did he get the rope?”

“I know not; but this I know: my brother Gerard bade me there farewell, and he is many leagues from Tergou ere this. The town, you know, was always unworthy of him; and when it imprisoned him, he vowed never to set foot in it again. Let the burgomaster be content, then. He has imprisoned him, and he has driven him from his birthplace and from his native land. What need now to rob him and us of our good name?”

It was sense, and had Dierich been only a townsman he might have felt it. But he was mortified—mortified at the escape, and mortified at the thought of the hundred crowns slipping away like fish in a net.

“What need had he to steal?” he flung back bitterly.

“Gerard stole not the trash,” Kate answered hotly. “He but took it to spite the burgomaster, who stole his liberty. But he shall answer to the Duke for it, he shall. As for these skins of parchment you keep such a coil about—look in the nearest brook or stye, and ’tis odds but you find them.”

Dierich’s eyes flashed, not with piety for the records, but with a sudden greedy hope. “Think ye so, mistress?—think ye so?” And the words came out as though he were tasting them, turning them on his tongue, as one turns a rumour that might lead to profit.

“Mayhap you know ’tis so,” said Kate, and her voice lowered. “This I know, that Gerard is too good to steal, and too wise to load himself with rubbish, going a journey.”

“Give you good day, then,” snapped Dierich. “The sheepskin you scorn, I value it more than the skin of any in Tergou.” And he went off hastily on the false scent she had thrown him—toward brooks and styes, toward any place where wet and filth might hide what a man in fear had cast away.

Kate went back into the house, and the familiar noises there—spoons, a creak of a stool, the soft breathing of stored linen—felt suddenly fragile, as if the house were a loaf that might collapse if jarred. She drew Giles aside—Giles, whom folk called Perpusillus, small in name if not in bone.

“Giles, my heart misgives me. Breathe not to a soul what I say to you. I have told Dirk Brower that Gerard is out of Holland, but much I doubt he is not a league from Tergou.”

“Why, where is he, then?” asked Giles, his blunt face earnest.

“Where should he be, but with her he loves?” Kate said; and the thought was like smelling a remembered herb—sweet, piercing, and sorrowful. “But if so, he must not loiter. These be deep and dark and wicked men that seek him. Giles, I see that in Dirk Brower’s eye makes me tremble.” She clasped her hands, angry at her own body. “Oh, why cannot I fly to Sevenbergen and bid him away? Why am I not lusty and active like other girls? God forgive me for fretting at His will; but I never felt till now what it is to be lame and weak and useless.”

Then, forcing tenderness into a coaxing tone, she laid her hope on him. “But you are strong, dear Giles—you are very strong.”

“Yes, I am strong,” thundered Perpusillus, swelling with it; then, catching what she meant, he fell back into the sulk of a boy asked to labour. “But I hate to go on foot.”

“Alas! alas!” Kate breathed. “Who will help me if you will not? Dear Giles—do you not love Gerard?”

“Yes,” said he, and the sulk cracked. “I like him best of the lot. I’ll go to Sevenbergen on Peter Buyskens his mule. Ask you him, for he won’t lend her me.”

Kate began to remonstrate at once. A mule taken openly would be a bell rung in the market. The whole town would have ears for it; folk would follow with their eyes; and in a place where every voice knew every name, it would soon be known whither Giles had gone—toward Sevenbergen, toward danger.

Giles parried it with a plan of his own, half-boyish, half-shrewd. He would ride out of town the opposite way, as if bound on some idle errand, and not turn the mule’s head toward Sevenbergen till he had shaken off the curious. Kate, measuring the town’s hunger for gossip as carefully as she would measure spice into broth, saw it was the best she could do. She assented, and borrowed the mule.

Then she charged Giles with a short message—few words, but heavy with meaning—and made him repeat it after her again and again until he could say it word for word, as a cook repeats a recipe that must not fail: no ingredient forgotten, no step altered, or the whole dish spoiled and the eater poisoned.

Giles mounted and started, the mule’s hooves making a steady, living percussion down the street—sound carrying farther than sight, and Kate listening until it thinned into the town’s general murmur.

Little Kate withdrew to a corner of the house where the daylight fell like a pale cloth. She knelt, and did the last thing now left in her power for her beloved brother: she prayed, long and earnestly, for his safety—sending the prayer after him as one sends bread after a traveller, knowing it may be all that stands between him and hunger.

Gerard and Margaret set their faces toward Sevenbergen with the lightness of folk new loosed from a snare. The road itself seemed to sing them free: the wet reeds hissed by the ditch, larks stitched their small notes into the high air, and the cart-ruts held yesterday’s rain like dull mirrors. Yet liberty, like fresh bread, cools quickly when one sits down to taste it. Before they had well warmed their hands at Peter’s hearth, the savor of safety thinned, and bitter thoughts came up as if a sour leaven were working underneath.

Gerard was still a man broken out of bonds. Any hour might bring the hand that would clap him back into misery, and then—God help them—punishment. So, though they had found each other again, they must part.

Worse, he had taken a harsh distaste to his own place, as a man turns from meat that has been served him with insult. Margaret urged him to leave the country awhile; but the very word Italy—sunny in other mouths—made her heart go cold, as if someone had spoken of the sea and she could already taste the salt of drowning. Gerard, on the contrary, could bear the thought of leaving her only because Italy drew him like a strong spice one has never yet smelled but knows will change the whole dish. There, he said, he would earn money and name; there, his hand and eye—wasted among boors—would be valued; there, every obstacle between them and marriage would be ground small as pepper under the heel.

He had told her already all that the demoiselle Van Eyck had spoken—how she had weighed him with her painter’s judgment, how she had put gold into his palm for that very journey. Now he repeated it, as men repeat a recipe when they fear the hearer will forget one step and spoil all.

“Those gold pieces were given me to go,” he said. “It is for my good, Margaret. Here I am as a fine flour thrown to pigs. In Italy they will know what to do with me.”

It was on that ground, more than on any plea of his longing, that the unselfish girl consented. Yet the consent came salted with tears. She wept, and he—young, loving, and as quick to feel—broke down with her, and they asked each other, over and over, what they had done that so many should be their enemies, and why different persons, who had no common love, seemed to have one common will: to part them.

They sat hand in hand till midnight. The cottage noises went on around them with their homely faithfulness—Peter’s slow breathing by the settle, the mouse in the thatch, the soft ticking of a drip where the eaves shed into a pan—but in their ears those little sounds were like a world that would continue without them. Now they lamented their hard lot; now they built bright pictures of the time to come, when Gerard would return with skill made famous and pockets heavy; and in the midst of that shining future Margaret’s tears would start afresh, sudden as sap rising, and then Gerard’s brave talk would die away in a sigh.

Morning found them resigned to part—resigned as one is resigned to eating bitter herbs because hunger will not wait—but neither had courage to say when. And it is likely the hour of parting would never have struck, for love will always find one more task, one more word, one more look to delay the knife.

But about three of the afternoon Giles rode up to the door, having made a wide circuit to shun eyes. The horse steamed; the man’s voice came before he had well swung down.

“Brother Gerard!” he cried, in those tremendous tones that seemed to shake the very smoke in the chimney. “Kate bids you run for your life. They charge you with theft; you have given them a handle. Think not to explain. Hope not for justice in Tergou. The parchments you took, they are but a blind. She hath seen your death in the men’s eyes; a price is on your head. Fly! For Margaret’s sake and all that love you, loiter not life away, but fly!”

It fell like a thunder-clap in clear air, leaving two white faces staring at him—and then at each other, as if each would read in the other’s eyes whether the world had truly turned so suddenly cruel.

Giles, who till now had spoken like a messenger repeating another’s words, added hastily from his own fear: “All the constables were at our house after you, and so was Dirk Brower. Kate is wise, Gerard. Best give ear to her rede, and fly!”

“Oh, yes, Gerard!” Margaret cried, wild as if she had been struck. “Fly on the instant. Ah, those parchments—my mind misgave me. Why did I let you take them?”

“Margaret, they are but a blind,” said Gerard, catching at Giles’s phrase as at a rung. “No matter. The old caitiff shall never see them again. I will not go till I have hidden his treasure where he shall never find it.”

He thanked Giles in words that came quickly and hot, bade him farewell, and charged him to ride back and tell Catherine he was gone. “For I shall be gone ere you reach home,” said he.

Then he shouted for Martin and told him what had happened, and begged him go a little way toward Tergou and watch the road.

“Ay,” said Martin, “and if I see Dirk Brower or any of his men, I will shoot an arrow into the oak-tree that is in our garden; and on that you must run into the forest hard by, and meet me at the weird hunter’s spring. Then I will guide you through the wood.”

With that net set against surprise, Gerard breathed again, though it was a breath that seemed to scrape his throat like dry bread.

He went out with Margaret into the little garden. The earth there was dark and kindly, smelling of roots and old leaves; cabbages sat heavy as green stones, and the last onions lay with their necks bent, as if listening. Margaret stood watching the oak-tree, trembling so that the hem of her kirtle quivered against the wet grass; each moment she looked for the sudden thud of an arrow among the branches—the agreed signal that danger had come running.

Gerard took a spade and dug deep. The iron bit into the soil with a dull, satisfying sound—thok, thok—each stroke a coarse music that steadied his hands. He made the hole as a cook makes a pit for a slow fire: deep enough that what you lay in it will be swallowed by darkness and kept.

He threw the parchments in, one by one. They were mostly charters and records of the burgh—dry skins covered with words that ruled men’s lives as surely as iron bars. Yet even as he handled them, he felt how strange it was that so much power should sit in silence, needing only a reader’s tongue to become a weapon. One sheet, thicker and more private in look, bore a different air, like a family loaf amid market bread. It seemed a deed between Floris Brandt, father of Peter, and Ghysbrecht.

“Why,” said Gerard, peering, “this is as much yours as his. I will read this.”

“Oh, not now, Gerard, not now,” Margaret pleaded, and fear sharpened her voice. “Every moment you lose fills me with terror; and see—large drops of rain are beginning to fall, and the clouds lower.”

Indeed, the first heavy drops struck the leaves with a broad sound, like fingers tapping on a drumhead. The air changed its smell: the sharp green of crushed herb gave way to the metallic odor of rain on earth.

Gerard yielded; but he slipped the deed into his bosom, as a man tucks away a precious spice to keep it from damp. Over the rest he flung the earth, patted it down, and stamped it firm.

As he did so, lightning tore the sky with a white crack, and a peal of thunder answered far off. Then the rain came in earnest, thick as thrown grain. They ran for the house, the wet striking their faces and making their hair cling. Martin came in close behind them.

“The road is clear,” said he, shaking the water from his cap, “and a heavy storm coming on.”

His words were proved at once. The thunder came nearer and nearer till it crashed overhead; flashes followed one another close, like the strokes of a whip; and the rain poured in torrents, drumming on thatch and shutter so the whole cottage seemed a kettle boiling. Margaret hid her face, not to see the lightning; at that Gerard put up the rough shutter and lighted a candle. Its small flame made a warm pool of amber against the storm’s cold roaring, and the smell of tallow rose, mingling with wet wool and the faint, comforting ghost of yesterday’s broth that lived in the stones of the hearth.

They consulted together in that strained little circle of light; and Gerard, with a lover’s selfish gratitude, blessed the storm because it gave him a few hours more beside Margaret. Outside, the world was a great, loud thing—branches beating, water rushing, thunder rolling like carts of stone; inside, their voices were low and close, like hands touching in the dark.

The sun set unperceived behind the clouds. Supper was set—Peter’s plain fare, honest and nourishing, the kind that keeps a body fit to reap and sow: bread, cheese, and what else the house afforded. The knife rang softly on the board; a crust cracked. Yet Gerard and Margaret could not eat. The thought that this might be the last time they should sup together choked them, so that even the smell of warm bread, usually a solace, turned to an ache. It was as if the very taste of the food would bind the moment to memory too tightly, and memory was pain.

The storm lulled a little. Peter, old and worn, retired to rest. But Gerard was to go at peep of day, and neither he nor Margaret could afford to lose an hour in sleep, not when hours were now dearer than coin.

Martin sat with them awhile. He was fitting a new string to his bow—a task he did with a nicety like a careful cook tying a roast so it will turn evenly. He tested the twist, smoothed it, drew it, listened for the right taut note. In such small exactness there was comfort: a world where one thing, at least, could be made true by patience.

The lovers murmured their sorrows and their love beside him, their words half drowned at times by the hiss of rain and the long retreating growl of thunder. And even in that, Margaret felt how the sounds of the place—rain on thatch, wind in the oak, the low creak of timber—held a kind of shelter. There was no harsh clang of forge or shouted market here, only the old, natural voices; and yet those very peaceful sounds were now haunted, because any other sound—an alien footfall, a whispered order—could cut through them like a knife through curd.

Suddenly Martin held up his hand for silence.

They stopped at once. The candle’s flame quivered. They listened, and heard nothing but the soft drip and the far, fading mutter of the storm.

Then, as if the earth itself had exhaled a warning, a footstep crackled faintly upon the autumn leaves strewn in the garden at the back door. To those with no enemies it would have meant nothing; to those who were hunted it was dreadful. For it was a foot trying to be noiseless.

Martin fitted an arrow and in the same breath blew out the candle. Darkness fell thick, and with it the sharpening of every sound: their own breathing loud, Margaret’s stifled sob, the minute creak of the bow as Martin drew it a hair to test.

At that instant, to their horror, they heard more than one footstep approach the other door—not quite so noiselessly as the first, but very stealthily—and then a dead pause.

Their blood froze.

“Oh, Kate, oh, Kate!” Margaret moaned in the blackness. “You said fly on the instant.” And she wrung her hands in anguish and terror and wild remorse for having kept Gerard.

“Hush, girl!” whispered Martin, stern as a man who has faced wolves.

A heavy knock fell on the door—and on the hearts within.

The first blow upon the back door came so sudden and so brutish that the very hearth seemed to start. A second followed, and a third, and with them the wet roar of the storm that had been battering Sevenbergen all night—rain worrying the thatch, wind whining down the eaves, and the thin iron note of a latch-plate struck with knuckles that had no patience left in them.

They were ringed.

At that sound Margaret’s terror did a strange thing: it did not vanish, but it gathered itself into shape, as dough gathers under a practiced hand when the baker will have it rise true. She leaned close to Gerard; her breath smelled faintly of warm milk and the brown crust of the bread she had eaten earlier, as if the house, even in peril, insisted on being a house.

“Say he was here,” she breathed, “but is gone.”

And before he could answer, she had seized him—no weak clutching, but a grip with sinew in it—and almost dragged him up the rude steps to her father’s sleeping-room. Hers lay beyond; the narrow stair creaked like an old fiddle-string tuned too tight. Below, the pounding resumed, and the whole dwelling listened, every board and beam, as if sound itself were the law that governed men.

“Who knocks at this hour?” Martin Wittenhaagen called, voice roughened by sleep and by the peat-smoke that lived in his beard.

“Open, and you will see!”

“I open not to thieves—honest men are all abed now.”

“Open to the law, Martin Wittenhaagen, or you shall rue it.”

Martin’s answer came slow, and, in it, recognition: “Why, that is Dirk Brower’s voice, I trow. What make you so far from Tergou?”

“Open, and you will know.”

Martin drew the bolt as if the act were a kindness done to the door rather than to the men outside. The wind snatched at the gap the instant it opened; rain-spatter and cold rushed in, with Dierich Brower and four more behind him, their boots dragging mud and ditch-water onto the clean-swept boards. A sixth slipped in at the back, as if the night itself had posted him there.

The kitchen—its soot-dark rafters, its hanging pots, the smell of yesterday’s onions clinging to the stone—was suddenly full of wet wool, steel, and authority.

“Now, Martin,” said Dierich, shaking off rain like a dog, “where is Gerard Eliassoen?”

Martin blinked at him with a sleepy insolence that was almost artistry. “Gerard Eliassoen? Why, he was here but now!”

“Was here?” Dierich’s face fell, as if a purse had been cut from it. “And where is he now?”

“They say he has gone to Italy. Why, what is to do?”

“No matter. When did he go? Tell me not he went in such a storm as this!”

“Here is a coil about Gerard Eliassoen,” Martin said, contempt in every syllable. He went to the fire and, with the unhurried air of one doing a homely task, lighted the candle. Then he sat himself down as if this were some neighborly visit and began whipping fine silk round his bow-string where the nick fretted it—winding and smoothing, winding and smoothing, with fingers as exact as a cook trussing a bird.

“I’ll tell you,” he said carelessly. “Know you his brother Giles?—a little misbegotten imp, all head and arms? Well, he came tearing over here on a mule, and bawled out something. I was too far off to hear the creature’s words, but only its noise. Any way, he started Gerard. For as soon as he was gone, there was such crying and kissing, and then Gerard went away. They do tell me he has gone to Italy—mayhap you know where that is, for I don’t.”

Dierich listened, and the more Martin kept to one plain thread, the more it held. A subtler man might have embroidered, and the embroidery would have betrayed him; Martin lied once, and let the rest be honest.

“Mates,” said Dierich at last, sourly, “I doubt he speaks sooth. I told the burgomaster how ’twould be. He met the dwarf galloping Peter Buyskens’s mule from Sevenbergen. ‘They have sent that imp to Gerard,’ says he, ‘so, then, Gerard is at Sevenbergen.’ ‘Ah, master!’ says I, ‘’tis too late now. We should have thought of Sevenbergen before, instead of wasting our time hunting all the odd corners of Tergou for those cursed parchments that we shall never find till we find the man that took ’em. If he was at Sevenbergen,’ quoth I, ‘and they sent the dwarf to him, it must have been to warn him we are after him. He is leagues away by now,’ quoth I. Confound that chalk-faced girl! she has outwitted us bearded men; and so I told the burgomaster, but he would not hear reason. A wet jerkin apiece, that is all we shall get, mates, by this job.”

Martin grinned in his face as if to say, You have come far for nothing and brought your clatter with you. Yet when Dierich added, “However, to content the burgomaster, we will search the house,” Martin’s grin died as quick as a candle snuffed.

That shift did not pass Dierich unnoticed. His eyes narrowed, and he weighed the room as a man weighs a loaf by the hand, knowing by feel if it is hollow.

“Watch outside, two of you,” he ordered. “One on each side of the house, that no one jump from the upper windows. The rest come with me.”

He took the candle and mounted the stairs, his men following, their heavy tread making the whole dwelling ring. The sound was worse than speech; it was the noise of men who do not need to ask permission. Martin was left below with the fire’s low crackle and the wet hiss of his own thoughts.

For a moment he stood very still, hearing the house like a living creature hears: the wind’s bass in the chimney, the rain’s fingers on the panes, the men’s boots thudding overhead. If Gerard meant to escape, it must be from Peter’s room or Margaret’s; neither was too high to leap. Dierich had left a watcher below—but then, what of that? For half a minute Gerard and the watcher would be two to one, and in half a minute much can be done: a man can break a wrist, crack a skull, vanish into a hedge-row, or into the night that swallows sound.

Martin went to the back door and held it ajar, peering out. The storm breathed in like a cold animal.

A light shone above—in Peter’s room. Martin’s mouth tightened. “Curse the fool!” he muttered. “Is he going to let them take him like a girl?”

The light moved, passed along, slid into Margaret’s chamber. Still no window opened. If Gerard had meant to jump, he would have done it before the men were in the room. Martin saw that at once, and closed the door softly, the bolt sliding home with a small final click that sounded too loud in his ear.

He crossed to the foot of the stair and listened. The men’s voices were muffled above, but their boots spoke plainly: prying, rummaging, stamping from board to board. Then a lull—so long a lull that it began to persuade Martin. Perhaps Gerard had slipped away while all were in the house. Perhaps he was already out in the storm, soaked to the bone, but free.

Then the silence was ripped by faint cries from the inner bedroom—Margaret’s.

“They have taken him,” groaned Martin. “They have got him.”

In that instant he saw, as if the fire flared and showed it, what taking Gerard away would mean. A man hauled off for parchments and accusations in such times did not come back with his skin whole. And if Gerard were broken—or hanged—Margaret’s heart would be broken with him, and the house would be emptied of its best sound: a girl’s laugh in the kitchen, a song under breath while kneading, the clink of a spoon against a pot. There are silences that last longer than storms.

Martin’s eyes ranged the room, wild as a trapped beast’s, and then steadied. A resolve came over him, not gentle, not modern—made for iron times and for a soldier driven into a corner.

He stepped to each door in turn—the front and the back—and, mimicking Dierich Brower’s voice, snapped out, “Watch the window!”

Then, very quietly, he closed and bolted both doors. The house was now a sealed oven, heat within, men within, and no easy way out.

He took up his bow and six arrows. One he fitted to the string; the others he dropped into his quiver with a soft, dry tap, like beans into a wooden bowl. His knife he placed upon a chair behind him, the hilt turned so that his hand could find it without looking—like a cook laying ready a blade before carving.

And there he waited at the foot of the stair.

He counted it coldly. Two men he could take with arrows before they closed; then Gerard and he must go hand-to-hand with the remaining pair—if Gerard were not bound, if Gerard could move. And panic—panic was always a spice in men’s blood; if Brower and his fellows hesitated a breath, Martin might loose three shafts instead of two, and the odds would shift.

He did not wait long. Heavy steps sounded overhead, then nearer, then the scrape of a boot on the top stair. The candlelight approached, throwing long trembling bars of brightness down the stairwell. Voices came with it, low and exasperated.

Martin’s heart beat hard—not from fear of dying, but from the knowledge of what he was about to do: to make this narrow space, ten feet square, into a slaughter-pen. Four against one, maybe two; and exile if he lived, death if he failed. Yet the man who had been seen shaking at a foolish lantern in a marsh did not waver now that the danger was honest and made of flesh and steel. His body braced itself; his eye burned. He was ready to take life, ready to lose it.

Above, Dierich Brower and his men had found Peter Buyskens in his first sleep. They flung open cupboards, upsetting the quiet order of a room that smelled of dried herbs and old paper. They ran their knives into an alligator Peter had nailed to the wall—a foolish trophy pierced for no reason but suspicion. They stooped and looked beneath the bed. The chamber was large, full of corners that might have hidden a man, and yet it hid nothing of what they wanted.

Then they went on to Margaret’s room. At the threshold, the sight of it discouraged them: small, bare, no cupboards, no deep shadows to tuck a fugitive into. Only a large fireplace and chimney, black-mouthed and honest. Dierich’s eye went straight there, for men hunting men learn to read stone and soot.

In that room they found the beauty of Sevenbergen asleep on an old chest scarcely a foot high. There was no careful attempt at hiding, no bed-curtains drawn close in guilt. The sheets were snowy white, and so was Margaret’s own linen—cleanliness like a silent witness. She lay as if fallen there, pale and still, a lily dropped into a rut of the world.

Presently she woke and sat up, staring like one pulled from a dream into a nightmare. Seeing the men, she began to scream—faintly at first, from shock—and then to pray for mercy. The sound of her fear, thin as it was, made Dierich Brower oddly ashamed, as if a sour note had crept into his own music.

“Here is a to-do,” he said, a little confused, trying for a jest to cover the ugliness of his errand. “We are not going to hurt you, my pretty maid. Lie you still, and shut your eyes, and think of your wedding-night, while I look up this chimney to see if Master Gerard is there.”

“Gerard! in my room?” Her voice gathered strength; indignation warmed it, and the warmth gave it flavor, like pepper shaken over bland broth. “Why not? They say that you and he—”

“Cruel!” she cried. “You know they have driven him away from me—driven him from his native place. This is a blind. You are thieves; you are wicked men; you are not men of Sevenbergen, or you would know Margaret Brandt better than to look for her lover in this room of all others in the world. Oh, brave! Four great hulking men to come, armed to the teeth, to insult one poor honest girl! The women that live in your own houses must be naught, or you would respect them too much to insult a girl of good character.”

Dierich, who had meant to be hard, found himself flinching beneath words sharper than steel. He glanced at his comrades, as if fearing the contagion of shame.

“There! come away, before we hear worse,” he said hastily. “He is not in the chimney. Plaster will mend what a cudgel breaks; but a woman’s tongue is a double-edged dagger, and a girl is a woman with her mother’s milk still in her.”

And with that, he beat a hasty retreat, the candle bobbing as he went, his men stumbling after him.

“I told the burgomaster how ’twould be,” he muttered, as if the storm outside could be blamed for everything that did not go as planned.

Where is the woman that cannot put on another face? Where is she who will not, for one fierce instant, borrow craft from fear, and use it—neatly, swiftly—to save the man she loves? On such nights Nature herself turns actress, and even the simplest girl learns how to blind Solomon.

The men had no sooner clumped from the chamber than Margaret slid out of the bed as silently as a cat in a dairy. She was still dressed beneath the linen—skirt and petticoat, stockings, and over all the nightdress she had flung on in haste—yet she moved with the practised thrift of a housewife who knows every board that creaks and every latch that sings.

The long chest, that had served her for a bed, stood by the wall. With both hands she lifted the lid, and, with it, the bedclothes, and set the whole—lid and coverlet together—upright against the plaster, as one props a kneading-board. Then she glided to the door and pressed her ear to the wood.

Footsteps, heavy with beer and authority, dwindled through her father’s room and down the stair; their iron-shod soles beat time on the boards, then sank into the duller hush below. A last mutter. A door. The house settled, as houses do, into its own breathing.

Now that chest had a secret, the sort of household ingenuity that grows in poor rooms the way leaven grows in a warm bowl. A strip of boarding had once been broken; Gerard had been asked to mend it, and, being short of timber, he had sawed away a space just wide enough to receive Margaret’s so-called bed. With the planks so stolen back from necessity, he had patched the floor till no stranger’s eye would note the theft. The chest, in truth, rested on the rafters a foot beneath the boards; it looked scarce a foot deep, but it held near two. In such small carpentry lay the difference between a hearth kept and a life taken.

All was quiet.

Margaret sank to her knees on the bare boards and gave thanks—quickly, breathlessly—because gratitude, too, can be fear’s habit. Then she rose and bent over the chest, her hair loosening about her cheeks, and whispered as one calls a child from a pantry:

“Gerard.”

No answer.

She whispered again, a shade louder, careful still—as careful as when one lifts a lid from simmering pottage not to let the steam betray its savour to a passer-by.

“Gerard, all is safe, thank Heaven! You may rise; but oh—be cautious!”

No answer.

A coldness went along her spine. She reached down and laid her hand upon his shoulder.

“Gerard!”

Nothing—no shifting of cloth, no rasp of breath, no impatient little sound a man makes when cramped.

“Oh, what is this?” she breathed, and her fingers flew, not tender now but blind, over his face and breast as if searching in meal for a lost coin. She took him by the shoulders; she shook him; she lifted; but he slipped from her trembling grasp and fell back—not like a man who resists sleep, but like a weight that has forgotten will.

Dread—thick as smoke—filled her mouth. The lid had been down. She had lain upon it. The men had stood there, questioning, listening, lingering. The air inside that hidden depth—how little there is, how soon it turns sour, as when a crock is sealed too tight and the milk within goes wrong.

With the strength of frenzy she tore him out of the chest. Splinters bit her palms; she did not feel them. She bore him to the window as if he were a sack of grain, precious and ruinously heavy. She flung the casement wide.

Night rushed in—cool, clean, smelling of wet earth and distant peat-smoke; it carried, too, the village’s sleeping music: a far dog’s single bark, the faint creak of a sign in the wind, the soft settling of thatched roofs. The air poured over Gerard’s face, but he did not drink it.

She laid him in the moonlight, on the sill and against the wall where the draught could find him. His skin was the colour of ashes; his mouth slack; his whole body limp, as dough before the first working.

She put her hand to his breast.

Horror: the heart beneath her fingers was as still as stone.

Horror of horrors: she had smothered him with her own body—the very warmth that had seemed a shelter had turned to a weight, and the hiding place, meant to keep him from hands and ropes, had become a coffin of boards.

The mind will not swallow such a thing at once; it sticks in the throat like dry bread. Gerard had slid alive into that chest scarce five minutes before. How could death have travelled so quickly through so little space?

She called him by all the names love invents in the instant it dares to speak—names she had never given him aloud, though her tongue had shaped them in secret as she kneaded and stirred and swept. She kissed him—forehead, cheek, lips—pressing her mouth to his as if she might blow life back into him the way one fans a coal to wake it. She coaxed and implored him, urgent and low, as if he were only sulking.

No answer.

Then, trembling from head to foot, she began to say over that grey face little foolish things, broken and dreadful, as a child babbles over a spilled pot.

“Oh, Gerard! I am very sorry you are dead. I am very sorry I have killed you. Forgive me for not letting the men take you; it would have been better than this. Oh, Gerard! I am very, very sorry for what I have done.”

And suddenly the dam in her mind burst; words rushed out wild, not chosen, not measured—like water let loose from a millpond.

“No! no! such things can’t be, or there is no God. It is monstrous. How can my Gerard be dead? How can I have killed my Gerard? I love him. Oh, God! you know how I love him. He does not—I never told him. If he knew my heart, he would speak to me; he would not be so deaf to his poor Margaret. It is all a trick to make me cry out and betray him; but no! I love him too well for that. I’ll choke first!”

She seized her own throat, crushing down the scream that fought to tear free—because she heard, even through madness, the house’s listening: the timbers that carried sound, the stairwell that drank it and returned it, the night itself that would carry her voice like a hunted thing across roofs and yards.

“If he would but say one word. Oh, Gerard! don’t die without a word. Have mercy on me and scold me, but speak to me: if you are angry with me, scold me! curse me! I deserve it—the idiot that killed the man she loved better than herself. Ah, I am a murderess—the worst in all the world. Help! help! I have murdered him. Ah! ah! ah! ah! ah!”

She tore at her hair, and the screams that she had tried to swallow tore out at last—shriek after shriek, so wild, so piercing, they rang like a death-bell in the ears of Dierich Brower and his men below. All started to their feet and looked at one another.

Martin Wittenhaagen stood planted at the stair-foot like an oak in winter, shoulders squared, bow bent and drawn so far the goose-feathered shaft nearly kissed the head. His knife lay ready behind his back, a cold comfort against warm blood. When the men blundered in again—breathing hard, boots slick with thawed snow and ditch-water—without Gerard among them, wonder struck him clean through. The cord slackened; the bow lowered. He stared, mouth open, as if he had bitten into something that should have been sweet and found it bitter.

They stopped short as well, their eyes taking in the posture they had walked into.

“Why, mates,” one muttered, half-laughing, half-angered, “was the old fellow making ready to shoot at us?”

“Stuff!” said Martin, hauling his face back into its usual dull mask. His voice came out thick as barley porridge left too long on the fire. “I was but trying my new string. There! I’ll unstring my bow, if you think that.”

“Humph!” Dierich answered, suspicion sharp as vinegar. “There is something more in you than I understand. Put a log on, and let us dry our hides a bit ere we go.”

A log went down; then another. Soon the hearth roared. Resin in the wood cracked and spat, sending up that sweet, piney breath that clings to hair and wool. The men crowded in, steaming like horses after a hard pull, their long hair and sodden jerkins beginning to smoke. Water ran off them and hissed on the stones. The room filled with the homely racket of boots thumping, leather creaking, breath whistling through teeth, and the fire’s own busy music—a soundscape that could have been comfort, if every snap had not seemed a warning.

Then the shrieks came.

Not from the wind, nor from any beast in the dark yard, but from Margaret’s room above—thin, raw cries that cut through the hearth-crackle as a knife slices sinew.

Every man started. One seized the candle, its tallow already softening from the heat, and ran up the steps. The flame jerked and flared, throwing greasy light on the walls.

Martin moved too—too quickly for an old man who had just been “trying a string.” Confusion—and something worse—showed itself in him. He lurched after the candle-bearer, as if to bar the way with his body.

Dierich caught the meaning of that at once. He sprang behind Martin and locked both arms around him like a clamp.

“Hold him!” Dierich barked to the others, his breath loud in Martin’s ear. “Keep him!”

The man with the candle wrenched free of the tangle and went on, his feet drumming overhead. The rest fell upon Martin in a heaving mass. They struggled long and fiercely, the hearth’s heat at their backs, sweat and wet wool stinging their noses. More than once they all rolled on the floor—elbows in ribs, knees on thighs—with Martin in the middle, as if the old man were the hard knot in a net they could not loosen.

For all his age, he fought like a man saving his last loaf from hungry mouths. He growled low, a sound like a dog guarding a pot, and the rope they carried—meant for Gerard—was needed at last. They wound it around him, rough hemp biting into skin, and bound him hand and foot until the great arms that had once lifted barrels lay useless as tied hams on the slab.

Martin groaned aloud—not only from the rope’s cruel bite, but from what he knew was happening above. During the struggle, the candle had gone on into Margaret’s room, and now he was powerless to follow, powerless to stop any eyes and hands that might pry.

“Ay, grind your teeth, you old rogue,” Dierich said, panting, hair sticking to his brow with sweat and smoke. “You shan’t use them.”

“It is my belief, mates,” said another, rubbing a bruised wrist, “that our lives were scarce safe while this old fellow’s bones were free.”
