“He makes me think this Gerard is not far off,” put in a third, glancing toward the stair as if expecting some shadow to slide down it.

“No such luck,” Dierich answered, with the sour certainty of a man who has bought bad meat and will not admit it disappoints him. Then, after a moment, his eyes narrowed. “Hallo, mates. Jorian Ketel is a long time in that girl’s bedroom. Best go and see after him, some of us.”

A rude laugh went up—coarse as spilt ale on rushes—trying to turn fear into sport. Yet beneath it the house listened: the fire clicking; the wind finding cracks in the shutters; the bound man’s breath coming heavy through his nose. Even the candlelight upstairs seemed to have its own voice, a faint, wavering hiss in the minds of those below.

The laugh had hardly died when rapid footsteps ran along overhead—quick, uneven, as if someone were fleeing not for play but for life. The sound skittered across the planks, and every man’s head tilted, hunters reading the forest by ear.

“Oh, here he comes, at last,” Dierich called up, his tone too loud, as if to drown a doubt he would not name. “Well, Jorian—what is to do now up there?”

Jorian Ketel went straight as a draught through a broken shutter to Margaret’s room, the candle he carried making a timid, butter-yellow puddle of light that wavered with every step. The house itself seemed to hold its breath. The boards did not creak; the rafters did not settle; even the winter wind at the eaves came muffled, as if the night had laid a thumb upon the mouth of the world. In that hush he found what he had not expected to find at all.

Gerard—whom they had hunted through kitchen and loft as if he were a wolf—lay pale and motionless, his head sunk in Margaret’s lap. She knelt over him, not weeping now, not crying out, but turned to stone: eyes wide and emptied, as though all her sight had been poured into the white face she cradled. She neither saw the candle nor heard the man; the room might have been a chapel after the last bell, the congregation gone, the candles guttering, and one stubborn soul still praying.

Jorian stopped, struck dumb for a heartbeat, the grease of the candle running down his fingers. “Why, where was he, then, all the time?” he said, half to her and half to the baffled night.

Margaret did not so much as flicker.

He looked from Gerard to the empty chest, lid thrown back, its belly gaping and bare. The trick of it began to piece itself together in his mind—hiding, flight, search, the burlap and skins, the false promise of a clever nook. It had all ended here, on a girl’s knees. Her despair, so mute it had no language left to it, pricked him like a fishbone.

“This is a sorry sight,” he muttered. “A black night’s work—all for a few skins! Better have gone with us than so. She is past answering me, poor wench. Stop—let us try whether—”

He took down a little round mirror—no bigger than his hand—from where it hung, and held it close to Gerard’s mouth and nostrils. The candle’s flame trembled in the glass; Jorian’s own breath fogged it a little. He waited, counting the small sounds he could still hear: the wick’s faint hiss; the far-off tick of some settling timber; the blood pounding in his ears like a drum under cloth.

When he drew the mirror away, its surface was dulled.

There was the smallest smear of life upon it, a mist like dawn on cold water.

“THERE IS LIFE IN HIM!” Jorian said to himself—only muttered, only breathed, yet the words fell into that air like a stone into a still pond.

Margaret snatched them at once. It was as if the statue had cracked and a living woman burst out. She sprang up and flung both arms round the great fellow’s neck, clutching him with a fierce gratitude that had no measure.

“Oh, bless the tongue that tells me so!” she cried, and kissed him—cheek, beard, jaw—again and again, as if each touch could nail Gerard to the world. “Bless it! bless it!”

“There, there,” said Jorian, shaken and embarrassed by so much passion, yet softened in spite of himself. “Let us lay him warm.”

He lifted Gerard as if he were a heavy sack of meal—careful, though, with the head—and laid him on the bedclothes. Then he drew from his coat a flask; the sharp smell of Schiedamze leapt out into the room, clean and biting as crushed juniper, like a kitchen suddenly overrun by a spirit too strong for any pot.

He filled his broad hand and flung the liquor sharply in Gerard’s face—once, twice. The cold wet slap, the pungent sting, the violent scent, all conspired like rough nurses.

Gerard gave a faint sigh.

To Margaret that thin sound was richer than any song. It was a bell rung at the right hour; it was a hearth catching after long coaxing. She flew toward him, then stopped short, trembling, afraid her very love might bruise him. Her confidence in her own hands had fled.

“That is right—let him alone,” said Jorian, in a voice that tried to sound careless and came out kind. “Don’t go cuddling him as you did me, or you’ll drive his breath back again. Let him alone: he is sure to come to. ’Tisn’t like as if he was an old man.”

Gerard sighed more deeply; a faint streak of colour crept back to his lips as warmth returns to bread set near the fire. The room, that had been a tomb, began to be merely a room again: four walls, a bed, a candle, two living people.

Jorian turned for the door. If he lingered, someone might wonder where he had gone; suspicion, like smoke, found every chink. He had scarcely reached the latch when something seized his legs from behind.

It was Margaret.

She curled about his knees like a thing that will not be shaken off—no longer statuesque, no longer cold—kissing his hand, pressing her cheek to it, pleading with a body before she could find words.

“You won’t tell?” she whispered, hoarse with fear. “You have saved his life; you have not the heart to thrust him back into his grave—to undo your own good work?”

“No, no!” Jorian answered roughly, as if roughness could hide feeling. “It is not the first time I have done you two a good turn; ’twas I told you in the church whither we had to take him. Besides, what is Dierich Brower to me? I’ll see him hanged ere I’ll tell him.”

He paused; the thought that always sat nearest his tongue pushed forward—his own hearth, his own mouths to fill, his own wife with her practical hands, his children with their hungry mornings. Gain, like a strong spice, will assert itself even in a kindly stew.

“But I wish you’d tell me where the parchments are! There are a hundred crowns offered for them. That would be a good windfall for my Joan and the children, you know.”

Margaret’s fingers tightened on him, not with greed, but with the desperate quickness of one snatching at any rope flung into deep water. “Ah! they shall have those hundred crowns.”

“What! are the things in the house?” Jorian asked eagerly, his voice dropping.

“No; but I know where they are; and by God and St. Bavon I swear you shall have them to-morrow. Come to me for them when you will—but come alone.”

“I were made else,” said Jorian, and a grin flashed and vanished. “What! share the hundred crowns with Dirk Brower? And now may my bones rot in my skin if I let a soul know the poor boy is here.”

With that oath—and the odd blend of mercy and profit that had fathered it—he slipped out quickly, for delay was danger. Margaret sank again to her knees, quivering from head to foot as a flame trembles in a draught, and prayed beside Gerard and for Gerard, as if prayer were another blanket she could tuck about him.

When Jorian returned to the others, Dierich Brower turned on him with the blunt impatience of a man whose blood had been stirred and wanted a conclusion.

“What is to do?” asked Brower. “What saw you?”

Jorian made his face a careless mask. “Why, we have scared the girl out of her wits. She was in a kind of fit.”

“We had better all go and doctor her, then,” said another, with that officiousness that mistakes noise for help.

“Oh, yes!” Jorian replied, in a tone that mocked them without their hearing it, “and frighten her into the churchyard. Her father is a doctor, and I have roused him, and set him to bring her round. Let us see the fire, will ye?”

The words were thrown off as lightly as a man tosses a crust to a dog. Their very ease disarmed suspicion. Men who have been straining their ears for a cry of “Here he is!” will accept a shrug and a hearth as a relief; they are glad to be told there is nothing more to do.

Soon enough, cold and half-ashamed and hungry, the party agreed that the kitchen of the Three Kings was much warmer than Peter’s house. They departed, not without untying Martin first—an afterthought, as if a man bound in a corner were no more than a sack that had been in the way.

At the door Dierich Brower could not resist his little triumph of hindsight. “Take note, mate, that I was right, and the burgomaster wrong,” said he. “I said we should be too late to catch him, and we were too late.”

Thus, in one terrible night, Gerard grazed the prison and the grave.

And how did he get clear at last? Not by the cunning of a hiding-place; not by the sharpness of Margaret’s wits; but by a sudden good impulse in one of his captors—by the scrap of humanity left in a somewhat reckless man’s heart—helped along by that same man’s desire of gain. In such mixed measures are men compounded: mercy and money, pity and profit, kneaded together like dark flour and white, and baked by chance into the loaf that saves or ruins us.

Within the room, as danger receded like footsteps down a lane, joy came in upon them—first timidly, then with a flood that made everything else seem small. Gerard’s colour returned by degrees: a faint warmth in the cheeks, a breath that no longer faltered, an eyelid that fluttered as if waking from a deep, strange sleep. Margaret watched each change as a housewife watches the first sign of rising in dough she has feared would never lift—hope in the smallest swelling, salvation in a simple softness.

At last Gerard’s eyes opened upon her.

He woke from his trance to find his head pillowed on her arm. The scent of her hair was about him, loosened in great waves, warm with the heat of her body and the close air of the room. The candle-smoke lay thin as a veil; the hush that had been terror now felt like safety. He heard her voice—broken, new, eloquent with a love that had no need of fine words because it spoke first in breath, in tears, in the trembling of fingers against his face.

She bent close and kissed him, and then kissed him again, and tears fell—hot drops, each one a proof that she was alive and he was alive and the world had not taken him after all. She murmured endearments in the tongue that belonged to her childhood and her heart; and in those sounds, not to be translated without loss, he understood more than he had ever understood before. It struck him with a sweet shock how ardently, how tenderly, she loved him—how much of her very self was bound up in those familiar syllables no stranger could quite pronounce.

He whispered thanks—not to his enemies as saints might counsel, but to the strange chain of accidents that had let him return to her. Trouble and danger seemed suddenly a far country, a whole age behind them. They drew together, arms twining as naturally as if they had always been so, and called each other husband and wife.

Were they not solemnly betrothed? Had they not stood before the altar together? Was not the blessing of Holy Church upon their union—her curse on all who would part them?

In that hour their words were simple, domestic even: a vow spoken low, like something said at the hearth when the door is barred against the weather. Outside, the night had its own noises—distant feet in the street, a dog somewhere giving one lonely bark, the city’s faint murmur like the sea heard through walls—but in the room the soundscape had changed entirely. No longer the racket of pursuit, no longer the clatter of men; only breath, heartbeats, the soft rustle of linen, the small, sacred creak of the bed as life resumed its ordinary weight.

But no woman’s nerves bear such a strain without recoil. Presently Margaret’s strength ebbed as suddenly as it had flared. She turned faint and sank upon Gerard’s shoulder, smiling—oh, so feebly—yet with a smile that said she had won a battle. She was quite, quite unstrung.

Gerard started up in alarm, seeking help with his eyes, his whole body eager to rise, to call, to do something.

But she held him with a gentle grasp and pleaded, “Do not leave me for a moment. While I can lay my hand on you, I feel you are safe—not else. Foolish Gerard! nothing ails me. I am weak, dearest, but happy—oh! so happy.”

Then it was Gerard’s turn to be steady. He supported that dear head, and her great loose hair fell over him like a cloak. He nursed her as carefully as if she were the precious thing and he the strong one set to guard it—soothing her quivering on his bosom with soft words, with murmurs of love, with gentle caresses that asked no more than that she stay, that she breathe.

Poor things—they were happy.

To-morrow they must part. Yet the thought, hovering at the edge of their bliss, could not sting them now. They had looked into Death’s face; all other troubles seemed light as air. While there is life there is hope; while there is hope there is joy. Separation for a year or two—what was it to two so young, who had caught even a glimpse of the grave?

The future shone. The present was heaven. So the hours passed—sweet, perilous, and unguarded; for innocence, when visible danger has slipped away, runs risks of its own, and they lay not in prisons or pursuers, but in the beating of their own hearts, and in the inexperience that can scarcely tell one kind of hunger from another.

Ghysbrecht van Swieten lay all that night with his eyes open and his heart thumping as if a fist beat time upon his ribs. The storm had passed over Sevenbergen like a drum—first the long roll of wind along the eaves, then the sudden crack of lightning that split the dark with a sound too bright for any mortal ear, then the heavy sluicing rain that made every gutter sing. To Ghysbrecht, thunder was no grand voice of God but a threat with teeth; each peal seemed to come hunting for his very bed. So he had not dared join the men who had gone to turn Peter’s poor house inside out. He listened instead—counting the pauses between the flashes, straining to hear through the weather for any footfall, any shout, any sound that meant his prey had slipped the net.

When at last the sky tired of striking and the rain thinned to a dripping, steady whisper, he rose like a man who has been held under water and is allowed, grudgingly, one breath. He crept down the stairs, careful as a thief in his own home, and the boards answered him with little groans. Outside, the night smelled washed and raw—wet earth, bruised grass, the sharp iron tang storms leave behind. He saddled his mule with hands that worked too quickly to be gentle; the leather was cold and damp, and the buckles rang faintly in the cleansed air. Then he rode for the “Three Kings” at Sevenbergen, the hoofs and the mule’s soft snorts the only sounds in a world still rinsed clean of clamor.

The inn received him with a different music: the stale hush after revelry, broken by snores—thick, varied, shameless. His men lay scattered like dropped garments: some folded over chairs, some sprawled on tables with their mouths open, some on the floor where the rushes had been trodden into a sour mat. A hearth had died down to a dull red eye; last night’s ale hung in the air with the tang of sweat and damp wool.

Ghysbrecht’s voice cut through it like a cleaver. He roused them furiously, kicking at boots, seizing shoulders, shaking heads as if to shake out the dregs and leave only obedience. Blinking, yawning, they gave him their tale: how they had searched and found nothing, and how zealously they had done it—each word a self-praise to sweeten failure.

“Fool! to let you go without me,” cried the burgomaster, his fear transmuted now into rage that tasted, on his tongue, like vinegar. “My life on’t he was there all the time.” His eyes gleamed with the fierce certainty of a man who cannot bear that the world should escape his ordering. “Looked ye under the girl’s bed?”

A man, still half-asleep, scratched at his beard. “No; there was no room for a man there.”

Ghysbrecht’s lip curled. “How know ye that, if ye looked not?” he snarled, each syllable sharp enough to draw blood. “Ye should have looked under her bed, and in it too, and sounded all the panels with your knives. Come, now, get up, and I shall show ye how to search.”

Dierich Brower got to his feet and shook himself like a dog flinging off river water. His tone carried the dull amusement of the confident. “If you find him, call me a horse and no man.”

In a few minutes they were abroad again, the street still glistening. The village had not yet found its morning voice; only a few hens muttered in their coops, and from far off a cart-chain clinked once and was still. Peter’s house stood as before—plain, closed, quiet—its silence now seeming to Ghysbrecht not innocence but insolence. They surrounded it as if it were a pot to be watched lest it boil over and spill what they wanted. The fiery old man handed his mule’s reins to Jorian Ketel, and with Dierich Brower and the rest pushed in.

The house met them with emptiness that had a taste: cold ashes, damp wood, yesterday’s air. Not a creature to be seen—not even Peter. No crying child, no scurrying girl, no startled man. They went from room to room, and the floors answered their boots with a hollow thud. Upstairs they climbed, their breath loud in the close stairwell, their weapons and buckles making small metallic chirps against the washed hush of the world outside.

Then, sudden as a pot-lid clapped down, one of the men gave a shout and thrust an arm out, pointing through Peter’s window. It stood open, letting in the fresh, wet smell of fields and the thin song of morning—larks beginning their work over the drenched land.

They crowded to look, faces pressed close, and there—at some little distance—walking quietly across the fields, as if there were no net at all, no burgomaster’s temper, no law’s teeth—went the man they sought. He kept his pace unhurried. With him were Margaret and Martin, their figures moving together through the wet grass, each step raising a faint darkening in the green where the storm-water clung.

Ghysbrecht’s answer was not a prayer. It was an exulting yell, raw and loud enough to make the very window-frame seem to quiver. He was down the stairs in a rush, the house’s silence broken and left behind like a snapped thread. He flung himself upon his mule; the saddle creaked, the animal stamped and snorted at the sudden weight. His men spilled out after him, roused at last into one purpose. And in the brightened, dripping morning—while the fields still rang with bird-song and the world smelled of wet soil and living roots—Ghysbrecht van Swieten and his company set off in hot pursuit.

Before the cocks had found their throats, Gerard started up as if the straw beneath him had turned to nettles. He shook Martin’s shoulder, and the old soldier, wrenched out of sleep, stared as though he looked on an apparition.

“By the rood,” muttered Martin, blinking, “I deemed you slipped out by the window yesternight.”

Gerard told him in broken haste what peril had brushed him so close that the warmth of it still clung to his skin. When he asked, low and quick, how a man might get out of Holland unseen, Martin’s answer came like a map he had carried folded in his head through twenty campaigns.

“There is but one safe way. I must take you through the great forest to a bridle-road I know—no cart-track, no village-lane where every dog knows a stranger’s step. It will carry you swift to a hostelry. There they’ll lend you a horse that can eat up miles. One day’s hard gallop and you are out of Holland. But we go ere the folk here so much as turn in their beds.”

Peter’s house lay scarce a furlong and a half from the black edge of the forest. They made ready with the economy of those who have fled before: no clatter, no shouted farewells, only hands that moved by habit. Martin took his bow and three arrows—it being Thursday, and the old man’s mind clung to the day’s rule as to a rosary. Gerard carried nothing but the stout oak staff Peter thrust into his palm, the wood smooth where a hand had worried it, the grain close as if it had grown stubborn on poor ground.

Margaret pinned up her kirtle and farthingale, for the road was wet, and the hem of a woman’s gown is a sponge that drinks mud and sorrow alike. Peter walked with them as far as his garden hedge. He was not a man prodigal of outward feeling; yet now his face worked, and his breath caught as if the cold had seized him.

He raised his hand over Gerard’s head. “God keep thee,” he said—only that, and it was a whole benediction.

The sun was just prying at the rim of the world when they crossed the stony field, dew clinging to every pebble and blade. The forest ahead stood like a dark loaf on a board, crusted with branches, smelling of damp needles and last year’s leaves. Halfway over the field Margaret kept turning her head, quick, like a hare that cannot help looking for the hawk. Then a sound, or a glimpse, or the tightening of some inward cord made her cry out.

She ran.

Not the measured running of one who knows she can outrun, but the wild flight of terror, skirts lifted, breath tearing her throat, screaming as she went as if the voice itself could push her feet faster. Martin and Gerard needed no second warning. Behind them, Ghysbrecht and his men came on hot, the clink and slap of pursuit crossing the open ground.

Resistance would have been madness there. They ran too.

“Only win the wood!” Martin shouted between breaths. “Only win the wood!”

The great trees seemed to stretch their boughs toward them like arms that promised shelter; the leaves—still and patient—hung as a screen. Hope leapt in Gerard’s chest with each stride, and in hope there was a strange lightness, as if his feet barely kissed the earth.

Then danger changed its shape.

Ghysbrecht, fiery even in age, flung himself upon his mule. The beast, goaded to a gallop, cut a wide semicircle; and while his men labored straight after the fugitives, their leader rode to head them off. He cared not though the others slipped into safety; he had set his malice on Gerard as a cook sets a spit: fixed, and turning it till it be done.

He gained the edge of the wood a heartbeat before Gerard. The mule’s breath steamed, sour with sweat. Ghysbrecht’s eyes blazed under his cap.

Margaret shrieked, threw herself against Gerard, clinging as if her body could be a shield. Gerard shook her off—no gentleness in the motion, only the hard necessity of a man whose life is measured in moments.

Ghysbrecht, in his ardor, forgot what hunters forget until it costs them: a beast at bay has teeth, and a man has more than teeth—he has hate, and he has the sudden fierce joy of striking back.

Gerard did not dodge. He sprang straight at the burgomaster with a savage, exulting cry, all the fear in him transmuted into one bright, brutal purpose. The oak staff whistled and came down on Ghysbrecht’s face with a crash like a cleaver on bone. The old man pitched under his mule’s tail, heels kicking a devil’s tattoo in the air, blood streaming and spattering his collar.

Before the mule’s startled snort had finished, the three were in the wood.

Behind them rose a yell—dismay first, then vengeance—like a pot boiling over. It told them what they already knew in the marrow: this was now a race for life.

“Why run?” Gerard panted, half turning. He held up the staff, darkened at the end. “You have your bow, and I have this.”

“Boy!” Martin roared, and his voice cracked like a whip. “The gallows! Follow me.”

They fled deeper, and soon the open field’s honest sounds were swallowed. The forest closed around them with its own breath: the hush of needles, the soft suck of wet earth underfoot, the far whisper of branches rubbing like old garments. Yet human noise followed—feet breaking twigs, men calling—and then, sharp and sickening, a cry like a pack of hounds opening on the scent.

Margaret moaned as she ran; her breath came in sobs that tasted of iron. Gerard’s jaw locked till his teeth ached, and his fingers clenched the staff as if it were rooted to his bones.

They came upon a stiff hazel coppice. Martin plunged into it as if it were standing corn, shouldering the young wood aside. Hazel switches slapped and sprang back, wet leaves smearing their faces. Fifty yards in, the ground forked into four blind paths—thin as scratches. Martin chose one without pause.

“Bend low,” he said.

Half crouching, they slid along, the hazel closing behind them as if it meant to erase their passage. Again little tortuous paths crossed theirs, weaving like threads in a net. They took one that seemed to turn them back upon themselves, and for a moment Gerard’s heart faltered; then it swung, and after a while led them into a thick pine grove.

Here the walking was firm and dry, the floor carpeted with needles that muted every footstep. Young firs stood so close you could not see three yards, their resinous scent thick in the air, clean and sharp as if the forest had been newly washed. No paths showed; it was a green room with a thousand narrow pillars.

When they had gone some way, Martin sat down as calmly as if he had reached a market bench. War had taught him this trick: when danger drops away for an instant, so does the trembling it leaves behind. He opened his wallet and drew out bread and a slice of ham.

The bread was coarse, dark with rye, its crust hard and honest. The ham was lean, salt-bitten, with a rim of fat that went translucent where his fingers warmed it. He chewed with the relish of a man who had lived on worse than hunger.

Gerard and Margaret stared at him, aghast, the chase still in their ears.

Martin jerked his chin at Gerard. “All Sevenbergen could not find you now. But you will lose your purse, Gerard, long before you get to Italy. Is that the way to carry a purse?”

Gerard looked down. A large triangular purse hung absurdly at his side, its chains entangled with the buckle and strap of his wallet as if it had grown there.

“This is none of mine,” he said. He tugged at it, but the coppice had snarled it past sense.

“It seems loath to leave me,” he said, and had to cut it loose with his knife.

They opened it. Silver coins of all sizes gleamed in the dim green light—some worn thin as wafers, some newer and sharp-edged. Yet the purse’s swollen look came chiefly from brown paper, folded and doubled, making a great show of wealth with no weight behind it.

A light broke on Gerard. “Why—it must be that old thief’s; see, stuffed with paper to deceive the world!”

How had it come to him? For a moment the thing seemed like a conjuration. Then the plain truth rose: the purse had hung at Ghysbrecht’s saddle-bow; and when Gerard flew at him, the staff and hand and fury had torn the chains away without his knowing it. With one gesture he had felled his enemy—and robbed him.

Gerard’s eyes shone, not with greed alone, but with that fierce, foolish delight a man feels when fortune appears to take his side in the midst of ruin. Margaret, however, went pale.

“Throw it away, Gerard,” she whispered, as if the coins could cry out their owner’s name. “Or let Martin take it back. Already they call you a thief. I cannot bear it.”

“Throw it away? Give it him back?” Gerard’s voice was low but hard. “Not a stiver. This is spoil lawfully won in battle from an enemy. Is it not, Martin?”

“Why, of course,” Martin said, mouth full, indifferent as a butcher weighing meat. “Send him back the brown paper, and you will. But the purse or the coin—that were a sin.”

“Oh, Gerard,” Margaret pleaded, and her hands trembled as if she were kneading dough that would not come together. “You are going to a distant land. We need the goodwill of Heaven. How can we hope for that if we take what is not ours?”

But to Gerard the happening wore a different color, like light through stained glass. “It is Heaven that gives it me by a miracle,” he said, and pressed the purse to him as if it were a relic. “Thus the favoured people spoiled the Egyptians, and were blessed.”

Margaret’s gaze fell. The damp of the forest lay on her lashes, making them heavy. “Take your own way,” she said humbly. “You are wiser than I am. You are my husband,” she added in a low murmur, as if the words were new on her tongue and tasted strange—like speaking in a dialect learned for love. “Is it for me to gainsay you?”

Those words—so yielding from Margaret, who till that day had held the whip-hand—made Martin glance at her, surprised, though he said nothing. Later they would return to him, and then he would understand them more.

Gerard, moved by her sudden obedience, kissed her. Then they went on hand in hand, Martin leading them deeper into the huge forest. The farther they pressed, the more the world of men seemed to thin behind them. Even the townspeople, bold enough on roads and in fields, did not venture so far into this trackless heart where sound itself changed—where a snapped twig could seem far as a horn-call, and a man could be lost a stone’s throw away.

And as danger fell behind like a cloak dropped in haste, Gerard’s nature—impetuous in both passion and repentance—turned upon itself. His conscience began to prick, each step giving it room.

“Martin,” he said at last, “would I had not struck quite so hard.”

“Whom?” Martin scoffed. “Oh, let that pass. He is cheap served.”

“I saw his grey hairs,” Gerard said, and his voice wavered. “As my stick fell on him. I doubt they will not from my sight this while.”

Martin grunted, contemptuous as ever of scruples that did not keep a man alive. “Who spares a badger for his grey hairs? The greyer your enemy is, the older; and the older, the craftier; and the craftier, the better for a little killing.”

“Killing?” Gerard stopped short, and shook all over, as if a cold wind had found him among the pines. “Killing, Martin? Speak not of killing!”

“I am much mistook if you have not,” Martin returned cheerfully, like a man pronouncing tomorrow’s weather.

“Now Heaven forbid!”

“The old vagabond’s skull cracked like a walnut. Aha!”

“Heaven and the saints forbid it!”

“He rolled off his mule like a stone shot out of a cart. Said I to myself, ‘There is one wiped out.’”

The old soldier grinned, ruthless as a blade that has been sharpened too long to pity the flesh it enters.

Gerard fell on his knees on the pine-needles, and began to pray for his enemy’s life. His lips moved fast, the words tumbling out in the learned tongue that had shaped his conscience—Latin, heavy with authority, yet in that instant feeling too grand and too rigid to carry the raw taste of fear and regret in his mouth.

At the sight of him, Martin’s patience broke like a snapped bowstring.

“Here’s mummery!” he cried. “What! you that set up for learning, know you not that a wise man never strikes his enemy but to kill him? And what is all this coil about killing old men? If it had been a young one now, with the joys of life waiting for him—wine, women, and pillage! But an old fellow at the edge of the grave, why not shove him in? Go he must, to-day or to-morrow; and what better place for greybeards? Now, if ever I should be so mischancy as to last so long as Ghysbrecht did, and have to go on a mule’s legs instead of Martin Wittenhaagen’s, and a back like this”—he struck the wood of his bow—“instead of this”—he struck the string—“I’ll thank and bless any young fellow who will knock me on the head, as you have done that old shopkeeper; malison on his memory.”

“Oh, culpa mea! culpa mea!” Gerard cried, smiting his breast, his prayer and shame spilling out in that same priestly tongue—words that meant much, yet could never quite translate the feel of a man’s staff striking a human face.

“Look there!” Martin sneered at Margaret. “He is a priest at heart still—and when he is not in ire, St. Paul, what a milksop!”

“Tush, Martin!” Margaret cried, sharply reproachful; then she went to Gerard, wound her arms about him, and drew him close. Her voice changed, soft and sure, as if she were laying a warm cloth over a burn.

“Sweetheart,” she murmured, “you forget. You went not a step out of the way to harm him who hunted you to your death. You fled from him. He it was who spurred on you. Then did you strike—but in self-defence, and a single blow, and with that which was in your hand. Malice had drawn knife, or struck again and again. How often have men been smitten with staves, not one but many blows, yet no lives lost! If then your enemy has fallen, it is through his own malice, not yours, and by the will of God.”

“Bless you, Margaret,” Gerard whispered, grasping at her words as a starving man grasps bread. “Bless you for thinking so!”

“Yes,” she said, and her tone hardened with practical dread, “but, beloved one, if you have had the misfortune to kill that wicked man, the more need is there that you fly with haste from Holland. Oh, let us on.”

“Nay, Margaret,” Gerard answered, rising slowly. “I fear not man’s vengeance, thanks to Martin here and this thick wood. Only Him I fear whose eye pierces the forest and reads the heart of man. If I but struck in self-defence, ’tis well; but if in hate—He may bid the avenger of blood follow me to Italy—to Italy? ay, to earth’s remotest bounds.”

“Hush!” Martin snapped, suddenly peevish, his head cocked as if his very skull were an ear. “I can’t hear for your chat.”

“What is it?” Gerard asked, the forest closing its damp silence around them.

“Do you hear nothing, Margaret? My ears are getting old.”

Margaret held her breath and listened. At first there was only the small music of the grove—the faint drip from needles, the soft stir where a branch settled. Then, threading through it, came a tuneful sound: one single stroke, deep and ringing, like a bell sounded once in some far church and carried here by miracle and air.

She described it so, in a whisper.

“Nay, I heard it,” Martin said.

“And so did I,” Gerard breathed. “It was beautiful. Ah—there it is again. How sweetly it blends with the air. It is a long way off. It is before us, is it not?”

“No, no,” Martin answered quickly. “The echoes of this wood confound the ear of a stranger. It comes from the pine grove.”

“What! the one we passed?”

“Why, Martin,” Margaret said, and now she saw his face in the dimness—drawn, almost ashen—“is this anything? You look pale.”

“Wonderful!” Martin said, with a sickly sneer that did not hide his dread. “He asks me is it anything? Come on, on! At any rate, let us reach a better place than this.”

“A better place—for what?” Gerard asked, though his stomach had already begun to sink, as if the sound had entered his body and weighed it down.

“To stand at bay, Gerard,” Martin said gravely; “and die like soldiers, killing three for one.”

“What’s that sound?” Gerard whispered, and the pines seemed to press in to listen too.

“It is the avenger of blood.”

“Oh, Martin, save him! Oh, Heaven be merciful—what new mysterious peril is this?”

“Girl,” Martin said, and the words came out like iron. “It’s a bloodhound.”

Courage, like any homely craft, often keeps to one narrow rut. A man may face rain, debt, wolves, and a hard winter as steadily as he kneads rye in a trough—because he has done it before. But take him one thumb’s breadth beyond his known labor, and his heart turns strange.

So it was with Martin Wittenhaagen. He had tramped more forests than most men have crossed market-squares; he had watched for poachers, smuggled bales, slept hungry, fought with fist and staff, and borne all the common hazards of a rough soldier’s life with a blunt endurance. Yet he had never been hunted by a bloodhound; never heard, in the deep of a wood, that measured music which was not music but sentence.

A few paces after they fled, he halted as if his joints had rusted. He leaned on his bow; the grain of the yew pressed into his palm, and still the strength ran out of him. The air itself seemed altered—no longer mere damp leaf-and-moss, but a fear-scent, sharp as bruised fern under heel.

Gerard, to whom danger always looked smaller when it stood a field away, urged him on with impatient breath.

“What avails it?” Martin said at last, his voice sunk and heavy. “If we get clear o’ the wood we shall die cheap. Here, hard by, I know a place where we may die dear.”

“Alas, good Martin,” cried Gerard, “despair not so quickly. There must be some way.”

Margaret, who had not once failed them in the day’s sharp turns, came closer, her eyes bright with a desperate kindness. “What if we part company? Gerard’s life alone is forfeit. Is there no way to draw the pursuit on us twain and let him go safe?”

Martin shook his head as if the very thought were childish. “Girl, you know not a bloodhound’s nature. He is not on this man’s track or that. He is on the track of blood. My life on’t they have taken him where Ghysbrecht fell; and from the dead man’s blood to the man that shed it that cursed hound will lead them, though Gerard run through an army or swim the Meuse.”

And again his head sank, and the bow’s horn nock gleamed dull in the green shade.

Then, far off, it came—one long note rolling between trunks as if the wood were a vaulted church. The hound’s bay was mellow, full-throated, almost beautiful; it had the roundness of a horn-call at harvest home, when men bring in sheaves and sing. But here that sweetness was a hook in the blood. It made the skin on Margaret’s arms rise; it made Martin’s stomach go slack as sour beer.

Strange, that what is fair to the ear can be deadly to the flesh. In the same breath that a lullaby calms a child, this sound steadied the hunters and shook the hunted. It seemed to lay its tongue upon Martin’s nerve, to hold him fast. Gerard too felt it—felt, with the sick clarity that comes in terror, the moral weight of his own act. He had struck an old man and shed blood; now blood itself had found a voice, four-footed and unerring, and it was coming.

Was there not something beyond man in it? Was it not as if Heaven had set a living instrument to play him down?

While the men stood thus benumbed, the woman’s wits ran like a quick hand at a hearth, doing three things at once. Her love was in peril; she would not watch him hunted like a hare without trying some cunning of her own.

“Lend me your knife,” she said to Martin.

He gave it, half in scorn, half in stupor. “’Twill be little use in your hands,” he muttered.

Margaret stepped behind Gerard as if only to keep close; and there, in the cover of their bodies and the wood’s shadow, she drew the blade clean across her arm. The cut was quick—no ragged sawing—like the slit a careful cook makes in a skin to drain and dress it. Blood welled at once, warm and startling, and she did not cry out. She stooped, and with deft fingers smeared her hose and shoes, again and again, letting the drops fall where she chose. All the while she kept her face composed; neither Gerard nor Martin saw what she did, though the iron tang rose sharp in the damp air.

Then she caught the soldier’s arm and shook him. “Come—be a man, and let this end. Take us to some thick place, where numbers will not avail our foes.”

“I am going,” Martin said, sulkily, as men go to an appointed whipping. “Hurry avails not. We cannot shun the hound, and the place is hard by.”

He turned left, and led them, not running but moving with the dull obedience of doom. Soon the wood closed into a hazel coppice, a tight-grown tangle of supple stems, as close as wattle in a byre wall—the sort of cover that catches at cloak and hair and keeps sound muffled, so that you hear your own breathing loud as a bell.

“There,” said Martin. “’Tis but a furlong broad, but it will serve.”

“What are we to do?” Gerard demanded.

“Get through, and wait on the other side. Then, as they come straggling through, shoot three, knock two on the head, and the rest will kill us.”

“Is that all you can think of?”

“That is all.”

“Then, Martin Wittenhaagen, I take the lead, for you have lost your head. Come—can you obey so young a man as I am?”

Margaret clutched Martin’s sleeve, pleading him into obedience. “Do not gainsay Gerard. He is wiser than his years.”

Martin gave a sullen nod.

“Do as you see me do,” Gerard whispered, and drew his great knife. At every step he cut a hazel shoot or two close by the ground, clean and low, and then twisted the severed wands breast-high behind him among the standing stems—braiding them so that the path would be easy for a nose that reads the earth, and hard for men who must shove with shoulder and shin. It was work like making a hurdle in haste, each bend and twist with purpose. Martin copied him, grudging and hopeless, the bow dragging in his hand.

They labored through the coppice, sweat mingling with leaf-mould smell. The bay came nearer. What had been mellow now grew louder, sterner, less like music and more like a mallet beating on a door. With it rose another sound: voices—hoops and halloos tossed through the timber, rough as crows. The whole wood’s soundscape shifted. Where earlier there had been only birds and their own footfalls, now the air was full of pursuit: bay, shout, branches snapping, breath.

Margaret trembled, not only from fear but from the slow drain at her arm. Martin went down on his stomach and pressed his ear to the earth.

“I hear a horse’s feet.”

“No,” Gerard whispered. “A mule’s. That cursed Ghysbrecht is still alive. None other would follow me up so bitterly.”

“Never strike your enemy but to slay him,” Martin returned, gloomily, as if quoting an old village proverb that had outlived its language.

“I’ll hit harder this time, if Heaven gives me the chance,” Gerard said between his teeth.

At last the coppice thinned. They forced their way out into an open wood where the trees stood wide apart, tall trunks with clean spaces between—no hiding, no slipping unseen, only long sight-lines and the naked sense of being watched. Behind them the bay and the hooting swelled, and the young hazel seemed to shiver with the passage of men.

“The whole village is out after us,” Martin breathed.

“I care not,” said Gerard. His voice steadied into command. “Listen, Martin. I have made the track smooth to the dog, but rough to the men, that we may deal with them apart. The hound will gain on the men; and as soon as he comes out of the coppice we must kill him.”

“The hound?” Martin’s eyes narrowed. “There is more than one.”

“I hear but one.”

“Ay—but one speaks; the others run mute. Let the leading hound lose scent, and another shall give tongue. There will be two dogs at least—or devils in dog’s hides.”

“Then we kill two instead of one,” Gerard said. “The moment they are dead, into the coppice again, and go right back.”

“That is a good thought,” Martin answered, and heart came back into him like warmth returning to a chilled hand.

“Hush. The men are in the wood.”

Gerard set them in place with quick, whispered orders. “Stand with your bow by the side of the coppice—there, in the ditch. I will go a few yards to yon oak and hide behind it. The dogs will follow me; and, as they come out, shoot as many as you can. The rest I’ll brain as they come round the tree.”

Martin’s eye flashed. He slid into the ditch, the damp earth cold through his hose, and held the bow as steady as if aiming at a deer in rut. Gerard went to the oak and melted behind it; Margaret hovered between, caught by the openness, by the way sound travelled in that space like a thrown stone.

The hooping and hallooing came nearer; the coppice rustled as if it were alive, as if the thicket itself had learned to speak in men’s feet. Now and then, above all, the single bay—like a church bell tolling for one soul.

A trembling hand touched Gerard’s shoulder. He started hard, strung as a drawn bow.

“Martin says,” Margaret whispered, “if we are forced to part company, make for that high ash-tree we came in by.”

“Yes—yes—yes,” Gerard breathed, impatient with tenderness in so sharp an instant. “But go back, for Heaven’s sake. Don’t come here, all out in the open.”

She ran back toward Martin; but before she reached him, a huge dog burst out of the coppice and stood a moment erect, head high, nostrils working as if he drank the world through scent. Margaret crouched instinctively. The brute did not even glance at her; smell was his sight, and her fear was nothing to him.

He lowered his nose. One instant—then, with an awful yell, he sprang straight at Gerard’s oak.

The bow twanged from the ditch like a snapped string on a viol. The hound rolled head-over-heels and fell dead as stone, spitted clean through with Martin’s arrow.

That same heartbeat another hound came out and bent over his dead comrade. Gerard rushed, cudgel up; but before wood met skull, a streak of white flew—another arrow—and the hound grovelled in the dust, desperately hurt, howling thinly, piteously, the sound cutting the ear worse than the bay had done.

Gerard had no time to despatch him. The coppice behind the dogs was already thrashing; it seemed to bulge with bodies. With a wild gesture he pointed Martin back, then ran a few yards to the right and slipped into the hazel just as three men burst out into the open.

Those three had outstripped their fellows. The rest were coming in scattered knots, voices rising and falling like rough chant. Gerard crawled on hands and knees, hazel switches slapping his face; instinct taught Martin and Margaret to do the same, back into the thick. So, within a few yards, the hunters and the hunted passed one another upon opposite tracks—men blundering forward where the fugitives were already sliding back.

A loud cry announced the dead and wounded hounds. Then a babble—arguments, orders, oaths—swelling as more pursuers arrived. Surprise always wastes time; the hunted stole it greedily.

“I hear no more hounds,” Martin whispered to Margaret, and his old soldier’s self came back, brisk as a man who has tasted hope.

It was Margaret’s turn to falter. The blood she had so cleverly spent now took its price; her head swam, and fear for Gerard—separate from her in that twisting brush—gnawed her like hunger.

“Oh, why did we part with Gerard?” she whispered. “They will kill my Gerard, and I not near him.”

“Nay, nay,” Martin breathed. “The head to catch him is not on their shoulders. You bade him meet us at the ash-tree?”

“And so I did. Bless you, Martin, for thinking of that. To the ash-tree!”

“Ay—but with less noise.”

They crept, they slid, they listened. Near the edge of the coppice, hooping and hallooing rose behind them again: the men had satisfied themselves the fugitives were in the thicket and were beating back through it.

“No matter,” Martin whispered, close to Margaret’s ear. “We shall have time to win clear and slip out of sight by hard running.”

He was about to burst from the brush when he stooped suddenly, struck still by what his eye caught through leaves.

A man sat sentinel on a mule.

It was Ghysbrecht Van Swieten. A bloody bandage crossed his face; the bridge of his nose was broken, and beneath the stained cloth his eyes peered keenly, alert as a butcher’s when he weighs a beast and misses no fault. By their very set it was plain he had heard the faint rustle and was searching the green for it.

Martin muttered an oath that seemed to sour the air. Slowly, carefully—careful as a cook lifting a lid lest steam betray him—he strung his bow and fitted his last arrow. Margaret put her hands to her face; she said nothing. She understood without words: this man must die, or Gerard would.

The bow rose. Martin drew steadily—back to the head—holding the aim with the patience of long practice, every breath measured.

And in that very instant, an active figure leaped upon Ghysbrecht from behind, swift as a hawk stooping. A kerchief flashed; in one turn of the hand Ghysbrecht’s head was muffled, his shout smothered. He was whirled from the mule and fell heavily, groaning with terror. Gerard sprang down after him.

“Hist, Martin! Martin!”

Martin and Margaret came out, blinking as if into daylight. Martin’s mouth opened in a great silent cry of relief. “Now fly—fly—while they are all in the thicket. We are saved.”

At the very edge of safety, fate twisted the knife. Margaret, who had held herself up with sheer will, sagged. The blood loss made the world reel; her voice came thin.

“Oh, my beloved—fly! Leave me, for I am faint.”

“No! No!” Gerard cried, fierce and tender together. “Death together, or safety. Ah—the mule! Mount her, you, and I’ll run by your side.”

In a moment Martin was on the mule. Gerard lifted Margaret as if she were a child, set her before the saddle, and took Martin’s bow from him. The mule shifted, uneasy, ears flicking to the noises behind, smelling sweat and fear.

“Help! treason! murder! murder!” shrieked Ghysbrecht, scrambling up on his hams like a man rising out of a nightmare.

“Silence, cur!” roared Gerard, and trod him down again by the throat, crushing him as men crush an adder’s neck.

“Now—have you got her firm? Then fly! For our lives! For our lives!”

But even as the mule, urged by Martin’s heel, scattered flints with his hind hoofs before he found his canter, and even as Gerard lifted his foot from Ghysbrecht’s throat to run—Dierich Brower and five men, returning for orders and drawn by the burgomaster’s cries, burst roaring out of the coppice upon them.

Speech is the familiar vent of human thought; yet there are moments—simple, brutal, and too swift for any tongue—when the heart breaks cover not in words, but in sound. The voice becomes not speech but a cry, raw as a struck bell in a lonely field. In that instant a man is no scholar, no lover, no tradesman with a name to keep; he is a creature in flight, listening with his whole skin for the next footfall behind him, the next branch snapped, the next breath that is not his own.

So it was when the pursuers burst from the thicket upon the three fugitives. Their shout of triumph rolled out like a hunting-horn blown too close to the ear, a rough, tearing noise that made the birds lift in a black scatter and the leaves tremble. And the hunted answered it with a single sharp cry—not shaped by language, not Dutch nor Latin nor any mother-dialect a hearth might cherish, but pure terror made audible. Then there was nothing in the world but the drumming of feet on turf, the whip of grasses against shins, the harsh rasp of breath, and, under all, the mule’s quick, steady snort, warm and animal, as if the beast itself were a bellows keeping a small life-fire going.

Hands clawed at empty air—scarce two feet behind—so near that Gerard could almost feel the heat of their fingers at his back as they sprang. For a heartbeat the men were checked, baffled like lions that have struck at a shadow; and in that breath’s-space Gerard and Martin and the mule stole ten yards as cleanly as if some invisible hand had pushed them forward.

Then the hunters flew after them again with uplifted weapons. They had measured speed before; they were sure of their prey. In the open ground that morning they had gained on the three; and now, at last, it was a fair race, to be settled by legs and lungs alone. A hundred yards vanished beneath them as if the earth were being rolled backwards. Yet those ten yards held—then held more.

It puzzled Dierich Brower, whose mind, for all its violence, could reckon simple things. Why did the distance not lessen? Why did it, by such faint degrees he could not at first believe, begin to widen?

The reason lay in the plain arithmetic of bodies. When three run together, the pace is the pace of the slowest. From Peter’s house to the edge of the forest Gerard had matched himself to Margaret’s gait, as one tempers a fire so it does not scorch the bread; but now he ran his own true pace. The mule was fleet, a creature made for roads and burdens, and it could have left them all behind as a cart-horse leaves children at play. And besides—youth, clean blood, sober living, all the small daily choices that seem as homely as kneading dough and yet make a man’s sinews honest—began to tell. It was as if the very air in his chest tasted clearer now, resinous with pine, damp with leaf-mould, and he drank it greedily. Each breath came with a scent: crushed fern, bruised nettle, the cold iron tang of stream-water somewhere under the roots. The world was not an abstraction; it was a mouthful of forest, and he swallowed it and ran.

Daylight—imperceptible at first—grew between the hunted and the hunters.

Dierich made a desperate effort, a long lunge that brought him two yards nearer, the sound of his boots suddenly loud as a mallet on a board. But in a few seconds Gerard stole those yards back again without seeming to alter anything, as quietly as a careful cook slides a pan away from flame before it spits.

The pursuers began to curse. Their oaths cracked through the wood and fell wrong upon it, like bad music in a holy place. Martin heard, and his face, drawn tight with fear a moment before, lit as if a candle had been shielded and then uncovered. “Courage, Gerard! courage, brave lad! they are straggling.”

It was true. The pack began to break. One of the men edged ahead of Dierich; another dropped behind altogether, his breath now a loud, ragged sawing that made him seem less a hunter than a broken bellows. Even the forest seemed to listen and judge them by their sound: the young ran silently, the old announced their coming with every gasp and stumble.

They came to rising ground—not sharp, but long—and there grit and youth and temperate living told more than ever. Before he reached the top, Dierich’s forty years weighed on him like forty bullets. His chest burned; his mouth tasted of sour sweat, as if he had chewed bitter herbs. He tried to call out a command and could only force it out in a strangled groan.

“Our cake is dough,” he gasped at last—an image dragged up from some remembered kitchen where batter had failed and hope had sunk with it. “Take him dead, if you can’t alive.” And he left running, sinking to a foot’s pace, stubbornly walking as if he could trample down the hill by mere will.

Jorian Ketel tailed off next; then another; and so, one by one, Gerard ran them all to a standstill—save one who kept on staunch as a bloodhound, though losing ground every minute. His name, if I am not mistaken, was Eric Wouverman. He ran with a grim economy, jaw clenched, the sound of his breath thin and measured, like a file at work; and though the distance grew, he did not break.

Followed by him alone, the three fugitives came to another rise in the wood—shorter but much steeper than the last. The trees stood close; the air was cooler; and the ground, where roots broke through the earth like knuckles, demanded nimbleness. Martin, who had eyes for the small aids of the world, cried out over the panting, “Hand on mane!”

Gerard obeyed. His fingers sank into the mule’s coarse hair—warm, living, salted with sweat—and he let the beast lend him its climbing strength. The mule heaved up the slope with a sure-footed urgency; its hooves struck the earth in quick, hard notes, and Gerard, half-running, half-drawn, found himself moving faster than before. It was a simple trick, like using a spoon to lift a delicate wafer from a hot stone: small knowledge that saves much loss.

At the sight of this manoeuvre Eric Wouverman’s heart faltered. He was now full eighty yards behind Gerard—and, worse for him, rather more than that ahead of his nearest comrades. Alone between prey and help, he felt suddenly the silence behind him where the pack ought to be. The wood seemed to widen; the space filled with nothing but his own breath and the pounding in his ears. He pulled up short.

Obeying Dierich’s brutal order, he took down his crossbow. The action had its own calm, like a cook pausing in the midst of panic to sharpen a knife—deliberate, practised, almost domestic in its routine. He set his feet, raised the weapon, levelled it carefully. The string creaked; the bolt lay ready, a small straight thing of wood and iron with death in its point. As the trio were sinking out of sight over the crest of the hill, he loosed.

The bolt went whizzing among them with a sound like a sudden wasp in the ear—thin, vicious, impossible to reason with.

There was a cry of dismay; and next moment, as if a thunderbolt had fallen on them, they were all lying on the ground—mule and all.

The change came so swift it seemed witch-work: one instant the bolt sang through the air, the next there was a stunned hush, as if the very birds had swallowed their notes. Even the man who had loosed the shot stood gaping for a heartbeat—then his voice cracked out, summoning the rest to help net the quarry, and he himself began to scramble up the rise.

He had not won halfway when a shape rose against the pale strip of sky: Martin Wittenhaagen, bow bent, the cord drawn to the cheek, the whole man turned into a single tense line—wood, sinew, and will. Eric Wouverman, who had the stomach to hunt lovers with iron and rope, had not the stomach to face that bow. He slipped behind a tree as a cook slips behind a hanging of herbs when a master’s eye is sharp, pressing himself flat to bark and shadow.

Martin’s name had long been salted with stories—how he could send a shaft so clean it seemed to part the air without disturbing it. The dead dog, still warm in memory, was proof enough. Wouverman craned out, cautious as a man lifting a lid from a pot he fears has boiled over; there—glinting, unwavering—was the arrowhead, fixed on him like a skewer poised above meat. He dared not stir. The forest held its own acoustics: the rasp of his breath against his teeth, the minute tapping of sap on leaf, a far-off jay’s complaint—each sound suddenly loud, each silence a threat.

He played that fearful little game of peeping round the trunk for minutes that felt like hours, until boots and voices came swelling up behind him—his companions arriving in a press. Only then did Martin let his scorn show. A short laugh—dry as old crust—broke the tension; and he vanished, as if the wood had folded him into itself. Almost at once the muffled drumming of hooves told the rest: he was off, riding the mule hard.

The men surged to the top together. From the high ground they looked down into a narrow glade that ran on and on, a green corridor seemingly without end. Far away—so far the eye could barely name them—Gerard and Margaret were fleeing, two dark motes on the bright strip, like gnats dancing at the edge of sight. And behind them, stretched low over the beast’s neck, Martin galloped ventre à terre. The hunters had been beaten twice over: outwitted, and outrun.

To understand Martin’s craft, one must be careful with “coincidences.” They are like a hare’s stumble at the very crack of a gun: it makes men cry, “Hit!” and then, with a contemptuous flick, the creature is off untouched, and their hopes lie flat in the dust.

So it had been with the burgomaster’s mule. At the very moment the crossbow-bolt hissed over her head—harmless as a curse that misses its mark—her hoof found a rabbit-hole. Down she went, sudden as a sack dropped from a cart, and threw both riders. Gerard caught Margaret as instinctively as hands catch a loaf slipping from the peel, but her weight and the impetus of the fall carried him under; and for an instant the earth was strewn with actors in the play—lover, maid, mule—tangled together.

The mule, docile as ever, was on her feet again almost at once, trembling all over, ears laid back, nostrils flaring at the smell of churned soil and fear. Martin rose next. A quick look told him the truth: only one pursuer had gained on them. In that instant he made his choice. He sent the young pair forward on foot—lightened of the beast—and stayed to hold the line, doing precisely what had just been seen: pinning Wouverman to a tree with the mere promise of a shaft.

Then Martin wheeled and drove after them. It was a long chase, the kind that is measured not by distance but by breath: the rasp in the throat, the sting of cold air in the lungs, the drum of blood in the ears louder than any shouting left behind. When he came up at last, he wasted no time in tenderness or talk. He hoisted Gerard and Margaret onto the mule, then ran at her side until his own breathing went ragged; when his wind failed, he took the saddle, and one of the lovers ran, and so they changed in turn—rider and runner alternating like hands at a kneading-trough, so the work never stopped and no one tired beyond recovery.

In that steady rotation—horseflesh, human sinew, and a grim intelligence that understood the value of rhythm—they slipped their enemies. Long before they dared to ease their pace, every sound of pursuit had thinned into nothing; no crack of twig, no clink of tackle, no far halloo came riding the air. The forest’s own music returned—wind in needles, leaf-talk, the distant chuckle of water—and with it the knowledge that the hunters were left with only their humiliation.

Dierich and his men, beaten and empty-handed, went trudging back—crestfallen—to seek their chief and the dog that had run on so bravely and so fatally, as if it had been given wings only to fly into death.

Life and liberty are like the daily loaf: while they sit warm on the board, no one marvels; let the oven go cold, let hunger prowl the threshold, and each crust becomes treasure, each mouthful a prayer. So it was with Gerard and Margaret. A little while ago the wood had been all alarm—dogs baying, men’s coarse shouts cracking through the trunks like whips—yet now, sliding between the friendly trees, they drank in the deep, sheltered quiet as if it were broth after fever. The forest’s hush was not emptiness: it had its own homely music—the soft comb of wind through needles, the distant tap of a woodpecker like a cook’s cleaver on a block, the muted tread of their feet in leaf-mould. Against that sane, green acoustics, the remembered noise of pursuit rang all the fouler in their ears, and made the present silence taste sweeter.

But Gerard, glancing down as they went, saw dark stains on Margaret’s ankles, smeared where her shoes had brushed her hose.

“Martin! Martin!” he cried, voice breaking as if a cord had snapped. “Help! they have wounded her—the crossbow!”

Martin, trudging with the mule’s bridle looped in his fist, wheeled round. Margaret did too, and smiled quickly—too quickly.

“No, no,” she said, laying the smile on him like a cloth over a hurt. “I am not wounded, nor hurt at all.”

“But what is it then, in Heaven’s name?” Gerard’s hands hovered, helpless, as if he could cover her whole with them.

“Scold me not, then!” She blushed—red rising through her pallor like wine through water.

“Did I ever scold you?”

“No, dear Gerard. Well—Martin said it was blood those cruel dogs followed; so I thought, if I could but have a little blood on my shoon, the dogs would follow me instead, and let my Gerard wend free. So I scratched my arm with Martin’s knife—forgive me! Whose else could I take? Yours, Gerard? Ah, no. You forgive me?” She pleaded and caressed in the same breath, like one offering herself up and asking pardon for it.

“Let me see this scratch first,” said Gerard, and his throat tightened.

She showed her forearm.

“There,” he whispered, turning white. “A scratch? I call it a cut—a deep, terrible, cruel cut.” The fresh blood had the bright, honest smell of iron, sharp as a struck coin; it made him shudder more than any battlefield tale. “Oh, Margaret—”

“She might have done it with her bodkin,” growled Martin. “Milksop, that sickens at sight of a scratch and a little blood.”

Gerard heard him, but the words had no hold. “No,” he said hoarsely. “I could look on a sea of blood—but not on hers. Oh, Margaret! how could you be so cruel?”

Margaret’s smile softened, not offended—only full. “Foolish Gerard,” she murmured, and flung the guilty arm round his neck as if to bind him there. “As if I would not give all the blood in my heart for you, let alone a few drops from my arm.”

And under the memory of how near he had been to losing her—of how near she had been to losing him—she began to weep upon his neck, tears warm as fresh milk. He wept too, and the wood took their sobs and dulled them, the way moss takes a footfall.

“And I must part from her,” he sobbed, the words forced out like breath from a broken bellows. “We two that love so dear—one must be in Holland, one in Italy. Ah me! ah me! ah me!”

At that, Margaret wept afresh, but made no lament. Something in her—an instinct that was as watchful as any housewife’s ear for a pot boiling over—kept her from speaking what she thought. To pour out her whole heart now would be to burden his already weighted going. So she bore it in silence, and let only her tears speak.

They came suddenly out upon a beaten path. It felt, after the forest, like stepping from a chapel into a market. The very gravel underfoot had a harsher sound. Martin stopped and pointed with his chin, hanging his head as if he pointed to a grave.

“This is the bridle-road I spoke of,” said he. “And there away lies the hostelry.”

Gerard and Margaret looked at one another—one quick, frightened glance, like two children caught at a forbidden cupboard.

“Come a step with me, Martin,” whispered Gerard.

He drew the soldier behind a thicket, where the leaves could hide faces, if not sorrow. Gerard’s voice came brokenly, as if each word must be fetched up from deep.

“Good Martin, watch over her for me. She is my wife; yet I leave her. See—here is gold—it was for my journey; it is no use my asking her to take it—she would not; but you will for her, will you not? Oh, Heaven! and is this all I can do for her? Money? But poverty is a curse. You will not let her want for anything, dear Martin? The burgomaster’s silver is enough for me.”

Martin’s hard mouth worked once, as if he chewed a tough morsel. “Thou art a good lad, Gerard. Neither want nor harm shall come to her. I care more for her little finger than for all the world; and were she nought to me, even for thy sake would I be a father to her. Go with a stout heart, and God be with thee going and coming.”

He wrung Gerard’s hand and turned his head away, ashamed of the softness in him.

After a moment he moved as if to go back; but Gerard caught his sleeve.

“No, good Martin—prithee, stay here behind this thicket, and turn your head away from us, while I—oh, Martin! Martin!”

So Martin, who had seen wounds and deaths without blinking, spared himself this. He did not witness the poor young things kneel and renew before Heaven those vows which rough men had broken with brute noise. He did not see them cling together as if stitched by the same thread, and then try to part, and fail, and return, and cling again like drowning creatures who cannot trust the shore. But he heard Gerard sob, and sob, and Margaret’s low moan—the kind of sound that lives under speech, untranslatable into any tongue a man can boast of learning.

At last there was a hoarse cry, and the quick patter of feet on the hard road. Martin started up—and there was Gerard running wildly, both hands clasped above his head as if in prayer against the air itself. Margaret tottered after him, palms stretched out piteously as if asking to be held up; her cheek was ashy, her eyes fixed on nothing, like a lamp gone out while the wick still smokes.

Martin caught her in his arms and spoke comfort—plain, soldierly words—but her mind could not take them in. Only the sound of a voice reached her, and at that she moaned and clutched him, trembling from head to foot.

He got her on the mule, set his arm round her, and so, supporting the body that had been strong as a boy’s and was now slack and powerless, he led her slowly and sadly home. She shed no tear now, spoke no word. Grief had stopped her like a clog in a millstream.

At the edge of the wood he took her down and bade her go across to her father’s house. She went, obedient as one walking in sleep.

Martin went on to Rotterdam; Sevenbergen was too hot for him.

Gerard, severed from her he loved, moved like a man under enchantment. He hired a horse and a guide at the little hostelry and rode swiftly toward the German frontier; yet nothing entered him. Trees and houses and men slid by as if seen through oiled parchment. His companions spoke twice; he answered nothing. Only once, as if the words leapt out of him of their own cruelty, he cried, “Shall we never be out of this hateful country?”

After many hours they reached the brow of a steep hill. A small brook ran at the bottom, its sound thin but continual—the patient talking of water over stones.

“Halt!” cried the guide, and pointed across the valley. “Here is Germany.”

“Where?” Gerard asked, as if he doubted that any land could be real after what he had left.

“On t’other side of the bourn. No need to ride down the hill, I trow.”

Gerard dismounted without a word and drew the burgomaster’s purse from his girdle. As he opened it the guide, half sulky, said, “You will soon be out of this hateful country. Mayhap the one you are going to will like you no better; any way, though it be a church you have robbed, they cannot take you, once across that bourn.”

At another time Gerard would have rebuked him, or struck him. Now the words fell on him like smoke and drifted away. He paid the lad in silence and went down the hill alone.

The brook was silvery. It murmured over little pebbles that glittered as if varnished, each stone a small, clean thing, rinsed and made itself again. He sat and looked stupidly at them, at the way water made a continuous song without knowing the meaning of its own notes. The sound steadied him more than any counsel.

Then he drank. The water was cold and pure, tasting of earth and leaf-shadow. He laved his hot feet and hands; the chill bit, and the bite woke him, the way sharp vinegar wakes the palate.

He rose; then, taking a short run, leaped across into Germany.

Even as his foot struck the strange bank, he turned and looked back.

“Farewell, ungrateful country!” he cried. “But for her it would cost me nought to leave you for ever, and all my kith and kin, and—the mother that bore me, and—my playmates, and my little native town. Farewell, fatherland—welcome the wide world! omne solum forti patria.”

The brave Latin sat oddly with the rawness in his mouth; and with it still there, he suddenly drooped, arms and legs turned weak, and he sat down on the foreign soil and sobbed bitterly, like a child who cannot name what hurts him.

When he had sat a while bowed down, he rose, dashed the tears from his eyes like a man, and—lest one look back should undo him—cast not a single glance behind. He stepped out into the wide world.

His love and heavy sorrow left no room for vulgar misgiving. Compared with tearing himself from Margaret, it seemed a small thing to go on foot to Italy in that rude age. All nations met in a convent; and thanks to the monks’ teaching and his own thirst of knowledge, he could speak most tongues needful on that long road.

“I will soon be at Rome,” he said to himself. “The sooner the better now.”

After walking a good league he came to a place where four ways met—country roads, serpentine, puzzling even to neighbors who had trudged them all their lives between field and village. Gerard took out a little dial Peter had given him, set it in the autumn sun, and by this small, honest instrument—this portable scrap of ordered light—chose his way unhesitatingly for Rome, inexperienced as a young swallow flying south; but unlike the swallow, wandering south alone.

Not far along the road Gerard overtook a little knot of people—two men in sober, workmanlike suits, each leaning with lazy confidence against a horse’s flank, their heads together in talk. The rider, by contrast, was dressed as if he had meant to be seen: a silk doublet, and bright green jerkin and hose of English cloth, smooth and shining as a mole’s fur. Yet this splendid creature lay full length on his belly in the afternoon sun, sprawled in the dust like a great lizard. His velvet cloak—flaming yellow—had been taken from him with care and spread across the horse’s loins, as though the beast were the more delicate body.

“Is aught amiss?” Gerard asked, for the sight jarred with any sober sense of order.

“Not that I wot of,” said one servant.

“But your master lies like a corpse. Are ye not ashamed to let him grovel so?”

“Go to,” the other answered, untroubled. “The bare ground is the best cure for his disorder. If you get sober in bed, it gives you a headache; but you leap up from the hard earth like a lark in spring. Eh, Ulric?”

“He speaks sooth,” said Ulric, warming to it.

“What—then the gentleman is drunk?”

Both servants broke into a hoarse laugh at the plainness of the question; and then Ulric checked himself, scanned Gerard from head to heel, and turned grave.

“Who are you, and where born, that know not the Count is ever drunk at this hour?”

Gerard felt suspicion snap about him like a cold cord. “I am a stranger,” he said steadily, “but a true man; and one that loves knowledge. Therefore I ask questions, not for love of prying.”

“If you be a true man,” Ulric returned, shrewd as a toll-gatherer, “then give us trinkgeld for the knowledge we have given you.”

Gerard’s purse was lean enough to show through his courage. Yet he put a good face on it. “Trinkgeld you shall have, such as I can spare—an if you will tell me why ye have taken his cloak from him and laid it on the beast.”

At the sweet prospect of coin they both became philosophers at once, and offered him two answers as swiftly as two cooks crying their own sauce the best. One swore it was prudence: should the Count wake (and seasoned topers do come to themselves in a breath) and find his horse sweating in the cold while his cloak lay idle, he would curse, and mayhap lay on. The other gave a grander reason, as if a stable were a school: a horse, drinking nought but water, must be cockered and warmed without; but a master, being ever filled with good beer, carries his heat inside to the skin, and a cloak is but a shred of vanity.

Each fell enamoured of his own doctrine; and to tell truth, each had taken a hair or two of the dog that bit his master. Their voices rose; their breath, strong with yesterday’s ale, steamed in the mild air; and as they wrangled the green lord began to growl instead of snore. In their heat they marked it not.

Soon the argument took the turn that, in that age, sooner or later enlivened most debates. Hans, holding the bridle in his right hand, cuffed Ulric soundly with his left. Ulric returned it with interest, his right being free. There they went—ding-dong—over the horse’s mane, pummelling each other and jagging the poor beast, until it backed and set an iron heel upon a tender promontory of the sprawled Count.

He started up with a howl, one hand clapped to his hurt, the other tugging at his hilt; and in an instant his naked sword was out and his tongue outstripped it in curses. The servants, frightened out of their courage, let go the horse. Off it went whinnying; off they ran after it crying; and after them plunged the green noble, sword in hand, rebounding from hedge to hedge in a headlong, zigzag fury down the narrow lane.

Gerard, in the midst of this hurtling folly, turned his back on them all and went calmly south—glad to have saved the four tin farthings he had actually made ready for trinkgeld, and far too heavy at heart to smile at the spectacle.

The sun drew low. For some time he had been hoping, and hoping in vain, to see an inn by the way; and now uneasiness crept up his wet sleeves. Worse followed: black clouds gathered and thickened, and the light that had gilded the road became a thin, frightened thing.

He quickened to almost a run; but it was in vain. The rain came down in torrents, drenching him to the skin, and it seemed to douse the very sun, whose rays, already failing, could not contend with this new assault.

He trudged on—dark, wet, and in an unknown region. “Fool! to leave Margaret,” he said aloud, as the water ran from his hair into his eyes.

Then the darkness thickened again. He was entering a great wood. Huge branches shot across the narrow road; the way became an inky passage, a cave with a rugged floor, and he stumbled and stumbled, hands out, feeling for the safer patches, his stomach hollow, his limbs shivering.

On, and on, and on, until the wolves rose from their lairs and bayed all round the wood. The sound was not a single cry but a ring of voices—near, far, high, low—crossing each other like notes in a cruel choir. There was no wind; each small noise carried: light feet pattered at times over the newly fallen leaves; low branches rustled with creatures gliding swiftly past. To Gerard’s strained ear the forest became an instrument played by unseen hands, every snap and scuff a message without words, and therefore the more dreadful for being untranslatable.

His hair bristled; he gripped his cudgel and made ready to sell his life dear.

Then, in the sea of ink, he saw a great fiery star close to the ground. He hailed it as he would his patron saint. “CANDLE! a CANDLE!” he cried, and tried to run; but the dark, broken way tripped him back to walking. The light was farther than he had thought, as hope often is when one is hungry and wet. Yet at last, in the very heart of the forest, he came upon a house. Candles shone in its windows; loud voices rolled out from within, thick as steam.

He looked up for a signboard. There was none. “Not an inn after all,” he said sadly. “No matter. What Christian would turn a dog out into this wood to-night?” And he went to the door that led to the voices.

He opened it slowly and put his head in, timidly. He drew it out at once, as if slapped in the face, and recoiled into the rain and darkness.

Within was a large but low room, and in the middle stood a huge round stove, a clay oven that rose nearly to the ceiling. About it wet clothes were drying—some on lines, and some more compendiously on rustics themselves. Those garments, soaked with the day’s wet and the dirt of a life, and lined with what a foot-traveller in these parts would call rammish clowns, breathed out rank vapours in steaming clouds. It was not one smell but a parliament of smells, each insisting on dominion: sour wool, old sweat, damp leather, wet mud scraped with knives, and beneath it the persistent animal note that clung to men who lived near beasts and seldom near clean water.

In one corner huddled a travelling family, and from it flowed the peculiar sickly smell of neglected brats—warm milk turned stale, unwashed skin, and bedding that had swallowed too many nights. Garlic filled the interstices of the air, as if someone had tried to plaster the room with it, clove by clove. All this with the windows shut, the furnace at full heat, and the breath of at least forty persons thickening the same small space. The room had a sound too: not music, but the constant chew of voices—laughs that broke like sticks, coughing, the scrape of boots, and over all a deep, communal exhalation, as if the house itself breathed.

They had just supped.
