Now Gerard, like most artists, had sensitive organs; and these potent effluvia struck dismay into him. Yet outside the rain lashed him, and inside the light and fire tempted him like warm bread to a fasting man.

He could not force his way through the palpable perfumes at once; he returned to the threshold again and again like a moth singed yet still drawn. At last he discovered that the smells did not entirely mix—no fiend was there to stir them round—so that each held its own little empire. The family’s sourness predominated in two corners; stewed rustic reigned in the centre; garlic ruled near the window. By hasty analysis he found, too, that garlic described the smallest aerial orbit, and the reeking rustic darted farthest—a flavour as if ancient goats, or the fathers of all foxes, had been dragged through a river and were here dried by Nebuchadnezzar.

So he crept into a corner close to the door. Even there the heat and vapours circulated and made the walls drip; and the home-nurtured novice felt a cold snake-wind about his legs while his head turned heavy as lead. Next came the strange mingling of choking, sweet slumber, and a sense of dying—three things in one cup.

He was within an ace of swooning; but he recovered into a deep disgust and a deeper discouragement, and resolved to go back to Holland at peep of day. The resolve gave him a thin comfort: it set an end, at least, to this road. Being faint with hunger, he asked one of the garlic men whether this was not an inn after all.

“Whence come you,” was the answer, “who know not ‘The Star of the Forest’?”

“I am a stranger; and in my country inns have aye a sign.”

“Droll country yours! What need of a sign to a public-house—a place every soul knows?”

Gerard was too tired and empty for argument. He asked where he could find the landlord.

At this new display of ignorance the man’s contempt rose beyond words. He pointed across the room to a middle-aged woman seated on the other side of the oven, and then told his mates what an outlandish animal had strayed among them. Loud voices stopped one by one as the news travelled. Eyes turned on pivots and followed Gerard and his every movement—silently, zoologically—as if they could read his origin in the cut of his wet sleeves.

The landlady sat on a chair an inch or two higher than the rest, between two bundles. From the first, a huge heap of feathers and wings, she plucked downy plumes and stripped the others from their quills, stuffing bundle two. The floor about her was littered ankle-deep; the feathers contributed a stuffy little malaria which in a sweet room might have been noticed, but here went for nothing.

Gerard asked if he could have something to eat.

She opened her eyes wide. “Supper is over this hour and more.”

“But I had none of it, good dame.”

“Is that my fault? You were welcome to your share for me.”

“But I was benighted, and a stranger; and belated sore against my will.”

“What have I to do with that? All the world knows ‘The Star of the Forest’ sups from six till eight. Come before six, ye sup well; come before eight, ye sup as pleases Heaven; come after eight, ye get a clean bed, and a stirrup cup, or a horn of kine’s milk, at the dawning.”

Gerard stared. “May I go to bed then, dame?” he said, sulky with hunger. “For it is ill sitting up wet and fasting, and the byword saith, ‘He sups who sleeps.’”

“The beds are not come yet,” she replied.

“The beds are not come?” Gerard echoed inwardly, but did not dare ask what she meant; every word he spoke seemed to astonish the room, and the eyes were on him—he could feel them as one feels a draught at the nape. He leaned against the wall and sighed audibly.

A titter ran round the watchful company.

“So this is Germany,” he thought bitterly; “and Germany is a great country by Holland. Small nations for me.”

He told himself it would be his first night in the land and his last. He was in that thin place between wakefulness and collapse when an elbow drove into his ribs. He turned sharply. The offender only pointed across the room. In a corner a woman beckoned him. He went toward her gingerly, surprised and irresolute, so that to a spectator her curling finger might have been pulling him across the floor by gut-line. When he reached her, she said in a fine hearty voice, “Hold the child.”

Before he could refuse, she plumped the bairn into his arms.

He stood transfixed, the child a sudden weight of living warmth in his hands, and a horror on his face long and plain as a confession.

At that rueful countenance the lynx-eyed conclave laughed loud and long.

“Never heed them,” the woman said cheerfully. “They know no better; how should they, bred an’ born in a wood?” She rummaged among her clothes with two busy hands—one of which Gerard had freed by shifting the child. Presently she fished out a small tin plate and a dried pudding; then, taking her child back under one arm, held plate and pudding out to Gerard with the other, keeping a thumb on the pudding to prevent it slipping.

“Put it in the stove,” she said. “You are too young to lie down fasting.”

Gratitude surged in him—sharp and clean as the first draught of fresh water after brine. He thanked her warmly. Yet as he went toward the stove, he caught the landlady’s eye and asked, almost pleading, “May I, dame?”

“Why not?” she said, as if he had asked whether he might breathe. Even that question surprised them, though less than the rest.

At the stove he found the oven door blocked by the rammish clowns. They did not budge. He hesitated, and the landlady, seeing, calmly put down her feathers and came. Without a word of temper she pulled a hircine man or two aside and pushed another hircine man or two this way and that, her impassive face the face of a housewife shifting furniture.

“Turn about is fair play,” she said. “Ye have been dry this ten minutes and better.”

Her eye was not deceived: Gorgonii had done stewing and begun baking. Debarred the stove they trundled away, all but one whom she had set like a table where she wished him, and there he stood like a table. Gerard slid the pudding into the oven, and, drawing near the heat, felt his own soaked clothes begin to steam. The smell of warm grain and fat rose faintly from the pudding as it revived; it was not a feast, but it spoke a language his body could understand without translation.

The door opened and in flew a bundle of straw, hurled by a hind with a pitchfork. Another and another followed until the room looked like a clean farmyard. Then the straw was spread in rings round the stove in layered ranks, like seats in an arena, and in a moment the whole company was down on its back.

The beds had come.

Gerard drew out his pudding. It was delicious—salt, brown, and honest; the heat had softened it, and hunger did the rest. While he relished it, the woman who had saved him from fasting, now abed, beckoned him again.

He went to her bundle-side. “She is waiting for you,” she whispered.

He hurried back to the stove, gobbled the rest, casting uneasy glances at the landlady, who sat silent as fate amid the prostrate multitude. When the last bite was swallowed, he went to her.

“Thank you kindly, dame, for waiting for me.”

“You are welcome,” she said calmly, making neither much nor little of it, and began again to gather feathers.

He stopped her. “Nay, that is my task,” he said, and went down on his knees to collect them with ardour, scooping the soft drift into order. The feathers clung to his wet fingers and to his sleeves; the room’s stale warmth made them stick as if the air itself were a paste.

She watched him demurely. “I wot not whence ye come,” she said, with the last relic of distrust; then, more cordially, “but ye have been well brought up. Y’ have had a good mother, I’ll go bail.”

At the door she committed the whole company to Heaven in a formula, and disappeared.

Gerard went to his straw in the very corner—for the guests lay round the sacred stove by seniority, that is, by priority of arrival. This punishment was a boon to him, for he lay upon the shore of odour and stifling heat instead of mid-ocean. He turned his face away from the steaming centre and began to drift.

He was just dropping off when he woke to a noise: the hind with the pitchfork was remorselessly shaking guest after guest to ask whether it was he who had picked up the mistress’s feathers.

“It was I,” Gerard cried.

“Oh, it was you, was it?” The man strode over the intermediate sleepers. “She bade me say, ‘One good turn deserves another,’ and so here’s your nightcap.” He thrust a great oaken mug beneath Gerard’s nose.

“I thank her, and bless her; here goes—ugh!” Gratitude ended in a wry face: the beer was muddy and carried a strange medicinal twang, new and wrong to a Hollander’s tongue, as if herbs had been boiled in it for a sick cow.

“Trinke aus!” shouted the hind reproachfully.

“Enow is as good as a feast,” Gerard murmured, Jesuitically, and stopped.

The hind looked at him with pity, as at a man lacking a sense. “Ich brings euch,” he said, took the mug, and drained it to the bottom.

Then Gerard turned to the wall, pulled up two handfuls of clean straw, and bored into them with his finger until he made a little scabbard; he sheathed his nose in it like a weapon he wished to keep from harm. Soon they were all asleep—men, maids, wives, and children—higgledy-piggledy and snoring in a dozen keys like an orchestra slowly tuning. The room’s sounds knitted into a thick blanket of breath and grunt; and in that coarse music Gerard’s body lay on straw in Germany, while his spirit went away to Sevenbergen, where the air was different, and a familiar voice spoke in a familiar tongue.

When he woke, morning had cleared the night’s foulness as much as it might. Nearly all his fellow-passengers were gone; one or two waited for dinner at nine o’clock—though it was but six. He paid the landlady her demand—two pfenning, about an English halfpenny. The hind demanded trinkgeld; getting a trifle more than usual, he saw Gerard eyeing a foaming milk-pail newly brought from the cow, and hoisted it bodily to his lips.

“Drink your fill, man,” he said.

The milk was cold and sweet and thick with the pasture’s own green breath; it rinsed away, for a moment, the night’s garlic and steam. Gerard offered to pay, but the hind told him in broad patois that a man might swallow a skinful of milk, or a breakfast of air, without putting hand to pouch.

At the door Gerard found his benefactress of the night, and with her a huge-chested artisan, her husband. Gerard thanked her, and in the spirit of the age offered her a creutzer for the pudding.

She repulsed his hand quietly, colouring faintly. “For what do you take me? We are travellers and strangers the same as you, and bound to feel for those in like plight.”

Gerard blushed and stammered excuses. The hulking husband grinned, superior to them both.

“Give the vixen a kiss for her pudding, and cry quits,” he said, with an air at once impartial, judge-like, and Jove-like.

Gerard obeyed the lofty behest and kissed the wife’s cheek—warm, flour-scented, and real as kindness. “A blessing go with you both, good people,” he said.

“And God speed you, young man!” they answered; and so they parted, and never met again in this world.

The sun had just risen. Rain-drops on leaves glittered like diamonds; the wood’s small birds tried their morning notes in the rinsed air, and each sound, clean and separate, was like a balm after last night’s choking chorus. Gerard steered south, and did not even remember his overnight resolve to turn back.

Eight leagues he walked that day. In the afternoon he came upon a huge building with an enormous arched gateway and a postern by its side.

“A monastery!” he cried, joyfully. “I go no further lest I fare worse.”

He knocked at the postern. On stating whence he came and whither bound, he was admitted at once and directed to the guest-chamber, a large lofty room where travellers were fed and lodged gratis by the charity of the monastic orders. Soon the bell tinkled for vespers, and Gerard entered the church. From his place he heard the service sung so exquisitely it seemed the choir of heaven. Yet one thing was wanting: Margaret was not there to hear it with him, and that absence pricked him so sharply he sighed bitterly in the midst of rapture, as if a sweet dish had been set before him without the one spice his tongue craved.

At supper they set before him and his fellows plain but wholesome, abundant food, and good beer brewed in the convent—clearer, kinder, and without the forest inn’s bitter herbs. At an early hour they were ushered into a large dormitory; the number being moderate, each had a truckle bed, and for covering sheepskins dressed with the fleece on.

Before this, a monk, struck by Gerard’s youth and beauty, questioned him, and soon drew out his projects and his heart. When he was found to be convent-bred and going alone to Rome, he became a personage. In the morning they showed him over the convent and made him stay to dine in the refectory. They pricked him a route on a slip of parchment; and the prior gave him a silver guilden to help him on the road, and advised him to join the first honest company he should fall in with, “and not face alone the manifold perils of the way.”

“Perils?” Gerard said to himself, the word echoing in him like a note struck on wood.

That evening he came to a small straggling town where there was one inn. It had no sign; but now, better versed in the country’s customs, he detected it at once by the coats of arms painted on its walls—tokens left by distinguished visitors who had slept there at different epochs since its foundation. At present it looked more like a mausoleum than a house of cheer. Nothing moved nor sounded in it or about it; the silence was so complete it seemed a policy, as if sound itself were taxed.

Gerard hammered on the great oak door. No answer. He hallooed. No reply. After a while he hallooed louder; and at last a little round window—rather a hole in the wall—opened. A man’s head protruded cautiously, like a tortoise from its shell, and eyed Gerard stolidly without a syllable.

“Is this an inn?” Gerard asked, with a covert sneer.

The head appeared to sink into a brown study; at length it nodded, lazily.

“Can I have entertainment here?”

Again the head pondered and ended by nodding, sullenly, like a skull overburdened with catch-penny questions.

“How am I to get within, an’t please you?”

At that the head popped in as if shot; a hand popped out, pointed round the corner of the building, and slammed the window.

Gerard followed, and after some search found the fortification’s one vulnerable point: a small low door on the flank. As for the main entrance, it was used to keep out thieves and customers, except once or twice a year, when they entered together—some duke or count arriving in pomp with his train of gaudy ruffians.

Once within the outer fort, Gerard found his way to the stove—the public room, so called from its principal article—and sat near the oven, where only a few live embers glowed, giving off a mild grateful heat.

He waited long. At last a grim old fellow with a long white beard stalked solemnly in, turned the hour-glass, and stalked out again. Gerard asked him when supper would be.

The grisly Ganymede counted the guests on his fingers. “When I see thrice as many here as now.”

Gerard groaned, the sound wrung from his belly more than his throat.

The old tyrant resented even that. “Inns are not built for one,” he said. “If you can’t wait for the rest, look out for another lodging.”

Gerard sighed and held his tongue, learning that here, too, a man’s needs must be translated into the inn’s rude grammar or not spoken at all.

By degrees company trickled in, until full eighty persons of various conditions crowded the room. To the novice it became a chamber of horrors—not by ghosts, but by what living bodies do when no one expects refinement. Mothers gathered and compared ringworms as openly as if they spoke of ribbons. Men scraped mud off shoes with their knives and left it on the floor, then combed their long hair out—guests and inmates alike—and made their toilet, which was generally a dry rub. Water came in ewers; Gerard pounced on one, but at sight of the liquid lost his temper.

“Wash you first your water,” he said to the waiter, “and then a man may wash his hands withal.”

“An’ it likes you not,” came the answer, “seek another inn!”

Gerard said nothing. Quietly and courteously he asked an old traveller how far it was to the next inn.

“About four leagues.”

Then Gerard understood the grim pleasantry: the inn’s rudeness was guarded by distance, and patience was forced on the legs.

The white-beard returned with an armful of wood, and, counting the travellers, put on a log for every six—so that the hotter the room grew, the more heat he added, by an obstinate arithmetic. Gerard noticed the flaw but carefully suppressed every symptom of intelligence, lest his feet be made to carry his brains four leagues farther that night.

When perspiration and suffocation were well advanced they brought in the table-cloths—brown, dirty, and coarse as sacks worn out in agriculture and come down to this, or as shreds from the mainsail of some worn-out ship. Gerard, who had never seen such linen even in nightmare, uttered a faint cry.

“What is to do?” asked a traveller.

Gerard pointed ruefully to the dirty sackcloth. The other stared with lack-lustre eye and comprehended nought.

A Burgundian soldier, an arbalest on his back, peeped over Gerard’s shoulder. Seeing what ailed him he laughed so loud the room rang, then slapped Gerard on the back.

“Courage! le diable est mort,” he cried.

Gerard stared; he doubted the good tidings and their relevance. Yet the tones were hearty, and the arbalestrier’s face, despite a formidable beard, was so gay and genial that Gerard smiled. After a pause he said drily, “Il a bien faite avec l’eau et linge du pays; on allait le noircir a ne se reconnaitre plus.”

“Tiens, tiens!” the soldier cried. “V’la qui parle le Francais peu s’en faut.” He sat by Gerard and at once began to talk volubly of war, women, and pillage, seasoning his speech with curious oaths at which Gerard drew away from him by degrees, as from a dish over-peppered—tasty to some, but burning to others.

Presently in came the grisly servant again, counted them all on his fingers superciliously like Abraham telling sheep, went out, and returned with a deal trencher and a deal spoon for each.

Denys had the good fortune to clutch at Gerard as he pitched headlong from the bough; yet it was not Denys’s arm that truly broke the fall. Gerard’s brow and shoulders sank into the shaggy bulk of the she-bear, whose last strength was already running out in hot panting. Denys hauled him clear; the brute still shuddered and pawed as if even dying were a kind of malice, then the quiver ceased, the breath went thin, and at last was gone. Denys, practical as ever, set Gerard’s back against the bear’s soft flank like a cushion and fanned him with his cap.

Gerard came round by little and little—bewildered, and then suddenly keenly aware of what had borne him up. Feeling hair against his cheek, he rolled away as if the earth itself were fouled, and let out a yell fit to bring the whole wood upon them.

“Courage,” cried Denys. “Le diable est mort.”

“Is it dead? quite dead?” Gerard called from behind a tree; his courage came in gusts and ebbs, and just then the chill fit had him.

“Behold!” Denys seized the dead beast’s ear and tugged it as if it were a tavern dog; then, to make his triumph complete, he prised open the jaws and thrust his own head between the teeth in a grotesque bravado. At that very instant Gerard’s stomach rose against him; he turned and was violently sick among the leaves.

Denys laughed, as one laughs at a comrade and not an enemy. “What now? And why tumble off thy perch when we had won the day?”

“I swooned, I trow.”

“But why?”

Gerard wiped his mouth with the back of his hand and shuddered. “She sent her nasty blood all over me. I think the smell did it. Faugh! I hate blood.”

“I do believe it potently.”

“See what a mess she has made me!”

“But with her blood, not thine. I pity the enemy that strives to satisfy thee.”

“You need not brag, Maître Denys; I saw you under the tree—the colour of your shirt.”

“Let us distinguish,” Denys answered, colouring in spite of himself. “It is permitted to tremble for a friend.”

For answer Gerard flung his arms round Denys’s neck and held him hard, not speaking.

Denys, blubbering his words to hide that he was touched, grumbled, “Was ever aught so like a woman? I love thee, little milksop—go to. Good! now on thy knees. What new caprice is this?”

“O Denys, ought we not return thanks to Him who saved both our lives against such fearful odds?” Gerard dropped to his knees and began to pray aloud. After a moment he heard the faint rustle of a heavier body settling; Denys was kneeling beside him, hands folded across his breast as his people did, his face drawn long and solemn.

When they rose, Gerard’s eyes shone. “Good Denys, Heaven will reward thy piety.”

“Ah bah! I did it out of politeness,” said Denys. “To please thee, little one. C’est égal; ’twas well and orderly prayed, and edified me while it lasted. A bishop had scarce handled the matter better. So now our evensong being sung, and the saints enlisted—marchons.”

They had scarce taken two steps when Denys halted. “By-the-by—the cub!”

“Oh, no, no!” Gerard cried; the very thought of the living bundle made his skin crawl.

Denys nodded. “Thou art right. It is late. We have lost time climbing trees, tumbling off ’em, swooning, vomiting, praying; and the brute is heavy to carry. And when I think on’t, we shall have papa after it next; these bears make such a coil about an odd cub. What is this? You are wounded! you are wounded!”

“Not I.”

“He is wounded; miserable that I am!”

“Be calm. I am not touched; I feel no pain anywhere.”

“You? you only feel when another is hurt,” Denys burst out, and dropped to his knees in the road. His hands went at Gerard’s leg with swift soldierly certainty, and his eyes glittered with something more than fear. “Quick, quick, before it stiffens!”

“Who makes the coil about nothing now?” Gerard asked, trying to be steady.

Denys did not answer straight. He got Gerard moving, supporting him, and spoke as if confessing to a priest. “Be pleased to note I have a bad heart. You were man enough to save my life, yet I must sneer at you, a novice in war. Was not I a novice once? Then you fainted from a wound, and I thought you swooned for fear, and called you milksop. Briefly, I have a bad tongue and a bad heart.”

“Denys!”

“Plaît-il?”

“You lie.”

“You are very good to say so, little one, and I am eternally obliged,” Denys mumbled, still angry with himself.

But the leg betrayed them. Before many furlongs the muscles drew tight, and each step was a nail driven. Gerard could at last only touch the ground with his toe, and that with a sharpness that turned his breath sour.

“Let me lie down and die,” he groaned. “This is intolerable.”

Denys told him it was afternoon and the nights were frosty; that cold and hunger were ill companions for a man who lay down; and that it would be unreasonable to lose heart, a certain great personage being notoriously defunct. So Gerard leaned on his axe and hobbled on, until, all at once, he gave in and sank helpless in the road.

Denys dragged him a little way into the wood where the undergrowth broke the sight from the path. Then, to Gerard’s astonishment, he thrust the crossbow and bolts into his hands. “Lie quiet. If any ill-looking fellows find thee, bid them keep aloof; if they refuse, shoot them dead at twenty paces. Honest men keep the path; knaves in a wood—none but fools do parley with them.”

With that he snatched up Gerard’s axe and set off at a run—not toward Düsseldorf, but back the way they had come.

Gerard lay with the pain throbbing like a drumbeat in the bone, thinking how Rome, that had looked so near at starting, seemed now a great stretch of world away—though he was two hundred miles nearer it than before. Yet his thoughts would not stay with Rome. They turned of themselves, like a needle, toward Sevenbergen. He saw Margaret’s hand in his—warm, clean, homely—saw her listening with parted lips while he told her what he had gone through for her. The thought soothed him as milk soothes a scalded mouth; and though his nerves were raw, he lay resigned and faintly smiling.

He had lain thus more than two hours when shouts burst suddenly, as if the forest had found a voice. The next instant something struck a tree close by with a hard thud and quivered there.

An arrow.

He struggled up. More missiles hissed and rattled among the boughs; the wood filled with cries—battle-cries—yet the vast trunks and hollows threw the sound about so that he could not tell from what quarter it came. The very air seemed to carry war. Then came a lull, and after it the fierce gallop of hooves; and louder shouting, mixed with shrieks and groans; and above all, strange dreadful noises like claps of thunder, bellowing loud and dying away in cracking echoes. Red tongues of flame stabbed out among the trees; sulphurous smoke drifted over his head, sharp as brimstone in the nose and throat.

Then—silence.

Gerard stood trembling, not knowing whether to pray or run. Awe pressed on him like a weight. “What will become of Denys?” he cried to the empty trunks. “Why did you leave me? O Denys, my friend! my friend!”

Just before sunset Denys returned, staggering under a hairy bundle. When he let it drop, it proved to be the bear’s skin.

Gerard welcomed him with such joy that Denys blinked at it. “I thought never to see you again, dear Denys. Were you in the battle?”

“No. What battle?”

“The bloody battle of men—or fiends—that raged in the wood a while agone.” And Gerard described what he had heard and seen: the arrows, the hooves, the thunder-claps, the flame, the choking smoke.

Denys patted him as one humours a fevered child. “It is well. Thou art a good limner, and fever is a spur to imagination. One day I lay in a cart-shed with a cracked skull, and saw two hosts manoeuvre and fight a good hour on eight feet square, and described it all fair to my comrade—only not so gorgeously as thou, for want of book-learning.”

“What—then you believe me not? when I tell you the arrows whizzed over my head, and the combatants shouted, and—”

“May the foul fiends fly away with me if I believe a word.”

Gerard took Denys’s arm and quietly pointed to the tree.

Denys went close, and his face changed. “Why—it looks like—it is—a broad arrow, as I live!” He stared up at it. “It came out of the battle,” Gerard said. “I heard it and saw it.”

“An English arrow.”

“How know you that?”

“By its length. The English draw to the ear; others to the right breast. So they loose a three-foot shaft, and this is one—perdition seize them!” He spat, half from superstition, half from old soldier’s hate. “Well, if this is not glamour, there has been a trifle of a battle. And if there has been a battle in so ridiculous a place for a battle, ’tis no business of mine; my duke hath no quarrel hereabouts. So let’s to bed.”

He scraped together a heap of leaves and made Gerard lie on it with the axe at his side; then lay down close, one hand on the arbalest, and drew the bear-skin over them, hair inward. The warmth came up at once, thick and animal, like being wrapped in fresh bread from an oven. They slept.

But long before dawn Gerard shook Denys. “What shall I do? I die of famine.”

“Do? why, go to sleep again incontinent: qui dort dîne.”

“I tell you I am too hungry to sleep,” Gerard snapped; pain had sharpened his temper.

“Let us march, then,” Denys said with paternal indulgence. He yawned hugely, then cut a strip of skin and rolled up the bear’s ears in it like a small grim bundle of provisions.

They took the road. Gerard leaned upon his axe and, on the other side, upon Denys; he hobbled with sighs.

“I hate pain,” Gerard said viciously.

“Therein you show judgment,” replied Denys.

The night was clear with stars; and when the moon rose it silvered the last ranks of trees ahead, showing the end of the wood not far off. Beyond lay Düsseldorf, a short league further—civil roofs, a fire, and bread that did not bleed.

At the very edge they came upon something that stopped them cold. Two white pillars rose pale in the moonlight, a few paces apart; between them stood shapes like men—too many, too still.

“I go no farther till I know what this is,” Gerard whispered, his throat tight. “Are they saints’ images set for prayer? or live robbers waiting to shoot down honest travellers? Nay, living men they cannot be, for they stand on nothing. Denys, let us turn back till daybreak; this is no mortal sight.”

Denys peered long and keenly. “They are men,” he said at last.

Gerard shrank the more. “But men that will never hurt us, nor we them,” Denys added. “Look not to their feet—for that they stand on.”

“Where, then, in the name of all saints?”

“Look over their heads.”

Gerard followed the line of Denys’s finger and made out a dark beam crossing from pillar to pillar; then, as they crept nearer, he saw cords—snake-like in the moon—running down from the beam to each slack body, each rope drawn tight as wire.

As they came beneath, a light air stirred. Several corpses swung or slowly turned, and every rope creaked. The sound went through Gerard like cold water down the back. He could not take his eyes away. Death was not silent here; it had a voice of hemp and timber.

So held were they by that sickening sight that they did not at first mark a fire burning under the gallows, and a living man huddled over it. An axe lay beside him; its bright edge shone red in the glow. He slept.

Gerard started; Denys only whispered, “Courage, comrade; here is a fire.”

“Ay—but there is a man at it.”

“There will soon be three.” Denys began calmly to heap on wood the watcher had already gathered, feeding the coals as if they were a kitchen hearth. At that, prudent Gerard slid forward, took the stranger’s axe, and sat down tight upon it, his own laid ready, eyes fixed on the sleeper.

The man wore a country dress and the local hat—a stiff three-cornered Brunswicker with a thick brass band, heavy enough to turn a sword-cut. Its weight had flattened his ears down like a fancy rabbit’s; but they had met scores of such dog-eared rustics. The strangeness was not his clothes. It was his post: why should a clown keep watch under a laden gallows?

Denys would not show curiosity. He drew two bear’s ears from his bundle, ran sticks through them, and held them to the fire. The fat began to hiss faintly; the air filled with a rank, meaty smell—wild, oily, like singed hair and smoked marrow. Denys sniffed as a cook might judge a roast. “’Twill be eating coined money,” he said, “for the burgomaster of Düsseldorf would have given us a rix-dollar for these ears as proof of the bear’s death; but better a lean purse than a lere stomach.”

“Unhappy man!” Gerard cried, glancing up at the creaking bodies. “Could you eat food here?”

“Where the fire is lighted there must the meat roast, and where it roasts there must it be eaten; for nought travels worse than your roasted meat.”

“Well, eat thou, Denys, an thou canst! I am cold and sick; there is no room for hunger in my heart after what mine eyes have seen. Oh, how they creak! And who is this man, I wonder? what an ill-favoured churl!”

Denys studied the sleeper as if judging a face in a painting. “I take him to be of the refuse of that company”—he nodded carelessly upward—“whereof these were the cream; and so ran their heads into danger.”

“At that rate, why not stun him before he wakes?” Gerard fidgeted, gripping his axe.

Denys opened his eyes wide in mock amazement. “For one that sets up for a milksop, you have the readiest hand. Why should two stun one? Tush—he wakes. Note what he says at waking, and tell me.”

The watcher opened his eyes. Seeing the fire built up and two strangers watching him, he stared, and you could see him struggling into calm; yet a tremor ran over him as if the cold ground crept into his bones. He forced out, “Good morrow.” But at that moment he missed his axe and saw Gerard sitting upon it with his own ready. His face fell.

Denys smiled grimly at the little play.

“Good morrow,” Gerard returned, quiet as a drawn knife.

The man could not bear the silence. “You make free with my fire,” he said—then, faltering, “you are welcome.”

Denys whispered; Gerard interpreted: “My comrade says, since we share your fire, you shall share his meat.”

“So be it!” the man answered quickly, brightening with a show of hearty goodwill. “I have half a kid hanging on a bush hard by—I’ll go fetch it.” He rose, turning as if to go.

In the same instant Denys had the crossbow up and levelled at his head. The man dropped on his knees as if the string had jerked him down.

Denys lowered the weapon and, with a mere tilt of his chin, ordered him back. The fellow obeyed, moving in a sick, disjointed way, like a mouse that the cat has let run a little only to tap it down again.

“Sit down, friend,” Denys said in French, the tone doing the work the words could not.

The man sat, though he understood no French.

“Tell him,” Denys murmured, “the fire is not big enough for more than thee. He will take my meaning.”

Gerard conveyed it; the man grinned. Since Denys had spoken, he seemed oddly relieved. “I wist not ye were strangers,” he said to Gerard.

Denys cut a piece of bear’s ear—brown at the edge now, the fat bubbling—and offered it with a courtly little gesture to the same man he had just covered with the bow.

The watcher accepted as calmly as if such hospitality were common. He drew bread from his wallet and broke it, sharing it with them. Then, with a wink that tried to make comradeship of peril, he thrust his hand into the heap of leaves he sat on. Gerard’s fingers tightened on his axe. Out came a great leathern bottle, near two gallons. The man drank first, then offered it to Gerard, who passed it untouched to Denys.

“Mort de ma vie!” Denys cried, drinking. “Rhenish—and fit for an archbishop’s gullet. Here’s to thee, thou prince of good fellows: wishing thee a short life and a merry one! Come, Gerard, sup! Pshaw—never heed them, man! they heed not thee.” He jerked his head upward as if the dead were no more than sacks in a barn. “Natheless, did I hang over such a skin of Rhenish as this, and three churls sat beneath drinking it and offered me not a drop, I’d soon be down among them.”

“Denys! Denys!”

“My spirit would cut the cord, and womp would come my body amongst ye, with a hand on the bottle, and one eye winking, t’other.”

Gerard sprang up with a cry of horror, clapped his hands to his ears, and started to run; then his eye fell on the watcher’s axe and the common sense of danger dragged him back. He sat down again on the axe, hands still pressed to his ears.

“Courage, l’ami, le diable est mort!” Denys shouted gaily, and thrust the roasted bear’s ear under Gerard’s nose. The smell turned Gerard’s stomach; he turned away.

“Wine!” he gasped. “Heaven knows I have need of it, with such companions as thee and—” He took the bottle and drank. The Rhenish went through him like warm copper, glowing in the chest, loosening the knot of fear; yet each gust of wind that set the ropes creaking sent a shiver back through him.

Denys and the watcher, meanwhile, ate and drank as if at a fair. They caroused beneath that creaking sepulchre, as though sound itself—rope on beam, flame on stick, bottle against teeth—were the only music men needed.

“Ask him how they came here,” Denys said at last, mouth full, pointing up without looking.

Gerard asked. The watcher, warmed by drink and by the importance of having listeners, replied that treason had been their end—diabolical treason and priest-craft. Then, in a long, prosy tale, he set forth the matter as he understood it.

Those “honest gentlemen” now dangling had been stout men and true, living in the forest by their wits; their thriving freedom had bred envy in mankind, and many had tried to take their lives and liberties, but the Virgin and their patron saints, with their own courage, had ever baffled such attempts. Yet yestereve, a party of merchants had come from Düsseldorf on mules. The forest-men let them creep near a league into the wood, then fell on them to make them disgorge a portion of their ill-gotten gains. Alas, the merchants were no merchants, but soldiers of more than one nation in the Archbishop of Cologne’s pay, with haubergeons hidden beneath their gowns and weapons ready. Still, the honest men fought stoutly and pressed the traitors hard—when lo, horsemen that had lain in ambush for hours galloped up; and with new diabolical engines of war they shot leaden bullets, laying many a fellow low, and so broke the rest that they yielded. The victors, with malice inconceivable, had brought cords already knotted about their waists and hanged them speedily, even hanging the dead beside the living “to make the gallanter show.”

“And that one at the end,” the watcher went on, using the neck of the bottle like a showman’s pointer, “was the captain. He never felt the cord; he was riddled with broad arrows and leaden balls ere they could take him. A worthy man as ever cried, ‘Stand and deliver!’—but a little hasty. Stay! I forgot; he is dead. Very hasty, and obstinate as a pig. That one in the buff jerkin is the lieutenant, as good a soul as ever lived: he was hanged alive. This one here—I never could abide; no, not that one, that is Conrad, my bosom friend—this one overhead in the chicken-toed shoon: you were always carrying tales, thief, making mischief; you know you were; and I am a man would rather live united in a coppice than in a forest with backbiters and tale-bearers. Strangers, I drink to you.”

So he went down the string, describing each man with a confidence that would have been comical had the creaking not answered him from above. His judgments were pithy—and almost all false; he had no true eye for character, and his words put masks upon the dead as easily as a tavern jester puts on faces. Gerard, listening, felt how words could be made to turn murder into “honesty,” and ambush into “priest-craft”; the same tongue that called theft a trade could make virtue into treason. In that talk he heard, dimly, the power of names—how a man might hang by a rope and also by a word.

“Enough palaver!” Denys broke in. “Marchons! Give me his axe. Now tell him he must help you along.”

The watcher’s face fell. He saw resistance in Denys’s eye and swallowed it. Gerard protested. “Y pensez-vous? To put my hand on a thief, it maketh my flesh creep.”

“Childishness! all trades must live. Besides, I have my reasons. Be not you wiser than your elder.”

“No. Only if I am to lean on him, I must have my hand in my bosom still, grasping the haft of my knife.”

“It is a new attitude to walk in; but please thyself.”

So they went, a strange three—one giving aid, one taking it, and both ready to strike; tenderness and distrust yoked together like ill-matched oxen. The gallows behind them kept creaking a while, then the sound thinned as the night swallowed distance.

When they cleared the wood, the watch-tower light of Düsseldorf showed like a steady star set on earth. It heartened Gerard. After an hour’s march the black outline of the tower and other buildings stood clear, and then their companion halted and said gloomily, “You may as well slay me out of hand as take me nearer the gates of Düsseldorf town.”

Gerard told Denys.

“Let him go then,” Denys said at once; “for in sooth his neck will be in jeopardy if he wends further with us.”

Gerard agreed as a matter of course. His horror of a criminal did not make him eager to hand a man to the rope. In those days a private citizen meddled little with criminals, save in self-defence.

Freed, the man asked for his axe. Denys returned it. To their surprise he lingered, shifting his feet like one bargaining. Was he to have nothing for coming so far?

“Here are two batzen, friend,” said Gerard shortly.

“Add the wine—the good Rhenish?”

“Did you give aught for it?”

“Ay—the peril of my life.”

“Hum! what say you, Denys?”

“I say it was worth its weight in gold.” Denys tossed him silver groshen. “One for every acorn on that gallows tree; and here is one more for thee, who wilt doubtless be there in due season.”

The man took the coins, yet still lingered, awkward now, his greed turning into a sort of shame.

“Well! what now?” Gerard cried. “Dost seek the hide off our bones?”

“Nay, good sirs. But you have seen to-night how parlous a life is mine. Ye be true men, and your prayers avail. Give me then a small trifle of a prayer, an’t please you; for I know not one.”

Gerard’s choler rose; pain had made him irritable, and the rogue’s self-pity soured him. Yet he bit his lip and asked, “Is it true what men say of you Rhenish thieves, that ye do murder innocent and unresisting travellers as well as rob them?”

The man answered sullenly, “They you call thieves are not to blame for that; the fault lies with the law.”

“Gramercy! so ’tis the law’s fault that ill men break it?”

“I mean not so,” the other said, “but the law in this land slays an honest man an if he do but steal. What follows? He would be pitiful, but is discouraged. Pity gains him no pity, and doubles his peril. An he but cut a purse his life is forfeit; therefore cutteth he the throat to boot, to save his own neck: dead men tell no tales. Pray then for the poor soul who by bloody laws is driven to kill or else be slaughtered. Were there less of this unreasonable gibbeting on the highroad, there should be less enforced cutting of throats in dark woods, my masters.”

“Fewer words had served,” Gerard replied coldly. “I asked; I am answered.” And, doffing his bonnet suddenly, he spoke his “prayer” in a clear Latin that rang strangely in the night air, like church-speech thrown into the face of the road:

“Obsecro Deum omnipotentem, ut, qua cruce jam pendent isti quindecim latrones fures et homicidae, in ea homicida fur et latro tu pependeris quam citissime, pro publica salute, in honorem justi Dei cui sit gloria, in aeternum, Amen.”

“And so good day.”

The outlaw blinked, then nodded, satisfied. “That is Latin,” he muttered. “More than I bargained for.”

He turned away at last, back into his perilous life, with his mind oddly at ease—as if the very sound of an unknown tongue could serve him for comfort, though he knew not what it had asked.

Denys and Gerard went on in silence, each chewing his own thoughts as men chew tough bread. The creak of ropes was gone now; only their steps, and far off the calm human sounds of a town waking—faint clinks, a dog’s bark, the low stir of morning.

At last Gerard said, thoughtfully, “That she-bear saved both our lives—by God’s will.”

The next afternoon brought a thin, grey light, and with it a Gerard altered. The swimming in his head was gone; in its place came a fretful heat, as if his very thoughts had been salted and left too long by the fire. He lay picking at the linen, inventing miseries out of shadows, until in one of those restless fancies he fixed upon a single desire.

“Denys,” he whispered, swallowing with pain, “get me a lemon. I would suck it. My mouth is ashes.”

Denys—who had marched through camps hard as iron, and yet, by some quiet miracle of companionship, had turned tender as an old grandsire over this sick youth—started up at once.

“A lemon? Thou shalt have lemons in the twinkling of a quart-pot,” he said, as if he were calling for salt in a kitchen, not a fruit in a northern town. “Set thy mind at ease.”

He was out, boot-heels fading down the stair.

Lemons, however, were no common thing there: not like onions that hang in every market, or cabbages you could smell before you saw. Those sharp golden suns came by long road and longer sea, and changed hands like relics. Denys was gone so long that Gerard’s thirst grew spiteful; he listened to every footfall as if it were water being poured, and each time it passed his door he clenched the sheet.

At last the latch gave softly.

Gerard lifted his head, ready to snap at Denys for delay—and saw, not Denys at all, but an old man who entered as solemnly as if he came with the Host.

He wore a long sober gown, yet trimmed richly with fur at the edges; cherry-coloured hose and pointed shoes; a sword hung at his side in a morocco sheath. About his neck rose a ruff starched into cruel furrows, stiffened by hidden wood so that it held his head like a yoke. Above a majestic white beard sat a four-cornered cap bordered in fur. Behind him followed a boy with a basket carried in both hands; and the basket was a little portable apothecary—phials that caught what light there was, rolls of lint, instruments of iron that glimmered like fish-bones.

The old gentleman drew near, and, leaning to the bed with a practiced softness of step and voice, said under his breath, “How is’t with thee, my son?”

Gerard, schooled to gratitude even when peevish, answered, “My wound pains me little now, sir; but my throat is parched, and my head lies heavy.”

“A wound! They told me not of that. Let me see.” The doctor’s fingers went at once, deft and curious. “Ay, ay—a good clean bite. The mastiff had sound teeth that took this out, I warrant me.” And in his tone there was almost a fond respect, as if the brute’s jaw were the true artist and he but the interpreter.

“This must be cauterized forthwith,” he continued briskly, “or we shall have thee starting back from water and turning somersaults in bed under our hands. ’Tis the year for raving curs, and one hath done thy business; but we will baffle him yet. Urchin—go heat thine iron.”

“But, sir,” Gerard put in, with that weary politeness sick men use when they are being hurried, “’twas no dog, but a bear.”

“A bear!” The physician drew himself up, offended, as if a patient had contradicted a Gospel. “Young man, think what thou sayest. ’Tis ill jesting with the man of art who brings his grey hairs and long study to heal thee. A bear, quotha! Hadst thou dissected as many bears as I, or the tithe, and drawn their teeth to keep thine hand in, thou wouldst know no bear’s jaw ever made this foolish trifling wound. I tell thee ’twas a dog—nay, since thou puttest me to it, I deny ’twas even a dog of magnitude; it was one of these little furious curs that run devious, biting each manly leg and laying its wearer low—but for me and my learned brethren, who stay the mischief with knife and cautery.”

“Alas, sir,” said Gerard, trying not to lose patience, “when said I ’twas a bear’s jaw? I said, ‘a bear’: it was his paw.”

“And why didst not tell me that at once?”

“Because you kept telling me instead,” Gerard murmured—then bit his tongue for having spoken at all.

“Never conceal aught from thy leech, young man,” the doctor went on, as if he had not heard him. He was a torrent in a narrow channel: swift, loud, and heedless of stones. “This is ill business. All horny excrescences of animals—to wit, claws of tigers, panthers, badgers, cats, bears, and the like, and horn of deer, and nails of humans, especially children—are imbued with direst poison. Thou hadst better have been bitten by a cur than scratched by bear. Yet we will do what may be done. A good biting cataplasm for thy leg; meantime keep we the body cool. Put out thy tongue—good—fever. Pulse—good—fever. I ordain flebotomy, and on the instant.”

“Flebotomy?” Gerard repeated, and the word tasted sour in his mouth, like wine gone to vinegar. “That is bloodletting. Humph. Well—if it be sure to cure, for I will not lie idle here.”

The physician assured him, with the confidence of a man who has never doubted himself long enough to learn fear, that it was infallible—especially in this case.

“Hans,” he said to the boy, “go fetch the things needful, and I will entertain the patient meantime with reasons.”

And now the old man began to lecture as if Gerard’s sickbed were a chair of medicine, and the room a disputation hall. He spoke of blood as of stew set too close to the coals: it grew hot, distempered, more or less poisonous; draw off a portion of the corrupted broth, and Nature would be forced to make a fresher pot. Bleeding cooled and purified, and so was a specific in all diseases, “for all diseases are febrile, whatever empirics may say.”

“But think not,” he added, warming to his own voice, “that it suffices to bleed; any paltry barber can open a vein—though not all can close it again. The art is to know what vein to empty for what disease. T’other day they brought me one tormented with earache. I let him blood in the right thigh, and away flew his earache. By-the-by, he hath died since then. Another came with toothache. I bled him behind the ear and relieved him in a jiffy. He is also since dead, as it happens. I bled our bailiff between thumb and forefinger for rheumatism. Presently he comes with a headache and drumming in the ears and holds out his hand over the basin; but I smiled at his folly and bled him in the left ankle sore against his will, and made his head as light as a nut.”

Gerard lay and listened as one listens to church bells when fevered: the sound is beautiful and tormenting, each peal striking not only the air but the bone. Beyond the window the town had its own music—the scrape of carts, the holler of children, a hammer on metal—yet inside the chamber the doctor’s voice ruled everything, booming and clacking, drowning even the faint swallow of Gerard’s parched throat.

Then, like a cook who cannot name a sauce without reciting all the kitchens of Christendom, the physician diverged into schools and authorities. Arabia and Greece marched through the room in his phrases; Avicenna and Rhazes stood and bowed; Hippocrates entered with bandages; Aristotle named the aorta as if he had kneaded it out of dough. The doctor’s words were thick with learned titles—rich, heavy, difficult to digest—like meat overspiced to hide its age.

“Surely, sir,” Gerard ventured at last, in humble pain, “the Almighty gave us all that is in our bodies, and not Aristotle, nor any Grecian man.”

“Child!” snapped the physician. “Of course He gave us the thing; but Aristotle did more—he gave us the name. Comprehension is your only true possession. Are you answered?”

“I am put to silence, sir.”

“And that is better still; for garrulous patients are ill to cure—especially in fever.” His voice swelled again into the litany of anatomists, nerves, vessels, pia mater, milk-veins—until the room seemed packed with invisible parts being discovered and christened by men long dead.

Hans returned with a basin and other gear; another boy—or perhaps the same, moving with quick practiced hands—had a little chafer, and blew it so that coals glowed red as pomegranate seeds. The air took on that faint choking smell of heated iron and smouldering cloth: a smell that makes the skin remember pain before it arrives.

It was in this posture—Gerard’s ankle half-bared, the basin ready, the coals brightening—that Denys came back at last with lemons, their skins dimpled, pale-gold, and fragrant as a southern memory. He paused in the doorway, startled by the tableau.

“What sport is toward?” he asked, brows lifted.

Gerard coloured and said, trying to make it small, “The learned doctor is going to flebotomize me and cauterize me; that is all.”

“Ay, indeed,” said Denys, looking from basin to chafer. “And yon imp, what bloweth he hot coals for?”

“What should it be for,” the doctor answered Gerard, not Denys, “but to cauterize the vein when opened and the poisonous blood let free? ’Tis the only safe way. Avicenna indeed recommends a ligature, but how it is to be done he saith not, nor knew he himself, nor any of the spawn of Ishmael. For me, I have no faith in tricksy expedients; and take this for a safe principle: whatever an Arab or Arabist says is right, must be wrong.”

“Oh, I see now,” said Denys, and his voice sharpened like a knife on a stone. “And art thou so simple as to let him put hot iron to thy living flesh? Didst ever keep thy little finger but ten moments in a candle? And this will be as many minutes. Art not content to burn in purgatory after thy death? Must thou buy a foretaste on’t here?”

“I never thought of that,” Gerard said gravely, because he had indeed been lulled by syllables. “The good doctor spake not of burning, but of cautery. To be sure ’tis all one—but cautery sounds not so fearful as burning.”

“Imbecile!” Denys broke out. “That is their art: to confound a plain man with dark words, till his hissing flesh tells him their meaning. Now listen to what I have seen.” And he launched into the bitter witness of battlefields: how leeches bleed men already bleeding; how weakness follows fever, and the poor wounded needs every drop; how veterans die under lancet and fire, while those far from chirurgeons live by chance and frost and ignorance. His voice rose and filled the chamber; each sentence struck the air like the crack of a whip.

The physician, deaf to anything but opposition, roared back, calling Denys a brute whose trade was killing not curing, and cursed the meddling of unlearned men. Denys answered with mock courtesy, naming himself a man of blood indeed, but claiming the doctor spilt more lives with a bodkin than soldiers with swords. The doctor thundered that a sickroom was no place for jesting; Denys retorted it was no place for bawling.

Gerard’s head throbbed with the noise; each shout was a hammer on his temples. He had lived among chants and choir-like calm; he knew what sound could do to a soul. Here was a kind of noise that did not merely offend the ear—it undid the mind, took hold of the nerves and shook them, as a rough hand shakes a bell to make it clang too loud.

When the physician began boasting of Montpellier—of dririmancy, scatomancy, anatomy—and how authorities “winked,” and how twice a year a living condemned criminal was sent for science to “deal with as science asks,” Denys bellowed blasphemies in disgust. Gerard actually squeaked, clapped fingers to his ears, then—suddenly stung past endurance—dragged them away and shouted, with a fury that surprised even him:

“You great roaring, blaspheming bull of Basan, hold your noisy tongue!”

Denys fell contrite at once, but the doctor flowed on, grandly, describing inoculations and watched diseases—words that made suffering into a lesson, as if men were pigs to be fattened and opened for knowledge.

The wrangling swelled again, and with it the threat of steel: Denys, pale now, folded his arms and said coldly that if the physician pricked Gerard, his sword-hilt would knock against the man’s ribs.

Gerard, exhausted by their clamor, lifted a hand.

“Now,” he said, very quietly, “as all this is about me, give me leave to say a word.”

The stillness that fell was immediate; even the coals seemed to hush, though they continued to glow. Gerard spoke with a gentleness that shamed the room.

“I doubt not you both mean me well; but you assassinate me between you. Calmness and quiet are everything to me; but you are like two dogs growling over a bone. And in sooth, bone I should be, did this uproar last long.

“First, venerable sir, I thank you for coming to see me, whether from humanity or in the way of honest gain; all trades must live.

“Your learning seems great, to me at least, and your age vouches experience.

“You say you have bled many, and of these many, many have not died thereafter, but lived and done well. I must needs believe you.”

The physician bowed; Denys made a sound between scorn and impatience.

“Others, you say, you have bled—and they are dead. I must needs believe you.

“Denys knows few things compared with you, but he knows them well. He is not given to conjecture; this I myself have noted. He says he has seen the fevered and blooded for the most part die; the fevered and not blooded live. I must needs believe him.

“Here, then, all is doubt.

“But thus much is certain: if I be bled, I must pay you a fee, and be burnt and excruciated with a hot iron, who am no felon.

“Pay a certain price in money and anguish for a doubtful remedy—that will I never.

“Next to money and ease, peace and quiet are certain goods, above all in a sick-room; but ’twould seem men cannot argue medicine without heat and raised voices. Therefore, sir, I will essay a little sleep; and Denys will go forth and gaze on the females of the place; and I will keep you no longer from those who can afford to lay out blood and money in flebotomy and cautery.”

The physician’s face, which had held itself in dignified patience, reddened and tightened. He drew himself up as if to leave with lofty silence—the only dignity left him—turned, and strode to the door with Hans and the basket at his heels.

At the threshold his anger choked him; he swelled, burst, and whirled back, mouth open. Hans and the basket had to dodge like ducklings before a cart.

“Ah! You reject my skill, you scorn my art. My revenge shall be to leave you to yourself. Lost idiot, take your last look at me—and at the sun. Your blood be on your head!”

He stamped away—then at the door turned again, rage dragging him as a hook drags a fish.

“In twelve hours at furthest,” he cried, “you will be in the secondary stage of fever. Your head will split. Your carotids will thump. Aha! And let but a pin fall, you will jump to the ceiling. Then send for me—and I’ll not come!”

Again he went—again he returned, fury gathering like wind that cannot find an outlet.

“Next will come—CRAMPS of the STOMACH. Aha!

“Then—BILIOUS VOMIT. Aha!

“Then—COLD SWEAT, and DEADLY STUPOR.

“Then—CONFUSION OF ALL THE SENSES.

“Then—BLOODY VOMIT.

“And after that nothing can save you—not even I; and if I could I would not—and so farewell!”

Even Denys, who had faced cannon, changed colour at so precise a curse. Gerard’s eyes, however, lit with a kind of desperate rage—not at the prophecy, but at the noise, the pounding, the assault on his already battered head. He seized his hard bolster as a man seizes a shield.

This motion brought the physician back yet again, as if the sight of resistance was wine to his temper.

“And after that—MADNESS!

“And after that—BLACK VOMIT!

“And then—CONVULSIONS!

“And then—THAT CESSATION OF ALL VITAL FUNCTIONS THE VULGAR CALL ‘DEATH,’ for which thank your own Satanic folly and insolence. Farewell!”

He turned, but could not let the door go without one last barb.

“And think not to be buried in any Christian church-yard; for the bailiff is my good friend, and I shall tell him how and why you died: felo de se! felo de se! Farewell!”

That did it. Gerard sprang to his feet on the bed with a sudden strength, unnatural and fierce, as if the soul itself lent muscle to the body for one instant. His face was white with pain and fury, his hearing raw as flayed skin. The physician, seeing him so moved, came back at him with fist shaking to launch some final thunder.

Gerard hurled the bolster straight into his face.

The old man went down like a felled ox. His falling head struck the boy; the boy’s skull cracked against his master’s mass; and both went crashing into the basket. Phials shattered with bright, sharp noises, and odors burst out—the sour bite of spirits, the bitter sweetness of tinctures, the rank medicinal stink that clings to a leech’s hands. The doctor and boy landed wedged absurdly, like grotesque specimens arranged by size: the smaller flung aside, squatting and howling.

Then the physician’s face changed from anger to horror. He uttered a screech more unearthly than all his threats, and kicked and struggled with astonishing agility for so old a man.

He was sitting on the hot coals.

They had singed the cloth; now they bit into flesh. He writhed but could not free himself from the basket’s grip. The basket rolled sideways with him, and there came a great hiss as spilled compounds met the heat. The sickroom filled with steam and stench—burning wool, scorched skin, sharp alcohol, and the sickly-sweet rot of herbs kept too long.

Gerard’s rage broke at once into humane alarm. He leapt down, ignoring the pull of his wound, and with Denys’s help wrenched off the tight basket—not without struggle, for it clung like a crab. The doctor lay on his face, groaning, his handsomely singed palms and backside slaked a moment too late by his own villainous mixtures. Those same mixtures, spilled and splattered, had painted his sober robe in stains of green and violet and rusty red, gaudier than any jester’s and far less neat.

Gerard and Denys raised him up between them. The physician gasped, half-choked with pain and humiliation, his stiff ruff askew, his beard damp with tears and spilt physic. Gerard, still trembling with the aftershock of noise and fury, tried to soothe him.

“Courage, man,” he said, with a faint, bitter edge the room could not help but hear. “’Tis but cautery—balm of Gilead. Why, you recommended it but now to my comrade here.”

The worthy leech went home with his fingers wrapped and his pride rawer than the skin. To his housekeeper he called it, not a cauterizing, not a salutary application—no; a “bad burn.” Such are the words men keep for their own pain: we sear our neighbour’s flesh with the gravity of science, and cry out like children when the flame licks our own.

His housekeeper—an old hand at kitchens and sickness both—set him down by the hearth where the pot always murmured, and dressed him with one of those village salves that smell of churn and herb-garden: sweet whey thickened with goose-grease, plantain bruised fine on a board, and a pinch of soot from the chimney to “draw.” She warmed the poultice at the edge of the coals until it turned glossy and gave up a faint green breath, then laid it on as gently as she would butter on new bread. He submitted like a lamb to her homely certainty; for here, whatever his temper toward travellers, his sole object was cure.

Meanwhile, with his other hand, he made out his bill for broken phials, and with his tongue—sharp as his lancet when gain was in question—he laid plans to have the strangers clapped in prison. He swore before the magistrate that they, being unknown men and owing him money, meant to slip away at once from the town.

Alas, it was his unlucky day. His sincere desire and honest endeavour to forswear himself were baffled by a circumstance he had never dreamt of, nor indeed believed possible: he had spoken the truth—and in an affidavit.

The officers went to the Silver Lion and found the birds flown. They hurried down to the river; there, on hearing which way the boat had gone, they started up the bank in hot pursuit.

This brief start the friends owed to Denys’s cool eye. He had laughed—laughed till it rang out like a bell over the inn-yard, a peal that would have heartened a dying man—and had flung his watchword to the air thrice; then, in a breath, he sobered, as if some change in the very sounds around them warned him.

“Gerard,” said he, “Dusseldorf is no place for us. That old fellow went off too quiet for such a babbler; and strangers here have short shrift. The bailiff is his friend. In five minutes we shall lie in a dungeon for laying hands on a Dusseldorf dignity. Art strong enough to hobble to the water? It is hard by. Once there, thou hast but to lie down in a boat instead of a bed; and what’s the odds?”

“The odds, Denys? untold—and all in favour of the boat,” cried Gerard, with that sudden heat in him the fever loved to ride. “I pine for Rome; for Rome is my road to Sevenbergen; and then we shall lie in the boat, but on the Rhine—the famous Rhine; the cool, refreshing Rhine. I feel its breezes coming. The very sight will cure a little hop-o’-my-thumb fever like mine. Away! away!”

Denys, seeing his friend thus kindled, paid the landlord in haste, and they made for the river, Gerard limping but eager as if the sound of water already ran in his blood. At the bank they learned, to their dismay, that the public boat had put off half an hour since, and no other would start that day, the afternoon being already advanced. But by dint of asking many questions—questions thrown as one flings grain to call fowl, till folk gathered—and by the bustle of it, they drew out an offer: an old man with two sons would take them in a private boat.

A bystander mocked aloud. “The current is too strong for three oars.”

“Then my comrade and I will help row,” said Gerard, the invalid, whose spirit had forgotten his weakness.

“No need,” said the old man, dry as old bread. “Bless your silly heart—he owns t’other boat.”

A powerful breeze sat right astern as if the river itself were in league with escape. The boatmen stepped a broad sail; it filled with a clap and a long breathing sound, and at the same time they dipped their oars. The Rhine answered in its own language—rush and slap, the creak of rowlocks, the soft hiss along the planks—and all that moving music, so clean and living, seemed to scour the inside of Gerard’s head where the fever had hammered. The town’s noise fell behind; the river’s sound took possession, and with it came that strange easing of the mind that follows when one’s ears are no longer flogged by angry voices and street-clatter, but bathed in a steadier element.

“Art better, lad, for the river breeze?” asked the old man.

“Much better,” said Gerard, drawing in the damp air that smelt of mud and reeds and far-off fires. “But indeed the doctor did me good.”

“The doctor?” the boatman sniffed. “Why, you would none of his cures.”

“No,” said Gerard, colouring, “but I mean—you will say I am nought—but knocking the old fool down—somehow—it soothed me.”

“Amiable dove!” cried Denys. “How thy little character opens more and more every day, like a rosebud. I read thee all wrong at first.”

“Nay, Denys, mistake me not,” said Gerard quickly, anxious even in confession to keep his own measure. “I trust I had borne with his idle threats, though in sooth his voice went through my poor ears; but he was an infidel, or next door to one, and such I have been taught to abhor. Did he not as good as say we owed our inward parts to men with long Greek names, and not to Him whose name is but a syllable, but whose hand is over all the earth? Pagan!”

“So you knocked him down forthwith—like a good Christian.”

“Now, Denys, you will still be jesting. Take not an ill man’s part. Had it been a thunderbolt from Heaven, he had met but his due; yet he took but a sorry bolster from this weak arm.”

“What weak arm?” Denys’s eyes danced. “I have lived among arms, and by Samson’s hairy pow never saw I one more like a catapult. The bolster wrapped round his nose and the two ends kissed behind his head, and his forehead resounded; and had he been Goliath, or Julius Caesar, instead of an old quacksalver, down he had gone. Saint Denys guard me from such feeble opposites as thou! and above all from their weak arms—thou diabolical young hypocrite.”

The Rhine took its bends; at times the wind struck them on the quarter, and the boat would heel and shiver, sail straining with a low thunder in its cloth. Then all aboard shifted to the weather side to trim her—save one small body that weighed nothing in the world’s balances: a child of five years or so, the old man’s grandson and darling, who had slipped aboard at the last instant. He sat where he pleased, little hands on the wet gunwale, his hair blown into his eyes; the river’s breath and the sail’s great sigh seemed to make him more solemn than any chapel.

They went merrily enough, not knowing that a whole posse of constables, with the bailiff’s writ, were striding the east bank after them, and that their pursuers gained as much by the current as the fugitives by the wind.

And now, while the oars rose and fell and the sail boomed, Gerard’s mind, always running ahead of his feet, suddenly took alarm at their direction.

“Oh, Denys,” he cried, almost startled, “this is not your road.”

“I know it,” said Denys quietly. “But what can I do? I cannot leave thee till the fever leaves thee; and it is on thee still—for thou art both red and white by turns; I have watched thee. I must e’en go on to Cologne, I doubt, and then strike across.”

“Thank Heaven,” said Gerard, with sudden joy that had in it, too, a hidden relief. Then, as if to make that detour seem piety and not need, he added eagerly, “’Twere a sin to be so near Cologne and not see it. Oh, man, it is a vast and ancient city such as I have often dreamed of, but ne’er had the good luck to see. Me miserable, by what hard fortune do I come to it now? Well then, Denys,”—and he warmed to his tale, as if words themselves could build the city on the air—“it is old enough to have been founded by a Roman lady in the first century of grace, and sacked by Attila the barbarous, and afterwards sore defaced by the Norman Lothaire. And it has a church for every week in the year, forbye chapels and churches innumerable of convents and nunneries; and above all, the stupendous minster yet unfinished; and therein, but in their own chapel, lie the three kings that brought gifts to our Lord—Melchior gold, and Gaspar frankincense, and Balthazar the black king, he brought myrrh; and over their bones stands the shrine the wonder of the world. It is of ever-shining brass brighter than gold, studded with images fairly wrought, and inlaid with exquisite devices, and brave with colours; and two broad stripes run to and fro, of jewels so great, so rare, each might adorn a crown or ransom its wearer at need; and upon it stand the three kings curiously counterfeited, two in solid silver, richly gilt—these be bareheaded; but he of Aethiop ebony, and beareth a golden crown; and in the midst our blessed Lady, in virgin silver, with Christ in her arms; and at the corners, in golden branches, four goodly waxen tapers do burn night and day. Holy eyes have watched and renewed that light unceasingly for ages, and holy eyes shall watch them in saecula. I tell thee, Denys, the oldest song, the oldest Flemish or German legend, found them burning, and they shall light the earth to its grave.”

Denys listened, half amused, half taken—less by saints than by Gerard’s tongue, which could salt and spice a tale till it became sustenance. The river’s steady chant under Gerard’s speech made it seem as if the Rhine itself were carrying old names forward, lest they die on land.

“And there is Saint Ursel’s church,” Gerard went on, “a British saint’s, where lie her bones and all the other virgins her fellows; eleven thousand were they who died for the faith, being put to the sword by barbarous Moors, on the three-and-twentieth day of October, two hundred and thirty-eight. Their bones are piled in the vaults, and many of their skulls are in the church. Saint Ursel’s is in a thin golden case, and stands on the high altar, but shown to humble Christians only on solemn days.”

“Eleven thousand virgins!” Denys burst out. “What babies German men must have been in days of yore. Well—would all their bones might turn flesh again, and their skulls sweet faces, as we pass through the gates. ’Tis odds but some of them are wearied of their estate by this time.”

“Tush, Denys!” said Gerard, stung. “Why wilt thou, being good, still make thyself seem evil? If thy wishing-cap be on, pray that we may meet the meanest she of all those wise virgins in the next world, and to that end let us reverence their holy dust in this one. And then there is the church of the Maccabees, and the cauldron in which they and their mother Solomona were boiled by a wicked king for refusing to eat swine’s flesh.”

“Oh, peremptory king!” cried Denys. “And pig-headed Maccabees! I had eaten bacon with my pork liever than change places at the fire with my meat.”

“What scurvy words are these? It was their faith.”

“Nay, bridle thy choler,” said Denys, lightly, as if stroking a cat the wrong way on purpose. “Tell me—are there nought but churches in this thy so vaunted city? For I affect rather Sir Knight than Sir Priest.”

“Ay, marry,” said Gerard, glad to display other treasures, “there is an university near a hundred years old; and there is a market-place, no fairer in the world, and at the four sides of it houses great as palaces; and there is a stupendous senate-house all covered with images, and at the head of them stands one of stout Herman Gryn, a soldier like thyself, lad.”

“Ay,” said Denys, pricked at once. “Tell me of him! what feat of arms earned him his niche?”

“A rare one. He slew a lion in fair combat, with nought but his cloak and a short sword. He thrust the cloak in the brute’s mouth, and cut his spine in twain; and there is the man’s effigy and eke the lion’s to prove it. The like was never done but by three more, I ween: Samson was one, and Lysimachus of Macedon another, and Benaiah, a captain of David’s host.”

“Marry! three tall fellows. I would like well to sup with them all to-night.”

“So would not I,” said Gerard drily.

Denys eyed him with a soldier’s wonder. “But tell me—when wast thou in Cologne?”

“Never but in the spirit,” said Gerard. “I prattle with the good monks by the way, and they tell me all the notable things both old and new.”

“Ay, ay, have not I seen your nose under their very cowls?” Denys chuckled. “But when I speak of matters that are out of sight, my words they are small, and the thing it was big; now thy words be as big or bigger than the things. Art a good limner with thy tongue; I have said it. And for a saint—art as ready with hand, or steel, or bolster—as any poor sinner living. And so—shall I tell thee which of all these things thou hast described draws me to Cologne?”

“Ay, Denys.”

“Thou—and thou only; no dead saint, but my living friend and comrade true. ’Tis thou alone draws Denys of Burgundy to Cologne.”

Gerard hung his head, and for a moment the river’s voice seemed louder, as if to cover what could not be put into any dialect without losing its heart.

At that instant the boat’s little world was broken by a new sound: a thin, sudden crying from aft. One of the younger boatmen looked round and snapped, half in jest, half in anger, “What ails little turnip-face now?”

The child—thus christened—had come back from the bow grave as a judge, and burst out wailing without warning. The men fell upon him with questions, some coaxing, some sharp: Had he hurt himself? Had he over-ate? Was he frightened? Cold? Sick? An idiot? To all he made but one answer, the same syllables over and over, such as English pens write “oh! oh! oh!” and French pens “hi! hi! hi!”—as if the very shapes men give to a child’s cry belonged to their own tongues, not his pain.

“Who can tell what ails the peevish brat?” snarled the young boatman at last. Then, shading his eyes, he cried, “Rather look this way and tell me whom be these after!”

The old man and his other son peered to the east bank. Four men were coming along there, walking fast, keeping the boat abreast as the bends allowed. At the sight, the rowers held their stroke a moment and huddled in the stern, whispering, throwing looks first at their passengers, then back at the men on shore.

If they had spent their wits on the turnip-face mystery, they might have done better; but grown minds are often deaf to the meanings of small cries, and quick to the whisper of law and profit.

“If ’tis as I doubt,” muttered one of the sons, “why not give them a squeak for their lives? Let us make for the west bank.”

The old man set his jaw. “What,” said he, “run our heads into trouble for strangers? Are ye mad? Nay—let us rather cross to the east side; still side with the strong arm! That is my rede. What say you, Werter?”

“I say—please yourselves,” returned the other, as one who had learned that a man’s peace lies sometimes in not choosing.

What age and youth could not settle, the wind decided, without malice and without mercy. A squall struck sudden; the sail snapped like a whip, the little vessel heeled over, and the men sprang to windward to save her trim.

Then—horror: in the very boat, from stem to stern, a ditch of water came rushing to leeward, a cold weight that did not belong to wind or wave but to treachery. In the next breath the world turned, and there was no boat as a sheltering thing—only the Rhine, the cold and rushing Rhine, closing over heads and words alike.

Turnip-face had drawn the plug.

Gerard, flung out, felt the river take him like a giant hand. Though he could swim like a duck, yet the best swimmer, pitched from a capsized boat, must sink ere he can strike. The dark water bubbled loudly over his head; it filled his ears so that for an instant he was blind and deaf, as if all sound and sight had been kneaded into one blackness. Then he broke up again, choking, the air tasting of wet wood and river-mud; he saw the black boat-bottom uppermost, and figures clinging to it like beetles to bark.

He shook his head like a water-dog and made for it, driven by mere instinct. But before he reached it he heard behind him—not loud, but deep with manly distress, as if the river had stolen half the breath from the speaker—“Adieu, comrade, adieu!”

He turned, and there was poor Denys sinking, sinking, dragged down by his wretched arbalest. His face was gone pale as whey; his eyes stared wide, fastened on Gerard with a despair that no jests could sweeten.

Gerard gave a wild cry—love and terror together—and struck out toward him, cleaving the water madly. The next moment Denys went under. The next, Gerard plunged after him.

On the bank the officers, coming up, unwound cords from their waists; one knotted a rope in haste, and flung the end out over the rushing, clamorous Rhine.

Good and ill will keep their own tally, as if God Himself weighed them in His hand.

The steel bow lashed across the arbalestier’s back had dragged him down; yet that same burden, perched above his shoulders, offered Gerard a purchase like a handle on a drowning man’s coffin-lid. Gerard’s fingers closed on the cold curve of it; his other hand thrust in between bow and cord—anything to keep Denys from slipping away into the Rhine’s blind green pull.

The next instant Denys, hoisted by that very crossbow, came up with a gulping jerk, half his body bobbing out of the water.

“Now, grip me not! grip me not!” Gerard cried, white with the terror of the one mistake that kills—the drowning man’s clutch.

“Pas si bête,” Denys gurgled back; and hearing sense in the wet voice, Gerard’s panic steadied into command.

“On thy back,” he ordered sharply. He seized the arbalest, struck forward, and forced Denys into the right posture. “Hand on my shoulder! Slap the water with the other. No—downward; so. Do nothing more than I bid thee.”

He got hold of Denys’s long hair—streaming like river-weed—twisted it hard, and caught the end between his side teeth. With the stout muscles of his young neck he held Denys’s head up, while his arms and legs worked in a dogged rhythm against the current.

For a heartbeat he hung between two banks, ignorant of the dreadful weight of so small a choice; then, seeing the west side a shade nearer, he made for it—turning, without knowing it, from prison as a man turns from a road that would have changed his whole tale.

The Rhine swept them slantwise. After near a hundred yards Denys muttered uneasily, “How much more of it?”

“Courage,” Gerard mumbled round the hair between his teeth. “Whatever a duck knows, a Dutchman knows; art safe as in bed.”
