And then, to their astonishment, their feet scraped gravel. The water slackened; their knees emerged; they waded ashore, dripping, choking, blinking like men hauled back into the world.

On terra firma they stared at one another from head to foot, as if their eyes could eat the sight and be satisfied. Then, by one impulse, they flung an arm round each other’s neck and panted there, hearts too full for speech.

In that raw moment, with river-water running down their sleeves and the air tasting of silt and reeds, life was sweet as heaven; sweetest, perhaps, to the poor exile with love in his breast, who had dragged his friend from death. There are joys no poet can climb to: to save a human life—and that life a loved one.

When at last they could breathe like men again, they took hands and walked along the bank hand in hand, like a pair of simple sweethearts, scarcely knowing or caring whither their feet carried them.

Out on the Rhine, the boat folk were all safe on the late concave, now convex craft—Herr Turnip-face, the Inverter of Things, sitting in the midst of the muddle as if the world had only performed a trick for his diversion. The whole uproar seemed not to have discomposed his habits: he had been greeting when he shot the two into the river, and he was greeting still when they crawled out again.

“Shall we wait till they right the boat?” asked Denys.

“No,” said Gerard. “Our fare is paid; we owe them nought. Let us on—and briskly.”

Denys agreed; it was easy enough, he said, to walk all the way to Cologne on this bank.

“I fare not to Cologne,” Gerard answered, very calmly.

“Why, whither then?”

“To Burgundy.”

“To Burgundy? Ah, no! that is too good to be sooth.”

“Sooth ’tis, and sense into the bargain. What matters it to me how I go to Rome?”

“Nay, nay; you but say so to pleasure me. The change is too sudden; and think me not so ill-hearted as take you at your word. Also did I not see your eyes sparkle at the wonders of Cologne?—the churches, the images, the relics—”

“How dull art thou, Denys; that was when we were to enjoy them together. Churches! I shall see plenty, go Rome-ward how I will. The bones of saints and martyrs—alas, the world is full of them; but a friend like thee, where on earth’s face shall I find another? No, I will not turn thee farther from the road that leads to thy dear home—and her that pines for thee. Neither will I rob myself of thee by leaving thee. Since I drew thee out of Rhine I love thee better than I did. Thou art my pearl: I fished thee; and must keep thee. So gainsay me not, or thou wilt bring back my fever; but cry courage, and lead on; and hey for Burgundy!”

Denys gave a joyful caper, as if the wet on his boots were a badge and not a discomfort. “Courage! va pour la Bourgogne. Oh! soyes tranquille! cette fois il est bien décidément mort, ce coquin-là.”

So they turned their backs on the Rhine.

But as the meaning of that turn made itself plain, there was commotion among the little group that had watched their parley from the far side. The friends had not gone many steps when a voice came over the water, sharp as a thrown stone.

“HALT!”

Gerard turned. One of the four held up a badge of office and a slip of parchment. The sight struck him in the pit like hunger: he was a good citizen by breeding and habit, and the voice that now called him back towards Düsseldorf was the Law’s.

Denys did not share the scruple. He was French; and he despised every other nation’s laws, inmates, and customs together. He was a soldier; he saw the situation as he would a field: force on the far bank, a river between, the rear open—retreat made easy. The boat still drifted mid-stream, and there was no ferry nearer than Düsseldorf.

“I shall beat a quick retreat to that hill,” he said, “and then, being out of sight, quick step.”

They sauntered off, as if their feet were ruled by leisure.

“Halt! in the bailiff’s name,” cried a voice from the shore.

Denys turned and snapped his fingers at the bailiff, and went on.

“Halt! in the archbishop’s name.”

Denys snapped his fingers at his grace, and went on.

“Halt! in the emperor’s name.”

Denys snapped his fingers at his majesty, and went on.

Gerard watched this needless pantomime with regret; but when they had passed the brow of the hill and were hidden from the river, he said, “There is now but one course: we must run to Burgundy instead of walking,” and set off at such a pace that the road itself seemed to fly under him. He ran the best part of a league without stopping.

Denys, for all his hardihood, was fairly blown. “What on earth,” he panted, “has become of thy fever? I begin to miss it sadly.”

“I dropped it in Rhine, I trow,” Gerard answered.

Towards evening they came to a little village. Denys went in and came out with a loaf under his arm and a huge bottle of Rhenish wine—green glass sweating in the cool air.

“For,” said he, “we must sleep in some hole or corner. If we lie at an inn, we shall be taken in our beds.”

It was plain prudence. In that age the official net for catching law-breakers—especially plebeian ones—was drawn tight indeed. The people might care little to help the law, but innkeepers were watched and questioned, and held answerable for strangers’ comings and goings far more than for their comfort.

Both were glad when the sun went down; and delighted when, after a long trudge under the stars (the moon, if one keeps true account, not rising until about three), they found a great barn belonging to a house some distance off.

A heap of barley had been lately threshed. On one side of the threshing-floor the straw lay piled almost as high as the unthreshed corn on the other. The barn held the day’s work in its smell—broken stalk, dry chaff, the faint sweetness of grain bruised under the flail, and that clean, warm breath straw gives off when you bury your hands in it.

“Here be two royal beds,” said Denys. “Which shall we lie on—the mow, or the straw?”

“The straw for me,” said Gerard at once.

They sat on the heap and ate their brown bread, coarse but honest, with that faint sourness of rye and the grit of bran that makes a hungry mouth rejoice. Denys uncorked the Rhenish; it came out with a small sigh, and the wine ran pale into their throats—sharp as apples, smelling of river hillsides and last year’s sun. It warmed them as if the Rhine itself, so murderous a moment ago, had been pressed into kindness and bottled for their need.

When they had finished, Denys covered Gerard in straw and heaped it high above him, leaving only a breathing hole.

“Water, they say, is death to fevered men,” Denys muttered, settling the straw with the care of an old campaigner arranging a bivouac. “I’ll make warm water on’t, anyhow.”

Gerard bade him easy. “These few drops from Rhine cannot chill me. I feel heat enough in my body now to parch a kennel—or boil a cloud if I was in one.”

With that little jest his senses slid away as if the straw had been a pillow of poppy; he might truly be said to fall asleep.

Denys lay awake awhile, listening. The barn creaked softly as it cooled; somewhere a night bird measured the dark with a thin call. Then there came a sound that changed the air—horses’ hoofs ringing up from Düsseldorf, the hard drumming of pursuit. The wooden barn vibrated as they rattled past, and with them rose the howling—one of those fierce cries men used to fling into the night in the fifteenth century, understood then as plainly as a trumpet-call, but now as strange in Europe as a red Indian’s war-whoop.

Denys shook where he lay. Gerard slept like a top.

The troop swept by; the hoof-beats dwindled; the howls died into distance. Denys drew a long breath, whistled in a whisper, and at last closed his eyes and slept like a top too.

In the morning he sat up and put out his hand to wake Gerard. His palm lit on the young man’s forehead—and found it quite wet. Denys, in his quality of nurse, forbore.

“It is ill to check sleep or sweat in a sick man,” he said softly to himself. “I know that far, though I ne’er minced ape nor gallows-bird.”

He waited a good hour, gnawed by hunger. At last, in sheer self-defence, he turned and went to sleep again; poor fellow, his hard life had taught him that trick—when there is nothing to eat, let sleep do the feeding.

At high noon he was waked by Gerard moving. Gerard sat up, and the straw about him smoked faintly, as a damp dung-hill smokes when the sun strikes it—animal heat wrestling with moisture.

“Lazy loon,” Gerard called Denys.

Denys only grinned, unoffended.

They set out again; and the first thing Denys did was give Gerard his arbalest and gear, then climb a high tree by the road. From that perch he listened and watched like a man reading a landscape as if it were a map.

“Coast clear to the next village,” he said, dropping down; and on they went.

As they drew near the village Denys halted and eyed Gerard. “How feelest thou?”

“What! can you not see? I feel as if Rome was no further than yon hamlet.”

“But thy body, lad—thy skin?”

“Neither hot nor cold; and yesterday ’twas hot one while and cold another. But what I cannot get rid of is this tiresome leg.”

“Le grand malheur! Many of my comrades have found no such difficulty.”

“Ah! there it goes again—itches consumedly.”

“Unhappy youth,” said Denys, with solemn relish in the pronouncement, “the sum of thy troubles is this: thy fever is gone, and thy wound is—healing. Sith so it is,” he added indulgently, “I shall tell thee a little piece of news I had otherwise withheld.”

“What is’t?” Gerard asked, his eyes bright with sudden fear and curiosity.

“THE HUE AND CRY IS OUT AFTER US: AND ON FLEET HORSES.”

“Oh!”

Gerard reeled as if a hand had struck him behind the ear. The message—so sudden, so plain—drove the blood up into his face and then drained it again, leaving him white and hot by turns. His jaw set; his whole body took the posture of a man who has been hunted too near, too long, till fear itself curdles into anger and he would rather turn and gore than be driven another step.

Then, as swiftly, the heat sank out of him. His shoulders dropped with a sort of miserable childishness, and he said, not to Denys only but to the wet night and the hard earth, “And my axe is in Rhine.”

It was as if he had confessed he had left his right hand behind.

They stood close, heads together, the wind worrying at their cloaks and making a thin, fretful music in the hedges. Prudence spoke first—Prudence that sees a village as a net and every lighted window as an eye. “Avoid it,” said that cautious voice within them. Hunger answered with the belly’s blunt logic: “Buy food.”

Hunger spoke loudest. Prudence argued best.

So they took the third counsel, old as flight itself: not to go through the mouth of danger, but round it, and feed like field-mice while they ran. They struck away from the road, sliding over clods and through wet grass that hissed underfoot. A haystack loomed, darker than the dark, breathing out the warm, sweet smell of summer stored—sun caught and dried, with the faint sharpness of last year’s weeds. They did not so much steal as borrow from it, for men on the road make compacts with the dead generosity of harvest. Two bundles came away with them, prickling their fingers, shedding seeds that clung to their sleeves like small memories.

In a ditch—dry at the bottom though nettles licked the sides—they laid the hay as a poor man’s bed. It crackled softly, a domestic sound, like bedding shaken in a cottage loft, and for a moment that sound did more to steady them than any prayer: the world still knew the old language of comfort, even here. But the nettles were fluent too, and wrote their stinging script along wrist and neck.

By turns they slipped out, low as foxes, and came back with turnips pulled from the field. The bulbs were cold with earth; their skins carried the scent of clay and rain, and when they broke them with their teeth the juice was harsh, peppery, almost bitter—no cook’s dish, no hearth’s kindness, only raw sustenance bitten straight from the ground. Yet even that had its honest flavor: the field speaking in root and fibre, in the old peasant tongue that needs no interpreter. They munched at intervals, sharing without ceremony, chewing slowly to make the most of what little sweetness there was, and listening between bites for any footstep, any call, any dog’s bark that might translate into pursuit.

At sunset the light bled away; the sky shut like a lid. They crept out again, shivering into rain and darkness, and found the road on the farther side of the village. The storm had made a world without edges. The wind drove in gusts that roared and then fell away into a sullen moan; the rain rattled on leaves and whispered over mud. It was so black they could neither see nor, for long moments together, truly hear—only feel the night’s great pressure, as if they were pushing through a slab of black marble. In such weather, men are half-blind and half-deaf, and that dulled sense was a shield: they could not be seen, and their own tread was swallowed. For aught they knew they might have passed close to those they feared—close enough for a man’s breath to mingle with another’s—yet the tempest made all living things ghosts to one another.

They had almost forgotten their pursuers in the presence of the natural terror itself: not the clamor of men, but the huge indifferent noise of sky and water. And still they trudged, one foot after another, the road sucking at their soles, their cloaks heavy, the raw turnip taste lingering like penance.

When the moon rose, it did not bring warmth, only a pale witness. It found them many leagues from Düsseldorf, trudging still, bent into the wind, their shadows broken in the puddles.

At last a vast building bulked up out of the wet night, the stones shining dully where the moon caught them. Denys drew breath as if he had smelled bread. “Courage!” he cried, and his voice rang strangely clear against the wall, a human sound in all that weather. “I think I know this convent. Aye—it is. We are in the see of Juliers. Cologne has no power here.”

And with that one piece of knowledge—place-names like charms, jurisdictions like borders drawn in air—they went in at the gate, and the wind’s howl fell behind them as if a door had been shut on it.

The next moment they were safe within the walls.

Gerard had no sooner crossed the threshold of that house than he felt the place speak to him in two tongues at once: the low, continuous Latin of rule and ritual, and the bright, vernacular chatter of tools and timbers—pegs tapped home, a plane singing on oak, a wheel murmuring where water took its turn. The cloister had its own music, not merely in the choir, but in the whole ordered soundscape of living: footsteps softened by worn stone, the dry rustle of a friar’s sleeve as he passed, the far-off cough of a kitchen fire settling into embers. After the road’s coarse din—shouting, tramping, the sudden clang of danger—this was a meadow of sound to rest the mind in.

It was here he made acquaintance with an old monk who was never without some contrivance in hand. The prior’s garden, they told him, bore witness: a great dial that could catch the sun and tell the hours as soberly as any bell; a wheel for drawing water, obedient as a beast; a machine to winnow grain, so that the chaff fled and the good kernels stayed. The man had fashioned psalteries too—several—and two dulcimers; and now he was at work on regalles, a little organ for the choir, its wooden pipes laid out like clean bones waiting for breath.

Gerard, who could play a humble psaltery a little, came forward with the pleased modesty of one who has a craft and meets another craftsman. But the monk touched the instrument as if he were not plucking strings so much as loosening prayer from them; and in a few moments Gerard’s pride in his small skill was turned, not to shame, but to that wholesome wonder which makes youth eager to learn. In return, Gerard’s penmanship—clear, patient, and beautiful—shone beside the monk’s, for the old man illuminated finely, yet his hand in letters could not match Gerard’s steady elegance. Comparing their acquirements with the earnestness and simplicity of an age when “accomplishments” were not ornaments but true bends of nature, the two were soon like brothers: Youth leaning toward Age, and Age warming to Youth as to a late-found son.

So the monk pressed Gerard hard to stay the night.

Gerard consulted Denys. Denys assented with a rueful shrug, as one who had grown used to choosing between hardships and mercies and taking either with the same stiff neck. Then, in the monk’s cell—where the smell was of clean wood, beeswax, and the faint sour sweetness of leather stops—Gerard told his old new friend whither he was bound, and of their late adventures, softening down the bolster, as was his wont.

“Alack!” said the good old man. “I have been a great traveller in my day, but none molested me.”

He shook his head and began to give counsel with that affectionate authority monasteries breed.

“Avoid inns,” said he. “They are ever haunted by rogues and roysterers; and though thy body should escape, thy soul may take harm by what it hears and sees. Shape each day’s journey so thou mayst lie at some peaceful monastery.”

Then he broke off, and his keen eyes—sharp as a needle—ran Gerard through.

“How long since thou wast shriven?”

Gerard coloured. “Better than a fortnight,” he said, but feebly.

“And thou an exorcist!” cried the monk. “No wonder perils have overtaken thee. Come—thou must be assoiled out of hand.”

“Yes, father,” said Gerard, with all his heart; and he began to sink to his knees, hands joined.

But the monk stopped him, half fretful, half troubled.

“Not to me! not to me! not to me!” he cried. “I am as full of the world as thou, or any that lives in’t. My whole soul is in these wooden pipes and sorry leathern stops, which shall perish—with them whose minds are fixed on such like vanities.”

“Dear father,” said Gerard, honest and eager, “they are for the use of the Church, and surely that sanctifies the pains and labour spent on them?”

“That is just what the devil has been whispering in mine ear this while,” said the monk; and he put one hand behind his back and wagged a finger at Gerard, half threateningly, half playfully, as if he scolded temptation itself. “He was even so kind as to mind me Solomon built the Lord a house with rare hangings, and it was counted gracious and no sin. Oh, he can quote Scripture rarely.”

Then suddenly, with a flash of defiance not to Gerard but to Vacancy—to the air where an invisible adversary might be supposed—he cried:

“But I am not so simple a monk as you think, my lad! This one toy finished—vigils, fasts, and prayers for me; prayers standing, prayers lying on the chapel floor, and prayers in a right good tub of cold water.”

He nudged Gerard and winked, conspirator against hell.

“Nothing he hates and dreads like seeing us monks at our orisons up to our chins in cold water. For corpus domat aqua. So now go confess thy little trumpery sins—pardonable in youth and secularity—and leave me to mine, sweet to me as honey, and to be expiated in proportion.”

Gerard bowed his head; yet he could not help saying, with the instinct that seeks the best, “Where shall I find a confessor more holy and clement?”

“In each of these cells,” replied the monk simply—for they were now in the corridor. “There. Go to Brother Anselm—yonder.”

Gerard went; but the cell-doors were close, one to another, and it seems he mistook. For just as he was about to tap, he heard his old friend behind him in an agitated whisper:

“Nay! nay! nay!”

He turned—and there stood the monk at his own cell-door, in a strange state of anxiety, going up and down, beating the air double-handed like a bottom sawyer. For a moment Gerard truly believed the cell he was approaching held some dangerous wild beast; if not that darker personage whose presence the old man had so distinctly proclaimed.

He looked back, inquiring, and went on to the next door.

At once his old friend nodded rapidly, relief breaking over his face, and shot back into his den like a hare to cover. He took his hour-glass, turned it, and went again to work on his regalles; and often, pausing to look at the running sand, he murmured to himself, “Well-a-day, the sands how swift they run when the man is bent over earthly toys.”

Father Anselm proved venerable indeed: ample head, a face in which dignity sat as naturally as kindness, and love did not soften authority but crowned it. Gerard, confessing to him, answered gentle though searching questions; and even in the midst of shame and contrition his artist’s hunger rose up like a child tugging at his sleeve.

Here is a head, he thought—oh dear! oh dear! I wonder whether you will let me draw it when I have done confessing.

And so his own head got a little confused, and he forgot a crime or two. Yet he did not lower the bolstering this time; nor was he so uncandid as to detract from the pagan character of the bolstered. When all was said, the penance was brief and plain.

“You shall enter the convent church,” said Anselm, “and prostrating thyself, kiss the lowest step of the altar three times; then kneel on the floor and say three paternosters and a credo. This done, come back to me on the instant.”

Gerard obeyed. The church had that cool breath that stone keeps even when winter claws at the world outside; it smelled faintly of old incense and damp mortar, and the silence there was not empty but held, as in a bowl, by the distant tick of the place—some small sound of life in the building’s body. Gerard kissed the lowest step, and the cold bit his lips. He said the prayers, his voice low, and felt his own words come back to him in his native cadence even when the Latin was fixed; for the heart has its dialect, and it will not always be forced to march in another’s measure. Then he returned at once.

He found Father Anselm spreading plaster.

“After the soul, the body,” said the monk. “Know that I am the chirurgeon here, for want of a better. This is going on thy leg—to cool it, not to burn it; the saints forbid.”

As the plaster was laid—smooth, careful, with the practised touch of one who has seen pain often and learned to be swift—Anselm, who had naturally been interested by the Düsseldorf branch of Gerard’s confession, leaned rather to Denys upon the matter of bleeding.

“We Dominicans seldom let blood nowadays,” said he. “The lay leeches say ’tis from timidity and want of skill; but in sooth, we have long found that simples will cure most of the ills that can be cured at all. Besides, they never kill in capable hands; and other remedies slay like thunderbolts. As for the blood, the Vulgate saith expressly it is the life of a man. And in medicine or law, as in divinity, to be wiser than the All-wise is to be a fool.

“Moreover, simples are mighty. The little four-footed creature that kills the poisonous snake—if bitten herself—finds an herb powerful enough to quell that poison, though stronger and swifter of operation than any mortal malady; and we, taught by her wisdom and our own traditions, still search and try the virtues of those plants the good God hath strewed this earth with: some to feed men’s bodies, some to heal them.”

At the word feed, Gerard’s mind, which never quite let go of the earth even in holy talk, ran for a moment to the monastery’s stores—the smell of clean grain, the bins of beans, the dried herbs that were not only physic but seasoning; and he heard, somewhere beyond the wall, the steady hush and clatter of the house’s daily bread being made ready: water poured, a knife on board, a pot-lid set down with care. Such domestic sounds were more than comfort. They were memory made audible, and he felt—without quite knowing why—that where a people keeps its food and its prayers, it keeps its language too; and where those die, even saints’ names grow strange upon the tongue.

“Only in desperate ills,” Anselm went on, “we mix heavenly with earthly virtue. We steep the hair or the bones of some dead saint in the medicine, and thus work marvellous cures.”

“Think you, father, it is along of the reliques?” asked Gerard; “for Peter a Floris, a learned leech and no pagan, denies it stoutly.”

“What knows Peter a Floris? And what know I?” said Anselm simply. “I take not on me to say we can command the saints, and, will they nill they, draw corporal virtue from their blest remains. But I see that the patient drinking thus in faith is often bettered as by a charm. Doubtless faith in the recipient is for much in all cures. So ’twas ever. A sick woman, that all the Jewish leeches failed to cure, did but touch Christ’s garment and was healed in a moment. Had she not touched that sacred piece of cloth, she had never been healed. Had she without faith not touched it only, but worn it to her grave, I trow she had been none the better.

“But we do ill to search these things too curiously. All we see around us calls for faith. Have then a little patience; we shall soon know all. Meantime I—thy confessor for the nonce—do strictly forbid thee, on thy soul’s health, to hearken learned lay folk on things religious. Arrogance is their bane; with it they shut heaven’s open door in their own faces. Mind, I say—learned laics. Unlearned ones have often been my masters in humility, and may be thine.

“Thy wound is cared for. In three days ’twill be but a scar. And now God speed thee, and the saints make thee as good and as happy as thou art thoughtful and gracious.”

Gerard hoped there was no need to part yet; he was to dine in the refectory, and his heart was hungry for company as well as meat. But Father Anselm told him—with a shade of regret just perceptible and no more—that he did not leave his cell this week, being himself in penitence. Then, as if to make amends for the rigour of that solitude, he took Gerard’s head delicately in both hands, kissed him on the brow, and almost before the cell-door had closed, was back to his pious offices, swallowed up in the silence he had chosen.

Gerard went away chilled to the heart by the isolation of the monastic life, and saddened too.

“Alas!” he thought, “here is a kind face I must never look to see again on earth; a kind voice gone from mine ear and my heart for ever. There is nothing but meeting and parting in this sorrowful world. Well-a-day! well-a-day!”

A young monk came for him and led him to the refectory. As they went, Gerard heard the place change its note: the corridor’s hush gave way to the mild clink of trenchers, the soft scrape of benches, the controlled murmur that is not talk but many men breathing near one another, and above it all the single voice that read aloud, steady as a metronome. The sound was as ordered as the fare.

There he found several monks seated at a table, and Denys standing like a poker, being examined as to the towns he should pass through. The friars then clubbed their knowledge and marked out the route, noting all the religious houses on or near that road; and this they gave Gerard, as if handing him not merely directions but a chain of safe hearths strung across the winter world.

Then supper: plain, wholesome, made not for display but for strength. Yet even simplicity had its savor here—bread with a crust that crackled properly, pottage whose steam carried the honest smell of leeks and herbs, and that faint, blessed tang of ale which tells you grain has been coaxed, not abused. Gerard, who had lived too long upon chance morsels and the harshness of the road, felt the food go into him like a benediction. The monks ate with that quiet economy of movement that keeps a refectory’s peace: spoons rising and falling like a small tide, a cup set down with care rather than thumped. It struck him, oddly, how much a man’s soul may be guarded by such manners; for noise, he had begun to learn, is not only nuisance but temptation, and a mind battered by din grows raw and easily led.

After, the old monk carried Gerard to his cell, and they had an eager chat. The friar’s hands kept straying to his regalles as he spoke, as if his thoughts and fingers were one creature; but his eyes were on Gerard, quick and affectionate. Incidentally he revealed the cause of his pantomime in the corridor.

“Ye had well-nigh fallen into Brother Jerome’s clutches. Yon was his cell.”

“Is Father Jerome an ill man, then?” asked Gerard.

“An ill man!” cried the friar, and crossed himself. “A saint, an anchorite, the very pillar of this house! He had sent ye barefoot to Loretto. Nay—I forgot, y’are bound for Italy: the spiteful old saint upon earth had sent ye to Canterbury or Compostella.”

Gerard stared, half amused, half dismayed.

“But Jerome was born old and with a cowl,” the monk went on. “Anselm and I were boys once, and wicked beyond anything you can imagine.”

Gerard wore a somewhat incredulous look.

“This keeps us humble more or less,” said the monk, “and makes us reasonably lenient to youth and hot blood.”

Then, at Gerard’s earnest request, the old man took up the psalterion and drew from it one more heavenly strain—so clear, so tender, it seemed to cleanse the very air of the day’s dust, and to lay a soft hand upon Gerard’s troubled spirit. Outside, winter might grind its teeth; inside, the strings spoke a language older than Gerard’s own and yet intimately understood, as if sound itself could translate what words cannot.

So to bed: the sore heart soothed, the mind quieted, the body given its little mercy.

That day, marked only by contrast—coming like oil upon waves after so many passions and perils—must stand here as the representative of many such days that now succeeded. For on their weary way the travellers learned what most learn on the longer road of life: stirring events are not evenly dealt out, but come by fits and starts, and in clusters, as if each drew the next by hidden links. Between those knots of fate lie long stretches where nothing “happens” save the plain business of staying alive: walking, eating, seeking shelter, mending what can be mended, and carrying one’s own language in one’s mouth as a man carries fire from hearth to hearth.

So it was with them. Though there were no more vivid adventures for a long while, one day’s march succeeded another; one monastery after another fed and lodged them gratis with a welcome always charitable, sometimes genial. They met no enemy but winter and rough weather—antagonists not always contemptible. The road had its own hard music now: boots sucking at mud, wind worrying the bare branches into a thin complaining, rain drumming on hood and cloak; yet, again and again, the bell of a house would answer that wilderness, and the door would open on warmth, broth, bread, and the gentler acoustics of human order.

And so the pair—Gerard bronzed in the face and travel-stained from head to foot, Denys with his shoes in tatters, stiff and footsore both—drew near the Burgundian frontier.

Gerard hungered for Burgundy almost as keenly as Denys did, though each in his own fashion. Denys sang of it the way a vintner praises his own cask: not in great speeches only, but in every small vexation on the road—every sour host, every greasy trencher, every featherless pallet—he must needs point with his whole body and voice toward that promised country where, he swore, folk washed their hands and their linen as if God Himself were to dine.

And it was ever the linen that Denys used to bait Gerard with—knowing well the Hollander’s tenderness on that score.

“I ask no more,” Gerard would say, half laughing and half sick. “To think I have not lain once in a naked bed since I left home! When I look at their sheets, instead of doffing habit and hose, it is my eyes and nose I would fain be shut of.”

Denys—who loved his country as some men love a mistress, with blind fidelity and sharp jealousy—carried that fondness to folly. He would tramp twenty leagues in shoes that had burst their seams and gaped like mouths, rather than buy a stitch of leather from a German churl; for, said he, the fellow would not sell without first flinging his sulks, his dinner, and his big body across the bargain, setting a man to struggle through a hedge of discourtesies for the bare right to pay.

Toward sunset they came to a choice. A little town lay ahead on the road, its smoke faint against the paling sky; a monastery lay aside, a black mass of roof and wall set back from the track among trees. The one promised an inn, noise, and trade; the other, quiet, charity, and rule.

Denys turned his toes toward the town at once. Gerard, who had lived on convent bread and convent shelter more than once, and found in it a clean simplicity after the world’s rank cookery, pointed his staff toward the cloister.

Denys yielded—after a struggle that showed plain his whole body was an argument. But he laid down his terms like a captain striking a truce.

“Once in Burgundy,” said he, “we stop always at an inn.”

Gerard agreed the readier because the little chart he carried—the careful list of houses where a traveller might find a pallet and a bowl—ended there. So they left the road and took the side way.

The air changed as they went: less of hoof and cart-rattle, more of hedge-birds and their own footfalls; and then, as the great building drew near, there came upon the wind that peculiar smell which clings to such places—cold stone that has never wholly dried, wax long burned into wood, boiled pottage worked into the very mortar by centuries of ladles, and, faintly, the sharp clean breath of herbs from a physic garden.

Gerard, surprised at Denys’s sudden sourness, asked him whence this new dislike of houses that had fed and lodged them for nothing so often.

Denys hemmed, hawed, spat to one side, and for a time would only shrug. But at last his wrongs—long banked up—broke through; and when he spoke, it was not new dislike at all, but an old horror that had been biting him all the way, only held back (so he pretended) out of politeness and because, as he said, he had seen powder put in Gerard’s drink and had therefore forborne to offend men who might do worse.

“However,” he added, with the air of one who grants a favour to himself, “being this the last, why not ease my mind? Know then, I have been like a fish out of water in all those great dungeons. You straightway levant with some old shaveling; so you see not my purgatory.”

Gerard’s face softened. “Forgive me. I have been selfish.”

“Ay, ay, I forgive thee, little one; ’tis not thy fault. Art not the first fool that hath been priest-rid and monk-hit. But I’ll not forgive them my misery.”

And then, as if he were some commissioner come a century too soon to pull down abbeys, he delivered his indictment—hot, particular, and full of the bodily things that make a man’s days either human or hellish.

“These gloomy piles,” said he, “are all built alike. Inns differ—God bless them for it!—one hath a buttery that smells of ale and roast; another a kitchen where the onions and dripping tell you supper is at hand; another a hall full o’ talk and a hearth that crackles like good company. But here—monotony! Great gate, little gate, so many steps, then a gloomy cloister where your voice dies on the stones. Here the dortour; there the great cold refectory, where you must sit mumchance—or, at least, whisper like a thief—he that likes to speak his mind out.”

He flung his hand toward the walls as if they had already begun to close on his throat.

“And then,” he cried, “nobody is a man here, but all are slaves—and of what? Of a peevish, tinkling bell, that never sleeps. An ’twere a trumpet now, aye sounding alarums, ’twouldn’t freeze a man’s heart so. But this—tinkle, tinkle, tinkle—and you must sit to meat, with may be no stomach for food. Ere your meat settles warm in your belly, tinkle, tinkle! and ye must to church, with may be no stomach for devotion: I am not a hog at prayers, for one. Tinkle, tinkle, and now you must to bed with your eyes open. Well, by then you have contrived to shut them, some uneasy imp o’ darkness hath got to the bell-rope, and tinkle, tinkle, it behoves you say a prayer in the dark, whether you know one or not. If they heard the sort of prayers I mutter when they break my rest with their tinkle! Well, you drop off again and get about an eyeful of sleep: lo, it is tinkle, tinkle, for matins.”

To Denys, sound was not mere air: it was command and compulsion. The bell, small as a child’s toy, made a world of men into puppets; it stole sleep, it turned hunger into duty, it turned the body’s honest needs into sins measured by a rope and a clapper. Gerard heard in Denys’s wrath not only blasphemy, but a true misery—the tyranny of a soundscape a soldier could not master, the way a perpetual thin ringing can rasp a mind rawer than any cold stone.

“And the only clapper you love is a woman’s,” Gerard said, half contempt, half teasing.

“Because there is some music in that even when it scolds,” Denys retorted stoutly; and for a moment his face lightened, as if the memory of a human voice—warm, various, full of breath and laughter—had driven off the bell’s thin tyranny.

Then he plunged back.

“And to be always checked! If I do but put my finger in the salt-cellar, straightway I hear, ‘Have you no knife that you finger the salt?’ And if I but wipe my knife on the cloth to save time, then ’tis, ‘Wipe thy knife dirty on the bread, and clean upon the cloth!’ Oh small of soul! these little peevish pedantries fall chill upon good fellowship like wee icicles a-melting down from strawen eaves.”

“I hold cleanliness no pedantry,” said Gerard, with that quiet firmness that could be more cutting than Denys’s oaths. “Shouldst learn better manners once for all.”

“Nay; ’tis they who lack manners. They stop a fellow’s mouth at every word.”

“At every other word, you mean; every obscene or blasphemous one.”

“Exaggerator, go to! Why, at the very last of these dungeons I found poor travellers sitting all chilled and mute round one shaveling, like rogues awaiting their turn to be hanged; so to cheer them up, I did but cry out, ‘Courage, tout le monde, le dia—’”

“Connu! what befell?” asked Gerard, despite himself; Denys’s tales always had a smell of smoke and ale about them, even when they were told in the open air.

“Marry, this. ‘Blaspheme not!’ quo’ the bourreau. ‘Plait-il,’ say I. Doesn’t he wheel and wyte on me in a sort of Alsatian French, turning all the P’s into B’s. I had much ado not to laugh in his face.”

Gerard’s eyes narrowed. “Being thyself unable to speak ten words of his language without a fault.”

“Well, all the world ought to speak French. What avail so many jargons except to put a frontier atwixt men’s hearts?”

There was truth there too—yet Gerard felt how such a saying could be a kind of conquest, taking from each man his mother-words and calling the theft a courtesy. He thought of how a thing tasted different when named in a different tongue—how one word could carry a whole childhood’s kitchen in it, and another, meaning the same by rule, could leave it cold as a translation of prayer.

“But what said he?” Gerard persisted.

“What signifies it what a fool says?”

“Oh, not all the words of a fool are folly, or I should not listen to you.”

Denys snorted, but he had been caught; he must go on.

“Well then, he said, ‘Such as begin by making free with the devil’s name, aye end by doing it with all the names in heaven.’ ‘Father,’ said I, ‘I am a soldier, and this is but my consigne, or watchword.’ ‘Oh, then, it is just a custom?’ said he. I—not divining the old fox, and thinking to clear myself—said, ‘Ay, it was.’ ‘Then that is ten times worse,’ said he. ‘’Twill bring him about your ears one of these days. He still comes where he hears his name often called.’ Observe! no gratitude for the tidings which neither his missals nor his breviary had ever let him know.”

“And he was wrong?” Gerard asked quietly.

Denys, guarded now, shifted his ground like a man who feels the earth hot beneath him.

“Then he was so good,” Denys went on, “as to tell me soldiers do commonly the crimes for which all other men are broke on the wheel; a savoir murder, rape, and pillage.”

“And is’t not true?” said Gerard, not cruelly, but as one who will not let a thing hide behind laughter.

“True or not, it was ill manners,” Denys replied, fencing. “And so says this courteous host of mine, ‘Being the foes of mankind, why make enemies of good spirits into the bargain, by still shouting the names of evil ones?’ and a lot more stuff.”

“Well, but, Denys,” Gerard said, “whether you hearken his rede or slight it, wherefore blame a man for raising his voice to save your soul?”

“How can his voice save my soul,” Denys shot back, triumphant, “when he keeps turning of his P’s into B’s?”

Gerard was staggered, as if Denys had flung a dish in his face. He had no answer ready to that gross mockery of speech—the very instrument by which men carry law, love, prayer, and bread from one to another. Before he could recover, Denys—having found the weak spot—bounded away from the point and fell upon a larger prey.

“All monks are hypocrites,” he cried. “Do but look at them, how they creep about and cannot eye you like honest men.”

“Nay,” said Gerard quickly, eager to defend what he loved in them, “that modest downcast gaze is part of their discipline—’tis custodia oculorum.”

“Cussed toads eating hoc hac horum?” Denys bellowed. “No such thing; just so looks a cut-purse. Can’t meet a true man’s eye. Doff cowl, monk; and behold, a thief; don cowl thief, and lo, a monk. Tell me not they will ever be able to look God Almighty in the face, when they can’t even look a true man in the face down here.”

By now the shadow of the monastery lay upon them. The walls rose blacker than the trees; the way narrowed; the sound of their steps became a small hard thing in the deepening hush. And then—thin as a thread, yet cutting through all other sounds—came a bell.

“Ah, here it is, black as ink!” Denys cried, with a shiver that was half rage and half jest. “Into the well we go, comrade. Misericorde, there goes the tinkle already.”

He paused, cocking his head like a dog that hears meat being carved.

“’Tis the best of tinkles though; ’tis for dinner. Stay—listen! I thought so: the wolf in my stomach cried ‘Amen!’”

This last he sealed with two oaths, as if seasoning his hunger with profanity; and with that he marched into the convent like a victorious gamecock, taking Gerard’s silence for defeat, and never dreaming how deeply he had disgusted him.

In the refectory that night—where the long boards shone with the wear of many elbows and the air hung with the warm, yeasty breath of trenchers and broth—Gerard caught, at his own end of the table, a low talk that pricked him sharper than any bell.

The brother who had been set to write out fair new copies of the house’s charter and rule had died suddenly.

A quill laid down in mid-stroke, a hand stilled before the ink dried—so much order depending on one man’s fingers. It made a gap in the monastery’s memory, and the gap had to be bridged with a living hand.

Gerard’s own fingers, stained by travel and hunger, twitched as if they already held a pen. Timidly, as one asks not alms but leave, he offered his service.

There was a moment’s pause among the monks near him, a weighing. Gerard mistook it for suspicion of hire, and hastened, reddening:

“Nay, not for hire, my lords, but for love; and as a small return for many a good night’s lodging your order hath bestowed on me, a poor wayfarer.”

One monk’s mouth softened, approving; yet he shook his head a little, as if to caution the company. The dead brother, he hinted, had been an excellent penman; his work could not be taken up and carried on save by a master.

That word—master—drew from Gerard a quiet courage. From his wallet he brought out, with a tremor he could not wholly hide, a vellum deed. The back of it he had cleaned and scraped, and on that pale, rescued space he had written a specimen: letters laid as carefully as herbs in a mortar, each stroke measured, each flourish obeying its own law.

The monk started as at some rare spice recognized by scent alone. Without another word he rose and went swiftly up the hall to the high table. Gerard, watching, saw him bend his knee so that it just touched, in passing, the fifth step and then the tenth, and then present the vellum to the prior, whispering comments.

At once a dozen knowing eyes fixed on the piece; a buzz ran like bees about a hive. Gerard saw the prior point more than once; then the monk came back with the strut of a man sent with an honour. In his hands were not only praise, but supper: a savoury crustade ryal—a game pie whose lid had been lifted and set back, so that the gravey steamed up, thick with spice and wine—and with it a silver grace-cup brimming with rich pimentum.

The spiced drink sent up a perfume of honey and pepper and warmed herbs; it was like being invited into the kitchen without having scrubbed one’s hands first. Gerard took the cup, and, bowing low first to the distant prior and then to his own company, quaffed and passed it on.

Instantly the whole table hailed him as of their own kin.

“Art convent bred, deny it not?”

He confessed it; and in that moment he thanked Heaven for his cloister-breeding, for he saw clearly how else he might have been as blunt and hungry-minded as his brothers Sybrandt and Cornelis, taking food and shelter as mere filling and roof, and missing the hidden customs that bind men together like a shared loaf.

“But ’tis passing strange how you could know,” said he.

Two monks answered together, as if a rubric had been recited: “You drank with the cup in both hands.”

So slight a gesture, and yet it spoke a whole dialect of the refectory—one of those untranslatable languages that live in the body: how to hold, how to bow, how to receive. A man may travel far and learn many tongues, and yet betray himself by the way he lifts a vessel.

While Gerard was still wondering at the power lodged in such little forms, a rougher sound rose at the bottom of the hall. Voices there had been loudish for some time, but now came a burst of mirth so obstreperous and so long that the prior sent even the sub-prior striding down to check it and lay penance on every monk at that table.

Gerard’s cheek burned with shame; for in the heart of the unruly laughter his ear had caught the word “courage!” and then, clear above the rest, the trumpet tones of Denys of Burgundy.

The monastery’s sound—normally measured as a chant—had been cracked by that soldier’s brass. It jarred the place like a cracked pot in a still dairy. Gerard felt, too keenly, how noise could bruise the mind; yet he could not help loving Denys’s very excess, since it sprang from life.

Soon after, Gerard was installed in the dead Werter’s cell, with wax lights that made the walls swim in gold, and a little writing-frame that could be set at any angle like a cook’s board tilted to catch the best light for trimming, and all the materials of calligraphy: quills cut clean, inks of several strengths, pumice, knife, colours, and the smooth waiting vellum.

Work began at once. Gerard’s hand went steadily, as if the long road had been only a prelude to this stillness. Each letter he laid down was a morsel of order; the strokes joined like stitched seams, binding the monastery’s past so it should not fray.

Yet the labour was too much for one evening; the charter and the rule were not short dishes to be turned in a hurry. Then came a question more difficult than any flourish: how could he ask Denys—the monk-hater—to stay longer?

He spoke to him plainly at last, offering to abide by his decision. And here Denys surprised him. The big man, who had sworn and scoffed at cowls, answered graciously:

“A day’s rest will do neither of us harm. Write thou, and I’ll pass the time as I may.”

Gerard wrote on. When the monks saw what he had done, their admiration was honest and unfeigned; they agreed, with a solemnity that was almost cheerful, that the records had gained by poor Werter’s death. The sub-prior, in the warmth of this discovery, forced a rix-dollar on Gerard and thrust into his hands several brushes and colours from the convent stock, which was very large—pigments like ground berries and burnt bone, all the palette of memory.

Next day Gerard resumed his march, warm at heart; for this was a good omen. It was on the pen he relied to make his fortune, and through that fortune to recover his well-beloved. The road might be harsh, but a man who carries skill carries a hearth with him.

He showed Denys the gifts as they walked.

“Come, Denys. See what the good monks have given me; now do try to be fairer to them. For, to be round with you, it chilled my friendship for a moment to hear even you call my benefactors hypocrites.”

Denys did not snarl, as Gerard expected. Instead he threw up his hand with a soldier’s frankness.

“I recant.”

“Thank you! thank you! Good Denys.”

“I was a scurrilous vagabond.”

“Nay, nay; say not so, neither!”

“But we soldiers are rude and hasty. I give myself the lie, and I offer those I misunderstood all my esteem. ’Tis unjust that thousands should be defamed for the hypocrisy of a few.”

“Now are you reasonable. You have pondered what I said?”

“Nay. It is their own doing.”

Gerard crowed a little—who does not like to be proved in the right?—and then gave him all his attention when Denys offered to tell how his conversion had been wrought.

“Well then,” began Denys, with the relish of a man describing a feast, “at dinner the first day a young monk beside me did open his jaws and laughed right out—most musically.”

Denys’s voice, even telling it, seemed to fill the road like a horn in a narrow lane.

“‘Good,’ said I, ‘at last I have fallen on a man and not a shorn ape.’ So, to sound him further, I slapped his broad back and administered my consigne.”

“‘Heaven forbid!’ says he. I stared—for the dog looked as sad as Solomon; a better mime saw you never, even at a Mystery. ‘I see war is no sharpener of the wits,’ said he. ‘What are the clergy for but to fight the foul fiend? and what else are the monks for? The fiend being dead, The friars are sped. You may plough up the convents, and we poor monks shall have nought to do—but turn soldiers, and so bring him to life again.’”

Denys laughed at the recollection; he could taste again the laughter that had run round the table at his expense.

“Then there was a great laugh at me. ‘Well, you are the monk for me,’ said I. ‘And you are the crossbowman for me,’ quo’ he; ‘and I’ll be bound you could tell us tales of the war should make our hair stand on end.’ ‘Excusez! the barber has put that out of the question,’ quoth I—and then I had the laugh.”

“What wretched ribaldry!” Gerard said, half to himself, his mind still in the quiet cell where letters behaved.

Denys, candid as a child in some matters, admitted at once he had seen merrier jests hatched with less cackle.

“’Twas a great matter to have got rid of hypocrisy,” he went on, satisfied with his own conclusion. “So said I, ‘I can give you the chaire de poule, if that may content ye.’ ‘That we will see,’ was the cry, and a signal went round.”

Then Denys—bursting with glee—told how at bedtime he had been taken, not to the great dortour, but to a cell, and strictly forbidden to sleep; and to aid his vigil, a book had been lent him, full of pictures of a hundred merry adventures of monks pursuing the female laity. How, in due course, he had been taken out barefoot, down to the parlour, where waited a supper fit for a duke, and at it twelve jolly friars, roaring boys, he declared, the merriest he had met in peace or war.

How the story, the toast, the jest, the wine-cup went round. How some played cards with a gorgeous pack in which Saint Theresa and Saint Catherine, bedizened with gold, stood for queens; and black, white, grey, and crutched friars for knaves; and how they staked their very rosaries and swore like troopers when they lost.

And how about midnight a sly monk stole out, and Denys and others followed him into the garden and saw him thrust his hand into the ivy and draw out a rope-ladder. With this he ran up upon the wall—ten feet broad—yet not so nimbly but a russet kirtle popped up from the outer world as quick as he; and then the two fell to billing and cooing.

“That situation,” said Denys, delighted at his own wit, “struck me as rather feline than ecclesiastical, and drew from me the appropriate comment of a ‘mew!’”

The monks joined his mewsical chorus; the visitor shrieked and was sore discomforted. But the monk on the wall—Abelard, Denys named him—only cried:

“What, are ye there, ye jealous miauling knaves? Ye shall caterwaul to some tune to-morrow night. I’ll fit every man-jack of ye with a fardingale.”

That brutal threat, Denys confessed, had reconciled him to stay another day—at Gerard’s request.

Gerard groaned aloud. Denys, unable to disconcert so brazen a monk and the demoiselle beginning to whimper, told how they danced caterwauling in a circle, then bestowed a solemn benediction on the two wall-flowers, and off they went back to the parlour. There they found a pair lying dead drunk, and two others affectionate to tears. They carried off the inanimate, dragged off the loving and lachrymose, and kicked each merrily into his cell.

“And so,” concluded Denys, “shut up in measureless content.”

Gerard’s stomach turned, not with hunger but with disgust. “I am disgusted,” said he. “And I tell you so.”

Denys only chuckled, as if Gerard’s displeasure were a seasoning to his tale, and proceeded to tell how next day he and the young monks drew the fish-ponds and secreted pike, carp, tench, and eel for their own use; and how, in the dead of night, he was taken again, shoeless, by crooked ways into the chapel—a ghost-like place, being dark—and then down steps into a crypt below the floor, where suddenly paradise burst on him.

“’Tis there the holy fathers retire to pray,” Gerard put in quickly, eager to rescue at least the place with a better meaning.

“Not always,” said Denys. “Wax candles by the dozen were lighted, and princely cheer. Fifteen soups maigre—with marvellous twangs of venison, grouse, and hare in them—and twenty different fishes (being Friday), cooked with wondrous art. And each he between two buxom lasses, and each lass between two lads with a cowl—all but me. And think I had to woo by interpreter! I doubt the knave put in three words for himself and one for me; if he didn’t, hang him for a fool.

“And some of the weaker vessels were novices and not wont to hold good wine; had to be coaxed ere they would put it to their white teeth; mais elles s’y faisaient. And the story, and the jest, and the cup went round—by-the-by they had flagons made to simulate breviaries. And a monk touched the cittern and sang ditties with a voice tunable as a lark in spring. The posies did turn the faces of the women folk bright red at first—but elles s’y faisaient.”

Here Gerard could bear no more. He broke out like a man whose native tongue has been mocked and trampled, not with words but with deeds.

“Miserable wretches! Corrupters of youth! Perverters of innocence! But for your being there, Denys—who have been taught no better—oh, would God the church had fallen on the whole gang. Impious, abominable hypocrites!”

“Hypocrites?” cried Denys, honestly amazed. “Why, that is what I clept them ere I knew them—and you withstood me. Nay, they are sinners; all good fellows are that; but by St. Denys his helmeted skull, no hypocrites—right jolly roaring blades.”

“Denys,” said Gerard solemnly, and lowered his voice till the road itself seemed to hush and listen, “you little know the peril you ran that night. That church you defiled amongst you is haunted. I had it from one of the elder monks. The dead walk there; their light feet have been heard to patter o’er the stones.”

“Misericorde!” whispered Denys, and for once the loud man became a child in the dark.

“Ay, more,” Gerard went on, the whisper drawing its own dreadful music from the air, “celestial sounds have issued from the purlieus of that very crypt you turned into a tavern. Voices of the dead holding unearthly communion have chilled the ear of midnight; and at times, Denys, the faithful in their nightly watches have even heard music from dead lips. Chords—made by no mortal finger—swept by no mortal hand—have rung faintly, like echoes, deep among the dead in those sacred vaults.”

Denys’s face altered; the colour left him as if a hand had wiped it away.

“Ugh!” said he. “If I had known, mules and wain-ropes had not hauled me thither.” Then, after a breath, with the stubborn regret of the flesh: “And so I had lost a merry time.”

Whether more might have been drawn from this talk—whether that other, older music of the place could ever be understood by two such men—who can tell? For up came a bearded lay brother from the monastery, spurring his mule, waving a piece of vellum.

It was the deed between Ghysbrecht and Floris Brandt.

Gerard’s heart leapt as if he had been struck. The deed was home in his hand: Sevenbergen in ink, a scrap of the language of his beginnings. He turned pale at first, thinking how near he had been to losing it; and then, to Denys’s infinite amusement, he gave money to the lay brother—and kissed the mule’s nose in gratitude, as if the beast had carried not parchment but a living child back into his arms.

“I’ll read you now,” said Gerard to the vellum, almost tenderly, “were you twice as ill written; and—to make sure of never losing you—”

There, by the roadside, he sat down, drew out needle and thread, and with a dexterity that might have shamed many a housewife, sewed the deed fast to his doublet. The stitches went in and out like steady footfalls; and with each pull of the thread his mind, heart, and soul were away to Sevenbergen—its ovens and fields, its familiar speech, the very household noises that no other country could reproduce.

So they went on, and at last reached the promised land. Denys, in high spirits again, doffed his bonnet to all females; they curtsied and smiled in return. He fired his consigne at most men; some stared, some grinned, some did both.

And so he landed Gerard at one of the long-promised Burgundian inns.

“It is a little one,” said he, “but I know it of old for a good one; Les Trois Poissons.” Then he stopped short. “But what is this writ up? I mind not this.”

He pointed to an inscription that ran across the whole building in a single line of huge letters. Denys, proud of his pains, spelled it out as if it were a hard crust to be chewed.

“Oh, I see. ‘Ici on loge a pied et a cheval,’” said he, going minutely through it and looking bumptious when he had effected it.

Gerard looked too; and the sentence that met his eye was not that at all, but a harsher proverb, written large enough for the blind and the dishonest alike:

ON NE LOGE CEANS A CREDIT; CE BONHOMME EST MORT, LES MAUVAIS PAIEURS L’ONT TUE.

They met the host in the narrow passage, where the smell of damp stone, yesterday’s smoke, and frying fat clung like a second plaster.

“Welcome, messieurs,” said he, lifting his cap with a bow so low his forehead nearly met his own apron-string.

“Come,” said Gerard, half laughing, half weary, “we are not in Germany.”

In the common room the hostess held court—a broad, red-cheeked woman with sleeves rolled for work and eyes quick as a knife in a kitchen. She dipped a curtsey and beamed as though they were kin come home at Martinmas.

“Give yourself the trouble of sitting ye down, fair sir,” she said to Gerard, and swept two chairs with her apron, though they were clean enough.

“Thank you, dame,” Gerard answered; and to himself, with the sour mirth of a tired traveller: “A polite nation indeed. First the trouble of sitting; then the labour of eating; then the toil of digesting; and at last, by Hercules, the strain of going to bed and the struggle of falling asleep.”

Denys had already taken command of the victuals.

“Why, Denys,” cried Gerard, “what are you doing—ordering supper for only two?”

“Why not?”

“What, can we sup without waiting for forty more? Burgundy for ever!”

“Aha! Courage, camarade. Le dia—”

“C’est convenu.”

In that house, and in France by the look of it, the women ruled as naturally as fire draws smoke. The host drifted about like a cap on a pond, forever doffing it because he had nothing else to do; and as the women went by, they shifted him aside without so much as turning their heads—no more ceremony than brushing a living twig from one’s sleeve in a thicket.

Supper came in on a maid’s arms—steam, grease, and garlic rising before the dishes like a banner. The hostess followed empty-handed, as if her presence were itself a course.

“Fall to, my masters,” she said briskly. “Y’have but one enemy here; and he lies under your knife.”

They fell to with the honest hunger of men who have walked their meat a dozen leagues. There was bread with a crackling crust and a warm, sour scent; there was a stew dark with wine and onions cooked down till they had turned to sweetness; there were eggs—always eggs in such houses—fried in brown butter till the edges laced and crisped. The fat sang faintly in the pan somewhere beyond the door, and that small domestic music made the room feel less like an inn than a kitchen where a family ate.

The hostess drew her chair near enough to make them company as well as feed them, and talked as though she had known them since they were weaned; then, business calling, she rose and sent in her daughter to take the vacant place. The girl was near twenty, fair and gentle, and when she learned how far Gerard had come and still must go, her eyes softened with a tenderness that warmed him more than the stew.

She stayed almost half an hour. When she went, Gerard looked after her and said low, amazed, “This an inn? Why, it is like home.”

“Qui fit François il fit courtois,” said Denys, swelling with pleased pride.

“Courteous?” Gerard shook his head. “Christian—this is beyond courtesy. To welcome us like home-guests and old friends, us that are here to-day and gone to-morrow. But who merits kindness more than a worn traveller, far from his folk? Hola—here comes another.”

This one brought in not gentleness but a gust of rude health and laughter. She was the chambermaid, about five-and-twenty, with a cocked nose, a wide mouth that seemed made for merriment, a black eye like a berry in sunshine, and bare arms stout as a dairymaid’s, fit to wring linen dry or swing a pail without spilling.

The moment she entered, a traveller tossed her a free jest. Before the jest had cooled in the air, the whole room was roaring—at the jester. Her tongue had turned on him and pricked him like a master fencer touching a novice, swift and sure. Another tried; then another. Marion planted her fists on her hips and held the room at play, beating them with a bludgeon of country humour—coarse as the rind on a winter cheese, but hearty, and spoken so fast it carried all before it.

Gerard sat staring as if he had discovered a new beast in the menagerie of the world. He leaned to Denys and whispered, “Now I see why you Frenchmen say a woman’s tongue is her sword.”

At that moment she downed another assailant, and Denys, chivalrous as ever, flung her his threadbare refrain to hearten “the weaker vessel”—though she looked more like the iron pot among earthenware.

“Courage, ma mie, le—”

She wheeled on him. “How can he be dead as long as there is an archer left alive?” The room shouted, and Denys laughed with them, caught in his own snare.

“It is washing day, my masters,” Marion said suddenly grave, as if announcing a fast.

“Aprés? We travellers cannot strip and go bare while you wash our clothes,” grumbled an old fellow by the fire—one who had held his tongue through the raillery and now ventured into the safe sunshine of commonplaces.

“I aimed not your way, ancient man,” Marion replied, looking him over slow from bald pate to cracked shoe. “But since you ask—methinks you might take a turn i’ the tub, clothes and all, and no harm done.” Laughter shook the benches. Then her bright eye slid to Gerard. “But what I spoke for, I thought this young sire might like his beard starched.”

Gerard’s chin wore only a thin, silky crop. Denys, traitor, laughed the loudest, for Denys’s own beard was a stiff, bristling hedge.

Gerard took the jest calmly; vanity was no great burden on him. “Nay, chambrière,” said he, smiling, “mine is all unworthy your pains; take you this fair growth in hand,” and he pointed at Denys’s vegetable.

“Oh, time for that, when I starch the besoms.”

They were still shouting when the hostess re-entered; and in the instant it took her to cross the threshold Marion turned from Amazon to Madonna—meek face, demure hands, eyes down. But it was wasted craft. The hostess had heard the laughter and did not, at heart, disapprove.

“Ah, Marion lass,” she said, good-humoured, “if you laid me an egg every time you cackle, ‘L’es Trois Poissons’ would never lack an omelet.”

At “omelet” Gerard’s mind flew, as it often did, to the comfort of food well done: the eggs beaten just enough to marry yolk and white, not to froth; the pan warmed, not scorched; the butter browned to hazelnut and poured off before it blackened; a pinch of salt between finger and thumb, measured by habit, not miserly. It pleased him that even a scold could speak of cookery as coin.

“Now, dame,” said Gerard aloud, “what is to pay?”

“What for?”

“Our supper.”

“Where is the hurry? cannot you be content to pay when you go? Lose the guest, find the money—that is the rule of ‘The Three Fish.’”

“But, dame—outside ‘The Three Fish’ it is thus written—‘Ici-on ne loge—’”

“Bah! Let that flea stick on the wall!” She pointed up at the smoky ceiling, which was scribbled all over with scratches—scores, accounts, rude hieroglyphs cut through soot till the pale plaster showed. “Look hither. We write there to scare moneyless folk from the inn altogether, or to be acted on when a non-paying face comes in and insists on being served. We can’t refuse them plump, you know. The law forbids us.”

“And how know you mine is not such a face?”

“Out fie! it is the best face that has entered ‘The Three Fish’ this autumn.”

“And mine, dame?” Denys asked, thrusting his chin forward. “Dost see no knavery here?”

She looked at him without blinking. “Not such a good one as the lad’s; nor ever will be. But it is the face of a true man. For all that,” she added dryly, “an I were ten years younger, I’d as lieve not meet that face on a dark night too far from home.”

Gerard stared. Denys laughed, taking it for a compliment.

“Why, dame,” said Denys, “I would but sip the night dew off the flower; and you needn’t take ten years off, nor ten days, to be worth risking a scratched face for.”

Marion had slipped back in. “There, our mistress,” she cried. “Said I not t’other day you could make a fool of them still, an if you were properly minded?”

“I dare say ye did,” the hostess retorted. “It sounds like some daft wench’s speech.”

“Dame,” Gerard said, bewildered, “this is wonderful.”

“What? Oh—no, no. That is no wonder at all. I have been here all my life; and reading faces is the first thing a girl picks up in an inn.”

“And frying eggs the second,” Marion put in. “No—telling lies. Frying eggs is the third, though.”

“And holding her tongue the last,” said the hostess, “and modesty the day after—never at all.”

“Alack!” Marion flung up her hands. “Talk of my tongue. But I say no more. She under whose wing I live now deals the blow. I’m sped—’tis but a chambermaid gone. Catch what’s left on’t!” And she staggered and sank backwards onto the handsomest fellow in the room—which happened to be Gerard.

“Tic! tic!” Gerard cried, peevish as a man whose thoughts have been interrupted mid-sentence. “There—don’t be stupid! That is too heavy a jest for me. See you not I am talking to the mistress?”

Marion sprang upright again like a ball, made two little bounds into the middle of the floor, and turned a pirouette. “There, mistress,” she said. “I give in; ’tis you that reigns supreme with the men—leastways with male children.”

“Young man,” the hostess said to Gerard, “this girl is not so stupid as her deportment. In reading of faces and frying of omelets, there we are great. ’Twould be hard if we failed at these arts, since they are about all we do know.”

“You do not quite take me, dame,” said Gerard. “That honesty in a face should shine forth to your experienced eye—that seems reasonable. But how by looking on Denys here could you learn his one little foible—his insanity—his miserable mulierosity?” The more he thought on it, the more it vexed him, as though language itself were being forced to carry a meaning it did not fit.

“His mule—his what?” The hostess crossed herself at the polysyllable, as if he had named a devil.

“Nay, ’tis but the word I was fain to invent for him.”

“Invent? What, can a child like you make other words than grow in Burgundy by nature? Take heed what ye do! why, we are overrun with them already, especially bad ones. Lord, these be times. I look to hear of a new thistle invented next.”

“Well then, dame—mulierose means wrapped up, body and soul, in women. So prithee tell me: how did you ever detect the noodle’s mulierosity?”

“Alas, good youth,” she said, “you make a mountain of a molehill. We that are women be notice-takers; and out of the tail of our eye see more than most men can, glaring through a prospect glass. Whiles I move to and fro doing this and that, my glance is still on my guests. I did notice that this soldier’s eyes were never off the womenfolk—my daughter, or Marion, or even an old woman like me—all was gold to him. And there you sat, turning to the speaker, her or him, and that is common sense.”

Denys burst into a hoarse laugh. “You never were more out. Why, this silky, smooth-faced companion is a very Turk—all but his beard. He is more wrapped up in one single Dutch lass called Margaret than I am in the whole bundle of ye, brown and fair.”

“Man alive,” said the hostess, “that is just the contrary. Yourn is the bane, and hisn the cure. Cling you still to Margaret, my dear. I hope she is an honest girl.”

“Dame, she is an angel.”

“Ay, ay, they are all that till better acquainted. I’d as lieve have her no more than honest, and then she will serve to keep you out of worse company. As for you, soldier, there is trouble in store for you. Your eyes were never made for the good of your soul.”

“Nor of his pouch either,” Marion struck in, “and his lips—they will sip the dew, as he calls it, off many a bramble bush.”

“Overmuch clack! Marion, overmuch clack.”

“Ods bodikins, mistress; ye didn’t hire me to be one o’ your three fishes, did ye?” Marion sulked for the space of thirty seconds and no more.

At that moment the landlord slipped in, scenting, as timid men do, that there had been noise and he might claim a share of authority.

“Is that the way to speak to our mistress?” he ventured.

“Hold your whisht,” said his wife sharply. “It is not your business to check the girl; she is a good servant to you.”

“What,” he muttered, “is the cock never to crow, and the hens at it all day?”

“You can crow as loud as you like, my man, out o’ doors. But the hen means to rule the roost.”

“I know a byword to that tune,” said Gerard.

“Do ye, now? Out wi’t then.”

“Femme veut en toute saison, Estre dame en sa mason.”

“I never heard it afore,” said the hostess, “but ’tis as sooth as gospel. Ay, they that set these bywords a rolling had eyes and tongues, and tongues and eyes. Before all the world give me an old saw.”

“And me a young husband,” Marion cried. “Now there was a chance for you all, and nobody spoke. Oh! it is too late now—I’ve changed my mind.”

“All the better for some poor fellow,” Denys suggested.

Later, when the “little mistress” returned, they all drew round the fire—travellers, host, hostess, even the servants in the outer ring—as though the room were a hearth and not a trade. The flames clicked and the embers settled with soft sighs; outside, the wind worried at the shutters; within, voices rose and fell, and the very sound of company—laughter, tale-telling, the scrape of a boot, the thump of a log—seemed a kind of nourishment. Gerard told, in his turn, one of his most terrible saints’ stories from his manuscript store, and made them shudder deliciously; then his head nodded, spent by walking, eating, and the effort of making strangers his kin for an hour.

The young mistress saw and gave Marion a look. Marion lit a rush, and laying her hand on Gerard’s shoulder, bade him follow. She led him to a chamber with two clean white beds that smelled of sun-dried flax and the faint iron tang of freshly pressed linen.

“Choose,” said she.

“Either is paradise,” said Gerard. “I’ll take this. Do you know—I have not lain in a naked bed once since I left my home in Holland.”

“Alack! poor soul,” Marion said. “Well then, the sooner my flax and your down—he! he!—come together, the better; so—allons!” And she held out her cheek, as brisk and business-like as if it were her hand for a tip.

“Allons? What does that mean?”

“It means good-night. Ahem! What—don’t they salute the chambermaid in your part?”

“Not all in a moment.”

“What, do they make a business on’t?”

“Nay, perverter of words—I mean we make not so free with strange women.”

“They must be strange women,” she said, sniffing, “if they do not think you strange fools then. Here is a coil. Why, all the old greasy greybeards that lie at our inn do kiss us chambermaids—faugh! and what have we poor wretches to set on t’other side the compt but now and then a nice young—? Alack! time flies. Chambermaids can’t be spared long in the nursery, so how is’t to be?”

“An’t please you,” said Gerard, trying to laugh it off, “arrange with my comrade for both. He is mulierose; I am not.”

“Nay, ’tis the curb he will want, not the spur. Well! well! you shall to bed without paying the usual toll; and oh, but ’tis sweet to fall in with a young man who can withstand these ancient ill customs, and gainsay brazen hussies. Shalt have thy reward.”

“Thank you. But what are you doing with my bed?”

“Me? oh, only taking off these sheets, and going to put on the pair the drunken miller slept in last night.”

“Oh, no! no!” Gerard cried, horror-struck. “You cruel, black-hearted thing! There—there!”

“A la bonne heure!” She clapped her hands softly. “What will not perseverance effect? But note now the frowardness of a mad wench! I cared not for’t a button. I am dead sick of that sport this five years. But you denied me; so then forthwith I behoved to have it; belike had gone through fire and water for’t. Alas, young sir, we women are kittle cattle—poor perverse toads. Excuse us: and keep us in our place, savoir, at arm’s length; and so good-night!”

At the door she turned, and her face changed as if another woman had stepped into it. Her voice fell from banter to something grave and tender.

“The Virgin guard thy head, and the holy Evangelists watch the bed where lies a poor young wanderer far from home! Amen!”

Then she was gone, tearing down the stairs; and a moment later a peal of laughter from the salle told where she had landed.

“Now that is a character,” Gerard murmured, and yawned over his discovery.

He was in a dry bath of cold, clean linen—an inexpressible refreshment after such long disuse. The chill passed; a glow rose up; and then—Sevenbergen, as if the body, warmed and fed, had boiled memory to the surface like broth.

In the morning Gerard woke refreshed and would have risen, but found himself a close prisoner. His linen was gone. In that age a nightgown was no common thing: men crept into clean sheets clothed in their innocence, and out of them, it seemed, took most after Adam’s eldest son. Without his shirt, Gerard was pinned to the bed as surely as a beetle under a glass.

He bewailed his captivity to Denys; but even as the words left his mouth, the door opened and in sailed Marion with their linen newly washed and ironed, laid along her arms like a baker bearing loaves, white and warm from the oven. The cloth smelled of lye, clear water, and the faint sweetness of sun—cleanliness made almost edible.

She set it down on the table.

“Oh, you good girl,” Gerard cried, as if she had brought him freedom itself.

“Alack, have you found me out at last?”

“Yes, indeed. Is this another custom?”

“Nay, not to take them unbidden,” she said. “But at night we aye question travellers, are they for linen washed. So I came into you, but you were both sound. Then said I to the little mistress, ‘La! where is the sense of waking wearied men, t’ask them is Charles the Great dead, and would they liever carry foul linen or clean—especially this one with a skin like cream?’ ‘And so he has, I declare,’ said the young mistress.”

“That was me,” Denys put in, with the air of a glossator.

“Guess once more,” said Marion, “and you’ll hit the mark.”

“Notice him not,” Gerard said warmly. “Marion, he is an impudent fellow; and I am sure we cannot be grateful enough for your goodness—and I am sorry I ever refused you—anything you fancied you should like.”

“Oh, are ye there,” said l’espiegle, turning at once. “I take that to mean you would fain brush the morning dew off, as your bashful companion calls it. Well then—excuse me—’tis customary, but not prudent. I decline. Quits with you, lad.”

“Stop! stop!” Denys cried as she was making off, victorious. “I am curious to know how many of ye were here last night a-feasting your eyes on us twain.”

“’Twas so satisfactory a feast as we weren’t half a minute over’t,” Marion answered. “Who? why, the big mistress, the little mistress, Janet, and me, and the whole posse comitatus, on tiptoe. We mostly make our rounds the last thing, not to get burned down; and in prodigious numbers. Somehow that maketh us bolder, especially where archers lie scattered about.”

“Why did not you tell me? I’d have lain awake.”

“Beau sire, the saying goes that the good and the ill are all one while their lids are closed. So we said, ‘Here is one who will serve God best asleep. Break not his rest!’”

“She is funny,” said Gerard, as if delivering judgment.

“I must be either that or knavish.”

“How so?”

“Because ‘The Three Fish’ pay me to be funny. You will eat before you part? Good. Then I’ll go see the meat be fit for such worshipful teeth.” And off she went, her feet quick on the boards, as if she could taste the seasoning with her ears.

“Denys,” said Gerard, watching her go, “I wish that was a great boy, and going along with us, to keep us cheery.”

“So do not I,” Denys replied. “But I wish it was going along with us as it is.”

“Now Heaven forefend! A fine fool you would make of yourself.”

They broke their fast, settled their score, and said farewell. Then they found Marion had not exaggerated the “custom of the country.” The three chief women took and kissed them heartily, and they kissed the three chief women. The landlord took and kissed them, and they kissed the landlord; and the cry followed them out like a blessing and a bargain both:

“Come back, the sooner the better!”

“Never pass ‘The Three Fish.’ Should your purses be void, bring yourselves: le sieur credit is not dead for you.”

So they took the road again.

They came to a little town where Denys would buy shoes. The shoemaker stood in his doorway, wide awake, and bowed as if he were greeting a noble. Denys was fitted quickly; the leather creaked fresh as bark, and the new soles smelled of oak-tan and wax.
