The tradesman followed them to the street and dismissed them with such graceful salutes that Gerard, who loved order and civil sound in the world as he loved good bread, felt himself soothed.

They agreed it was Elysium to deal with such a man.

“Not but what my German shoes have lasted well enough,” Gerard added, just.

Outside the town ran a pebbled walk, the stones set close for dry footing.

“This is to keep the burghers’ feet dry,” Denys said, “a-walking o’ Sundays with their wives and daughters.”

Those simple words—wives and daughters, and dry feet on a Sunday, and the quiet ritual of walking together—painted “home” so suddenly in Gerard’s heart that it ached like a hunger.

“Oh, how sweet!” he said.

A little farther on, sweetness ended. They came on a gibbet, and on it two skeletons swayed and clacked softly when the wind moved them—bones answering the air with a dry, obscene music.

“Mercy!” Gerard cried. “A gibbet! and—ugh—two skeletons thereon! Oh, Denys, what a sorry sight to woo by!”

“Nay,” said Denys, shrugging, “a comfortable sight; for every rogue i’ the air there is one the less a-foot.”

A little farther, and worse: two stone pillars, and between them a huge wheel studded thick with iron prongs. Tangled in those prongs were bones and rags of cloth—what had once been a man scattered and displayed like refuse for crows. The air smelled of old corruption and iron, and above it the cawing and wing-beat made a harsh canopy of sound that set Gerard’s teeth on edge.

He hid his face in his hands. “Oh, to think those patches and bones are all that is left of a man! of one who was what we are now.”

“Excusez,” said Denys. “A thing that went on two legs and stole. Are we no more than that?”

“How know ye he stole? Have true men never suffered death and torture too?”

“None of my kith ever found their way to the gibbet, I know.”

“The better their luck. Prithee, how died the saints?”

“Hard. But not in Burgundy.”

“Ye massacred them wholesale at Lyons,” Gerard answered hotly, “and that is on Burgundy’s threshold. To you the gibbet proves the crime, because you read not story. Alas! had you stood on Calvary that bloody day we sigh for to this hour, I tremble to think you had perhaps shouted for joy at the gibbet builded there; for the cross was but the Roman gallows, Father Martin says.”

“The blaspheming old hound!”

“Oh, fie! fie!” Gerard cried. “A holy and a book-learned man. Ay, Denys, y’had read them, that suffered there, by the bare light of the gibbet. ‘Drive in the nails!’ y’had cried: ‘drive in the spear!’ Here be three malefactors—three roues—yet of those little three one was the first Christian saint, and another was the Saviour of the world which gibbeted him.”

Denys, stung, protested on his honour that in Burgundy they managed things better. After a moment’s thought he added, more softly, that those very horrors had once made him curse with rage when the good curé in his village told the Passion at Eastertide—but that was in an outlandish nation, near a thousand years ago. “Mort de ma vie,” he said, trying to laugh it away, “let us hope it is not true; or at least sore exaggerated. Do but see how all tales gather as they roll!”

Then his blood rose again, quick as a pot boiling over. “Do ye not blush to play with your book-craft on your unlettered friend, and throw dust in his eyes, evening the saints with these reptiles?”

But as suddenly he slid back into lightness. “Since your heart beats for vermin, feel for the carrion crows! They be as good vermin as these. Would ye send them to bed supperless, poor pretty poppets? Why, these be their larder; the pangs of hunger would gnaw them dead, but for cold cut-purse hung up here and there.”

Gerard, who had held silence a while, said at last, very quietly, “The subject is closed between us, and for ever. There are things wherein our hearts seem wide as the poles asunder, and eke our heads. But I love thee dearly all the same.” And he said it with such grace and tenderness that Denys had not the heart to jest.

Towards afternoon they heard, ahead, a faint wailing—thin at first like wind through reeds, then clearer, many-voiced, rising and falling as if the road itself cried out. Being fast walkers, they soon came upon its cause.

A score of pikemen marched with several constables; and before them a herd was driven, more than a hundred souls of various ages. Few were old; many were in their strength; and there were children—some scarce able to walk, some in arms. The men went downcast and silent. The women made the outcry, keening and calling, their voices torn and hoarse, a sorrowful music that soured the very air.

“Good Heaven!” Gerard cried. “What a band of them! But stay—surely all those children cannot be thieves; why, there are some in arms. What on earth is this, Denys?”

Denys nodded toward an officer with a badge. “Ask that bourgeois. This is Burgundy: here a civil question ever draws a civil reply.”

Gerard went up, removed his cap—a courtesy instantly returned—and said, “For our Lady’s sake, sir, what do ye with these poor folk?”

“Nay, what is that to you, my lad?” the functionary answered, suspicious, though not unmannerly.

“Master,” said Gerard, “I’m a stranger, and athirst for knowledge.”

“Where be the true men?”

“Here be we. God bless you all! God bless you!”

The cry, half prayer and half battle-call, burst into the upper room and seemed to shake the very rafters. There was a rush for the stairs; torchlight leaped and wavered like a storm of fireflies; and half-a-dozen hands—hard with bow and bill, yet friendly as hearth-stones—caught at Denys and Gerard and hauled them safe among the archers.

“Y’have saved our lives, lads,” Denys cried, breathless, with that loud gratitude a man spends the more freely when his skin is still upon him. “Y’have saved our lives this night.”

A wild sight met the rescued pair: torches flaring in pitchy gusts, the glitter of breastplates slicked with soot, bronzed faces shining with sweat, and the bound thieves with cheeks turned paper-white under rope. In the midst lay the giant’s great body, bleeding out upon the boards; and these seasoned men left it there in its own gore as if it were no more than a butchered ox, already beyond reckoning. The soundscape of the room was a harsh music: boots scuffing, cords rasping, steel rings clinking, men speaking over one another, and underneath it all the thin, insect-like hiss of torches eating tallow—an ugly chorus that made the safe, domestic noises of a true inn (spoons against bowls, a kettle’s homely mutter) feel like a story told in some other language.

Gerard went round the archers and took them each by the hand, his eyes bright and wet. They, moved by that frank clasp, kissed him; and for once, shy no longer, he kissed them in return, tasting smoke and salt on their cheeks as if war itself had a flavor.

Then he turned to one handsome archer of his own years. “Prithee, good soldier, have an eye to me. A strange drowsiness overcomes me. Let no one cut my throat while I sleep—for pity’s sake.”

The archer laughed, thinking him merry with relief, and promised. Gerard’s lids sank as if a heavy cloth had been laid upon them. He went off into a sleep so sudden it looked like a swoon; his breath deepened at once, and his body slackened where he sat, as if all the fear and fasting of the night had been a debt called in at last.

Denys stared at him a moment, surprised; but the surprise did not ripen into care. It served Denys’s purpose that the lad was out of hearing.

Two of the archers were already prodding at the Abbot’s huge corpse with their feet, turning it half over to marvel at the weight of him and the manner of his fall. They asked which of the two had flung that enormous rogue down from an upper storey, for they would fain have the trick of his arm.

Denys at first pished and pshawed, and in his heart feared the sleeping youth might wake and speak of Providence and miracles, and so make him look a braggart. But with Gerard sunk like a stone in water, Denys found his courage swelling into a tale.

“Well then, you see, comrades,” he began, drawing their eyes as neatly as a cook draws diners to the steaming pot, “I had run my sword through this one up to the hilt, and one or two more of ’em came buzzing about me; so it behoved me have my sword or die. So I just put my foot against his stomach, gave a tug with my hand and a spring with my foot, and sent him flying to kingdom come! He died in the air, and his carrion rolled in amongst you without ceremony: made you jump, I warrant me. But pikestaves and pillage! what avails prattling of these trifles once they are gone by? Buvons, camarades, buvons.”

The archers answered that it was easy to say buvons when there was no liquor, but not so easy to do it.

“Nay, I’ll soon find you liquor,” said Denys, with a sniff that might have belonged to a hound or a vintner. “My nose hath a natural alacrity at scenting out the wine. You follow me; and I my nose. Bring a torch!”

They went, leaving the upper room with its ropes and blood, and found a short flight of stone steps that went down into the belly of the house. The air thickened as they descended: damp, stale, and close, with that cold mineral taste old walls keep. The cellar was large and low, and the torch’s yellow light stroked the stones to a greasy shine. Here and there the walls were crusted with what looked like cobwebs until the flame showed them to be saltpetre oozed from the wet stone and crystallized like hoarfrost in a cave.

“Oh! the fine mouldy smell,” said Denys, drawing it into his lungs as some men draw in a roast’s first scent when the joint is turned. “In such places still lurks the good wine. Advance thy torch. Diable! what is that in the corner? A pile of rags? No—’tis a man.”

They gathered around the torch, and there indeed crouched the landlord on a heap, pale as ashes, shivering as if the damp had got into his bones.

“Why, it is the landlord,” said Denys. “Get up, thou craven heart!”

One of the archers shouted at him. “Why, man, the thieves are bound, and we are dry that bound them. Up! and show us thy wine; for no bottles see here.”

“What, be the rascals bound?” stammered the landlord, his teeth knocking as if in a fever. “Good news. W-w-wine? That will I, honest sirs.” He rose on unsure joints and offered to lead them to the wine.

But Denys slid in like a knife under a joint. “You are all in the dark, comrades. He is in league with the thieves.”

“Alack, good soldier, me in league with the accursed robbers! Is that reasonable?” The landlord’s voice tried for injured honesty; it came out thin as sour ale.

“The girl said so anyway.”

“The girl! What girl?” The man’s eyes darted. “Ah! Curse her, traitress!”

Another archer, cooler, cut in. “The girl is not here, but gone on to the bailiff. So let the burghers settle whether this craven be guilty or no: for we caught him not in the act. And let him draw us our wine.”

“One moment,” said Denys, shrewd as a man who knows when a pot has been watered. “Why cursed he the girl? If he be a true man, he should bless her as we do.”

“Alas, sir,” said the landlord, licking his lips, “I have but my good name to live by, and I cursed her to you because you said she had belied me.”

“Humph!” Denys gave him a look like a cook gives a piece of meat that smells fair but feels wrong under the thumb. “I trow thou art a thief, and where is the thief that cannot lie with a smooth face? Therefore hold him, comrades: a prisoner can draw wine an if his hands be not bound.”

The landlord offered no objection. He even said, with a wretched politeness, he would show them where his little stock of wine lay, and only begged they would pay for what they drank, for his rent was two months due. The archers smiled grimly at his simplicity as they took him—one hand firm on his shoulder, another man leading with the torch.

They had reached the threshold when Denys halted them with a sharp “Halt!”

“What is’t?”

“Here be bottles in this corner; advance thy light.”

The torch-bearer, a man called Philippe, turned. Denys had slipped off his scabbard and was prodding at the very heap the landlord had crouched upon.

“Nay, nay,” cried the landlord, sudden in his fear. “The wine is in the next cellar. There is nothing there.”

“Nothing is mighty hard, then,” said Denys, and put his hand into the heap. He drew out something and held it up. It was only a bone. He tossed it down; it rattled on stone.

“There is nought there but the bones of the house,” said the landlord quickly, as if words could salt away suspicion.

“Just now ’twas nothing. Now that we have found something ’tis nothing but bones.” Denys rummaged again. “Here’s another. Humph? Look at this one, comrade; and you come too and look at it—and bring you smooth knave along.”

Philippe took the bone into the torchlight and turned it about, measuring it with a soldier’s eye.

“Well?” said Denys.

“Well—if this was a field of battle, I should say ’twas the shankbone of a man; no more, no less. But ’tisn’t a battlefield, nor a churchyard; ’tis an inn.”

“True, mate,” said Denys; and his voice had changed, growing colder, like a pot taken off the fire and left to stand. “But yon knave’s ashy face is as good a light to me as a field of battle. I read the bone by it. Bring yon face nearer, I say. When the chine is amissing, and the house dog can’t look at you without his tail creeping between his legs, who was the thief? Good brothers mine, my mind it doth misgive me. The deeper I thrust the more there be. Mayhap if these bones could tell their tale they would make true men’s flesh creep that heard it.”

“Alas! young man,” the landlord whined, “what hideous fancies are these! The bones are bones of beeves, and sheep, and kids, and not, as you think, of men and women. Holy saints preserve us!”

“Hold thy peace! Thy words are air.” Denys’s contempt cracked like dry wood. “Thou hast not got burghers by the ear, that know not a veal knuckle from their grandsire’s ribs; but soldiers—men that have gone to look for their dear comrades, and found their bones picked as clean by the crows as these I doubt have been by thee and thy mates. Men and women, saidst thou? And prithee, when spake I a word of women’s bones? Wouldst make a child suspect thee. Field of battle, comrade! Was not this house a field of battle half an hour agone? Drag him close to me, let me read his face. Now then—what is this, thou knave?”

He thrust a small object into the landlord’s sight so suddenly the man jerked back as if struck.

“Alas! I know not.”

“Well, I would not swear neither; but it is too like the thumb bone of a man’s hand.” Denys swallowed, and for all his bravado there was a shiver in him now, as if the cellar’s damp had found his spine. “Mates, my flesh it creeps. Churchyard! How know I this is not one?”

He drew his sword and began to rake the heap apart: earth, broken crockery, and bones scraped out onto the floor with a sound like a shovel in a midden. The landlord protested that Denys wasted his time.

“We poor innkeepers are sinners,” he babbled, clutching at common, petty guilt as if it might hide the greater. “We give short measure and baptize the wine—we are fain to do these things; the laws are so unjust to us; but we are not assassins. How could we afford to kill our customers? May Heaven’s lightning strike me dead if there be any bones there but such as have been used for meat. ’Tis the kitchen wench flings them here: I swear by God’s holy mother, by holy Paul, by holy Dominic, and Denys my patron saint—ah!”

Denys held up a bone under his eye and said nothing.

It was a bone no man, however ignorant, however lying, could confound with those of sheep or oxen. The sight stopped the man’s mouth as if a hand had clapped it. His hair rose visibly, bristling; his knees gave way as if the stones had slid out from under him.

But the archers dragged him upright and held him under the torch. Denys had raked free a skull—white as chalk, and yet no whiter than the living cheek set opposite it. Its empty sockets stared, and in that stare the murderer’s courage collapsed. His lips opened and opened, but no sound came.

“Ah!” said Denys, and now rage shook him harder than fear. “Look on the sockets out of which thou hast picked the eyes, and let them blast thine eyes, that crows shall pick out ere this week shall end. Now hold thou that while I search on. Hold it, I say, or here I rob the gallows—”

He threatened the quaking wretch with his naked sword until, with a groan, the landlord took the skull and held it, swaying, almost fainting—forced into a dreadful parody of a host offering, bearing not bread nor wine but the very proof of his own slaughterhouse.

The heap scattered wider. Alas—there were not one nor two. Many skulls came to light; many bones, too many for any kitchen’s honest leavings. Each time Denys uncovered another, the landlord moaned, and each moan sounded like the creak of a door in an empty house, a noise with no comfort in it.

Then Denys gave a cry stranger still, a note of distress that seemed to tear itself out of him against his will. He had drawn up, from the foulness, a mass of human hair.

It was long, glossy, golden—woman’s beautiful hair, still shining even in that cellar’s sour air, as if the dead carried a stubborn memory of sunlight.

At sight of it the archers shook the landlord by instinct, as men shake a sack to learn what foul thing lies inside. He only whined.

“I have a little sister with hair just so fair and shining as this,” Denys said hoarsely, and the words came not in French bravado now but in something deeper and more native, where feeling clung to the consonants like steam clings to a kitchen ceiling. “Jesu! If it should be hers! There—quick—take my sword and dagger, and keep them from my hand, lest I strike him dead and wrong the gibbet. And thou, poor innocent victim, on whose head this most lovely hair did grow, hear me swear this, on bended knee, never to leave this man till I see him broken to pieces on the wheel even for thy sake.”

He dropped to his knee upon the wet stone. The torches hissed above him; somewhere overhead the inn settled with a creak as if it listened.

He rose. “Ay, had he as many lives as here be hairs, I’d have them all, by God,” and he put the golden hair into his bosom as tenderly as a man stows away a relic.

Then fury took him like a fever. He seized the landlord by the neck and forced him down, grinding his face among the bones where they lay thickest. The assassin first yelled, then whined and whimpered, as a dog yells and then whines when its nose is forced into the body of some innocent it has killed.

“Now lend me thy bowstring, Philippe!”

He passed the string through the eyes of a skull and hung the ghastly thing round the man’s neck like an accursed collar. Then he hauled him up and kicked him—kicked him steadily, industriously—toward the kitchen, where an alderman of the burgh had arrived with constables and was taking an archer’s deposition.

The grave burgher started at the sight: the landlord driven in bleeding from a dozen scratches—scratches made, as it were, by the very dead—carrying his horrible ensign.

Denys came panting after and in a few hot words made the matter plain.

“Bind him like the rest,” said the alderman sternly. “I count him the blackest of them all.”

While they bound his hands, the poor wretch begged, as if begging for a cup of water, that “the skull might be taken from him.”

“Humph!” said the alderman, eyeing it. “Certes, I had not ordered such a thing to be put on mortal man. Yet being there, I will not lift voice nor finger to doff it. Methinks it fits thee truly, thou bloody dog. ’Tis thy ensign, and hangs well above a heart so foul as thine.”

He asked Denys whether they had secured the whole gang or only part.

“Your worship,” said Denys, “there are but seven of them, and this landlord. One we slew upstairs, one we trundled down dead, the rest are bound before you.”

“Good! Go fetch the dead one from upstairs, and lay him beside him I caused to be removed.”

Here a voice broke in—thin, peevish, like a guinea-fowl’s cry in a farmyard, an officious little sound amid so much blood and judgment.

“Now, now, now, where is the hand? That is what I want to see.”

It was a little pettifogging clerk, eyes bright with the hunger not for justice but for documentation. The world to him was a ledger; even horror must be translated into items that could be counted, labeled, and displayed.

“You will find it above,” said someone, “nailed to the door-post by a crossbow bolt.”

“Good!” squeaked the clerk, and leaned to whisper his master: “What a goodly show will the pièces de conviction make!” He began to write them down, enumerating each in separate squeaks as his quill scratched: Skulls—Bones—A woman’s hair—A thief’s hands—1 axe—2 carcasses—1 crossbow bolt. His words made a strange dominion: Latin and French tags turned lived terror into official tokens, as if a change of language could drain the warm, untranslatable weight from what men had seen and smelled.

He itched to search the cellar himself; there might be other valuable morsels of evidence—an ear, or even an earring. The alderman assented. The clerk seized a torch and hurried toward the stair—

—and an accident stopped him and carried him, in a heartbeat, a step or two the opposite way.

The constables had gone up the stair in single file. But the head constable no sooner saw the phosphorescent corpse seated by the bedside than he stood stupefied. Next he began to shake like one in an ague, terror gaining on him until he uttered a sort of howl and recoiled swiftly. Forgetting the steps in his recoil, he tumbled backward over his nearest companion. The second, shaken by that shout and catching a glimpse of something horrid, was already staggering back and could not sustain the head man’s weight—who, like most head constables, was ponderous. The two carried away the third, and the three the fourth, and they streamed into the kitchen and settled on the floor overlapping each other like a sequence laid out on a card-table.

The clerk, coming hastily with his torch, ran into the fourth man and was knocked flat on his back—the ace of that fair quint. There he lay kicking and waving his torch, seeming for a moment to flourish it in triumph, but in truth convulsed, wind and sense driven out together by the blow.

“What is to do now, in Heaven’s name?” cried the alderman, starting up in alarm.

Denys explained with a quick, contemptuous brevity, and offered to accompany his worship.

“So be it,” said the alderman. His men picked themselves up, rueful and red, and he put himself at their head and examined the premises above and below, the torches’ hiss and the men’s uneasy footsteps making a sour accompaniment in every room.

As for the prisoners, their questioning was postponed until they could be confronted with the servant.

Before dawn the thieves—alive and dead—and all the relics and evidences of crime and retribution were swept away into the law’s net. The inn, which should have been a place of bread-scent and clinking cups, fell silent and almost deserted, as if the stones themselves held their breath to forget what they had heard.

There remained but one constable, and Denys and Gerard—the latter still sleeping heavily, as if the night, with all its smoke and shouting, had been muffled for him into a single deep, wordless sound.

Gerard woke as one rises from a cauldron that has boiled over in the night and been skimmed at dawn—his mind still filmed, but the worst scum gone. Denys sat near, not dozing, but watching, with that soldier’s vigilance that listens even with the eyes. Through the small casement came the town’s noon—distant hammering on wood, a cart’s iron hoop crying on stone, pigeons clapping and cooing under the eaves; and underneath all, a steady human murmur like a hearth-fire heard from the next room.

“It is you for sleeping!” Denys broke out. “Why, ’tis high noon.”

“It was a blessed sleep,” said Gerard, and his voice surprised him with its steadiness. “Methinks Heaven sent it me. It hath put as it were a veil between me and that awful night. To think that you and I sit here alive and well. How terrible a dream I seem to have had!”

“Ay, lad; that is the wise way to look at these things when once they are past—why, they are dreams, shadows.” Denys nodded toward the table as if that were the proper altar for gratitude. “Break thy fast, and then thou wilt think no more on’t. Moreover, I promised to bring thee on to the town by noon, and take thee to his worship.”

Denys spoke of breakfast as if it were a remedy compounded by old women and proved by generations. Gerard obeyed him with the obedience of a man newly returned to his body. He took coarse rye bread, dark as tilled earth, tore it with his hands, and sopped it in red wine. The wine ran into the bread’s pores, staining it a purplish brown, softening its stubborn grain until it yielded like muscle warmed. He ate—slow at first, then with the simple hunger that comes when fear has at last loosened its grip. The sourness of rye, the fruit and bite of the wine, the faint smell of woodsmoke in the room—these things, homely and exact, stitched him back into daylight.

Then Denys would not let him brood. They went out.

The road beyond the lodging lay innocent enough; birds chattered in the hedgerows as if no human throat had cried there. Yet Gerard’s feet, having learned the night’s lesson, led him unwillingly over the very place where steel had sung. He saw again, with his waking eyes, what his sleep had tried to fold away: trampled grass, a smear of earth where bodies had wrestled, the broken twigs in the ditch. The sounds of noon—children calling somewhere, a dog’s bark, the rhythmic thud of a mallet—did not belong to that patch of ground, and that mismatch made him shudder. It was as if the world had changed its language between one hour and the next, and his memory could not translate.

They turned back, and took the road for the little town. Gerard’s gaze kept slipping to the hedges, as if every green bank hid an ambush; he hated his own unreasonable expectation of sudden hands and knives, but could not lay it down at once. Denys walked with the ease of a man who trusts walls and people more than open fields; he hummed once under his breath, a tune without words, as though to set the air right again.

At length the houses gathered, close-shouldered, the street narrowing into a throat that swallowed hoofbeats and spat them back in echoes. The town had its own music: the clink of a blacksmith’s tools, a churn of voices in a market nook, the splash of water poured from a pail. Compared with the wild silence of the road, it was a kind of safety. Noise, here, was not menace but proof—proof of hearths tended, of loaves baked, of lives continuing.

Denys led him straight to an inn whose sign creaked gently: The White Hart. From within came the warm breath of men and cooking—yeast and ale, fat meeting flame, onions sweating down in a pot. A woman’s laugh rose, then was swallowed by the room’s general rumble.

“No fear of cut-throats here,” said Denys, with a confidence born of familiarity. “I know the landlord this many a year. He is a burgess, and looks to be bailiff. ’Tis here I was making for yestreen. But we lost time, and night o’ertook us—and—”

“And you saw a woman at the door, and would be wiser than a Jeanneton; she told us they were nought,” Gerard finished, unable to keep the tartness from his tone.

Denys’s eyebrows lifted, then lowered as if in honest shame. “Why, what saved our lives if not a woman? Ay, and risked her own to do it.”

“That is true, Denys.” Gerard’s chest tightened, not with fear now, but with a fierce, almost childlike gratitude that demanded a shape, a name, a face. “And though women are nothing to me, I long to thank this poor girl, and reward her—ay, though I share every doit in my purse with her. Do not you?”

“Parbleu.”

“Where shall we find her?”

“Mayhap the alderman will tell us. We must go to him first.”

So they went to the alderman—through streets that smelled of damp stone and stale straw, past a baker’s where hot crust breathed out into the air, past a yard where someone split kindling with measured strokes that sounded, to Gerard’s startled nerves, like blows. In each tongue he heard in the street—Burgundian turns, French clipped by trade, words thrown quick between neighbors—there was that hidden power of a place: the way a town speaks can make a stranger feel either invited or judged. Gerard, who carried other sounds within him and other names for bread and wine and mercy, felt the edges of his own speech press against theirs.

The alderman received them with a most singular and inexplicable expression of countenance. It was not displeasure exactly, nor welcome; rather the look of a man who has tasted something and cannot decide whether it is sweet or spoiled. He studied them as though the two travelers had walked in carrying a story already half-known to him.

However, after a moment’s reflection, he let a grim smile creep over his mouth, like a knife slid back into its sheath. Then he began to question Gerard closely—where they had come from, what hour they had been set upon, how many assailants, what weapons, what words were spoken. He wrote down the answers with careful strokes, as exact as a cook measuring spices that might, misjudged, ruin the whole dish.

When he had done, he looked up and said in a tone that made law sound as everyday as buying salt: they must stay in the town till the thieves were tried, and be at hand to give evidence, on peril of fine and imprisonment.

They looked very blank at that; Denys’s mouth opened a little, then shut. Gerard thought of Rome and of Margaret as of a loaf left half-baked—time and heat required, but now interrupted; his impatience rose like yeast.

“However,” the alderman added, as if offering a small sweet after a bitter draught, “’twill not be long, the culprits having been taken red-handed.”

Then, with that same odd gleam in his eye, he said, “And you know, in any case you could not leave the place this week.”

Denys stared at this remark, his face hardening in puzzlement. Gerard, thinking the old gentleman’s provincial mind had made a harmless jest, smiled—smiled at the simplicity of dreaming that a little town in Burgundy could detain him from Rome and Margaret, as if the world’s great fire burned no hotter than their own small hearth.

But what lay nearest both their hearts was not Rome at that instant, nor even freedom. It was the memory of a girl in the dark, the sudden brave voice that had bent danger aside.

“Your worship,” said Gerard, and the words came out with a warmth that surprised even him, “we cannot find our benefactress in the town.”

“Nay,” said the alderman, “but who is your benefactress?”

“Who?” Gerard leaned forward, the room’s sounds falling away as if a door had closed on them. “Why, the good girl that came to you by night and saved our lives at peril of her own. Oh sir, our hearts burn within us to thank and bless her; where is she?”

“In prison, sir? Good lack—for what misdeed?”

“Well, she is a witness, and may be a necessary one.”

“Why, Messire Bailiff,” Denys broke in, smooth as warm butter on trenchers, “you lay not all your witnesses by the heels, I trow.”

The alderman—pleased to be titled bailiff, as a man is pleased when a fine spice is named in his honor—grew looser of tongue. “In a case of blood we detain all testimony that is like to give us leg-bail, and so defeat justice; and that is why we still keep the women folk. For a man at odd times hides a week in one mind; but a woman, if she do her duty to the realm o’ Friday, she shall undo it afore Sunday, or try. Could you see yon wench now, you should find her a-blubbering at having betrayed five males to the gallows. Had they been females, we might have trusted to a subpoena. For they despise one another. And there they show some sense. But now I think on’t, there were other reasons for laying this one by the heels. Hand me those depositions, young sir.”

He set his glasses upon his nose as carefully as a cook sets a pot to simmer, and began to read, lips moving to each line. “Ay! she was implicated; she was one of the band.”

A loud denial sprang from Denys and Gerard together, like two staves struck at once.

“No need to deave me,” said the alderman. “Here ’tis in black and white. ‘Jean Hardy (that is one of the thieves), being questioned, confessed that—humph? Ay, here ’tis—‘And that the girl Manon was the decoy, and her sweetheart was Georges Vipont, one of the band; and hanged last month: and that she had been deject ever since, and had openly blamed the band for his death, saying if they had not been rank cowards, he had never been taken; and it is his opinion she did but betray them out of very spite—and—’”

“His opinion!” Gerard flamed, indignation ringing in his voice like a clapper in a bell. “What signifies the opinion of a cut-throat, burning to be revenged on her who has delivered him to justice? And an you go to that, what avails his testimony? Is a thief never a liar? Is he not aye a liar? and here a motive to lie—revenge—why, ’tis the strongest of all the passions. And oh, sir! what madness to question a detected felon and listen to him lying away an honest life—as if he were a true man swearing in open day, with his true hand on the Gospel laid!”

“Young man,” said the alderman, “restrain thy heat in presence of authority! I find by your tone you are a stranger. Know then that in this land we question all the world. We are not so weak as to hope to get at the truth by shutting either our left ear or our right.”

“And so you would listen to Satan belying the saints!”

“Ta! ta! The law meddles but with men and women, and these cannot utter a story all lies, let them try ever so. Wherefore we shut not the barn-door against any man’s grain. Only having taken it in, we do winnow and sift it. And who told you I had swallowed the thief’s story whole like fair water? Not so. I did but credit so much on’t as was borne out by better proof.”

“Better proof?” Gerard stared, the blood in his cheeks cooling. “Why, who but the thieves would breathe a word against her?”

“Marry, herself.”

“Herself, sir? What—did you question her too?”

“I tell you we question all the world. Here is her deposition; can you read? Read it yourself, then.”

Gerard took the paper, and, leaning so Denys could see, read the words that smelt of ink, fear, and stale stone walls:

“I am a native of Epinal. I left my native place two years ago because I was unfortunate: I could not like the man they bade me. So my father beat me. I ran away from my father. I went to service. I left service because the mistress was jealous of me. The reason that she gave for turning me off was, because I was saucy. Last year I stood in the marketplace to be hired with other girls. The landlord of ‘The Fair Star’ hired me. I was eleven months with him. A young man courted me. I loved him. I found out that travellers came and never went away again. I told my lover. He bade me hold my peace. He threatened me. I found my lover was one of a band of thieves. When travellers were to be robbed, the landlord went out and told the band to come. Then I wept and prayed for the travellers’ souls. I never told. A month ago my lover died.

“The soldier put me in mind of my lover. He was bearded like him I had lost. I cannot tell whether I should have interfered, if he had had no beard. I am sorry I told now.”

The sheet seemed to weigh more than parchment ought; it nearly slipped from Gerard’s fingers. Now, at last, he heard—beneath the alderman’s dry voice and the scrape of quills—the sentence humming like a rope under strain. Manon’s life stood in the very draft of death.

He dropped to his knees, not as a courtier kneels, but as a man flung down by a sudden blow. “Oh, sir! think of the difference between those cruel men and this poor weak woman! Could you have the heart to send her to the same death with them; could you have the heart to condemn us to look on and see her slaughtered, who, but that she risked her life for ours, had not now been in jeopardy? Alas, sir! show me and my comrade some pity, if you have none for her, poor soul. Denys and I be true men, and you will rend our hearts if you kill that poor simple girl. What can we do? What is left for us to do then but cut our throats at her gallows’ foot?”

The alderman was tough, yet mortal; Gerard’s shaking fervor first amazed him, then found a tender place like a knife finding a joint. He showed it oddly—by turning peevish, as if moved against his will. “There, get up, do,” said he. “I doubt whether anybody would say as many words for me. What ho, Daniel! go fetch the town clerk.”

The clerk entered from the next room, smelling of wax and ledger dust; a man built of refusals.

“Here is a foolish lad fretting about yon girl,” said the alderman. “Can we stretch a point? say we admit her to bear witness, and question her favourably.”

The clerk shook his head as steadily as a mill-wheel. “Nay, sir, we cannot do that: she was not concerned in this business. Had she been accessory, we might have offered her a pardon to bear witness.”

“But she did better,” Gerard cried. “Instead of being accessory, she stayed the crime; and she proffered herself as witness by running hither with the tale.”

“Tush, young man, ’tis a matter of law.”

They argued long: the alderman pushing, the clerk barring every opening with “cannot,” “may not,” “is not done.” And this, by a turn of temper as sudden as a gust in a chimney, proved Manon’s salvation; for the alderman, nettled by so much denial, struck the table and swore he would show the man he could do anything he chose.

So Manon was brought out. Her eyes were raw as if washed in brine; her face had the whiteness of flour before it is wetted, and the tremble of a small creature held too long. Upon the landlord of “The White Hart” becoming bondsman, and Denys laying down five gold pieces—bright, round suns fallen into a clerk’s palm—and upon Manon promising (after Denys coaxed her, voice low, almost like a lullaby) to attend as witness, the alderman released her.

Yet, to ease his conscience, he must season his mercy with a coarse jest, like a man sweetening sour wine with honey and calling it charity. “The town had to buy a new rope for everybody hanged, and present it to the bourreau, or compound with him in money: and she is not, in my opinion, worth this municipal expense—whereas decided characters, like her late confederates, are.”

Thus they carried her off: Gerard capering round her in sheer relief; Denys speaking briskly of a troublesome personage’s speedy demise, as if to prop her courage the way one props a failing fire with kindling. But Manon wept—soft, miserable drops that foretold nothing fair.

The street had its own breath and ear, as a village has: the clop of hooves, the rasp of wheels on cobbles, the shrill cries that pass from mouth to mouth faster than any runner. Word slid ahead of them. Before they reached “The White Hart,” folk had found her out; and, having heard the tale from the archers—who told it warmly in her favour—followed her with hurrahs and rough encouragement. The sound of it, swelling behind her like a tide, steadied her; being backed by numbers, she dared lift her head.

The landlord, too, measured the thing in his own scales: not of justice, but of custom. A heroine under his roof would draw drinkers like the scent of roasting meat draws hungry men. He received her politely, and gave her an upper chamber—high, safe, and yet a cage. There she shut herself away, and, alone, let tears run again, as water runs when no hand turns the sluice.

Her mind was but a little ripple: up and down, down and up—now bold with the street’s shouts in her ears, now sunk again in private dread. Gerard and Denys bade the landlord be kind to her, and keep her a prisoner without letting her feel it; then they went out.

And lo, as they stepped into the street, two processions came toward them from opposite ends, like two currents meeting where the channel narrows.

One was large, loud, thick with noise—howls, hoots, and those cries by which rude throats confess, now and then, their kinship to beasts of field and forest: a pack-sound, hungry for spectacle. The other was thin: a few nuns and friars, slow and silent, feet whispering, beads clicking faintly like small bones.

The prisoners were going to exposure in the market-place.

The gathered bones of the victims were coming to the churchyard.

The two met in a narrow street almost at the inn door, and could not pass. The bier that bore the relics of mortality wedged against the cart that carried the men who had made those bones what they were—and in a few hours must die for it themselves. For a space the crowd’s mind, dulled by habit, did not take the meaning. Then a woman—sharp-voiced as a jay—cried, “Look at your work, ye dogs!”

The cry flew. A horrible yell rose, a whole town’s throat turned into one. The culprits groaned and tried to hide their heads upon their bosoms, but could not, their hands being tied. There they stood—pale, hollow-eyed—despair made visible. How their eyes clung to the bier; how they envied those bones, already past fear, already beyond jeers, already out of the market’s noise and into silence.

Denys and Gerard, the cause of both processions, stood and looked. Even Manon, hearing the uproar, crept to her window; and, like women will, hid her face and peeped trembling through her fingers.

That meeting parted the two friends. Denys yielded to curiosity and revenge and went with the noisy crowd. Gerard doffed his bonnet and, with a piety that sat in him as naturally as hunger, followed the poor remains of those whose fate had so nearly been his own.

For a time he was the one lay mourner, solitary amid the thin file. But when they reached the suburbs, far from the louder lure of the market-place, others began to join: an artisan wiping his hands and dropping his tools, a shopman shutting his door, men drawn by pity, by common humanity, and perhaps by the example of Gerard—bareheaded now, and grave. Together they watched the bones laid, with the Church’s prayers, in hallowed ground. The air there was different: the coarse roar of town life dulled to a distant murmur; what you heard was footfall, prayer, and the soft scrape of earth—sounds that do not mock the dead.

When the rites were done, Gerard stepped to the curé and offered to buy a mass for their souls.

Gerard, son of Catherine, ever looked at two sides of a penny; so he tried, with the nimblest conscience, to purchase the mass a trifle under the usual terms, pleading the pitiable circumstances. But the good curé parried him gently and adroitly, like a man turning aside a small knife with the flat of a spoon, and screwed him up to the market price with a bland smile.

In the bargaining they found a likeness of spirit. Piety and worldly prudence do keep company, though not often do they walk so arm in arm as in these two. Their collision in the prayer-market bred esteem, as when knight meets knight worthy of his steel. Moreover, the curé loved a morsel of gossip; and finding his customer was one who had fought the thieves at Domfront, he drew him into the parlour to hear all from his own lips.

His heart warmed. “God was good to thee,” said he. “I thank Him for’t with all my soul. Thou art a good lad.” Then, dryly, as if pinching out a candle: “Shouldst have told me this tale in the churchyard. I doubt I had given thee the mass for love. However—’tis ill luck to go back upon a bargain. But I’ll broach a bottle of my old Médoc for thee: and few be the guests I would do that for.”

He went to a cupboard, and while he groped for the choice bottle he muttered, half to himself, “At their old tricks again!”

“Plaît-il?” said Gerard.

“I said nought. Ay, here ’tis.”

“Nay, your reverence. You surely spoke: you said, ‘At their old tricks again!’”

“Said I so in sooth?” The curé smiled, and set to work with practiced hands, drawing the cork so the sound was a soft, satisfying sigh, like a loaf cracking as it cools. He filled a cup for each. Then he put a log on the fire—for stoves were none in Burgundy—and the flames caught with a low crackle, a homely sound that made the room feel inhabited, safe.

“And so I said ‘At their old tricks!’ did I? Come, sip the good wine; and, whilst it lasts, story for story, I care not if I tell you a little tale.”

Gerard’s eyes brightened. “As my life.”

“Nay, but raise not thine expectations too high neither. ’Tis but a foolish trifle compared with thine adventures.”

And the curé told his tale: of a poor priest in a stingy parish who, having found most of his baptised babes later cheated the Church by ending as pendards—hanged and “buried in air”—demanded burial fees at the christening table, taking greed by the sleeve and turning it back upon itself. How parishioners plotted, how a churchwarden complained, how the bishop summoned him with a frown; how the curé confessed the fact, then laid out his reason: to keep them from the gallows by making them fear paying fees twice. How the bishop laughed till tears ran, approved the stratagem, and later moved the curé to a better parish, where he might offer old Médoc to worthy guests.

As the tale ended, a light broke in on Gerard’s face; he saw the man behind the story.

“Ay,” said his host, meeting his look, “I am that curé. So now thou canst guess why I said ‘At their old tricks.’ My life on’t they have wheedled my successor into remitting those funeral fees. You are well out of that parish. And so am I.”

At that moment the curé’s little niece burst in, breathless. “Uncle, the weighing—la! a stranger!” and fled again as quickly, the very sound of her slippers darting away like a small bird’s panic.

The curé rose at once, yet would not loose Gerard. “Wet thy beard once more, and come with me.”

In the church porch they found the sexton with a huge pair of scales and weights of all sizes. Several humble folk stood by, their talk subdued by the place, though the world’s noises still leaked in—wheels in the street, a vendor’s cry thinning with distance.

Soon a woman stepped forward with a sickly child. “Be it heavy be it light, I vow, in rye meal of the best, whate’er this child shall weigh, and the same will duly pay to Holy Church, an if he shall cast his trouble. Pray, good people, for this child, and for me his mother hither come in dole and care!”

The child was weighed and yelled as if the scale had been the font, his thin cry echoing off stone, a little creature protesting the world’s measures.

“Courage! dame,” cried Gerard. “This is a good sign. There is plenty of life here to battle its trouble.”

“Now, blest be the tongue that tells me so,” said she, and hushed him against her breast, rocking as if her arms were a cradle and a prayer. She stood aside while another mother brought her child.

Presently a loud dictatorial voice cut the air. “Way there—make way for the seigneur!”

The small folk parted like waves before a lordly galley, and in strode the lord of the manor, gorgeous as a painted saint: cap with feather and a topaz at its root, furred jerkin, satin doublet, red hose, shoes like skates, diamond-hilted sword in velvet scabbard, and a hawk on his wrist. He flung himself into the scales as if he were lord of the zodiac too. The hawk balanced, flapped, then settled and winked.

While the sexton heaved in the great weights, the curé told Gerard, “My lord had been sick unto death, and vowed his weight in bread and cheese to the poor, the Church taking her tenth.”

The seigneur, pressing his staff on the other scale, grinned at the trick of it.

“Permit me, my lord,” said the curé, “if your lordship continues to press your lordship’s staff on the other scale, you will disturb the balance.”

His lordship removed it—but then leaned on it. The curé objected again, politely and firmly.

“Mille diables! what am I to do with it, then?” cried the seigneur.

“Deign to hold it out so, my lord, wide of both scales.”

When the seigneur did, and so fell into the trap that Holy Church had laid for him, the curé whispered to Gerard, “Cretensis incidit in Cretensem!”—diamond cut diamond. Then, aloud, with an obsequious air, “If that your lordship grudges Heaven full weight, you might set the hawk on your lacquey, and so save a pound.”

“Gramercy for thy rede, cure,” cried the great man, reproachful. “Shall I for one sorry pound grudge my poor fowl the benefit of Holy Church? I’d as lieve the devil should have me and all my house as her, any day i’ the year.”

“Sweet is affection,” whispered the curé.

“Between a bird and a brute,” whispered Gerard.

“Tush!” The curé looked frightened, as if words themselves could summon peril in sacred stone.

The seigneur’s weight was booked. And men—then as now—did not bargain only over wheat or cloth; they bargained with Heaven too, striving always for the sunny side. In that age, body being master, all sentiments took material form: repentance by scourge, prayer by bead, bribery by candle, sanctity by fish, and gratitude weighed out in bread and cheese down to the last ounce.

While this went on, the curé had been soliciting the seigneur to step into the church and give order what should be done with his great-great-grandfather.

“Ods bodikins! what, have you dug him up?”

“Nay, my lord, he never was buried.”

“What, the old dict was true after all?”

“So true that the workmen this very day found a skeleton erect in the pillar they are repairing. I had sent to my lord at once, but I knew he would be here.”

“It is he! ’Tis he!” cried the descendant, quickening his pace. “Let us go see the old boy. This youth is a stranger, I think.”

Gerard bowed.

“Know then,” said the lord, as they entered the porch, “that my great-great-grandfather held his head high; and being on the point of death, revolted against lying under the aisle with his forbears for mean folk to pass over. So, as the tradition goes, he swore his son—my great-grandfather—to bury him erect in one of the pillars of the church. ‘For,’ quoth he, ‘NO BASE MAN SHALL PASS OVER MY STOMACH.’ Peste!”

Even as he spoke, his lordship parried with his stick a skull that came hopping at him, bowled by a boy in the middle of the aisle. The child took to his heels yelling the moment he saw what he had done. The seigneur, in a gust of temper, flung the skull after him. The curé cried out and put forth his arm to hinder him—but too late.

The curé groaned aloud. As if the groan had loosed a nest of devils, up started a whole pack of children from some ambuscade; unseen, but heard loud enough, they clattered out of the church like a covey rising in a thick wood, the racket of their flight turning holy hush to a barnyard din.

“Oh! these pernicious brats,” cried the curé. “The workmen cannot go to their nonemete but the church is rife with them. Pray Heaven they have not found his late lordship; nay, I mind, I hid his lordship under a workman’s jerkin, and—saints defend us! the jerkin has been moved.”

His worst fear was true. The rising generation of plebeians had played mischief with the haughty old noble: jockeyed for the bones, pocketed such pieces as suited their rude games, scattered the rest with the careless cruelty of children who have not yet learned what a body once held.

“I’ll excommunicate them,” roared the curé, “and all their race.”

“Never heed,” said the scapegrace seigneur, stroking his hawk as one strokes a beloved beast. “There is enough of him to swear by. Put him back! put him back!”

“Surely, my lord,” pleaded the curé, “’tis your will his bones be laid in hallowed earth, and masses said for his poor prideful soul?”

The noble stroked his hawk again, as if weighing devotion in feathers. “Are ye there, Master Cure? Nay, the business is too old: he is out of purgatory by this time, up or down. I shall not draw my purse-strings for him. Every dog his day. Adieu, messires—adieu, ancestor!” And he sauntered off, whistling to his hawk and caressing it, his whistle sharp and bright in the vaulted air.

His reverence watched him go, rueful as a man who has set bread to rise and finds the oven cold.

They set the three of them up in the market-place, pinioned like felons on a painter’s board, arms strained back, shoulders wrenched, so that the very posture made confession seem to creep out of the bones. The town had ordained two full hours of this misery, not for punishment alone, but for recognition: that any man or woman who had met these night-prowlers on a lonely road, and carried the bruise of it in memory or flesh, might come forward and add fresh crimes to the count.

Yet the hours wore through, measured by the marketplace’s own small noises—the slap of sandals on cobble, the creak of carts, the shrill calls of hawkers, the sparrows quarreling in the eaves—and no new voice rose to accuse. It was not so strange: such men hunted weary strangers, and strangers, once plundered, went on, nursing their fear in another parish and another tongue.

At last the officers stepped in to take them down.

Then, as the ropes were loosened, a scream cleft the air—one of those cries that makes every sound after it seem thin and guilty. A woman in the crowd thrust out her hand and pointed, eyes wide as if they would leave her skull; her lips shaped a name, a word, a whole tale—and she fell like a sack, senseless on the stones.

People surged to her, some with pity, more with that sharp appetite a crowd has for calamity. As she came back to herself, their guesses bubbled and collided.

“’Twas him she marked.”

“Nay, this one.”

“No, no,” cried another, “yon hangdog with the hair down round his neck.”

The woman’s mind cleared in a flash—cleared and broke. She sprang up and flew, not at the pinioned man’s face but at his throat, like a mother-beast. “My child!” she cried. “Man! man! give me back my child!” And with both hands she seized the glossy golden hair the officers had hung about the culprit’s neck—some trophy of the road—and tore it free. She pressed it to her mouth, kissed it again and again as if warmth might return to it by sheer will.

Then the token told its own truth: hair without the head, a relic without the living. She sank down shrieking, clutching it to her breast, sobbing till her whole body shook over those poor locks as over a grave.

The market, that had been a market an instant before, turned wolf. A low growl ran through it; men’s hands went to their girdles. In those days every man carried death close, and the difference between justice and slaughter was often no thicker than a breath.

The assassin would have been torn and hacked where he stood, but Denys was on them like steel drawn from a sheath. He whipped out his sword, planted himself, and shouted, “A moi, camarades!” Other archers sprang in, and their blades made a hedge. “Who lays a finger on him dies,” Denys cried, and his voice, hard as a struck bell, rang above the snarling.

“What vengeance is this?” he called to them. “Would you be so mad as rob the wheel, and give the vermin an easy death?”

Words did little; naked iron did more. The crowd held back, lips pulled from teeth, eyes bright with the lust to strike. Seeing how the temper ran, the municipal officers drew close; with archers and staves they made a guard and carried the prisoners back toward gaol, prudently, before the market-place could boil over.

They went amid hoots that struck officer and culprit alike. Denys watched them safely lodged, and then, thinking of Gerard and the strange mishap of that dawn, turned his steps toward the White Hart; he expected to find his comrade there.

On the way he glanced up and saw two girls at a first-floor window, hands busy at their work. Their cheeks were high-colored, their laughter ready. Denys saluted; they smiled; words flew as easily as swallows under an eave. Their voices braided with the street’s music—hoofbeats, a distant hammer, a peddler’s chant—as if they belonged to the town’s own soundscape.

He invited them to eat at the White Hart. They refused. He accepted the refusal with the art of a man who knows refusal is sometimes merely the first seasoning. They consented.

And in that bright, unguarded company he let the thought of Gerard slip away like a coin through a careless finger.

Meanwhile Gerard, the very man forgotten, was marched off toward gaol. His heart had been a trapped bird at first; then, step by step, it beat itself steadier. He stopped short in the street and demanded, with such dignity as fear allows, by what authority he was taken.

“By the vice-baillie’s,” said the constable.

“The vice-baillie?” Gerard’s voice faltered into bewilderment. “Alas! what have I, a stranger, done to offend a vice-baillie? This charge of sorcery must be a blind. No sorcerer am I; but a poor true lad far from his home.”

The vagueness displeased the officer. “Show him the capias, Jacques,” he said.

Jacques held the writ out in both hands at arm’s length as if paper itself might scorch him; at the same moment the big constable pinned Gerard, sudden and rough. Both were on edge, guarding the document with superstitious care, fearing he might snatch it and work some devilry by touching it.

Gerard had no such thought. Indeed, he looked on it as on a snake. He only craned his neck and read. To his astonishment, the name signing it was the very alderman who had spoken him fair before. Courage stirred. He told them there must be error and demanded to be taken before the alderman.

“What say you to that, Jacques?” asked the constable, hesitating.

“Impossible. We have no orders to take him before his worship. Read the writ!”

“Nay, but good kind fellows,” Gerard pleaded, “what harm can it be? I will give you each an ecu.”

The constable’s eyes flicked. “Jacques, what say you to that?”

“Humph! I say we have no orders not to take him to his worship. Read the writ!”

“Then say we take him to prison round by his worship.”

It was agreed with the speed that silver gives. The money passed; they told Gerard, with the air of men performing a kindness, that he should be grateful too. He tried to show it, but gratitude, feigned, stuck in his throat like dry crust. He could not season his face with falsehood to please another man’s appetite.

So he came again into the alderman’s presence, heart thudding like a pestle in a mortar, and begged in a voice that shook to know what he had done since he had left that very room with Manon and Denys.

“Nought that I know of,” said the alderman.

When the writ was shown, he nodded. “I signed it at daybreak. I get old, and my memory faileth me: in discussing of the girl I quite forgot your own offence. But I remember now. All is well. You are he I committed for sorcery. Stay! ere you go to gaol, you shall hear what your accuser says: run and fetch him, you.”

The messenger fumbled about and could not find the man at once. The alderman, growing impatient, turned back to Gerard and told him bluntly the charge: he was said to have set a dead body burning with diabolical fire—flame that shone and yet did not consume. “And if ’tis true, young man,” the alderman added, “I’m sorry for thee; for thou wilt assuredly burn with fire of good pine logs in the market-place of Neufchasteau.”

The words brought in their own smell—the resinous bite of pitch, the thick smoke that catches in the throat. Gerard’s mouth went dry. “Oh, sir, for pity’s sake let me have speech with his reverence the curé.”

The alderman advised against it. “The Church is harder upon sorcerers than is the corporation.”

“But, sir, I am innocent,” Gerard burst out, somewhere between a snarl and a whine, shame and terror wrestling on one tongue.

“Oh, if you think you are innocent—officer, go with him to the curé; but see he ’scape you not. Innocent, quotha?”

They found the curé not in stole and dignity but in his doublet, mending a wheelbarrow as calmly as if no man in his parish ever faced a stake. Gerard poured out the whole matter—his phosphorus, his fright, his desperate trick—and pleaded as if pleading could season fate. “Just for using a little phosphorus in self-defence against cut-throats they are going to hang.”

It stood Gerard in good stead that he had already told the tale at length; the priest had the facts in hand, and could grasp them where the corporation clutched at mere terror. The curé put on a grave face and said aloud, “I must question you privately on this untoward business.” He led Gerard to a small room, bade the officer stand without and guard the door, and be ready if called.

The big constable remained outside, quaking, as though the room might lift away on a gust of brimstone and leave only a stench behind.

The moment the door closed, the curé’s countenance unlocked; his eyes brightened with pure curiosity. “Show me the trick on’t,” he said.

“I cannot, sir, unless the room be darkened.”

The curé shut the wooden shutter and made twilight. “Now, then.”

“But on what shall I put it?” Gerard asked. “Here is no dead face. ’Twas that made it look so dire.” The priest groped, found a carved figure. “Good; here is an image: ’tis my patron saint.”

“Heaven forbid!” Gerard recoiled. “That were profanation.”

“Pshaw! ’twill rub off, will’t not?”

“Ay, but it goes against me to take such liberty with a saint,” Gerard said, and his scruple was honest—his conscience had a dialect of its own, not easily translated into another man’s impatience.

“Fiddlestick!” said the divine.

“To be sure,” Gerard argued, trying to make devotion serve his case, “by putting it on his holiness will show your reverence it is no Satanic art.”

“Mayhap ’twas for that I did propose it,” the curé replied, shrewd as any lawyer under a cassock.

Thus heartened, Gerard took his bottle and, with careful finger, laid the substance where he had laid it before—eyes, nostrils, hair. In the half-dark the saint’s gaze sprang into a sharp, eerie light; the nostrils flared as if breathing fire; patches of hair kindled and shone, and then the whole face glimmered like a glow-worm pinned to wood. The curé jumped back, and even in his readiness to laugh he crossed himself.

“By’r Lady,” he cried, “’tis strange; and small my wonder they took you for a magician, seeing a dead face thus fired. Now come thy ways with me!”

He flung on his grey gown and great hat, and in a few minutes they stood again before the alderman. Beside him—like a spice too bitter for any stew—stood the accuser: a singular figure in red hose and red shoes, black gown with blue bands, and cocked hat. His very clothes seemed to shout, as if he tried to win authority by loud colors when his truth was pale.

The curé saluted the alderman, then turned on the man with a good-humored contempt. “So, Mangis, at thy work again, babbling away honest men’s lives! Come, your worship, this is the old tale! Two of a trade can ne’er agree. Here is Mangis, who professes sorcery, and would sell himself to Satan to-night, but that Satan is not so weak as buy what he can have gratis—this Mangis, who would be a sorcerer, but is only a quacksalver—accuses of magic a true lad, who did but use in self-defence a secret of chemistry well-known to me and all churchmen.”

“But he is no churchman,” objected the alderman, “to dabble in such mysteries.”

“He is more churchman than layman,” the curé returned instantly, “being convent bred, and in the lesser orders. Therefore, sorcerer, withdraw thy plaint without more words!”

Mangis stiffened. “That I will not, your reverence. A sorcerer I am, but a white one, not a black one. I make no pact with Satan, but on the contrary still battle him with lawful and necessary arts. I ne’er profane the sacraments, as do the black sorcerers, nor turn myself into a cat and go sucking infants’ blood, nor e’en their breath, nor set dead men o’ fire. I but tell the peasants when their cattle and their hens are possessed, and at what time of the moon to plant rye, and what days in each month are lucky for wooing of women and selling of bullocks and so forth: above all, it is my art and my trade to detect the black magicians—as I did that whole tribe of them who were burnt at Dol but last year.”

“Ay, Mangis,” said the curé, and his voice sharpened like a knife on a stone. “And what is the upshot of that famous fire thy tongue did kindle?”

“Why, their ashes were cast to the wind.”

“Ay. But the true end of thy comedy is this. The parliament of Dijon hath since sifted the matter, and found they were no sorcerers, but good and peaceful citizens; and but last week did order masses to be said for their souls, and expiatory farces and mysteries to be played for them in seven towns of Burgundy; all which will not of those cinders make men and women again.”

The curé leaned forward, staff in hand. “Now ’tis our custom in this land, when we have slain the innocent by hearkening false knaves like thee, not to blame our credulous ears, but the false tongue that gulled them. Therefore bethink thee that, at a word from me to my lord bishop, thou wilt smell burning pine nearer than e’er knave smelt it and lived, and wilt travel on a smoky cloud to him whose heart thou bearest—for the word devil in the Latin it meaneth ‘false accuser’—and whose livery thou wearest.”

He pointed his staff straight at Mangis.

“That is true i’fegs,” said the alderman, eager to join the music of authority, “for red and black be the foul fiendys colours.”

Mangis’s cheek went suddenly the color of parchment, so that his own gaudy hose seemed to mock him. He stammered, “I respect Holy Church and her will; he shall fire the churchyard, and all in it, for me. I do withdraw the plaint.”

“Then withdraw thyself,” said the vice-baillie.

When Mangis had slunk away, the curé’s tone softened into business. He told the alderman that the accused had received the chemical substance from Holy Church and had restored it, by giving it all to him.

“Then ’tis in good hands,” said the alderman. “Young man, you are free. Let me have your reverence’s prayers.”

“Doubt it not! Humph! Vice-baillie,” the curé added, as if recalling a recipe’s missing pinch of salt, “the town owes me four silver franks, this three months and more.”

“They shall be paid, curé, ay, ere the week be out.”

So Church and State parted in decent amity, each having tasted a morsel of power and found it to their liking.

Once in the street, Gerard seized the priest’s hand and kissed it. “Oh, sir—oh, your reverence—you have saved me from the fiery stake. What can I say, what do? what?”

“Nought, foolish lad,” the curé said. “Bounty rewards itself. Natheless—Humph?—I wish I had done’t without leasing. It ill becomes my function to utter falsehoods.”

“Falsehood, sir?” Gerard stared, lost.

“Didst not hear me say thou hadst given me that same phosphorus? ’Twill cost me a fortnight’s penance, that light word.” He sighed, but his eye twinkled with a cunning that knew how to keep accounts between Heaven and earth.

“Nay, nay,” cried Gerard, eager as a man bringing bread to a hungry table. “Now Heaven forbid! That was no falsehood, father: well you knew the phosphorus was yours, is yours.” And he thrust the bottle into the curé’s hand. “But alas, ’tis too poor a gift: will you not take from my purse somewhat for Holy Church?” His eyes shone as he held it out.

“Nay,” said the priest brusquely, and put his hands behind him too quickly. “Not a doit. Fie! fie! art pauper et exul. Come thou rather each day at noon and take thy diet with me; for my heart warms to thee.” And he went off abruptly, hands clasped behind his back.

They itched.

But they itched in vain.

Where there’s a heart there’s a Rubicon.

Gerard, still shaken, hastened to the White Hart to relieve Denys of what he must suppose to be anxiety at so long and strange an absence. The inn breathed out its usual odors—smoke, sour wine, damp straw, meat-fat clinging to the rafters like old gossip. In the common room, Denys sat at his ease, dice rattling, playing with two young women—those same high-colored girls—whose laughter rose and fell with the click of bone on wood.

Something in Gerard tightened. “N’oubliez point la Jeanneton!” he said, coloring.

“What of her?” Denys answered, gayly, shaking the dice as if they were his whole creed.

“She said, ‘Le peu que sont les femmes.’”

“Oh, did she?” Denys turned, smiling at the girls. “And what say you to that, mesdemoiselles?”

“We say that none run women down,” said one, “but such as are too old, or too ill-favoured, or too witless to please them.”

“Witless, quotha?” Gerard flared, lofty with indignation and wounded loyalty. “Wise men have not folly enough to please them, nor madness enough to desire to please them; but ’tis to my comrade I speak, not to you, you brazen toads, that make so free with a man at first sight.”

Denys laughed. “Preach away, comrade. Fling a byword or two at our heads. Know, girls, that he is a very Solomon for bywords. Methinks he was brought up by hand on ’em.”

“Be thy friendship a byword!” Gerard shot back. “The friendship that melts to nought at sight of a farthingale.”

“Malheureux!” cried Denys. “I speak but pellets, and thou answerest daggers.”

“Would I could,” said Gerard. “Adieu.”

“What a little savage!” said one of the girls, with the easy cruelty of the uninvested.

Gerard opened the door, put his head back in, and tossed one more sentence like a stone into their laughter. “I have thought of a byword,” he said spitefully:

“Qui hante femmes et dez
Il mourra en pauvretez.”

“There.” And he slammed the door before any of them could season a reply.

The day’s fear had hollowed him; the quarrel had drained what was left. He went to the bar for a morsel of bread and a cup of wine, craving something simple to anchor him—crust under teeth, warmth down the throat, the humble, faithful comfort that asks no questions.

The landlord would sell nothing less than a pint bottle. Gerard agreed; but when the bottle came, its body seemed to promise more than it gave. He held it up, eyed the glass; saw the cheat: thin where it tapered, thick and treacherous at the bottom.

He pointed it out.

The landlord answered with a supercilious shrug. He did not make bottles; he was not accountable for their shape.

“That we will see presently,” said Gerard. “I will take this thy pint to the vice-baillie.”

“Nay, nay, for Heaven’s sake,” cried the landlord, and his tone changed as swiftly as a sauce saved from burning. “I love to content my customers. If by chance this pint be short, we will charge it and its fellow three sous instead of two sous each.”

“So be it,” Gerard said. “But much I admire that you, the host of so fair an inn, should practise thus. The wine, too, smacketh strongly of spring water.”

“Young sir,” said the landlord, leaning in with the sour frankness of a man long pinched by law and life, “we cut no travellers’ throats at this inn, as they do at most. However, you know all about that. The White Hart is no lion nor bear. Whatever masterful robbery is done here, is done upon the poor host. How then could he live at all if he dealt not a little crooked with the few who pay?”

Gerard objected root and branch: honest trade, small profits, quick returns; neither to cheat nor be cheated.

The landlord sighed as if Gerard had described an inn in paradise where every measure was true and every guest paid gladly. “So might one keep an inn in heaven, but not in Burgundy. When foot soldiers going to the wars are quartered on me, how can I but lose? Two sous per day is their pay, and they eat two sous’ worth, and drink into the bargain. The pardoners are my good friends; but palmers and pilgrims—what think you I gain by them? Marry, a loss. Minstrels and jongleurs draw custom and so claim to pay no score, save for liquor. By the secular monks I neither gain nor lose; but the black and grey friars have made vow of poverty, but not of famine: eat like wolves and give the poor host nought but their prayers—and mayhap not them: how can he tell?”

His grievances spilled like thin broth from an overfilled pot. Weddings no longer filled inns; gentry hired out plate and benches, so even mechanics feasted at home. Wine sold by the cup in the market-place now, under privilege, undercutting those who must buy from growers. The law forbade innkeepers to go into market the first hour; so they bought only refuse. They might buy but three bushels of meal at a time though market came but once a week. Butchers demanded bribes to kill for them.

“Courage,” Gerard said gently, hearing under the rant the worn music of a trade trapped between hunger and statute. “The shoe pinches every trader somewhere.”

“Ay,” groaned the landlord, “but not as it pinches us. If we pay not the merchants we buy of, they can cast us into prison and keep us there till we pay or die. But we cannot cast into prison those who buy our victuals. A traveller’s horse we may keep for his debt—but where? In our stable, eating his head off at our cost. The traveller himself we may keep—but where? Not in gaol; in our own house—and then must we lodge and feed him gratis. Merci; no. Our honestest customers are the thieves. Would to Heaven there were more of them. They look not too close into the shape of the canakin, nor into the host’s reckoning: lightly come, lightly go. Also they spend freely, not knowing but each carouse may be their last.”

He told too of provost’s men who pretended suspicion of noble travellers and demanded searches, forcing the host to “stop their mouths with meat and wine”; and of excisemen—town, royal, parliament—who swarmed like flies, each with a wolf in the belly and a sponge in the gullet. Prices rose; yet inns might not raise their own. Mustard, pepper, salt, firewood—no charge allowed, though none were free. Candle a sou the pound. Salt five sous the stone. Pepper four sous the pound. Mustard twenty deniers the pint. A cook at a hundred sous a year. A waiter thirty, and richer than his master by perquisites.

Even sermons lashed innkeepers: godless for this, godless for that—opening doors during mass—though law forced them to admit travellers at all hours.

A man speaking of himself in general is a babbling brook; of his wrongs, a shining river—rolling on and on.

“Labitur et labetur in omne volubilis aevum.”

The river was cut short by a new flood.

Denys burst in, face livid, voice cracking the air. “I am robbed!” he swore, cursing as if each oath might summon back the coins. “Did those hussies pass this way? Who are they? Where do they bide? They have ta’en my purse and fifteen golden pieces. Raise the hue and cry! Ah! traitresses! vipers! These inns are all guet-apens.”

“There now,” cried the landlord triumphantly to Gerard, as if the loss proved his philosophy as a burnt crust proves a careless oven.

Gerard caught Denys’s arm and begged him to be calm and tell how it happened.

“First one went out on some pretence,” Denys snapped; “then after a while the other went to fetch her back, and neither returning, I clapped hand to purse and found it empty. Ungrateful creatures! I was letting them win it in a gallop; but loaded dice were not quick enough—they must claw it all in a lump.”

Gerard, who still had the alderman’s bench and the curé’s shuttered room in his bones, was for running straight to authority and setting officers on their track.

“Not I,” Denys said. “I hate the law. No: as it came so let it go.”

Gerard would not let it go. At a hint from the landlord—who had his own reasons for wanting thieves chased away from his doorstep—he forced Denys along to the provost-marshal.

That dignitary listened and shook his head. “We have no clue to occasional thieves—girls that work honestly at their needles, till some gull comes and tempts them with an easy booty, and then they pluck him.”

Denys flung up his hands. “Come away!” he cried furiously. “I knew what use a bourgeois would be to me at a pinch.” And he marched off, rage making his steps loud on the boards.

“They are clear of the town ere this,” Gerard said, bitterly.

“Speak no more on’t if you prize my friendship,” Denys answered. Then, mastering himself a little, he added, “I have five pieces with the bailiff, and ten I left with Manon, luckily; or these traitresses had feathered their nest with my last plume.”

Gerard stared at him, and Denys’s anger softened into confession. “What dost gape for so? Nay, I do ill to vent my choler on thee. I’ll tell thee all. Art wiser than I. What saidst thou at the door? No matter. Well, then—I did offer marriage to that Manon.”

Gerard stopped as if struck. “What? You offered her what?”

“Marriage. Is that such a mighty strange thing to offer a wench?”

“’Tis a strange thing to offer to a strange girl in passing.”

“Nay, I am not such a sot as you opine,” Denys said, and there was a kind of grim pride in it. “I saw the corn in all that chaff. I knew I could not get her by fair means, so I was fain to try foul. ‘Mademoiselle,’ said I, ‘marriage is not one of my habits, but struck by your qualities I make an exception; deign to bestow this hand on me.’”

“And she bestowed it on thine ear.”

Beyond the last low roofs of the town the road lay white and raw, the new-fallen snow stamped and fretted by countless pads. The tracks crossed and re-crossed—broad, splayed toes, claw-marks bitten deep—so that the whole way looked as if it had been kneaded by invisible hands.

“We did well to take the old man’s counsel, Denys,” Gerard said; yet his voice had the distant note of one who hears more within than without.

“Ay, did we,” Denys answered, peering at the print of a great wolf as if it were a seal on some letter of doom. “For now I mind me, I heard ’em yesternight scurrying under our window, and howling and whining for man’s flesh in yon market-place. But no fat burgher did pity the poor vagabones, and drop out o’ window.”

Gerard smiled, but the smile did not sit at home upon his face. Their boots made a soft, dry squeak in the cold; the hedges answered with a small, brittle hiss as the wind combed their twigs. Far off, a crow cracked the silence once, as if to see whether the world still held.

“What dost meditate so profoundly?” Denys asked at last.

“Thy goodness.”

Denys stopped short, the snow gritting under his heel. That answer—so mild, so grateful—touched him on one of his odd nerves and made him flare where no spark had been cast.

“A civil question merits a civil reply,” said he, very drily.

“Alas, I meant no other,” Gerard replied, startled.

“Then why pretend you were thinking of my goodness, when you know I have no goodness under my skin?”

Had another spoken thus, Gerard would have crossed him with a hearty contradiction. With Denys he only looked and listened, as one who knows the turns of a beloved temper.

“Hast no eye for men’s qualities,” said Gerard gently, “but only for women’s. Yet once more I defy thy unreasonable choler and say I was thinking on thy goodness of overnight. Wouldst have wedded me to the ‘Tête d’Or’—or rather to the tête de veau dorée—and left thyself solitary.”

“Oh, are ye there, lad?” Denys’s frown broke at once like ice under a warm hand. “Well, to speak sooth, I meant that not for goodness, but for friendship and true fellowship, no more. And let me tell you, my young master, my conscience pricketh me even now for letting you turn your back thus on fortune and peaceful days. A truer friend than I had ta’en and somewhat hamstrung thee.
