Then hadst thou been fain to lie smarting at the ‘Tête d’Or’ a month or so; yon skittish lass had nursed thee tenderly, and all had been well. Blade I had in hand to do’t; but remembering how thou hatest pain, though it be but a scratch, my craven heart failed me at the pinch.”

He looked so abashed at his own lack of this dreadful “virtue” that Gerard could only stare, half laughing, half aghast; and the very thought of Achilles’ tendon and friendship was cut short by the sudden trumpet of another sound—a mule’s hooves skidding on hard snow and a man riding as if pursued by the devil’s own horn.

“Here cometh one in our rear,” cried Denys, shading his eyes, “a-riding on his neighbour’s mule.”

“And how know ye ’tis not his own, pray?” Gerard asked, turning.

“Oh, blind! Because he rides it with no discretion.”

The rustic came galloping like a fury. When he reached them his eyes opened saucer-wide; he hauled the rein with both hands; the mule threw out her forelegs and slid between the two travelers like a four-legged table on castors, snorting white breath that steamed in the keen air.

“I trow ye are from the ‘Tête d’Or’?” the clown panted.

They assented.

“Which o’ ye is the younger?”

“He that was born the later,” said Denys, winking.

“Gramercy for the news. Come, divine then!”

“And shall. Thy beard is ripe, thy fellow’s is green; he shall be the younger. Here, youngster.” He held out a packet.

“Ye left this at the ‘Tête d’Or,’ and our mistress sends it ye.”

“Nay, good fellow,” Gerard said, and felt at his pouch by old habit, “methinks I left nought.”

“Would ye make our burgess a liar?” the rustic returned, reproachful as a priest; then, with reproach doubled and sharpened by hunger, “and shall I have no pourboire? and came ventre à terre.”

“Nay, thou shalt have pourboire.” Gerard gave him a small coin.

“A la bonne heure!” The man’s whole face flowered in sudden, almost childish gladness, as if the bright ring of metal were itself a kind of music in that bleak world. “The Virgin go with ye; come up, Jenny!” And he was away again, belly to earth as his nation called it, the mule’s shoes clattering and slipping, the sound dying into the open whiteness.

Gerard unwrapped the packet. It was a square of folds upon folds—linen, then paper, then paper again—each tied and turned with a carefulness that had in it both modesty and art, like the way a good housewife will hide a sweetmeat in layers so that a child cannot steal it with one quick grab. At the fourth packet his patience snapped; he flung the whole into the snow.

Denys stooped, fished it out, and rebuked him. Gerard pleaded that he hated affectation.

“‘The great toe of the little daughter of Herodias!’” Denys cried. “There is no affectation here, but only woman’s good wit. Doubtless the wraps contain something which—out of delicacy, or her sex’s lovely cunning—she would not her hind should see her bestow on a young man: thy garter, to wit.”

“I wear none.”

“Her own then; or a lock of her hair.” Denys tore another fold away. “What is this? A piece of raw silk fresh from the worm. Well, of all the love-tokens!”

“Now who but thee ever dreamed she is so naught as send me love-tokens? I saw no harm in her—barring her hands.”

“Stay; here is something hard lurking in this soft nest.” Denys’s fingers, sure as a cook’s when he lifts a dumpling from dough, searched the silk. “Come forth, I say, little nestling! Saints and pikestaves! Look at this!”

A gold ring lay in his palm, heavy and warm even in the cold, set with an amethyst that glowed as if it held a drop of dusk-purple wine caught and clarified. It seemed to drink the pale day and give it back richer.

“How lovely,” Gerard said, simply, as if naming bread or water.

“And here is something writ,” Denys went on. “Read it thou. I read not so glib as some, when I know not the matter beforehand.”

Gerard took the paper. The ink, a little blurred at the edges as if by hurried breath, held lines set down with more courage than craft. He read, and as he read the blood came up in him like a hearth-fire suddenly fanned.

“’Tis a posy,” said he, “and fairly enough writ.”

He read aloud, blushing like a maid:

“Youth, with thee my heart is fledde,
Come back to the ‘golden Hedde!’
Wilt not? yet this token keepe
Of hir who doeth thy goeing weepe.
Gyf the world prove harsh and cold,
Come back to ‘the Hedde of gold.’”

“The little dove!” Denys purred; then he broke into a gruffer tone. “The great owl! To go and risk her good name thus. However, thank Heaven she has played this prank with an honest lad that will ne’er expose her folly. But oh, the perverseness! Could she not bestow her nauseousness on thee?”

He sighed and shrugged, as if the world’s wisdom and its foolishness were both beyond mending.

“On thee that art as ripe for folly as herself?” Gerard said, unable not to prick him back.

Denys confessed with a look that Gerard had struck his very thought. To Denys it was a matter as puzzling as a bad seasoning: why should a damsel with eyes in her head pass by a man and set her heart on a boy? Yet he could not but grant, with a kind of soldier’s rough philosophy, that Nature had her bounties: boys were human creatures after all, and but for women’s occasional caprice their lot would be too terrible—out of the sun altogether, blighted, and never come to anything; since only the fair could make a man out of such unpromising materials as a boy.

This discourse Gerard cut short.

“Denys,” said he earnestly, “take thou the ring.”

Denys refused flatly. He pressed instead that Gerard should turn back to the “Tête d’Or” at once, ring and all, and not let a poor girl hold out her arms in vain.

“Her hands, you mean,” Gerard said, despite himself.

“Her hand,” Denys retorted, “with the ‘Tête d’Or’ in it.”

Failing in that, Denys would have set the ring on Gerard’s finger by force of argument. Gerard drew back.

“I wear a ring already.”

“What, that sorry gimcrack? Why, ’tis pewter, or tin at best; and this virgin gold, forbye the jewel.”

“Ay,” Gerard answered, and his voice softened as if he spoke a secret name in his own tongue, “but ’twas Margaret gave me this one; and I value it above rubies. I’ll neither part with it nor give it a rival.” He kissed the base metal, as one might kiss the crust that holds the memory of a mother’s oven, and half laughed through his ache. “Fear nought.”

“I see the owl hath sent her ring to a goose,” Denys said sorrowfully.

Yet he prevailed so far that Gerard consented to fasten the amethyst ring inside his bonnet. That he did readily; for in every inn-yard and by every hearth such stones were spoken of as talismans, with sovereign virtues against poison and ill chance. The jewel lay hidden against his brow; he felt it there like a small, strange warmth.

When it was done, Gerard begged Denys to let the matter fall. Talk of women, even in jest, set a hunger in him—not for any new face, but for one dear face far away; and every step southward seemed to pull a thread tighter in his chest.

“I am no general lover, Denys,” said he. “There is room in my heart for one sweetheart, and for one friend. I am far from my dear mistress; and my friend, a few leagues more, and I must lose him too. Oh, let me drink thy friendship pure while I may, and not dilute it with any of these stupid females.”

“And shalt, honey-pot, and shalt,” Denys replied, kindness smoothing his voice. “But as to my leaving thee at Remiremont, reckon thou not on that! For”—and he salted the air with three consecutive oaths—“if I do. Nay, I shall propose to thee to stay forty-eight hours there while I kiss my mother and sisters, and the females generally; and on go you and I together to the sea.”

“Denys! Denys!”

“Denys nor me! ’Tis settled. Gainsay me not! or I’ll go with thee to Rome. Why not? His Holiness the Pope hath ever some little merry pleasant war toward, and a Burgundian soldier is still welcome in his ranks.”

At that, Gerard’s heart, long held tight as a clenched fist, opened of itself.

“Denys,” he said, “ere I fell in with thee, I used often to halt on the road, unable to go farther: my puny heart so pulled me back. And then, after a short prayer to the saints for aid, would I rise and drag my most unwilling body onward. But since I joined company with thee, great is my courage. I have found the saying true, that better is a bright comrade on the weary road than a horse-litter. And, dear brother, when I do think of what we have done and suffered together—savedst my life from the bear, and from yet more savage thieves; and even poor I did make shift to draw thee out of Rhine—and somehow I loved thee double from that hour. How many ties tender and strong between us! Had I my will, I’d never, never, never, never part with my Denys on this side the grave. Well-a-day! God His will be done.”

“No, my will shall be done this time,” Denys shouted, as if he could out-cry Fate itself. “Le bon Dieu has bigger fish to fry than you or me. I’ll go with thee to Rome. There is my hand on it.”

“Think what you say! ’Tis impossible. ’Tis too selfish of me.”

“I tell thee, ’tis settled. No power can change me. At Remiremont I borrow ten pieces of my uncle, and on we go; ’tis fixed.”

They struck hands upon it; and Gerard, being young and sudden, could not keep his joy in the bounds of walking. He ran twice round Denys as they went, then danced backwards before him, then caught his hand. So they went hand in hand like sweethearts; and their boots, their breath, and the faint whirr of winter wind made a little household music in the open road—as if companionship itself were a hearth one could carry.

Then, over the brow of a hill, a company of mounted soldiers rose into sight—about fifty—black dots that grew to men, to steel, to harness, to banners that took the sun like flame.

“See the banner of Burgundy,” Denys cried joyfully. “I shall look out for a comrade among these.”

“How gorgeous is the standard in the sun,” Gerard said, his eye caught by the bright things of the world as a boy’s will be: velvet, feathers, steel breastplates shining like glass. Even the pack-mules seemed to wear their great brass frontlets proudly, as if the metal were a face and the face could preen.

“No wonder men itch to be soldiers,” Gerard murmured, almost in spite of his own troubles; for the jingle of their harness and the measured thunder of hooves made a kind of martial song that filled the cold air and changed the road’s loneliness.

When they drew near enough to see faces, Denys gave a sharp cry.

“Why, ’tis the Bastard of Burgundy, as I live. Nay then; there is fighting afoot since he is out. A gallant leader, Gerard—rates his life no higher than a private soldier’s, and a soldier’s no higher than a tomtit’s. And that is the captain for me.”

In the midst of their innocent admiration the troop came up.

“Halt!” cried a stentorian voice.

The whole body checked as one beast. The Bastard of Burgundy bent his brow on Denys, and his gaze was like iron laid to the skin.

“How now, arbalestrier,” said he, “how comes it thy face is turned southward, when every good hand and heart is hurrying northward?”

Denys answered respectfully that he was going on leave after some years’ service, to see his kindred at Remiremont.

“Good,” said the Bastard. “But this is not the time for’t; the duchy is disturbed. Ho! Bring that dead soldier’s mule to the front; and thou mount her and forward with us to Flanders.”

“So please your highness,” Denys said firmly, though the words cost him, “that may not be. My home is close at hand. I have not seen it these three years; and above all I have this poor youth in charge, whom I may not—cannot—leave, till I see him shipped for Rome.”

The Bastard stared, as if he had heard a dog reason; amazement turned quick to wrath.

“Dost bandy words with me? Art weary o’ thy life? Let go the youth’s hand, and into the saddle without more idle words.”

Denys made no reply. He only held Gerard’s hand tighter, and his look was a wall.

At that the Bastard roared, “Jarnac, dismount six of thy archers, and shoot me this white-livered cur dead where he stands—for an example.”

The young Count de Jarnac, second in command, gave the order; the men swung down, bows and belts creaking.

“Strip him naked,” the Bastard added, in the cold voice of one giving kitchen orders. “Put his arms and accoutrements on the spare mule. We’ll maybe find some clown worthier to wear them.”

Denys groaned aloud, not for death, but for the shame.

“Am I to be shamed as well as slain?”

“Oh, nay! Nay! Nay!” Gerard cried, waking as if a hand had struck him. “He shall go with you on the instant. I’d liever part with him for ever than see a hair of his dear head harmed. Oh, sir—oh, my lord—give a poor boy but a minute to bid his only friend farewell! He will go with you. I swear he shall go with you.”

The leader’s mouth tightened; he nodded a cold assent.

“Thou, Jarnac, stay with them, and bring him on alive or dead. Forward!”

The troop moved again, the banner dipping and rising; the sound of them rolled away like a storm withdrawing, leaving behind a thin, stunned silence. Only Count Jarnac remained with six archers and the spare mule.

Denys and Gerard looked at one another. There are looks that are meals in themselves—bread, salt, and a cup of water shared at the end of a long day; and there are looks that empty the body. This one emptied them. Words came in a rush, because time ran like sand between fingers.

“Thou goest to Holland,” Denys said hoarsely. “Thou knowest where she bides. Tell her all. She will be kind to thee for my sake.”

“Oh, sorry tale that I shall carry her!” Gerard gasped. “For God’s sake, go back to the ‘Tête d’Or.’ I am mad!”

“Hush! Let me think—have I nought to say to thee? My head! my head!”

Then Denys’s eyes cleared as if a thought had cut through smoke.

“Ah! I have it. Make for the Rhine, Gerard! Strasbourg. ’Tis but a step. And down the current to Rotterdam. Margaret is there. I go thither. I’ll tell her thou art coming. We shall all be together.”

“My lads,” Count Jarnac said, firm but not harsh now, “haste ye, or you will get us into trouble.”

“Oh, sir, one moment!” Gerard panted. “One little moment!”

Denys, driven beyond himself, flung his face up at the dull sky and screamed, “Cursed be the land I was born in! Cursed be the race of man! and he that made them what they are!”

“Hush, Denys, hush!” Gerard cried, as if he could clap a hand over his friend’s soul. “Blaspheme not! Oh, God forgive him; he wots not what he says. Be patient, Denys, be patient: though we meet no more on earth, let us meet in a better world, where no blasphemer may enter. To my heart, lost friend; for what are words now?”

He opened his arms. Denys came into them; they locked together, close as brothers and closer than many lovers. They kissed one another again and again, speechless, the tears raining down hot on cold cheeks. Count Jarnac watched amazed; but the rough archers, to whom comrade was a sacred name—more sacred than banner or pay—looked on with a kind of pity that could not soften their orders.

At Jarnac’s signal they used a kind force, half lifting Denys onto the mule. They placed him in the middle of them, and spurred after their leader.

Gerard ran wildly after them—for the lane turned—and strained his eyes for the last of him. The last glimpse he caught, Denys was rocking to and fro upon the mule and tearing his hair out.

At that sight something rose in Gerard’s throat so high, so high, he could run no more nor breathe. He staggered to the snow-clad hedge and seized it, choking piteously. Thorns ran into his hand; he did not feel them until he saw the red blossom on the white. Then he fought for breath, and the sound he made was smaller than the world’s silence, yet seemed to fill his own skull like a bell.

When he could draw air again, his legs carried him without counsel. He went on, scarce feeling or caring whither. Every few paces he stopped; his arms fell; his head sank upon his chest; he stood motionless as a post. Then the thought would strike him anew—clear, incredulous, cruel.

“Can this thing be? This must be a dream. ’Tis scarce five minutes since we were so happy, walking hand in hand, faring to Rome together; and we admired them and their gay banners and helmets—oh, hearts of hell!”

All nature seemed to stare, as lonely as himself. Not a creature in sight. No colour but white. Trees stood like pale ghosts; hedges like ribs; the fields like shrouds. He was a ghost of his former self wandering among the ghosts of things.

Desolate. Desolate. Desolate.

He knelt and gathered a little snow. It was dry and stinging; it squealed faintly as he pressed it, a thin winter cry. He held it a moment, then let it sift away.

“Nay, I dream not,” he whispered, “for this is snow—cold as the world’s heart.” He saw the red on it. “It is bloody too: what may that mean? Fool! ’tis from thy hand. I mind not the wound. Ay, I see: thorns. Welcome, kindly foes: I felt ye not; ye ran not into my heart. Ye are not cruel like men.”

He rose and dragged himself on. Then behind him he heard horses’ feet and gay voices—a bright splashing of sound, laughter and jingling harness, a careless tune tossed into the air as one tosses crumbs to birds. For a breath his heart leapt with a wild hope: the soldiers had relented; they were bringing Denys back.

But no. A gay cavalcade swept by: a gentleman of rank and his favourites in velvet and furs and feathers, and four or five armed retainers in buff jerkins. They passed like a flash of colour and noise over white ground, leaving behind only the faint diminishing clatter—then the road’s hush returned, heavier for having been broken.

Gerard did not look after them. Certain bright shadows had come and gone; that was all.

He had gone a little way when a harsh voice in front of him cried, “Stand and deliver!”

Three of the gentleman’s servants had ridden back to plunder him. Their horses steamed; leather creaked; iron bits clicked; their breath came loud in the cold. The nobleman and his companions had halted scarce a hundred yards off and sat on their horses watching, too proud to do their own dirty work, not too proud to take its fruit, and to mark, with sharp eyes, that their agents robbed clean.

“How, ye false knaves,” Gerard said, very calmly, as if grief had drained fear out of him, “would ye shame your noble master? He will hang ye to the nearest tree.”

With that he drew his sword doggedly and set his back to the hedge.

One of the men levelled his petronel at him. The mouth of it looked like a black hole into which a man’s life might fall.

But another—less eager for blood, and perhaps with a memory still in him of some mother’s kitchen and the clean clack of wooden spoons—put out his hand.

“Be not so hasty! And be not thou so mad! Look yonder!”

Gerard looked. He saw the nobleman and his friends waiting, idle as spectators at a bear-baiting.

The milder servant spoke on, almost apologetic, as if explaining the price of spices to a stranger at market.

“Resistance is vain. Common thieves take the life as well as the purse. And it costs a mint to be a gentleman. My master lost money at play overnight, and is going to visit his leman, and so must take money where he sees it. Therefore, good youth, consider that we rob not for ourselves, and deliver us that fat purse at thy girdle without more ado; nor put us to the pain of slitting thy throat and taking it all the same.”

“This knave is right,” Gerard said aloud, but it sounded as if he spoke to his own soul. “I ought not to fling away my life; Margaret would be so sorry.” He unknotted his purse and flung it to them. “Take then the poor man’s purse to the rich man’s pouch; and with it this: tell him, I pray the Holy Trinity, each coin in it may burn his hand, and freeze his heart, and blast his soul for ever. Begone, and leave me to my sorrow!”

They rode away muttering, his words pricking them a little—no more than a thorn pricks a hide. The nobleman turned his horse; the whole bright knot moved off, their laughter rising and fading like a tune played at a distance.

Gerard went on, penniless now as well as friendless, until he came to the edge of a wood. Here the wind changed; it came through bare branches with a low, hollow moan, as if the trees remembered wolves and spoke their names without tongue. The road under his feet was hard; the snow at the edges lay like flour thrown down and left. He thought of flour, and of the smell of warm bread, and of milk foaming in a pail; the thought was torture. Hunger, till then muffled by shock, stirred and bit him.

His heart could hardly feel this second blow; his judgment did. Rome he could never reach without money. Denys had said, “Go to Strasbourg, and down the Rhine home.” He would obey Denys. But how to get to Strasbourg without money?

Then, like a refrain caught in the ear, the posy rang again within him—each word sharp as frost, yet oddly tender, as if it had been wrapped in silk before it was sent:

“Gyf the world prove harsh and cold,
Come back to ‘the Hedde of gold.’”

“And if I do,” he whispered, “I must go as her servant—I who am Margaret’s.”

The weariness came over him heavier than cloak or mail. The world’s sounds seemed to thin, as if his ears themselves were filling with snow.

“I am a-weary, a-weary,” he murmured. “I will sleep, and dream all is as it was. Ah me, how happy were we an hour agone; we little knew how happy.”

He saw a house not far off, and a barn, and imagined the warmth that must live there—the sour-sweet smell of hay, the animal breath, the thick quiet of stored grain; imagined a bowl of milk, not as fuel, but as comfort, the very whiteness of it like a promise. Yet he dared not ask.

“There is a house,” he told himself. “The owner well-to-do. What if I told him my wrong, and prayed his aid to retrieve my purse, and so to Rhine? Fool! is he not a man, like the rest? He would scorn me and trample me lower.”

Denys had cursed the race of men. Gerard would not. Yet dread and loathing crept in him like a cold that finds the bone.

“Nay,” he said, “here will I lie till sunset: then darkling creep into this rich man’s barn, and take by stealth a draught of milk or a handful o’ grain, to keep body and soul together. God, who hath seen the rich rob me, will peradventure forgive me.”

He looked toward the wood and remembered the old man’s warning. Wolves. Yet even that seemed less bitter than men.

“They say ’tis ill sleeping on the snow. Death steals on such sleepers with muffled feet and honey breath. But what can I? I am a-weary, a-weary. Shall this be the wood where lie the wolves yon old man spoke of? I must e’en trust them: they are not men.”

He crawled to the roadside and stretched himself upon the snow with a deep sigh, as one lays down a burden and cannot take it up again.

“Ah, tear not thine hair so! teareth my heart to see thee.”

“Margaret,” he whispered, and the name came out as if in his own native dialect—unborrowed, untranslatable, the one word that still meant what it had always meant. “Never see me more. Poor Margaret.”

Then the too-tender heart grew still. The constant lover, and friend of antique mould, lay silent on the snow—in peril from the weather, in peril from wild beasts, in peril from hunger; friendless and penniless in a strange land, and not halfway to Rome.

Rude travel, men say, is a salt relish to English blood, and the telling of it sets many a cold hearth glowing. Yet the true loaf of this history was kneaded in Holland, and it is time to go back to the low rooms, the familiar thresholds, the common pots and pans where most lives are boiled down—slowly, with small daily stirrings that decide great matters.

In Sevenbergen, Jorian Ketel came up to Peter Brandt’s door as if he owned the very lintel, and demanded Margaret’s promise like a debt long overdue. But Margaret lay sick abed; the fever had made her more like a pale candle than a girl, and Peter, hearing Ketel’s errand, flamed up. He affronted him openly—drove him off the premises with hard words, and one or two in the street were ready enough to take the rest of the argument to the horse-pond; for father and daughter were beloved, and the whole matter was in every mouth, and Sevenbergen was in that hot, undiscriminating temper that comes of public pity.

So Jorian Ketel went away in dudgeon, and repented of a good deed he had done once; which kind of repentance is common enough, and is at least honest.

And Dierich Brower—found at “The Three Kings,” with ale at his elbow and a poor chattering fellow opposite, making him drunk, not from generosity but to draw from him Martin Wittenhaagen’s whereabouts—was discovered, seized, and flung into a horsepond. The splash of him went through the little town like a bell-note: men laughed, women cried shame, and the water frothed round his ears while threats fell on him thicker than droplets. He was told, with more emphasis than courtesy, that if ever he showed his face again in that burgh he should taste worse than pond-water.

Municipal jealousy pricked up its ears. The burgomaster of Sevenbergen, resenting Ghysbrecht Van Swieten’s high-handed forays, sent a formal missive to the burgomaster of Tergou, telling him plain he had overstepped the law, and that, next time he had a complaint—real or imaginary—against any of Sevenbergen’s townsfolk, he must apply where he ought.

Ghysbrecht, wily as a pike in still water, swallowed his rage and sent back a civil answer: the person he had followed, he said, was no Sevenbergen man at all, but a Tergovian—one Gerard—who had stolen the town records; and that Gerard, having escaped into foreign parts and likely carried the documents with him, the whole matter was now at an end. Thus he made a virtue of necessity, and a lie into a salve.

But his smoothness was only a lid. Baffled at Sevenbergen, he turned his eyes elsewhere and set emissaries to learn, from the family at Tergou, whither Gerard had fled. To his “infinite surprise,” they did not know. That ignorance—genuine as it was—added a sour drop to his cup. It made him fear Gerard was not far off at all, but lurking in the neighbourhood like a knife in a sleeve; that he would make some sure discovery and come back to take a dreadful revenge.

From that time those about Ghysbrecht noticed a change for the worse. The man who had once strutted in his authority became moody and irritable. A dread lay on him like a low, ceaseless hum in the ear—one of those sounds you cannot point to, yet cannot escape. His eyes began to cast furtive glances, as of one who expects a blow and knows not from what quarter it will fall. Making others wretched had not made him happy. It seldom does.

At Tergou, the little household that, but for violent interference, might in time have healed its own difference without banishing its hope of the flock to far roads, kept the same outward look, but inwardly was altered. Little Kate knew what share Cornelis and Sybrandt had in driving Gerard away; and though she never told her mother—fearing to breed worse mischief—there were moments when the bare sight of those two made her shudder, and she reddened at their hypocritical regrets.

Catherine, with a woman’s vigilance, noticed this. With a woman’s subtlety she said nothing, but held her tongue and watched—watched as one watches a pot that must not boil over, hearing not only the clink of spoons and the scrape of wooden trenchers, but the pauses between voices, the quickened breath, the wrong note in a laugh. The black sheep, trying to wear mourning faces and take their share in the general sorrow, imposed well enough on their father and Giles. Yet the demure satisfaction under their gloom could not escape feminine eyes—those eyes “that, noting all, seem nought to note.”

Thus mistrust and suspicion sat at table—poor substitutes for Gerard’s quick, intelligent face that had brightened the circle, unobserved till it was gone. The old hosier’s pride had been wounded by his son’s disobedience; so he bore up stiffly and did his best never to mention Gerard’s name. Yet under his Spartan cloak Nature tugged at his heart-strings. One anxiety he never pretended to hide.

“If I but knew where the boy is,” he would say, “and that his life and health are in no danger, small would be my care.” And then a deep sigh would follow, like a bell heard far off across flat land.

It seemed to me that if Gerard had opened the door at that instant and walked in, there would have been more tears and embraces than reproaches—few, or none.

One thing took the old couple by surprise: publicity. Ere Gerard had been gone a week, his adventures were in every mouth; and to make it sharper, the town sympathy ran warmly on the lovers’ side, and against Gerard’s “cruel parents,” and against that old busybody of a burgomaster who must put his nose into a matter that nowise concerned him.

“Mother,” said Kate one day, coming in with the sound of street-talk clinging to her like flour dust to a sleeve, “it is all over the town that Margaret is down with a fever—a burning fever; her father fears her sadly.”

“Margaret? what Margaret?” asked Catherine, with a treacherous calmness that did not reach her eyes.

“Oh, mother! whom should I mean? Why, Gerard’s Margaret.”

“Gerard’s Margaret,” screamed Catherine; and the very syllables were as if someone had dashed vinegar into milk. “How dare you say such a word to me? And I rede you never mention that hussy’s name in this house, that she has laid bare. She is the ruin of my poor boy, the flower of all my flock. She is the cause that he is not a holy priest in the midst of us, but is roaming the world, and I a desolate broken-hearted mother.”

Then, seeing Kate’s lip tremble, her voice broke and softened, as fire softens when you lay a lid on it.

“There, do not cry, my girl; I do ill to speak harsh to you. But oh, Kate! you know not what passes in a mother’s heart. I bear up before you all; it behoves me swallow my fears; but at night I see him in my dreams, and still some trouble or other near him: sometimes he is torn by wild beasts; other times he is in the hands of robbers, and their cruel knives uplifted to strike his poor pale face, that one should think would move a stone. Oh! when I remember that, while I sit here in comfort, perhaps my poor boy lies dead in some savage place—and all along of that girl: there, her very name is ratsbane to me. I tremble all over when I hear it.”

“I’ll not say anything, nor do anything to grieve you worse, mother,” said Kate tenderly; but she sighed, and kept her promise with difficulty.

The name forbidden in that house was spoken freely elsewhere—and with pity. All Sevenbergen was sorry for Margaret. Young men and maidens cast many a compassionate glance, as they passed, toward the little window where the village beauty lay “dying for love.” In that familiar phrase they wronged her. Gerard was not dead, and she was too loyal to doubt his constancy. Her father was dear to her and helpless; and but for bodily weakness, all her love for Gerard would not have kept her from her duties—though she might have gone about them with a drooping head.

But the strain of body and mind had brought on a fever so fierce that nothing but youth and constitution saved her. When the malady at last released her, it left her in that terrible weakness where the patient feels life not a gift but a weight. Then love and friendship by the bedside are mortal angels—comfort in the voice, healing in the hand. Yet this poor girl had to climb back into strength as she could, largely alone.

Many days she lay with no company but the soft crackle of the fire below and the changing noises of the street—cart wheels grumbling on the stones, a distant dog’s bark, the thin cry of a hawker—sounds that should have tethered her to the world, yet seemed to come from another life. The hours rolled over her like leaden waves. In her enfeebled state existence itself felt done and over. She could not stir herself to get well. Gerard was gone. She had not him to get well for. Often she lay for hours quite still, with tears welling gently out of her eyes as if her body had learned the habit of sorrow.

One day, waking from an uneasy slumber, she found two women in her room. One was a servant; the other, by the deep fur on her collar and sleeves, was a person of consideration. A narrow band of silvery hair, spared by her coiffure, showed she was past the age when sensible women pretend to be younger than they are. Both faces were kind.

Margaret tried to raise herself, but the older lady laid a hand on her—very gently, as one sets down a warm loaf so it will not break its crust.

“Lie still, sweetheart; we come not here to put you about, but to comfort you, God willing. Now cheer up a bit, and tell us, first, who think you we are?”

“Nay, madam,” whispered Margaret, “I know you, though I never saw you before: you are the demoiselle Van Eyck, and this is Reicht Heynes. Gerard has oft spoken of you, and of your goodness to him. Madam, he has no friend like you near him now.”

At that thought her strength went out of her, and tears sprang again in a moment.

Reicht Heynes, good-natured as a warm kitchen, began to cry too—for company, as some do; but her mistress checked her sharply.

“Well, you are a pretty one for a sick-room,” said she; and then she turned all her art—not the loud gaiety of the young, but the quiet, seasoned skill of one that has seen trouble and knows its smell—toward cheering the patient. She spoke of small things, safe things, the way one coaxes appetite back: the weather that would turn, the neighbours’ doings, the comfort of a clean bed, the need for broth when strength is low, and how a little patience is a sort of prayer. She knew what to say and what to avoid; she knew when silence was the better medicine.

Ere an hour was gone, Margaret’s head lay on her shoulder instead of on the pillow, and her soft eyes dwelt on the older woman with a gratitude as quiet as it was deep.

“Ah! this is hair,” said the dame, running her fingers through it with a housewife’s approving touch, as if weighing flax. “Come and look at it, Reicht!”

Reicht came, handled it, and praised it unaffectedly. The poor girl that owned it was not quite beyond the reach of flattery—owing, doubtless, to not being dead.

“In sooth, madam,” said Margaret faintly, “I did use to think it hideous; but he praised it, and ever since then I have been almost vain of it, saints forgive me. You know how foolish those are that love.”

“They are greater fools that don’t,” said the old lady sharply.

Margaret opened her eyes wide, as if a new sound had rung in her hearing.

This was only the first of many visits. Either Margaret Van Eyck herself, or Reicht, came nearly every day until their patient was convalescent; and she mended rapidly under their hands. Reicht said it was chiefly the nourishing dishes she made in Peter’s kitchen—thin gruels strengthened with egg, broths drawn long from bone and herb till they held the very marrow of comfort, little pans of stewed fruit with spice just enough to wake the tongue, and possets that slid warm and mild down a sore throat. She was a woman who knew that healing has a smell: the clean steam of barley, the sweet breath of simmering milk, the homely sharpness of onion softened to sweetness, the honest perfume of browned crust.

Margaret herself thought more of the kind words and eyes that told her, day by day, she had friends to live for; and of the hushed, merciful quiet the two women brought into the room, as if they laid a soft cloth over harsh noises. Even the street, heard through the shutter, seemed less cruel when one was not alone.

While this homely miracle went on, Martin Wittenhaagen went straight to Rotterdam to take the bull by the horns. The bull, in this case, walked on two legs and wore a crown for horns: Philip the Good—duke of this, earl of that, lord of the other.

Arrived at Rotterdam, Martin found the court was at Ghent. To Ghent he went; and there he sought an audience, but was put off by lackeys and pages, turned aside as if he were a dog nosing at a door. So he took another tack, such as soldiers learn: he threw himself in his sovereign’s way out hunting, and, contrary to court precedents, began the conversation by roaring lustily for mercy.

“Why, where is the peril, man?” cried the duke, looking all round and laughing.

“Grace for an old soldier hunted down by burghers!” bawled Martin.

Now kings differ in character like other folk; but there is one trait they share: they are often wonderfully affable to men of very low estate. Such folk vie with them in nothing; jealousy does not wake. Their bluntness amuses them; their plain speech brings a breath of nature into courts where every word is perfumed and weighed.

So Philip reined in his horse and gave Martin almost a tête-à-tête. Martin reminded him of a certain battlefield where he had taken an arrow meant for his sovereign. The duke remembered the incident perfectly, and could afford to look on it cheerfully—having not been the one struck.

Then Martin told him of Gerard’s first capture in the church, his imprisonment in the tower, the manoeuvre by which they got him out, and all the details of the hunt; and whether Martin told it better than others might, or the duke had heard fewer good stories than common folk, certain it is Philip grew so wrapped up in it that, when courtiers came galloping up and cut across them, he swore like a costermonger, and threatened—only half in jest—to cut off the next head that came between him and a good tale.

When Martin ended, the duke cried out:

“St. Luke! what sport goeth on in this mine earldom—ay, in my own woods—and I see it not. You base fellows have all the luck.”

Fortune’s partiality offended him like a spoiled child’s. “Lo you now! this was a man-hunt,” said he. “I never had the luck to be at a man-hunt.”

“My luck was none so great,” replied Martin bluntly; “I was on the wrong side of the dogs’ noses.”

“Ah! so you were; I forgot that.” And royalty, thus comforted, was reconciled.

“What would you, then?”

“A free pardon, your highness, for myself and Gerard.”

“For what?”

“For prison-breaking.”

“Go to; the bird will fly from the cage. ’Tis instinct. Besides, coop a young man up for loving a young woman? These burgomasters must be void of common sense. What else?”

“For striking down the burgomaster.”

“Oh, the hunted boar will turn to bay. ’Tis his right; and I hold him less than man that grudges it him. What else?”

“For killing of the bloodhounds.”

The duke’s countenance fell, as if a pleasant tune had jarred.

“’Twas their life or mine,” said Martin eagerly.

“Ay! but I can’t have my bloodhounds—my beautiful bloodhounds—sacrificed to—”

“No, no, no! They were not your dogs.”

“Whose dogs, then?”

“The ranger’s.”

“Oh.” The duke drew breath again, as a man does when he learns the loss is not his own. “Well, I am very sorry for him; but as I was saying, I can’t have my old soldiers sacrificed to his bloodhounds. Thou shalt have thy free pardon.”

“And poor Gerard.”

“And poor Gerard too, for thy sake. And more—tell thou this burgomaster his doings mislike me. This is to set up for a king, not a burgomaster. I’ll have no kings in Holland but one. Bid him be more humble; or by St. Jude I’ll hang him before his own door, as I hanged the burgomaster of—what’s the name—some town or other in Flanders it was; no, ’twas somewhere in Brabant—no matter—I hanged him, I remember that much—for oppressing poor folk.”

Then he beckoned his chancellor, a pursy old fellow that rode like a sack strapped to a saddle, and bade him draw a free pardon for Martin and one Gerard. The precious document was made in form and signed next day; and Martin hastened home with it, carrying that strip of parchment as if it were a loaf for starving people.

Margaret had left her bed some days and sat pale and pensive by the fireside, the warmth on her face and the weakness in her bones, when Martin burst in waving the parchment as if it were a banner and crying:

“A free pardon, girl, for Gerard as well as me! Send for him back when you will; all the burgomasters on earth daren’t lay a finger on him.”

Color rushed into her cheeks like wine into a thin cup. Her hands trembled as she took the parchment, devoured it with her eyes, kissed it again and again—as if the ink itself were a sacrament—and then flung her arms round Martin’s neck and kissed him.

When she was calmer, she told him Heaven had raised her up a friend in the dame Van Eyck.

“And I would fain consult her on this good news; but I have not strength to walk so far.”

“What need to walk?” said Martin. “There is my mule.”

“Your mule, Martin?”

The old soldier—professional pillager, as folk called him—laughed, and confessed he had got so used to the beast that at times he forgot Ghysbrecht had a prior claim. To-morrow, he said, he would turn her into the burgomaster’s yard. But to-night she should carry Margaret to Tergou.

It was nearly dusk. The town sounds softened; the day’s sharp clatter sank into evening murmurs. Margaret ventured. And about seven o’clock she astonished and gladdened her new, ardent friend by arriving at her house with unwonted roses on her cheeks, and Gerard’s pardon warm in her bosom.

Some folk grow old in the heart before their hair is grey; others keep a sap-green courage that no winter can bite. Margaret Van Eyck was of the latter sort. She loved her young namesake with a bright, almost girlish heat—partly because she had a quick eye for what is real in people, and had found in Margaret Brandt a thing rarer than beauty: plain truth. But there was another bond, older than judgment and stronger than gratitude.

It is a crooked piece of human nature that we often cling most warmly to those we have helped. Kindness, once spent, comes back like an echo in the giver’s own breast, and makes a home there.

So it was with the old painter. She had broken her settled habits to go out to Sevenbergen; she had sat by the sickbed; she had warmed broths and sharpened the smell of herbs in the room—sage bruised between finger and thumb, a sting of vinegar in the air, and the slow, comforting whisper of a fire that never quite died. She had coaxed life back with patience that was half art, half mothering; and the very act of saving Margaret had drawn her to her more tenderly than ever she had been drawn even to Gerard—though it was for Gerard’s sake she had crossed that threshold at first.

Now she saw the colour come back to the girl’s cheek, as if some invisible hand had rubbed in a rose-tint; and she saw the cause of it too—the little strip of parchment Margaret held as reverently as if it were a relic.

Margaret Van Eyck read it, and her own long-laid plan yielded without a sigh.

“Sweetheart,” said she, “I did desire he should stay in Italy five or six years, and come back rich, and above all an artist. But your happiness is before all; and I see you cannot live without him. So we must have him home as fast as may be.”

“Ah, madam! you see my very thoughts.” The girl’s voice ran shy; she lowered her eyes and blushed, like one caught tasting honey. “But how to let him know? That passes my skill. He is gone to Italy; but what part I know not. Stay—he named the cities he should visit: Florence was one, and Rome.”

Then sense, which was strong in her, fought down the first wild impulse. A letter flung into the world with no better direction than “My Gerard—Italy” might wander like a lost pilgrim and never reach the shrine. She looked up, beseeching counsel.

“You are come to the right place, and at the right time,” said the old lady. “Here was this Hans Memling with me to-day; he is going to Italy, girl, no later than next week, ‘to improve his hand,’ he says. Not before ’twas needed, I do assure you.”

“But how is he to find my Gerard?”

“Why, he knows your Gerard, child. They have supped here more than once, and were like hand and glove. Now, as his business is the same as Gerard’s, he will visit the same places; and soon or late he must fall in with him. Wherefore, get you a long letter written, and copy out this pardon into it, and I’ll answer for the messenger. In six months at farthest Gerard shall get it; and when he shall get it, then will he kiss it, and put it in his bosom, and come flying home. What are you smiling at? And now what makes your cheeks so red? And what you are smothering me for, I cannot think. Yes—happy days are coming to my little pearl.”

While that hopeful scheme took shape in the upper room, Martin Wittenhaagen sat in the kitchen with a black-jack of ale before him, and Reicht Heynes at her wheel. The distaff hummed; the treadle made its steady, soothing thump, as if the house itself had a pulse. But the old woman’s questions were sharper than any kitchen knife, and she pumped Martin till his answers rose like bubbles and burst in spite of him.

Hans Memling, meanwhile, was a former pupil of Jan Van Eyck and his sister. Painter he was, for all Margaret Van Eyck’s dry gibes; and good-hearted enough—save for one fault that sat on him like a leech. He loved the nipperkin and the brown bowl more than they loved him. It kept his purse light and his feet often at Margaret Van Eyck’s threshold, hungry for a meal and sometimes for a groat. That dependence gave her a hold on him; she knew he would not trifle with any errand she placed in his hand.

So the letter was written—long, urgent, warm with the girl’s very breath—and the duke’s pardon copied within it as carefully as a cook lays pastry over a precious filling, sealing it from all harm. It was left with Margaret Van Eyck; and the following week, sure enough, Hans Memling came back from Flanders. The old artist put the letter into his wallet and slipped him a piece of gold for the road.

He seemed in a mighty hurry to be gone.

“All the better,” said Margaret Van Eyck. “He will be the sooner in Italy.”

But there are horses that fret to start and then, after the first furlong, need whip and spur. Hans’s eagerness cooled into a lazy heat as soon as he reached the chief hostelry of Tergou and spied two boon companions planted in the bay-window like crows on a branch. He went in for a parting glass; and once he lifted the cup, the ale and wine did the rest. When he offered to pay, they cried shame on it—he was bound for a long journey; everybody must treat him, landlord and all.

The more they treated him, the more his tongue ran as if oiled. He boasted he would teach Italians how to paint; then sang of his battle feats—he had handled a pike, he swore; and then, warming further, told of amorous victories with women not present to contradict the tale. In short, he leaked words in every direction; and among the things that oozed out, he blabbed he carried a letter for a townsman, one Gerard—a good fellow; and to prove the point that all present were good fellows too, he slapped Sybrandt on the back with such hearty fellowship it drove the breath from him.

Sybrandt slid round the table to escape further brotherly blows, but he listened. For the first time he learnt Gerard was gone to Italy. To be sure, he affected to doubt it.

“My brother Gerard is never in Italy.”

“Ye lie, ye cur!” roared Hans, the drink turning him quick to wrath. He was too muddled to see the man he now cursed was the one he had praised a moment before. “If he is ten times your brother, he is in Italy. What call ye this? There—read me that superscription!” And he flung the letter down upon the board, where ale had soaked the grain dark.

Sybrandt took it up and peered as gravely as a clerk; then set it down again with a shrug. “I cannot read.”

One of the company, by some happy chance, could; and proud as a minstrel with a new song, he read aloud:

“To Gerard Eliassoen, of Tergou. These by the hand of the trusty Hans Memling, with all speed.”

“’Tis excellently well writ,” said the reader, eyeing each stroke.

“Ay!” cried Hans, swelling. “And small wonder: ’tis writ by a famous hand—by Margaret, sister of Jan Van Eyck. Blessed and honoured be his memory! She is an old friend of mine, is Margaret Van Eyck.”

After that, Hans wandered into forty matters as a drunkard wanders through streets he does not know, laughing at corners and singing to doorposts.

Sybrandt stole away and sought Cornelis. The brothers put their heads together; their talk had the hiss of damp wood on a fire.

Italy was far—an immense distance. If only Gerard could be kept there.

“Keep him there?” said Cornelis. “Nothing would keep him long from his Margaret.”

“Curse her!” Sybrandt’s voice came like spit. “Why didn’t she die when she was about it?”

“She die?” Cornelis snarled. “She would outlive the pest to vex us.”

So the black sheep of the family chewed their envy and fed it, till it grew bold enough to shape a plan: keep Gerard in Italy all his life, and so secure his share of their father’s substance.

They had the wickedness for it, but not the wit. The scheme stuck—until, as if a malicious whisper slid between their two skulls at once, they both said together:

“THE BURGOMASTER!”

They went straight to Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, and he received them at once. The man who sits in suspense catches at knowledge as a starving man catches at crust.

“You have news of Gerard?” he cried.

They told him of the letter, and of Hans Memling with the wallet. Ghysbrecht’s eye flickered with a restless light.

“Who writ the letter?”

“Margaret Van Eyck,” they answered—supposing, naturally, the inside matched the outside hand.

“Are ye sure?” He opened a drawer and drew out a paper Margaret Van Eyck had written in the business of her house. “Was it writ like this?”

“Yes. ’Tis the same writing,” said Sybrandt, boldly lying.

“Good. And now what would ye of me?” Ghysbrecht asked, beating heart carefully masked under a show of indifference so neat it nearly fooled them.

They fumbled with their bonnets and their words, edging round the matter as cats edge round a hot pot. At last it came out: they wanted him to write a letter—something that would keep Gerard in Italy—and they meant to swap it into Hans Memling’s wallet for the true letter.

While they stammered, the old man’s spirit ran a swift race between vengeance and prudence. Vengeance cried: let Gerard return and be crushed by law. Prudence murmured: better a thousand miles between you and him. Prudence also warned: why dirty your hands for these two? why give them power to smear your name? Yet fear tugged too—a fear Gerard held some secret that could wound him to the quick. At last he spoke.

“It is my duty to aid the citizens that cannot write. But for their matter I will not be responsible. Tell me, then, what I shall write.”

“Something about this Margaret.”

“Ay, ay—that she is false, that she is married to another, I’ll go bail.”

“Nay, burgomaster, nay! not for all the world!” cried Sybrandt. “Gerard would not believe it—or but half—and then he would come back to see. No; say that she is dead.”

“Dead! what, at her age, will he credit that?”

“Sooner than the other. Why she was nearly dead: so it is not to say a downright lie, after all.”

“Humph! And you think that will keep him in Italy?”

“We are sure of it, are we not, Cornelis?”

“Ay,” said Cornelis. “Our Gerard will never leave Italy now he is there. It was always his dream. He would come back for his Margaret, but not for us. What cares he for us? He despises his own family; always did.”

“This would be a bitter pill to him,” said Ghysbrecht, tasting the bitterness with a secret relish.

“It will be for his good in the end,” replied Cornelis coolly.

“What avails Famine wedding Thirst?” he added, with a hard little laugh.

“And the grief you are preparing for him so coolly?” Ghysbrecht’s voice held sarcasm, though his heart enjoyed the cruelty.

“Oh, a lie is not like a blow with a curtal axe. It hacks no flesh, and breaks no bones.”

“A curtal axe?” said Sybrandt; “no, nor even like a stroke with a cudgel.” And he shot a sly glance at Ghysbrecht’s broken nose.

The hit landed. The burgomaster’s face darkened; the old hurt burned as if the blow were new. Rage rose, and with it hatred.

“Well,” said he, “tell me what to write for you, and I must write it; but take notice, you bear the blame if aught turns amiss. Not the hand which writes, but the tongue which dictates, doth the deed.”

They agreed eagerly, sneering inwardly. Ghysbrecht drew his inkhorn close, laid the sample of Margaret Van Eyck’s hand before him, and began to ask of the size and fold of the letter—when the door flew open.

Jorian Ketel burst in, quick and flurried, and looked vexed to find company.

“Thou seest I have matter on hand, good fellow,” said Ghysbrecht.

“Ay; but this is grave. I bring good news; but ’tis not for every ear.”

Ghysbrecht rose and drew him aside into the deep embrasure of the window. The brothers heard low, eager murmuring—words clipped and urgent, like knives on a board. It ended with Ghysbrecht sending Jorian out to saddle his mule. Then he turned on the two brothers with sudden coldness that chilled them.

“I prize the peace of households; but this is not a thing to be done in a hurry: we will see about it, we will see.”

“But, burgomaster, the man will be gone. It will be too late.”

“Where is he?”

“At the hostelry, drinking.”

“Well, keep him drinking! We will see, we will see.” He dismissed them; they went off, baffled.

To understand this change, one must step back a little.

That very morning Margaret Brandt had met Jorian Ketel near her door. He passed her with a scowl. It pricked her memory: this was the man who had saved Gerard.

“Stay,” said she. “Yes! it is the good man who saved him. Oh! why have you not been near me since? And why have you not come for the parchments? Was it not true about the hundred crowns?”

Jorian snorted; but her open face made him suspect some misunderstanding. He told her he had come—and how he had been received.

“Alas!” she said. “I knew nought of this. I lay at Death’s door.” Then she led him out into the garden. The air there smelled of damp earth and bruised leaves; a spade stood stuck in the ground, and somewhere a hen muttered to herself. Margaret showed him the place, a patch where the soil lay oddly loose, as if recently turned. “Martin was for taking them up, but I would not let him. He put them there; and I said none should move them but you, who had earned them so well of him and me.”

“Give me a spade!” cried Jorian, eyes bright. Then he checked himself. “But stay! He is a suspicious man. You are sure they are there still?”

“I will openly take the blame if human hand hath touched them.”

“Then keep them but two hours more, I prithee, good Margaret,” said Jorian, and ran off to the Stadthouse of Tergou as if he smelt gold on the wind.

Now Ghysbrecht jogged towards Sevenbergen on his mule, with Jorian striding beside, full of assurances that in an hour the missing parchments would be safe in the burgomaster’s hands.

“Ah, master,” said Jorian, “lucky for us it wasn’t a thief that took them.”

“Not a thief? not a thief? what call you him, then?”

“Well—saving your presence—I call him a jackdaw. This is jackdaw’s work, if ever there was: take the thing you are least in need of, and hide it—that’s a jackdaw. I should know,” he added solemnly, “for I was brought up along with a chough. He and I were born the same year, but he cut his teeth long before me, and wow! but my life was a burden for years all along of him. If you had but a hole in your hose no bigger than a groat, in went his beak like a gimlet; and, for stealing, Gerard all over. What he wanted least, and any poor Christian in the house wanted most, that went first. Mother—she was notable—so if she did but look round, away flew her thimble. Father lived by cordwaining, so about sunrise Jack went diligently off with his awl, his wax, and his twine. After that, make your bread how you could! One day I heard my mother tell him to his face he was enough to corrupt half-a-dozen other children; and he only cocked his eye at her, and next minute away with the nurseling’s shoe off his very foot. Now this Gerard is tarred with the same stick. The parchments are no more use to him than a thimble or an awl to Jack. He took ’em out of pure mischief and hid them, and you would never have found them but for me.”

“I believe you are right,” said Ghysbrecht. “And I have vexed myself more than need.”

But when they reached Peter’s gate, uneasiness crept over him like a draught under a door.

“I wish it had been anywhere but here.”

Jorian reassured him. “The girl is honest and friendly. She had nothing to do with taking them, I’ll be sworn.” He led him into the garden. “There, master—if a face is to be believed, here they lie; and see, the mould is loose.”

He ran for the spade and began to dig. The blade bit with a soft, wet sound; the earth gave up its smell, rich and cellar-cool. Soon the corner of a parchment showed. Ghysbrecht thrust Jorian aside, dropped to his knees, and tore it out as if it were a living thing. His hands trembled; his face shone. He flung parchment after parchment up into the light, while Jorian dusted and shook them, clearing the clinging soil.

But as the heap grew, Ghysbrecht’s expression changed. The shine dulled; his brow drew down. When he reached the last, he clapped both hands to his temples as if the world had struck him.

“What mystery lies here?” he gasped. “Are fiends mocking me? Dig deeper! There must be another.”

Jorian drove the spade in again and turned up hard mould in chunks. In vain.

And even as he dug, Ghysbrecht’s mood snapped from bewilderment to rage.

“Treason! treachery!” he cried. “You knew of this.”

“Knew what, master, in Heaven’s name?”

“Caitiff, you knew there was another one worth all these twice told.”

“’Tis false,” cried Jorian, suspicion flaring because suspicion was shown to him. “’Tis a trick to rob me of my hundred crowns. Oh! I know you, burgomaster.” And he was on the edge of whining.

Then a mellow voice slid into the quarrel, smoothing it like warm oil on choppy water.

“No, good man, it is not false, nor yet is it quite true: there was another parchment.”

“There, there, there! Where is it?” Ghysbrecht panted.

“But,” said Margaret calmly, “it was not a town record—so you have gained your hundred crowns, good man—it was but a private deed between the burgomaster here and my grandfather Flor—”

“Hush, hush!” Ghysbrecht’s command cracked.

“—is Brandt.”

“Where is it, girl? that is all we want to know.”

“Have patience, and I shall tell you. Gerard read the title of it, and he said, ‘This is as much yours as the burgomaster’s,’ and he put it apart, to read it with me at his leisure.”

“It is in the house, then?” Ghysbrecht asked, gathering his face back into control.

“No, sir,” said Margaret gravely, “it is not.” Then her voice faltered, as if some old pain pressed her throat. “You hunted—my poor Gerard—so hard—so close—that you gave him no time to think of aught but his life and his grief. The parchment was in his bosom, and he hath ta’en it with him.”

“Whither, whither?”

“Ask me no more, sir. What right is yours to question me thus? It was for your sake, good man, I put force upon my heart and came out here, and bore to speak at all to this hard old man. For when I think of the misery he has brought on him and me, the sight of him is more than I can bear.” She shuddered, as if a cold sound had passed through her—like a door slammed in a quiet house—and went slowly in, hand to head, crying bitterly.

Remorse, dread of what must come, avarice, fear—these four tugged at Ghysbrecht in a single moment. His head sank; his arms fell heavy.

A coarse chuckle snapped him round. There stood Martin Wittenhaagen, leaning on his bow, grinning as if he chewed mockery for pleasure. At sight of that grin, Ghysbrecht’s worst passions sprang up anew.

“Ho! attach him, seize him, traitor and thief!” he cried. “Dog, thou shalt pay for all.”

Martin answered without a word: he only drew the duke’s pardon from his doublet and thrust it beneath the burgomaster’s nose. Ghysbrecht read—and the law in his own hands turned suddenly to ash.

Martin pressed the advantage, his voice blunt as a cleaver.

“The duke and I are soldiers. He won’t let you greasy burghers trample on an old comrade. He bade me carry you a message too.”

“The duke send a message to me?” Ghysbrecht could scarcely swallow the words.

“Ay! I told him of your masterful doings—of your imprisoning Gerard for loving a girl; and says he, ‘Tell him this is to be a king, not a burgomaster. I’ll have no kings in Holland but one. Bid him be more humble, or I’ll hang him at his own door.’”

Ghysbrecht trembled; he believed the duke capable.

“‘As I hanged the burgomaster of Thingembob.’ The duke could not mind which of you he had hung, or in what part; such trifles stick not in a soldier’s memory. But he was sure he had hanged one of you for grinding poor folk—‘and I’m the man to hang another,’ quoth the good duke.”

To be so handled by a man he counted mean, and yet to find the man untouchable under the duke’s shadow, drove the old burgomaster into an impotent fury. He shook his fist, tried to threaten, but rage choked him. Then he gave a sort of screech, and drew himself up, coiling in face and body like a striking snake, and spat full on Martin’s doublet.

Martin wiped nothing; he only looked at him with a soldier’s contempt.

“Here’s a venomous old toad! he knows a kick from my foot would send him to his last home; and he wants me to cheat the gallows. But I have slain too many men in fair fight to lift limb against anything less than a man; and this I count no man. What is it, in Heaven’s name? an old goat’s-skin bag full o’ rotten bones.”

“My mule! my mule!” screamed Ghysbrecht.

Jorian helped him up, the burgomaster shaking in every joint. But once in the saddle, unnatural vigour came into him; and the figure that fled back to Tergou was like something out of a fever-dream: wizened face under streaming white hair, eye baleful, fury shaking the bent frame as he spurred like mad. His quavering voice carried back on the road like a harsh, persistent crow-call:

“I’ll make their hearts ache. I’ll make their hearts ache. I’ll make their hearts ache. All of them. All—all—all!”

Back at the hostelry, the black sheep sat among the drinkers, sick at heart and staring at Hans Memling’s wallet. For ease, the painter had taken it off and flung it on the table; it lay there, slack-mouthed, ready. How easily they might have slid out the true letter and put in another. For the first time in their lives, they were sorry they had not learned to write, like their brother.

Hans began to talk of going; the brothers whispered and agreed to abandon their plan—for the moment.

They had scarcely settled it when Dierich Brower appeared in the doorway and gave them a wink.

They went out to him.

“Come to the burgomaster with all speed,” said he.

They found Ghysbrecht seated at a table, pale and restless. Before him lay the sample of Margaret Van Eyck’s handwriting.

“I have written what you desired,” said he. “Now for the superscription. What were the words? did ye see?”

“We cannot read,” said Cornelis.

“Then is all this labour lost,” cried Ghysbrecht, anger flaring. “Dolts!”

“Nay, but,” said Sybrandt quickly, “I heard the words read, and I have not lost them. They were: ‘To Gerard Eliassoen, these by the hand of the trusty Hans Memling, with all speed.’”

“’Tis well. Now—how was the letter folded? how big was it?”

“Longer than that one, and not so long as this.”

“’Tis well. Where is he?”

“At the hostelry.”

“Come, then. Take you this groat, and treat him. Then ask to see the letter, and put this in place of it. Come to me with the other letter.”

The brothers took the false letter and went. They had not been gone a minute when Dierich Brower slipped out after them, under orders to keep them in sight until the true letter lay safe in his master’s hands. He watched from outside the hostelry like a hound that has been taught which door to guard.

He did not wait long. The brothers came out almost at once, faces fallen.

“Too late!” they cried. “Too late! He is gone.”

“Gone? How long?”

“Scarce five minutes. Cursed chance!”

“You must go back to the burgomaster at once,” said Dierich Brower.

“To what end?”

“No matter; come!” He hurried them back.

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten was not the man to accept defeat.

“Well,” said he, when he heard. “Suppose he is gone. Is he mounted?”

“No.”

“Then what hinders you to come up with him?”

“But what avails coming up with him! There are no hostelries on the road he is gone.”

“Fools!” said Ghysbrecht. “Is there no way of emptying a man’s pockets but liquor and sleight of hand?”

A look passed between Ghysbrecht and Dierich—cold, swift, understanding. It carried meaning enough. The brothers paled; the zeal ran out of them as if a bung had been pulled.

They set Denys in the very midst of them, elbowed and hemmed as if his grief itself were a kind of weapon. Yet no cord could bind what tore inside him. He rode like a man who has swallowed fire: now spitting it at heaven and earth in raving curses, now dropping into a silence so black and sharp that even rough soldiers, who had heard dying men rattle prayers through split throats, looked sideways and decided it was wiser to take his arms away.

All his thought went in one ring, round and round, wearing the same groove deeper: for his sake Gerard had forsaken the German road to Rome—and for that mercy what came? Gerard left alone in the very belly of Burgundy, where vineyards climbed the slopes like patient hands and every lane might hide a knife. Denys felt the bargain of friendship turn to ashes in his mouth.

They overtook their leader just beyond the town gates, and the whole cavalcade drew bridle and baited at the Tête d’Or. The inn steamed like a pot set on coals. From the kitchen came the fat, consoling breath of broth, onions sweated down to sweetness, a hare somewhere turning on a spit and weeping its own perfume into the smoke; the clack of trenchers and the hiss of ale drawn bright and quick were a kind of rough music—one that should have steadied a man’s heart. But Denys heard none of it rightly. The clang of harness, the barked orders, the scrape of boots on rushes all rasped him raw, as though sound itself had turned against him.

The young landlady—nimble as a cook who can turn from sauce to guest without spilling either—was much taken up with the count, and more still with the bastard; yet her eyes, sharp as a carver’s knife, found Denys in his misery. She came near enough to smell the road-dust on him and asked, with an uneasiness she tried to cover, what had become of his young companion.

Denys’s grief broke out like a pot boiling over. He told her all—how Gerard was parted from him—and begged her to send after him.

“Now he is sundered from me, he will maybe listen to my rede,” he cried; “poor wretch, he loves not solitude.”

The landlady tossed her head, colour rising in her cheeks as if the very request had touched a sore place. “I trow I have been somewhat over-kind already,” said she.

“You will not?”

“Not I.”

Then Denys—who had nothing left but the sting of his tongue—poured out a volley of curses that made even the nearest trooper shift. She turned her back as if he had flung dirty dishwater at her, and went off whimpering that she was not used to be cursed at. Yet, even while she spoke so, she snapped orders to her hind to saddle two mules.

Denys rode north with his troop, mute now, drooping over the saddle like a man whose spine had been cut. He did not know—could not know—that the same “veracious” young woman, who had sworn him no help, made herself ready in forty minutes as briskly as one trussing a capon, threw on cloak and riding-gear, and spurred away with her servant in the opposite direction. Her haste had the clean, clipped rhythm of purpose; her horse’s hoofbeats dwindled on the road like a receding drum.

At dark, after a long march, the bastard and his men reached the White Hart. Their arrival turned the inn inside out. Doors banged; voices rose; dogs yelped; the stable rang with iron on stone. Pots were set to boil and ladles struck rims in a hurry, and the air filled with the sharp-sweet promise of bread warming and meat being sliced too fast, the knife scraping bone. In that uproar Denys moved like a shadow.

It took Manon time to find him among so many. When at last she did, her only sign was a sudden heightening of colour, as if she had leaned too close to a hearth. She did not claim the acquaintance. She stood in her worshipful place now, among those who mattered, and the poor soul within her had already begun that slow new scorn of the ladder she had climbed—those base degrees by which she did ascend. Denys saw it all and could not so much as twist his mouth into a smile. This inn, with its smells of stew and spilled wine, its familiar smoke and grease and trampled rushes, reminded him too much of Gerard—of shared crusts, of meat divided by a blade and laughter caught between mouthfuls. His loss sat in his throat like dry bread.

Before the night closed, the wind changed, and with it the whole sound of the place: the draught found cracks and whistled; the sign creaked; a far-off owl called as if counting the living. Manon looked into the room and beckoned Denys with her finger.

He rose sulkily—and his guards rose with him, for they watched him like men watch a dog that has been beaten but may still bite.

“Nay,” said Manon, quick and low, “I would speak a word to thee in private.”

She drew him to a corner where the noise thinned to a dull wash, and there, under her breath, she asked would he do her a kindness.

Denys answered aloud, brutal as a man who has been rubbed raw and then asked for velvet. “No, I will not. I am not in the vein to do kindnesses to man or woman. If I did a kindness it should be to a dog; and not that if I could help it.”

“Alas, good archer,” said Manon, humbly as a beggar at a buttery hatch, “I did you one eftsoons—you and your pretty comrade.”

“You did, dame, you did,” he said, the edge dulling a little at Gerard’s name. “Well then, for his sake—what is’t to do?”

“Thou knowest my story,” she murmured. “I had been unfortunate. Now I am worshipful. But a woman did cast him in my teeth this day. And so ’twill be ever while he hangs there. I would have him ta’en down; well-a-day!”

“With all my heart,” said Denys, fierce with a sudden, misplaced generosity.

“And none dare I ask but thee,” she whispered. “Wilt do’t?”

“Not I,” he said, and the word struck like a mallet, “even were I not a prisoner.”

On this stern refusal Manon sighed and clasped her palms together, a gesture as old as hearth-prayer, despairing. Denys, who had no patience left for her delicacy, told her not to fret. There were soldiers of a lower stamp—men who would not make two bites of such a cherry. It was a mere matter of money. If she could find two angels, he would find two soldiers to do the dirty work.

The suggestion sat ill on her tongue. She had wanted the deed washed clean by friendship and secrecy, not bought like salt pork. Yet she reflected—slowly, as one who turns a thought over like a dumpling to see if it is cooked through—that soldiers were birds of passage: drinking here to-night, knocked on the head there to-morrow. At last she said, soft as if ashamed of her own voice, “Send them out to me. But prithee, tell them that ’tis for one that is my friend; let them not think ’tis for me; I should sink into the earth. Times are changed.”

Denys found two warriors glad to win an angel apiece so easily. He sent them out, and instantly, with contempt for the whole matter, dropped his mind back into its old trench, brooding on his lost friend as a man worries a crust he cannot swallow.

Manon and the mail-clad fellows soon came to understanding. Yet even agreed sin has its housekeeping: what were they to do with the body when it was taken down? Manon’s voice trembled, but her words were practical—she had thought upon it more than once, as a cook thinks upon storage and spoilage.

“The river is nigh the—the place,” she murmured.

“Fling him in, eh?” one said, blunt as a cleaver.

“Nay, nay; be not so cruel!” she breathed, horror and need wrestling. “Could ye not put him—gently—and—with somewhat weighty?”

It was all speedily settled, save the time of payment. The mail-clad itched for their coin and asked for it in advance. Manon demurred. Did she doubt their word? Then let her come along with them, or watch from a distance.

“Me?” Manon cried, as if they had asked her to taste blood. “I would liever die than see it done.”

“Which yet you would have done,” they answered, with the rough justice of men who hear only the clink of money.

“Ay,” she said, and the confession came out like a cough, “for sore is my need. Times are changed.”

She had already forgotten her own caution to Denys. The night swallowed their footsteps. An hour later that disagreeable relic of caterpillar existence—hung up between past and present—ceased to canker the worshipful matron’s public life, and the grim eyes of what had been stopped looking down into a white hind’s clover field. The village air, so long tuned to the creak of rope and the small, constant complaints of the dead, seemed suddenly altered: the night had one less harsh note in it, as if a string had been cut.

Manon went on to make the landlord an average wife, and a prime house-dog, and to outlive everybody; for such is the stubbornness of lives that root themselves in bread and habit. But that was after.

When the two soldiers came back from their errand—having followed, with a kind of medieval naïveté, the precept “Off wi’ the auld love”—they received a shock. They found the market-place black with groups; it had been empty an hour ago. Voices swarmed like bees. Lanterns bobbed. The very air was thick with whispering, and every sound—shuffling feet, quick prayers, a child’s sudden cry—seemed to strike the ear too loud.

Conscience smote them, for even hard men feel the world listen when they have meddled with the dead. The bolder of the two, heartened by darkness, stole forward alone and slyly mingled with a group. He listened a moment, then ran back to his fellow and said, in a tone of reproach not strictly reasonable:

“Ye born fool, it is only a miracle.”

Letters, the color of live coals, had asked their question on the church wall with a blunt, almost household curiosity—why, in such troubled weather of men’s souls, there was no mass for the duke. People who had gone to market for onions and eels found themselves instead standing with necks craned, mouths ajar, staring at scripture written by no human hand. It shone, it wavered, and it thinned like lard in a hot pan, fading slowly until only the lime-washed stones remained and the cold of daylight returned to its proper dominion.

Yet the question lingered as stubbornly as the smell of smoke in a cloak.

The magistrates, not wishing the heavens to outbid them in loyalty, began to buy masses with a generosity that had the clink of coin in it. The curé—an old acquaintance—took this sudden piety in hard cash, and with it indulged a very pretty taste. But miracles, like cheap wine, grow stale if you sip them too long; life moved on, as it always does, from wonder to bargaining.

Denys had begged for his arms.

“Why disgrace him as well as break his heart?” he pleaded, thinking of Gerard.

“Then swear,” came the answer, “on the cross of thy sword thou wilt not leave the bastard’s service until the sedition is put down.”

Need is a hard master. Denys poured out oaths in volleys—thick, quick, and bitter—till they were satisfied. His arms were restored; his liberty, too, in that narrow soldier’s sense which means a man may walk where he is ordered and die where he is paid.

They halted at an inn called The Three Fish, a place that smelled of damp straw, ale-sour boards, and frying fat that had done duty too many days. Marion, catching sight of him, cried out at once, as if she could keep fear at bay by making sport of it:

“I’m out of luck; who would have thought to see you again?”

Then she saw his face was not made for jesting and softened, the way a cook softens a tough scrap with patience and heat.

“What is amiss?”

He told her—of Gerard lost to him in this whirl of politics and steel, and of the promise that had bound him.

Marion’s mind, trained by hard streets and harder reckonings, took a bright view as naturally as it took a quick knife to an apple.

“Gerard is too handsome and too well-behaved to come to harm,” she said, as if those were protections like armour. “Women will always be on his side. Besides, it must go either well or ill with him. If it goes well, he will strike in with good company to Rome; if ill, he will come home again—perhaps there before you, for you have, by all accounts, a trifle of fighting to do in Flanders.”

She fetched the gold pieces he had entrusted to her. He urged her to keep one, then another, as a man presses bread on a hungry child. She refused steadily, with that honest obstinacy that is rarer than piety paid for by corporations. It eased him. It made him think a little better of the world—at least of the corners where a poor little friend walked alone and yet kept her hands clean.

Already the roads were dotted with foot soldiers in twos and threes, trudging lazily toward Flanders. Many were penniless, but bailiffs pushed them on from town to town, and the innkeepers—grumbling, sweating, and making do—were ordered to feed and lodge them. Anthony of Burgundy rode among these stragglers, gathering them as a man gathers loose ears of wheat into his apron, until he entered Flanders with six hundred men under his standard.

On the frontier Baldwyn, his brother, met him with arms, provisions, and more men. Their force was set in order and marched in battle array through several towns, not only unimpeded but acclaimed—shouts in the streets, bells in the air, the whole countryside sounding like a drum of loyalty. The noise of it, hearty and unanimous, sat ill on those who had been told they marched to chastise disaffection.

“This rebellion of ours is a bite,” growled a soldier named Simon, who had elected himself Denys’s comrade.

Denys said nothing. But inside him a vow hardened, like a crust set before the fire: if this rebellion that had cost him Gerard proved no rebellion at all, then, by St. Mars, he would shoot Anthony of Burgundy dead.

That afternoon they saw ahead a town that crouched behind walls thick as old bread and towers like clenched fists. A whisper ran through the ranks—this was a disaffected place. Yet as they approached, the great gate stood open, and each flanking tower showed only a single sentinel, as if the town had nothing to hide and no fear to show. Their formation loosened; men walked easier; harness creaked, and someone even laughed.

Then, when they were within a furlong, the drawbridge over the moat rose slowly, groaning on its chains until it stood upright against the fort. At that very instant the portcullis dropped with an iron rattle, and the walls bristled—lances, crossbows, sudden faces, the neat black mouths of slits alive with intent.

A stern hum rose from the front rank and shivered backward like a plucked string.

“Halt!” Anthony cried. The word ran down the line, and the whole body checked as if it had struck a wall of air.

“Herald to the gate!”
