A pursuivant rode out and stopped twenty yards from the gate. He lifted his bugle; the herald’s flag drooped round it, and the summons rang bright, thin, and insolent against the stone. A tall figure in brazen armour appeared over the gate. Fiery words passed—inaudible, but their meaning plain in the way the herald’s shoulders stiffened. He blew one keen note, a threat sharpened by brass, and galloped back with war in his face.

Anthony bent his head to him for the space of two breaths, then wheeled and shouted, “Pioneers, to the van!”

Hedges were levelled; the force took the field and encamped just out of shot. Mounted officers rode south, east, and west to friendly towns for mangonels and palisades, mantelets and raw hides, tar-barrels and carpenters, provisions and all the stubborn furniture of a siege. The camp settled into a new kind of life—mechanical, busy, and incessantly loud: mallets on stakes, saws biting wood, chains clinking, carts rattling, and, above all, the high thin hiss of arrows sewing the air.

At the first clang of the portcullis Denys’s eyes had brightened. When the herald came back with battle in his gaze, Denys saw it and, for the first time in days, cried out, “Courage, tout le monde, le diable est mort.”

If the great warrior whose name he had spoken could have heard, he might have grinned.

The besiegers encamped a furlong from the walls and made roads. Pikemen waited ready for assault; sappers and pioneers crept forward; catapultiers and crossbowmen took their stations. The siege began in the old patient way—filling the moat, mining, breaching, and all the while working under a close rain of quarrels, bolts, stones, and little rocks. A siege was a kind of craft, a trade of wood and rope and leverage, and it demanded a hundred eyes and a mind awake in every limb. To those who watched from safety it might even seem amusing, like a fair; to those beneath the missiles it was a daylong reckoning.

Carpenters advanced behind rolling mantelets to raise a stockade at the very edge of the moat. Some lives were lost—men dropped as suddenly as sacks of meal—but not many, for crossbowmen, Denys among them, rolled up their shields and shot over the workmen’s heads at every besieged who showed so much as a nose, and at every slit or loophole that commanded the ground. Their bolts made a dull, satisfying thunk when they struck wood; a sharper, uglier sound when they found meat.

Under that condensed fire the palisade rose—fresh-cut timber smelling green and raw, sap bleeding where axes had opened it. It stood between the besiegers and the ordinary missiles of the walls.

The defenders answered at night by running out wooden penthouses atop the curtains, fitting beams into square holes built for the purpose. These hoards—true teeth of a medieval fort—gave defenders freer range than any fixed loophole. From them they could drop and shoot with a cruel liberty, as if the wall had grown hands.

The besiegers brought up mangonels and battered those woodworks with huge stones until boards shattered, and the air filled with splinters like flying bones. They built, too, a triangular wooden tower as high as the curtain, kept ready just out of shot, and the sight of it brooding there chilled the town like a bad omen. The defenders began mining beneath the part of the moat where that tower would come, preparing a warm reception. The besiegers mined elsewhere, aiming to get under the square barbican and throw it down.

All this time Denys worked behind his mantelet with another arbalestrier. He made excellent shots—clean, purposeful, the way a cook trims away waste with a sure knife. His skill earned him the peculiar esteem of an unseen archer within the walls, who now and then sent a winged compliment quivering into Denys’s board. One struck within an inch of the narrow slit through which Denys was squinting.

“Peste,” Denys cried, more angry than afraid. “You shoot well, my friend. Come forth and receive my congratulations! Shall merit such as thine hide its head? Comrade, it is one of those cursed Englishmen with his half-ell shaft. I’ll not die till I’ve had a shot at London wall.”

On the defenders’ side a figure soon drew every eye—because he walked where any sensible man would crawl. A tall knight in complete brass paced the battlements under fire, carrying a light but prodigiously long lance with which he directed the defenders’ movements, as if he were conducting music. When disaster befell the besiegers, that knight and that lance were almost always part of it.

Why did not Denys shoot him? Denys did—every day. Other crossbowmen shot. Archers shot. Everybody shot; and the abomination was that he did not mind. Worse: he began to look as if he did not even know when he was hit. Bolts struck and glanced; arrows kissed the metal and fell. He kept pacing, glittering in the bright air, as calmly oblivious as a sailor in wool pacing his deck under harmless rain.

At last the besiegers, spiteful and practical, cursed him and his impervious coat and saved their good steel for softer targets.

The day was bright, clear, not quite frosty. The whole effort concentrated on about two hundred and fifty yards—two curtains and two towers. One tower was the square barbican; another had a pointed roof overlapping on a stone machicolation, so that a row of crenelets grinned between roof and masonry like a mouth of grinders. The curtains wore their hoards, battered by slinging engines.

Along the moat’s edge, on the besiegers’ side, the works sprawled like a gigantic arsenal—longer than broad, peopled by human ants. Levers groaned, winches squealed, pulleys creaked; capstans turned; carts came and went, rattling like bones in a box. Heaps of stone, piles of fascines, stacks of mantelets, rows of fire-barrels sat ready. And through that honest industry flew arrows, back and forth, stitching an invisible cloth. Here and there a man lay flatter than in any decent sleep with feathers stuck in him, and blood oozed darkly into the churned earth.

Opposite the wooden tower, a great penthouse called a “cat” crept toward the curtain, filling the moat with fascines and rubbish pushed out from its mouth. Ropes and pulleys and distant windlasses moved it with slow persistence. The tall knight burned the first cat with blazing tar-barrels. So the besiegers made the roof of this one very steep and covered it with raw hides; the tar slid off, spitting, and did no harm. The knight signalled, and a little trebuchet behind the wall began dropping stones into the moat. At last it found the range, and one stone punched through the cat’s roof, making an ugly wound.

Baldwyn saw, and his temper—always ready as flint—threw sparks. He ordered the great catapult that had been battering the hoards opposite to be turned and levelled, slantwise, at that invulnerable knight.

Denys and his Englishman went to dinner.

For all their murderous attentions, they had made a distant acquaintance, speaking by signs as men do who share a single, constant topic that keeps its importance in peace or war: food. Sometimes Denys would set a piece of bread atop his mantelet; sometimes the archer would dangle something from a string. Thus they dined together as if at the same board—each chewing, each watching, each listening to the battlefield’s rough orchestra: the thump of stones, the twang of bows, the low thunder of shouted orders.

Now the engineers took the unusual step of slinging fifty-pound stones at one man.

The catapult was a beautiful, brutal thing: a fir-tree trunk set to turn on an axis between uprights, not balanced—three-quarters of its length on one side. At the short thick end hung a weight like half a ton, butt toward the enemy. A winch forced the long end down to the earth and pinned it; the weight rose and strained aloft. A stone lay in a sling at the nose. Then the bolt was drawn, and gravity—old and patient—snapped the machine into motion: weight down, long arm up, sling whipping at the top, stone flying with a jerk that seemed to tear the very air.

The huge mass missed the knight but struck the hoard near him, went through roof and floor like paper, and made a gap as wide as a grave. Two things fell out—first the stone, then the mangled body of a besieger it had struck. Down the curtain they went, down, down, and struck the moat almost together. The water closed bubbling on them, swallowing both stone and bone.

“Aha! a good shot,” cried Baldwyn.

The tall knight retired, and the besiegers hooted. He reappeared on the barbican platform, helmet just visible above the parapet, busy as a man in a bakehouse. Soon an enormous Turkish catapult was hauled into place. From that height it flung a twenty-pound stone some two hundred and forty yards; it bounded and knocked dirt into Lord Anthony’s eye and made him swear. The next stone struck a horse drawing a cart of arrows, bowled it dead like a rabbit, and spilled the load.

Then the Turk turned on the besiegers’ wooden tower, supposed to be out of shot. He slung stones cut with sharp edges on purpose and struck it repeatedly, breaking it in several places. Two of the besiegers’ engines were turned on the barbican platform; they rained smaller stones and killed two engineers. But the Turk disdained to answer in kind. He sent a forty-pound stone crashing onto the besiegers’ great catapult near the axis and smashed the whole structure to pieces; the engineers fled, skipping and yelling like boys stung by bees.

In the afternoon Simon, running back to his mantelet from a palisade where he had been shooting, suddenly stared, held out his arms, and rolled face-first into the dirt with an arrow protruding from his back. The Englishman showed himself a moment to enjoy his work. Denys, already prepared, shot; his bolt struck, and the murderous archer staggered away wounded. Simon never moved again.

“I am unlucky in my comrades,” Denys said, and the words tasted like stale ale.

Next morning the besieged saw, with dismay, that the cat was now covered with mattresses and raw hides and was steadily filling the moat. The tall knight stoned it in vain; he flung burning tar-barrels in vain. Then, with his own hands, he lowered by a rope a bag of burning sulphur and pitch. The stench rolled out thick and choking—sulphur’s bitter bite, pitch’s oily reek—so that the men within were smoked like hams.

But Baldwyn, armoured like a lobster in shining plates, ran forward, bounded onto the cat’s roof, and cut the rope. The work went on while smoke curled and thinned, carried away by the indifferent wind.

Then the knight sent fresh engineers into the mine and underpinned the place with beams, smearing them thick with grease and tar, laying a trap in the earth as carefully as a cook lays kindling under a pot.

At break of day the moat was filled. The wooden tower began to move on its wheels toward the curtain where two catapults were already clearing the hoards. Its approach was awful, almost magical, for it moved without visible agency—driven by internal rollers worked by leverage. On its top platform stood the first assailing party, protected in front by the drawbridge of the turret, which stood upright until it would be lowered onto the wall; protected better still by full suits of armour.

The defenders slung stones at the tower and struck it often, but the hides and mattresses drank the blows. Presently it stood at the moat’s edge. The tall knight bade fire the mine beneath it.

At that moment the Turkish engine flung a stone of half a hundredweight right among the knights on the tower. Two were carried off it onto the plain. One lay and writhed; the other neither moved nor spoke.

Now the besieging catapults hurled blazing tar-barrels and set the hoards on both sides aflame. The assailants ran up ladders behind the tower; the drawbridge was lowered onto the battered curtain. In concert the engines fired adjoining works to drive defenders back. Armoured men sprang onto the bridge led by Baldwyn. The invulnerable knight and his men-at-arms met them, and a fearful combat began on that narrow plank of death. Men fell headlong, armour flashing, bodies tumbling like dropped pots.

Fresh besiegers swarmed up behind. The defenders were driven off the bridge. Another minute and the town might have been taken.

But the mine had been timed with a craft as exact as measuring spice: just then the underpinnings gave way. The tower sank suddenly away from the wall, tearing the drawbridge clear and pouring the soldiers off it—against the masonry and into the dry moat below, a heap of iron and limbs.

A fierce shout rose from the defenders. In a moment they surrounded Baldwyn and his fellows—and, strangely, offered quarter. While some disarmed and disposed of the prisoners, others fired the turret in fifty places with a kind of hand-grenades. The tall knight was busiest of all, loading fire-bags onto his long spear and thrusting them into the doomed structure that had lately been so terrible.

To do this he had to stand on a projecting beam of the shattered hoard, holding on by a pikeman’s hand to steady himself.

It provoked Denys. The confusion seemed a cloak. He ran out from behind his mantelet, levelled his crossbow, and shot—missing the knight clean, but driving the bolt into the pikeman’s brain. The hand let go. The tall knight fell heavily from the wall, lance and all.

Denys stared, wonder-struck. In that unlucky moment his arm burned hot, then went cold as if plunged into water. An English arrow had skewered it.

His small pain was swallowed by the larger drama. The knight, armour glittering in the morning sun, fell headlong, but turned as he struck the water and hit with a slap that sounded a mile off. No one thought to see him again. Yet he fell at the edge of the fascines where the turret stood cocked on one side. His spear stuck into them under water; by a mighty effort he worked to the side, but could not climb out.

Anthony sent a dozen knights with a white flag to take him prisoner. The fallen terror submitted like a lamb, saying nothing. They brought him dripping and mud-plastered to Anthony’s tent. At first Anthony laughed at the sight of that once-glittering armour fouled like a pot left too long in ashes. Then his face hardened.

“I marvel, sir,” he said, “that so good a knight as you should know his devoir so ill as turn rebel, and give us all this trouble.”

“I am n-n-n-n-no knight,” the prisoner stammered.

“What then?”

“A hosier.”

“A what? Then thy armour shall be stripped off, and thou shalt be tied to a stake in front of the works, and riddled with arrows for a warning to traitors.”

“N-n-n-no! Duda-duda-don’t do that.”

“Why not?”

“Tuta-tuta-townsfolk will h-h-h-hang t’other buba-buba-bastard.”

“What—whom?”

“Your bub-bub-brother Baldwyn.”

Anthony started as if a hot coal had fallen into his glove. “What, have you knaves ta’en him?”

The warlike hosier nodded.

“Hang the fool!” Anthony said peevishly, more angry at being checked than at the peril.

The hosier watched his eye, then doffed his helmet and drew from its lining a letter—intercepted. It was from the duke, bidding Anthony come to court immediately. He was to represent Burgundy at the court of England; to go over, receive the English king’s sister, and conduct her to her bridegroom, the Earl of Charolois.

The words had the power of perfume: they carried the scent of velvet halls, rich tables, music untroubled by screams, and a court famed as the gayest and most luxurious in Europe. The hosier saw desire rise in Anthony like hunger.

“We’ll gega-gega-give ye a thousand angels,” the hosier stammered, “to raise the siege.”

“And Baldwyn?”

“I’ll gega-gega-go and send him with the money.”

It was dinner-time. A flag of truce was hoisted on both sides. The sham knight and the true one dined together, and by the end of the meal—between bread broken and meat torn—came to a friendly understanding.

“But what is your grievance, my good friend?” Anthony asked, as if rebellion were merely a seasoning that had been overdone.

“Tuta-tuta-too much taxes,” said the hosier, with the plainness of a man who has counted every penny and felt each one taken.

Denys, discovering the arrow in his right arm, turned his back—protected by a long shield—and walked sulkily into camp, the noise of the siege dulled by the rush of blood in his ears. The wound throbbed with its own pulse, like a kettle beginning to simmer.

He met the Comte de Jarnac, who had seen his brilliant shot; finding him wounded into the bargain, the count dropped into his hand a handful of broad pieces, bright as freshly turned loaves.

“Hast got the better of thy grief, arbalestrier, methinks.”

“My grief, yes,” Denys replied, the words tight between his teeth. “But not my love. As soon as ever I have put down this rebellion, I go to Holland; and there I shall meet with him.”

The event was nearer than Denys thought. Next day he was relieved from service; and though his wound was no trifle, he set out with a stout heart to rejoin his friend in Holland, leaving behind him the siege’s clangour and its bitter smoke, and carrying with him the ache of iron in flesh and of a name that tasted, in his mouth, like home bread remembered in exile.

A change fell on Margaret Brandt like a frost that comes in the night and will not melt at noon. She moved through the hosier’s house as though the rooms were full of smoke and she must feel her way by touch alone. Her hands still did their work—kneading, rinsing, sweeping—yet without their old brisk certainty; she would pause with the dough half turned, as if the living warmth under her palms accused her.

If Peter but spoke a little sharp, the way a man will when accounts go awry or a strap will not buckle, she started so violently the pot-lids on the shelf would chatter. Then she would stare at him with wide, frightened eyes, and the sound of his voice seemed to ring too loud in her ears, as if every syllable were a hammer on the house’s thin peace.

She went less often to her warm old friend, Dame Margaret Van Eyck; and when she did go, she was ill at ease there. The dame’s caresses—those motherly embraces that had once drawn a smile—were now received with a passive trembling, and sometimes Margaret shrank from them as if love itself might burn.

But the strangest thing of all was this: she would not go outside her own door in daylight. If she went to Tergou, it was after dusk, when the street-sounds softened and faces blurred into shadow; and she would return before daybreak, while only the earliest birds and the far-off creak of a cart-wheel spoke in the dark. She would not even go to matins. The bell’s clean call that used to wash the town’s sleep away seemed now too public, too piercing, a sound that drew eyes as well as ears.

At last Peter—slow to observe anything that did not touch his trade—marked it and questioned her.

“Why ever will you not show your face by day?”

Margaret’s fingers tightened on the cloth she held. “Methinks the folk all look at me.”

Another day Dame Van Eyck, with that shrewd kindness which sees beneath excuses, asked her outright what ailed her. A scared look, and then a flood of tears, were all the answer. The old lady expostulated gently.

“What, sweetheart—afraid to confide your sorrows to me?”

“I have no sorrows, madam,” Margaret whispered, “but of my own making. I am kinder treated than I deserve—especially in this house.”

“Then why not come oftener, my dear?”

“I come oftener than I deserve,” said Margaret, and sighed so deep it seemed to draw the warmth out of the room.

“There—Reicht is bawling for you,” Dame Van Eyck said, easing the moment with homely impatience. “Go, child!—what on earth can it be?”

Left alone, the dame turned the matter over as women do when their hands are busy and their minds will not rest: perhaps the girl was mortified by the contempt with which she was treated by Gerard’s kin. The thought stung her. If that were it, she would take them to task—at least the women.

The very next day she put on hood and cloak, and with Reicht trotting after her, went to the hosier’s house. Catherine received her with much respect, and thanked her with tears for her kindness to Gerard; but when, encouraged by this, Dame Van Eyck turned the talk toward Margaret Brandt, Catherine’s eyes dried as suddenly as if a shutter had been drawn over them. Her lips pinched, and her face set into that look which belongs to obstinate, ignorant women—faces that, once settled thus, might as well be a brick wall for all the softening words in the world.

Dame Van Eyck tried. She tried as one tries to coax a sour leaven into sweetness—patiently at first, then more sharply when patience fails. All in vain. Not being used to be thwarted, she grew provoked; and at last, with an abrupt, half-broken curtsey that was more dismissal than farewell, she went out. Catherine returned it with an air of defiance rather than obeisance.

Outside the door Reicht stood talking with a pale girl on crutches. Dame Van Eyck, cheeks hot, was sweeping past them with a scornful toss meant for the whole household when suddenly a little delicate hand slid into hers—timid as a bird lighting. She looked round and met two dove-like eyes, wet with tears, that sought hers with gratitude and with entreaty in one.

The old woman read that look, complex as it was; and her anger dropped away, as if some unseen hand had turned down the flame.

“I see,” said she softly. Then she kissed the girl’s brow. “Mind, then—I leave it to you.”

When she returned home she said, half to herself, half to the room that listened, “I have been to a house to-day where I have seen a very common thing and a very uncommon thing. I have seen a stupid, obstinate woman; and I have seen an angel in the flesh, with a face—if I had it here, I’d take down my brushes once more and try and paint it.”

Little Kate did not belie that hasty good opinion. She watched, waited, and chose her hour. Then she told her mother what she had learned from Reicht Heynes: how Margaret Brandt had shed her very blood for Gerard in the wood.

“See, mother, how she loves him.”

“Who would not love him?” Catherine answered, as if that settled all.

“Oh, mother—think of it! Poor thing.”

“Ay, wench. She has her own trouble, no doubt, as well as we ours. I can’t abide the sight of blood—let alone my own.”

That was a gain: the first crack in a hardened crust. But when Kate tried to press further, she was stopped short; her mother’s temper was like a pot that will not simmer—either cold or boiling.

About a month after this, a soldier of the Dalgetty breed—one of those lean, roving blades who come and go with war as if war were weather—returned from service in Burgundy and brought a letter one evening to the hosier’s house. Peter was away on business; the rest sat at supper. The table held their plain fare: coarse bread, a bit of salted meat, and a pot that sent up a homely steam smelling of cabbage and onions browned in dripping. The spoons clicked; the hearth snapped; outside, the wind worried at the eaves.

The soldier laid the letter by Catherine’s hand, refused all guerdon for bringing it, and went off toward Sevenbergen as if he carried news for no one, as if messages were nothing but another road.

The letter lay unfolded and spread out. Curiously enough, though not one of them could read, they all knew it was Gerard’s hand. The strokes, the spacing, even the way the ink thinned at the end of a line—these were as familiar as his tread on the stair.

“And your father must be away,” cried Catherine, half anger, half shame. “Are ye not ashamed of yourselves—not one that can read your brother’s letter?”

Yet though the words were to them what strange runes are to a ploughman, there was something on the page they could read. There is an art that speaks without words, and needs no priest nor scholar to interpret it; it steals through the eye into the heart, learned and unlearned alike, and crosses frontiers without losing a syllable, because it has none to lose. It is at the mercy of no translator; it writes an universal tongue.

Between two short paragraphs Gerard had drawn, in pencil, two hands clasped together.

They read that. It went straight to the marrow. As they stared, Gerard seemed present—his very manner in every turn and line—and bidding them farewell. The women wept until tears blurred the simple sketch. Giles said, “Poor Gerard!” and his voice came out lower than seemed to belong to him. Even Cornelis and Sybrandt felt a momentary remorse and sat silent, gloomy, as if the hearth had dimmed.

But how to get the words read? Pride held them. They were loth to show both ignorance and grief to a stranger.

“The Dame Van Eyck?” Kate ventured timidly.

“And so I will,” said Catherine. “She has a good heart. She loves Gerard, too. She will be glad to hear of him. I was short with her when she came here; but I will make my submission, and then she will tell me what my poor child says to me.”

She wrapped herself and went at once. The night air had that winter bite that makes every sound seem sharper: her footsteps on frozen ground, the distant bark of a dog, the thin, far bell of some late hour. When she reached Dame Van Eyck’s, Reicht took her into a room and said, “Bide a minute; she is at her orisons.”

A young woman sat pensively by the stove. She rose at Catherine’s entrance and courteously made way. The stove breathed a steady warmth; it carried scents of peat and dried herbs, and in that warmth Catherine thawed her fingers, grateful as a starved body is grateful to broth.

“Thank you, young lady,” said Catherine. “The winter nights are cold, and your stove is a treat.”

While warming her hands she inspected the other furtively from head to foot, as women will. The young person wore a common wimple, but her gown was trimmed with fur—almost a sign, in those days, of superior rank or wealth. Yet what struck Catherine most was not the fur, but the face: so candid, so modest, it promised sympathy the way fresh bread promises comfort before ever it is cut.

Catherine’s tongue loosened with hope. “Now, what think you brings me here, young lady? It is a letter! a letter from my poor boy that is far away in some savage part or other. And I take shame to say that none of us can read it. I wonder whether you can read?”

“Yes,” said the young woman.

“Can ye, now? It is much to your credit, my dear. I dare say she won’t be long; but every minute is an hour to a poor longing mother.”

“I will read it to you.”

“Bless you, my dear; bless you!” Catherine cried, and in her unfeigned eagerness she never noticed the strange, suppressed eagerness with which the other slowly put out her hand to take the letter—nor the tremor that ran through the fingers as they closed upon it, as though the paper were a living thing.

“Come, then,” said Catherine. “Read it to me, prithee. I am wearying for it.”

The young woman’s voice began steady, but too careful, like one who walks on ice.

“The first words are—‘To my honoured parents.’”

“Ay! and he always did honour us, poor soul,” Catherine answered, and clutched her apron as if it were his sleeve.

“‘God and the saints have you in His holy keeping, and bless you by night and by day. Your one harsh deed is forgotten; your years of love remembered.’”

Catherine’s hand flew to her bosom. She sank back with one long sob, as if the words had struck and soothed her at once—salt and honey in the same mouthful.

“Then comes this, madam,” the reader went on. “It doth speak for itself: ‘a long farewell.’”

“Ay—go on,” Catherine pleaded. “Bless you, girl; you give me sorry comfort. Still ’tis comfort.”

“‘To my brothers Cornelis and Sybrandt—Be content; you will see me no more!’”

“What does that mean?” Catherine whispered; and then the meaning, like a knife’s cold edge, found its way in. “Ah!”

“‘To my sister Kate—Little angel of my father’s house. Be kind to her—’”

“Ah!” Catherine cried again, the sound dragged out of her as if by force.

“That is Margaret Brandt, my dear—his sweetheart, poor soul,” she broke in, as the thought rushed upon her. “I’ve not been kind to her, my dear. Forgive me, Gerard!”

The young woman read on, but the words seemed to cost her breath.

“‘—for poor Gerard’s sake: since grief to her is death to me—Ah!’”

That last cry—half in the letter, half in the reader’s own throat—broke what she had been holding shut. Nature, resenting the struggle for unnatural composure, suddenly had its way. The young woman swayed, slipped from her chair, and fell insensible, the letter still in her hand, her head coming to rest on Catherine’s knees like a child laid down after weeping itself to sleep.

Women who have baked bread through fevers, and watched children pale and swoon at the smell of blood or the crush of sorrow, do not scream at a faint as if a spirit had flown out of the window. Catherine, who had handled more than dough and dairy in her time, moved as briskly and surely as if she were laying a loaf to cool.

She caught Margaret as the girl went slack, lowered her at once to the floor, and set her flat—head low, as one sets a basin to drain—so the blood might find its road back. She tugged the laces loose at the throat and bodice, and threw the casement wide. Night-air slid in, damp with canal-mist and the faint sour-sweet of yeast from some baker’s yard beyond; with it came the street’s small soundscape: a distant watchman’s call, a hoof striking cobble, the soft clink of a tether chain, all of it clean and human, not the grinding din of carts at full market that makes the head ache and the heart skitter like a startled hen.

Only after she had done what hands must do did she step to the door and call, loud enough to carry over the house’s hush: “Come here, if you please.”

Margaret Van Eyck and Reicht entered and found the young woman stretched quite flat, and Catherine briskly beating her hands—hard enough to stir life, gentle enough not to bruise. The elder lady’s face went up like a flame.

“Oh, my poor girl! What have you done to her?”

“Me?” Catherine’s voice came out sharp as a knife on a board. “What has happened, then?”

“Nothing, madam; nothing more than is natural in her situation.”

Margaret Van Eyck coloured with ire. “You do well to speak so coolly,” she said, “you that are the cause of her situation.”

“That I am not,” said Catherine bluntly; “nor any woman born.”

“What! was it not you and your husband that kept them apart? and now he has gone to Italy all alone. Situation indeed! You have broken her heart amongst you.”

“Why, madam? Who is it then? in Heaven’s name!” Catherine threw out her hands. “To hear you, one would think this was my Gerard’s lass. But that can’t be. This fur never cost less than five crowns the ell; besides, this young gentlewoman is a wife; or ought to be.”

“Of course she ought. And who is the cause she is none? Who came before them at the very altar?”

“God forgive them, whoever it was,” Catherine answered, and for once her briskness dropped into gravity like a stone into a pot. “Me it was not, nor my man.”

“Well,” said Margaret Van Eyck, a little softened by that plain earnestness, “now you have seen her, perhaps you will not be quite so bitter against her, madam. She is coming to, thank Heaven.”

“Me bitter against her?” Catherine’s eyes went to the girl’s face, where the pallor was already loosening its grip. “No, that is all over. Poor soul! trouble behind her and trouble afore her; and to think of my setting her, of all living women, to read Gerard’s letter to me. Ay, and that was what made her go off, I’ll be sworn.”

She knelt, put her rough, warm palm to Margaret’s cheek, and spoke as one coaxes a child to swallow broth. “She is coming to. What, sweetheart! be not afeard; none are here but friends.”

They raised the girl into an easy chair. Colour crept back into lip and eyelid in slow, reluctant tides. Her breath, which had been a thin thread, thickened; her lashes trembled as if she listened for some sound only she could hear.

Catherine drew Margaret Van Eyck a little aside, as a housewife draws a neighbour from the hearth when there is counsel to be given. “Is she staying with you, if you please?”

“No, madam.”

“I wouldn’t let her go back to Sevenbergen to-night, then.”

“That is as she pleases. She still refuses to bide the night.”

“Ay, but you are older than she is; you can make her.” Catherine glanced at the girl. “There—she is beginning to notice.”

Then Catherine bent and put her mouth close to Margaret Van Eyck’s ear. The whisper lasted no longer than it takes to pinch salt between finger and thumb; yet the old lady started as if a coal had dropped on her skin.

“It’s false!” she breathed back. “It is a calumny! it is monstrous! look at her face. It is blasphemy to accuse such a face.”

“Tut! tut! tut!” Catherine returned, impatient as a cook contradicted about her own kitchen. “You might as well say this is not my hand. I ought to know; and I tell ye it is so.”

And then—most strangely to Margaret Van Eyck, who had expected coldness and found a storm—Catherine went straight to the young woman, took her round the neck, and kissed her with a warmth that had in it both pardon and claim.

“I suffered for Gerard,” she said aloud, and her voice shook, not with age but with the sudden rush of feeling; “and you shed your blood for him I do hear; his own words show me that I have been to blame, the very words you have read to me. Ay, Gerard, my child, I have held aloof from her; but I’ll make it up to her once I begin. You are my daughter from this hour.”

Another close embrace sealed the hasty compact, and the woman of impulse was gone, as if she had flung her heart on the table and swept out to tend some unseen task.

Margaret lay back in her chair. A feeble smile stole over her mouth—thin as the first scent of bread before it shows itself—because Gerard’s mother had kissed her and called her daughter. But the next moment she saw her old friend’s face set and vexed, as if some harsh note had been struck in a familiar song.

“I wonder you let that woman kiss you.”

“His mother!” Margaret murmured, half reproachfully, as though the word itself should hush all discord.

“Mother, or no mother, you would not let her touch you if you knew what she whispered in my ear about you.”

“About me?” The faintness came back in a shadow; the words scarcely left her throat.

“Ay, about you, whom she never saw till to-night.”

Margaret Van Eyck began—slowly, with that careful choosing of terms by which the old try to keep mercy in their mouths even when anger is hot—to shape her indignation into speech, to make the younger woman share it and be defended by it. But before the first full sentence could be born, the room altered.

The girl slid from the chair to her knees, as if the very wood would not hold her up under the weight of what she carried. The boards creaked under her small fall; outside, the street’s noises seemed to draw back and listen. She clasped Margaret Van Eyck’s hands and began to pray piteously for pardon—so humbly, so brokenly, that any bystander would have thought she had committed some cruel wrong, some intolerable insult, against her venerable friend, and could find no language—no dialect, no set of words—large enough to translate the pain in her breast except by kneeling and begging it away.

They were still at table in the hosier’s house, the little board set close to the hearth so the warmth might climb their knees. The trenchers had been scraped clean, yet the room kept its supper-breath: rye crust and onion, a sour-sweet tang of small beer, the last faint smoke of bacon that had hung in the rafters since morning. Even the sounds were homely and measured—the tick of the settle as one shifted, the soft rasp of a knife laid down, the hearth’s steady crackle like a patient animal chewing its cud.

They spoke, in low, broken starts, of the late matter that had troubled the house; each word fell as if it feared to ring too loud and draw more ill upon them. Then the door opened, and their mother came in.

Catherine did not hurry. She crossed the threshold with that noiseless economy a housewife learns by long service, as if her very feet knew where every loose board lay. In her hand she carried a letter. She did not clasp it to her breast like a love-token, nor wave it like a banner; she laid it flat upon the table, smoothing it with the palm as one smooths dough before the first fold. Her eyes travelled round the circle—one keen, piercing sweep that took each face as surely as the butcher’s hook finds the joint.

She bent over the paper. The signs on it were black and orderly, but they were not hers; and yet, by sheer hunger of heart, she followed them. She traced the lines with her finger, slowly, as if her nail could catch meaning the way it catches a thread in cloth. Then, word for word, she repeated the letter by memory—every turn of phrase, every stab and sob in it—keeping her finger moving to cheat herself and the hearers into thinking she read as others read. The room listened with the strange silence of a household when the bread is cut and no one dares speak until each has his share.

When she had done, she lifted her head suddenly.

Her gaze fell on Cornelis and Sybrandt. Their eyes, that had been bold enough when the matter was in doing, dropped now like dogs whipped off a bone. The hearth snapped; somewhere outside, a cart-wheel groaned in the street; a sparrow fussed in the eaves. Those small honest sounds made the stillness at the table sharper, like salt on a cut.

Then the storm that had been long brewing broke.

Catherine seemed to swell where she stood, as a hen swells and ruffles when some hand goes near her brood. And out of her mouth came a torrent—wisdom and twaddle together, high and low invective all in one breath; such a current as few men could have uttered and not many women, save one whose tongue had been sharpened on daily care and daily wrong.

“I have long had my doubts,” she began, and the words came swift and crowded, “that you blew the flame betwixt Gerard and your father, and set that old rogue, Ghysbrecht, on. And now here are Gerard’s own written words to prove it. You have driven your own flesh and blood into a far land, and robbed the mother that bore you of her darling—the pride of her eye, the joy of her heart.

“But you are all of a piece from end to end. When you were all boys together, my others were a comfort; but you were a curse: mischievous and sly; and took a woman half a day to keep your clothes whole—work wears cloth, but play cuts it. With the beard comes prudence; but none came to you: still the last to go to bed and the last to leave it; and why? because honesty goes to bed early, and industry rises betimes; where there are two lie-a-beds in a house there are a pair of ne’er-do-weels.

“Often I’ve sat and looked at your ways and wondered where ye came from. Ye don’t take after your father, and ye are no more like me than a wasp is to an ant. Sure ye were changed in the cradle, or the cuckoo dropped ye on my floor: for ye have not our hands, nor our hearts. Of all my blood, none but you ever jeered them that God afflicted. But often, when my back was turned, I’ve heard you mock at Giles because he is not as big as some; and at my lily Kate because she is not so strong as a Flanders mare. After that, rob a church an you will! for you can be no worse in His eyes that made both Kate and Giles—and in mine that suffered for them, poor darlings, as I did for you, you paltry, unfeeling, treasonable curs!”

Her daughter moved, as if to lay a hand on her arm and still the torrent; but Catherine shook her off with a glance.

“No,” she cried, “I will not hush, my daughter. They have filled the cup too full. It takes a deal to turn a mother’s heart against the sons she has nursed upon her knees; and many is the time I have winked and wouldn’t see too much, and bitten my tongue lest their father should know them as I do; he would have put them to the door that moment. But now they have filled the cup too full.

“And where got ye all this money? For this last month you have been rolling in it. You never wrought for it. I wish I may never hear from other mouths how ye got it. It is since that night you were out so late, and your head came back so swelled, Cornelis. Sloth and greed are ill-mated, my masters. Lovers of money must sweat or steal. Well, if you robbed any poor soul of it, it was some woman, I’ll go bail; for a man would drive you with his naked hand.

“No matter. It is good for one thing. It has shown me how you will guide our gear if ever it comes to be yourn. I have watched you, my lads, this while. You have spent a groat to-day between you. And I spend scarce a groat a week, and keep you all, good and bad.”

Her voice, that had run like boiling water, turned now hard and decisive, like a knife striking a board.

“No. I give up waiting for the shoes that will maybe walk behind your coffin; for this shop and this house shall never be yourn. Gerard is our heir—poor Gerard, whom you have banished and done your best to kill. After that, never call me mother again!”

At the name, something softened and flamed together in her face: grief and pride kneaded into one, as a cook kneads salt into the loaf because it must be there though it bites.

“But you have made him tenfold dearer to me. My poor lost boy! I shall soon see him again—shall hold him in my arms, and set him on my knees. Ay, you may stare! You are too crafty, and yet not crafty enow. You cut the stalk away; but you left the seed—the seed that shall outgrow you, and outlive you.

“Margaret Brandt is quick, and it is Gerard’s; and what is Gerard’s is mine. And I have prayed the saints it may be a boy; and it will—it must. Kate, when I found it was so, my bowels yearned over her child unborn as if it had been my own. He is our heir. He will outlive us. You will not; for a bad heart in a carcass is like the worm in the nut—soon brings the body to dust.”

She turned on her daughter with sudden household briskness, as if the rage must spend itself in doing some plain thing, the way sorrow often takes refuge in setting a pot to boil.

“So, Kate, take down Gerard’s bib and tucker that are in the drawer you wot of; and one of these days we will carry them to Sevenbergen. We will borrow Peter Buyskens’ cart, and go comfort Gerard’s wife under her burden. She is his wife. Who is Ghysbrecht Van Swieten? Can he come between a couple and the altar, and sunder those that God and the priest make one?”

Her voice held, beneath the anger, the old stubborn reverence for forms and words that bind—vows spoken in a tongue the people own, not clipped and traded like coin. In that room, where the mother could not read the black marks yet could keep a son’s sentences alive by sheer memory, the power of written words stood plain: a dominion that could banish, could name, could make a marriage denied by one man and affirmed by another. And Catherine, who had lived by the honest noises of hearth and shop-bell, flung back at that dominion her own authority: the mother’s claim, the household’s law.

“She is my daughter,” she went on, “and I am as proud of her as I am of you, Kate—almost. And as for you—”

Her eyes, black and sharp now, struck Cornelis and Sybrandt like stones.

“Keep out of my way awhile, for you are like the black dog in my eyes.”

Cornelis and Sybrandt needed no more. They rose and slunk out, their shoulders drawn in, their faces stung—not into penitence, but into a sore mixture of remorse and hate. The door closed behind them with a wooden thud that sounded louder than it should, as if the house itself had spoken.

For many days thereafter, Catherine never said them a word—good, bad, or indifferent. She had eased her mind. Liberaverat animum suum.

Catherine was of those housewives whose hands held the whole dwelling together as a net holds fish: lift it but for a day, and something slipped through—milk left to sour, dough forgotten, a child’s stocking mislaid, the very kettle seeming to take offence and boil over. She knew it, and watched for a slack tide in chores to go to Sevenbergen; yet still some small domestic fate thwarted her. One afternoon it might truly have been done—if only Peter Buyskens’ mule had not been out of the way.

At last Eli asked her, bluntly and before all the family, whether it was true she had been thinking to visit Margaret Brandt.

“Ay, my man.”

“Then I do forbid you.”

“Oh, do you?”

“I do.”

“Then there is no more to be said, I suppose,” she answered, colouring to the brow.

“Not a word,” said Eli, and his face shut like a chest-lid.

When she was alone with Kate, Catherine turned her wrath—not on her husband, but on herself, as if her own tongue had betrayed her like a careless cook who lifts the cover to boast of a stew and lets all the savor fly.

“Behoved me rather go thither like a cat at a robin,” she whispered, fierce with shame. “But this was me all over. I am like a silly hen that can lay no egg without cackling, and convening all the house to rob her on’t. Next time you and I are after aught the least amiss, let’s do’t in Heaven’s name then and there, and not take time to think about it, far less talk; so then, if they take us to task we can say, alack we knew nought; we thought no ill; now, who’d ever? and so forth. For two pins I’d go thither in all their teeth.”

Defiance so wild and painted in such homely images startled Kate. “Nay, mother; with patience father will come round.”

“And so will Michaelmas; but when?” Catherine’s voice fell, and with it some softer hunger showed—hunger not for bread but for certainty. “And I was so bent on you seeing the girl. Then we could have put our heads together about her. Say what they will, there is no judging body or beast but by the eye. And were I to have fifty more sons I’d ne’er thwart one of them’s fancy, till such time as I had clapped my eyes upon her and seen Quicksands. Say you, I should have thought of that before condemning Gerard his fancy; but there—life is a school, and the lesson ne’er done; we put down one fault and take up t’other, and so go blundering here, and blundering there, till we blunder into our graves.”

“Mother,” said Kate timidly.

“Well, what is a-coming now? no good news though, by the look of you. What on earth can make the poor wretch so scared?”

“An avowal she hath to make,” faltered Kate.

“Now, there is a noble word for ye,” Catherine said, proud in spite of herself. “Our Gerard taught thee that, I’ll go bail. Come then, out with thy vowel.”

Kate’s breath came thin. “Well then—sooth to say—I have seen her.”

“And?”

“And spoken with her to boot.”

“And never told me? After this marvels are dirt.”

“Mother, you were so hot against her. I waited till I could tell you without angering you worse.”

“Ay,” Catherine answered, half sad, half bitter. “Like mother, like daughter; cowardice it is our bane. The others I whiles buffet, or how would the house fare? but did you, Kate, ever have harsh word or look from your poor mother, that you—Nay, I will not have ye cry, girl. Ten to one ye had your reason. So rise up, brave heart, and tell me all, better late than ne’er; and first and foremost, when ever and how ever went you to Sevenbergen wi’ your poor crutches, and I not know?”

“I never was there in my life; and, mammy dear, to say that I ne’er wished to see her that I will not, but I ne’er went nor sought to see her.”

“There now,” said Catherine, disputatious with relief, “said I not ’twas all unlike my girl to seek her unbeknown to me? Come now, for I’m all agog.”

“Then thus ’twas. It came to my ears—no matter how—and prithee, good mother, on my knees ne’er ask me how—that Gerard was a prisoner in the Stadthouse tower.”

“Ah!” Catherine’s sound was like a knife turned in a wound.

“By father’s behest, as ’twas pretended.”

A sigh came from Catherine that was almost a moan. “Blacker than I thought,” she muttered, as if the word itself had a taste like burnt crust.

“Giles and I went out at night to bid him be of good cheer. And there at the tower-foot was a brave lass, quite strange to me I vow, on the same errand.”

“Lookee there now, Kate.”

“At first we did properly frighten one another—through the place his bad name, and our poor heads being so full o’ divels—and we whitened a bit in moonshine. But next moment, quo’ I, ‘You are Margaret.’ ‘And you are Kate,’ quo’ she. Think on’t!”

“Did one ever? ’Twas Gerard! He will have been talking backards and forrards of thee to her, and her to thee.”

Kate kissed her—a single kiss that spoke agreement, gratitude, and a sudden return to their old oneness.

“Now then,” said Catherine, with a catch in her throat, “speak thy mind, child. Gerard is not here. Alas, what am I saying? would to Heaven he were.”

“Well then, mother, she is comely, and wrongs her picture but little.”

“Eh, dear; hark to young folk! I am for good acts, not good looks. Loves she my boy as he did ought to be loved?”

“Sevenbergen is farther from the Stadthouse than we are,” said Kate, thinking it out as if weighing flour, “yet she was there afore me.”

Catherine nodded, understanding.

“Nay, more, she had got him out ere I came. Ay—down from the captive’s tower.”

Catherine shook her head. “The highest tower for miles! It is not feasible.”

“’Tis sooth though. She and an old man she brought found means and wit to send him up a rope. There ’twas dangling from his prison, and our Giles went up it. When first I saw it hang, I said, ‘This is glamour.’ But when the frank lass’s arms came round me, and her bosom did beat on mine, and her cheeks wet, then said I, ‘’Tis not glamour: ’tis love.’ For she is not like me, but lusty and able; and, dear heart, even I, poor frail creature, do feel sometimes as I could move the world for them I love. I love you, mother. And she loves Gerard.”

“God bless her for’t!” cried Catherine, and said it again, as if blessing were a kind of seasoning the heart needed. “God bless her!”

“But—”

“But what, lamb?”

“Her love—is it for very certain honest? ’Tis most strange; but that very thing which hath warmed your heart hath somewhat cooled mine towards her; poor soul. She is no wife, you know, mother, when all is done.”

“Humph! They have stood at the altar together.”

“Ay, but they went as they came—maid and bachelor.”

“The parson, saith he so?”

“Nay, for that I know not.”

“Then I’ll take no man’s word but his in such a tangled skein.” Catherine’s eyes narrowed; her mind, like a careful housekeeper’s, began to sort and stack facts. After a little she said, “Natheless art right, girl. I’ll to Sevenbergen alone. A wife I am but not a slave. We are all in the dark here. And she holds the clue. I must question her, and no one by—least of all you. I’ll not take any lily to a house wi’ a spot, no, not to a palace o’ gold and silver.”

The more Catherine chewed that talk over—slow, persistent chewing, as one works a tough crust—the more she felt drawn toward Margaret; and besides, curiosity, that strong spice which sharpens the dullest broth, tugged her on. At last, one fine day after dinner, when the house still held the smell of pottage and woodsmoke and the last loaf’s warm crumb, she whispered to Kate, “Keep the house from going to pieces, an ye can,” and put on her best kirtle and hood, her scarlet clocked hose and her new shoes, and went briskly off to Sevenbergen, troubling no man’s mule.

In Sevenbergen she asked where Margaret Brandt lived. The first person shook his head: “The name is strange to me.” A little farther a girl of fifteen stood in a doorway. Catherine asked her; the girl called into the house, loud as a jackdaw, “Father, here is another after that magician’s daughter.”

The man came out and said Peter Brandt’s cottage was just outside the east side. “You may see the chimney hence,” and pointed. Then, with a kind of relish in the telling, “But you will not find them there, neither father nor daughter; they have left the town this week, bless you.”

“Say not so, good man, and me walken all the way from Tergou.”

“From Tergou? then you must ha’ met the soldier.”

“What soldier? ay, I did meet a soldier.”

“Well, then, yon soldier was here seeking that self-same Margaret.”

“Ay, and warn’t a mad with us because she was gone?” put in the girl, with the heedless cruelty of youth. “His long beard and her cheek are no strangers, I warrant.”

“Say no more than ye know,” Catherine snapped, the way one slaps a child’s hand from the dough. “You are young to take to slandering your elders. Stay! tell we more about this soldier, good man.”

The man shrugged. “Nay, I know no more than that he came hither seeking Margaret Brandt, and I told him she and her father had made a moonlight flit on’t this day sennight, and that some thought the devil had flown away with them, being magicians. ‘And,’ says he, ‘the devil fly away with thee for thy ill news;’ that was my thanks. ‘But I doubt ’tis a lie,’ said he. ‘An you think so,’ said I, ‘go and see.’ ‘I will,’ said he, and burst out wi’ a hantle o’ gibberish—my wife thinks ’twas curses—and hied him to the cottage. Presently back a comes and sings t’other tune. ‘You were right and I was wrong,’ says he, and shoves a silver coin in my hand. Show it the wife, some of ye; then she’ll believe me; I have been called a liar once to-day.”

“It needs not,” said Catherine, though she took the coin and looked at it, weighing its cold shine.

“And he seemed quiet and sad like, didn’t he now, wench?” asked the man.

“That a did,” said the girl warmly; “and, dame, he was just as pretty a man as ever I clapped eyes on. Cheeks like a rose, and shining beard, and eyes in his head like sloes.”

“I saw he was well bearded,” said Catherine, “but for the rest, at my age I scan them not as when I was young and foolish. But he seemed right civil: doffed his bonnet to me as I had been a queen, and I did drop him my best reverence, for manners beget manners. But little I wist he had been her light o’ love, and most likely the—Who bakes for this town?”

The man’s eyes widened at so swift a turn, like someone interrupted mid-gossip by talk of grain and ovens.

“Well, dame, there be two; John Bush and Eric Donaldson, they both bide in this street.”

Catherine went to them, but her step had lost its cocking briskness; her foot came flatter now, as if the road itself had grown heavy. Bush said the Brandts were not customers. Donaldson said, “Not a stiver: his daughter had come round and paid him the very night they went. Didn’t believe they owed a copper in the town.”

“Can you tell me what sort this Margaret was?” Catherine asked, turning to go.

“Well, somewhat too reserved for my taste. I like a chatty customer—when I’m not too busy. But she bore a high character for being a good daughter.”

“’Tis no small praise,” Catherine said, and could not keep the respect from her voice.

“A well-looking lass, I am told?” she added, though she tried to sound indifferent.

“Why, whence come you, wyfe?”

“From Tergou.”

“Oh, ay. Well you shall judge: the lads clept her ‘the beauty of Sevenbergen;’ the lasses did scout it merrily, and terribly pulled her to pieces, and found so many faults no two could agree where the fault lay.”

“That is enough,” said Catherine. “I see, the bakers are no fools in Sevenbergen, and the young women no shallower than in other burghs.”

She bought a manchet—partly out of habit, for she kept a shop, partly out of justice, and partly so she might carry home, in her hands and nose, a measure by which to praise her own bread. The loaf steamed faintly through the paper; its crust gave a clean, nutty scent, and she breathed it as one might breathe courage. Yet she walked back to Tergou dejected, the town’s sounds behind her—the clack of wooden shoes, the far-off hammering, the stray shout—dulling into her own thoughts.

Kate met her outside the town, eyes bright with expectation.

“Well, Kate, lass,” Catherine said, and her voice broke, “it is a happy thing I went; I am heartbroken. Gerard has been sore abused. The child is none of ourn, nor the mother from this hour.”

“Alas, mother, I fathom not your meaning.”

“Ask me no more, girl, but never mention her name to me again. That is all.”

Kate bowed her head with a humble sigh, and they went home together through the familiar hush of fields, where even the birds seemed to keep their distance from such news.

Within, the hearthlight was alive, and a soldier sat tranquilly by their fire, as if the crackle and the smell of peat belonged to him. When they entered, he rose at once and saluted them civilly.

They stood and looked at him—Kate with a small surprise, but Catherine with a great deal, and indignation rising like yeast.

“What makes you here?” was Catherine’s greeting.

“I came to seek after Margaret.”

“Well, we know no such person.”

“Say not so, dame; sure you know her by name—Margaret Brandt.”

“We have heard of her for that matter—to our cost.”

“Comes, dame, prithee tell me at least where she bides.”

“I know not where she bides, and care not.”

Denys’s jaw tightened; he felt the lie in it as plainly as grit in bread. He bit his lip. “Well, I looked to find myself in an enemy’s country at this Tergou; but maybe if ye knew all ye would not be so dour.”

“I do know all,” Catherine replied bitterly. “This morn I knew nought.” Then, arms akimbo, she lifted her voice and flashed her eyes, wondering at his cheek to sit by that hearth of all hearths.

“May Satan fly away with your hearth to the lake of fire and brimstone,” shouted Denys—in fluent Flemish that rang against their rafters like a struck pan. “Your own servant bade me sit there till you came, else I had ne’er troubled your hearth. My malison on it, and on the churlish roof-tree that greets an unoffending stranger this way!” He strode, scowling, to the door.

“Oh! oh!” cried Catherine, frightened and, beneath it, pricked by conscience. The fierceness drained out of her as if someone had opened the tap of her courage; she dropped into a chair and burst into tears. Kate followed suit quietly, almost at once.

Denys halted at the threshold, dismayed at the ruin his words had made. The house sounded suddenly different: the fire snapped too loud, the bench creaked, even the little hiss of the kettle seemed to reproach him.

“Nay, wife,” he said, turning back, “weep not neither for a soldier’s hasty word. I mean not all I said. Why, your house is your own, and what right in it have I? There now—I’ll go.”

“What is to do?” said a grave, manly voice.

Eli had come in from the shop. The smell of flour clung to him, and cold air with it, as if he brought the outside world on his shoulders.

“Here is a ruffian been a-scolding of your women folk and making them cry,” Denys said, half angry, half ashamed.

“Little Kate, what is’t? for ruffians do not use to call themselves ruffians,” said Eli sensibly.

Ere she could speak, Catherine broke in between sobs. “Hold your tongue, girl. Muriel bade him sat down, and I knew not that, and wyted on him; and he was going and leaving his malison on us, root and branch. I was never so becursed in all my days—oh! oh! oh!”

“You were both somewhat to blame; both you and he,” said Eli calmly, as if settling a quarrel over a measure of grain. “However, what the servant says the master should still stand to. We keep not open house, but yet we are not poor enough to grudge a seat at our hearth in a cold day to a wayfarer with an honest face, and, as I think, a wounded man. So end all malice, and sit ye down!”

“Wounded?” cried mother and daughter together.

“Think you a soldier slings his arm for sport?”

“Nay, ’tis but an arrow,” Denys answered, forcing cheer, “a trifle.”

“But an arrow?” Kate said, horror gathered into one small voice. “Where were our eyes, mother?”

“Nay, in good sooth a trifle,” Denys went on. “Which, however, I will pray mesdames to accept as an excuse for my vivacity. ’Tis these little foolish trifling wounds that fret a man, worthy sir. Why, look ye now, sweeter temper than our Gerard never breathed, yet, when the bear did but strike a piece no bigger than a crown out of his calf, he turned so hot and choleric y’had said he was no son of yours, but got by the good knight Sir John Pepper on his wife dame Mustard; who is this? a dwarf? your servant, Master Giles.”

“Your servant, soldier,” roared the newcomer.

Denys started: he had not counted on meeting a powder-bomb in the shape of a man.

Yet it was Denys’s mention of Gerard that changed the air. All three—Eli, Catherine, and Kate—came creeping nearer him as if drawn by scent from a remembered kitchen: the name of their absent one was like hot bread set on a board. They stared down into him, lips parted, as if he were some marvel set by their fire.

Amazement grew into agitation.

“Now hush!” said Eli. “Let none speak but I.” His voice shook, though his back remained straight. “Young man, in God’s name who are you, that know us though we know you not, and that shake our hearts speaking to us of—the absent—our poor rebellious son: whom Heaven forgive and bless?”

“What, master,” said Denys, lowering his tone, “hath he not writ to you? hath he not told you of me—Denys of Burgundy?”

“He hath writ—but three lines, and named not Denys of Burgundy, nor any stranger.”

“Ay, I mind. The long letter was to his sweetheart, this Margaret, and she has decamped—plague take her—and how I am to find her Heaven knows.”

“What,” Catherine broke in sharply, “she is not your sweetheart then?”

“Who, dame? an’t please you.”

“Why, Margaret Brandt.”

“How can my comrade’s sweetheart be mine? I know her not from Noah’s niece; how should I? I never saw her.”

“Whist with this idle chat, Kate,” Eli said impatiently, and turned full on Denys again, like a judge. “How came you to know Gerard, our son? Prithee now think on a parent’s cares, and answer me straightforward, like a soldier as thou art.”

“And shall,” Denys replied, and sat more squarely by the fire, as if to give an account in a guard-room. “I was paid off at Flushing, and started for Burgundy. On the German frontier I lay at the same inn with Gerard. I fancied him. I said, ‘Be my comrade.’ He was loth at first; consented presently. Many a weary league we trode together. Never were truer comrades—never will be while earth shall last. First I left my route a bit to be with him; then he his to be with me. We talked of Sevenbergen and Tergou a thousand times; and of all in this house. We had our troubles on the road; but battling them together made them light.

“I saved his life from a bear; he mine in the Rhine—for he swims like a duck and I like a hod o’ bricks. And one another’s lives at an inn in Burgundy, where we two held a room for a good hour against seven cut-throats, and crippled one and slew two. And your son did his devoir like a man, and met the stoutest champion I ever countered, and spitted him like a sucking-pig. Else I had not been here.

“But just when all was fair, and I was to see him safe aboard ship for Rome—if not to Rome itself—met us that son of a—the Lord Anthony of Burgundy, and his men, making for Flanders, then in insurrection, tore us by force apart, took me where I got some broad pieces in hand, and a broad arrow in my shoulder, and left my poor Gerard lonesome. At that sad parting, soldier though I be, these eyes did rain salt scalding tears, and so did his, poor soul. His last word to me was, ‘Go, comfort Margaret!’ so here I be. Mine to him was, ‘Think no more of Rome. Make for Rhine, and down stream home.’ Now say, for you know best, did I advise him well or ill?”

“Soldier,” said Eli, and reached out his hand as if to clasp a plank in rough water, “take my hand. God bless thee! God bless thee!” His lip quivered; he could not find more, nor needed to.

Catherine said nothing at all. She darted from the room and bade Muriel bring the best that was in the house. She returned with wood in both arms and heaped the fire till it roared and threw a brighter, kinder light; then she pulled from the press a snow-white cloth, smelling faintly of flax and lavendered airing, and hurried to lay it as if setting a table were a prayer. But suddenly her strength ran out of her body like broth from a cracked pot; she sat down, white-lipped.

“Father!” cried Kate, quick-eyed with love.

Denys sprang up; Eli waved him back and flung a little water sharply in Catherine’s face. She gasped, “So sudden. My poor boy!” Eli leaned and murmured to Denys, “Take no notice. She thinks of him night and day.” They all pretended not to see her weakness; she shook it off and, hands trembling, smoothed the cloth—yet a tear or two fell upon it, darkening the white like drops of wine.

Then the house turned hospitable in earnest. They made much of Denys; they stuffed him, crammed him, pressed him as if feeding him could somehow feed the hollow place Gerard had left behind. Catherine’s pantry gave up its best: bread with a crackling crust, cheese that smelled of cellar and summer pasture, and warm ale that carried the malt’s sweet bitterness. The fire’s talk—its pops and sighs—kept time with their questions; and outside, the night lay listening, the village’s small sounds muffled, as if even the dogs had been told to hush.

They gathered round Denys and kept filling his glass in turn while, by that genial blaze and ruby drink and eager faces, he told all he had said—and far more besides: little turns of speech of Gerard’s, how he cleaned his hands and tended his clothes, how he could not abide coarse linen, how he had a proverb ready as a cook has salt.

Giles, after a while, crept in softly and curled himself before the fire, gazing at the soldier with a reverence almost canine. And when Denys, rough as oak-bark yet full of warmth for their absent one, let fall some proof of his rare affection for Gerard, Kate—timorous as a bird—stole her little hand into his huge brown palm. It lay there a moment like a spoonful of cream spilled on a platter; then, shyly, she pinched the ball of his thumb and served for a measurer of his heart’s beat, as if her fingers could read truth more surely than words.

Denys, who had known louder audiences, learned quickly that here the story’s danger could not be left to stand stark. When Gerard was in too sharp a peril, the women’s faces whitened and their throats made small, wet sounds; and in common humanity he was forced to spoil his own suspense.

“Now, dame, take not on till ye hear the end,” he would say, softening a horror with a jest. “Ma’amselle, let not your cheek blanch so; courage! it looks ugly; but you shall hear how we won through. Had he miscarried, and I at hand, would I be alive?”

Only once did he repay himself for the loss of such fine terrors: when he told of falling into the Rhine and sinking, Kate pinched him—hard. Denys felt it and, in his wicked way, lingered in that watery tale longer than needful, treading the imagined current as he spoke, chaffing the officers, making himself almost a fish, until even Eli’s stoic face tightened. At last he let the river release him, for very shame, and the pressure of Kate’s little fingers eased.

It was eleven o’clock—an hour unheard-of in that house—yet no one had marked time, for grief and hope were keeping their own clock. Denys had still much to tell when the door opened quietly and Cornelis and Sybrandt slipped in, hang-dog, smelling of ale and the last drop of their mysterious funds. Catherine feared Eli would rebuke them before the stranger, but he only looked sadly and motioned them to sit down in silence.

Denys alone seemed discomposed; he knitted his brows and eyed the two thoughtfully, gloomily, as if weighing them the way a man weighs flour and finds it light. Then he turned to Catherine.

“What say you, dame? the rest to-morrow; for I am somewhat weary, and it waxes late.”

“So be it,” said Eli.

Denys rose to go to his inn; but Catherine, all at once herself again where hospitality was concerned, stopped him like a hand on a door.

“And think you to lie from this house? Gerard’s room has been got ready for you hours agone; the sheets I’ll not say much for, seeing I spun the flax and wove the web.”

“Then would I lie in them blindfold,” Denys said gallantly. “Ah, dame, our poor Gerard was the one for fine linen. He could hardly forgive the honest Germans their coarse flax; and whene’er my traitors of countrymen did amiss, a would excuse them, saying, ‘Well, well; bonnes toiles sont en Bourgogne’—that means, there be good lenten cloths in Burgundy. But indeed he beat all for bywords and cleanliness.”

Denys chose his hour next day, when the house was quiet and the kettles no longer sang, to tell mother and daughter all that still lay unsaid. He did it with that rough, soldierly delicacy that will spare a foe’s name even while it shields a friend’s honour.

“It is not for me to blacken them,” said he, speaking of Cornelis and Sybrandt. “They come of good stock. But Gerard counts them no friends of his in this matter; and I am Gerard’s comrade. We soldiers have a rule—tell the enemy nothing—save lies.”

Catherine’s hands, that had been busy with a cloth and a trencher, went still. She drew breath, but answered him with silence. When he came to the parting of the friends—how one road cleft into two, and how a brave heart turned away alone—his voice thickened in spite of him; and they wept, all three, as if grief had been boiling there like broth too long left untended, rising sudden and salt to the brim.

Yet, as happens at hearths, sorrow did not end the day. It turned, by degrees, into a hungry hope: Gerard might return—soon, even any day. That prospect warmed them like a pan set near the embers; and Denys, who shared their confidence, would not let it soften him into neglect.

“All this joy,” said he, “is no reason to forget his last words. If he comes back next week and no Margaret to be found—what figure do I cut? What figure do you?”

Catherine, who had never once blessed the truant Margaret in her heart before, felt now a strange tenderness toward her, as if the girl were a loaf mislaid—no use to scold it into appearing; it must be sought, and when found, handled gently lest it crumble.

“I am as anxious as you to find her,” said she. “And to be kind to her before Gerard comes—Heaven knows I am. But I cannot agree to your roving from here. She must have told somebody whither she went. They owe not a stiver in Sevenbergen. And dear heart, Denys, you cannot hunt all Holland for her.”

“Can I not?” said Denys grimly. “That we shall see.”

Then, after a pause in which one could hear, outside, the steady, wholesome sound of a cart far off on the road and the nearer cluck of a hen settling—those homely noises that keep a mind from flying wholly to misery—he set his plan.

“We must divide,” said he. “You stay here, with eyes and ears wide open. I will ransack every town in Holland for her, if need be. But she will not be many leagues from here. They be three. Three fly not so fast, nor far, as one.”

“That is sense,” said Catherine; and because she was a woman that trusted in counsel tried nearest first, she insisted he go before all else to the demoiselle Van Eyck.

“She and our Margaret were bosom friends,” said Catherine. “If any know where the girl is gone, it is she—if she will but tell.”

Denys would have set off that instant; so Catherine, with that swift, household magic by which a woman can turn herself from apron to visiting-gown in the time a man takes to find his cap, made herself one shade neater and went with him.

The old lady received them graciously, seated in a rich room where the hangings drank the light, and the air held a faint, dear odour of dried pigments and old wood—like a chest where summer herbs have lain among linens. Catherine spoke straight.

At the word “gone,” the tapestry slid from Margaret Van Eyck’s hands as if it had been cut.

“Gone? Gone from Sevenbergen and not told me?” cried she. “The thankless girl!”

This heat surprised them.

“What,” asked Catherine, “you know not? When was she here last?”

“Maybe ten days agone,” said the old lady. “I had ta’en out my brushes—after so many years—to paint her portrait. I did not do it, though; for reasons.”

Catherine clasped her hands, half in prayer, half in domestic impatience at a mischance that would not be mended by wringing.

“’Tis a most strange thing,” said she, “she should go away bag and baggage like this, without with your leave or by your leave—why, or wherefore. Was ever aught so untoward? Just when all our hearts are warm to her; and here is Gerard’s mate come from the ends of the earth with comfort for her from Gerard, and cannot find her—and Gerard himself expected. What to do I know not. But sure she is not parted like this without a reason. Can you not give us a clue, my good demoiselle? Prithee now.”

“I have it not to give,” said the elder lady, peevish now, as if ashamed of her own surprise.

“Then I can,” said a voice from the doorway.

Reicht Heynes stood there, colour high, as if she had come in from a hot kitchen where the steam blinds and the pot-lids chatter.

“So you have been hearkening all the time, eh?” said her mistress.

“What are my ears for, mistress?”

“True. Then throw us light.”

“There is no darkness that I see,” said Reicht. “And the clue—why, an ye call’t a two-ply twine, and the ends on’t in this room e’en now, ye’ll not be far out. Oh, mistress, I wonder at you sitting there pretending.”

“Marry, come up!” cried the old lady, her cheek flushing till it matched the servant’s. “So ’twas I drove the foolish girl away.”

“You did your share, mistress,” said Reicht, steady as a chopping-knife. “What greeting gave you her last time? Think you she could miss it—she, and friendless? And you said, ‘I have altered my mind about painting of you,’ says you, a-turning up your nose at her.”

“I did not turn up my nose,” snapped the mistress. “It is not shaped like yours for looking heavenward.”

“Oh, all our noses can follow our hearts’ bent,” said Reicht. “Poor soul. She came into the kitchen to me. ‘I am not to be painted now,’ said she, and the tears in her eyes. She said no more. But I knew well what she meant. I had seen ye.”

Margaret Van Eyck drew a long breath, and her pride, like a pot taken suddenly from the fire, boiled over into explanation.

“Well,” said she, “I confess so much, and I make you judge, madam. These young girls can do nothing of their own heads, but are apt to mimic aught their sweethearts do. Your Gerard is handy at many things, and among the rest at the illuminator’s craft. Margaret is his pupil—patient as a nun. What marvel? Having a woman’s eye for colour, and eke a lover to ape.

“’Tis a trick I despise at heart: by it, the great art of colour—which should be royal and free—becomes slave to the petty crafts of writing and printing; is fettered and made little to match the littleness of books, and go to church in a rich fool’s pocket.

“Nathless affection rules us all. When the poor wench brought me her thorn-leaves, and lilies, and ivy, and dewberries, and ladybirds, and butterfly grubs—all the scum of Nature stuck fast in gold-leaf like wasps in a honey-pot—and withal her day-book, showing she had pored an hundred, or an hundred and fifty, or two hundred hours over each singular page—certes I was wroth that an immortal soul, and many hours, and much manual skill, should be flung away on Nature’s trash and barren letters.

“But having bowels, I restrained, and looked kindly to better it. I said, ‘Sith Heaven for our sins hath doomed us to spend time and soul and colour on great letters and little beetles, omitting saints and heroes—why not present the scum naturally? The grapes I see abroad hang i’ the air, not stick in a wall; and these insects—Nature’s slime in general—pass not their noxious lives wedged in metal prisons like flies in honey and glue, but hover at large, infesting air.’

“‘Ah, my dear friend,’ says she, ‘I see whither you drive; but this ground is gold; whereon we may not shade.’

“‘Who said so?’ quoth I.

“‘All teachers of this craft,’ says she—‘Gerard himself!’

“‘That for Gerard himself,’ quoth I, ‘and all the gang; gi’e me a brush!’”

Here Denys, who had been swallowing laughter and admiration together like a man trying to eat too-hot pottage without wincing, contrived at last to wedge in a word.

“Did she now?”

Margaret Van Eyck stared at him, then smiled, as one who finds a spice she did not expect in the dish.

Then she told them how, step by step, she had been drawn to take up again the art she had laid aside when her brothers died; and how she promised—God forgive her—once more to paint the Madonna, with Margaret for model. In passing, she let slip, with an old painter’s plainness, how girls are turned to saints by brush and by language.

“‘Thy hair is adorable,’ said I.

“‘Why, ’tis red,’ quo’ she.

“‘Ay,’ quoth I, ‘but what a red! how brown! how glossy! Most hair is not worth a straw to us painters; thine is the artist’s hue. Thy violet eyes—which smack of earth, being now languid for lack of one Gerard, now full of fire in hopes of him—these will I lift to heaven in fixed and holy meditation. And thy nose, which already somewhat aspires that way (though not so piously as Reicht’s), will I debase a trifle, and somewhat enfeeble thy chin.’”

“Enfeeble her chin?” cried Catherine, scandal and curiosity kneaded together in her voice. “Alack, what means that?”

“’Tis a resolute chin,” said the old lady. “Not a jot too resolute for this wicked world; but when ye come to a Madonna—no thank you.”

“A resolute chin,” echoed Denys, with soft absurd tenderness, as if he could see Margaret’s face before him.

“The darling!” he added.

“And now comes the rub,” said Margaret Van Eyck, her own voice lowering. “When you told me she was—the way she is—it gave me a shock. I dropped my brushes. Was I going to turn a girl that could not keep her lover at a distance into the Virgin Mary at my time of life?

“I love the poor ninny still. But I adore our blessed Lady. Most painters are men; men are fine fellows—they can do aught. Their saints and virgins are neither more nor less than their lemans, saving your presence. And half their craft is lost on me, which find beneath angels’ white wings the very trollops I have seen flaunting it in the streets, bejewelled like Paynim idols.

“I am not a fine fellow, but only a woman; and my painting is but one half craft, and t’other half devotion. So you may read me. ’Twas foolish, maybe, but I could not help it; yet am I sorry.”

She ended despondently, though she had begun defiant. Catherine, who measured holiness by kindness as much as by doctrine, answered gently:

“You must think it would go to the poor girl’s heart—she so fond of you.”

The old lady sighed and said no more. Then Reicht, who had been biting her lip as if holding back sharper words than any mustard, turned on Catherine.

“Why, dame,” said she, “think you ’twas for that alone Margaret and Peter hath left Sevenbergen? Nay.”

“For what else, then?”

“What else? Because Gerard’s people slight her so cruel. Who would bide among hard-hearted folk that ha’ driven her lad to Italy, and now he is gone, relent not, but face it out, and ne’er come anigh her that is left?”

“Reicht,” began Catherine, stung, “I was going—”

“Oh ay, going, and going, and going,” cried the Frisian girl. “Ye should ha’ said less or else done more. With your words ye uplift her heart and let it down wi’ your deeds. ‘They have never been,’ said the poor thing to me, with such a sigh.
