“Ay, here is one can feel for her; for I too am far from my friends, and when first I came to Holland I used to take a hearty cry all to myself. But ten times liever would I be Reicht Heynes with nought but leagues atwixt me and my kith, than be as she is in the midst of them that ought to warm to her, and yet to fare as lonesome as I.”

“Alack,” pleaded Catherine, tears rising in spite of her, “I did go but yestreen—and had gone before, but one plaguy thing or t’other did still come and hinder me.”

“Mistress,” said Reicht, “did aught hinder ye to eat your dinner any one o’ those days? I trow not. And had your heart been as good towards your own flesh and blood as ’twas towards your flesher’s meat, nought had kept you from her that sat lonely, watching the road for comfort—with your child’s child a-beating ’neath her bosom.”

At this, the old Van Eyck—nettled, and yet too proud to seem wounded—sprang from ambush.

“Since you disrespect my guests,” she cried, “seek another place!”

“With all my heart,” said Reicht stoutly.

“Nay, mistress,” put in Catherine, softening as one does when the pot threatens to boil over. “True folk will speak out. Her tongue is a stinger; but better she said it than thought it, so it will not rankle. And part with her for me—that shall ye not. Beshrew the wench, she wots she is a good servant and takes advantage. We poor wretches that keep house must still pay ’em tax for value.”

And then, half laughing through wet eyes, Catherine fell into that domestic confession that comes so readily among women when the air is charged.

“I had a good servant once, when I was young. Eh dear, how she did grind me down into the dust. In the end, by Heaven’s mercy, she married the baker, and I was my own woman again. ‘So,’ said I, ‘no more good servants shall come hither, a-hectoring o’ me.’ I get a fool and learn her; and whenever she knows her right hand from her left, she sauceth me: then out I bundle her neck and crop and take another dunce. ’Tis wearisome, teaching a string of fools by ones; but there—I am mistress.”

Here she forgot she defended Reicht, and turned, spite pricking through fondness, on the girl.

“And you be mistress here, I trow.”

“No more than that stool,” said the Van Eyck loftily. “She is neither mistress nor servant; but gone. She is dismissed the house, and there’s an end. What, did ye not hear me turn the saucy baggage off?”

“Ay, ay,” said Reicht, vast in her indifference. “We all heard ye.”

Then Denys, who had stood hitherto like a man at table watching a quarrel he cannot season to his liking, spoke, and his grave tone made them all wheel toward him as if on axles. The room, a moment before full of voices, fell quiet enough that the small sounds outside—the distant lowing of cattle, the faint tapping of a shutter—came in clear, and with them the sense of how much a house’s peace hangs upon what is said within its walls.

“Mistress Reicht,” said he, with a dignity so ceremonious it threatened to become comical, “you are turned off. If on a slight acquaintance I might advise, I’d say—since you are a servant no more, be a mistress, a queen.”

“Easier said than done,” replied Reicht bluntly.

“Not a jot,” said Denys. “You see here one who is a man, though but half an arbalestrier owing to that devilish Englishman’s arrow—in whose carcass I have, however, left a like token, which is a comfort. I have twenty gold pieces”—he showed them—“and a stout arm. In another week or so I shall have twain. Marriage is not a habit of mine; but I capitulate to so many virtues. You are beautiful, good-hearted, outspoken, and above all, you take the part of my she-comrade. Be then an arbalestriesse!”

“And what the dickens is that?” asked Reicht.

“I mean,” said Denys, “be the wife, mistress, and queen of Denys of Burgundy here present.”

A dead silence fell, like a cloth thrown suddenly over a table. It did not last; and when it broke it broke into a burst of female indignation so instant and unanimous it might have been rehearsed.

“Well, did you ever?” cried Catherine.

“Never in all my born days,” cried Margaret Van Eyck.

“Before our very faces,” said Catherine.

“Of all the absurdity and insolence of this ridiculous sex—” began the old lady.

Then Denys observed drily that the only female to whom he had addressed himself was mute; and the others, on whose eloquence there was no immediate demand, were fluent. At that, the voices stopped; eyes swung pivot-like upon Reicht.

She gave Denys a sly look from under her lashes, and said, “I mean to take a good look at any man ere I leap into his arms.”

Denys drew himself up as if on parade.

“Then look your fill,” said he, “and leap away.”

This, of all things, produced a new result. Margaret Van Eyck thrust out a long white finger straight at Denys’s face, as if taking aim.

“Stand!” she cried, in a shaken voice. “In the name of all the saints—stand!”

Then, as if seized by some fit between worship and folly, she exclaimed, “You are beautiful, so. You are inspired—with folly. What matters that? you are inspired. I must take off your head.”

And in a moment she had pencil in hand. The room, that had been a court of reproach, became a studio; the air seemed to change taste, as if chalk-dust and gum-water had been stirred. Her voice snapped like a cook’s command when the bread must be saved at the last moment.

“Come out, hussy!” she screamed to Reicht. “More in front of him, and keep the fool inspired and beautiful. Oh, why had I not this maniac for my good centurion? They went and brought me a brute with a low forehead and a shapeless beard.”

Catherine stood and stared, half scandalized, half amused, and secretly concluded her venerable hostess had been a disguised lunatic all this time and was now throwing off the mask. Reicht, for her part, was plainly unhappy and cross; and she made no scruple to say why.

“I left my caldron in a perilous state,” said she. “Duties so grave as mine leave no time to waste, a-playing the statee and the fool both at one time.”

Her mistress, without looking up from her furious sketching, reminded her that it was possible to be rude and rebellious to one’s poor, old, affectionate, desolate mistress without being utterly heartless and savage—and a trampler on arts. At that, Reicht stopped, pouted, and looked like a little basilisk at the “inspired” model who was the cause of her woe. Denys retorted with unshaken admiration, standing as still as a soldier ordered, while the pencil ran like a mouse over the paper.

At last the artist’s wrist cramped from long disuse; and only then did she let the moment die, though she had made a rough but noble sketch.

“I can work no more at present,” said she sorrowfully.

“Then, now, mistress,” said Reicht, “I may go and mind my pot?”

“Ay, ay, go to your pot!” cried the old lady. “And get into it, do; you will find your soul in it—so then you will all be together.”

“Well, but, Reicht,” said Catherine, laughing despite herself, “she turned you off.”

“Boo, boo, boo!” said Reicht contemptuously. “When she wants to get rid o’ me, let her turn herself off and die. I am sure she is old enough for’t. But take your time, mistress; if you are in no hurry, no more am I. When that day doth come, ’twill take a man to dry my eyes; and if you should be in the same mind then, soldier, you can say so; and if you are not, why, ’twill be all one to Reicht Heynes.”

And with that she went her way.

But her words did not fall to the ground. Catherine and Denys, walking back together, could not help tasting in them a bitter truth—like smoke in good milk: that blunt, solitary girl had likely read Margaret Brandt aright; and that she had left Sevenbergen not out of caprice, nor only for a painter’s rebuke, but broken-hearted—driven off by the coldness of those who should have spoken to her in the language of kin.

They bade the Van Eyck farewell; and that same afternoon Denys set out upon what Catherine, with a sigh, called his wild-goose chase.

His plan—like many great things—was simple. He would go to a hundred towns and villages and ask in each after an old physician with a fair daughter and an old long-bow soldier. He would inquire of burgomasters about all new-comers. He would go to fountains and watch the women and girls as they came with their pitchers, listening as much as looking—for the turn of a word, the burr of a dialect, the borrowed cadence of a stranger among natives can betray a whole history where eyes see only faces. And away he went.

He was months and months on the tramp, and could not find her.

Yet this chivalrous feat of friendship was in some degree its own reward. He that lives habitually by the drum and the sudden cry does not, between dangers, hunger chiefly for tranquil innocence; he thirsts for keen moments, for the world’s sharp savour. Denys was no exception. His soldier’s life had been half Sparta, half Capua; and he was too good a soldier and too good a libertine to have ever mixed either habit with the other.

But now, for the first time, he found them mixed: at peace, and yet on duty; for he chose to name this roaming a duty, and so kept himself in hand. So all these months he was a demi-Spartan—sober, prudent, vigilant, indomitable; and, though constantly disappointed, happy as men are who have a purpose that holds their heart tight.

He flirted gigantically upon the road; but wasted no time about it. Nor in these wanderings did he tell a single female that marriage was not one of his habits.

And so we leave him on the tramp—Pilgrim of Friendship—as his poor comrade was of Love.

Catherine’s hands would not keep still that evening. They went from spindle to hearth and back again, as if the very tools could be coaxed to answer what no one yet could tell her: where Margaret was, and what had become of her. The house held its common sounds—the soft hiss where broth breathed at the edge of boiling, the tick of settling embers, Kate’s tread on the flags, the faint, familiar water-voice of the canal beyond the wall—yet every noise came sharp to Catherine, like a knife touched to the tongue.

Gerard would be home within a month at farthest—more like a week, she counted it, tasting the numbers as bitter as burnt crust—and how was she to meet his eyes and say she had not even kept watch upon his betrothed? Worse than her shame was the blank where knowledge ought to be. In that blank the mind breeds monsters.

“Oh, Kate,” she broke out at last, her voice thick as dough not yet kneaded smooth, “if she should have gone and made herself away!”

Kate, who had been trimming a bit of onion fine enough to vanish into the pot and sweeten it without showing, turned quick. “Mother, she would never be so wicked.”

“Ah, my lass,” Catherine said, and the words came with the rough tenderness of a hand pressing salt into meat to keep it from spoiling, “you know not what hasty fools young lasses be, that have no mothers to keep ’em straight. They will fling themselves into the water for a man that the next man they meet would ha’ cured ’em of in a week. I have known ’em jump in like brass one moment and scream for help in the next—couldn’t know their own minds, ye see, even about such a trifle as yon.”

She jerked her chin toward the window, where the canal’s running never quite ceased, a constant under-song in their lives: sometimes a lullaby, sometimes an accusation. Catherine had always loved its plain, clean music—water on stone, water under plank, the reedy gossip of rushes when wind walked through them. Tonight it sounded to her like a beckoning finger.

“And then,” she went on, “there’s times when their bodies ail like no other living creatures ever I could hear of, and that strings up their feelings so, the patience that belongs to them at other times—beyond all living souls barring an ass—seems all to jump out of ’em at one turn, and into the water they go. Therefore I say that men are monsters.”

“Mother!”

“Monsters, and no less, to go making such heaps o’ canals just to tempt the poor women in. They know we shall not cut our throats, hating the sight of blood and rating our skins a hantle higher nor our lives; and as for hanging—why, while she is a fixing of the nail and a making of the noose she has time to alter her mind. But a jump into a canal is no more than into bed; and the water, it does all the lave, will ye, nill ye.”

As she spoke, she stirred the pot, though it needed no stirring, as if the spoon could turn fear into sense. A savour rose—bones and leek, pepper bruised between fingers, a whisper of thyme—homely, honest things that belonged to living mouths. Catherine breathed it in hard, as if to prove to herself the world still held nourishment.

“Why, look at me,” she said suddenly, and there was a flash of savage humour. “The mother o’ nine—wasn’t I agog to make a hole in our canal for the nonce?”

Kate’s knife paused mid-air. “Nay, mother, I’ll never believe it of you.”

“Ye may, though.” Catherine leaned her hip to the table, and her voice changed, slipping back along the years the way a tune will carry you to a long-closed door. “’Twas in the first year of our keeping house together. Eli hadn’t found out my weak stitches then, nor I his; so we made a rent, pulling contrariwise; had a quarrel. So then I ran crying, to tell some gabbling fool like myself what I had no business to tell out o’ doors except to the saints—and there was one of our precious canals in the way. Do they take us for teal?”

At the memory, she gave a short sound, half laugh, half choke. “Oh, how tempting it did look! Says I to myself, ‘Sith he has let me go out of his door quarrelled, he shall see me drowned next, and then he will change his key. He will blubber a good one, and I shall look down from heaven’—I forgot I should be in t’other part—‘and see him take on, and oh, but that will be sweet!’ And I was all a tiptoe and going in, only just then I thought I wouldn’t.”

“Why?” Kate asked, almost despite herself, as if she were listening to a tale told by the hearth that must end in the same place each telling, yet always draws a new breath from you.

“I had got a new gown a making, for one thing, and hard upon finished.” Catherine’s mouth softened. Even in shame she remembered cloth between fingers, the good pull of thread, the patient craft that binds a life. “So I went home instead, and what was Eli’s first word? ‘Let yon flea stick i’ the wall, my lass,’ says he. ‘Not a word of all I said t’ anger thee was sooth, but this, “I love thee.”’ These were his very words; I minded ’em, being the first quarrel.”

She saw it again as clearly as if the steam before her had taken shape: her own young arms flung about his neck; her sobbing that tasted of salt and milk; the canal’s cold lure forgotten under the warmer pull of being wanted and forgiven. “So then that was better than lying in the water,” she finished, “and spoiling my wedding kirtle and my fine new shoon—old John Bush made ’em, that was uncle to him keeps the shop now. And what was my grief to hers?”

Kate’s eyes shone, but she held to her point, as a careful cook holds to a recipe and still adjusts it for the day’s flour. “Margaret loves her father too much to think of leaving him so at his age,” she said. “He is father and mother and all to her, you know.”

“Nay, Kate.” Catherine’s gaze went past her daughter, past the pot, past the neat row of bread loaves cooling on the board. “They do forget all these things in a moment o’ despair, when the very sky seems black above them. I place more faith in him that is unborn, than on him that is ripe for the grave, to keep her out o’ mischief.”

Kate’s hand drifted, unconsciously, to the bowl of flour as if to anchor herself in something that could be measured. Catherine’s voice dropped, and the kitchen’s little sounds—spoon against pot, fire settling—seemed suddenly too loud, too near, as if the house itself were listening.

“For certes,” Catherine said, “it do go sore against us to die when there’s a little innocent a pulling at our hearts to let ’un live, and feeding at our very veins.”

Kate swallowed. “Well, then, keep up a good heart, mother.” She forced steadiness into her tone, the way one pinches a flame to keep it from guttering. “Very like all these fears are overgreat.”

Then, remembering another dread that had been fermenting in the women’s talk like yeast, she added—carefully, solemnly, as if naming it might change the very substance of fate—“And at all events, mother, do not persist in naming the sex of Margaret’s infant. It is so unlucky, all the gossips tell. Dear heart, as if there were not as many girls born as boys.”

The sensible words fell into the room and were met, not with reason, but with Catherine’s instant clamour, fierce as a pan set on too hot a fire.

“Have you the cruelty to threaten me with a girl!” she cried. “I want no more girls, while I have you. What use would a lass be to me? Can I set her on my knee and see my Gerard again as I can a boy? I tell thee ’tis all settled.”

“How may that be?” Kate asked, half shocked, half amused, because her mother’s certainty had always been its own kind of weather.

“In my mind,” Catherine said, and tapped her temple with the spoon as if it were a ladle on the rim of a pot. “And if I am to be disappointed i’ the end, ’tisn’t for you to disappoint me beforehand, telling me it is not to be a child, but only a girl.”

Outside, the canal went on singing its old, untroubled song in the dark—an ordinary music that had outlived a thousand quarrels, a thousand prayers, a thousand names spoken in dialects that were already thinning from the tongues of the young. Catherine listened as if she could wrest an answer from that water-voice, but it offered only what it always had: sound without meaning, and meaning only the listener could supply.

Margaret Brandt had never belonged to Sevenbergen the way other women did.

She lived among them, bargained with their merchants, nodded to them at church doors and market-stalls; yet she carried herself as if some thin pane of glass stood between her and their breath. They called it pride. She had heard the word passed like a dry crust from mouth to mouth, and she knew what hunger sat beneath it: jealousy, and that relish people have for another’s fall—especially when it can be served hot and public.

Now the fall was ripening within her, day by day, and could not be kept under cloak much longer.

It was not that she was blind to her own case. Margaret’s mind, though unlettered in the fine wire-drawn distinctions of law, had the plain, hard sense that in those times often sat more firmly in women’s judgment than in men’s. A betrothal, made solemnly, written and witnessed, was no child’s ribbon to be untied at whim; it was a bond. She knew, too, what old custom and both Church and State had long held: that a woman betrothed might rightly look on her troth as marriage; that children born of such union were not bastards in God’s sight nor always in man’s.

But law and conscience were not what tormented her. It was the world.

Her written contract—her “marriage lines,” the one stout paper that could have stood like a trencher before the barking of tongues—was not in her chest, not under her key. In a moment of foolish trust—trust that had felt as natural as taking bread from a hand she loved—she had let Gerard carry it away. And Gerard was far, far off; and the paper, like a spice locked in some distant cupboard, might scent nothing here until it was too late.

She hated herself for that oversight with an honest ferocity. If she could have boiled it out of her like bitterness from an over-strong herb, she would have done it. Yet this was the one thing that could not be strained away.

For what would the tale sound like, once her condition could no longer be hidden under dark gowns and hurried steps?

“I have my marriage lines, but I cannot show them.”

It was a story fit to be laughed into crumbs. Women would not believe it; and it was women’s belief she craved, not men’s easy pardon. Men might shrug and call it nature; women would measure her, taste the scandal on their tongues, and decide she had been wanton. A bare slander is bad enough; but here was slander glazed with the shine of visible fact.

In those days there was no fashion of a woman standing up and calling herself “strong-minded,” no neat word to varnish endurance. Margaret had been mistress of her father’s house since she was sixteen; she could rule servants, keep accounts, portion flour and salted fish through a hard winter without waste. Yet in this she was weak as water: not because her conscience accused her, but because she foresaw the pitch of public shame laid ready to smear her name.

A virtuous woman who foresees herself paraded as a frail one knows a torment that needs few words. It is like smelling smoke in one’s own kitchen while the door is shut and the baby sleeps: the dread is constant, and the mind runs in frantic circles—bucket, cloth, prayer—yet the flames are not in sight, only the certainty they will be.

So Margaret hid. She stayed indoors; she shunned daylight; when she must go out she went as if the air itself could point at her. She would sit for long stretches, hands idle in her lap, hearing nothing yet everything: the scrape of a neighbor’s shoe on cobbles beyond the shutters, the caw of a crow, the water’s faint slap against a wharf-pile—each sound seemed an omen, each laugh in the street a knife.

Often her father would talk to her, and she would answer properly, as one answers while kneading dough: the hands work, the mind is elsewhere. Then without warning her cheek would burn as if a coal had been set beneath the skin; and old Peter would pause and peer at her, wondering what word of his had stung her. It was no word. It was the ever-present fear rising like heat from an oven she could not cool.

But the fear leapt into panic after her visit to Margaret Van Eyck’s.

There, among women, her secret had been seen. The old artist, secluded in his own quiet, might keep counsel; his house was like a larder with the door shut—what was within stayed within. But Catherine—Catherine was in the middle of a large household and a tight neighborhood, where news traveled faster than yeast in warm milk. She had the habit of speech, the bright-eyed appetite for telling and being told.

One spark of hope remained: Catherine had spoken kindly, almost lovingly. Such a woman, once roused, must become either the warmest friend or the sharpest enemy; there was no lukewarmness in her.

Margaret waited as one waits for the kettle to boil when there is no firewood left—listening, listening. No word came. The silence itself began to taste like betrayal. Catherine was not going to shelter her; Catherine was going to talk. And then, in Margaret, the wish to flee began to grow—at first a small stirring, like a mouse in the thatch; then a gnawing that would not stop; then a wild, passionate craving to be gone and hidden somewhere no one knew her name.

Yet how could she wrench her father from his place? Old people cling to their hearthstones as ivy clings to a wall. Peter was very old, and infirm. To ask him to change his lodging was to ask a tree to walk.

There seemed only one course: to make him her confidant. Better to tell him than to run away without him. And still she could not do it. The thought of speaking it out to a man—even to her father—made her throat close and her hands go cold. Between the urge to fly and the dread to confess, she hung in a torment that vibrated every hour.

Then, one day, between those two pressures came a third thought, sudden and fatal, slipping into her mind like a knife into a sheath:

End all.

There were canals in this land, calm and deep, threading through daily life as naturally as a pot-hook hangs above the fire. People cursed them in winter, praised them in summer, crossed them, hauled goods along them, washed in them, drowned in them. Catherine had her superstitions about them, her fears of water’s quiet treachery; and now that same quiet tempted Margaret.

One afternoon she stood on a bank and looked down. The water lay smooth and dark, smelling of reeds and cold mud, a smell like shut cellars. It did not roar. It did not threaten. It offered repose. In the distance she heard the faint clop of a cart, the call of a child, the creak of a boat’s rope against a post. The ordinary sounds of living seemed far away from that still surface.

No more trouble. No more waiting for shame. No more imagining women’s eyes.

If Gerard had not loved her—if she had not been able to taste his love as surely as she could taste salt—she might have ended there. But love, even absent, has weight.

She sank to her knees by the water and prayed, breathless and fervent, as if her words could build a railing between her and the brink.

“Oh, keep such wicked thoughts from me,” she whispered. “Selfish wretch—to leave my father. Wicked wretch—to kill my child, and make my poor Gerard lose all his pain and peril undertaken for my sight.”

And then, as if the prayer itself had given her a new backbone, she said aloud, “I will tell father all—ay, ere this sun shall set.”

She rose and hurried home as if chased, fearing that her good resolve might ooze away like melted butter before she reached the door.

In the house, domestic matters had always been her realm. Learned Peter could read the world’s secrets in plants and stars, yet in household ordering he was as simple as a child. Margaret had governed gently but absolutely; her word had been the pinch of salt that makes a whole pot right.

So it was strange—almost unnatural—to see her now, standing before him with the faltering hesitation of a servant asking leave, while the true master of the house sat less important, in that moment, than Martin Wittenhaagen or even the little girl who came each morning for a pittance to scour vessels and went home at night.

“Father,” she began, and her voice was small, “I would speak to thee.”

“Speak on, girl,” said Peter, without lifting his eyes from the simple work before him.

“Wilt listen to me? And—and—not—and try to excuse my faults?”

He looked up then, mild in the face, and said, “We have all our faults, Margaret—thou no more than the rest of us; but fewer, unless parental feeling blinds me.”

“Alas, no, father.” Her hands twisted together. “I am a poor foolish girl, that would fain do well, but have done ill—most ill, most unwisely—and now must bear the shame. But, father, I love you, with all my faults; and will not you forgive my folly, and still love your motherless girl?”

“That ye may count on,” said Peter cheerfully.

“Oh—well—smile not.” The plea came out sharp with pain. “For then how can I speak and make you sad?”

“Why, what is the matter?”

“Father—disgrace is coming on this house; it is at the door. And I the culprit.” Her breath came quick. “Oh, father, turn your head away. I—I—father, I have let Gerard take away my marriage lines.”

Peter’s brows lifted. “Is that all? ’Twas an oversight.”

“’Twas the deed of a mad woman. But woe is me—that is not the worst.”

He cut in, comforting by habit. “The youth is honest, and loves you dear. You are young. What is a year or two to you? Gerard will assuredly come back and keep troth.”

“And meantime know you what is coming?” Her voice broke.

“Not I, except that I shall be gone first for one.”

“Worse than that. There is worse pain than death.” She shut her eyes as if bracing for a blow. “Nay, for pity’s sake turn away your head, father.”

“Foolish wench!” muttered Peter; yet he turned his head aside.

She trembled so hard her bones seemed to click. Her cheeks were aflame; it felt as if all the heat of the hearth had leapt into her face. She forced the words out, each one catching.

“I did look on Gerard as my husband—we being betrothed—and he was in so sore danger, and I thought I had killed him, and I—oh, if you were but my mother I might find courage: you would question me.” She made a helpless little motion with her hands. “But you say not a word.”

He turned his head back, astonishment and impatience mingled. “Why, Margaret, what is all this coil about? And why are thy cheeks crimson, speaking to no stranger, but to thy old father?”

“Why are my cheeks on fire?” A sob strangled her; the truth would not come shaped into decent speech. “Because—because—father, kill me; send me to heaven! Bid Martin shoot me with his arrow! And then the gossips will come and tell you why I blush so this day. And then, when I am dead, I hope you will love your girl again for her mother’s sake.”

Peter’s face hardened—not in cruelty, but in alarm. “Give me thy hand, mistress,” said he.

She held it out, trembling.

He took it gently, and, more physician than father in that instant, began to feel her pulse, his eyes intent, his mouth set. Anxiety crept into his features.

“Alas, nay,” she cried, snatching at breath. “’Tis my soul that burns, not my body, with fever. I cannot, will not, bide in Sevenbergen.” And she wrung her hands with an impatience that was half despair.

“Be calm now,” said the old man, softening at once, “nor torment thyself for nought. Not bide in Sevenbergen? What need to bide a day, as it vexes thee and puts thee in a fever? For fevered thou art, deny it not.”

“What!” Margaret stared at him as if a door had opened where she expected a wall. “Would you yield to go hence, and—and ask no reason but my longing to be gone?”

And suddenly she dropped to her knees beside him, seized his sleeve, then his arm, then clung to his shoulder, pouring out supplication with the fierce gratitude of the reprieved.

“Oh, go—go, father! Quit this place, and ask me not why. Alas, what needs it? You will soon see it. And I could never say it. I would liever die.”

“Foolish child,” he answered, and there was tenderness under the grumble, “who seeks thy girlish secrets? Is it I, whose life hath been spent in searching Nature’s?” He sighed, and his gaze wandered, as if the room itself had grown strange to him. “And for leaving Sevenbergen—what is there to keep me in it, thee unwilling? Is there respect for me here, or gratitude? Am I not yclept quacksalver by those that come not near me, and wizard by those I heal? And give they not the guerdon and the honour they deny me to the empirics that slaughter them? Besides, what is’t to me where we sojourn? Choose thou that, as did thy mother before thee.”

At that, Margaret’s strength ran out. She embraced him, and wept against his shoulder, her tears warm through his worn cloth. The reprieve was like cool milk after thirst: she drank it greedily, yet even as she wept she almost wished she had found the courage to tell him everything—had laid the whole truth on the table like a loaf sliced open, so it could not be misnamed by anyone.

After a while Peter would not be content until she took a medicine. He rose, went to fetch it with the briskness of one who can mend bodies if not reputations, and brought her a composing draught. She swallowed it obediently—if only to please him, for what else could she offer? Though given under a common error, it did her more good than harm. The heaviness of sleep came down on her like a clean linen cloth laid over fevered brow and thoughts.

She woke calmer after a long rest. That very day she began to prepare.

There were small domestic tasks that had to be done as if nothing world-shaking were at stake: linen counted and folded, jars checked, the good knife wrapped, little store of spices tied up—pepper that had cost dear, dried herbs from summer, a knob of nutmeg treasured like a relic. In such work there is a kind of prayer; the hands can obey when the heart cannot. The house made its accustomed noises: the scrape of a chest-lid, the thump of a bundle set down, the low hiss of embers. Outside, the town’s soundscape went on—voices, carts, bells—indifferent as ever. Margaret listened to it with a new hunger: soon those particular noises would no longer define her days.

The next week they went to Rotterdam, bag and baggage, and lodged above a tailor’s shop in the Brede-Kirk Straet, where the air smelled of cloth, chalk, and hot irons, and the street below stitched together many tongues into one restless murmur.

Only one person in Tergou knew whither they were gone: the Burgomaster. He locked the knowledge in his own breast. What use he would make of it ere long could not easily be divined—for he did not divine it himself. But time, which kneads all scattered things into consequence, would show.

Among strangers Margaret Brandt found a kind of peace, as if the very speech about her—strange vowels, new proverbs, different scolding—kept her own grief from being handled too roughly. In Rotterdam she could be merely “the leech’s daughter,” not the woman whose heart had been packed away with a traveller’s chest and sent beyond reach.

Then fortune, that capricious kitchen-maid, flung her a ladleful of comfort.

A civic dignitary, one of those men whose body is ruled by his imagination and whose imagination is ruled by his dignity, had been handed from physician to physician. Each had left a mark: this one had bled him to pallor, that had purged him to weakness; he lay at last like a linen bag that has been rinsed too often—empty of colour, empty of strength, yet still stuffed with complaints.

In desperation they sent for Peter Brandt.

Peter came in, smelt the room—stale sweat, sour possets, sharp vinegar of old cordials—and saw the battalion of bottles ranged like little glass soldiers, each promising salvation and delivering only thirst. His eyes flashed; with an anger that was half pity and half pride he swept the bottles up and sent them flying out of the window. He left the casement open, to let God’s air do what man’s drugs had failed to do.

Then he went to work like a cook who understands that a stomach is not a kettle to be scoured, but a hearth to be coaxed back into warmth.

He took yolks of eggs—fresh, thick as gold paint—beat them patiently, and laced them with neat Schiedam in small, careful measure, as one tempers a sauce so it warms without scorching. In little doses he fed it to the man, watching the swallowing, the blink of relief, the faint return of appetite. After that he gave meat stewed in red wine and water, and into the pot he shredded only mild herbs—febrifugal simples that would not fight the body, only help it. Nothing violent, nothing showy; just nourishment, warmth, and time.

The dignitary rose again. He looked, when first he came out, like something between a man and a pillow-case; but he was alive, and being voluble, he filled every street with Peter’s name. The old doctor, who had long deserved a reputation and been denied it, found it arriving at last—late, noisy, and public. The purse began to fill; the pride, too, which is a kind of hunger, was fed.

Yet Peter spent much of his gain on sovereign herbs and choice drugs, as if his very success made him fear scarcity. He would have poured all their money into jars and packets—roots, resins, powders—had not Margaret, with a wife’s thrift and a daughter’s clear sight, held him to earth and forced a portion into hoard.

The victory came too late. The excitement that should have cheered him killed him by degrees.

One evening, when she kissed him good-night, his voice stumbled; the words came thick, as if the tongue were suddenly a stranger in the mouth.

In the morning he was found speechless, and only just sensible.

Margaret, who had been her father’s attentive pupil for years—watching not only the prescriptions but the pauses, the listening, the laying on of fingers to a wrist—saw at once a paralytic stroke had struck him. Still, she would not trust herself alone; she ran for a doctor.

One of those men whom Peter had blocked from finishing off the civic dignitary came. He confirmed her judgement with a cheerful air, like a man pleased to find himself right. He was for bleeding the patient.

Margaret’s chin lifted. “He was ever against blooding,” said she, “and most of all the old.”

Peter lived; but he did not return. His memory faltered; his mind, once a cupboard of well-labelled simples, became a disorderly shelf where jars stood without names. He could not be trusted to prescribe. Yet patients came all the same—some waiting with stubborn faith for the “new doctor,” refusing any other hand.

Misery stared her in the face with an honest, hungry gaze. There were two men to lodge and feed, and she herself was with child; another mouth was already on its way into the world.

And that helpless mouth, still unbreathed, was her best friend.

Nature in Margaret was strong—the same nature that teaches birds to line nests before the eggs are laid, and beasts to hoard fat against winter. She sat and brooded as a hen broods: warming her fear with thought, thought with fear, till a plan hatched.

Though she had five gold pieces left, she could see starvation, steady as a clock, advancing foot by foot. If she was to be beaten, it would not be for want of craft.

She resolved first to seek counsel and comfort from her cousin William Johnson, whom pride and poverty had kept her from. She went to him, and found him in one room with his servant; and neither of them was the better for liquor. The air stank of spirits gone flat, and of talk that had turned sour.

She mastered her surprise, gave her greetings, and told him she came on a family matter; with that she glanced quietly at the servant—hinting for privacy.

The woman took the hint—and twisted it to a weapon.

“Oh, you can speak before me, can she not, my old man?”

At the familiarity Margaret reddened, and rose at once. “I cry you mercy, mistress. I knew not my cousin had fallen into the custom of this town. I must take fitter opportunity.”

“I wot not what ye mean by custom o’ the town,” the woman cried, bouncing up, “but this I know: ’tis the part of a faithful servant to keep her master from being preyed on by his beggarly kin.”

Margaret’s tongue was sharp when honour was touched. “Ye are too modest, mistress. Ye are no servant. Your speech betrays you. ’Tis not till the ape hath mounted the tree that she shows her tail so plain. Nay, there sits the servant; God help him! And while so it is, fear not thou his kin will ever be so poor in spirit as come where the likes of you can flout their dole.”

She cast one mute look of reproach at her cousin—sitting passive and silent—and went out haughtily. Not a tear fell until she reached home and thought on it. Then she wept, not for her own pride, but for the shame of seeing a man of her blood so tamed.

Now indeed she stood alone: two helpless men and a child-to-come depending on one girl.

She wiped her face, set her jaw, and went to work.

She bade Martin move Peter into another room. She made the front room very neat and clean, scrubbed till the boards gave up their old smells of damp and ash. She polished the glass globe till it shone like a pale moon. She suspended it from the ceiling. She dusted the crocodile—Peter’s odd trophy—and nailed it to the outside wall as a sign, as if a monster’s jaw could keep misfortune at bay.

Then she instructed Martin and set him to lounge like a sentinel by the street door.

When people stopped to stare at the crocodile, Martin was to say a great, aged, learned alchymist dwelt within—one so deep in secrets that curing mortal diseases was but his pastime.

The first patients came. They demanded to see the leech.

“That might not be,” said Margaret, in a voice she took care to keep steady. “He is deep in his studies, searching for the grand elixir. Not princes could have speech of him. Tell me your symptoms, and return in two hours.”

In two hours they returned. Oh, mystery of mysteries: the draught was ready, the powder measured, the potion labelled.

Sometimes, if the patient was worshipful, she studied his face, felt pulse and skin, listened closely, then went softly to Peter’s room. There she stood a while, thinking not only what he had taught her, but how he had chosen between remedies—the way he watched a man’s breathing, the way he distrusted a complaint that did not match the body’s smell. She asked herself, as she had asked a hundred times at his side, what her father’s system would do.

Then she wrote an illegible scrawl with a cabalistic letter, brought it down reverently, showed it the patient. “Can you read that?”

Most answered, “I am no reader,” or, “Nay, mistress, nought can I make on’t,” with admiration.

“Ay, but I can. ’Tis sovereign. Look on thyself as cured!”

If she had the materials, she compounded before them—economical as she was, favouring medicines already in her stock. She would consult the “prescription” anxiously, as if great Science trembled in her hands. And so she sent them away relieved of cash, but with pockets full of medicine, mouths tasting of bitters or honeyed cordials, and minds full of faith.

When they were gone, she took down two little boxes Gerard had made her, long ago—small, neat, beloved. On one she had written To-day, on the other To-morrow. She dropped the smaller coins into “To-day,” the larger into “To-morrow,” along with such gold pieces as had survived her journey and housekeeping. Thus she met current expenses and laid by against the rainy day she saw, sure as cloud.

She mixed drugs with simples, and vice with virtue.

Her conscience pricked her. Each evening, after the day’s comedy, she knelt and begged God’s pardon “for the sake of her child.” But then cures were reported. This neighbour’s fever broke; that burgher’s pain eased; some would have recovered without her, yet they credited her. Gradually her conscience hardened, as hands harden that must work in cold water.

Martin Wittenhaagen had become, of late, a dead weight. Like many men who have endured long hardship, he had stiffened suddenly. Yet he was as strong as ever, and at his own pace could have carried the doctor herself around Rotterdam. He carried instead her slops and errands.

In her new business he showed soldierly qualities: obedience without question, punctuality, accuracy, despatch—and drunkenness.

He fell among “good fellows.” Blackguards plied him with Schiedam. He babbled and bragged. Doctor Margaret rose high in his cups, not as Science but as something grander: Strategy. The crocodile as standard, the dotard hidden in back rooms, the money taken briskly—Martin admired it like a campaign.

And he boasted, before mixed company, how “me and my General we are a biting of the burghers.”

Words, once loosed, have their own legs. The tale walked through the city. Before long constables called.

They took Margaret—trembling, begging them to forgive her—before the burgomaster. By his side stood real physicians, a terrible row, in long robes and square caps, accusing her of practising unlawfully on the duke’s lieges.

At first she could not speak. The very word Law struck her like a cudgel; she felt again the helplessness of a poor girl in a town of strangers. But they questioned her—closely, not cruelly—and at last truth came out as breath comes out of a squeezed lung.

She told them she had long been her father’s pupil; she had followed his system; she had cured many. And then, forgetting caution, she pleaded, and the pleading betrayed her condition.

“It is not for myself in very deed, sirs,” she said, “but I have two poor helpless honest men at home upon my hands, and how else can I keep them? Ah, good sirs, let a poor girl make her bread honestly; ye hinder them not to make it idly and shamefully; and oh, sirs, ye are husbands, ye are fathers; ye cannot but see I have reason to work and provide as best I may—”

Even as the appeal left her lips she would have recalled it. She stood with one hand upon her heart and one before her face, hiding it—yet tears slipped out beneath.

But it went to the wrong address.

“What have we to do with that,” said the burgomaster, “save and except that if thou wilt pledge thyself to break the law no more, I will remit the imprisonment and exact but the fine?”

Margaret clasped her hands and vowed most penitently never, never, never to cure body or beast again. Dismissed with constables to pay the fine, she curtsied at the door and thanked the gentlemen for their forbearance—poor soul, grateful even for a whip laid lightly.

To pay, the To-morrow box must be opened that instant. With excess of caution she had nailed it up so temptation could not pry it. Now she could not draw the nails. The constables grew impatient, doubting its contents.

“Let us break it for you,” they said.

She would not let them. “Ye will break it worse than I shall.”

She took a hammer, struck too faintly, lost strength, and wept hysterically—breath catching, heart racing, belly heavy with child. At last she broke it. A little cry bubbled from her as the wood split. She paid the fine: it swallowed all her unlawful gains and two gold pieces besides.

When the men were gone, she drew the broken pieces together on the table with what little money remained. Her arms went round them as if she could hold the past intact by embrace. Her rich hair came loose and fell down like a curtain. She bowed her forehead on the wreck and sobbed, “My love’s box it is broken, and my heart withal.”

So Martin found her. She could not lift her head; she only sighed out what had befallen, ending again, “My love his box is broken, and so mine heart is broken.”

Martin’s grief turned to wrath. A traitor had betrayed them. Some stony heart had told. Whoever it was should feel his arrow’s point—he spoke as if vengeance were bread.

“Idle chat! idle chat!” moaned Margaret, not lifting her brow. “When you have slain all the gossips in this town, can we eat them? Tell me how to keep you all, or prithee hold thy peace, and let the saints get leave to whisper me.”

He held his tongue then, glancing uneasily at his defeated General.

Towards evening she rose, washed her face, did up her hair with a stubborn care, and bade Martin take down the crocodile and put out a basket instead.

“I can get up linen better than they seem to do it in this street,” said she, “and you must carry it in the basket.”

“That will I for thy sake,” said the soldier.

“Good Martin! forgive me that I spake shrewishly.”

Even while they spoke, a man came seeking advice. Margaret told him the mayor had forbidden her to sell drugs. “But I will gladly iron and starch your linen,” said she, “and come and fetch it from your house.”

“Are ye mad, young woman?” he cried. “I come for a leech, and ye proffer me a washerwoman.” He went out in dudgeon.

“There is a stupid creature,” Margaret said sadly—because he could not hear what a woman must hear in the city’s soundscape: not only voices, but the thin howl of need beneath them.

Soon after came a woman, frantic with the tale of her sick child. Margaret stopped her with the same words—no drugs, but she would wash, iron, and starch.

“Oh, ay,” said the woman. “I have smocks and ruffs foul. Come for them; and when you are there, you can look at the boy.” She told Margaret where she lived, and when her husband would be out; and yet she was fond enough of her husband to plan around him.

An introduction is an introduction. And so, out of those turned away from physic, two or three made Doctor Margaret their washerwoman.

“Now, Martin,” said she, “you must help. I’ll no more cats than can slay mice.”

“Mistress,” said he, “the stomach is not awanting for’t, but the headpiece, worst luck.”

“Oh, I mean not starching and ironing; that takes a woman and a handy one. But the bare washing—surely a man can contrive that. Why, a mule has wit enough to do’t with his hoofs, an’ ye could drive him into the tub. Come, off doublet, and try.”

“I am your man,” said he, stripping for the unwonted toil. “I’ll risk my arm in soapsuds, an you will risk your glory.”

“My what?”

“Your glory and honour as a—washerwoman.”

“Gramercy! if you are man enough to bring me half-washed linen t’ iron, I am woman enough to fling’t back i’ the suds.”

So the brave girl and the brave soldier worked with a will. The tub slopped; lye bit the hands; wet linen thumped on boards; steam rose with a homely smell of soap and sour cloth. Outside, Rotterdam clattered and shouted; inside, Margaret learned to measure time by the music of labour—water poured, cloth wrung, irons hissed—sounds that were honest and therefore soothing.

They kept the wolf from the door. More they could not do.

Margaret repaired the To-morrow box. As she leaned over the glue, her tears mixed with it; she cemented her exiled lover’s little chest with salt water from her own eyes. When mended it stood unreplenished. They paid the weekly rent and kept the pot boiling, but no more.

Then came a concatenation—one small link hooking another.

Recommended from house to house, Margaret washed for the mayor himself. Bringing home clean linen one day, she heard in his kitchen that his worship’s only daughter was stricken with disease and like not to live. Margaret could not help cross-questioning. A servant gave such symptoms as she had seen; too general at first—weakness, paleness, silence. But one gossip added one detail, another another, until a pattern formed in Margaret’s mind like a recipe glimpsed from scattered notes.

At last she met the mayor. He knew her at once.

“Why, you are the unlicensed doctor.”

“I was,” said she. “Now I’m your worship’s washerwoman.”

The dignitary coloured; it was a drop in state. Margaret met it without malice. “Your worship might have been harder. Rather would I do you a good turn. Sir, you have a sick daughter. Let me see her.”

He shook his head. “That cannot be. The law I do enforce on others I may not break myself.”

“Alack, sir,” she answered, “I seek no guerdon now for curing folk; why, I am a washerwoman. I trow one may heal all the world, an if one will but let the world starve one in return.”

“That is no more than just,” said he stiffly; then, as if reasoning with his own conscience, “an’ ye make no trade on’t, there is no offence.”

“Then let me see her.”

“What avails it? The learnedest leeches in Rotterdam have all seen her, and bettered her nought. Her ill is inscrutable. One saith spleen; another, liver; another, blood; another, stomach; and another, that she is possessed. In very truth she seems to have a demon. She shunneth all company; pineth alone; eateth no more victuals than might diet a sparrow. Speaketh seldom, nor hearkens them that speak, and weareth thinner and paler and nearer the grave.”

Margaret listened, taking in not only the words but the silences between them—the way the man’s voice cracked on “only daughter,” the harshness that grief gives to authority.

“Sir,” said she, “an if you take your velvet doublet to half-a-dozen shops in Rotterdam and speer is it fine or sorry velvet, and worth how much the ell, those traders will eye it and feel it and all be in one story to a letter, for they know their trade. But your leeches are all in different stories. Why? because they know not their trade. Each is enamoured of some one evil and seeth it with his bat’s eye in every patient. Had they stayed at home and never seen your daughter, they had answered all the same—spleen, blood, stomach, lungs, liver, lunacy, or as they call it possession. Let me see her. We are of a sex, and that is much.”

He still hesitated. The law was a bridle he feared to drop.

“Saints of heaven!” cried Margaret, the quick irritability of a breeding woman flaring. “Is this how men love their own flesh and blood? Her mother had ta’en me in her arms ere this and carried me to the sick room.”

Her violet eyes flashed fire.

“Come with me,” said the mayor hastily.

In the chamber, the mother sat pale, worn with watching. Near the fire, as if heat could fill what was empty, sat the girl: eighteen, thin as a fasting saint, her face drained of all summer.

“Mistress,” said the mayor, “I have brought thee a new doctor.”

The girl gave a contemptuous wrench of her shoulder and turned more decidedly to the fire.

Margaret came softly and sat beside her, as one sits beside a kettle that must not be jolted lest it boil over. “But ’tis one that will not torment you.”

“A woman!” said the young lady, surprised and scornful at once.

“Tell her your symptoms,” urged the father.

“What for? you will be no wiser.”

“You will be none the worse,” said Margaret.

“Well,” said the girl, “I have no stomach for food, and no heart for any thing. Now cure me, and go.”

“Patience awhile! Your food—doth it taste like nought in your mouth?”

“Ay. How knew you that?”

“Nay, I knew it not till you did tell me. I trow you would be better for a little good company.”

“I trow not. What is their silly chat to me?”

Margaret asked the father to leave them. When he was gone she put practical questions—about sleep, about mornings, about the body’s tremblings, about what sounds in the house were bearable and what were hateful. The girl tried to be sullen, but answered despite herself.

“When you wake i’ the morning you find yourself quiver, as one may say?” asked Margaret, lightly touching the wrist.

“Nay. Ay. How knew you that?”

Margaret smiled a little. “Shall I dose you, or shall I but tease you a bit with my silly chat?”

“Which you will.”

“Then I will tell you a story,” said Margaret, lowering her voice as if making a private music in the room. “’Tis about two true lovers.”

“I hate to hear of lovers,” said the girl. “Nevertheless canst tell me; ’twill be less nauseous than your physic—maybe.”

So Margaret told her, not as leeches tell symptoms but as women tell their own lives when they cannot speak them plainly. The maiden in the tale was Ursel, daughter to an old physician; the youth was Conrad, son of a hosier at Tergou. Margaret gave the story from the woman’s view, with that sweet, earnest voice that turns a room’s harsh noises soft. She spoke of trouble and waiting, of courage in small acts—like making a thin broth from bones when hunger is near; like keeping a hearth alive with a pinch of embers.

The sullen heart beside her began to listen. Breath steadied. The eye, dulled all day, sharpened. When Margaret stopped, the girl turned almost eagerly.

“Nay, nay, I must hear the end. I will hear it.”

“Ye cannot,” said Margaret gently, “for I know it not; none knoweth that but God.”

“Ah, your Ursel was a jewel of worth,” the girl said, earnest now. “Would she were here.”

“Instead of her that is here?”

“I say not that,” the girl murmured, and blushed.

“You do but think it.”

“Thought is free. Whether or no, an she were here, I’d give her a buss, poor thing.”

“Then give it me,” said Margaret, her voice suddenly thick with her own sorrow, “for I am she.”

“Nay, nay,” cried the girl, startled into life. “That I’ll be sworn y’ are not.”

“Say not so,” said Margaret. “In very truth I am she. And prithee, sweet mistress, go not from your word, but give me the buss ye promised me—and with a good heart, for oh, my own heart lies heavy: heavy as thine.”

The young gentlewoman rose, put her arms round Margaret’s neck, and kissed her.

“I am woe for you,” she sighed. “You are a good soul; you have done me good—a little.” Her throat gulped. “Come again! come again!”

Margaret came again, and again. She talked; she watched keenly under gentleness; she listened for what the girl’s voice quickened upon, what names made the pulse leap. There was but one.

At last Margaret said to the mayor, “I know your daughter’s trouble, and ’tis curable.”

“What is’t? the blood?”

“Nay.”

“The stomach?”

“Nay.”

“The liver?”

“Nay.”

“The foul fiend?”

“Nay.”

“What then?”

“Love.”

“Love? Stuff, impossible! She is but a child; she never stirs abroad unguarded. She never hath from a child.”

“All the better,” said Margaret. “Then we shall not have far to look for him.”

“I vow not. I shall command her to tell me the caitiff’s name that hath by magic arts ensnared her young affections.”

“Oh, how foolish be the wise!” cried Margaret. “What, would ye go put her on her guard? Nay, let us work by art first; and if that fails, then ’twill still be time for violence and folly.”

With difficulty she persuaded him to use the common ritual of Saturday wages. Let all his people be paid in his daughter’s presence, and Margaret’s.

It was done. Some fifteen came in, each receiving coin and a word. Margaret sat close by the girl, holding her hand as if for comfort, her finger lightly at the wrist like a listener at a wall.

Most entered and went as if dogs and cats had passed through the room—mere noise, no meaning. Then came a black-haired lad.

The girl’s pulse leaped beneath Margaret’s finger. Her eye shone; her mouth, which had forgotten taste, almost remembered sweetness. When he went out she sank back and sighed, as if the sun had gone out with him.

Margaret rose and slipped away. The mayor followed her.

“Sir,” she whispered, “how call you yon black-haired lad?”

“That is Ulrich, my clerk.”

“Well then—’tis he.”

The mayor’s face went startled, then hard. “Now Heaven forbid! A lad I took out of the streets.”

“Well,” said Margaret steadily, “you took him not up without some merit?”

“Merit? not a jot! I liked the looks of the brat, that was all.”

“Was that no merit? He pleased the father’s eye. And now he hath pleased the daughter’s. That has oft been seen since Adam.”

“How know ye ’tis he?”

“I held her hand,” said Margaret, “and touched her wrist. At others her pulse lay quiet. At Ulrich’s coming it did leap; at his going she did sink and sigh. ’Twas to be seen the sun had gone out of the room for her. Look not so scared. No witch am I, but a poor girl that hath been docile, and so bettered herself by a great neglected leech’s art and learning. Now bide thou there till I come, and prithee, prithee, spoil not good work wi’ meddling.”

She went back, asked the girl for a lock of hair.

“Take it,” said the girl, listless again, as if tenderness shamed her back into stone.

“Why, ’tis a lass of marble,” Margaret teased softly. “How long do you count to be like that, mistress?”

“Till I am in my grave, sweet Peggy.”

“Who knows?” said Margaret. “Maybe in ten minutes you will be altogether as hot.”

She ran down to the shop as if for some household errand. When she returned to the mayor her eyes were bright.

“Good news! He fancies her—and more than a little.”

“How is’t to be?” he demanded, torn between pride and fear. “Will you marry your child, or bury her? For there is no third way. Shame and love do rend her virgin heart to death.”

The dignitary chose the more cheerful rite, but not without struggle; the battle showed on his face as lines and colour. He went with Margaret to his daughter and stood silent, for men are seldom in haste to drink their wormwood.

So Doctor Margaret spoke for him, cheerfully, like one stirring a stubborn sauce so it will not catch.

“Mistress,” said she, “your lock is gone; I have sold it.”

“And who was so mad as to buy such a thing?” the young lady asked, scornful by habit.

“Oh, a black-haired laddie wi’ white teeth. They call him Ulrich.”

The pale face reddened at once—brow and all—like a flame had been put back into the room.

“Says he, ‘Oh, sweet mistress, give it me.’ I had told them all whose ’twas. ‘Nay,’ said I, ‘selling is my livelihood, not giving.’ So he offered me this, he offered me that, but nought less would I take than his next quarter’s wages.”

“Cruel,” murmured the girl, scarce audible.

“Why,” said Margaret, “you are in one tale with your father. Says he to me when I told him, ‘Oh, an he loves her hair so well, ’tis odd but he loves the rest of her. Well,’ quoth he, ‘’tis an honest lad, and a shall have her, gien she will but leave her sulks and consent.’ So what say ye, mistress—will you be married to Ulrich, or buried i’ the kirkyard?”

“Father! father!” cried the girl, and all her coldness cracked at once like thin ice.

“’Tis so,” said he hoarsely. “Speak thy mind.”

Denys had brought her more than tidings; he brought her a living voice from the road, full of turns and tones that made the room feel less like a cell and more like a hearth. Yet the day was sweet and bitter together: sweet, because in this strange place she had found a true comrade; bitter, because by Denys’s very news she learned, plain as salt on the tongue, that Gerard was alone in a foreign land. Denys spoke of men who always meant to come home and never did; and Margaret, who had once fed hope with both hands as if it were a child, could not force herself to swallow Denys’s belief that Gerard would appear at her door some morning. If he had been coming, she thought, he would have come ere this.

Still, Denys was balm—warm, sharp, and a little wild, like a draught spiced overmuch for health’s sake. He called her his she-comrade, and the name, half mock, half vow, rang in the small house like a tune that would not die. He was forever striving to make her laugh by repeating his soldier’s “formula” and turning it into burlesque; and she, who had so little left to pet, made much of him. She hectored him feebly, too—over Denys as over Martin—because scolding was the one kind of authority grief still allowed her.

And she ruled the table as a captain rules a gate. Denys was not suffered to eat a single meal out of her house. If he tried to slip away, she would catch him by the sleeve, as if hunger itself were a deserter.

“It spoils you, Denys,” she would say, setting before him what she had contrived from the market—dark bread still warm in the heart, a small pot of pottage kept at the edge of the coals so it thickened and did not scorch, a dab of salted fish rinsed and flaked to take the worst brine out, onions cut fine so their bite would soften in the steam. “Good lack, to hear such ugly words come forth so comely a head: forbear, or I shall be angry: so be civil.”

Then Denys would sit up, as if the bench were suddenly a throne, and his struggle began—between the native courtesy bred into him long ago and the ruffian tongue he had learned among camps where men speak like stones striking sparks. He would bite down on an oath, swallow it, and replace it with some courtly phrase that sounded to him as strange as a foreign spice. It was ludicrous and touching; and even Martin, red-armed from the wash, would laugh under his breath.

For the house was all labour and sound. The basin in the corner kept time with Martin’s hands, slap and swill, slap and swill; the wet linen made a soft, heavy music as it was wrung; Denys’s iron, clumsy in his soldier’s grip, hissed and rasped over cloth; and Margaret, plaiting ruffs, let the stiffening paste dry under her fingers until it held shape—each pleat a little fence against disorder. Outside, Rotterdam’s noises drifted in—carts, calls, the thud of hooves—but within, the domestic rhythm steadied the mind better than any sermon: the honest acoustics of work, not the jangling show-noise of men who sell delight.

And, as it never rains but it pours, other persons began to solicit Margaret’s friendship—friendship and its shadow, obligation.

She had written, some while ago, to Margaret Van Eyck: a humble letter, carefully worded, with all her pride pressed flat between the lines. She told the lady she knew she was no longer the favourite she had been; she would keep her distance; yet she could not forget past kindness. Then, briefly—because pain, once set down, need not be embroidered—she told how many ways she had battled for a living. And she ended with a plea that tasted like ash even as she wrote it: let not her residence be betrayed.

“Least of all to his people,” she had begged. “I do hate them; they drove him from me. And even when he was gone, their hearts turned not to me as they would an if they had repented their cruelty to him.”

The Van Eyck woman was perplexed, and what she could not digest alone she took to another mouth. At last she made a confidante of Reicht; and the secret ran through Reicht, as through a cylinder, to Catherine.

“Ay, and is she turned that bitter against us?” Catherine said—good woman, yet with a sting in her goodness, as nettles grow near clean water. “She stole our son from us, and now she hates us for not running into her arms. Natheless it is a blessing she is alive and no farther away than Rotterdam.”

Then came the great pageant, and with it the loudness of the world. The English princess—now Countess Charolois—made a stately progress through the northern states of the duchy, with her stepdaughter beside her, the young heiress, Marie de Bourgogne. The old duke, most magnificent prince in Europe, put out his splendour as a rich man lays out a feast: not to feed hunger, but to dazzle eyes.

Troops of knights went by in armour that flashed like fire struck from steel; bevies of ladies followed, their garments rustling like fields of dry grain in a wind. Minstrels and jongleurs, story-tellers and tumblers, bards and players swelled the train; in every town there was fencing and dancing and rejoicing—the kind of rejoicing that drowns out quieter songs. Margaret, hearing of it, could not help thinking how such uproar, clattering from street to street, can make a man forget the older music of a mother’s voice, a lover’s dialect whispered in the dark, the small syllables that carry a whole life and cannot be translated into courtly French without losing their savour.

Richart invited all his people to meet him at Rotterdam and view the glitter. They had been there some days when Denys met Catherine by chance in the street. A warm greeting passed between them, for Denys could not help liking honest folk, and Catherine, once she had decided you were not her enemy, could be hearty as bread.

“Rejoice!” Denys cried, crowing like a cock at sunrise. “I have found the she-comrade.”

Catherine’s face, that had lifted, cooled again. She showed him—plainly, as one pours cold water on a boil—how much earlier he would have found Margaret had he stayed quiet at Tergou instead of vagabondizing it all over Holland.

“And being found,” she added, “what the better are we? Her heart is set dead against us now.”

“Oh, let that flea stick,” said Denys. “Come you with me to her house.”

But Catherine shook her head. She would not go where she was sure of an ill welcome.

“Them that come unbidden sit unseated,” she said; and would not budge. Let Denys be mediator; let him carry words back and forth until the rough edges wore down.

Denys undertook the office at once, with great pomp and confidence, as if he were marching between two armies with a truce flag.

He trotted to Margaret and began, as if warming the dish before serving it. “She-comrade, I met this day a friend of thine.”

“Thou didst look into the Rotter then, and see thyself,” she answered, for she could still parry.

“Nay, ’twas a female, and one that seeks thy regard; ’twas Catherine, Gerard’s mother.”

Margaret’s fingers went on plaiting, but her hands trembled. “Oh, was it?” she said at last; and the words were ice laid on fire. “Then you may tell her she comes too late. There was a time I longed and longed for her; but she held aloof in my hour of most need, so now we will be as we ha’ been.”

Denys tried to shake this resolution. He coaxed her—he pleaded that old wrongs could be salted down and kept, but were better eaten up and done with. She would not. Her bitterness sat in her mouth like burnt crust; she was sullen, and not to be sweetened.

Then Denys, changing tack as soldiers do when the ground will not take a charge, scolded her well. At that, all her pent breath broke; her strength went out in hysterics, and the room filled with a sound worse than any street uproar—grief made loud and helpless. Denys, frightened at what his bold tongue had uncorked, was taken off guard; and before he rightly knew it she had trapped him into a solemn promise never to speak of Catherine again.

He went back to Catherine crestfallen and told her what he had met—how Margaret would not yield an inch, how her heart had turned hard.

Catherine fired up; she told the family, and they fired up in their turn. What had been a sore became a feud, and burned fiercer with each retelling—each word adding its own pepper, each hearer tasting offence where perhaps there had only been pain. Little Kate alone tried to make excuses for Margaret, as if she could still remember what it is to be young and frightened and too proud to beg.

The very next day, while the house rang with its familiar labour-music—Martin enslaved and degraded by soapsuds, Denys ironing with the grave clumsiness of a man used to sword-hilts not linen, Margaret plaiting ruffs and watching her raw levies with a mistress’s eye—another visitor entered.

An old man, venerable at first sight, came in: on nearer view keen and wizened, with something sharp about him that made Margaret’s skin draw back before her mind had named him.

“Ah,” she cried; and swiftly turned her back, hiding her face with an invincible repugnance. “Oh, that man! that man!”

“Nay, fear me not,” said Ghysbrecht. His voice was dry, yet steady; not kind, but not mocking. “I come on a friend’s errand. I bring ye a letter from foreign parts.”

“Mock me not, old man.” She turned slowly round, as if turning cost her. She had been mocked enough by fate.

“Nay, see.” And he held out an enormous letter.

At once all else in the room—iron, suds, ruffs, grievances, pageants—fell away like husks. Margaret darted upon it; the paper was thick, the seal rough under her thumb. Her hands shook; her eyes shone. It was Gerard’s handwriting—those strokes and turns she could have known among a thousand, as one knows a loved voice in a crowd.

“Oh, thank you, sir,” she cried, and the words came hot and sudden. “Bless you for this. I forgive you all the ill you ever wrought me.”

She pressed the letter to her bosom with one hand, as if to warm it with her own life, and glided from the room so swiftly the others could not stop her. The door shut; the house’s sounds went on without her, but they seemed muffled now, as if the letter had drawn all hearing into itself.

When she did not come back, Ghysbrecht went away. As he passed, he cast a scowl at Martha—old accounts remembered without being spoken. Then the street took him, with its pageant-noise and common cries.

Margaret was hours alone with her letter.

When she came down again, she was not the same woman who had gone up. The storm in her had spent itself in secret; what returned was quieter, and therefore more perilous. Her eyes still held tears, but the tears lay like clear water in a settled cup—no longer splashing, no longer bitter. Even her mouth, that could twist words into weapons, was softened, as if she had been tasting something sweet and would not waste it.

“Denys,” said she, very low, “I have got my orders. I am to read my lover’s letter to his folk.”

Denys stared, as if she had offered him a dish that looked fair yet smelt of treachery. “Ye will never do that?”

“Ay will I.”

“I see there is something in the letter has softened ye towards them.”

“Not a jot, Denys, not a jot.” Her voice did not rise; it fell, steady as a spoon into honey. “But an I hated them like poison I would not disobey my love. Denys, ’tis so sweet to obey, and sweetest of all to obey one who is far, far away, and cannot enforce my duty, but must trust my love for my obedience.”

As she spoke, the house noises below—footfalls, a chair grating, a pot-lid set down—seemed to come up through the boards and mix with her words, making them homely, almost pious, like grace said over bread.

“Ah, Gerard, my darling,” she murmured, and for an instant she was not addressing Denys at all, but some distance that had a voice of its own. “At hand I might have slighted thy commands, misliking thy folk as I have cause to do; but now, didst bid me go into the raging sea and read thy sweet letter to the sharks, there I’d go. Therefore, Denys, tell his mother I have got a letter, and if she and hers would hear it, I am their servant; let them say their hour, and I’ll seat them as best I can, and welcome them as best I may.”

Denys went off with the message. Downstairs the family sat at dinner: the thick brown bread on the board, the salt near at hand, the steam of the pottage lifting a familiar savour that, in that house, meant safety and custom. The room held also its own music: spoons against earthenware, the quiet chink of knife on trencher, the soft talk that breaks and gathers like a hearth-fire’s crackle.

Denys came in with news that struck straight through all these common sounds as a bell cuts through wind.

“There is a long letter from Gerard.”

Joy leapt like flame in dry straw; even the air seemed to brighten. In the midst of that warmth Denys added, with a soldier’s bluntness made oddly gentle by what he carried, “And her heart is softened, and she will read it to you herself; you are to choose your own time.”

“What does she think there are none can read but her?” Catherine cried at once, setting down her spoon with a sharp click that rang louder than it should in the little room. “Let her send the letter and we will read it.”

“Nay, but, mother,” put in little Kate, and the girl’s cheeks went red, as if the steam from the bowl had found them. “Mayhap she cannot bear to part it from her hand; she loves him dearly.”

“What, thinks she we shall steal it?” said Catherine, with the old suspicion, salted like cured meat.

Cornelis, who had been nursing his own sourness, said, “She would fain wedge herself into the family by means of this letter.”

Denys turned on him with a look like the flat of a blade. “There spoke a bad heart,” said he. “La camarade hates you all like poison. Oh, mistake me not, dame; I defend her not, but so ’tis; yet maugre her spleen at a word from Gerard she proffers to read you his letter with her own pretty mouth, and hath a voice like honey—sure ’tis a fair proffer.”

Eli, Gerard’s father, took the matter as he took the carving-knife: steady, with the wrist set, not without feeling but without flutter. “’Tis so, mine honest soldier,” said he, “and merits a civil reply; therefore hold your whisht, ye that be women, and I shall answer her. Tell her I, his father, setting aside all past grudges, do for this grace thank her; and would she have double thanks, let her send my son’s letter by thy faithful hand, the which will I read to his flesh and blood, and will then to her so surely and faithful return, as I am Eli a Dierich a William a Luke, free burgher of Tergou, like my forbears, and like them, a man of my word.”

“Ay, and a man who is better than his word,” cried Catherine, her sharpness turning all at once to warmth, as if a lump of butter had melted in the pot. “The only one I ever did foregather.”

“Hold thy peace, wife.”

“Art a man of sense, Eli,—a dirk, a chose, a chose,” shouted Denys, in a burst of admiration that made the room laugh in spite of itself. Then, with the gusto of a man tasting his own jest, he ran on: “The she-comrade will be right glad to obey Gerard and yet not face you all, whom she hates as wormwood, saving your presence. Bless ye, the world hath changed; she is all submission to-day: ‘obedience is honey,’ quoth she; and in sooth ’tis a sweetmeat she cannot but savour, eating so little on’t, for what with her fair face and her mellow tongue; and what wi’ flying in fits and terrifying us that be soldiers to death, an we thwart her; and what wi’ chiding us one while, and petting us like lambs t’ other, she hath made two of the crawlingest slaves ever you saw out of two honest swashbucklers. I be the ironing ruffian; t’ other washes.”

“What next?” cried Catherine, half amused, half scandalized.

“What next? Why, whenever the brat is in the world I shall rock cradle, and t’ other knave will wash tucker and bib. So, then, I’ll go fetch the letter on the instant. Ye will let me bide and hear it read, will ye not?”

“Else our hearts were black as coal,” said Catherine.

Denys went out briskly, as if fetching a flagon; and came back as if the flagon had been knocked from his hand. His shoulders drooped; his face wore that crestfallen look soldiers get when a campaign turns on a petty order.

“She will not let it out of her hand neither to me nor you, nor any he or she that lives.”

“I knew she would not,” Cornelis said at once, as if he had been waiting to salt the wound.

“Whisht! whisht!” said Eli. “And let Denys tell his story.”

“‘Nay,’ said I, ‘but be ruled by me.’ ‘Not I,’ quoth she. ‘Well, but,’ quoth I, ‘that same honey Obedience ye spake of.’ ‘You are a fool,’ says she; ‘obedience to Gerard is sweet, but obedience to any other body—who ever said that was sweet?’”

Denys paused, then drew from his pouch a paper folded small, as if it were a spice to be used sparingly. “At last she seemed to soften a bit, and did give me a written paper for you, mademoiselle. Here ’tis.”

“For me?” said little Kate, colouring deeper.

“Give that here!” said Eli, and took it before the girl’s fingers had quite closed. He scanned the writing; his lips moved without sound, tasting the words as if they were unknown meat. Then he spoke, almost in a whisper, for it was as though Gerard’s voice had entered the room and the room must mind its manners.

“These be words from the letter. Hearken!”

And he read:

“‘And, sweetheart, an if these lines should travel safe to thee, make thou trial of my people’s hearts withal. Maybe they are somewhat turned towards me, being far away. If ’tis so they will show it to thee, since now to me they may not. Read, then, this letter! But I do strictly forbid thee to let it from thy hand; and if they still hold aloof from thee, why, then say nought, but let them think me dead. Obey me in this; for, if thou dost disrespect my judgment and my will in this, thou lovest me not.’”

Silence fell—thick, not empty. The very dinner seemed to hold its steam and wait. Those words, copied by Margaret’s hand, went round the table and were looked at as folk look at relics: to be sure the thing is real, to read in the ink the pressure of a mind far off.

“Well,” said Catherine at last, and her tone changed, as when a cook finds the salt must be measured afresh. “That is another matter. But methinks ’tis for her to come to us, not we to her.”

“Alas, mother! what odds does that make?” said little Kate, and in her voice was the young instinct that words are bridges, not walls.

“Much,” said Eli. “Tell her we are over many to come to her, and bid her hither, the sooner the better.”

When Denys was gone again, Eli sat a moment with his hands on the board, as if feeling the grain of it, the old familiar ridges that had known so many meals and so many tidings. “When that lass shall cross my threshold,” said he, “all the mischief and misery she hath made here will seem to come in adoors in one heap. But what could I do, wife? We must hear the news of Gerard. I saw that in thine eyes, and felt it in my own heart. And she is backed by our undutiful but still beloved son, and so is she stronger than we, and brings our noses down to the grindstone, the sly, cruel jade. But never heed. We will hear the letter; and then let her go unblessed as she came unwelcome.”

“Make your mind easy,” said Catherine; but in her there was a small, unwilling ache, like hunger that comes even when pride would rather not eat. “She will not come at all.”

They had scarcely gathered up the board when Richart arrived at last from Amsterdam—grave and set, in his burgher’s robe and gold chain, with ruff starched clean and furred cap that smelt faintly of winter storage and city streets. With him came a different sound into the house: the faint jingle of his chain when he moved, the firmer step of a man risen in the world.
