He was received not with affection only, but with respect; in those days such steps upward were counted almost as clearly as those in a stair.

When he had been admitted to the council, and the matter told, his face showed plainly—though he kept his voice civil—that his pride was wounded by their having deigned to treat with Margaret Brandt at all.

“I see the temptation,” said he. “But which of us hath not at times to wish one way and do another?”

It cast a chill on the old folk; the room’s earlier warmth went thin, as if a door had opened to a draught. Little Kate, quick to mend the broken harmony of voices as a careful hand mends a torn cloth, spoke softly:

“Vex not thyself, dear Richart. Mother says she will not come.”

“All the better, sweetheart,” said he. “I fear me, if she do, I shall hie me back to Amsterdam.”

At that instant Denys popped his head in at the door—his entrance brisk as a ladle tapping the pot to say it is time.

“She will be here at three on the great dial,” said he.

They all looked at one another in silence, while outside the day went on with its ordinary sounds—the distant call in the street, the wind against the shutters—each noise a reminder that the world does not pause for any family’s bitterness, nor even for the taste of a son’s far-off words.

“Nay, Richart,” said Catherine at last, her hands still smelling faintly of the onions she had been slicing for supper, “for Heaven’s sake let not this one sorry wench set us all by the ears: hath she not made ill blood enough already?”

“In very deed she hath,” Richart answered. His jaw was set, as if he meant to carve the matter as clean as a roast, no more and no less. “Fear me not, good mother. Let her come and read the letter of the poor boy she hath by devilish arts bewitched, and then let her go. Give me your words to show her no countenance beyond decent and constrained civility: less we may not, being in our own house; and I will say no more.”

So it was agreed, and they waited—each with a different hunger. Not for meat, though the house was full of the honest homely odours that cling to a dwelling where bread is baked and pottage set on, and a ham has smoked in its season; but for the sharp, salt taste of news; for the bitter herb of jealousy; for the warm, dangerous draught of hope.

Denys had carried their message. He returned with it, too; and meanwhile Margaret Brandt, hearing she must come to them, curled her lip in solitude, as if their very dialect were a coarse cloth against her tongue.

“Well,” said she aloud, to a chamber that gave her no counsel, “I have not that excuse; so why mimic the pretty burgher’s pride, the pride of all unlettered folk? I will go to them for Gerard’s sake. Oh, how I loathe them!”

Poor Denys, good-natured as a kitchen boy that brings fire too near dry straw, was all unwitting bringing into one house the materials of an explosion.

Margaret made her toilet as knights arm for the lists—each point to ward a blow. She chose her kirtle of English cloth, dark blue, with a farthingale and hose of the same stuff but of glossy roan, claret-tinted as old wine. There was no fur to boast of; only plain snowy linen at the wrists, and linen curiously plaited from the bosom of the kirtle up to the commencement of the throat, framing it square, not choking it round. Her front hair showed in two waves; the rest was hid beneath a very small tight-fitting hood of dark blue cloth, hemmed with silver. Her shoes were red—red like a cook’s coals when they are at their best, red that said, I will not be trodden on.

Beauty knew its business then as now.

And with all this she kept her enemies waiting, though it was three by the dial. Outside, the street had its own music—carts creaking, a distant hammer, a dog barking at nothing, a thin winter wind worrying the eaves; yet within the house the silence grew so thick you could hear the tinder in the hearth snap.

At last she started, Denys at her side like an overgrown page. Halfway thither she stopped short.

“Denys!”

“Well, she-general?”

“I must go home,” she said piteously, like one that has forgotten the one spice that saves a dish.

“What, have ye left somewhat behind?”

“What?”

“My courage. Oh! oh! oh!”

“Nay, nay, be brave, she-general. I shall be with you.”

“Ay, but wilt keep close to me when I be there?”

Denys promised, and she resumed her march, but gingerly, as if each step might crack thin ice.

Meantime all were assembled at Eli’s—Eli, grave as a church door; Catherine, whose mother’s tenderness fought with a woman’s resentment; Richart, bristling; Cornelis and Sybrandt, hard-mouthed; and Kate, who did not rise when the rest rose, but sat as if her pain nailed her in place. The room smelt of woodsmoke and stale ale and that faint sweet that clings to dried herbs hung in rafters: domestic life refusing, stubbornly, to be driven out by drama.

Their feelings were a strange medley—mortification and curiosity, panting affection for Gerard, aversion to her who came to gratify it, and a sharper curiosity still to see what there was in her to bewitch him and breed such mischief.

At last Denys came alone, and whispered, “The she-comrade is without.”

“Fetch her in,” said Eli. “Now whisht, all o’ ye. None speak to her but I.”

They turned their eyes to the door in dead silence. Outside, a little muttering—Denys’s rough organ and a woman’s softer, mellower voice—rose and fell like two instruments that will not tune to one key.

Then the door opened slowly, and Margaret Brandt stood on the threshold, dressed as has been said, pale, but calm and lovely, looking straight before her as if she were stepping into judgment.

All rose but Kate, and remained mute and staring.

“Be seated, mistress,” said Eli gravely, and motioned to a chair set apart for her.

She inclined her head and crossed the apartment; and in that crossing her condition declared itself—not only by shape, but by a languor as if her blood were heavy. Cornelis and Sybrandt hated her for it. Richart thought it spoiled her beauty. It softened the women somewhat, as warm broth softens hard bread.

She drew a letter from her bosom and kissed it—not for show, but as if she had been alone with it by the fire at midnight. Then she set herself to read, with the air of one who knew she was there for that single purpose.

But she saw they had placed her all by herself, like a leper. Her eyes went to Denys; her hand dropped by her side, and she made him a swift furtive motion to come. He sprang to her shoulder with a soldier’s obedience; and because he did it too zealously, the whole room perceived he had been commanded. She coloured.

Then she began to read—Gerard’s letter, their Gerard’s—to their eager ears. Her voice was clear and soft, each syllable laid down tenderly, as a careful hand lays thin slices of bread to soak evenly in broth: no waste, no tearing, only a patient making-ready for what must be swallowed.

“I do nothing doubt, my Margaret, that long ere this shall meet thy beloved eyes, Denys, my most dear friend, will have sought thee out, and told thee the manner of our unlooked for and most tearful parting. Therefore I will e’en begin at that most doleful day. What befell him after, poor faithful soul, fain, fain would I hear, but may not. But I pray for him day and night next after thee, dearest. Friend more stanch and loving had not David in Jonathan, than I in him. Be good to him, for poor Gerard’s sake.”

The praise fell on Denys like a sudden hot draught in cold weather. He leaned his head on the back of Margaret’s high chair and groaned aloud. She turned quickly, found his hand, and pressed it; and so sweetheart and friend held hands while she read.

“I went forward all dizzied, like one in an ill dream; and presently a gentleman came up with his servants, all on horseback, and had liked to have rid o’er me. And he drew rein at the brow of the hill, and sent his armed men back to rob me. They robbed me civilly enough and took my purse and the last copper, and rid gaily away. I wandered stupid on, a friendless pauper.”

A general sigh went round the room; then Denys swore, his oath cracking the hush like a dropped plate.

“Presently a strange dimness came o’er me; I lay down to sleep on the snow. ’Twas ill done, and with store of wolves hard by. Had I loved thee as thou dost deserve, I had shown more manhood. But oh, sweet love, the drowsiness that did crawl o’er me desolate, and benumb me, was more than nature. And so I slept; and but that God was better to us, than I to thee or to myself, from that sleep I ne’er had waked; so all do say.

“I had slept an hour or two, as I suppose, but no more, when a hand did shake me rudely. I awoke to my troubles. And there stood a servant girl in her holiday suit. ‘Are ye mad,’ quoth she, in seeming choler, ‘to sleep in snow, and under wolves’ nosen? Art weary o’ life, and not long weaned? Come, now,’ said she, more kindly, ‘get up like a good lad;’ so I did rise up.

“‘Are ye rich, or are ye poor?’ But I stared at her as one amazed. ‘Why, ’tis easy of reply,’ quoth she. ‘Are ye rich, or are ye poor?’ Then I gave a great, loud cry; that she did start back. ‘Am I rich, or am I poor? Had ye asked me an hour agone, I had said I am rich. But now I am so poor as sure earth beareth on her bosom none poorer. An hour agone I was rich in a friend, rich in money, rich in hope and spirits of youth; but now the Bastard of Burgundy hath taken my friend, and another gentleman my purse; and I can neither go forward to Rome nor back to her I left in Holland. I am poorest of the poor.’

“‘Alack!’ said the wench. ‘Natheless, an ye had been rich ye might ha’ lain down again in the snow for any use I had for ye; and then I trow ye had soon fared out o’ this world as bare as ye came into it. But, being poor, you are our man: so come wi’ me.’

“Then I went because she bade me, and because I recked not now whither I went. And she took me to a fine house hard by, and into a noble dining-hall hung with black; and there was set a table with many dishes, and but one plate and one chair.

“‘Fall to!’ said she, in a whisper.

“‘What, alone?’ said I.

“‘Alone? And which of us, think ye, would eat out of the same dish with ye? Are we robbers o’ the dead?’

“Then she speered where I was born. ‘At Tergou,’ said I. Says she, ‘And when a gentleman dies in that country, serve they not the dead man’s dinner up as usual, till he be in the ground, and set some poor man to it?’

“I told her, ‘nay.’ She blushed for us then. Here they were better Christians.”

At that, in Eli’s room, the very air seemed to thicken with imagined food: the clink of trenchers, the steam from covered dishes, the sour-sweet wine that bites the tongue awake. Even those who hated Margaret could not help but feel the pull of that table in a hall hung with black—death and dinner bound together, charity served with ceremony.

“So I behoved to sit down. But small was my heart for meat. Then this kind lass sat by me and poured me out wine; and tasting it, it cut me to the heart Denys was not there to drink with me. He doth so love good wine, and women good, bad, or indifferent. The rich, strong wine curled round my sick heart; and that day first I did seem to glimpse why folk in trouble run to drink so.

“She made me eat of every dish. ’Twas unlucky to pass one. Nought was here but her master’s daily dinner.

“‘He had a good stomach, then,’ said I.

“‘Ay, lad, and a good heart. Leastways, so we all say now he is dead; but, being alive, no word on’t e’er heard I.’ So I did eat as a bird, nibbling of every dish. And she hearing me sigh, and seeing me like to choke at the food, took pity and bade me be of good cheer. I should sup and lie there that night.

“And she went to the hind, and he gave me a right good bed; and I told him all, and asked him would the law give me back my purse.

“‘Law!’ quoth he; ‘law there was none for the poor in Burgundy. Why, ’twas the cousin of the Lady of the Manor, he that had robbed me. He knew the wild spark. The matter must be judged before the lady; and she was quite young, and far more like to hang me for slandering her cousin, and a gentleman, and a handsome man, than to make him give me back my own. Inside the liberties of a town a poor man might now and then see the face of justice; but out among the grand seigneurs and dames—never.’

“So I said, ‘I’ll sit down robbed rather than seek justice and find gallows.’

“They were all most kind to me next day; and the girl proffered me money from her small wage to help me towards Rhine.”

“Oh, then, he is coming home! he is coming home!” shouted Denys, bursting like a lid lifted too soon from a pot.

Margaret shook her head gently at him by way of reproof.

“I beg pardon, all the company,” said he stiffly, and fell back, chastened.

“’Twas a sore temptation; but being a servant, my stomach rose against it. ‘Nay, nay,’ said I. She told me I was wrong. ’Twas pride out o’ place; poor folk should help one another; or who on earth would? I said if I could do aught in return ’twere well; but for a free gift, nay: I was overmuch beholden already.

“Should I write a letter for her? ‘Nay, he is in the house at present,’ said she.

“Should I draw her picture, and so earn my money? ‘What, can ye?’ said she. I told her I could try; and her habit would well become a picture. So she was agog to be limned, and give it her lad. And I set her to stand in a good light, and soon made sketches two, whereof I send thee one, coloured at odd hours. The other I did most hastily, and with little conscience daub, for which may Heaven forgive me; but time was short. They, poor things, knew no better, and were most proud and joyous; and both kissing me after their country fashion, ’twas the hind that was her sweetheart, they did bid me God-speed; and I towards Rhine.”

Here Margaret paused and gave Denys the coloured drawing to hand round.

The women took it first, as women will when cloth and cut are at issue. They bent over it as over a new recipe, noting each fold and fastening: the hair in a tight linen bag; a yellow half-kerchief crossed from ear to ear, throwing out a rectangular point down the centre of the forehead; two more points meeting over the bosom. A red kirtle with long sleeves, kilted high in front to show a green farthingale; a great red leather purse hanging over it; red stockings; yellow leather shoes—low-quartered and square-toed, strapped over the instep, rude forebears of finer buckles. Even in this room of quarrel, such particulars carried the quiet power of a people’s memory: the way a country ties its kerchief, the way it shapes its shoe, the way it marks itself without ever naming itself.

Margaret resumed.

“But oh! how I missed my Denys at every step! often I sat down on the road and groaned. And in the afternoon it chanced that I did so set me down where two roads met, and with heavy head in hand, and heavy heart, did think of thee, my poor sweetheart, and of my lost friend, and of the little house at Tergou, where they all loved me once; though now it is turned to hate.”

“Alas!” broke from Catherine, before she could swallow it down, “that he will think so.”

“Whisht, wife!” said Eli; and his rebuke was less anger than fear of the room’s sound turning wild. For sound has its own governance: once a babble begins, it drowns the one voice that matters.

“And I did sigh loud, and often. And me sighing so, one came carolling like a bird adown t’ other road. ‘Ay, chirp and chirp,’ cried I bitterly. ‘Thou has not lost sweetheart, and friend, thy father’s hearth, thy mother’s smile, and every penny in the world.’ And at last he did so carol, and carol, I jumped up in ire to get away from his most jarring mirth.

“But ere I lied from it, I looked down the path to see what could make a man so lighthearted in this weary world; and lo! the songster was a humpbacked cripple, with a bloody bandage o’er his eye, and both legs gone at the knee.”

“He! he! he! he! he!” went Sybrandt, laughing and cackling, as if pain were a jest to be tossed like bones to a dog.

Margaret’s eyes flashed; she began to fold the letter up, the paper creasing under her fingers like dough pressed too hard.

“Nay, lass,” said Eli, sharp as a cleaver brought down, “heed him not! Thou unmannerly cur, offer’t but again and I put thee to the door.”

“Why, what was there to gibe at, Sybrandt?” Catherine added, more mildly but with that steady scorn a mother keeps for cruelty. “Is not our Kate afflicted? and is she not the most content of us all, and singeth like a merle at times between her pains? But I am as bad as thou; prithee read on, lass, and stop our gabble wi’ somewhat worth the hearkening.”

Margaret let the paper fall open again.

“‘Then,’ said I, ‘may this thing be?’ And I took myself to task. ‘Gerard, son of Eli, dost thou well to bemoan thy lot, thou hast youth and health; and here comes the wreck of nature on crutches, praising God’s goodness with singing like a mavis?’”

“There you see,” murmured Catherine, triumphant and tender in one breath, as if the boy’s words were bread to her heart.

“Whisht, dame, whisht!” Eli insisted; but his eyes had softened.

“And whenever he saw me, he left carolling and presently hobbled up and chanted, ‘Charity, for love of Heaven, sweet master, charity,’ with a whine as piteous as wind at keyhole.

“‘Alack, poor soul,’ said I, ‘charity is in my heart, but not my purse; I am poor as thou.’

“Then he believed me none, and to melt me undid his sleeve, and showed a sore wound on his arm, and said he, ‘Poor cripple though I be, I am like to lose this eye to boot, look else.’ I saw and groaned for him, and to excuse myself let him wot how I had been robbed of my last copper.

“Thereat he left whining all in a moment, and said, in a big manly voice, ‘Then I’ll e’en take a rest. Here, youngster, pull thou this strap: nay, fear not!’ I pulled, and down came a stout pair of legs out of his back; and half his hump had melted away, and the wound in his eye no deeper than the bandage.”

A great “Oh!” broke from them all at once, as when a whole table tastes vinegar where it expected honey.

“Whereat, seeing me astounded, he laughed in my face, and told me I was not worth gulling, and offered me his protection. ‘My face was prophetic,’ he said. ‘Of what?’ said I. ‘Marry,’ said he, ‘that its owner will starve in this thievish land.’ Travel teaches e’en the young wisdom.

“Time was I had turned and fled this impostor as a pestilence; but now I listened patiently to pick up crumbs of counsel. And well I did: for nature and his adventurous life had crammed the poor knave with shrewdness and knowledge of the homelier sort—a child was I beside him.

“When he had turned me inside out, said he, ‘Didst well to leave France and make for Germany; but think not of Holland again. Nay, on to Augsburg and Nurnberg, the Paradise of craftsmen: thence to Venice, an thou wilt. But thou wilt never bide in Italy nor any other land, having once tasted the great German cities. Why, there is but one honest country in Europe, and that is Germany; and since thou art honest, and since I am a vagabone, Germany was made for us twain.’

“I bade him make that good: how might one country fit true men and knaves! ‘Why, thou novice,’ said he, ‘because in an honest land are fewer knaves to bite the honest man, and many honest men for the knave to bite. I was in luck, being honest, to have fallen in with a friendly sharp.

“‘Be my pal,’ said he; ‘I go to Nurnberg; we will reach it with full pouches. I’ll learn ye the cul de bois, and the cul de jatte, and how to maund, and chaunt, and patter, and to raise swellings, and paint sores and ulcers on thy body would take in the divell.’ I told him shivering, I’d liever die than shame myself and my folk so.”

“Good lad! good lad!” cried Eli, unable to keep the pride from his voice; and in that cry you heard a whole lineage speak, the old stubbornness of farmers and craftsmen that would rather go hungry than eat dishonour.

“Why, what shame was it for such as I to turn beggar? Beggary was an ancient and most honourable mystery. What did holy monks, and bishops, and kings, when they would win Heaven’s smile? why, wash the feet of beggars, those favourites of the saints. ‘The saints were no fools,’ he told me. Then he did put out his foot. ‘Look at that, that was washed by the greatest king alive, Louis, of France, the last Holy Thursday that was. And the next day, Friday, clapped in the stocks by the warden of a petty hamlet.’

“So I told him my foot should walk between such high honour and such low disgrace, on the same path of honesty, please God.

“Well then, since I had not spirit to beg, he would indulge my perversity. I should work under him, he be the head, I the fingers. And with that he set himself up like a judge, on a heap of dust by the road’s side, and questioned me strictly what I could do.

“I began to say I was strong and willing. ‘Ba!’ said he, ‘so is an ox. Say, what canst do that Sir Ox cannot?’ I could write; I had won a prize for it. ‘Canst write as fast as the printers?’ quo’ he, jeering. ‘What else?’ I could paint. ‘That was better.’ I was like to tear my hair to hear him say so, and me going to Rome to write. I could twang the psaltery a bit. ‘That was well. Could I tell stories?’ Ay, by the score. ‘Then,’ said he, ‘I hire you from this moment.’

“‘What to do?’ said I.

“‘Nought crooked, Sir Candour,’ says he. ‘I will feed thee all the way and find thee work; and take half thine earnings, no more.’

“‘Agreed,’ said I, and gave my hand on it.

“‘Now, servant,’ said he, ‘we will dine. But ye need not stand behind my chair, for two reasons—first I ha’ got no chair; and next, good fellowship likes me better than state.’

“And out of his wallet he brought flesh, fowl, and pastry, a good dozen of spices lapped in flax paper, and wine fit for a king. Ne’er feasted I better than out of this beggar’s wallet, now my master.”

In Eli’s room, where the day’s broth had been stretched with barley and a rind, the mention of that wallet did more than paint a picture: it drew forth the imagined crackle of crust, the hot peppery breath of spices that travel farther than men, the thick sweetness of wine on an empty stomach. Hunger itself is a language, and every land speaks it with a different accent.

“When we had well eaten I was for going on. ‘But,’ said he, ‘servants should not drive their masters too hard, especially after feeding, for then the body is for repose, and the mind turns to contemplation;’ and he lay on his back gazing calmly at the sky, and presently wondered whether there were any beggars up there.

“I told him I knew but of one, called Lazarus.

“‘Could he do the cul de jatte better than I?’ said he, and looked quite jealous like.

“I told him nay; Lazarus was honest, though a beggar, and fed daily of the crumbs fal’n from a rich man’s table, and the dogs licked his sores.

“‘Servant,’ quo’ he, ‘I spy a foul fault in thee. Thou liest without discretion: now the end of lying being to gull, this is no better than fumbling with the divell’s tail. I pray Heaven thou mayest prove to paint better than thou cuttest whids, or I am done out of a dinner. No beggar eats crumbs, but only the fat of the land; and dogs lick not a beggar’s sores, being made with spearwort, or ratsbane, or biting acids, from all which dogs, and even pigs, abhor. My sores are made after my proper receipt; but no dog would lick e’en them twice. I have made a scurvy bargain: art a cozening knave, I doubt, as well as a nincompoop.’”

Margaret’s voice gave those words their due disgust; and the room, so careful to keep its own tongue—its own right names for bread and broth and work—felt the power of that rogue’s patter: how he could twist holy story into mockery, and make a counterfeit knowledge sound like truth.

“I deigned no reply to this bundle of lies, which did accuse heavenly truth of falsehood for not being in a tale with him. He rose and we took the road; and presently we came to a place where were two little wayside inns, scarce a furlong apart.

“‘Halt,’ said my master. ‘Their armories are sore faded—all the better. Go thou in; shun the master; board the wife; and flatter her inn sky high, all but the armories, and offer to colour them dirt cheap.’

“So I went in and told the wife I was a painter, and would revive her armories cheap; but she sent me away with a rebuff. I to my master.

“He groaned. ‘Ye are all fingers and no tongue,’ said he; ‘I have made a scurvy bargain. Come and hear me patter and flatter.’

“Between the two inns was a high hedge. He goes behind it a minute and comes out a decent tradesman.

“We went on to the other inn, and then I heard him praise it so fulsome as the very wife did blush. ‘But,’ says he, ‘there is one little, little fault; your armories are dull and faded. Say but the word, and for a silver franc my apprentice here, the cunningest e’er I had, shall make them bright as ever.’

“Whilst she hesitated, the rogue told her he had done it to a little inn hard by, and now the inn’s face was like the starry firmament.

“‘D’ye hear that, my man?’ cries she, ‘“The Three Frogs” have been and painted up their armories; shall “The Four Hedgehogs” be outshone by them?’

“So I painted, and my master stood by like a lord, advising me how to do, and winking to me to heed him none, and I got a silver franc.

“And he took me back to “The Three Frogs,” and on the way put me on a beard and disguised me, and flattered “The Three Frogs,” and told them how he had adorned “The Four Hedgehogs,” and into the net jumped the three poor simple frogs, and I earned another silver franc.

“Then we went on and he found his crutches, and sent me forward, and showed his ‘cicatrices d’emprunt,’ as he called them, and all his infirmities, at “The Four Hedgehogs,” and got both food and money.

“‘Come, share and share,’ quoth he: so I gave him one franc.

“‘I have made a good bargain,’ said he. ‘Art a master limner, but takest too much time.’

“So I let him know that in matters of honest craft things could not be done quick and well.

“‘Then do them quick,’ quoth he.

“And he told me my name was Bon Bec; and I might call him Cul de Jatte, because that was his lay at our first meeting.

“And at the next town my master, Cul de Jatte, bought me a psaltery, and set himself up again by the roadside in state like him that erst judged Marsyas and Apollo, piping for vain glory.

“So I played a strain.

“‘Indifferent well, harmonious Bon Bec,’ said he haughtily. ‘Now tune thy pipes.’

“So I did sing a sweet strain the good monks taught me; and singing it reminded poor Bon Bec, Gerard erst, of his young days and home, and brought the water to my een.

“But looking up, my master’s visage was as the face of a little boy whipt soundly, or sipping foulest medicine.

“‘Zounds, stop that bellyache blether,’ quoth he, ‘that will ne’er wile a stiver out o’ peasants’ purses; ’twill but sour the nurses’ milk, and gar the kine jump into rivers to be out of earshot on’t. What, false knave, did I buy thee a fine new psaltery to be minded o’ my latter end withal? Hearken! these be the songs that glad the heart, and fill the minstrel’s purse.’

“And he sung so blasphemous a stave, and eke so obscene, as I drew away from him a space that the lightning might not spoil the new psaltery.

“However, none came, being winter, and then I said, ‘Master, the Lord is debonair. Held I the thunder, yon ribaldry had been thy last, thou foul-mouthed wretch.’”

Margaret’s voice, in giving Gerard’s rebuke, rang like clean iron struck. Even Sybrandt held his tongue, for the sound of true anger—righteous, not petty—has a way of steadying a room. Outside, a wagon passed; its wheels groaned; a chain clinked; a man called to a horse. The ordinary world went on, indifferent, while within this house a letter carried Gerard’s very breath, his chosen words, his Dutch soul wrestling with foreign tongues that would rename him Bon Bec and teach him to live by lies.

“‘Why, Bon Bec, what is to do?’ quoth he. ‘I have made an ill bargain. Oh, perverse heart, that turneth from doctrine.’

“So I bade him keep his breath to cool his broth, ne’er would I shame my folk with singing ribald songs.

“‘Then,’ says he sulkily, ‘the first fire we light by the wayside, clap thou on the music box! so ’twill make our pot boil for the nonce; but with your,

Good people, let us peak and pine, Cut tristful mugs, and miaul and whine Thorough our nosen chaunts divine,”

When Margaret’s senses came back to her, her cheek lay against Catherine’s firm forearm, as if she had been set there like dough to rise under a warm cloth. Around her stood the honest half of the household she had stormed as one might storm a gate—plain faces, plain hands, and plain, hearty counsel spoken with the clumsy kindness of people who have salted much meat and wasted few words. Giles, great-voiced as a market bell, bellowed straight over her.

“Thou’rt not to take on so! Gerard’s alive and well, or he could not ha’ writ thee that letter—aye, the biggest mankind hath seen as yet—and,” he added with a reverence almost comic in his rough throat, “the beautifullest, and most moving, and smallest writ.”

“Ay, good Master Giles,” Margaret breathed, her voice thin as steam from a cooling pot, “he was alive. But how know I what hath since befallen him? Oh, why left he Holland to go among strangers fierce as lions? And why did I not drive him from me sooner than part him from his own flesh and blood? Forgive me—you that are his mother!”

She slid Catherine’s arm away with a gentleness that was more apology than strength, and made a trembling attempt to slip down upon her knees. The attempt ended—after a brief, helpless struggle against hands that would not let her fall—in her being gathered back against Catherine’s bosom, where she clung as if that plain wool gown were the one safe shore in all Europe.

Then, with a little shiver like a leaf in draught, she held out the letter to Eli.

“I will trust it from my hand now,” she whispered—sweetly, faintly. “In sooth, I am little fit to read any more—and—and—loth to leave my comfort.” And she wreathed her free arm round Catherine’s neck, as a child will cling when thunder has passed but the air still trembles.

“Read thou, Richart,” said Eli. “Thine eyes be younger than mine.”

Richart took the letter as if it were a consecrated wafer.

“Well,” said he, turning it this way and that to catch the light, “such writing saw I never. A writeth with a needle’s point; and clear to boot. Why is he not in my counting-house at Amsterdam instead of vagabonding it out yonder!”

And he began.

“When I came to myself I was seated in the litter, and my good merchant holding of my hand. I babbled I know not what, and then shuddered awhile in silence. He put a horn of wine to my lips.”

“Bless him! bless him!” cried Catherine, as if the wine had been poured for her own son.

“Whisht!” said Eli; but his face softened.

“And I told him what had befallen. He would see my leg. It was sprained sore, and swelled at the ankle; and all my points were broken, as I could scarce keep up my hose, and I said, ‘Sir, I shall be but a burden to you, I doubt, and can make you no harmony now; my poor psaltery it is broken;’ and I did grieve over my broken music, companion of so many weary leagues. But he patted me on the cheek, and bade me not fret; also he did put up my leg on a pillow, and tended me like a kind father.

“January 19.—I sit all day in the litter, for we are pushing forward with haste, and at night the good, kind merchant sendeth me to bed, and will not let me work. Strange! whene’er I fall in with men like fiends, then the next moment God still sendeth me some good man or woman, lest I should turn away from human kind. Oh, Margaret! how strangely mixed they be, and how old I am by what I was three months agone. And lo! if good Master Fugger hath not been and bought me a psaltery.”

“Eli, my man,” Catherine broke in, brisk as a cook taking stock of a pantry, “an yon merchant comes our way let us buy a hundred ells of cloth of him, and not higgle.”

“That will I,” said Eli; “take your oath on’t!”

While Richart shifted his stance to go on, Kate stole a glance at her mother and, with a blush that came and went like a quick flame under ash, drew a bit of sewing from beneath her apron. Her head bent lower than need was. Her needle began to travel again—soft, secret, sure. Catherine, catching the look, answered with a look, and drew out her own sewing from her pocket with the same guilty dexterity. They stitched in silence, the thread whispering through linen.

The two pieces—now first betrayed to common sight—were babies’ caps, more than half finished; and horror, for all their tenderness, they were shaped like little monks’ cowls, fine as frostwork.

Richart read on.

“January 20.—Laid up in the litter, and as good as blind, but halting to bait, Lombardy plains burst on me. Oh, Margaret! a land flowing with milk and honey; all sloping plains, goodly rivers, jocund meadows, delectable orchards, and blooming gardens; and though winter, looks warmer than poor beloved Holland at midsummer, and makes the wanderer’s face to shine, and his heart to leap for joy to see earth so kind and smiling. Here be vines, cedars, olives, and cattle plenty, but three goats to a sheep. The draught oxen wear white linen on their necks, and standing by dark green olive-trees each one is a picture; and the folk, especially women, wear delicate strawen hats with flowers and leaves fairly imitated in silk, with silver mixed. This day we crossed a river prettily in a chained ferry-boat. On either bank was a windlass, and a single man by turning of it drew our whole company to his shore, whereat I did admire, being a stranger. Passed over with us some country folk. And an old woman looking at a young wench, she did hide her face with her hand, and held her crucifix out like knight his sword in tourney dreading the evil eye.

“January 25.—Safe at Venice…”

At the name, the room seemed to widen. Even the loom and the hearth, the daily tools that had heard so much human talk, fell attentive. Outside, the house’s small noises—wood settling, a distant cluck, the sigh of winter air—made a kind of homely counterpoint, like a drone under a song.

“A place whose strange and passing beauty is well known to thee by report of our mariners. Dost mind too how Peter would oft fill our ears withal, we handed beneath the table, and he still discoursing of this sea-enthroned and peerless city, in shape a bow, and its great canal and palaces on piles, and its watery ways plied by scores of gilded boats; and that market-place of nations… But I, lying at my window in pain, may see none of these beauties as yet, but only a street, fairly paved, which is dull, and houses with oiled paper and linen, in lieu of glass, which is rude; and the passers-by, their habits and their gestures, wherein they are superfluous. Therefore, not to miss my daily comfort of whispering to thee, I will e’en turn mine eyes inward…”

Margaret listened as if each line were broth spooned into her mouth—too hot to swallow at once, yet necessary.

Gerard’s voice, carried by ink, began to do what his hands could not: set in order the world for the woman he loved. He wrote of nations as a baker speaks of different flours—each with its own temper, its own rising, its own sourness.

He told of Germans who drank till sobriety itself was suspect; of English who sugared their wine; of French courtesy that could be as light as foam and as treacherous as a thin crust over a hollow pie.

“‘Tis sooth! ‘tis sooth!” Catherine burst out at one passage, recognizing a wife in Tergou who gave her man leave to go abroad. “’Twas Beck Hulse, Jonah’s wife. This comes of a woman wedding a boy.”

Denys, lounging with his soldier’s ease, laughed at the French, and then rose with a flourish of hand to breastplate when France was praised, as if he would accept compliments on behalf of a whole kingdom.

Yet Gerard’s letter, for all its jests and observations, kept returning—like a song’s refrain—to the things that struck deeper: what words did in different mouths, how custom could gild cruelty, how nations named their sins with silken names. It was not philosophy in the air; it was the bite and smell of lived places—the stale beer breath of taverns, the clean shine of German windows, the dust of roads where a grape might cost a life.

When Richart read that Gerard had called Denys foul-mouthed, Denys bristled like a cat.

“My foul mouth! Is that so writ, Master Richart?”

“Ay, in sooth; see else.”

Denys peered at the letter with comical gravity, tracing the tiny strokes as if they were battle-maps.

“I read not the letter so.”

“How then?”

“Humph! ahem—why just the contrary.” He straightened, and appealed to the women with injured innocence. “’Tis kittle work perusing of these black scratches men are agreed to take for words. And I trow ’tis still by guess you clerks do go, worthy sir. My foul mouth! This is the first time e’er I heard on’t. Eh, mesdames?”

Margaret, caught between love and laughter, only blushed and lowered her eyes. Kate and Catherine bent over their needlework with a silence that had a sly curl at the edge. Denys studied their faces as intently as if reading a proclamation. Whatever he read there satisfied him; he turned back with patient martyrdom.

“Read on,” said he.

So the letter flowed—Italy polished and subtle; Venice temperate at table, yet crawling with itch-ointment hawked on corners; bread “lovely white,” salt “black;” meat “spoiled” with cheese; innkeepers who would sell clean sheets, and sometimes sell murder; women’s hair turned yellow by sun and art; and the State itself taking tax from sin as from spice.

Eli sighed once, deep in his chest, when Gerard prayed that in little Holland an assassin might be called assassin, and an harlot harlot, till doomsday.

“He should have been a priest,” Eli murmured, “saving your presence, my poor lass.”

At last Richart came to the last dated entry; and the room leaned in, as if nearer words could bring nearer the man.

“January 26.—Sweetheart, I must be brief, and tell thee but a part of that I have seen, for this day my journal ends. To-night it sails for thee, and I, unhappy, not with it, but to-morrow, in another ship, to Rome.

“Dear Margaret, I took a hand litter, and was carried to St. Mark his church…”

As Richart read of the church—of pillars like a forest of stone, and horses that seemed ready to leap, and jewels blazing like fruit set in gold—Margaret’s heart tightened and loosened with each marvel, for all that glittering wealth was only the crust upon another hunger: Gerard’s hunger to share what his eyes had seen, since he could not share it with her in person.

Then came the tale of relics and miracles, told with a man’s mixture of awe and doubt: St. Mark’s body breaking through marble at midnight; the crevice that would gape “while the world lasts;” the Virgin’s chair; the picture carried out to call down rain. There was a shiver in the room when Richart read, “I wish I had not seen it,” as if Gerard’s very voice had faltered.

He wrote, too, of darker civic customs: babes slid through a wall-niche into the State’s net; a corpse carried with bare face and feet; three rotting heads tainting the air upon a porphyry slab; a gallows of alabaster set before the Duke’s own eyes to whisper him memento mori. Even here—amid trade and prayer and music—the city’s soundscape rang with its own harsh bells: the clack of law, the creak of discipline, the steady hum of power saying, in stone, Remember.

He told of four brothers who poisoned each other at one table—wine drugged, marchpane envenomed—so that land might not be quartered, and souls were bartered for acreage. Catherine’s needle paused at marchpane, as if the very name of sugared paste should have been safe from such corruption.

Then, abruptly, the letter turned from poisoned banquets and stone effigies to a small, human sign that could be read without Latin or law.

“And after this they took me to the quay, and presently I espied among the masts one garlanded with amaranth flowers. ‘Take me thither,’ said I, and I let my guide know the custom of our Dutch skippers to hoist flowers to the masthead when they are courting a maid. Oft had I scoffed at this saying, ‘So then his wooing is the earth’s concern.’ But now, so far from the Rotter, that bunch at a masthead made my heart leap with assurance of a countryman. They carried me, and oh, Margaret! on the stern of that Dutch boy, was written in muckle letters,

RICHART ELIASSOEN, AMSTERDAM.”

Two months before ever Eli’s hearth began to glow in our sight, there was a little sea-town between Naples and Rome where the people left their nets to dry, their olives to cure, their pots to simmer, and streamed down to the strand as if summoned by a bell. The whole beach was alive with bodies and voices—old men with salt in their beards, women with wet hands still smelling of dough and brine, boys whose pockets held nothing but figs and pebbles—and all eyes were flung seaward, fixed upon a ship that laboured as a beast does under a cruel load.

The gale blew dead on shore. The sea did not merely move; it shoved and shouldered, it hammered with a rhythm that made the very air throb. There was a soundscape to it—wind keening through rigging like a thin flute, surf booming like a drum struck with a wet cloth, cries snapped short by spray—and on that harsh music the town’s murmuring rode: pity spoken aloud, and something meaner kept under the tongue, for men are seldom sorry to watch another man’s peril so long as their own feet are dry.

The vessel was ill-fated in her very bones: not built with the clean, clever lines that slip through water, but with an extravagant poop that caught the wind like a sail set wrong; she was, if truth be told, better fashioned for going ashore than for avoiding it. From the beach the battered frame of wood looked almost living—struggling, panting, driven back, lunging forward—yet if one could have been carried onto her deck, one would have found not one heart but many, and many sorts of courage and baseness breaking through as the hour grew black.

The sailors staggered and lurched, hands on ropes as each man’s fear taught him; they cursed, then prayed, then cursed again, as if oaths were ballast. The passengers were huddled amidships about the mast—some sitting, some kneeling, some flat as if they would press themselves into the planks—and every roll tore at their stomachs and their dignity alike. Among them stood a comely young man with an ashen cheek and lips clamped tight, as though he could bite terror into obedience. He held fast by a shroud, wincing with each heave of the sea.

It was Gerard.

Around the mast, vows rose as thick as spray. To listen, one might think there were nearly as many gods aboard as souls. The mariners, at least, clung to one Queen, though they dressed her in a dozen titles—Star of the Sea, Haven of Safety, Mistress of the World—each name flung upward like a rope. But the landsmen’s prayers were a market of divinities. An English merchant vowed gold to Our Lady of Walsingham; a Genoese promised a silver collar to Our Lady of Loretto; a Tuscan noble pledged ten pounds of wax lights to Our Lady of Ravenna; even the Cross itself must be specified by city, as if God’s wood needed a street-name to be found. In such moments men bargain with Heaven the way cooks bargain in a fish-market: loudly, greedily, and with a curious confidence that the price named must bind the seller.

Then came a gust more vicious than the rest. It struck the sail at the worst angle; rotten shrouds snapped. There was a crack like a cleaver through bone, and the torn sail went away downwind, dwindling, blackening, fluttering, and at last fell into the sea half a mile off like a paper dropped by a careless hand. Before the helm could bring the ship’s head about, a wave caught her on the quarter and drenched the whole poor company to the marrow, giving them a chill foretaste of death—salt water in the mouth, salt in the eyes, and the taste of fear that is like iron.

Vows turned frantic. One cried he would turn Carthusian if St. Thomas saved him. Another swore he would go barefoot to Compostella, bareheaded and with nothing but mail on naked skin, if St. James would draw him out. Names flew—Thomas, Dominic, Denys, and above all Catherine of Siena—like crumbs scattered to birds.

Two petty Neapolitan traders stood shivering, their teeth chattering a drumbeat on that furious sea-song. One bellowed, “I vow to St. Christopher at Paris a waxen image of his own weight if I win safe to land!”

The other nudged him, half drowned and half sensible. “Brother, brother, take heed. Sell all you have by auction and ’twill not buy his weight in wax.”

“Hold thy tongue, fool!” the other roared—then, bending close so the wind would steal the words, hissed, “Think ye I am in earnest? Let me but touch land and I’ll not give him a rush dip.”

Some, in their terror, prayed not to saints at all but to the sea itself, as if it were a capricious lord who might be softened by flattery. “Merciful sea! bountiful sea! beautiful sea! be gentle—be kind—preserve us!” And others only moaned, the animal sound that comes when speech breaks and the body remembers it is only flesh.

Yet amid this wailing throng there sat a Roman woman of the humbler sort, a child at her half-bared breast. She was pale as ash, but her eye was calm. Her lips moved at times in silent prayer; she neither wept nor bargained. When the ship seemed to sink under their feet and men with beards squeaked like frightened boys, she only kissed her child and held him closer, letting him draw what comfort he could while there was still milk and warmth in the world. There was something ancient in her—an unruined gravity, as if sixteen hundred years had not diluted the old blood; she died, if she must die, with decent dignity, and fed her child at the edge of the grave as naturally as another woman might do so beside a hearth.

On the poop stood a gigantic friar, feet apart as if planted in rock. He did not so much defy the danger as ignore it. His voice rang out steady and sonorous above wind and wave as he recited verses from the Canticles, and he invited the passengers to confess. Some crawled to him on their knees, clutching planks, and he heard them and laid his hands on them and absolved them as if he stood in a snug sacristy and not on a deck that pitched like a tossed trencher.

Gerard, drawn by an instinct older than thought, edged nearer and nearer to that immovable man—toward composure as a moth goes to flame. Heroic courage against fleshly odds might have looked small beside the friar’s vast, quiet self-command.

The sail was gone. The sailors cut down the useless mast a foot above the board and sent it, with its remaining hamper, over the side. The ship seemed to lift a little, relieved of that top-hampering weight, but now the hull could not keep ahead of the sea. Again and again the waves struck her on the poop; each blow felt like a mountain of rock, not water.

The captain left the helm and came amidships, pale as paste. “Lighten her!” he cried. “Fling all overboard, or we shall founder ere we strike, and lose the one little chance of life.”

As sailors began to obey, the captain—more like a superstitious pilgrim than a blunt skipper—spoke to the faces crowding him. “Friends,” said he, “last night when all was fair—too fair, alas—there came a globe of fire close to the ship. When a pair of them come, it is good luck, and nought can drown her that voyage. We mariners call them Castor and Pollux. But if Castor come without Pollux, or Pollux without Castor, she is doomed. Therefore, like good Christians, prepare to die.”

A wail went up, and the wind snatched it away in tatters. “How long?” a voice trembled.

“She may, or may not, last half an hour,” said the captain. “Over that, impossible. She leaks like a sieve. Bustle—lighten her!”

So the deck became a frantic larder being emptied in a fire: chests, bundles, spare gear, all heaved overboard with hands that shook. Presently they seized a heavy sack. An old man lay on it, sea-sick and helpless. They dragged it from under him; it rattled. Two began to heave it to the side.

Up sprang the owner with a cry raw enough to curdle milk. “Holy Moses! What would you do? ’Tis my all—the whole fruits of my journey—silver candlesticks, silver plates, brooches, hanaps—”

“Let go, thou hoary villain!” others shouted. “Shall all our lives be lost for thy ill-gotten gear?”

“Fling him in with it!” cried one. “’Tis this Ebrew we Christian men are drowned for.”

They wrenched the sack away and cast it into the sea. It splashed, then sank as if the water had swallowed it with appetite. The old man gave one cry of anguish and stood with white hair streaming, glaring like a mad prophet. He would have leapt after it had it floated; but it went down and was gone. He staggered, tore his hair, and cursed them, the ship, the sea, and all powers of heaven and hell together, as if he would season the water with blasphemy.

Then the captain cried, pointing: “See! there is a church in sight. Steer for that church, mate; and you, friends, pray to the saint, whoever he be.”

They tried to steer, and prayers shifted to this new, unknown patron like a sauce altered at the last moment because the cook has run out of herbs. But a tremendous sea broke over the stern, smashed the rudder, jammed it immovable, and flooded the deck. Panic turned to suspicion, and suspicion sought a scapegoat as naturally as hunger seeks bread.

Some, wild with superstition, came on Gerard. “Here is the cause of all! He has never invoked a single saint. He is a heathen—a pagan aboard!”

“Alas, good friends, say not so,” Gerard stammered, his teeth chattering with cold and terror. “Rather call these heathen that lie praying to the sea. Friends, I do honour the saints—but I dare not pray to them now—there is no time. What avail me Dominic, and Thomas, and Catherine? Nearer God’s throne than these St. Peter sitteth; and if I pray to him, I shall be drowned ere he has time to plead my cause with God. I must go straight to Him that made the sea, and the saints, and me.”

And he cried out into the storm, not bargaining now but begging like a man whose mouth is full of salt water: “Our Father which art in heaven, save these poor souls and me that cry for the bare life! Oh, sweet Jesus—pitiful Jesus—that didst walk Genezaret when Peter sank, and wept for Lazarus dead when the apostles’ eyes were dry—oh, save poor Gerard—for dear Margaret’s sake!”

At that moment the sailors were seen preparing the little boat every ship carried. A rush of selfishness answered them: thirty souls crowded in, pushing with elbows and curses. Left behind were three bewildered who ran to and fro wringing hands without the wit to leap; two more sat paralyzed like heaps of wet cloth. One man knelt over a wooden statue of the Virgin Mary, as large as life, which the sailors had reverently detached from the mast. As water slushed in and out through scuppers, the image washed about the deck, and the poor devotee followed it on his knees, hands clasped toward it, as if the statue were a floating loaf he dared not let drift away.

The Jew sat cross-legged, not palsied by fear but emptied of it—capable now only of grief for his lost silver. When spray lashed him, he shook his fist at the sea and cursed Nazarenes, their gods, their devils, their ships, and their waters, to all eternity.

The gigantic Dominican, having shriven the whole ship, stood calmly communing with his own spirit.

And the Roman woman still sat, pale and patient, only drawing her child closer as death came nearer.

Gerard saw her, and something in him hardened into manhood. “See—see!” he cried. “They have taken the boat and left the poor woman and her child to perish.”

His heart set his wits to work. “Wife,” he said to her—calling her so with the sudden fellowship of peril—“I’ll save thee yet, please God.” He ran seeking a cask, a plank, anything that would bear her. There was none.

Then his eye fell on the wooden image of the Virgin. He caught it in his arms. A wail burst from the kneeling worshipper like a child robbed of its toy, but Gerard, heedless, ran aft with it.

“Come,” he cried. “I’ll lash thee and the child to this. ’Tis sore worm-eaten, but ’twill serve.”

The woman lifted her great dark eyes to him and spoke one word, rich with question and tenderness: “Thyself?!”

“I am a man,” said he, “and have no child to take care of.”

“Ay,” she breathed; and the hope of life touched her face like sudden warmth. He lashed the image to her side—rope biting into old wood, knots drawn tight with numbed fingers, as if he were trussing a cask for travel. Her body trembled a little now, but her gaze held steady. The ship rode so low that Gerard, using an oar as a lever, could slide her into the waves.

“Come,” he urged, “while yet there is time.”

She turned to him, eyes wet. “Poor youth—God forgive me—my child!”

He launched her onto the surge, and with the oar kept her from being battered against the ship’s side, pushing her clear as one might guide a fragile bowl through a crowded kitchen.

Then a heavy hand fell on Gerard, and a deep voice sounded in his ear. “’Tis well. Now come with me.”

The gigantic friar.

Gerard turned, and the friar took two strides and seized the broken mast. Gerard did likewise, obeying by instinct. Together, with a prodigious effort, they hoisted the remainder and carried it.

“Fling it in,” said the friar, “and follow it.”

They cast it into the sea. But one of the bewildered passengers had chased them and leapt first, scrambling onto one end. Gerard seized the other; the friar took the middle. The mast rose and plunged with each wave like a kicking horse. Spray flogged their faces, filled their mouths with brine, and blinded them as if the sea were trying to knock them off by sheer violence.

A long grating noise sounded ahead. The ship had struck. Being now stationary, she became a wall for the waves to use. The three on the mast were hurled against the black hull with tremendous force. Their companion’s head struck the jagged upper part of the broken rudder with a crack that ended speech for ever; it was smashed like a nut beneath a hammer. He sank at once, leaving only a red stain on the water, a white clot on the splintered rudder, and a death-cry ringing in their ears as Gerard and the friar drifted clear under the lee of the hull.

The friar murmured a short Latin prayer for the dead man’s soul, then set himself again with composed strength.

They rolled along, alternately swallowed and lifted. One moment they saw nothing but the dim basin of watery hills; the next, a glimpse of shore speckled bright with people, arms flung up in wild Italian gestures. They saw, too, the black boat bottom-up, and between it and them the woman—rising and falling. She had come by a paddle and held her child with her left arm, paddling with her right—gallant, steady, her movements timed to the sea’s brutal rhythm. Even in that chaos there was a domestic obstinacy to her: the ancient duty of keeping a small mouth fed and a small body warm, even while the world roared.

After long tumbling, the friar said quietly, as if remarking upon a road: “I touched the ground.”

“Impossible, father,” cried Gerard. “We are more than a hundred yards from shore. Prithee, prithee, leave not our faithful mast.”

“My son,” said the friar, “you speak prudently. But know I have business of Holy Church on hand, and may not waste time floating when I can walk in her service. There—I felt it with my toes again. See the benefit of wearing sandals, and not shoon. Again; and sandy. Thy stature is less than mine: keep to the mast! I walk.”

He left the mast and, extending his powerful arms, rushed through the water. Gerard soon followed. At each overpowering wave the monk stood like a tower: he closed his mouth, flung his head back, vanished under the green weight, then emerged and ploughed on. Near shore, the outward suction fought them, dragging at their legs like unseen hands. The natives sent stout fishermen into the sea holding long spears, linked in a triple chain, and so hauled them ashore.

The friar shook himself like a great dog, bestowed a short paternal benediction, and went on toward Rome with eyes bent on the earth according to his rule, not pausing, not looking back upon the sea that had so nearly taken him. It could harm him no more than his Master permitted.

Gerard, who was not bound by a rule that forbade looking, stayed. Hands seized him, voices pressed him with questions, and they brought him to an enormous fire whose crackle and roar sounded, after that savage ocean, like sanity itself. The heat drew salt out of his clothes; steam rose from him; the smell of wet wool and smoke mingled with the sharp, clean stink of seaweed drying on stones. With a delicacy he might not have met farther north, they left him alone to dry.

Then he did a thing that showed what he valued most. From his bosom he drew a parchment and a paper, and he dried them with infinite care—turning them, shielding them from sparks, warming them gradually so ink would not run—tending them as a cook tends precious yeast, knowing that a careless heat can kill what time has made. Not until this was done to his mind did he consent to put on a fisherman’s dress, leaving his own garments by the fire, and go down to the beach to see what the sea would give back.

The rest may be told briefly. The captain clung to the ship, less from gallantry than from a conviction that it was idle to resist Castor or Pollux, whichever fiery messenger had come for him. Yet the sea broke up the vessel and swept the poop—captain and all—clear away, and then, in mockery, took him safe ashore. Gerard had a principal hand in dragging him out of the water.

The disconsolate Hebrew landed on another fragment, and the moment his feet touched earth he offered a reward for his bag. The offer stirred little sympathy and some amusement.

Two more were saved on pieces of wreck. The thirty who had crowded into the boat came ashore too—but one at a time, and dead; only one breathed still. The natives, with excellent intention and no knowledge, took him close to a hot fire. So he, too, went out of this shifting world, as if warmth were always kindness.

As Gerard stood by the sea, watching with horror and a grim curiosity the bodies of his late companions washed ashore to the sound of surf and lamentation, a hand touched his shoulder lightly.

He turned. It was the Roman woman, her face burning with gratitude as if life itself were a flame in her. She took his hand gently and raised it to her lips and kissed it—so nobly it seemed she conferred honour upon a deserving hand rather than begged favour from it. Then, with moist eyes and cheeks alight, she lifted her child and made him kiss his preserver.

Gerard kissed the child more than once; he was fond of children. But he did not speak. The woman spoke scarcely at all—only with her gaze and that antique, stately gesture—large, simple, and untranslatable into the little coinage of common words. Perhaps she was right. Gratitude is not a thing of talk.

Next day toward afternoon Gerard—twice as old as last year, thrice as learned in the ways of men, no boy now but a man who had shed blood in self-defence and grazed the grave by land and sea—reached the Eternal City; post tot naufragia tutus.

Gerard lodged in a modest house on the west bank of the Tiber, where the river talked all night under the windows—no clatter of carts here, only water worrying its stones, and, at dawn, the thin bell-notes from far churches threading the damp air. He lived by those sounds. They steadied him; they measured his hours when his purse would not.

Every day, after a mouthful, he went out with his best specimen—clean, severe lines, ink laid as evenly as a cook lays oil in a pan, neither too stingy nor too lavish. He carried it from shop to shop, to the booksellers and stationers he could hear of, men whose doors smelled of glue and old calfskin, whose counters were dusted with pumice and scraped vellum.

They met him with Roman coldness.

“We make our letter somewhat thinner,” said one, as if he spoke of slicing onions.

“How dark your ink is,” said another, wrinkling his nose like a man offered over-salted broth.

But the true answer came, again and again, in a chorus that made Gerard feel the city itself had turned its back.

“What avails this? Scant is the Latin writ here now. Can ye not write Greek?”

“Ay,” Gerard said, “but not nigh so well as Latin.”

“Then you shall never make your bread at Rome.”

Bread. The word went through him with a hunger that was more than hunger: a boy’s memory of his mother’s table, of a crust warmed at the hearth, of broth that comforted because it carried a familiar tongue in its very smell. Here, he could copy Virgil as cleanly as a knife can pare an apple, but Rome—Rome wanted other shapes, other letters, other mouths.

He borrowed a beautiful Greek manuscript at a high price—paying for it as one pays for a rare spice, dearly, with a wince—and went home with a sad hole in his purse but none in his courage. He set himself to the new characters as a cook sets himself to a strange fish: first learning its bones, then its flesh, then the exact heat that will not spoil it. In a fortnight he had made vast progress. Thereafter he worked at Greek till noon, and hunted customers the rest of the day.

When he carried round a Greek specimen better than any they possessed, the traders shrugged and smiled as if he had brought them a fine dish to a table already groaning.

“Greek and Latin are alike unsaleable,” they told him. “The city is thronged with works from all Europe. You should have come last year.”

So he bought a psaltery—cheap enough, and it gave him something to do with his hands when his head grew too loud with refusal. In the evenings he picked up canzonets as one picks up scraps in a kitchen: a phrase here, a cadence there. Rome’s streets had their own acoustic law—fountains, sandals, disputing voices, the slap of laundry in courtyards—and he found he could not think without some order in the sound.

His landlady, pleased with his looks and manners, spoke him kind words in passing. She was from Siena, and she said so the way another woman might show a medal of Our Lady: proudly, as protection. One day she made him dine with her—she herself tending the pot, stirring and tasting, and letting the broth speak before she did. The room was warm with garlic and stewed herbs; the spoon rang against the earthen bowl with a homely, honest note.

She watched him eat like a woman who has fed men all her life and can read their hearts in their jaws.

“What hath dashed thy spirits?” she asked at last.

Gerard, who had tried to swallow his discouragement with his bread and could not, told her plainly: no work, no patron, and Rome full to bursting of other men’s manuscripts.

She gave him her reading of it at once, her voice sharp as vinegar.

“Those sly traders have writers in their pay. For whose work they receive a noble price, and pay a sorry one. So no wonder they blow cold on you. Methinks you write too well.”

He stared.

“How know I that? say you,” she rattled on, delighted with her own certainty. “Marry—marry—because you lock not your door, like the churl Pietro, and women will be curious. Ay, ay, you write too well for them.”

Gerard sighed, half amused, half troubled. “Alas, dame, you read folk on the ill side, and you so kind and frank yourself.”

“My dear little heart,” said she, with a toss, “these Romans are a subtle race. Me? I am a Siennese, thanks to the Virgin.”

“My mistake was leaving Augsburg,” Gerard said, thinking of honest German cities and honest German work.

“Augsburg?” She drew herself up as if the name were a beggar at her door. “Is that a place to even to Rome? I never heard of it, for my part.”

Yet she would not let him sink. Her kindness had the briskness of a woman who will not have a guest die under her roof, because it brings a bad name upon the house and upon her own cooking besides.

“Seeing thee a stranger, they lie to thee without sense or discretion,” she said. “Why, all the world knows our great folk are bitten with the writing spider this many years, and pour out their money like water, and turn good land and houses into writ sheepskins, to keep in a chest or a cupboard. God help them, and send them safe through this fury—as He hath through a heap of others. And in sooth there hath been somewhat less cutting and stabbing among rival factions, and vindictive eating of their opposites’ livers, minced and fried, since Scribbling came in.”

She named two that made Gerard’s heart lift: Cardinal Bessarion, and the Pope himself.

“There be a pair could keep a score such as thee a-writing night and day,” she vowed. “But I’ll speak to Teresa; she hears the gossip of the court.”

The next day she returned with names—five more signori, each said to be mad for books and writing. Gerard wrote them down carefully, as if the names themselves were provisions to be measured. He bought parchment—good stuff, smooth under the finger, that faint animal sweetness of skin still clinging to it—and busied himself for days preparing specimens. He left one at each door, with his name and his lodging, and waited.

There was no answer.

Day after day passed, each one sounding the same: the same street cries, the same bell-hours, the same scuff of his own shoes on stone, and—worse than hunger—the same silence at his door. It was strange, and bitter, that this should be the very time when, far away at Rotterdam, Margaret fought like a wolf to feed her male dependents, and was arrested for curing without a licence instead of killing with one. A man can starve on coincidence as on crusts: slowly, incredulous at first, then with a dull certainty.

Gerard saw ruin staring him in the face. He spent his afternoons gathering canzonets as if hoarding crumbs, mastering them note by note. He bought playing cards to colour, because even poor work must be work. Then he struck off a meal a day.

That stroke of economy—so clever in his mind—brought him into fresh trouble at once, because in these camere locande the landlady dressed all meals though the lodgers bought the provisions. She knew the sound of a man’s hunger. She knew the silence of a plate not set.

She confronted him with a brusque “Are you not ashamed?” that made him blush and look scared. But she pacified herself as quickly as she had flamed, and appealed to his good sense as a mistress of kitchens appeals to a foolish boy who thinks he can live on air.

“Adversity is a thing to be overcome on an empty stomach?” she demanded. “Patienza, my lad! times will mend; meantime I will feed you for the love of heaven.”

“For gratis,” Gerard understood, and his pride rose like yeast.

“Nay, hostess,” he said, “my purse is not yet quite void; and it would add to my trouble an if true folk should lose their due by me.”

“Why, you are as mad as your neighbour Pietro, with his one bad picture.”

Gerard pricked up his ears.

“How know you ’tis a bad picture?”

“Because nobody will buy it.”

So she told him of Pietro: a Florentine who had come with money and an unfinished panel; how he had taken the room opposite Gerard’s and furnished it neatly, as if order could protect him; how, when the picture was finished, visitors came and made offers—liberal ones in her opinion—but he refused them with such disdain he made enemies of customers. Since then he had often carried it out to try to sell, and always brought it back; and these last weeks she had seen one movable after another go out of his room. Now he wore but one suit and lay at night on a great chest.

She had discovered this by peeping through the keyhole, for he locked his door vigilantly whenever he went out.

“Is he afraid we shall steal his chest,” she scoffed, “or his picture, that no soul in all Rome is weak enough to buy?”

“Nay,” said Gerard gently, “’tis his poverty he would screen from view.”

“And the more fool he! Are all our hearts as ill as his? A might give us a trial first, anyway.”

She compared them with a woman’s unmerciful fairness: Gerard, golden-haired and mannerly; Pietro, dark, sour-visaged, taking no pains to please. Yet she feared Pietro starving to death in her house would stain her name. One starveling, she declared, was enough.

“You are far from home,” she said, and her voice softened just a little, “and it is for me, which am the mistress here, to number your meals—for me and the Dutch wife, your mother, that is far away. We two women shall settle that matter. Mind thou thine own business, being a man, and leave cooking and the like to us, that are in the world for little else that I see but to roast fowls, and suckle men at starting, and sweep their grown-up cobwebs.”

Her talk of roasting fowls and numbering meals stabbed Gerard with the clean pain of memory; it made his need for his own mother’s tongue, his own hearth-sounds, rise in him till it was almost a thirst.

“Dear kind dame,” he said, “in sooth you do often put me in mind of my mother that is far away.”

“All the better,” said she, beaming. “I’ll put you more in mind of her before I have done with you.”

Gerard, who was not an egotist and could see his own grief mirrored in another’s, thought of Pietro’s pride and loneliness until he could bear it no more. If he had little, he would share it; and, he told himself, Pietro’s companionship would repay him in coin no moneychanger carried—sympathy, and perhaps some counsel in this city that listened only to its own dialects.

He tried to waylay Pietro on the stair; Pietro slipped past like a cat. He tried again; again the locked door and silence.

One day, passing, he heard a groaning in the room opposite—low, stubborn, as if wrung out of a man who hated to let sound betray him. Gerard knocked. No answer. He knocked again. A surly voice bade him enter.

He pushed the door and stepped in, timid as a man entering another’s hunger.

It was a garret: bare as a scraped board. A chair, an iron basin, an easel; a picture turned face to wall; and a long chest that served for bed and throne. On that chest lay a haggard young man coiled like a serpent, his eye unnaturally bright. The air smelled of stale oil, old sweat, and the faint sharpness of pigments ground too sparingly—as if even colour were rationed.

“Good Signor Pietro,” said Gerard, “forgive me that, weary of my own solitude, I intrude on yours; but I am your nighest neighbour in this house, and methinks your brother in fortune. I am an artist too.”

“You are a painter?” The man sprang up in a sudden blaze of courtesy, as quick as a match to tow. “Welcome, signer. Sit down on my bed.”

He leapt off the chest and waved Gerard into the place with a magnificent gesture, as if the bare wood were damask.

Gerard bowed and smiled, but hesitated a heartbeat.

“I may not call myself a painter. I am a writer—a calligraph. I copy Greek and Latin manuscripts, when I can get them to copy.”

“And you call that an artist?”

“Without offence to your superior merit, Signor Pietro.”

“No offence, stranger, none.” Pietro’s mouth twisted. “Only, meseemeth an artist is one who thinks, and paints his thought. Now a caligraph but draws in black and white the thoughts of another.”

“’Tis well distinguished,” said Gerard. “But then, a writer can write the thoughts of the great ancients, and matters of pure reason, such as no man may paint: ay, and the thoughts of God, which angels could not paint. But let that pass. I am a painter as well; but a sorry one.”

“The better thy luck. They will buy thy work in Rome.”

“Yet seeking to commend myself to one of thy eminence, I thought it well rather to call myself a capable writer than a scurvy painter.”

At that moment a step sounded on the stair—the landlady’s tread, with its kitchen authority. Gerard’s heart leapt, not for food alone, but for the familiar rhythm of a home’s service.

“Ah! ’tis the good dame,” he cried. “What, hostess! I am here in conversation with Signor Pietro. I dare say he will let me have my humble dinner here.”

Pietro bowed gravely, as if granting audience.

The landlady entered with a dish set steaming and savoury, the smell of it filling the poor room like music—meat and herbs, onion softened till sweet, the fat carrying the scent like a chorus. She set it down on the chest with a face stripped of expression—only her hands spoke, efficient and kind—and went without a word.

Gerard fell to, thankful as a man rescued. Yet after a few mouthfuls he stopped. Eating alone in another man’s misery felt like singing in a sickroom.

“I am an ill-mannered churl, Signor Pietro,” he said. “I ne’er eat to my mind when I eat alone. For Our Lady’s sake put a spoon into this ragout with me; ’tis not unsavoury, I promise you.”

Pietro’s glittering eye fixed on him, and for a beat the only sound was the far-off drip of a roof and Rome’s muffled street below.

“What,” said Pietro slowly, “thou a stranger, and offerest me thy dinner?”

“Why, see,” said Gerard, “there is more than one can eat.”

“Well, I accept,” said Pietro—and took the dish with an appearance of calmness.

Then, with a violent sweep, he flung the contents out of the window.

The smell of the ragout, broken and wasted, went out into the air like a prayer strangled.

He turned back, trembling—half with mortification, half with rage—and said, “Let that teach thee to offer alms to an artist thou knowest not, master writer.”

Gerard’s face flushed hot. For an instant it cost him a bitter struggle not to strike the man—if not for insult, then for the sacrilege of good food destroyed. Somewhere in him, his mother’s careful thrift rose up, indignant as a saint. Yet pity came too: the pride of a starving man is a sharp thing; it cuts the hand that touches it.

He spoke coldly.

“Likely what thou hast done might pass in a novel of thy countryman, Signor Boccaccio; but ’twas not honest.”

“Make that good!” Pietro snapped, sullen as a dog that knows it has bitten.

“I offered thee half my dinner; no more,” said Gerard. “But thou hast ta’en it all. Hadst a right to throw away thy share, but not mine. Pride is well, but justice is better.”

Pietro stared, then his brow shifted as the thought worked in. His anger, like oil, settled and showed its dregs.

“’Tis well,” he said at last. “I took thee for a fool, so transparent was thine artifice. Forgive me! And prithee leave me. Thou seest how ’tis with me. The world hath soured me. I hate mankind. I was not always so. Once more excuse my discourtesy, and fare thee well.”

Gerard sighed and moved to the door. But a new thought struck him—half Dutch stubbornness, half a kind of jest to salve the sting.

“Signor Pietro,” said he, “we Dutchmen are hard bargainers. We are the lads ’een eij scheeren’—to shave an egg. Therefore I, for my lost dinner, do claim to feast mine eyes on your picture, whose face is toward the wall.”

“Nay, nay,” Pietro cried hastily, stepping between him and the panel as if between a child and a knife. “Ask me not that. I have already misconducted myself enough towards thee. I would not shed thy blood.”

“My blood?” Gerard blinked.

“Stranger,” said Pietro, voice low, “irritated by repeated insults to my picture, which is my child, my heart, I did in a moment of rage make a solemn vow to drive my dagger into the next one that should flout it—and the labour and love I have given to it.”

“What,” said Gerard, “are all to be slain that will not praise this picture?” He could not help looking at its back with curiosity.

“Nay, nay—if you would but look, and hold your parrot tongue. But you will be talking. So I have turned it to the wall for ever. Would I were dead, and buried in it for my coffin!”

Gerard weighed him with one glance: pride like fever, despair like a draft in winter. He answered quietly.

“I accept the condition. Show me the picture. I can but hold my peace.”

Pietro went and turned its face, set it in the best light the garret could give, and then coiled himself again upon his chest—his eye bright, his stiletto nearer his hand than any rosary.

The picture showed the Virgin and Christ flying through the air in a cloud of shadowy cherubic faces; beneath stretched a landscape vast as a traveller’s life—fields, river, roads, little houses and moving specks of men—forty or fifty miles of earth unrolled like a tablecloth; above, a purple sky deep as wine.

Gerard stood and looked without a word. He stepped close and looked. He retreated as far as the poor room allowed and looked again. He paced between nearness and distance as a careful taster moves between pot and plate, letting the whole and the parts speak in turn. Half an hour passed, filled only with the hush of his breathing and the far city’s murmur.

At last Pietro’s voice broke, querulous and inconsistent as a starving man’s pride.

“Well—have you not a word to say about it?”

Gerard started, as if recalled from a chapel.

“I cry your mercy,” said he. “I forgot there were three of us here. Ay, I have much to say.”

And he drew his sword.

“Alas! alas!” Pietro cried, springing up in terror. “What wouldst thou?”

“Marry,” said Gerard, “defend myself against thy bodkin, signor—and at due odds, being, as aforesaid, a Dutchman. Therefore hold aloof while I deliver judgment, or I will pin thee to the wall like a cockchafer.”

“Oh! is that all?” Pietro sagged with relief. “I feared you were going to stab my poor picture with your sword—stabbed already by so many foul tongues.”

So Gerard, “pursuing criticism under difficulties,” stood with his sword’s point covering Pietro, one eye on the man, the other sliding back to the painted sky.

“First,” he said, “I would have you know that, in the mixing of certain colours, and in the preparation of your oil, you Italians are far behind us Flemings. But let that flea stick. For as small as I am, I can show you certain secrets of the Van Eycks that you will put to marvellous profit in your next picture.”

“I will! I will!” Pietro cried, leaning forward like a man offered bread.

“Meantime,” said Gerard, and his voice warmed, “I see in this one the great qualities of your nation. Verily, ye are solis filii. If we have colour, you have imagination. Mother of Heaven! an he hath not flung his immortal soul upon the panel.”

Pietro’s breath hitched, and even the stiletto seemed to forget to glitter.

“One thing I go by is this,” Gerard went on: “it makes other pictures I once admired seem drossy, earth-born things. The drapery here is somewhat short and stiff—why not let it float freely, the figures being in air and motion?”

“I will!” Pietro cried again, his whole face changing as if lit from within. “I will do anything for those who will but see what I have done.”

“And this landscape,” said Gerard, turning his head to take it all in, “it enlightens me. Henceforth I scorn those little huddled landscapes that did erst content me. Here is nature’s very face: a spacious plain, each distance marked, and every tree, house, figure, field, and river smaller and less plain, by exquisite gradation, till vision itself melts into distance. O, beautiful!”

His voice began to gather like a song. Outside, the street noises rose and fell, but in the garret another world had taken the air.
