“And the cunning rogue hath hung his celestial figure in air out of the way of his little world below. Here, floating saints beneath heaven’s purple canopy. There, far down, earth and her busy hives. And they let you take this painted poetry, this blooming hymn, through the streets of Rome and bring it home unsold. But I tell thee, in Ghent or Bruges—or even in Rotterdam—they would tear it out of thy hands. It is a common saying that a stranger’s eye sees clearest.”

Then, as if calling a man back from the brink with his true name, he cried, “Courage, Pietro Vanucci! I reverence thee; and though myself a scurvy painter, do forgive thee for being a great one. Forgive thee? I thank God for thee and such rare men as thou art; and bow the knee to thee in just homage. Thy picture is immortal; and thou, that hast but a chest to sit on, art a king in thy most royal art. Viva, il maestro! Viva!”

At that, Pietro—Italian to the marrow, all abandon where a moment ago he had been all suspicion—flung himself upon Gerard’s neck and sobbed.

“They said it was a maniac’s dream.”

“Maniacs themselves!” Gerard shouted, laughing with anger and joy together. “No—idiots!”

“Generous stranger,” Pietro cried, his voice broken, “I will hate men no more since the world hath such as thee. I was a viper to fling thy poor dinner away; a wretch, a monster.”

“Well, monster,” said Gerard, and his sternness melted like butter in heat, “wilt be gentle now, and sup with me?”

“Ah, that I will. Whither goest thou?”

“To order supper on the instant,” said Gerard. “We will have the picture for third man.”

“I will invite it whiles thou art gone,” Pietro said softly, turning toward his panel as to a hearth. “My poor picture—child of my heart.”

“Ah, master,” said Gerard, pausing at the door, “’twill look on many a supper after the worms have eaten you and me.”

“I hope so,” said Pietro.

A week, and a world of small hungers, had gone by. The two friends sat at the same trestle again, bent over their colors as monks over an antiphoner, yet their spirits were as far apart as Rome from Holland.

Pietro worked in storms. He would pounce on a card, hatch it with three daring strokes, and in a few minutes conjure a face so alive you could almost hear it breathe; then, as if the very speed shamed him, he would fling the brush down and curse the work, curse the buyers that did not come, curse Rome, curse the sun for shining on a city so hard of heart. Presently he would seize the brush again like a man taking up a dagger, and attack the paper with a fury that was half genius and half starvation.

Gerard, beside him, moved with that quiet thrift of hand and mind that had carried him over so many roads: steady, patient, smiling a little as if he listened to a music the other could not hear. He had, in plain truth, put his Onagra in harness. Pietro might rear and foam, but the yoke was on: they must eat. And so, to boil the pot, they painted playing cards.

The little squares lay in a sunbeam like wafers on a paten. The smell of gum and size rose with the faint, sharp sweetness of crushed pigment—vermilion with its hot, metallic tang; lampblack, sooty and dry; a whiff of garlic from the kitchen below that slid in under the door and made even their poor workroom feel for an instant like a home. Outside, through the shutter, Rome sounded as Rome always sounded: a far bell, a nearer shout, the patter of sandals on stone, a donkey’s complaint, and then—too often—those harsh cries of hawkers that made the street ring like a cracked cymbal. Gerard found himself counting the kinder noises: the sparrows under the eaves, the soft clink of a pot-lid below, the whisper of brush on paper. Those were the sounds a man could live with. The rest were like a tax laid on the nerves.

When the pack was done, Pietro, still indignant at the world for not falling at his feet, took up his larger picture for his daily round of doors that did not open. Gerard begged him to take the cards too and try their fortune.

Pietro turned on him with the look of a rattle-snake that has been asked to do a mole’s work. Yet need is a stronger master than pride. He embraced Gerard with sudden Italian warmth, took the packet—after first setting the last-wet cards in the sun at the window, where the light was already hot and full, and would bake the paint to dryness in a little while—and went out.

Left alone, Gerard made a Greek letter or two with the scrupulous care of a clerk who believes that meaning lives and dies in strokes. It was a comfort, that exactness: each curl and angle a small refusal to let the world’s words be trampled into one loud, easy tongue. Then, as if the hand must always be doing something useful, he drew his hose across his knee and mended a little rent with neat stitches.

His landlady found him so employed, needle in hand, and laughed in her throat.

“Are there no women in the house?” said she, with a bite of irony, as if mending were a woman’s trade and he stole it.

“When you have done that,” she added, “come and talk to Teresa—my friend I spoke to thee of—that hath a husband not good for much, which brags his acquaintance with the great.”

Gerard went down. The kitchen’s warmth met him like an embrace: steam on the air, herbs bruised in a mortar, yesterday’s bread re-toasted on a corner of the hearth to make it almost new again. The very pots had their own language—dull, honest notes when the ladle struck, a quick bright ring when copper was set down too sharply. It was homely music, better for a man’s heart than all the street’s bellowing.

And there stood Teresa.

She was the Roman matron from the river, the one with the fair-haired boy.

“Ah, madama,” cried Gerard, and his voice altered in spite of him, “is it you? The good dame told me not that. And the little fair-haired boy—he is well? he is none the worse for his voyage in that strange boat?”

“He is well,” said the matron; and the words were plain, but her eyes shone as if she said a prayer.

The landlady stared from one to the other. “Why, what are you two talking about?” she demanded; “and why tremble you so, Teresa mia?”

“He saved my child’s life,” Teresa answered, gathering herself as a woman gathers a cloak about her when the wind takes her. “He saved him.”

“What! my lodger?” the landlady cried. “And he never told me a word of that. Art not ashamed to look me in the face?”

Gerard colored, and would have made some poor excuse—he never could bear to be praised; praise, like rich food, oppressed him—but Teresa spoke quickly, almost fiercely, as if to shield him.

“Alas! speak not harshly to him.”

Then she turned to her friend, and gratitude unfastened her tongue. She poured out a glowing account of Gerard’s conduct—how he had not thought, but done; how he had flung himself into danger as another man flings bread to a starving child. Gerard stood there blushing like a girl, and hardly knew the deed as she told it; gratitude had painted it fairer than memory.

“And to think,” Teresa went on, “thou shouldst ask me to serve thy lodger, of whom I knew nought but that he had thy good word, oh, Fiammina; and that was enough for me. Dear youth, in serving thee I serve myself.”

So the two women fell to eager counsel—what had been done, what must be done—how to pierce that thick wall of fees and commissions and chicanery that stood between those who could pay for beauty and the unknown hand that made it. It was as if Rome had built, not one, but many gates, and hired men to stand at each, jangling their keys and demanding coin to open them; and if you had not the right words—if you did not speak the dialect of servants and brokers and whisperers—your meaning died on your lips, untranslated.

Teresa smiled sadly at Gerard’s simplicity.

“What!” she said. “Thou leavest specimens of thy skill at the doors of the great—without promising the servants a share—without even feeing them, to let the signors see thy merchandise! As well have flung it into Tiber.”

“Well-a-day!” sighed Gerard, and the sigh had hunger in it and weariness. “Then how is an artist to find a patron? for artists are poor, not rich.”

“By going to some city nobler and not so greedy as this,” Teresa replied. “La corte Romana non vuol’ pecora senza lana.” The Roman court will not have a sheep without wool.

She fell into thought; and Gerard watched her face the way he watched a page of Greek—seeking the sense beneath the surface. The room held its little domestic noises—fire snapping, a spoon scraping a bowl, the soft drip of water—while outside a cart rattled by like a threat. Teresa’s eyes narrowed as if she listened past both, toward some plan.

At last she said she would come again to-morrow.

When she had gone, the landlady nodded, pleased as a woman is pleased when her own shrewdness is justified. “Teresa has got something in her head,” said she.

Teresa was scarce out of the door when Pietro returned, his picture under his arm, his brow black as thunder. The air about him seemed to crackle; even the stair creaked louder at his feet.

Gerard exchanged a glance with the landlady and followed him up, ready with such comfort as one poor man can give another.

“What,” said Gerard, “have they let thee bring home thy masterpiece?”

“As heretofore,” Pietro answered between his teeth.

“More fools they, then.”

“That is not the worse.”

“Why, what is the matter?”

Pietro’s voice broke out like a volley. “They have bought the cards!” he yelled, and hammered the air right and left with both hands, as if he would beat Rome itself.

“All the better,” said Gerard, cheerful as if a loaf had been set down on the table.

“They flew at me for them,” cried Pietro. “They were enraptured with them. They tried to conceal their longing for them, but could not. I saw, I feigned, I pillaged; curse the boobies.”

He flung down a dozen small silver coins on the floor. Then, in a passion that was half triumph and half insulted pride, he jumped on them and danced on them, his eyes shining like a basilisk’s. He kicked them assiduously, sending them spinning and flying, running all abroad like frightened beetles.

Down went Gerard on his knees at once. He followed those maltreated innocents with the tenderness of a man who has known empty pockets too often. One by one he gathered them, the silver cool and weighty in his fingers, and transferred them carefully to his purse, as if each coin were a seed that must not be lost.

“Shouldst rather smile at their ignorance,” said he quietly, “and put it to profit.”

“And so I will,” said Pietro, and the indignation in him drew in, concentrated like a flame under a pot. “The brutes! We will paint a pack a day; we will set the whole city gambling and ruining itself, while we live like princes on its vices and stupidity.”

He began to pace, then stopped short, his face changing as a man’s face changes when, in the midst of hunger, he remembers a sweetness.

“There was one of the queens, though,” he said more lowly, “I had fain have kept back. ’Twas you limned her, brother. She had lovely red-brown hair and sapphire eyes, and above all, soul.”

Gerard’s hand tightened on the purse, not from greed but from some inward pain that money could neither cure nor cause.

“Pietro,” he said softly, “I painted that one from my heart.”

The quick-witted Italian nodded; his eyes twinkled with knowledge that was almost tenderness. “You love her so well, yet leave her.”

“Pietro,” Gerard answered, and the words tasted of long roads and salted tears, “it is because I love her so dear that I have wandered all this weary road.”

Before Pietro could press him further, the landlady’s voice came up from below, sharp as a spoon on a pan. “Come down, you are wanted.”

Gerard went down, and there was Teresa again.

“Come with me, Ser Gerard.”

Gerard went beside Teresa through the Roman streets as if they were moving along the margin of a great, warm sea. He did not question her; he watched her instead, the way a draughtsman watches a face before he dares a first line—waiting to learn what she meant to make of him, and what she meant to make of the city.

She spared him the asking.

“A friend,” she said at last, “told me of a goldsmith’s wife that would have a writer. Her shop is hard by; thou wilt not have far to go.”

So they turned into a lane where metal rang under hammers in quick bright strokes, and the air tasted of charcoal, hot filings, and the sharp, clean bite of vinegar used to brighten dull gold. The goldsmith’s wife stood in her doorway among glittering trifles and little scales, her hands white with polishing-powder.

“Madama,” said Teresa, with the grave courtesy that made her seem taller than she was, “Leonora telleth me you want a writer. I have brought you a beautiful one; he saved my child at sea. Prithee look on him with favour.”

The woman looked—looked as women look at comely youth with idle leisure—and could scarce take her eyes away; but her tongue gave small comfort.

“Nay. I have no use for a writer. Ah! I mind now—’tis my gossip Claelia, the sausage-maker, wanteth one. She told me, and I told Leonora.”

Teresa answered smoothly, as if refusal were but another door to be opened with patience, and drew Gerard away.

Claelia lived farther; the city’s sounds changed by degrees as they walked—less of jewellers’ tinkling, more of carts and donkey-bells, and the long hum of voices that makes Rome like a hive. When they reached the sausage-maker’s house, the door was shut and the place smelled—though even from the street—of smoke and pepper, of rendered fat that had clung to rafters for years. But Claelia herself was out.

“I will await her return,” said Teresa.

She seated herself with such stillness, such composed weight, as if she had been carved for a niche. Gerard, who lived by the hand and the eye, found his fingers itching to steal her outline on paper. He had already begun, furtively, in his mind, when footsteps and a burst of warm spiced air announced the woman’s return.

Claelia came in with her sleeves pushed up, a red string of sausages over one arm like a rosary of meat. Her hands were stained with wine and garlic, and her hair carried the scent of smoke.

“Madama,” Teresa began again, “I hear from the goldsmith’s wife, the excellent Olympia, that you need a writer.” Here she took Gerard’s hand and led him forward as one presents a chosen knife to a cook. “I have brought you a beautiful one; he saved my child from the cruel waves. For our Lady’s sake look with favour on him.”

“My good dame, my fair Ser,” cried Claelia, laughing with the easy mirth of women who have vats to stir and no time for courtly fears, “I have no use for a writer. But now you remind me—my friend Appia Claudia asked me for one but the other day. She is a tailor; liveth in the Via Lepida.”

Teresa withdrew as calmly as if she had gained a point.

“Madama,” said Gerard, when they were in the street again, “this is like to be a tedious business for you.”

Teresa opened her eyes slowly, as if he had spoken a childish thing. “What was ever done without a little patience?” Then, with that mild iron in her voice, she added, “We will knock at every door at Rome, but thou shalt have justice.”

He hesitated, and lowered his voice. “But, madama, I think we are dogged. I noticed a man that followeth us—now afar, now close.”

“I have seen it,” said Teresa coldly; but a faint colour stirred under her cheek like a blush hidden under marble. “It is my poor Lodovico.”

She stopped, turned, and beckoned with one finger.

A figure that had been hovering like a shadow in the bustle approached unwillingly. When he came up, Teresa looked full into his face. He wore the sheepishness of a man caught doing what he has no right to do.

“Lodovico mio,” she said, “know this young Ser, of whom I have so often spoken to thee. Know him and love him; for he it was who saved thy wife and child.”

At the last words Lodovico’s face broke, and what had been false bowing and grinning fell away. He embraced Gerard warmly, with a gratitude that seemed honest enough. Yet something—his first manner, and the stealth of his following—made Gerard’s skin tighten beneath the friendly arm, as if a dish too richly spiced had left a bitterness on the tongue.

Gerard drew back and kept his courtesy. “We shall have your company, Ser Lodovico?”

“No, signor,” answered Lodovico quickly. “I go not on that side Tiber.”

“Addio, then,” said Teresa, and there was meaning in the word, as in a lid set down on a pot.

“When wilt thou return home, Teresa mia?” he asked.

“When I have done mine errand, Lodovico.”

They went on. Teresa’s face had altered; the calm remained, but it was now the calm of a shut door. The sounds of Rome—fiddles from a courtyard, boys crying fruit, the slap of sandals on stone—seemed to leave her untouched. Gerard, who could not keep the world out of his senses, felt the city’s noise press closer, and wished, in spite of himself, for the simple hush of a Dutch field where wind and birds do the speaking.

Appia Claudia, the tailor, proved at least merciful: she did not send them over Tiber again, only a hundred yards down the street to Lucretia of the glove-shop.

“She it is,” said Appia, half amused, half puzzled, “that wanteth a writer; but what for, I cannot conceive.”

Lucretia was a little merry dame, with quick eyes and quicker hands. The shop was hung with gloves like pale fruit—kid as soft as cream, tanned leather smelling of oak-bark and smoke, and new-dyed pairs whose colour still breathed pungently: madder-red, walnut-brown, saffron, and the bluish black that catches the light like a raven’s wing. The air within was thick with that intimate perfume of leather, oil, and the faint sweetness of starch.

She received them heartily enough and laughed at the notion.

“A writer? I want no writer. I keep all my accounts in my head. ’Twas for my confessor, Father Colonna. He is mad after them.”

“I have heard of his excellency,” said Teresa.

“Who hath not?” Lucretia tossed her chin. “But, good dame, he is a friar; he hath made vow of poverty. I cannot let the young man write and not be paid. He saved my child at sea.”

“Did he now?” Lucretia gave Gerard an approving glance, as if measuring a roast before buying. “Well, make thy mind easy. A Colonna never wanteth for money. The good father hath but to say the word, and the princes of his race will pour a thousand crowns into his lap. And such a confessor! the best in Rome. His head is leagues and leagues away all the while; he never heedeth what thou sayest. I think no more of confessing my sins to him than of telling them to that wall.”

Teresa waited, patient as a woman who has watched bread rise slowly and knows haste ruins it. Lucretia, delighted with her own talk, went on, seasoning her tale with relish.

“Once, to try him, I confessed—along with the rest—how I had killed my lodger’s little girl and baked her in a pie. A fine pie too, mind you—crust browned, edges pinched fair as a collar, steam smelling o’ pepper and sweet herbs. Well, when my voice left off, he started out of his dream and mustered up a gloom. ‘My erring sister,’ saith he, ‘say three Paternosters and three Ave Marias kneeling, and eat no butter nor eggs next Wednesday, and pax vobiscum!’ And off he went with his hands behind him, looking as if there were no such thing as me in the world.”

Teresa, without a change of brow, brought her back as one brings a pot to the fire again.

“Would you be so kind as go with this good youth to the friar and speak for him?”

“Alack! how can I leave my shop?” cried Lucretia. “And what need? His door is aye open to writers and painters and scholars—and all such cattle. Why, one day he would not receive the Duke d’Urbino, because a learned Greek was closeted with him; the friar’s head and his so close together over a dusty parchment new come from Greece, as you could put one cowl over the pair. His wench Onesta told me. She mostly looks in here for a chat when she goeth an errand.”

“This is the man for thee, my friend,” said Teresa, and there was a warmth under the gravity.

“All thou hast to do,” continued Lucretia, “is go to his lodgings—my boy shall show you—and tell Onesta you come from me, and you are a writer, and she will take you up to him. If you put a piece of silver in the wench’s hand, ’twill do you no harm: that standeth to reason.”

“I have silver,” said Teresa promptly.

“But stay,” said Lucretia, and her tone sharpened like a knife finding bone. “Mind one thing. What the young man saith he can do, that he must be able to do, or let him shun the good friar like poison. He is a very wild beast against all bunglers. ’Twas but t’other day one brought him an ill-carved crucifix. ‘Is this how you present Salvator Mundi?’ saith he, ‘who died for you in mortal agony; and you go and grudge him careful work. This slovenly gimcrack—a crucifix? But that it is a crucifix of some sort, and I am a holy man, I’d dust thy jacket with thy crucifix.’ Onesta heard every word through the key-hole; so mind.”

“Have no fears, madama,” said Teresa loftily, as if the matter were already judged. “I will answer for his ability; he saved my child.”

Gerard, who could not follow her leap from courage at sea to neatness of hand, felt his confidence ebb.

He begged a respite. He would rather not go to the friar to-day: would not to-morrow do as well?

“Here is a coward for ye,” cried Lucretia.

“No, he is not a coward,” said Teresa, and for the first time her quiet caught fire; “he is modest.”

“I am afraid of this high-born, fastidious friar,” Gerard confessed, ashamed and honest together. “Consider he hath seen the handiwork of all the writers in Italy, dear dame Teresa. If you would but let me prepare a better piece of work than yet I have done, then to-morrow I will face him with it.”

“I consent,” said Teresa, and the flame went out as quickly as it had risen.

They walked home together. The city smelled now of supper beginning—onion frying in oil, fish newly gutted by the river, sour wine in cups, bread cracked open with warm hands. Voices rose and fell; a lute was tried and tuned; a quarrel started and ended in laughter. Gerard heard it all as one hears water running, and it soothed him; yet beneath it he thought of the friar’s “wild beast” temper and of his own trembling hand.

Not far from his lodging was a shop that sold vellum. In the window lay a skin, white as milk, with a faint sheen like the inside of a shell. It seemed to drink the late light and give it back. Gerard’s eye rested on it; his throat tightened; he sighed and hurried on, knowing he could not pay.

But as he went, his mind—always hungry, always contriving—chose another way. He parted from Teresa at his own door, then ran upstairs and drew from his bundle the bond he had carried from Sevenbergen as if it were a relic and a burden both. He laid it on the table with a sigh.

He set out his little chemicals to erase old writing—materials that smelled acrid and sour, like sharp fruit turning. Yet before he destroyed anything, he forced himself—once, and for the last time—to look hard at the crabbed hand upon the parchment. He loathed bad writing as some men loathe rancid butter; it offended his whole sense of order. Still he deciphered, slowly, wincing at each detestable contraction.

It appeared Ghysbrecht Van Swieten was to advance money to Floris Brandt on a piece of land, and repay himself out of the rent.

At that Gerard stopped, as if the parchment had spoken. It would be imprudent—improper—to destroy such a deed. Instead he vowed to decipher every word at leisure, and keep it safe.

He went downstairs resolved to buy a small piece of vellum with his half of the card-money, and so do his sample honorably. But at the bottom of the stairs he found his landlady and Teresa in talk, their heads close as if over a bowl.

At sight of him the landlady cried, triumphantly, “Here he is. You are caught, donna mia. See what she hath bought you?” And she whipped from under her apron the very skin of vellum Gerard had coveted.

His breath left him.

“Why, dame! why, donna Teresa!” He could not find words enough for the pleasure that flooded him, warm as broth after fasting. “Dear donna Teresa, there is not a skin in all Rome like it. However came you to hit on this one? ’Tis glamour.”

“Alas, dear boy,” said Teresa simply, “did not thine eye rest on it with desire? and didst thou not sigh in turning away from it? And was it for Teresa to let thee want the thing after that?”

“What sagacity! what goodness!” He took it as if it were bread in a famine. “Oh, dame, I never thought I should possess this. What did you pay for it?”

“I forget.” And already she was withdrawing, as if gifts were nothing and gratitude a burden. “Addio, Fiammina. Addio, Ser Gerard. Be happy; be prosperous, as you are good.”

She glided away while Gerard stood hesitating—half longing to press money on her, half knowing money would insult the stateliness of her charity.

The next day, in the afternoon, he went to Lucretia, and her boy led him to Fra Colonna’s lodgings. Gerard had his vellum page safe, like a fresh loaf wrapped against dust. He fed Onesta with the silver as Lucretia had advised; the coin clicked softly in her palm, and she smiled, practical as any market-woman weighing figs.

She took him up to the friar.

Gerard entered with a heart that beat so loudly he feared it would be heard above the house’s own sounds—the faint scrape of quills, the shifting of paper, the creak of a chest-lid, a distant chant passing like wind through a cloister.

The room was large, and strewed and heaped with objects of art, antiquity, and learning lying about in rich profusion and confusion: manuscripts piled like loaves cooling after baking, pictures leaned face to wall, carvings in wood and ivory, musical instruments with their bellies catching light. The place had its own smell too—dust, ink, old glue, the dry sweetness of parchment, and a faint musk from stored fabrics and leather bindings—like a pantry of memory where everything is kept but nothing is labelled in a tongue the living speak.

In the midst of this glorious chaos sat the friar, poring intently over an Arabian manuscript. He looked up a little peevishly at the interruption.

Onesta whispered in his ear.

“Very well,” said he. “Let him be seated. Stay; young man, show me how you write?” And he threw Gerard a piece of paper and pointed to an inkhorn.

“So please you, reverend father,” Gerard said, his mouth dry, “my hand it trembleth too much at this moment; but last night I wrote a vellum page of Greek, and the Latin version by its side, to show the various character.”

“Show it me.”

Gerard brought the work to him in fear and trembling, and then stood heart-sick, awaiting sentence as a cook waits while a great lord tastes.

When the verdict came, it staggered him; for the verdict was not words at all, but a Dominican falling on his neck.

The next day an event took place in Holland, the effect of which on Gerard’s destiny no mortal then—nor even my intelligent reader now—could, I think, foresee.

Marched up to Eli’s door a pageant brave to the eye of sense, and to the vulgar judgment noble, but to the philosophic pitiable more or less. It looked one animal, a centaur; but on severe analysis proved two. The human half was sadly bedizened with those two metals to clothe his carcass with which and line his pouch man has now and then disposed of his soul. Yet the horse was the vainer brute of the two, far worse beflounced, bebonneted, and bemantled than any fair lady regnante crinolina; for the man, under the colour of a warming-pan, retained Nature’s outline—subaudi equum! Scarce a pennyweight of honest horse-flesh was to be seen. Great sheaths of white linen tipped with silver and blue swallowed the ears; stiff gorgeous cloths swaddled the body down to the ground, save where room was left in front to mince; the tail—dear to memory, no doubt—was lost to sight, tucked in Heaven knows how. Only the eyes shone out like goggles through holes in that wall of haberdashery, and the little front hoofs peeped in and out like rats.

Yet did this compound, gorgeous and irrational, represent power—absolute power. It came straight from a tournament at the Duke’s court, which being on a progress lay last night at a neighbouring town—to execute the behests of royalty.

“What ho!” cried the upper half; and on Eli emerging with his wife behind him, saluted them. “Peace be with you, good people. Rejoice! I am come for your dwarf.”

Eli looked amazed and said nothing. But Catherine screamed over his shoulder, “You have mistook your road, good man; here abides no dwarf.”

“Nay, wife,” said Eli, slow and grave, “he means our Giles, who is somewhat small of stature. Why gainsay what gainsayed may not be?”

“Ay!” cried the pageant. “That is he, and discourseth like the big taber.”

“His breast is sound for that matter,” said Catherine sharply.

“And prompt with his fists though at long odds.”

“Else how would the poor thing keep his head in such a world as this?”

“’Tis well said, dame,” returned the emissary. “Art as ready with thy weapon as he; art his mother, likely. So bring him forth—and that presently. See, they lead a stunted mule for him. The Duke hath need of him, sore need. We are clean out o’ dwarven and tiger-cats, which may not be, whiles earth them yieldeth. Our last hop o’ my thumb tumbled down the well t’other day.”

“And think you I’ll let my darling go to such an ill-guided house as you,” cried Catherine, “where the reckless trollops o’ servants close not the well mouth, but leave it open to trap innocents, like wolven?”

The representative of autocracy lost patience at this unwonted opposition. He set his stern look on her and bade her bethink which was better: “to have your abortion at court fed like a bishop and put on like a prince, or to have all your heads stricken off and borne on poles, with the bellman crying, ‘Behold the heads of hardy rebels, which having by good luck a misbegotten son did traitorously grudge him to the Duke, who is the true father of all his folk, little or mickle!’”

“Nay,” said Eli sadly, “miscall us not. We be true folk, and neither rebels nor traitors. But ’tis sudden, and the poor lad is our true flesh and blood, and hath of late given proof of more sense than heretofore.”

“Avails not threatening our lives,” whimpered Catherine; “we grudge him not to the Duke; but in sooth he cannot go—his linen is all in holes. So there is an end.”

But the male mind resisted the crusher. “Think you the Duke will not find linen—and cloth of gold to boot? None so brave, none so affected, at court as our monsters, big or wee.”

How long the dispute might have lasted, before the iron arguments of despotism achieved the inevitable victory, I know not; but it was cut short by a party neither disputant had deigned to consult. The bone of contention walked out of the house and sided with monarchy.

“If my folk are mad, I am not!” Giles roared. “I’ll go with you—and on the instant.”

At this Catherine set up a piteous cry. She saw another of her brood escaping from under her wing into some unknown element. Giles was not quite insensible to her distress, so simple yet so eloquent.

“Nay, take not on, mother!” he said. “Why, ’tis a godsend. And I am sick of this, ever since Gerard left it.”

“Ah, cruel Giles!” she sobbed. “Should ye not rather say she is bereaved of Gerard: the more need of you to stay aside her and comfort her.”

“Oh! I am not going to Rome. Not such a fool. I shall never be farther than Rotterdam; and I’ll often come and see you; and if I like not the place, who shall keep me there? Not all the dukes in Christendom.”

“Good sense lies in little bulk,” said the emissary approvingly. “Therefore, Master Giles, buss the old folk, and thank them for misbegetting of thee; and ho! you—bring hither his mule.”

One of the retinue brought up the dwarf mule. Giles refused it with scorn; and being asked the reason, said it was not just.

“What! would ye throw all into one scale? Put muckle to muckle, and little to wee! Besides, I hate and scorn small things. I’ll go on the highest horse here—or not at all.”

The pursuivant eyed him attentively a moment, then adopted a courteous manner. “I shall study your will in all things reasonable. (Dismount, Eric; yours is the highest horse.) And if you would halt in the town an hour or so while you bid them farewell, say but the word, and your pleasure shall be my delight.”

Giles reflected. “Master,” said he, “if we wait a month, ’twill be still the same. My mother is a good soul, but her body is bigger than her spirit. We shall not part without a tear or two, and the quicker ’tis done the fewer; so bring yon horse to me.”

Catherine threw her apron over her face and sobbed.

The high horse was brought, and Giles was for swarming up his tail like a rope; but one of the servants cried out hastily, “Forbear, for he kicketh.”

“I’ll kick him,” said Giles. “Bring him close beneath this window, and I’ll learn you all how to mount a horse which kicketh, and will not be clomb by the tail, the staircase of a horse.”

He dashed into the house, and almost immediately reappeared at an upper window with a rope in his hand. He fastened an end somehow, and holding the other descended as swift and smooth as an oiled thunderbolt in a groove, and lighted astride the high horse as unperceived by the animal as a fly settling on him.

The official lifted his hands to heaven in mawkish admiration. “I have gotten a pearl,” thought he. “And wow but this will be a good day’s work for me.”

“Come, father, come, mother—buss me and bless me—and off I go.”

Eli gave him his blessing and bade him be honest and true, and a credit to his folk. Catherine could not speak, but clung to him with many sobs and embraces; and even through the mist of tears her eye detected in a moment the little rent in his sleeve he had made getting out of window. She whipped out her needle and mended it then and there; her tears fell on his arm the while, unheeded—except by those unfleshly eyes, with which they say the very air is thronged.

So the dwarf mounted the high horse and rode away complacent, while the old hand laid the court butter on his back with a trowel. Little recked Perpusillus of two poor silly females that sat by the bereaved hearth, rocking themselves and weeping and discussing all his virtues and how his mind had opened lately—blind as two beetles to his faults—who rode away from them jocund and bold:

Ingentes animos angusto pectore versans.

Arrived at court he speedily became a great favourite. One strange propensity of his electrified the palace; but on account of his small size, and for variety’s sake, and as a monster, he was indulged on it. In a word, he was let speak the truth.

It is an unpopular thing.

He made it an intolerable one.

Bawled it.

Happy is the man, they said in Rome, who has two stout cables to haul himself up by: merit, and women. Gerard had only the first, and even that he used as a rope-ladder to climb back—always back—to one plain room in the North where Margaret’s hands moved about bread and linen, and where his name, spoken in her own homely tongue, meant more than any Latin flourish.

Yet Rome, that day, meant ink, parchment, and the hum of minds sharpening themselves on dead syllables as if on whetstones.

Fra Colonna—Francesco of Florence, Dominican by habit and pagan at heart—moved through the city as through a gallery. He loved antiquity the way a careful cook loves old sourdough: not as a relic, but as a living ferment that, once fed, lifts everything. He had wandered the East and come home freighted with manuscripts the way a merchant comes home with sacks of spice—Greek and Latin, Hebrew and Syriac, each language a different aroma rising when you break the seal. Coins, inscriptions, broken marbles: to him they were all ingredients, and he distrusted the stories Rome told about itself when the stones told him otherwise.

In religion he had the friar’s robe, and in thought the philosopher’s shrug. Ceremonies were for the crowd, he would say with a smile; but if he discovered a rite had been borrowed from the ancients, then he would handle it with an odd tenderness—like a man who scorns sweetmeats until he learns the recipe is older than Christendom.

He had taken Gerard, with his clear hand and grave patience, as one takes in a rare tool. He praised him everywhere—too everywhere—until one morning he began, without warning, to pry Gerard out of his own contentment.

“Princes want you,” he announced, as if reporting the weather.

“But I am so happy with you, father,” Gerard said, and meant it; the convent quiet, the steady labour, the sense that each line he traced was a rung homeward.

“Fiddlestick about being happy with me,” snapped the friar. “You must not be happy; you must be a man of the world. The grand lesson I impress on the young is—be a man of the world. Now these Montesini can pay you thrice what I can, and they shall too—by Jupiter.”

And with that pagan oath—so cheerfully lodged in a Dominican mouth—Fra Colonna clapped a price on Gerard’s pen that made even noble purses blink. They agreed at once. In those years a fair copy of a Greek book was dearer than the thoughts in it; for the printing press was still unborn, and every page had to be coaxed into being as patiently as a cheese must be turned and rubbed and guarded from spoil.

Three hundred crowns Gerard earned for Aristotle on rhetoric alone. He watched the number as he watched his letters: carefully, without allowing his heart to dance. A vain man might have grown drunk on it. Gerard, Dutch to the backbone, could taste the steel beneath Rome’s velvet. The great, he saw, were lavish as long as their fancy held; when it turned, their hand closed like a trap. So he did not presume; he bent, and wrote, and stored each crown as if it were a grain of wheat meant for winter.

Fra Colonna’s pushing and praising carried him into rooms where his old life would have seemed a fable. One day he found himself seated—far down the length, a mile from the head if truth be told—at the table of Cardinal Bessarion, that Greek-born prince of the Church whose very presence smelled faintly of libraries: vellum warmed by hands, cedar chests, wax, dust that had slept for centuries.

Gerard, whose senses were always awake, saw as much as he ate. Roast pheasants came in dressed as if they had only just been snatched from a coppice, their feathers returned to them in proud disarray—an artful lie, a theatre of the spit. There were chickens cooked in bottles, the glass clouded with their own steam; when they were poured out they fell to pieces, so tender they might have been fruit. The air held layered smells: browned fat, sharp herbs bruised in the mortar, citrus peel pricked over sweetness.

But the strangest marvel to Gerard was not the meat. It was linen.

Napkins, finer than any he had touched, lay folded into cocked hats and birds’ wings and fans, like white sculptures waiting to be used and ruined. This, more than cardinal and peacock-feathers, nearly overturned his composure; the domestic made ceremonial, the simplest cloth turned into a language of display.

After the savouries came the miracle of more tables. The boards were lifted away in pieces, and beneath each was another table already laid, as if the feast were a book with hidden pages. Sweetmeats appeared—pastilles, candied fruits, sugared almonds glistening like polished stones. The ladies fell upon them with bright fingers and laughter, gormandizing without shame; the gentlemen watched with that reasonable suspicion a man gives anything that looks too pretty to be safe.

Gerard, remembering travellers’ tales, leaned to Fra Colonna. “But, dear father,” he whispered, “I see not the bifurcal daggers with which men say his excellency armeth the left hand of a man.”

“Nay,” said the friar, with scorn that was almost affectionate, “’tis Cardinal Orsini invented that peevish instrument for his guests to fumble their meat withal. One, being in haste, did skewer his tongue to his palate with it, I hear. O tempora, O mores! The ancients, reclining godlike at their feasts, how had they spurned such pedantries.”

When the ladies had done their sweet assault, the tables vanished again. Guests were set in a row against the wall, as if the meal had been only the prologue. Two ecclesiastics entered with lutes, ducking and scraping, and knelt at the cardinal’s feet. They sang the service of the day—music poured low and careful, the notes hovering in the room like incense. Gerard listened not only with devotion but with a craftsman’s ear: how the sound settled, how it softened the chatter, how the space itself seemed kinder when it was filled with ordered harmony and not with the clatter of forks, the scrape of stools, the barking of men. He thought, fleetingly, how cities could crush the mind by noise, how a single well-shaped melody could restore breath. Then the singers withdrew with deep obeisance; the cardinal touched his skull-cap in reply, as curtly as a soldier tipping his hat; the company dispersed. Gerard went away with the odd knowledge that he had dined with a cardinal and with a man who had thrice come near the papacy—and had been more astonished by folded linen than by any mitre.

Greater honour, and stranger, followed.

One morning Cardinal Bessarion sent for him, praised the beauty of his hand, and took him in his coach to the Vatican. They climbed a private stair into a small luxurious room with a great oriel window that caught the light like a net. Everything there was made for writing: sloping frames, knives for trimming quills, pumice, rulers, inkstands rich outside like reliquaries.

The cardinal whispered to a courtier; presently the Pope’s private secretary entered carrying a glorious grimy old manuscript of Plutarch’s Lives. The book looked as if it had travelled farther than armies—its skin stained with age, its leaves smelling of dust, oil, and the old animal life of parchment. When it was opened, a faint breath rose—mould and leather, a bitter-sweetness like cellars where apples have been stored too long.

Soon Gerard sat alone, charged with copying it for the Holy Father’s own use. Awe chilled him; delight warmed him through. His holiness would handle his work; his holiness would read his letters. For a moment Gerard felt himself not merely a man earning passage money, but a hand in the long chain of transmission—one more link forged in silence.

Yet the papal ink, when he tried it, was vile: thin, sour, prone to bleed. Rome could gild an inkstand and neglect the ink within, as it could dress pheasants in feathers and hide the spit’s brutality. Gerard took out his own inkhorn—a dirty little thing he always carried—and with it his home-made ink, black and honest, that bit the page and stayed. He knelt and prayed for a firm and skilful hand, and then began.

The room had one wall nearly swallowed by a massive curtain, divided in the centre but overlapping in deep folds. It stood there like a closed mouth. At first he worked without thinking of it, the steady scrape of his pen the only sound besides the far-off murmur of the Vatican—feet on stone, a door shutting, a faint clink of arms.

After a while his eyes began to stray. The curtain drew him, not with desire so much as with that dreadful curiosity that creeps upon a man when he is alone with power nearby. He resisted. The impulse returned. It thickened, like smoke in the mind. At last it overpowered him.

He laid Plutarch aside, crossed the matted floor on quiet feet, and with two fingers gathered the folds, as gently as one lifts the lid of a pot to see if the broth boils. He put his nose to the chink—and ran it straight against cold steel.

A halberd. Then another. Two soldiers stood beyond, armed cap-à-pie, their glittering weapons crossed in a triangle. In that instant he also caught the soft murmur of voices, and saw a knot of figures cringing before some hidden presence deeper within.

He drew back swiftly, heart hammering. He did not try again. But the curtain remained in his mind like a line of untranslatable text: it promised meaning, withheld it, and reminded him that in Rome the most important things were often spoken behind fabric.

And as if to underline it, every hour or so an ecclesiastic would peep in, let his eyes run over Gerard and the page, chill the room with suspicion, and vanish. The visits were wordless and mechanical, like the ticking of a clock that exists only to measure obedience.

The next day brought a different kind of intrusion.

A gentleman richly armed burst in with a soldier’s energy and a courtier’s insolence. He stared at Gerard as if at a curious instrument.

“What is toward here?” he demanded.

Gerard, pen poised, answered mildly that he was writing out Plutarch, with the help of the saints.

The newcomer frowned. He did not know this Plutarch, he said, as if that were Plutarch’s fault.

Gerard explained, as politely as possible, the circumstances of time and space that had deprived the Signor Plutarch of the advantage of the gentleman’s acquaintance.

“Oh! one of those old dead Greeks they keep such a coil about,” the man said, and waved his hand as if brushing away dust.

“Ay, signor,” Gerard replied. “One of them, who, being dead, yet live.”

“I understand you not,” said the noble, with all the dignity of ignorance. “What did the old fellow write? Love stories?” His eyes brightened. “Merry tales, like Boccaccio.”

“Nay,” said Gerard. “Lives of heroes and sages.”

“Soldiers and popes?”

“Soldiers and princes.”

The man’s mood softened into curiosity. “Wilt read me of them some day?”

“And willingly, signor. But what would they say who employ me, were I to break off work?”

“Oh, never heed that,” cried the other. “Know you not who I am? I am Jacques Bonaventura, nephew to his holiness the Pope, and captain of his guards. And I came here to look after my fellows. I trow they have turned them out of their room for you.”

And with that he bounced away again, leaving behind him a faint jingle of metal and the disturbed air of authority.

From that day Signor Bonaventura fell into the habit of running in upon Gerard. Perhaps the solitude of guarding secrets made him hunger for a living voice; perhaps the quiet of the scribe’s room was a relief from the louder court. He chattered of trifles while Gerard wrote of men who had founded kingdoms and conquered themselves. The contrast amused Gerard: the eternal set down in ink while the momentary strutted and sighed beside it.

One day Bonaventura came in changed, his face overcast, his bravado cracked. He flung himself into a chair.

“Ah, traitress! traitress!” he cried.

Gerard asked gently what had befallen him.

“Traitress! traitress!” was all the answer.

So Gerard returned to Plutarch, as a man returns to kneading when the kitchen quarrels; work, at least, obeys the hands.

At last Bonaventura spoke again, with a kind of plea beneath his pride. “I am melancholy; and for our Lady’s sake read me a story out of Ser Plutarcho, to soothe my bile. In all that Greek is there nought about lovers betrayed?”

Gerard turned the leaves and read to him the life of Alexander. The words—translated through Gerard’s careful Latin—fell into the room like measured steps. Bonaventura’s sorrow shifted shape as he listened; the tale of conquest and discipline stirred him like a trumpet heard at dawn across a field.

He rose, paced, clenched his hands, then came back in sudden heat and threw his arms about Gerard, half laughing, half fierce. He vowed to shun “soft delights,” that bed of nettles, and to follow glory.

Gerard smiled, moved and a little sad. The young man’s pain had not been cured; it had only been seasoned into another flavour, as sour wine can be spiced and served as something grand.

And Gerard—who had eaten of Rome’s dainties and still longed most for Margaret’s plain table—felt himself, for a time, almost happy. His hand was honoured; gold accumulated; in a year or two he would go by sea to Holland with enough to begin. He pictured Bruges, or Antwerp, or dear Augsburg—some city where he and Margaret might set up together, work honestly, live in peace, and let the days circle like seasons: baking, planting, harvest, winter fires, children’s voices in the house, and the old dialect spoken without shame.

His heart did not stray one instant from her.

Nor, in his prosperity, did he forget poor Pietro. He took Fra Colonna to see Pietro’s painting. The friar inspected it with a severe face and a long silence; then, suddenly softened, he flung his arms about the artist’s neck. He carried the picture to one of the Colonnas, who paid a noble price. Pietro, lifted by that single act as by a tide, descended from his garret to the first floor and began to live like a gentleman.

Gerard stayed where he was, in his own high room, for he measured comfort by a different rule. To increase his expenses would be to postpone his return to Margaret; and luxury, to him, had no savour when it stood between him and love.

Jacques Bonaventura introduced him to other gay young fellows, idle as cats in sunshine, sharp as knives in the dark. They took a liking to Gerard’s steady humour and tried to draw him into their pleasures—and, with them, into vice and lavish spending. Gerard begged humbly to be excused. He escaped that snare by sheer singleness of purpose.

But even as he wrote the immortal lives, even as he counted his crowns like saved seeds, a greater temptation waited behind the curtain of his days, folded and overlapping like the heavy drapery in the Vatican—something armed, watched, and not meant for such as him.

Fra Colonna had the freedom of the Pope’s library, and by that freedom Gerard had, as it were, a key to Rome itself. Many a day, when the ink in the Vatican had dried upon their labours, the friar would shut a manuscript with the flat of his hand, and the two would go out together, walking where the streets were narrow, and the stones underfoot were a patchwork of the living and the dead.

To Gerard, whose eye could never keep itself from beauty, Rome came upon him like a feast brought in course after course: churches like vast loaves broken open to show gold within; palaces glittering as if sugared; ruins that had the savour of antiquity, dry and wholesome as old wine. The city’s very air seemed seasoned—smoke from braziers, damp from fountains, incense from open doors; and always, underneath, the hum and clink of a populous place: sandals and wheels, bells, a snatch of chant, a vendor’s cry. It was a music that fed the spirit as broth feeds the body.

The friar granted him the ruins—granted them as a man grants bread to the hungry—yet he dashed cold water on the rest.

“This place Rome?” said he. “It is but the tomb of mighty Rome.”

And, as if he were a cook turning the lid off a pot to show what lies beneath, he made Gerard look down—down through the present into the buried past. Here, twenty or thirty feet of a triumphal arch lay sunk as if the earth had swallowed it. There, a modern street ran right over what had been a palace; and columns that once bore roofs and emperors’ dreams now showed only their crowns, like bones through thin soil. He pointed with a dry finger, and his voice took that relish it always had when he could season a lesson with a sharpness from antiquity.

“I tell thee this village they call Rome is but as one of those swallows’ nests ye shall see built on the eaves of a decayed abbey.”

“Old Rome must indeed have been fair then,” said Gerard, with the simple reverence of a man who feels greatness as he feels warm bread in the hand.

“Judge for thyself, my son. Thou seest the great sewer, the work of the Romans in their very childhood, and it shall outlast Vesuvius. Thou seest the fragments of the Temple of Peace. How wouldst thou look couldst thou see also the Capitol with its five-and-twenty temples? Note this Monte Savello: what is it, an it please you, but the ruins of the ancient theatre of Marcellus? And as for Testacio—one of the highest hills in modern Rome—it is but an ancient dust heap; the women of old Rome flung their broken pots and pans there, and lo—a mountain.”

Then, as if the sound of Latin itself were a savour he could not be without, he added, “Ex pede Herculem; ex ungue leonem.”

Gerard listened, as he always did, with the respect due to learning; but when the friar, by a glide of words, began to hint that the moral greatness of those heathen must have matched their stone and their works, Gerard’s heart rose against it.

“Has then the world lost by Christ His coming?” said he; and he blushed for the boldness of it, for he knew he spoke to a benefactor.

“Saints forbid!” cried Fra Colonna. “‘Twere heresy to say so.”

Yet the friar had an art of conceding with the front of his face, and retreating with the rest of him by a back stair of subtlety; and while he fenced and circled, they came to a church where a knot of folk stood in the porch. Within, a demon was being exorcised.

Now Fra Colonna had a certain little moan—half pity, half disdain—that he would utter when men brought him things Zeno or Epicurus would not have swallowed, and called them fact. It was a sound that belonged as much to him as his thin hand and his quick, keen eye. He moaned now.

“Then come away.”

“Nay, father, prithee! prithee!” said Gerard, his youth eager for marvels as for spices he had never tasted. “I ne’er saw a divell cast out.”

The friar went in with him, but first gave such a shrug as would have shaken dust from a cassock.

Within, they found the demoniac forced down on his knees before the altar. A scarf was tied round his neck, and by it the priest held him as one holds a dog in a chain. There were not many present; fame had whispered that the last demon cast out in that place went no farther than into one of the company—as a cony ferreted from one burrow runs to the next.

When Gerard and the friar drew near, the priest seemed to count the spectators sufficient, and began as a man begins a task he has done often and with pride.

He faced the demoniac, breviary in hand, and set himself to learn the name of the guest within.

“Come out, Ashtaroth. Oho! it is not you then. Come out, Belial. Come out, Tatzi. Come out, Eza. No; he trembles not. Come out, Azymoth. Come out, Feriander. Come out, Foletho. Come out, Astyma. Come out, Nebul. Aha! what, have I found ye? ’Tis thou, thou reptile; at thine old tricks. Let us pray!”

And he prayed with a zeal that would have been better bestowed upon bread for the hungry, thought Gerard, had he been free to judge; yet the sound of the prayer filled the vaulting as steam fills a kitchen.

“Oh, Lord, we pray thee to drive the foul fiend Nebul out of this thy creature: out of his hair, and his eyes, out of his nose, out of his mouth, out of his ears, out of his gums, out of his teeth, out of his shoulders, out of his arms, legs, loins, stomach, bowels, thighs, knees, calves, feet, ankles, finger-nails, toe-nails, and soul. Amen.”

Then, rising, the priest turned with a genial quietness to the little company. “Gentles, we have here as obstinate a divell as you may see in a summer day.” And facing the patient again, he spoke with great rigour, now to the man, now to the fiend; and through that one mouth came two sorts of answer—now hatred of the holy names, now complaint of pains within.

But it was the priest himself who first muddled victim and culprit in the eyes of the onlookers. He fell upon the poor wretch as if beating the devil could bruise the sin out of him: cuffed him soundly, kicked him, spat in his face again and again. He took a candle, lit it, turned it down, and burned it till it scorched his own fingers, then dropped it hastily. He fetched the custodial and showed the Corpus Domini. He burned another candle, more wary. At last he spoke civilly to the demoniac in his human character, dismissed him, and received the compliments of the company as if he had carved a roast and served it well.

“Good father,” said Gerard, when they were out, “how you have their names by heart. Our northern priests have no such exquisite knowledge of the hellish squadrons.”

“Ay, young man,” said the priest, overhearing and pleased, “here we know all their names, and eke their ways, the reptiles. This Nebul is a bitter hard one to hunt out.”

And he told them, affably, of feats he had done; ending with yesterday’s triumph, when he had driven a great hulking fiend out of a woman by her mouth, leaving nails and pins and a tuft of his own hair behind, and crying in anguish, “’Tis not thou that conquers me. See that stone on the window sill. Know that the angel Gabriel coming down to earth once lighted on that stone: ’tis that has done my business.”

Fra Colonna moaned his small moan. “And you believed him?”

“Certes! who but an infidel has discredited a revelation so precise?”

“What, believe the father of lies? That is pushing credulity beyond the age.”

“Oh, a liar does not always lie.”

“Ay doth he whenever he tells an improbable story to begin, and shows you a holy relic; arms you against the Satanic host. Fiends (if any) be not so simple. Shouldst have answered him out of antiquity—Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes. Some blackguard chopped his wife’s head off on that stone, young man; you take my word for it.” And, having given that, he hurried Gerard away.

“Alack, father,” said Gerard, troubled, “I fear you abashed the good priest.”

“Ay, by Pollux,” said the friar, with a chuckle that rang like a dry nut cracked between teeth. “I blistered him with a single touch of Socratic interrogation. What modern can parry the weapons of antiquity?”

One afternoon, when Gerard had finished his day’s work, a fine lackey came and demanded his attendance at the Palace Cesarini. Gerard followed, and was ushered into a noble apartment, where a girl sat working tapestry. She rose, went out, and said she would let her mistress know.

A full hour Gerard cooled his heels there, listening to the palace-sounds—soft steps, a far-off laugh, a door murmuring shut; and beneath all, the faint city-noise like the sea heard through walls. At last he began to fret. These nobles thought nothing of a poor fellow’s time. Yet just as he was gathering himself to slip away, the door opened, and a superb beauty entered, followed by two maids.

It was the young princess of the house of Cesarini. She came in talking loudly and haughtily to her dependents; but at sight of Gerard her voice dropped into a tone as sweet as it was sudden.

“Are you the writer, messer?”

“I am, Signora.”

“’Tis well.”

She seated herself on a chair so high it was almost a throne. Gerard and her maids remained standing until she bade him.

“What is your name, good youth?”

“Gerard, signora.”

“Gerard?” she cried. “Body of Bacchus! is that the name of a human creature?”

“It is a Dutch name, signora. I was born at Tergou, in Holland.”

“A harsh name, girls, for so well-favoured a youth; what say you?”

The maids agreed with an alacrity that showed their training.

“What did I send for him for?” said the lady, with lofty languor, as if even her own wishes were beneath her memory. “Ah, I remember. Be seated, Ser Gerardo, and write me a letter to Ercole Orsini, my lover; at least he says so.”

Gerard sat, drew forth paper and ink, and looked up, waiting as a scribe waits for dictation.

She, enthroned, looked down at him, eyes inquisitive as a cat’s.

“Well, Gerardo.”

“I am ready, your excellence.”

“Write, then.”

“I but await the words.”

“And who, think you, is to provide them?”

“Who but your grace, whose letter it is to be?”

“Gramercy! what, you writers, find you not the words? What avails your art without the words? I doubt you are an impostor, Gerardo.”

“Nay, Signora, I am none. I might make shift to put your highness’s speech into grammar, as well as writing. But I cannot interpret your silence. Therefore speak what is in your heart, and I will empaper it before your eyes.”

“But there is nothing in my heart. And sometimes I think I have got no heart.”

“What is in your mind, then?”

“But there is nothing in my mind; nor my head neither.”

“Then why write at all?”

“Why, indeed?” cried she, and her lip curled with amusement. “That is the first word of sense either you or I have spoken, Gerardo. Pestilence seize him! why writeth he not first? then I could say nay to this, and ay to that, withouten headache. Also is it a lady’s part to say the first word?”

“No, signora,” said Gerard. “The last.”

“It is well spoken, Gerardo. Ha! ha! Shalt have a gold piece for thy wit. Give me my purse!”

And she paid him on the nail, in the frank medieval fashion. The weight of the gold warmed his palm; money never yet chilled zeal. Having got it so cheaply, he felt bound to pull her out of her difficulty if the wit of man might do it.

“Signorina,” said he, “these things are only hard because folk attempt too much, are artificial and labour phrases. Do but figure to yourself the signor you love—”

“I love him not.”

“Well, then, the signor you love not—seated at this table, and dict to me just what you would say to him.”

“Well, if he sat there, I should say, ‘Go away.’”

Gerard, who had lifted his pen ready to run, laid it down with a groan.

“And when he was gone,” put in Floretta, one of the maids, quick with mischief, “your highness would say, ‘Come back.’”

“Like enough, wench.” The princess frowned, and the maids fell silent in a breath. She turned her head away, and fell into deep thought, her noble chin resting on her white hand, half clenched. “Now silence, all, and let me think. He pestered me to write, and I promised; so mine honour is engaged. What lie shall I tell the Gerardo to tell the fool?”

She sat so still, so lovely, so statuesque, that for a moment the room seemed to hold its breath. Even the faint palace-sounds seemed to retreat, as if they too waited upon her thought. Gerard forgot letter and Orsini and all else. Here was art offered to him as a dish set down steaming. He took his paper and, with hungry delight, began to draw that exquisite profile—pure line, pure light, the curve of cheek and chin that made her beauty imperial even in repose.

He had nearly finished when the fair statue turned brusquely and caught him.

“Nay, Signora,” said he, a little peevishly, like a cook whose dish is jostled at the last moment, “for Heaven’s sake change not your posture—’twas perfect. See, you are nearly finished.”

Instantly all eyes were on the work, and all tongues active.

“How like! and done in a minute: nay, methinks her highness’s chin is not quite so.”

“Oh, a touch will make that right.”

“What a pity ’tis not coloured. I’m all for colours. Hang black and white! And her highness hath such a lovely skin. Take away her skin, and half her beauty is lost.”

“Peace,” said the princess, but her eyes had kindled. “Can you colour, Ser Gerardo?”

“Ay, signorina. I am a poor hand at oils; there shines my friend Pietro; but in this small way I can tint you to the life, if you have time to waste on such vanity.”

“Call you this vanity? And for time, it hangs on me like lead. Send for your colours now—quick, this moment—for love of all the saints.”

“Nay, signorina, I must prepare them. I could come at the same time.”

“So be it. And you, Floretta, see that he be admitted at all hours. Alack! Leave my head! leave my head!”

“Forgive me, Signora,” said Gerard. “I thought to prepare it at home to receive the colours. But I will leave it. And now let us despatch the letter.”

“What letter?” she asked, as if the very word were tasteless.

“To the Signor Orsini.”

“And shall I waste my time on such vanity as writing letters—and to that empty creature, to whom I am as indifferent as the moon? Nay, not indifferent, for I have just discovered my real sentiments. I hate him and despise him. Girls, I here forbid you once for all to mention that signor’s name to me again; else I’ll whip you till the blood comes. You know how I can lay on when I’m roused.”

“We do. We do,” murmured the maids, cowed and accustomed.

“Then provoke me not to it;” and her eye flashed daggers; then, in the same heartbeat, she turned to Gerard all honey. “Addio, il Gerardo.”

And Gerard bowed himself out of that velvet tiger’s den.

He came next day and coloured her; and the next he was set to make a portrait of her on a large scale; and then a full-length figure. He had to set apart two hours each afternoon for drawing and painting this princess, whose beauty and vanity were alike prodigious, and whose admirers were numerous enough to make her likeness a kind of coin. The thriving Gerard found there a new and fruitful source of income—income that, like a well-kept store of grain, made the thought of Margaret feel nearer and nearer.

It was Holy Thursday. No work that day. Fra Colonna and Gerard sat in a window and saw the religious processions pass beneath, like rivers of men flowing between stone banks. Their number, their ardour, the press of bodies and voices—chants rolling like waves, bells striking, the beat of hoofs and the shiver of armour—thrilled Gerard with devotion. It was as if the whole city, lately bent on earthly joys, had turned in one hour to a great act of piety; and the sound of it all—the city’s breath made audible—entered him, and moved him.

Presently the Pope came pacing majestically at the head of his cardinals: red hat, white cloak, a capuchin of red velvet, riding a lovely white Neapolitan barb, caparisoned with red velvet fringed and tasselled with gold. Behind him rode a hundred horsemen armed cap-a-pie, lances erected, butt-ends resting on their thighs. The cardinals went uncovered, all but one—de Medicis—who rode close and conversed with the Pope as with an equal. At every fifteen steps the Pope halted a single moment, blessed the people, and went on.

Gerard’s heart beat fast, as it does when one hears a great organ fill a church; and with it came, half-unbidden, his own homelier memories—bread broken at home, voices in his native tongue—things no Latin blessing could translate, and which yet rose in him at the sound of so many voices made one.

The two came down, and threading by-streets reached the portico of one of the seven churches. It was hung with black. Soon the Pope and cardinals, who had entered by another door, issued forth and stood with torches on the steps, separated by barriers from the people. Then a canon read a Latin Bull, excommunicating several by name, especially such princes as kept the Church out of any of her temporal possessions.

At the awful words, Gerard trembled, and the crowd with him, as when a sudden hush falls over a market and even the hawkers swallow their cries. But two cardinals laughed unreservedly the whole time, and their laughter, light and careless in the midst of thunder, jarred upon the ear like tin struck in a chapel.

When it was ended, the black cloth was removed, and a gay panoply was revealed; the Pope blessed the people, and ended by throwing his torch among them. Two cardinals did likewise. Instantly there was a scramble. The torches were fought for and torn in pieces with a devotion that paid for splinters with black eyes, bloody noses, and burnt fingers. In that hurtling, his holiness and suite withdrew in peace.

Then a cry rose; the crowd rushed to a square where a large open stage had been set. Several priests were upon it praying. They rose, and with great ceremony donned red gloves. One knelt, and with signs of the lowest reverence drew forth from a shrine a square frame like that of a mirror, and within it, as it were, the impression of a face.

It was the Verum icon—the true impression of our Saviour’s face, taken at the very moment of His most mortal agony for men. Received without a grain of doubt, it moved every Christian heart as the smell of fresh bread moves the hungry: instantly, without argument, straight to the centre.

The people threw themselves on their faces when the priest raised it on high; cries of pity rose everywhere, and tears stood in almost every eye. After a time they rose; then the priest went round the platform, showing it for a single moment to the nearest; and at each glimpse loud cries of devotion burst forth, wave upon wave.

Soon after, they fell in with a procession of Flagellants, flogging their bare shoulders till blood ran streaming down; yet there was no pain in their faces, and many of them laughed and jested as they lashed. The bystanders, out of pity, offered them wine. They took it—few drank it; most used it to soften and cleanse the tails of the cat, hard with clotted blood, that the next stroke might bite the better. Many were boys. A young woman took pity on one fair urchin.

“Alas! dear child,” said she, “why wound thy white skin so?”

“Basta,” said he, laughing, “’tis for your sins I do it, not for mine.”

“Hear you that?” said the friar. “Show me the whip that can whip the vanity out of man’s heart! The young monkey; how knoweth he that stranger is a sinner more than he?”

“Father,” said Gerard, sickened by the sound of laughter mingled with the wet smack of scourges, “surely this is not to our Lord’s mind. He was so pitiful.”

“Our Lord?” said Fra Colonna, crossing himself. “What has He to do with this? This was a custom in Rome six hundred years before He was born. The boys used to go through the streets at the Lupercalia flogging themselves; and the married women used to shove in and try and get a blow from the monkeys’ scourges; for these blows conferred fruitfulness in those days. A foolish trick, this flagellation; but interesting to the bystander; reminds him of the grand old heathen. We are so prone to forget all we owe them.”

So even here, amid blood and prayer, the friar’s mind returned to older names, older rites—memory laid like one language over another, the later words drowning the first, yet never quite silencing it.

Next they got into one of the seven churches and saw the Pope give the mass. The ceremony was imposing; incense rose like visible breath, the chant flowed and echoed, candles trembled in their own heat—yet again it was spoiled by the inconsistent conduct of the cardinals and prelates, who sat about the altar with hats on, chattering all through the mass like a flock of geese. Their talk, that small domestic noise of pride and ease, crept into the sacred soundscape and soured it, as smoke from a bad fire will taint a whole pot.

The eucharist in both kinds was tasted by an official before the Pope would venture on it; and this surprised Gerard beyond measure.

“Who is that base man? and what doth he there?”

“Oh, that is the Preguste,” said the friar, “and he tastes the eucharist by way of precaution. This is the country for poison; and none fall oftener by it than the poor Popes.”

“Alas! so I have heard; but after the miraculous change of the bread and wine to Christ His body and blood, poison cannot remain; gone is the bread with all its properties and accidents; gone is the wine.”

“So says Faith; but experience tells another tale. Scores have died in Italy poisoned in the host.”

“And I tell you, father,” cried Gerard, hot with certainty, “that were both bread and wine charged with direst poison before his holiness had consecrated them, yet after consecration I would take them both withouten fear.”

“So would I,” said Fra Colonna, “but for the fine arts.”

“What mean you?”

“Marry, that I would be as ready to leave the world as thou, were it not for those arts which beautify existence here below, and make it dear to men of sense and education. No; so long as the Nine Muses strew my path with roses of learning and art, me may Apollo inspire with wisdom and caution, that knowing the wiles of my countrymen, I may eat poison neither at God’s altar nor at a friend’s table; since, wherever I eat it or drink it, it will assuredly cut short my mortal thread; and I am writing a book—heart and soul in it—The Dream of Polifilo, the man of many arts. So name not poison to me till that is finished and copied.”

And now the great bells of St. John Lateran rang with a clash at short intervals, as if the city itself were struck like a great brazen vessel. The people hurried thither to see the heads of St. Peter and St. Paul.

Gerard and the friar got a good place within. A great curtain hung; long, breathless expectation held the multitude in a silence broken only by the restless rustle of bodies and the whisper of prayers. Then the curtain was drawn by jerks, and at a height of about thirty feet were two human heads with bearded faces that seemed alive. They were shown no longer than the time to say an Ave Maria; then the curtain fell again. But they were shown thus three times.

St. Peter’s complexion was pale, his face oval, his beard grey and forked; his head crowned with a papal mitre. St. Paul was dark-skinned, with a thick square beard; his head and face were more square and massive, full of resolution.

Gerard was awe-struck, as a child is when first he tastes wine and feels it go straight to the blood. The friar approved—after his fashion.

“This exhibition of the imagines,” said he, “or waxen effigies of heroes and demigods, is a venerable custom, and inciteth the vulgar to virtue by great and invisible examples.”

“Waxen images?” cried Gerard, startled, as if told that a loaf was only painted. “What, are they not the apostles themselves, embalmed, or the like?”

The friar moaned.

“They did not exist in the year 800. The great old Roman families always produced at their funerals a series of these imagines, thereby tying past and present history together, and showing the populace the features of far-famed worthies. I can conceive nothing more thrilling or instructive. But then the effigies were portraits made during life or at the hour of death. These of St. Paul and St. Peter are moulded out of pure fancy.”

“Ah! say not so, father,” pleaded Gerard, who felt in himself the ache of the untranslatable—the way one man’s certainty cannot be poured into another man’s cup.

“But the worst is,” continued the friar, “this humour of showing them up on a shelf, and half in the dark, and by snatches, and with the poor mountebank trick of a drawn curtain.

Quodcunque ostendis mihi sic incredulus odi.

Enough; the men of this day are not the men of old. Let us have done with these new-fangled mummeries, and go among the Pope’s books; there we shall find the wisdom we shall vainly hunt in the streets of modern Rome.”

And the idea, once planted, took root in him at once. He plunged and tore through the crowd, looking neither right nor left, till he had escaped the glories of Holy Week that had brought fifty thousand strangers to Rome, and had got quiet among the dead in the Vatican library—where the loudest sound was a page turned, and the air smelled not of sweat and torches but of vellum, dust, and the faint sharpness of ink.

Presently, going into Gerard’s room, he found a hot dispute afoot between him and Jacques Bonaventura. That spark had come in all steel from head to toe; he doffed his helmet, puffed, and railed with scorn upon a ridiculous ceremony at which he and his soldiers had been compelled to attend the Pope: to wit, the blessing of the beasts of burden.

Gerard said it was not ridiculous; nothing a Pope did could be ridiculous.

The argument grew warm. Fra Colonna stood grimly neuter, waiting like the stork in the fable that ate frog and mouse at the close of their combat—to grind them both between the jaws of antiquity. When lo, the curtain was gently drawn, and there stood a venerable old man in a purple skull-cap, with a beard like white floss silk, looking at them with a kind though feeble smile.

“Happy youth,” said he, “that can heat itself over such matters.”

They all fell on their knees. It was the Pope.

“Nay, rise, my children,” said he, almost peevishly, as one who had stepped aside for quiet and found ceremony thrust upon him. “I came not into this corner to be in state. How goes Plutarch?”

Gerard brought his work, and kneeling on one knee presented it. His holiness seated himself; the others stood.

He inspected the writing with interest. “’Tis excellently writ,” said he.

Gerard’s heart beat with delight; praise from that mouth seemed to make even the ink on his page more black and sure.

“Ah, this Plutarch,” said the Pope to Francesco, “he had a wondrous art. How each character standeth out alive on his page: how full of nature each, yet how unlike his fellow!”

Jacques Bonaventura, who cared for nothing that did not march or strike, broke in bluntly. “Give me the Signor Boccaccio.”

“An excellent narrator, capitano,” said the Pope, “and writeth exquisite Italian. But in spirit a thought too monotonous. Monks and nuns were never all unchaste: one or two such stories were right pleasant and diverting; but five score paint his time falsely, and sadden the heart of such as love mankind. Moreover, he hath no skill at characters. Now this Greek is supreme in that great art: he carveth them with pen; and turning his page, see into how real and great a world we enter—of war, and policy, and business, and love in its own place: for with him, as in the great world, men are not all running after a wench. With this great open field compare me not the narrow garden of Boccaccio, and his little mill-round of dishonest pleasures.”

“Your holiness,” said Jacques, half-curious, half-mocking, “they say, hath not disdained to write a novel.”

“My holiness hath done more foolish things than one,” replied the Pope, and the tiredness in his voice made him sound suddenly older than his beard, “whereof it repents too late. When I wrote novels I little thought to be head of the Church.”

“I search in vain for a copy of it,” said Jacques, “to add to my poor library.”

Princess Claelia had set her heart on a full-length likeness—herself, entire, to outface time.

Gerard, who knew the temper of patronage and the price of it, ventured gently, “Signora, there is in Rome a master—Pietro Vanucci—my friend—who—”

She cut him off with a small, queenly lift of the chin. “’Twill be time enough to slight Gerardo when his work discontents me.”

The refusal did not wound him; it warmed him. He had, besides, a notion that belonged to his craft like a secret spice in a sauce: he could make paper look like marble.

“Then stand to me,” he pleaded, “as a Roman statue. I will draw you so—so cold and noble—that a man would think you carved, not born.”

At the first, she was half amused. But when he explained, with the innocent zeal of an artist who forgets everything but form, that she must wear tunic, toga, and sandals like the ancients—

“Why,” she said, with that mediaeval frankness that could be more startling than rudeness, “I had as lieve be presented in my smock.”

He fell to praising the antique habit—free, ample, simple, and noble—and, with the heedless sincerity that is the truest flattery, told her Heaven had given her Roman features, and an arm and hand that modern sleeves did but wrong.

She narrowed her eyes, smiling as if to weigh whether he mocked her. “What, can you flatter, like the rest, Gerardo? Well—give me time to think on’t. Come o’ Saturday, and then I will say ay or nay.”

Saturday came; but all the week between had been spent in her private rooms with needle and pins and trying-on—toga folded, tunic set, sandals chosen—antiquity measured against the face in the mirror, a thousand years of fashion argued with a single woman’s vanity.
