Gerard, hurrying to the appointed sitting, was stopped dead in the street by a shop-window, as if a hand had gripped his collar.

There lay a Lactantius open; the page was so even, so fair, that his calligrapher’s eye drank it like clear wine. He leaned closer. No pen had done that. No hand, however patient, however trained to thin strokes and swelling hairlines, could have made letters so uniform, so inexorably alike.

It was printed.

A groan came from him, low and bitter, like a man hearing his own trade pronounced dying.

“I am sped,” he whispered. “Mine enemy is at the door. The press is in Rome.”

He went in, schooling his face to indifference. “How long hath the printing-press been in Rome?” he asked, as carelessly as if inquiring the price of figs.

The trader laughed. “In Rome? There is no such thing, messer. Oh, you mean the Lactantius. That was printed on the top o’ the Apennines.”

“What,” said Gerard, staring, “did the printing-press fall down there out o’ the moon?”

“Nay; it shot up there out of Germany. See the title-page.”

Gerard took the book with the eagerness of a man handling his rival’s blade. The black, mechanical letters sat on the page with a cold perfection:

Opera et impensis Sweynheim et Pannartz Alumnorum Joannis Fust. Impressum Subiacis. A.D. 1465.

“Will ye buy?” the man coaxed. “See how fair and even be the letters. Few are left can write like that; and scarce a quarter of the price.”

“I would fain have it,” Gerard answered, and the sadness in him was like hunger turned to ash, “but my heart will not let me. Know I am a caligraph, and these disciples of Fust run after me round the world, taking the bread out of my mouth. Yet I wish them no ill. Heaven forbid!”

He fled the shop, and the street seemed altered: every sound sharper, every shout and iron-shod hoof a prophecy of pounding type. “Dear Margaret,” he said within himself, as if she walked beside him, “we must lose no time. We must make our hay while shines the sun. One month more, and an avalanche of printer’s letters shall roll down on Rome from those Apennines and lay us waste that writers be.”

He quickened his pace toward Claelia, as though he could outrun the press by speed alone.

He was ushered into an apartment he had not seen before—small, rich, cunningly contrived for softness. A fountain played in the center, its thin jets making a continual whisper; the floor was strewn with panthers’ skins, hair upward, so that no footfall spoke. Even the air seemed trained to hush itself. Beyond, instead of a door, a great curtain of tapestry hung, heavy as a wall.

Gerard was left there long enough to doubt whether he had been misplaced. The fountain’s voice became a kind of counting—time, time—each drop like a tiny admonition. Then, behind the curtain, came a step: light, swift, almost noiseless on the furred floor. The tapestry parted.

She stood there in tunic and toga and sandals, not modern in a single line. The figure might have been worshipped by pagans: not wholly Venus, not wholly Minerva, but something between—nobler than the one, more womanly than the other. Beauty, which laughs at centuries, had taken the antique dress and made it present.

Gerard started, the artist in him flushing as if someone had set a lamp behind his eyes. “Oh!” he cried—nothing more, because nothing else would come—and he stared in rapture.

That cry was the sweetest praise she had ever heard, because it was not dressed in courtly phrases. A blush tinted her cheek; her eyes brightened; her mouth curved into complacency that tasted like honey to her pride.

When his eloquence proved to be only gaze and breath, she spoke first. “Well, Gerardo, thou seest I have made myself an antique monster for thee.”

“A monster?” he said, still drinking in line and proportion. “Fra Colonna would fall down and adore your highness, seeing you so habited.”

“Nay,” she returned quickly, “I care not to be adored by an old man. I would liever be loved by a young one—of my own choosing.”

He set to work at once—pencils out, paper stretched on his canvas—so absorbed that he forgot her pulse, her lungs, the weight of her arms held aloft. He had the mercilessness of concentration. Near an hour passed before she spoke again, and then faintly: “Gerardo, I can stand so no more—even for thee.”

“Sit down and rest awhile, signora,” he said, startled at his own cruelty when it was named aloud.

“I thank thee,” she breathed; and sinking into a chair, she turned pale and sighed as if the toga had suddenly become lead.

He was alarmed. He dipped his hand into the fountain and, thinking like a simple man with a simple remedy, would have flung water on her face; but she lifted her hand, deprecating.

“Nay. Hold it to my brow with thine hand—prithee, do not fling it at me.”

Timidly, hesitating as if the touch were a sacrilege, he laid his wet hand on her forehead.

“Ah,” she sighed, “that is reviving. Again.”

He did it again, and her lashes fluttered; she thanked him and bade him ring the little bell on the table. A maid came. Claelia sent her to Floretta for a large fan.

Floretta arrived quickly, fan in hand—and before she could even kneel, the princess’s nostrils dilated like a bloodhorse scenting something foul.

“Wretch!” Claelia cried.

In an instant she was on her feet, vigor returning like flame to dry straw. With her left hand she seized Floretta by the hair; with her right she struck—once, twice, thrice—sharp, resounding blows. The bare arm the toga displayed was beautiful, and in that moment seemed terrible in its strength: it rose and fell with a brutal regularity, as if power were a machine. The slaps cracked through the hush-room and even drowned the fountain’s whisper. Floretta screamed and sobbed, and was driven through the tapestry as if through a storm.

From beyond the curtain her crying went on, bitter as smoke.

“Saints of heaven!” Gerard cried. “What is amiss? What hath she done?”

“She knows right well,” Claelia snapped, still breathing hard. “’Tis not the first time. The nasty toad! I’ll learn her to come to me stinking of the musk-cat.”

Gerard, whose senses were not dulled to smell—who knew how a rank perfume could spoil clean air the way a wrong spice ruins broth—still winced at the violence. “Alas, signora,” he ventured, “’twas a small fault, methinks.”

“A small fault? Nay—’twas a foul fault.”

Then, as if a cord had been cut within her, she dropped from fury into sweetness with amazing speed. “Are you wroth with me for beating her, Gerar-do?”

“Signora,” he said, uneasy, “it ill becomes me to school you; but methinks such as Heaven appoints to govern others should govern themselves.”

“That is true,” she answered softly. “How wise you are, to be so young.” She called the other maid, gave her a little purse. “Take that to Floretta, and tell her ‘the Gerardo’ hath interceded for her; and so I must needs forgive her. There, Gerardo.”

He coloured, caught between shame and the awkward pleasure of being made powerful by another’s words. To hide it, he asked if he should resume her picture.

“Not yet. Beating that hussy hath somewhat breathed me. I’ll sit awhile, and you shall talk to me. I know you can talk, an it pleases you, as rarely as you draw.”

“That were easily done,” he said, lightly.

“Do it then, Gerardo.”

The command struck him dumb. He searched for a safe subject, like a man groping for the right herb to temper a too-hot dish. “But, signora, I know not what to say. This is sudden.”

“Say your real mind,” she said. “Say you wish you were anywhere but here.”

“Nay,” he replied, honestly, “that would not be sooth. I wish one thing though.”

“Ay? and what is that?” The gentleness was almost dangerous.

“I wish,” he blurted, “I could have drawn you as you were beating that poor lass. You were awful—yet lovely. Oh, what a subject for a Pythoness!”

She sighed as if disappointed. “Alas, he thinks but of his art. And why keep such a coil about my beauty, Gerardo? You are far fairer than I am. You are more like Apollo than I to Venus. Also, you have lovely hair and lovely eyes—but you know not what to do with them.”

“Ay, do I,” he said, clinging to his refuge. “To draw you, signora.”

“Ah, yes—see my features. But you cannot see what any Roman gallant had seen long ago in your place.” Her voice sank, and the room’s hush seemed to lean closer to listen. “Yet sure you must have noted how welcome you are to me, Gerardo?”

“I can see your highness is ever passing kind to me; a poor stranger like me.”

“No,” she said, and the word fell like a stone into still water. “I am not. I have often been cold to you—rude sometimes—and you are so simple you see not the cause. Alas! I feared for my own heart. I feared to be your slave—I, who have hitherto made slaves.” Her breath trembled. “Gerardo, I am unhappy. Ever since you came here I have lived upon your visits. The day you are to come I am bright; the other days I am listless. You are not like the Roman gallants. You make me hate them. You are ten times braver to my eye; and wise, and scholarly, and you never flatter and lie. I scorn a man that lies. Gerar-do—teach me thy magic; teach me to make thee as happy by my side as I am still by thine.”

As she spoke, her mellow voice slid toward a whisper; her hand—white, careful, almost timid—stole down his arm and came to rest upon his wrist, as lightly as a bird that might fly at the least alarm.

Gerard, wrapped in Margaret as in a garment under all his garments, had not foreseen this. Admiration of Claelia’s beauty had never displaced the absent image that governed him. Yet here was regal loveliness wooing with a grace he had never imagined, and he stood as helpless as a boy asked to translate a language he does not know.

He blushed. He trembled.

The siren saw it and mistook it for yielding. “Poor Gerardo,” she murmured. “Fear not. None shall ever harm thee under my wing. Wilt not speak to me, Gerar-do mio?”

“Signora!” he muttered, pleading without words.

His lowered eye fell upon that same shapely arm and delicate hand curled round his elbow—and in a flash he saw it as he had just seen it: rising and falling on Floretta. Beauty and violence braided together. His skin went cold beneath the blush.

“Alas!” Claelia said, misreading his recoil. “I scare him. Am I then so very terrible? Is it my Roman robe? I’ll doff it, and habit me as when thou first camest to me. Mindest thou? ’Twas to write a letter to yon barren knight Ercole d’Orsini. Shall I tell thee? ’twas the sight of thee—thy pretty ways—thy wise words—made me hate him on the instant.” Her voice quickened with its own memory. “Tell me now how many times hast thou been here since then. Ah! thou knowest not—lovest me not, I doubt, as I love thee. Eighteen times, Gerardo. And each time dearer to me. The day thou comest not, ’tis night, not day, to Claelia. Cruel boy—am I not worth a word? Hast every day a princess at thy feet? Prithee, prithee—speak to me, Gerar-do.”

“Signora,” he faltered, “what can I say that were not better left unsaid? Oh, evil day that ever I came here.”

“Ah! say not so. ’Twas the brightest day ever shone on me—or indeed on thee. I’ll make thee confess so much ere long, ungrateful one.”

“Your highness,” he began, low and earnest.

“Call me Claelia,” she breathed.

He could not. The word stuck. “Signora, I am too young and too little wise to know how I ought to speak to you, so as not to seem blind nor yet ungrateful. But this I know: I were both naught and ungrateful—the worst foe e’er you had—did I take advantage of this mad fancy. Sure some ill spirit hath had leave to afflict you withal; for ’tis all unnatural that a princess adorned with every grace should abase her affections on a churl.”

Her hand withdrew from his wrist, slowly—yet, as it passed over his arm, it lingered a heartbeat, like a leaf that clings before falling.

“You fear the daggers of my kinsmen,” she said, half sad, half contemptuous.

“No more than I fear the bodkins of your women,” Gerard answered, with a sudden honest haughtiness. “But I fear God and the saints—and my own conscience.”

“The truth, Gerardo, the truth!” she said sharply. “Hypocrisy sits awkwardly on thee. Princesses, while they are young, are not despised for love of God, but of some other woman. Tell me whom thou lovest; and if she is worthy thee, I will forgive thee.”

“No she in Italy,” he said, “upon my soul.”

“Ah!” Her eyes flashed. “There is one somewhere then. Where? where?”

“In Holland—my native country.”

“Ah! Marie de Bourgoyne is fair, they say—yet she is but a child.”

“Princess,” he said, and his voice steadied on what was sacred to him, “she I love is not noble. She is as I am. Nor is she so fair as thou—yet is she fair—and linked to my heart for ever by her virtues, and by all the dangers and griefs we have borne together, and for one another.” He swallowed, but did not retreat. “Forgive me; but I would not wrong my Margaret for all the highest dames in Italy.”

The change in Claelia was like winter coming in a breath. She sprang to her feet and stood opposite him—beautiful still, but far more terrible now than when she struck Floretta; then her cheeks had been red, but now they were pale, and her fury was gathered and quiet, like a blade held steady.

“This to my face, unmannered wretch!” she cried. “Was I born to be insulted as well as scorned by such as thou? Beware! We nobles brook no rivals. Bethink thee whether is better—the love of a Cesarini, or her hate. After all I have said and done to thee, it must be love or hate between us—and to the death. Choose now!”

Gerard looked up at her with wonder and awe. In her Roman drapery, towering, imperious, she seemed some antique goddess affronted by a mortal. He sighed—deep, patient—and could not bring himself to answer.

The sigh struck some hidden string. Or perhaps passion, spent in its own blaze, made room for another. Claelia sank down, suddenly languid, and tears began to fall rapidly, bright in the soft room, each drop audible in that muffled place as if the very skins and tapestry listened.

“Alas! alas!” Gerard cried, miserable. “Weep not, sweet lady; your tears do accuse me, and I am like to weep for company. My kind patron—be yourself. You will live to see how much better a friend I was to you than I seemed.”

“I see it now, Gerardo,” she whispered. “Friend is the word—the only word can ever pass between us twain. I was mad. Any other man had ta’en advantage of my folly. You must teach me to be your friend—and nothing more.”

He seized upon the escape as a man seizes shore after a long current. He spoke to her of friendship out of Cicero—how godlike, how rare, how lasting beyond love’s fever—and, to prove himself capable of it, he even told her of Denys and himself. She listened with half-closed eyes, not merely hearing but studying, as though each phrase were an ingredient to be tasted for what it revealed.

At last she said calmly, “Leave me now, Gerardo, and come as usual to-morrow. You will find your lesson well bestowed.”

She held out her hand. He kissed it and went away, pondering, wondering whether he had walked wisely or only narrowly.

The next day he was received with marked distance. She stood before him literally like a statue—still, cold, offering him her outlines and nothing else—and after a very short sitting she excused herself and dismissed him. He felt the change like a draft in a once-warm room; yet he told himself, “She is wise.” In her way, she was.

The next day he found her surrounded by young nobles, their voices buzzing in the muffled chamber like insects that did not know silence had rights. They flattered her to the skies, and she and they treated Gerard as one treats a dog that can do a trick—useful, contemptible, amusing. The cavaliers leaned over his work and criticised it with such ignorance married to insolence that his cheeks burned.

Claelia watched his face, demure, half-lidded, at each sting; and when at last the insects had flown, she had her doors closed against every one of them—for their pains.

The next day she was alone again: cold, silent. After standing so long she said abruptly, “You treated my company with less respect than became you.”

“Did I, signora?”

“Did you? You fired up at the comments they did you the honour to make on your work.”

“Nay, I said nought.”

“Oh—high looks speak as plain as high words. Your cheeks were red as blood.”

“I was nettled a moment,” he confessed, “at seeing so much ignorance and ill-nature together.”

“Now it is me—their hostess—you affront.”

“Forgive me, signora, and acquit me of design. It would ill become me to affront the kindest patron and friend I have in Rome but one.”

“How humble we are all of a sudden,” she said, and her voice had the edge of a thin knife. “In sooth, Ser Gerardo, you are a capital feigner. You can insult—or truckle—at will.”

“Truckle? to whom?”

“To me, for one,” she said. “To one whom you affronted for a base-born girl like yourself; but whose patronage you claim all the same.”

He rose and put a hand to his heart, as if to keep the words from cutting too deep. “These are biting words, signora. Have I really deserved them?”

“Oh, what are words to an adventurer like you?” she returned. “Cold steel is all you fear?”

“I am no swashbuckler,” he said, stung into courage, “yet I have met steel with steel; and methinks I had rather face your kinsmen’s swords than your cruel tongue, lady. Why do you use me so?”

“Gerar-do,” she said, and for once it was almost honest, “for no good reason but because I am wayward, and shrewish, and curst—and because everybody admires me but you.”

“I admire you too, signora,” he answered. “Your friends may flatter you more; but believe me, they have not the eye to see half your charms. Their babble showed me that. None admire you more truly, or wish you better, than the poor artist, who might not be your lover, but hoped to be your friend; but no—I see that may not be between one so high as you and one so low as I.”

“Ay—but it shall,” she said quickly, seizing on the word “friend” as though it were a rope. “I will not be so curst. Tell me now where abides thy Margaret; and I will give thee a present for her; and on that you and I will be friends.”

“She is a daughter of a physician called Peter,” he said, and his voice softened into homesickness like broth cooling, “and they bide at Sevenbergen. Ah me—shall I e’er see it again?”

“’Tis well,” Claelia replied, and something in her tone closed like a clasp. “Now go.”

He went, more uneasy than before. He had stepped into deep water the day he met this Italian princess—callida et calida, the sun’s own child in craft and heat. He resolved to go no more when once her likeness was finished; already he repented having taken so long and laborious a task.

That resolution wavered at his next reception, for she met him all gentleness. After standing to him awhile she said she was fatigued and would have his aid in another way: would he teach her to draw a little?

He sat beside her and guided her hand through easy lines. She was wonderfully apt—quick as fire catching. He told her so.

“I had a teacher before thee, Gerar-do,” she said softly. “Ay—and one as handsome as thyself.”

She went to a drawer and brought out several heads—patiently done, ignorant of rules, yet full of spirit. All were Gerard’s face, again and again, as though she had been trying to learn him the way a cook repeats a dish until it matches the taste in the mind. One was his very image.

“There,” she said. “Now thou seest who was my teacher.”

“Not I, signora,” he murmured, astonished.

“What—know you not who teaches us women to do all things?” She laughed, and the laugh held hunger. “’Tis love, Gerar-do. Love made me draw because thou drawest. Love prints thine image in my bosom. My fingers touch the pen, and love supplies the want of art, and lo—thy beloved features lie upon the paper.”

His astonishment turned to dismay. “Oh, signora—you promised me to be friends and nothing more.”

She laughed outright. “How simple you are! Who believes a woman promising nonsense—impossibilities? Friendship, foolish boy—who ever built that temple on red ashes?” Then the gaiety fell away. “Between thee and me it must be love or hate.”

“Which you will, signora,” Gerard said, firm now as a man who has found the one language he will not betray. “But for me I will neither love nor hate you; but with your permission I will leave you.” He rose abruptly.

She rose too, pale as death. “Ere thou leavest me so, know thy fate: outside that door are armed men who wait to slay thee at a word from me.”

“But you will not speak that word,” he said, clinging to the last hope of her better self.

“That word I will speak,” she answered, quiet and dreadful. “Nay, more: I shall noise it abroad ’twas for proffering brutal love to me thou wert slain. And I will send a special messenger to Sevenbergen—a cunning messenger, well taught his lesson. Thy Margaret shall know thee dead and think thee faithless. Now go to thy grave—a dog’s. For a man thou art not.”

He went ashen, struck dumb. The room seemed suddenly louder, though no one spoke: the fountain’s whisper mocked him, the tapestry held its breath, the skins swallowed even the scuttle of panic. “God have mercy on us both,” he said at last.

“Nay—have thou mercy on her and on thyself,” she said, leaning toward him with cruel persuasion. “She will never know in Holland what thou dost in Rome—unless I be driven to tell her my tale. Come, yield thee, Gerar-do mio. What will it cost thee to say thou lovest me? I ask thee but to feign it handsomely. Thou art young—die not for the poor pleasure of denying a lady what—the shadow of a heart. Who will shed a tear for thee? Men will laugh, not weep, over thy tombstone—ah!”

She broke off with a little scream, for he flung himself at her feet and poured out, in one torrent, the whole story—his and Margaret’s—raw as newly bled truth. Imprisoned; hunted with bloodhounds for her; driven to exile; how she had shed her blood for him and now pined at home; how he had walked across Europe ringed with perils—torn by savage brutes, attacked by furious men with sword and axe and trap, robbed, shipwrecked—for her.

She tried to pull away, but he clung to her robe, held her there with the desperate strength of one who has nothing left but speech. He caught her hand and clasped it between both of his, and his tears fell fast upon it as he begged her to think on all the woes of true lovers she would part; and what could come of so deep a love betrayed, and so false a love feigned, with hatred lurking at the bottom, but remorse—swift and lasting.

In such moments none ever resisted Gerard. His sincerity was like a plain, strong bread: no ornament, but it fed.

Claelia wavered. Her breath came in broken sighs; her bosom rose and fell; her fiery eyes filled. At last she sobbed, “You conquer me—you, or my better angel. Leave Rome!”

“I will,” he cried. “I will.”

“If you breathe a word of my folly,” she whispered, “it will be your last.”

“Think not so poorly of me,” he answered. “You are my benefactress once more. Is it for me to slander you?”

“Go,” she said, and the command was half a plea. “I will send you the means. I know myself; if you cross my path again, I shall kill you. Addio—my heart is broken.”

She touched the bell. “Floretta,” she called, voice choked, “take him safe out of the house—through my chamber—and by the side postern.”

At the door he turned. She leaned with one hand on a chair, crying, her head averted. In that moment he remembered only her mercy, not her threat. He ran back and kissed her robe. She never moved.

Once clear of the house he darted home, thanking Heaven for escape—soul and body.

“Landlady,” he said, breath still unsteady, “there is one would pick a quarrel with me. What is to be done?”

She flashed her eyes. “Strike him first, and at vantage! Get behind him; and then draw.”

“Alas, I lack your Italian courage,” he said. “To be serious—’tis a noble.”

She crossed herself. “Oh, holy saints, that is another matter. Change thy lodging awhile, and keep snug; and alter the fashion of thy habits.”

She took him to her niece, who let rooms some little distance off, and installed him there.

He had little to do now—no princess to draw, no soft-footed visits to live upon—and the sudden leisure felt like a silence after music. So he set himself resolutely to read the deed of Floris Brandt, from which he had hitherto been driven by its abominably bad writing. He bent to it as one bends to a pot whose crust must be scraped, not because it is pleasant, but because the meal depends on it. Slowly the crabbed lines yielded; slowly the sense rose.

When he mastered it, he saw at once what had been hidden plain in the words: the loan on the land must have been paid over and over by the rents, and Ghysbrecht was keeping Peter Brandt out of his own.

“Fool!” Gerard cried, striking his palm with the paper’s edge. “Not to have read this before.”

He hired a horse and rode to the nearest port. A vessel was to sail for Amsterdam in four days. He took a passage and paid a small sum to secure it.

“The land is too full of cut-throats for me,” he told himself, tasting again the muffled menace of Claelia’s house, the invisible men beyond a door. “And ’tis lovely fair weather for the sea. Our Dutch skippers are not shipwrecked like these bungling Italians.”

When he returned, there sat his old landlady, her eyes sparkling, as if she had news that crackled like a hearth newly fed.

Gerard came back to himself as a man comes back to a burnt house—alive, and therefore capable of counting what is gone.

The second day his mind took fire. Fever rattled in his skull; his words ran off like scalding broth that will not be held in the pot. Close at hand, on the table, lay the spoil of him: his rich auburn hair, shorn clean, long as a woman’s—coiled like a rope of bright cinnamon on a trencher, too beautiful to be only waste. From hour to hour the signs thickened; one peril succeeded another as in a kitchen where the fat has caught and the flame hunts the rafters.

On the fifth day the leech—learned, grave, and weary of trying to rescue what seemed already over-boiled—stood back, wiped his hands, and gave him up. At sunset, when the room had that coppery light which makes even clean linen look stained, Gerard fell into a sleep so deep that it frightened those who had watched him struggle.

Some said he would wake only to die. But an old gossip, whose word carried weight because she had been paid for her nursing in better houses than this, listened to his breathing as a cook listens for the first steady murmur of a pot that has settled. “His youth may save him yet,” she said, “if he sleep twelve hours.”

At that, his old landlady, who had fed more lodgers than she could count and knew the comfort that comes from simple routines—hearth, bowl, bed—cleared the room and sat alone to keep the vigil. She vowed a wax candle to the Virgin for every hour he should sleep. She marked the time by the sounds more than by any clock: the creak of a stair, the clack of a shutter in the wind, the far-off cry of a hawker, and, beneath all, that one precious, even draught of breath.

He slept twelve hours.

The good soul dropped to her knees and thanked the Virgin with her face in her apron, as if it were a clean cloth laid over a loaf.

He slept twenty-four.

Her joy began to sour into a worried wonder, as milk will turn if you cannot keep it cool.

At the thirtieth hour she could bear it no longer and sent for the woman of art. “Thirty hours!” she whispered. “Shall we wake him?”

The other came in, bent over him, and watched long—watching not only his face but the small signs that women learn without books: the moisture of the palm, the looseness of the jaw, the way the ribs lift, the steadiness between one breath and the next, like the hush between two phrases of a chant.

“His breath is even,” said she at last, “his hand moist. I know there be learned leeches would wake him to look at his tongue, and be none the wiser; but we that be women should have the sense to let bon Nature alone. When did sleep ever harm the racked brain or the torn heart?”

So they let him lie.

When he had been eight-and-forty hours asleep it got wind, as all strange things do in a street of close doors and quick ears. Curious folk pressed on the stair; they had much ado to keep them out. But they admitted only Fra Colonna, and with him the gigantic Fra Jerome.

These two relieved the women and sat silent. Fra Colonna’s eyes watered as he watched, the tears slipping down as quietly as oil on warm bread. Fra Jerome fingered his beads, and looked on as calmly as he had looked upon the sea when he and Gerard had met it hand to hand—calm, because his calm was a kind of iron.

The house itself listened. Even the hearth, usually snapping and gossiping with its own small noises, seemed chastened; and the street sounds came softened, as if the air had been thickened with wool.

At last—about the sixtieth hour of that strange sleep—the landlady touched Fra Colonna with her elbow.

He looked.

Gerard opened his eyes as gently as if he had been only dozing after a long meal. He stared, not knowing at first what he saw. He drew himself a little higher in the bed. His hand went to his head—habit, hunger, the old gesture of the living—and met the nakedness there. He found his hair gone.

He saw Colonna and smiled—an honest flash, like sunshine finding a crack in a shutter.

But in the midst of smiling his face stopped, as if some hand had dashed cold water into it. The features convulsed in a moment with anguish unspeakable. A cry tore out of him, loud and raw, and he turned his face to the wall.

His landlady wept at that; she had known what it is to wake bereaved, when the room is the same and yet the world is not. Fra Jerome began to recite canticles and prayers from his breviary, the Latin falling into the chamber like measured drops—sound meant to soothe, meant to bind a mind back into obedience.

Gerard rolled himself hard into the bedclothes as if he would smother memory.

Fra Colonna went to him, and, whimpering with grief that was half selfish—because he loved the boy and also loved his hopes—reminded him that all was not lost. The divine Muses were immortal. He must transfer his affection to them; they would never betray him nor fail him like creatures of clay.

Then the good, simple father hurried away; his own heart could not keep its footing on so steep a sorrow.

Fra Jerome remained.

“Young man,” said he, standing as if he were already at the door of a tribunal, “the Muses exist but in the brains of pagans and visionaries. The Church alone gives repose to the heart on earth, and happiness to the soul hereafter. Hath earth deceived thee, hath passion broken thy heart after tearing it, the Church opens her arms: consecrate thy gifts to her! The Church is peace of mind.”

He spoke solemnly, as if the very cadence of his voice were a chain meant to be felt; and as soon as the words were uttered he was gone, leaving behind him the echo of his own authority.

“The Church!” cried Gerard.

He sprang up with a sudden fury that made his weak limbs seem for an instant strong. He shook his fist after the departing friar.

“Malediction on the Church! But for the Church I should not lie broken here, and she lie cold, cold, cold, in Holland. Oh, my Margaret! oh, my darling! my darling! And I must run from thee the few months thou hadst to live. Cruel! cruel! The monsters, they let her die. Death comes not without some signs. These the blind selfish wretches saw not, or recked not; but I had seen them, I that love her. Oh, had I been there, I had saved her, I had saved her. Idiot! idiot! to leave her for a moment.”

The words poured out of him with the bitter salt of tears. He wept long—deep, shaking sobs, the kind that leave a man as empty as a scraped pot.

Then rage took him again, sharp and sudden.

“The Church! for whose sake I was driven from her; my malison be on the Church! and the hypocrites that name it to my broken heart. Accursed be the world! Ghysbrecht lives; Margaret dies. Thieves, murderers, harlots, live for ever. Only angels die. Curse life! curse death! and whosoever made them what they are!”

Fra Jerome did not hear the blasphemies—only the howl of rage flung after him like a stone. It was well. Had he caught the words, he would have had his late shipmate burned in the forum with as little hesitation as he would have roasted a kid and called it duty.

The landlady, who had gone down the stair with Fra Colonna, heard the raised voice and turned back, her fear running ahead of her feet. She found Gerard dressing—his hands clumsy with weakness, his cheeks wet, his eyes bright and terrible. He had chosen his best clothes, as if for a feast-day, though his flesh looked ashy and drawn, and the cap he set on his head sat too jauntily for such a face.

She caught at him with words, as women do—trying to fold a man back into the small mercies of order. She remonstrated, begged, commanded.

“What avails my lying here?” he said gloomily, fastening a point with fingers that trembled. “Can I find here that which I seek?”

“Saints preserve us!” she cried. “Is he distraught again? What seek ye?”

“Oblivion.”

“Oblivion, my little heart? Oh, but y’are young to talk so.”

“Young or old, what else have I to live for?”

He smoothed his doublet, took his belt, made himself ready as if he were going into the street to buy spice or wine, though he was going to purchase nothing that can be weighed.

The good dame tried once more, clutching at a practical thing, the way one clings to a ladle when the kitchen tilts.

“My pretty Gerard, know that it is Tuesday, not Sunday.”

“Tuesday is it?” he muttered, as if time had become a foreign tongue in his mouth. “I thought it had been Saturday.”

“Nay, thou hast slept long. Thou never wearest thy brave clothes on working days. Consider.”

“What I did, when she lived, I did. Now I shall do whatever erst I did not. The past is the past. There lies my hair, and with it my way of life. I have served one Master as well as I could. You see my reward. Now I’ll serve another, and give him a fair trial too.”

“Alas!” sighed the woman, turning pale, for she heard in his voice a resolve colder than any winter draft. “What mean these dark words? and what new master is this whose service thou wouldst try?”

“SATAN.”

And with that horrible declaration on his lips, the miserable creature walked out—cap and feather set on one side as if to mock his own ruin; limbs feeble, face sinister and pale as ashes, all drawn down as if by age—leaving behind him the close room, the muttered prayers, the coiled hair on the table, and the hearth that crackled on, indifferent, while the house listened to his retreating step on the stair.

A shadow fell, not on Rome, but on a single man moving through Rome as if the streets had become sea and he a boat whose star had been blown out.

Margaret had been the fixed point by which Gerard steered—north in his blood, warmth in his mouth, bread in his hand. When that point went dark, he did not merely grieve; he raged. What stung him was the cruel arithmetic of it: all his watchings and wanderings, his temperance and his prayers, his nights slept hard and his days spent brave—wasted, and worse than wasted. If he had stayed at home, if he had been lazy and selfish like other men, then—so the thought bit and bit again—he might have saved her life.

Two poisons, despair and exasperation, worked together in him like sour wine in a young stomach. His mind, once so orderly, took to breaking its own rules. He rushed at pleasure as men rush at arrows when they are tired of dodging them. In those days, pleasure was not a neat pastime sold in bright wrappers; it was vice with its sleeves rolled up.

He learned the taverns by their sounds before he learned them by their names: the slap of dice on boards, the clack of cups, the hoarse chorus of men trying to drown their own thoughts in other men’s voices. Wine came first—thick, hot, and rough, with a smell like crushed skins and stale barrels; it warmed his throat as if it could warm the place behind his ribs where all had gone cold. Then women, whose laughter rang like coins in a purse, and gaming, whose little rattle of bone and wood could make a night feel busy enough to pass. Whatever could buy him an hour’s excitement, a moment’s oblivion—he paid for it lavishly.

He had money for this, money he had saved with a lover’s thrift, coin meant for Margaret’s comfort. Now he spent it as if scattering it might cover the grave. And because he never did anything by halves, he did not become vicious by halves. He was soon the foremost of companions he had once shunned, loud among the loud, reckless among the reckless. His heart spoiled with his habits; he grew short with gentle words. When his old landlady—homely, sharp-eyed, motherly—dared to press counsel on him, he sulked at her as if advice were an insult. At last he moved away to another quarter, to put distance between himself and both remonstrance and memory.

He could still draw; the old discipline of the hand remained a while after the discipline of the soul had begun to loosen. But even that art betrayed him. His hand shook at times; the fine patience needed for writing and delicate work would not come when his blood was full of fumes and late nights. So he left the pen more and more, and took to likenesses in colours—broad, indulgent strokes, easier to excuse than a line too thin. Yet he neglected even that whenever the idle rakes came to knock and call and laugh him into the street.

He dived in foul waters seeking that sorry oyster-shell, Oblivion.

His humble women friends gossiped of him in low kitchens and over shared loaves; the old landlady, grieving, told Teresa he was “going to the bad,” and begged her to find where he had gone. Teresa, who knew the taste of misfortune and the smell of courage in poor rooms, carried the tale home to her husband, Lodovico, and made him promise to look about.

“Shouldst remember his face, Lodovico mio?” she asked, her voice quiet, as if quietness could keep trouble from hearing.

“Teresa,” said he, “a man in my way of life never forgets a face, least of all a benefactor’s. But thou knowest I seldom go abroad by daylight.”

Teresa sighed, and the sigh seemed to carry all the city’s night-air with it. “And how long is it to be so, Lodovico?”

“Till some cavalier passes his sword through me. They will not let a poor fellow like me take to any honest trade.”

While these poor honest folk fretted in their narrow rooms, chance brought into Gerard’s new lodging one who bore prosperity worse than adversity: Pietro Vanucci. He had been thrust out, late and noisy, by his own landlady; and meeting Gerard in the street, greeted him with a warmth that belonged less to affection than to appetite for company. Soon after, Pietro installed himself in the same house.

He brought with him a lad named Andrea, who ground his colours, ran his errands, learned his tricks, and served him as model besides—being a youth of rare beauty and sharp as a needle. Pietro remembered old times enough to profess friendship; Gerard, in whom warmth seemed burned away, received the protestations coldly, as one receives rain when already drenched.

A fine acquaintance it was. Pietro was not merely a libertine; he had the sourness of one who despises what he pursues. Half misanthrope, open infidel, he made mock of piety as lightly as he made mock of fidelity, and yet clung to companions as if he could not bear to hear his own thoughts. So they ran together like mismatched dogs, coupled by accident and habit rather than kinship.

One day—when Gerard’s health had begun to show the underground labour he was doing to himself, and the bloom of his face had faded as fruit fades left too long in heat, and much of his money had found its way into other men’s pockets—Vanucci devised a revel that pleased the town’s idle mouths.

They were to mount the Tiber in a galley drawn from the bank by buffaloes—great blunt-brained brutes newly brought to Rome, a novelty Lorenzo de’ Medici had set in fashion elsewhere. Vanucci, beggar on horseback, must needs be drawn by monsters to prove himself a conqueror of novelty. Each libertine was to bring a lady, and she must be handsome or he should pay a fine; and he whose companion was adjudged the loveliest should be crowned with laurel and proclaimed a public benefactor. So did they read virtue: “Vir bonus est quis?”—a good man is he that brings the prettiest sin.

A splendid galley was hired; twelve buffaloes were yoked; the riverbank filled by degrees with silks, laughter, and the clink of flasks. The air smelled of wet rope, animal breath, and perfume fighting sweat. Men called to one another, women’s voices rose and fell like birds in a marketplace, and the Tiber made its old thick sound, patient as always beneath their froth.

But Gerard did not come.

They waited; impatience began to nip the merriment. Vanucci excused him with a sneer made smooth.

“I heard him say he had forgotten to provide himself with a fardingale. Comrades, the good lad is hunting for a beauty fit to take rank among these peerless dames. Consider the difficulty, ladies, and be patient!”

At last Gerard was seen in the distance, leading a female by the hand.

“She is long enough,” said one woman, measuring from afar with a jealous eye.

“Gemini, what steps she takes,” said another.

“Oh, it is wise to hurry into good company,” Vanucci answered, laughing, and the party made ready with their little stings.

But when the pair came up, satire choked in their throats.

Gerard’s companion was a peerless beauty—a figure that made the rest of the boat-load seem, in one glance, like candles beside a sun. Tall without being too tall; straight as a thrown spear yet supple as a young panther. Her face was a clean oval; her forehead white; her cheeks a rich olive with living blood mantling below. Her eyes—glorious, dark, and large—were fringed with long thick lashes that looked made to sweep hearts into captivity by the half-dozen. Her lips were red and saucy; her teeth ivory. She carried herself with a bold ease, as if all the world were a stage and she had paid for it.

The women drooped visibly, their mouths tightening as if they had bitten something bitter. The men broke into shouts, waving caps; one enthusiast even went down on his knees on the gunwale and hailed her as divine. His own chere amie answered by pulling his hair, and the goddess by giving him a small kick; the man sprawled, and she stepped lightly over his body as if he were part of the decking, taking her place at the prow without deigning him a glance.

Pietro Vanucci sat in collapse, staring at her, gaping like a fish on a board. Then his look narrowed, as if some private delight had begun to coil.

The drover spoke to the buffaloes; ropes tightened; the beasts leaned, and the galley began to move up-stream with a slow, stubborn drag. The animals’ breathing came in deep bellows; their hooves on the damp bank made a dull, sodden percussion. The river murmured thickly under them, and the city’s noises—vendors’ cries, distant bells, the slap of oars from other boats—wove themselves into a coarse tapestry.

“What think ye of this new beef, mesdames?” one gallant cried.

“We ne’er saw monsters so viley ill-favoured,” answered a lady, wrinkling her nose. “With their nasty horns that make one afeard, and their foul nostrils cast up into the air. Holes be they; not nostrils.”

“Signorina,” returned another with mock gravity, “the beeves are a present from Florence the beautiful. Would ye look a gift beef i’ the nose?”

“They are so dull,” objected a lively one. “I went up Tiber twice as fast last time with but five mules and an ass.”

“Nay, that is soon mended,” cried a gallant. He sprang ashore, drew his sword, and, despite the drovers’ protests, went down the line goading the dozen buffaloes. Steel flashed; the beasts snorted and whisked their tails—but they went no faster. The boat-load laughed loud and long, the laughter bouncing off the water and coming back oddly hollow.

At last he prodded a patriarch bull. The bull turned instantly on the blade, took the spark on its long horns, and with a furious jerk of its prodigious neck tossed him into the air. The man described a brave parabola and fell sitting into the yellow Tiber, still unconsciously waving his glittering sword.

The laughing ladies screamed and wrung their hands—all but Gerard’s fair companion. She uttered something very like an oath, seized the helm with quick competence, and steered the boat out so the swimmer would not be sucked under or struck. The gallant came up sputtering, gripped the gunwale, and was hauled in dripping, his doublet pierced, his skin spared by fortune’s mockery.

He glared round, confused and peevish. “I understand not that,” said he. “How ’tis that one moment a gentleman is out yonder a-pricking of African beef, and the next moment—”

“Disporting in his native stream,” said Gerard’s companion coolly, as if she had been born with a river in her mouth.

“Tell him not, a soul of ye,” cried Vanucci. “Let him find out ’s own riddle.”

“Confound ye all,” growled the spark. “I might puzzle my brains till doomsday, I should ne’er find it out. Also, where is my sword?”

“Ask Tiber!” returned the beauty. “Your best way, signor, will be to do it over again; and, in a word, keep pricking of Afric’s beef, till your mind receives light. So shall you comprehend the matter by degrees, as lawyers mount heaven, and buffaloes Tiber.”

A chevalier declared that the speaker transcended the sons of Adam in wit as much as she did the daughters of Eve in beauty. Compliments rained; she wore them as one wears sunlight—without gratitude, without shame.

Pietro’s conduct was singular. His staring had ceased; he sat coiled, snake-like, mouth muffled, bright eyes fixed on her, twinkling and scintillating with a secret glee. Yet she returned him no special notice. Her eyes swept him now and then, calm as a broom sweeping a floor, scarcely distinguishing him from benches and rope.

Soon the party’s harmony cracked. The women, mortified by the men’s attention to this newcomer, began to pick her to pieces, first under breath, then with small audible barbs. The lovely creature showed that if she was rich in beauty she was poor in feminine tact. Instead of revenging herself through the men as women of the world do, she let herself overhear and answered openly.

“There is not one of you that wears Nature’s colours,” said she, loud enough to sting. “Look here.” And she pointed rudely in one lady’s face. “This is the beauty that is to be bought in every shop. Here is cerussa; here is stibium; and here purpurissum. Oh, I know the articles—bless you—I use them every day; but not on my face, no thank you.”

Pietro’s eyes twinkled nearly out of sight.

“Why, your lips are coloured, and the very veins in your forehead—not a charm but would come off with a wet towel. And look at your great coarse black hair like a horse’s tail, drugged and stained to look like tow. And then your bodies are as false as your heads and your cheeks, and your hearts I trow. Look at your padded bosoms, and your wooden-heeled chopines to raise your little stunted limbs up and deceive the world. Skinny dwarfs ye are, cushioned and stultified into great fat giants. Aha, mesdames—well is it said of you, grande—di legni: grosse—di straci: rosse—di bettito: bianche—di calcina.”

The retort flew back at once.

“Avaunt, vulgar toad, telling the men everything. Your coarse ruddy cheeks are your own, and your little handful of African hair. But who is padded more? Why, you are shaped like a fire-shovel.”

“Ye lie, malapert!”

“Oh, the well-educated young person! Where didst pick her up, Ser Gerard?”

Gerard, roused by the shrill rise of voices from a black reverie, lifted his head as if waking from fever. “Hold thy peace,” said he. “Be not so insolent. The grave shall close over thy beauty as it hath over fairer than thee.”

“They began,” she said petulantly, but her eyes softened toward him.

“Then be thou the first to leave off.”

“At thy request, my friend.” She leaned and whispered him, and for a moment her tone lost its bravado and became almost tender. “It was only to make you laugh; you are distraught, you are sad. Judge whether I care for the quips of these little fools, or the admiration of these big fools. Dear Signor Gerard—would I were what they take me for! You should not be so sad.”

Gerard sighed, deep as if it came from under ruins, and shook his head. Yet the young voice, earnest beneath its impudence, moved him; he lifted his hand and caressed her jet-black locks, not like a lover but as one strokes an affectionate creature that follows him faithfully.

At that moment another galley, drifting slowly down-stream, got entangled for an instant in their ropes. The Tiber turned there; their boat had shot out; the stranger slid between them and the bank. Under a canopy sat a lady of great beauty, with gallants and dependents behind her like a carved retinue.

Gerard looked up. It was the Princess Claelia.

Colour rose to his face—shame, memory, the ghost of a nobler self. He withdrew his hand from the black hair as if it had burned him.

His companion, however, broke into admiration, careless as a bird. “Aha! ladies,” she cried, “here is a rival an ye will. Those cheeks were coloured by Nature—like mine.”

“Peace, child! peace!” Gerard said quickly, low and urgent. “Make not too free with the great.”

“Why, she heard me not,” the girl returned, delighted. “Oh, Ser Gerard, what a lovely creature!”

Two of the women had been whispering together, casting glances at Gerard’s companion. Now one addressed her with a false sweetness.

“Signorina, do you love almonds?” she asked, showing a lapful.

“Yes, I love them—when I can get them,” the other answered, eyeing the nuts with desire she did not care to hide. “But yours is not the hand to give me any, I trow.”

“You are much mistook,” said the second. “Here, catch!” And she flung a double handful into the beauty’s lap.

In the instant, the receiver snapped her knees together by an instinct too swift to counterfeit.

“Aha! you are caught, my lad,” cried the almond-thrower, triumphant. “’Tis a man; or a boy. A woman still parteth her knees to catch the nuts the surer in her apron; but a man closeth his for fear they should fall between his hose. Confess now—didst never wear fardingale ere to-day?”

“Give me another handful, sweetheart, and I’ll tell thee,” the beauty replied, calmly cracking an almond as if the world’s discovery were a small thing.

“There!” cried one. “I said he was too handsome for a woman.”

“Ser Gerard, they have found me out,” observed the epicaene, with perfect composure.

The libertines protested it was impossible, and stared as if their eyes could force the truth back into womanhood again. Pietro Vanucci, however, burst in, and reminded them of an old dispute in which they had laughed him and Gerard to scorn for saying that men were as beautiful as women to a true artist’s eye.

“Where are ye now?” he cried, delighting in their discomfiture. “This is my boy Andrea. And you have all been down on your knees to him. Ha! ha! But oh, my little ladies, when he lectured you and flung your stibium, your cerussa, and your purpurissum back in your faces—’tis then I was like to burst; he that grinds my colours. Ha! ha! he! he! he! ho!”

“The little impostor! Duck him!” cried a man, stung at being fooled.

“What for, signors?” Andrea cried in dismay, and his rich carnation faded beneath the sudden fear.

But the women, swift in their changes, flocked around him, shielding him with hands and laughter, as if tenderness were a cloak they could throw on and off at will.

“The dear child! How well his pretty little saucy ways become him.”

“Oh, what eyes and teeth!”

“And what eyebrows and hair!”

“And what lashes!”

“And what a nose!”

“The sweetest little ear in the world!”

“And what health! Touch but his cheek with a pin the blood should squirt.”

“Who would be so cruel?”

“He is a rosebud washed in dew.”

So they revenged themselves for their beaux’ earlier admiration by lavishing all their fondness on Andrea now.

But one man sat among these butterflies and was no longer of them. The passing glimpse of Princess Claelia had torn open Gerard’s wound, as a snag tears a garment already thin. Three months ago scarce, he had refused her—a love illicit and mad, yet refined in its very danger. He had been able then to stand in loyalty, as a man stands in clean air and thinks he can breathe forever. Now—what was he?

He had blushed to have Claelia see him with such company. Yet it was his daily company. He leaned over the gunwale, silent, watching the river’s thick glide and hearing in it an invitation. The buffaloes’ hooves thudded on the bank; the rope creaked; the galley’s boards groaned; above it all rose the shrill human laughter—noise meant to be music, music meant to be forgetfulness. None of it soothed. It only made the stillness inside him more absolute.

From that hour another phase of misery began and grew upon him. Some fools try to drown care in drink; the fumes vanish, and care remains, heavier, because the body has been poisoned and the spirit lowered. Gerard’s whole conduct had been of a piece with those maniacs. To survive his blow he needed all his forces—his virtue, his health, his labour, the calm sleep that is labour’s satellite; above all, his piety. Yet he flung these balms away and trusted to moral intoxication.

Its brief fumes fled. The bereaved heart lay still heavy as lead within him, and now the dark vulture Remorse sat upon it and tore.

Broken health; means wasted; innocence fled; Margaret parted from him by another gulf wider than the grave—by his own defilement. The hot fit of despair passed. The cold fit came, and it numbed instead of burning.

Then he spurned his gay companions and all the world. He wandered alone. He drank wine alone, not for company now, but as a drug—trying to stupefy himself, to paralyze for a moment the dark foes that preyed upon his soul. He walked among the temples of old Rome, where echoes live longer than men; he lay stony-eyed among the ruins, worse wrecked than they, and the city’s sounds—cart-wheels, distant singing, the hammer on an anvil, the far-off chant from a church—came to him as if from another life, not his. Even the river’s voice seemed to speak a language he could not translate into comfort.

Last came the climax to which solitude—gloomy, fascinating foe of diseased minds—pushes the hopeless. He wandered at night by dark streams and eyed them, and eyed them, with repugnance slowly lessening. There glided peace—perhaps annihilation. What else was left him?

Such spells have been broken by kind words, by loving and cheerful voices. The humblest friend the afflicted possesses may speak, or look, or smile, and stand like a sunbeam between him and that worst madness. Where was Teresa? Where the hearty old landlady? Their homely swiftness would have seen; their plain affection would have saved. But they knew not where he lodged now, nor where he walked, nor how near he slid to the edge.

Was there no mortal eye upon the poor wretch and the dark road he went?

Yes—one eye watched him; marked his steps abroad; tracked him home.

And that eye was the eye of an enemy. An enemy to the death.

The chamber had been dressed for triumph, yet it felt like a lair. Striped and spotted pelts lay in careless pomp upon the floor, their long hairs catching the lamplight like watered silk; the walls held heavy hangings that swallowed sound until every small noise—an ankle-ring’s faint chink, a curtain’s hush—came sharp as a knife-edge. The lady who sat there seemed not to breathe with the room. She sat rigid, arms thrust forward, hands half clenched as though she were kneading some invisible, bitter dough that would not soften. The colour ran and fled in her cheeks; now a feverish flush, now a pallor like stone. Her foot worried the carpet without cease, tapping out a restless, broken rhythm that made the skins seem to quiver.

A domestic drew the curtain that screened the outer door. The soft scrape of the ring against the rod was loud in that muffled place. The lady’s brow darkened and burned.

In an awe-struck whisper the maid said, “Altezza… the man is here.”

“Admit him.”

She snatched up a little black mask. It covered her as quickly as a lid shuts upon a flame. The colour went out of her face at once, and the black upon the whiteness made her look carved, cold, and dreadful—like marble that has been bruised.

The man entered bowing and scraping, a figure so common that a crowd could have yielded a hundred like him: cropped hair, roundish head, plain decent clothes, features neither fair nor foul. Only his eye would not be still; it darted, watched, measured, as if it listened with the pupil. After a profusion of reverences he stood opposite her, waiting as tools wait.

“They have told you for what you are wanted?” she asked.

“Yes, Signora.”

“And those who spoke to you—did they agree what you are to receive?”

“Yes, Signora. It is the full price, and it purchases the greater vendetta—unless of your benevolence you choose to content yourself with the lesser.”

She drew herself a hair’s breadth back, as one does from a smell that offends. “I understand you not.”

“Ah.” He spread his hands with the patience of a man explaining weights to a buyer. “This is the Signora’s first. The lesser vendetta is the death of the body only. We watch our man come out of a church; or take him in an innocent hour; and so deal with him. In the greater vendetta we watch him, and catch him hot from some unrepented sin, and so slay his soul as well as his body. But this vendetta is not so run upon now as it was a few years ago.”

A little shiver ran over the white of her throat above the mask; her fingers tightened until the nails bit into her own palm. “Man—silence me his tongue, and let his treasonable heart beat no more. But his soul I have no feud with.”

“So be it, Signora.” His voice showed no surprise; it was as level as a board. “He who spoke to me knew not the man, nor his name, nor his abode. From whom shall I learn these?”

“From myself.”

At that, for the first time, anxiety touched him; it flickered in the restless eye. “Signora,” he said quickly, “be cautious. Be particular. In this part of the business a word amiss is like salt mistaken for sugar—it spoils all.”

“Fear me not.” Her voice struck like flint. “Listen. It is a young man—tall of stature; auburn hair; dark blue eyes; an honest face that would deceive a saint. He lives in the Via Claudia, at the corner house—the glover’s. In that house lodge but three males: he; and a painter, short of stature and dark-visaged; and a young slim boy. He that hath betrayed me is a stranger, fair, and taller than thou art.”

The bravo drank the particulars as a cook drinks the recipe that will make or mar the dish. He nodded once. “It is enough.”

She lifted one hand, commanding. “Stay. Haunteth he any secret place where thou mayst deal with him?”

“My spy”—the word came out with a bitter relish—“doth report me he hath of late frequented the banks of Tiber after dusk; doubtless to meet his light o’ love, who calls me her rival. Even there slay him. Let my rival come and find him—the smooth, heartless, insolent traitor.”

“Be calm, Signora. He will betray no more ladies.”

“I know not that.” Her breath made the mask seem to stir. “He weareth a sword, and can use it. He is young and resolute.”

“Neither will avail him.”

The certainty in the man’s tone stung her pride into scrutiny. “Art so sure of thy hand? What are thy weapons?”

He answered not with boasting but with a show, as if laying out knives upon a board. He held up a steel gauntlet. “We strike with such force we need must guard our hand. This is our mallet.”

Then, with a practised motion, he undid his doublet and gave her a glimpse of mail beneath—small linked rings, hard as scales. Last, he laid a glittering stiletto upon the table. The metal caught the lamplight and threw it back in a thin, cold line.

She shuddered—one involuntary tremor, the flesh remembering what the mind commands it to forget. Then she took up the dagger in her white hand and tried its point against her finger, as a housewife tests a new blade on the skin of an apple.

“Beware, madam,” said the bravo, sharply.

“What—is it poisoned?”

“Saints forbid! We steal no lives. We take them with steel point, not drugs. But ’tis newly ground, and I feared for the Signora’s white skin.”

“His skin is as white as mine,” she said, and for a breath a strange pity gleamed through the anger, like a pale flame seen through smoke. It died as quickly as it came. “But his heart is black as soot. Say—do I not well to remove a traitor that slanders me?”

“The Signora will settle that with her confessor. I am but a tool in noble hands—like my stiletto.”

She did not seem to hear him. Her thoughts went racing, not in the language of prayer, but in the quick, stinging idiom of pride wounded in its own house. “Oh, how I could have loved him—to the death—as now I hate him. Fool! He will learn to trifle with princes; to spurn them and fawn on them, and prefer the scum of the town to them, and make them a by-word.”

She looked up, and the black mask made the movement terrible, as if some idol had turned its face. “Why loiter’st thou here? Haste thee. Revenge me.”

“It is customary,” he said without change of tone, “to pay half the price beforehand, Signora.”

“Ah—I forgot; thy revenge is bought.” She thrust a bag across the table; the coins within made a heavy, clotted sound, dull as a mortar’s thud. “Here is more than half. When the blow is struck, come for the rest.”

“You will soon see me again, Signora.” And he retired with the same bows and scrapings, the humbleness of a man who can kill.

When he was gone, the room seemed to expand, as if it had been holding its breath with him. The princess sat where he had left her, still masked, arms straight out before her, the nails of her clenched hand nipping the table’s edge. So sat the fabled sphinx; so sits a tigress—motionless, yet full of crouched violence.

And yet, when the hired step had ceased upon the stones outside, a chill crept upon her. In the silence she could hear more than she wished: the faint drip of a fountain beyond the wall, the far-off call of a watchman, the whisper of the hangings as the air shifted. Those small honest sounds, unbought and unbribed, made her mood waver. Misgivings rose in her like a cold vapour from a river at dusk—precursors of a remorse that would be too late to serve.

For Gerard and Margaret were before their age.

This was the true mediaeval creature: proud, amorous, vindictive, generous, foolish, cunning, impulsive, unprincipled—and ignorant as dirt. Power is the curse of such a nature. Had she been forced to do her crimes with her own hands, the weakness of her nerves might have balanced the violence of her passions; her bark would have been worse than her bite. But power gives a feeble furious woman male instruments; and that unholy joining is terrible in its effect.

Here it had whetted an assassin’s dagger for a poor, forlorn wretch—one who, even now, was but meditating suicide.

Two days after that sore encounter of his soul, Gerard, driven by mere restlessness, strayed through one of the poorest lanes of Rome, where the houses crouched close as if for warmth, and the gutters ran black with yesterday’s washings. The sky had been sulky all morning; then, without warning, it broke. Thunder rolled over the tiles like cartwheels on a bridge, and rain came down in a hard, slanting sheet that made the street hiss and sparkle. The city’s usual din—hawkers, sandals, quarrels—was blotted and replaced by the rain’s iron drumming, the gurgle of sudden rivulets, and the deep animal groan of the storm.

He took refuge in a low hostelry whose door breathed out sour warmth: wet wool, old smoke, vinegar, and the sharp bite of cheap wine. The room was narrow and dim, with a hearth that struggled under damp wood; it gave more smell than heat—resin, soot, and a faint, stubborn sweetness where some cook had spilled must or honey long ago and it had baked into the stones.

“Wine,” said Gerard; and because the rain would not ease, and because the noise of the water on the roof seemed to hammer his thoughts flat, he drank again and again—thin red stuff that rasped the throat and left a bitter, leathery aftertaste. It dulled him not into comfort but into a heavy half-stupor, as if his head were packed in wool. He leaned forward, his hands on the table, his forehead on his hands, and dozed in the mixed perfume of damp cloaks, garlic, and stale lees.

By degrees the room filled. Men shook the rain from their hoods; benches scraped; cups clacked; voices rose—coarse laughter, oaths, arguments that burst and died like sparks. The storm outside made its own choir: thunder far off, rain nearer, and in the pauses the long, watery drip from the eaves. That layered sound—the world’s great drum above, the petty clatter within—brought Gerard back to a dull awareness.

Near him, two figures spoke low, close enough for their words to thread into his stupor. One, by his wallet and the confident swing of his hand, was a pardoner—one of those merchants of mercy that haunted roads and taverns, selling heaven in measured portions. The other wore clean but modest clothes such as a decent tradesman might; yet he had pulled his hat down over his brows in a way that hid his face and left only his beard to show. That slouched brim was an old language in Rome: it meant, “Do not know me.”

They were bargaining, not over bread or oil, but over sin itself; and in that traffic—common enough in those days—the wares were not yet delivered. The crime to be forgiven was still to be done, purchased beforehand under a sort of celestial contract.

The man with the hidden eyes grumbled at the price.

“If they go up any higher,” said he, “we poor fellows shall be shut out of heaven altogether.”

The pardoner answered with practiced indignation, the way a butcher denies his scales are false.

“Indulgences were never cheaper to good husbandmen.”

The other gave a short, dry laugh, as if at a jest without mirth. “Who are they?”

“Why,” said the pardoner smoothly, “such as sin by the market, like reasonable creatures. But if you will be so perverse as go and pick out a crime the Pope hath set his face against, blame yourself, not me!”

Then, to prove his point—like a cook unrolling a cloth of spices to show there is something for every purse—he drew out a written parchment and read a scale of prices. Gerard, with his head still bowed, heard the murmured catalogue drift through the tavern’s smells and sounds: rain, smoke, wine, and that low, obscene arithmetic. It was a curious list—too foul for clean ink here—yet it had the cold exactness of an account-book, as if a soul were merely another measure to be bought, like salt by the handful. Some sins, that many a layman would call light, carried a higher fee than the taking of a life; and the taking of a layman was named almost as casually as ordering a cup topped.

That was the pivot of the bargain. A little haggling followed—small concessions, like pennies tossed across a board. At last the coin clinked, and the pardoner’s hand closed upon it with the quick certainty of long habit. The buyer, by that payment, was absolved in advance for removing one layman. For the disposing of a clerk the rate bore no proportion; but the man under the slouched hat had not come to pay that dearer sum. Neither of them spoke the word that would have made the deed sound like what it was. They did not say “assassination.” They spoke as traders speak, trimming words as a fishmonger trims off heads and entrails, to leave only what sells.

All of it buzzed in Gerard’s ear, thickened by drink and grief. He did not lift his head. He listened, stupidly, as one listens to a nightmare while unable to wake.

When the two rose and parted—one to go on selling pardon like rancid oil sweetened with honey, the other to go purchase blood with clean coin—Gerard half raised his face. The lamplight caught his eyes; they were dark and raw with sleeplessness. He followed the departing figure with a scowl that was almost a snarl.

“If Margaret was alive,” he muttered hoarsely, “I’d take thee by the throat and throttle thee, thou cowardly stabber.”

His voice cracked on the name, as if it were a word in a language he could not bear to lose, yet could not speak without pain.

“But she is dead; dead; dead.” The tavern noise seemed to pull back, as if even the rude guests had moved away from that utterance. “Die all the world; ’tis nought to me: so that I die among the first.”

He stumbled home afterward through the washed streets, where the storm had left the stones shining like black glass and the air smelled momentarily cleaner—wet lime, wet dust, the sharp green of bruised leaves. Yet even that freshened breath of Rome could not reach whatever had gone numb in him. The city’s sounds—water running, distant bells muffled by rain, the occasional shout—came to him as if through a wall.

And when he turned into his own way, he saw, on the opposite side, a man in a slouched hat walking briskly to and fro, as if measuring the street with his feet. The brim hid the face; only the beard showed, and the posture of one who will not be looked at.

“Why, there is that cur again,” thought Gerard.

But he was in such a mind that the sight, though it ought to have struck fire in him, fell like a spark into wet ash. He went on, taking no heed; and the rain, still dripping from roofs and ledges, kept up its steady, indifferent music behind him.

Two nights after, Pietro Vanucci and Andrea sat with the board laid and supper cooling itself into reproach, waiting on Gerard.

The lamp made a small island of light on the table. Beyond it the lodging was all shadow and ticking stillness, broken only by the faint creak of the settling beams and the distant night-noises of Rome—an oar-charm from some late boatman far off, a dog that barked once and thought better of it, the thin cry of a seller packing up his tray. But here, within, the loudest thing was the food losing its voice: the crackle of a crust gone quiet, the steam no longer singing from the dish, the smell of warm bread turning from invitation to accusation.

Pietro had done what he always did when his mind was uncertain: he had made order. The trencher was set straight. The knife lay just so. A jug of common wine stood breathing out its tartness. He had even contrived a modest comfort—a little pan of onions softened in oil till they were sweet at the edge, and a handful of herbs bruised between finger and thumb for the scent, because Gerard, when he ate at all of late, had been won less by hunger than by fragrance. Andrea hovered about the table like a faithful hound, sniffing and listening in turns, as if the very air might bring news.

Nine o’clock went by, and the supper, once so full of promise, grew dull and stale, as if it too had lost heart.

Pietro’s patience, which was never fat, began to lean and show its bones.

“At this hour,” said he, drumming his fingers, “a man is either eating, or sleeping, or dead. Go—try his chamber. Perhaps the philosopher hath come in like a ghost and thinks none see him.”

Andrea shrugged, the gesture of one who obeys and doubts in the same breath, and went.

He came back without Gerard; yet he carried something between finger and thumb as carefully as a spice that costs dear. It was a slip of paper.

Andrea could not read—no more than the charity lads that stumble at their letters with a stick at their back—but his eye was quick, and he had learned the look of Pietro’s name upon a page as one learns the shape of a loaf before it is cut.

“That is for thee, I trow,” said he, with a kind of proud craft. “See—the words have thy face.”

Pietro snatched it, and as he read his voice tried to be light, as men do when they feel their insides go cold.

“‘Dear Pietro, dear Andrea, life is too great a burden.’”

He gave a short laugh, and made a jest of it as if jesting could salt away fear and keep it from rotting.

“‘So ’tis, my lad,’” said he aloud, turning the line as though he spoke to Gerard across the table, “‘but that is no reason for being abroad at supper-time. Supper is not a burden.’”

He read on; the lamp flame wavered as if it listened.

“‘Wear my habits!’”

Pietro’s lip curled; he would have mocked, but his cheek had gone pale and his teeth chattered, betraying his brave disdain.

“‘Said the poplar to the juniper bush.’”

He ran his eye downward.

“‘And thou, Andrea, mine amethyst ring; and me in both your hearts a month or two.’”

Pietro looked up sharply; there are gifts that are blessings, and gifts that are last wills. The mention of the ring—Gerard’s ring, so often turned and stared at in brooding—hit Andrea like a blow.

“Why, Andrea?” Pietro said, with a forced levity that cracked at the edge.

But he could not hold it; the paper seemed to grow heavier in his hand. He read the next words, and now the room, with its cooling supper and its obedient stillness, felt suddenly like a chamber where a corpse lies.

“‘For my body, ere this ye read, it will lie in Tiber. Trouble not to look for it. ’Tis not worth the pains. Oh unhappy day that it was born—oh happy night that rids me of it.’”

Pietro’s mouth opened, but no jest came out. Only a dry breath.

“‘Adieu! adieu!

“‘The broken-hearted Gerard.’”

He tried one more time to wrap his fear in sarcasm, as one wraps bitter herbs in bread.

“Here is a sorry jest of the peevish rogue,” said he.

Yet his face was the face of a man who has tasted ashes where he looked for salt; and Andrea, hearing those words, did not believe them. He burst like a jar struck by accident—sound pouring out of him, raw and uncontrollable.

“O, miserable day! O, calamity of calamities! Gerard, my friend, my sweet patron! Help! help! He is killing himself! Oh, good people, help me save him!”

He filled the house with cries. Doors opened. Feet shuffled. Voices rose, drowsy at first, then sharp with alarm. Andrea ran into the street bareheaded, his hair tossed by the night air, imploring every soul he met as if Christ might be found at any corner.

A knot of people gathered—some in nightcaps, some with cloaks flung over their shirts, all reluctant, as folk are reluctant to step from their own hearth into another man’s despair.

“Down to the river?” said one, and spat as if the word itself was unlucky. “No. What business is that of mine?”

“What part of the river?” said another. “It is a wild goose chase.”

“And after sunset?” muttered an old woman, crossing herself. “Too many ghosts walk those banks all night. The water takes what it takes.”

Andrea’s sobbing would not move them; grief is a noise that many men shut their ears against, lest it become their own.

But a lackey—one who had been standing some time opposite the house, watching with the patient stillness of paid eyes—stepped forward.

“I will go,” said he.

His readiness shamed three or four younger men into following, for youth is proud of courage when it costs little. So this small band set off toward the Tiber, Andrea leading like a hound on a scent, the lackey close behind him.

As they walked, the street-sounds altered. There was less laughter and less clatter of pots from taverns. The city’s voice thinned and grew wary. Andrea, gulping tears, told the lackey of the letter and of Gerard’s moody ways of late—the long silences, the untouched bread, the way he stared at the wine as if it were a medicine he dared not drink. Their Italian tongues went fast, words tumbling over one another, until they neared the river.

Then, at the first breath of the Tiber’s air, speech died in every mouth.

The river has its own smell: green and cold, with mud beneath, and a faint rot of reeds. It slid into their nostrils and into their minds, and with it came the hush that falls on men when the world’s great, indifferent things draw near. The night was a calm spring night, the moon bright and clean in a cloudless sky. Their feet, that had seemed ordinary a moment before, now sounded loud and ominous on the stones, as if each step were a knock on some locked door.

Presently, hurrying round a corner, they met a man.

He stopped at sight of them, hesitated as one caught in a net, and the moon showed his face and head. He was bareheaded; his hair clung in wet strands and glittered like fish-scales. His clothes were drenched, water darkening them from collar to hem, and drops fell from him to the ground with a steady patter.

“Here he is!” cried one of the young men, who did not know Gerard’s face and shape well enough to read them in a glance.

At the cry, the stranger turned and fled.

They ran after him with might and main, the sound of their chase striking off the walls. Andrea, desperate as hunger, gained on him; the lackey was next, silent and quick. The fugitive twisted suddenly into a narrow alley. Andrea, too hot and too swift to check himself, shot past the turning, and the others, stumbling after, found themselves in a little labyrinth of lanes where a quickfooted man who knew every stone could vanish like breath from a cup.

For a moment they tried to follow him by ear alone—listening for the slap of wet shoes, the rasp of a breath—but the city swallowed those sounds the way a market swallows a single voice.

They came back, panting, to the spot where the man had stood, and found those who had not run standing there, staring like men in a dream. Pietro, who had followed with the others as far as his fear would drive him, spoke now with a strained certainty.

“That was not he,” said he. “The fugitive had neither the features nor the stature of Gerard.”

“Are ye verily sure?” they demanded, uneasy. “He had been in the river. Why, in the saints’ names, fled he at our approach?”

Pietro’s wit, that usually pricked like vinegar, had gone flat; he looked from face to face, seeking sense where none lay ready.

“Friends,” said he, “methinks this has nought to do with him we seek.” Then, turning upon Andrea, whose eyes were swollen with weeping and whose mouth trembled, “What shall we do, Andrea?”

Here the lackey put in his word, calm as a man who has rehearsed his part.

“Let us track him to the water’s side, to make sure,” said he. “See, he hath come dripping all the way.”

The advice pleased them, for it required action and promised an end. They bent themselves to it. The drops were plain enough on the stones in that moonlight—dark coins spilled from a purse. With very little difficulty they followed the trail.

And soon they met a new enigma.

They had gone scarcely fifty yards when the drops turned away from the river and led them to the gate of a large gloomy building that loomed up like a black cliff: a monastery. They stopped before it, irresolute, and gazed at the dark pile. It seemed to them to hide some horrible mystery, as if men could wash their sins and their secrets alike in the same water.

For a moment none spoke. Even Andrea’s sobbing paused, as if the night itself listened.

But presently Andrea, peering down, gave a shout.

“Here be the drops again!” cried he. “And this road leadeth to the river.”
