They resumed the track. Soon it became plain that the drops were now leading them back toward their own quarter, as if the man had run in circles like a hare that doubles. The closer they drew to the Tiber, the wetter the track grew, until the stones shone with it. At last it took them to the river’s edge.

There, upon the bank, a bucketful seemed to have been flung out of the stream—one heavy splash, and then trickles running back. The sight made them all cry out at once; hope is quick to leap at any shape that resembles its desire. But reflection came hard on its heels.

Certainly a man had been in the water, and had come out again in safety; but that man was not Gerard. The river lay as smooth as oil under the moon, giving back light without giving back truth. It made no sound but the small whisper of itself against stone and weed—voiceless, as if it took pride in keeping what it knew.

One of the men said he knew a fisherman hard by, a fellow with nets and drags.

They found him, roused him, and paid him liberally—silver now, and the promise of gold if he found the body. He listened, half asleep, with the slow, wary look of one who knows the river’s appetite and does not like to bargain with it. Yet money has its own voice, and he agreed.

So nets were sunk below the place, and the dragging went on above and below, ropes grating, water slapping, the fisherman’s men calling to one another in low tones that carried oddly over the calm surface. The sound of rope and water, of men’s short orders and answers, seemed to cut the night into strips.

Andrea and Pietro ran up and down the bank, calling and listening, as if Gerard might answer from behind a willow or from under a boat. The city behind them slept, and the river before them flowed on with that quiet that is not peace but indifference, holding this and a thousand more strange secrets. Now and then a night-bird gave a thin note; now and then the distant bell of a convent marked time with a soft iron mouth. Those sounds—so few, so clear—made their hearts feel larger and more empty, as if the whole world were a listening ear.

At last Andrea, with a cry of sudden hope, ran back toward the house. Pietro watched him go, helpless, as if hope were now something that must be chased on foot.

In less than half an hour Andrea returned. His face told the tale before his tongue could shape it.

“No,” he groaned, and wrung his hands. “No!”

The lackey, who had not spent his breath in running, asked coldly, “What is the hour?”

“Four hours past midnight,” said Andrea, as if each word were a stone laid on a grave.

The lackey drew himself up with a solemnity that might have been pity, or might have been performance.

“My pretty lad,” said he, “say a mass for thy friend’s soul: for he is not among living men.”

The morning broke at last, pale and reluctant. The moon’s white authority faded; the river took on the dull color of pewter. The city’s first sounds—carts beginning far away, a rooster somewhere daring to declare the day—came like insults to their vigil.

Worn out with fatigue, Andrea and Pietro went home, heart-sick. The supper on the table was cold now, its smells turned sour, as if the very food had forgotten its purpose. The days rolled on, mute as the Tiber as to Gerard’s fate.

With the scant signs those men held in their hands, it would have been a marvel if they could have read what had just been written—wet, dark, and irrevocable—upon the river’s brink. Yet there, in that commonplace strip of stone and ooze where the water lapped like a tongue tasting its own story, a thing had taken place so singular that, taken whole, it may have no fellow in the chronicles of men, and perhaps never shall. It can be told in few words—some by the plain voice of the teller, some by the mouth of one who acted in it.

Gerard, after he had written his brief farewell to Pietro and Andrea, stole down at nightfall toward the river. He went as one who has measured every step and will not be turned: that obstinate, household sort of resolve—like dough kneaded past the point of softness—only here it was kneaded toward death. He stuffed his pockets with all the silver and copper he had, not to buy bread or a warm pot, but to weigh his body, that the water might take him quicker and keep him surer.

He chose a part of the stream he had marked before as little frequented. There are some—especially women—who, even in despair, glance about as if to set a witness by their side. But this man’s eye went hunting for the opposite mercy: he looked to be certain there was nobody.

And to his annoyance he saw a single figure leaning against the corner of an alley, as still as a post, as patient as a cat by a pantry door. Gerard, with a forced carelessness, strolled away; then turned back. Lo, the same figure slid out of a side street and loitered there as if the night air were his only business.

“Can he be watching me? Can he know what I am here for?” thought Gerard. “Impossible.”

He went off briskly, took a street or two, made a detour, and returned again, the way a man doubles back to test whether footsteps follow. The man had vanished. But when Gerard cast his gaze round, pricking the dark with suspicion, there—only a few yards behind—was the same shadow, stooping as if to fasten his shoe.

Gerard saw then that he was watched; and at that moment the moon, like a thin coin held up to light, showed him a glint—a steel gauntlet in the sentinel’s hand. The chill of that shine went through him. He knew it for an assassin.

Strange to say, it never entered his mind that his own life was the life in question. He knew of no enemy; he carried no feud in his pocket. The river’s murmur, the distant slap of oars, the small city noises settling down for sleep—these were the sounds that had drawn him; and now another sound, silent as a held breath, pressed behind him.

He turned and walked straight up to the bravo.

“My good friend,” he cried eagerly, as if begging a cook for a last bowl of broth, “sell me thine arm! a single stroke! See, here is all I have;” and he thrust his money into the man’s hands—silver and copper, warm from his body, cold as their purpose. “Oh, prithee! prithee! do one good deed, and rid me of my hateful life!”

And even as he spoke he undid his doublet and bared his bosom to the night air.

The man stared into his face as if he had been offered not a purse but a riddle in an unknown tongue.

“Why do ye hesitate?” shrieked Gerard. “Have ye no bowels? Is it so much pains to lift your arm and fall it? Is it because I am poor, and can’t give ye gold? Useless wretch, canst only strike a man behind; not look one in the face. There, then—do but turn thy head and hold thy tongue!”

With a snarl of contempt at the living and all their bargains, he ran from him, and flung himself into the water.

“Margaret!”

The heavy plunge broke the river’s surface with a dull, bread-dough sound—weight meeting wet—and the stream closed over him, hushing him as a cloth laid over a loaf. At that, the bravo seemed to wake from some stupor of his own. He ran to the bank; and with a strange cry, the assassin plunged in after the self-destroyer.

What followed shall be told by the assassin.

A woman carries her griefs as a man carries his—only she is expected to carry them quietly, like a pot kept from boiling though the fire is fierce beneath. So it had been with Margaret Brandt. Up to that day when she crossed Eli’s threshold in anger, read her sweetheart’s letter, and—against her own intent—found her heart softened into friendship, her troubles had been many; yet she spoke of them as sparingly as a cook salts a broth when there are hungry mouths and little meat. Now the greatest trial drew near, and Gerard was far away.

Eli’s sudden favor might have been a shelter, had she been free to take it. But she was not. In that house were two men whose very looks made the skin behind her ears prickle, as if an unseen fiddle-string had been drawn too tight. She had read malice in their faces and a kind of noiseless understanding passing between them—little signals, swift as a knife’s glint, that told of secrets and of hate. She invented reasons, plausible enough, to stay away. She said she must mind her father; she said she was more at ease at home; she said the walk tired her. She never once named the true reason: dread.

So Catherine came to her instead—Catherine, who had the air of a woman born for nothing but the multiplying and the rearing of the multiplied. There are such, in every town and hamlet: when their own arms at last cease to be burdened with babies, they hover about the younger wives as hens about pullets, clucking, advising, warming, forever making nests where another must lay. Catherine went daily, and wrapped herself in Margaret’s expected hour as if it were her own.

It was in this spirit she begged Eli to let her remain in Rotterdam while he returned to Tergou.

“The poor lass hath not a soul about her,” she said, “that knows anything about anything. What avail a pair o’ soldiers? Why, that sort o’ cattle should be putten out o’ doors the first, at such an a time.”

To Margaret those words were comfort, plain and sustaining as brown bread. Yet comfort did not silence fear. As the time drew nearer she was full of it. She would die. Many died. And Gerard away. There was a loneliness in that thought like a room after a feast, when the platters are scraped clean and the hearth is ashes—only the emptiness was not in her kitchen but in her breast.

Still, life balances itself in odd ways. The very poverty that had bowed her, and her father’s helplessness that had forced her into struggles other girls never knew, now stood her friend. Adversity’s hard hand had long ago driven her from softness. She had learned to be always on her feet, always doing—scouring, kneading, lifting, stirring—because idleness was a luxury she could not afford. Catherine, wise in the rude wisdom of women, kept her so to the last. “Keep thyself moving,” she would say; “keep the blood warm; keep the house sweet.” So Margaret worked, not in a fever, but steadily—airing linen, setting water to heat, wiping the table, laying by clean cloths as carefully as if she were preparing for a guest of honor.

Outside her door the town went on with its own accustomed music: the gulls crying over the river, a boatman’s call, the faint thud of mallets from some distant cooper’s yard, and now and then the blessed hush that follows when wind drops and even Rotterdam seems to hold its breath. Catherine listened as much as she watched; she liked to know the world by its sounds. A harsh shout in the street could tighten a woman’s nerves more than a sour taste on the tongue; a quiet house, with only the purr of a kettle and the soft pad of feet, could make courage return. Catherine would silence unnecessary clatter as if she were shooing flies from milk.

So it came, one fine evening, just at sunset, when the sky had that pale-gold look of skimmed cream touched with saffron, and the air smelled of cooling brick and river-water, that Margaret’s hour took her. The room was kept dim and warm. Clean sheets lay like fresh flour. Water steamed; cloths were warmed; Catherine’s hands moved with the practised certainty of one who has fed and tended more lives than she can count. The noises of the street seemed to recede, and the house’s own small sounds—the breath, the whisper, the low directions—became the whole world.

When it was done, Margaret lay weak as water, but safe. By her side was a little face—creased, astonished, already searching the air with a mouth that knew nothing and yet demanded everything. And over Margaret’s tired spirit opened, sudden and immense, that heaven women enter when they become mothers, where pain is not denied but transfigured into a fierce, tender joy.

Catherine bent over her, wiping her brow as one wipes a board after kneading, tenderly, to keep it clean and cool.

“Why dost weep, sweetheart?” she asked. “All of a sudden?”

Margaret’s tears slid silently; her hands, so used to work, lay spent upon the coverlet.

“He is not here to see it.”

“Ah, well, lass,” said Catherine, forcing brightness into her voice the way a cook will coax warmth from a dying fire, “he will be here ere ’tis weaned. Meantime God hath been as good to thee as to e’er a woman born; and do but bethink thee it might have been a girl; didn’t my very own Kate threaten me with one; and here we have got the bonniest boy in Holland, and a rare heavy one, the saints be praised for’t.”

“Ay, mother,” said Margaret, and the word mother to Catherine came natural as the smell of bread to an oven, “I am but a sorry, ungrateful wretch to weep. If only Gerard were here to see it. ’Tis strange; I bore him well enow to be away from me in my sorrow; but oh, it does seem so hard he should not share my joy. Prithee, prithee, come to me, Gerard! dear, dear Gerard!”

And with that she stretched out her feeble arms, as if she could draw him bodily across miles by the sheer pull of longing.

Catherine busied herself—folding, rinsing, setting things straight—busywork like stirring a pot you cannot bear to watch; but she avoided Margaret’s eyes. For the cry had pierced her. Hearing her own absent child named so passionately, she felt her throat thicken and her sight blur. She would not let her tears fall where the young mother could see; she turned them into motion, into orders, into the small domestic duties that can sometimes hold a heart together.

Then, when she turned again, Margaret was looking at her with a strange stillness—as if the room had gone quiet in a deeper way than before, as if even the cradle of sound had been altered.

“Heard you nought?” Margaret whispered.

“No, my lamb. What?”

“I did cry on Gerard, but now.”

“Ay, ay, sure I heard that.”

“Well—he answered me.”

Catherine gave a sharp little sound, half rebuke, half fear. “Tush, girl: say not that.”

“Mother, as sure as I lie here, with his boy by my side, his voice came back to me—‘Margaret!’ So.” Margaret’s eyes were wide, not wild; rather, filled with a solemn wonder. “Yet methought ’twas not his happy voice. But that might be the distance. All voices go off sad like at a distance.” She paused, and the wonder melted into a soft radiance. “Why art not happy, sweetheart? and I so happy this night? Mother, I seem never to have felt a pain or known a care.”

And her gaze turned, hungry and adoring, to the child’s small face, lingering there as if drinking it in the way one drinks in the smell of broth after long hunger—slowly, gratefully, beyond words.

That very night Gerard flung himself into the Tiber.

And that very hour, when Margaret heard him speak her name, he cried aloud from death’s jaws and despair’s:

“Margaret!”

Account for it those who can. I cannot.

In the guest-chamber of a Dominican convent there lay a single stranger, spent as a man is spent who has wrestled all night, not with an enemy, but with his own body. The violent retchings that had shaken him like a sail in a squall were over at last; they had left him emptied and trembling, as weak as a child new-born. A great log-fire laboured on the hearth, resinous and sweet, cracking as the sap hissed out; its warmth licked the stone and made a small summer in that cold, high room. By the blaze his garments hung to dry, giving off the sour river-smell of drowned cloth—mud and rank weed and the sharp tang of wet leather—until the fire, little by little, conquered it with smoke and pine.

Beside the bed sat a gigantic friar, solid as an oaken settle. He read aloud from his breviary, the Latin rolling slow and even, like a mill-wheel that will not be hurried. Sometimes the sick man—Gerard—watched him with a dull, questioning gaze, and seemed to catch at the words as at driftwood. At other times he closed his eyes and only moaned, his throat raw, his lips salted with dried vomit and river-water.

The monk at length knelt, his broad brow touching the floor, and prayed for him with a whole body’s devotion; then rose and drew his cloak about him.

“Day breaks,” said he. “I must prepare for matins.”

“Good Father Jerome,” whispered Gerard hoarsely, “before you go—how came I hither?”

“By the hand of Heaven. You flung away God’s gift. He bestowed it on you again. Think on it! Hast tried the world and found its gall. Now try the Church! The Church is peace. Pax vobiscum.”

He went; and Gerard lay back, staring at the dark rafters where the firelight wavered, wondering at the strange turn of events, until weakness folded him down into a doze.

When he woke again the room had altered in those small ways a sick man notes before he knows why: the fire was newly fed; the air had a faint clean scent of warmed water and herbs, as if someone had rinsed a cloth and steeped something bitter in it. And by the bedside sat not the tranquil giant, but a layman—slight, alert—his eye small and restless, darting like a rat’s in lamplight.

He leaned in. “How feel you now, signor?”

“Very—very weak.” Gerard’s tongue felt too big for his mouth. “Where have I seen you before, messer?”

“None the worse for my gauntlet?” The man’s voice held anxious pride. “I was fain to strike you with it, or both you and I should be at the bottom of Tiber.”

Gerard stared, trying to fit memory to this face as one fits a lid to a pot. “What—’twas you saved me? How?”

“Well, signor, I was by the banks of Tiber on—on an errand, no matter what.” He licked his lip; even the motion was quick and wary. “You came to me and begged hard for a dagger stroke. But ere I could oblige you—ay, even as you spoke—I knew you for the signor that saved my wife and child upon the sea.”

A coldness ran through Gerard that was not fever. “It is Teresa’s husband. And an assassin?!!?”

“At your service.” The fellow’s mouth twitched, half grimace, half salute. “Well, Ser Gerard, the next thing was you flung yourself into Tiber, and bade me hold aloof.”

“I remember that,” Gerard muttered; and with the words came a flash of black water, the choking, and the mad sweetness of letting go.

“Had it been any but you, believe me I had obeyed you, and not wagged a finger. Men are my foes. They may all hang on one rope, or drown in one river for me.” He spoke with a brutal simplicity, as if stating the price of fish in a market. “But when thou, sinking in Tiber, didst cry ‘Margaret!’—”

“Ah!” Gerard’s breath caught on the name like a bone in the throat.

“My heart it cried ‘Teresa!’ How could I go home and look her in the face, did I let thee die, and by the very death thou savedst her from? So in I went; and luckily for us both I swim like a duck. You, seeing me near, and being bent on destruction, tried to grip me, and so end us both. But I swam round thee, and”—he lifted his gloved hand, awkwardly apologetic—“receive my excuses—so buffeted thee on the nape of the neck with my steel glove, that thou lost sense; and I with much ado, the stream being strong, did draw thy body to land, but insensible and full of water.

“Then I took thee on my back and made for my own home. ‘Teresa will nurse him, and be pleased with me,’ thought I. But hard by this monastery, a holy friar—the biggest e’er I saw—met us and asked the matter. So I told him. He looked hard at thee. ‘I know the face,’ quoth he. ‘’Tis one Gerard, a fair youth from Holland.’ ‘The same,’ quo’ I.

“Then said his reverence, ‘He hath friends among our brethren. Leave him with us! Charity, it is our office.’ Also he told me they of the convent had better means to tend thee than I had. And that was true enow. So I just bargained to be let in to see thee once a day—and here thou art.”

As he finished, the man let his gaze rest on Gerard with a strange, dog-like affection—pride of possession mingled with genuine concern. But Gerard’s spirit recoiled as if from a snake warmed on the hearthstone. He turned his face away and shut his eyes.

“Ah, thou wouldst sleep,” said the miscreant eagerly, and rose at once, light on his feet. “I go.” He backed out on tiptoe, promising to come every day.

Left alone, Gerard lay with eyes closed—not sleeping, but sinking through thought after thought as through cold water. Saved from death by an assassin. Was not this the finger of Heaven? Of that Heaven he had insulted, cursed, defied. The memory of his blasphemies burned him worse than the river-water in his lungs.

He tried to pray. Words he had learned as a boy came readily to his lips; his mouth could shape them. But his heart would not lift with them. It was as if the true meaning—the very savour and warmth of them—had been taken away, leaving only husk and sound.

“I am doomed eternally,” he whispered, and then louder in his despair, “doomed, doomed.”

At that instant the convent church—close by, yet in another world—sent its great organ-voice through the stone. It did not come like speech, but like weather: a solemn wind filling the room with harmony. Then rose the choir, a full service, the Latin syllables placed like measured steps. Among the voices one soared, a sweet boy’s voice, pure and high, seeming to hover above the rest and yet to spring from them, as a lark’s song springs from the same earth that bears wheat.

Gerard lay still and listened. The sound was not merely heard; it was felt, as the fire’s warmth was felt—entering the ribs, quieting the pulse, settling the mind. In those cadences his own boyhood came back, not as a thought, but as an atmosphere: cloistered mornings, clean rushes on stone, the smell of wax and old wood, and the untroubled certainty of a world ordered by bells.

No earthly dross there, no foul, fierce passions rending and corrupting the soul. Only peace—peace—sweet, balmy peace.

“Ay,” he sighed, the tears coming without his leave, “the Church is peace of mind. Till I left her bosom I ne’er knew sorrow, nor sin.”

And even as he wept, there beamed on him the sweet and reverend face of one he had never thought to see again. It was Father Anselm.

The good priest had come to the convent only the night before last. He was worn with travel, but his eyes were the same as ever—tender, steady, as if they had listened long to the world’s harshness and yet refused to become harsh.

Gerard knew him in a moment and stretched out a shaking hand. “Oh, Father Anselm! You cured my wounded body in Juliers: now cure my hurt soul in Rome! Alas, you cannot.”

Anselm sat by the bedside and laid his hand upon Gerard’s head, and first spoke a few soothing words that were like cool water to a scorched mouth. Then—having learned how Gerard had come there—he grew kind but solemn, and made him feel his crime, and urged him to repentance and to gratitude toward the Divine Power that had thwarted his will in order to save his soul.

“Come, my son,” said he, “first purge thy bosom of its load.”

“Ah, father,” Gerard groaned, “in Juliers I could; then I was innocent. But now, impious monster that I am, I dare not confess to you.”

“Why not, my son? Thinkest thou I have not sinned against Heaven in my time, and deeply? oh, how deeply! Come, poor laden soul; pour forth thy grief, pour forth thy faults; hold back nought! Lie not oppressed and crushed by hidden sins.”

The words—simple, homely, spoken in a tone that carried no curiosity, only pity—broke the last stubbornness in Gerard. He slid from his pillow as far as weakness allowed and, with a sob, was at Father Anselm’s knees, pouring out everything: his sins, his angers, his despair; each confession dragged up like something foul from a well, stinking in the air the moment it saw light, yet lighter once spoken. He sighed and groaned with penitence until his throat ached and his body shook as if the river’s current still ran through him.

When all was told, Anselm’s face did not harden; it saddened.

“Thy sins are great,” said he. “Thy temptation also was great—terribly great. I must consult our good prior.”

He kissed Gerard’s brow and left him to seek the superior, to learn what penance should be laid upon this torn, worn soul.

And lo—Gerard could pray now. Not with the tongue alone, but with the whole being. The phase through which his remarkable mind now passed might be summed in a word: Penitence.

He turned with terror and aversion from the world, and begged passionately to remain in the convent. To one nurtured among cloisters it was like a wounded bird, weary of storms, finding again the gentle nest. The days that followed were made of prayer, mortification, pious reading, and long meditations broken only by the measured music of the house: the bells that divided darkness and dawn; the soft scuff of sandals on stone; the breath and rise of chanting that entered his room like bread enters a hungry body, sustaining him more truly than broth.

Meanwhile, beyond those quiet walls, the world went on with its loud bargains and its sudden cruelties.

The Princess Claelia’s spy returned and told her, with the certainty of a man reporting coin counted, that Gerard was certainly dead, though the manner of his death was not yet known.

For a moment she seemed struck dumb. When at last she found breath, it was not to accuse herself, but to bemoan her lot as one ill-served by tools.

“So soon,” she sighed. “See how swift these monsters are to do ill deeds. They come to us in our hot blood, and first tempt us with their venal daggers, then enact the mortal deeds we ne’er had thought on but for them.”

And yet, ere many hours had passed, her pity for Gerard and her hatred of his murderer rose to fever heat—blood heat; for with such as she, feeling and appetite ran the same course.

“Poor soul!” she cried. “I cannot call thee back to life. But he shall never live that traitorously slew thee.”

She sent and set armed men in ambush, keeping them on guard all day, ready that when Lodovico should come for his money they should fall upon him in a certain antechamber and hack him to pieces.

“Strike at his head,” she commanded, “for he weareth a privy coat of mail; and if he goes hence alive your own heads shall answer it.”

So she sat weeping her victim, and all the while pulling the strings of her machines to shed the blood of a second—for having been her machine to kill the first.

One of the penances novice Gerard laid upon himself was this: when Lodovico came near, he must meet him with gentleness—though, in the hidden place of his mind, the man still felt like something cold and slick that had once slid through blood. He took that task as a fasting of the heart, and for a little while it bit him hard. Yet no abstinence is so wisely chosen as the kind that opens a door; and when a door is once ajar, a whole household of better motions can steal in on their own feet.

At first Lodovico’s bearing had in it something almost laughable—an assassin wearing, as if it were a new velvet doublet, the complacency of having spared a life. He would look at Gerard as a cook looks at a dish that did not burn, and marvel in secret at his own restraint. But it is a great thing, even for a ruined man, to taste the sweetness of saving instead of spoiling. That taste lingers on the palate. It begins as a sharp, surprising note—like vinegar on the tongue—then warms, then calls for bread.

So the miscreant, finding the saving of life pleasant, grew by degrees averse to taking it; and from that aversion stumbled into remorse; and from remorse, as from a dark corridor, into something so like penitence that it began to shape his days. Teresa, who had long managed him as a housewife manages a hearth that will smoke unless watched, helped the change with the one threat she knew would reach him: not for the first time she told him she would leave him—leave him utterly—unless he consented to live honestly.

The good fathers of the convent, who understood that souls, like bodies, sometimes mend better when removed from old air and old sounds, lent their counsel. And so Lodovico and Teresa were sent by sea to Leghorn, where Teresa had friends. There, where the quay creaked under barrels and the tide made its steady lap against stone, the assassin settled down and became a porter.

At first he found it miserably dull work, and said so—said it with the sulk of a man whose ears have been fed on sudden cries and now must learn the long, patient music of labour. A porter’s day has its rhythm like kneading: lift, set down, tighten the rope, bear the weight, breathe. It is not the rattle of a stiletto in a sleeve, nor the quickened hush before a blow. It is the plain chant of bodies at work: the thud of bales, the grating of sledges, the calls of boatmen crossing one another like counterpoint over the water. Dull, yes—but better, one may think, than the brief excitement of being hewn in pieces by Princess Claelia’s myrmidons. His exile saved the unconscious penitent from that end.

The princess, balked of her revenge, turned inward as a lamp turned down too low: she brooded until her very rooms seemed to swallow their echoes, and she fell into a profound melancholy. In her restlessness she dismissed her confessor and took a new one—one with a great reputation for piety—to whom she poured out what she called her griefs.

The new confessor was no other than Fra Jerome.

She could not have fallen into harder hands, nor better. He heard her grimly out—standing like a mast in a storm, letting her words beat against him. Then, as a cook will shake a maid out of her dainty airs when the broth is scorching and there is no time for affectation, he took her and shook the delusions out of her as roughly as if she had been a kitchen-girl dawdling over spice. For, to do this hard monk justice, on the path of duty he feared the anger of princes as little as he did the sea.

He showed her, in a few words all thunder and lightning, that she was the criminal of criminals.

“Thou art the devil,” he cried, “that with thy money hath tempted one man to slay his fellow; and then, blinded with self-love, instead of blaming and punishing thyself, art thirsting for more blood—of guilty men, but not so guilty as thou.”

At first she resisted, for she was used to priests who smoothed and sweetened, like merchants adulterating wine for noble lips; and she told him, with a wounded pride, that she was not accustomed to be taken to task by her confessors. But Fra Jerome did not barter truth. He overpowered her; he threatened her with the Church’s curse here and hereafter; he tore the scales from her eyes as one scrapes burnt crust from a pot; he thundered and crushed her until the lofty lady—so practised in masks and measured speech—sank down and grovelled with remorse and terror at the feet of the gigantic Boanerges.

“Oh, holy father,” she sobbed at last, “have pity on a poor weak woman, and help me save my guilty soul. I was benighted for want of ghostly counsel like thine, good father. I waken as from a dream.”

“Doff thy jewels,” said Fra Jerome sternly.

“I will. I will.”

“Doff thy silk and velvet; and in humbler garb than wears thy meanest servant, wend thou instant to Loretto.”

“I will,” said the princess faintly, as though the sentence had struck the breath from her.

“No shoes; but a bare sandal.”

“No, father.”

“Wash the feet of pilgrims both going and coming; and to such of them as be holy friars tell thy sin, and abide their admonition.”

The princess shivered as if the very word wash had turned the water cold. Yet she whispered, “Oh, holy father—let me wear my mask.”

“Humph!”

“Oh, mercy! Bethink thee! My features are known through Italy.”

“Ay,” he said with a hard contempt, “beauty is a curse to most of ye. Well—thou mayst mask thine eyes; no more.”

On this concession she seized his hand, like a drowning woman snatching at wood, and was about to kiss it; but he snatched it rudely away.

“What would ye do?” he said. “That hand handled the eucharist but an hour agone: is it fit for such as thou to touch it?”

“Ah, no.” Her voice broke into the small sounds of one unmade. “But oh, go not without giving your penitent daughter your blessing.”

“Time enow to ask it when you come back from Loretto.”

Thus that marvellous occurrence by Tiber’s banks left its mark on all the actors, as prodigies are said to do: not only in the great gestures men remember, but in the daily motions—what hands lifted, what feet bore, what mouths learned to confess.

The assassin, softened by saving the life he had been paid to take, turned from the stiletto to the porter's knot. The princess went barefoot to Loretto, weeping her crime and washing the feet of base-born men—learning, with every basin filled and emptied, that the same act cannot be named “grief” by a lady and “sin” by a monk without changing its weight, and that some truths refuse the fine vocabulary of power.

And Gerard—carried from the Tiber into that convent a suicide—now passed for a young saint within its walls. Loving but experienced eyes were on him, watching the quiet signs by which men read souls as bakers read dough: the patience under pressure, the rising after collapse, the steadying of the breath when old temptations hissed like fat in a pan.

Upon a shorter probation than usual, he was admitted to priest’s orders. Soon after, he took the monastic vows and became a friar of St. Dominic. Dying to the world, the monk parted with the very name by which he had lived in it, and so broke the last link of association with earthly feelings.

Here Gerard ended, and Brother Clement began.

“As is the race of leaves so is that of men.”

A great man, like a slow-risen loaf, was swelling unremarked this year in a tailor’s narrow house at Rotterdam; and a large man, loudly trumpeted, was dropping to earth at Bruges.

Philip, Duke of Burgundy, Earl of Holland, and a pageant of other titles besides, lay sick there; and in that age sickness was a question not of Nature’s sober kitchen, but of what meddling hands chose to do to her broth. A poor man fell ill and, if his constitution were stout, might be up again as quietly as a hen returns to her scratching after a shower. But woe to the rich: for where one Mr. Malady carried off his victim, three more were hustled out of life by Dr. Remedy.

The Duke’s ailment had no name then—names are a kind of memory, and memory comes late to pain. We call it now diphtheria: a smothering, weakening thing, like a cloth laid over the mouth of breath. The Duke was old besides; so, to “strengthen” him, the learned remedy was to drain him. They opened him as you would tap a cask, and let out his warmth by the bowlful. Presently he turned cold—marvellous!—as if men had never noticed that you cannot ladle away a man’s life and still expect the pot to simmer.

Then science, impatient as a cook who has burnt the first dish, cried for a stranger experiment.

“Ho! this is grave. Flay me an ape incontinent, and clap him to the Duke’s breast!”

Straightway officers of state scurried, their feet clattering on Bruges stone—an ill-tempered percussion that set dogs barking and made the very rafters of the palace seem to listen. They ran seven ways at once, hunting an ape as if salvation lay in fur and heat. But perdition! the Duke was out of apes. There were buffaloes, lizards, Turks, leopards—any unreasonable beast that men cage and name for sport—anything except the right creature for this bloodthirsty piece of folly.

“Why, there used to be an ape about,” said one. “If I stand here I saw him.”

So there had; but the mastiff had mangled the sprightly thief for stealing his supper. The crunch of bone, the yelp, the sudden silence—those are sounds every courtyard remembers. Thus the dog had obeyed, with honest teeth, the human maxim, “Soyez de votre siecle!”—be of your age; eat what you can, and call it wisdom.

In this need the seneschal cast his desperate eyes around the antechamber, where silk whispered, chain-mail chimed, and every soft shoe tiptoed as if quiet itself could hold back death. This time his gaze did not return empty. A hopeful light leapt into it.

“Here is this,” said he, sotto voce. “Surely this will serve: ’tis altogether apelike, doublet and hose apart.”

“Nay,” snapped the chancellor, sour with fear. “The Princess Marie would hang us. She doteth on this.”

And “this” was Giles—our friend Giles—strutting there, all unconscious, in cloth of gold, making the very air smell of new-dyed wool and rich people’s perfumes, while men weighed him like meat. For in a court, even affection has its price, and language itself becomes a knife: one man says “this,” and another man hears “thing.”

Dr. Remedy, thwarted and growing peevish, flung away the ape and reached for the next rung down the ladder of creatures.

“Then flay a dog. A dog is next best to an ape; only it must be a dog all of one colour.”

So they fetched a liver-coloured dog—poor, whole-coloured wretch that had perhaps known the honest music of fields and kitchens, the scrape of a trencher, the fall of scraps, the familiar calls in some homely dialect of whistle and name. They flayed it; and while its heart still battered its last rhythm against the world, they clapped the palpitating hide upon their sovereign’s breast, as if warmth were a garment you could borrow from the powerless and dress upon the mighty.

He died.

Thus Philip the Good was “scientifically” disposed of; and left behind him thirty-one children, of whom one—somehow or another—was legitimate, and reigned in his stead. The good duke had provided for nineteen out of the other thirty; the rest must shift, like unclaimed loaves in a market, to whatever hands would take them.

According to a Flemish chronicle, the deceased prince was descended from the kings of Troy through Thierry of Aquitaine and Chilperic, Pharamond, and the old kings of Franconia. But in truth this lineage was no distinction: in that day, I have not been able to discover a prince who did not come down from Troy. “Priam” was but the mediaeval way of saying “Adam”—a grand old word that made every lord feel native to every legend, and so helped them forget the plain, local tongue of truth.

The Duke’s body was carried into Burgundy and laid in a noble mausoleum of black marble at Dijon. Holland rang with his death—bells tolling, hoofbeats drumming, sermons swelling in the vaulted echoes—sound after sound thrown upon the air as if noise could prove importance. Yet Holland little dreamed that anything more famous was being born within her territory that year, not with tolling and proclamation, but with the small domestic hush of a working house: the snip of shears, the prick of needle, the soft fall of cloth, a woman’s breath counted between pains.

That judgment has long since been reversed. Men gaze now at the tailor’s house: here, they say, the great birth of the fifteenth century took place. In what house the good duke died “no one knows and no one cares,” as the song says.

And why?

Because dukes like Philip the Good come and go, and leave mankind not a halfpenny wiser, nor better, nor other than they found it. But when, once in three hundred years, such a child is born to the world as Margaret’s son—lo, a human torch, lighted by fire from heaven; and “FIAT LUX” thunders from pole to pole, while the cradle rocks to its own quiet rhythm, and the common sounds of home—spoon against bowl, hearth crackle, a mother’s low speech in her own dear dialect—keep time with a light the powerful never knew how to name.

The Black Friars had once held Rome and Christendom by the throat, not by violence, but by voice—by trained tongues that could turn a market-place into a chapel and make a prince feel poor. Yet now the Order’s power ebbed. The Franciscans, brown and barefoot, took the people’s ear, and the Dominicans, in their black cloaks, felt the world sliding away from them like dough from an unfloured board.

Therefore the prudent heads of the convent were hungry—hungry as men are when a pantry thins—to lay hands on any rare gift, salt it, and send it out where it might preserve what was decaying. Word went quickly through the cloister that young Brother Clement—shaven, pale, newly vowed—had a mouth made for more than prayer: Latin came to him as naturally as breath; Italian, French, high and low Dutch, he moved among them as a cook among herbs, knowing which leaf to bruise and which to keep whole.

It was already spoken, half in admiration and half in policy, that he should be sent to England to preach and to write, to answer Rome as a well-tuned bell answers another across a valley.

But Jerome stood in the way.

“He has still the milk of the world in his veins,” said Jerome to the prior—Jerome whose voice, even in kindness, carried iron filings. “Let not new-born zeal and a meek face cheat us. Try him. Temper him. Better to bend green wood now than find, in the day of need, we have taken a reed for a staff.”

The prior, who had watched many fine promises turn brittle under strain, nodded. “It is well advised. Take him in hand thyself.”

So Jerome took Clement as a man takes a knife to a stone, not to spoil it, but to see if it holds an edge.

One day he led him out beyond the cloister walls, into the sun and noise of a field where young men played at their rough games, shouting and laughing, the sound of it running like a brook through the air. It was a place Clement had known in other days; Jerome knew it too, as a cook knows where the temptations are kept—where the fat hangs, where the sweetmeats lie.

They had not stood long before two citizens passed by, Pietro Vanucci and Andrea—companions of Clement’s former life. Their eyes slid over the two friars as over stones on a road. They did not know their dead friend beneath a tonsure and a habit.

Clement gave a tiny start, like a hand that has touched a hot dish by accident; then he dropped his eyes and said a paternoster, low and swift, as if he would cover the old warmth with prayer.

Jerome’s test came quietly. “Would ye not speak with them, brother?”

“No, brother.” Clement’s voice was steady, though his mouth had gone dry. “Yet it was good for me to see them. They remind me of sins I can never repent enough.”

“It is well,” said Jerome, and his face betrayed nothing. But his report, when he made it, was coldly in Clement’s favour, like watered wine—truth, yet without warmth.

Then Jerome set him to harsher airs.

He brought him to death-beds where the room smelled of sour linen and stale breath, of wax and fear; where the last words rasped out like the last scraping of a spoon in an empty pot. Clement bent over the dying, held their hands, moistened cracked lips, prayed as if prayer were broth to be sipped by a failing body. And after that Jerome took him into dungeons—holes where the air was thick as old stew, where darkness sat on the eyes, and men, coiled in rags and filth, lay like beasts in a pen, their voices half growl, half sob. The place tried Clement’s body hard; the stench clung to his habit and hair as smoke clings to a cook’s sleeve. Yet his soul gathered itself and went among those poor wretches that were not past comfort, and there he shone—gentle, patient, fearless of the foulness of flesh.

Jerome reported: the spirit willing, the flesh weak.

“Good,” said Anselm the prior. “His flesh is weak, but his spirit is willing.”

Yet Jerome had one trial more in store—one that was like the moment a man is forced to watch the killing of an animal, not in the clean economy of a kitchen where death serves life, but in a street where death is a spectacle and the crowd feeds on it with its eyes.

It was seen by many.

On a morning when the sun came up clear and indifferent over Rome, a principal street filled as a granary fills with grain. Heads packed the ways; children were hoisted up onto shoulders; vendors cried out as if it were a fair. The city’s noise—foot-shuffle, cough, the clack of sandals, the murmur of anticipation—made a living skin of sound. Even the air had a taste in it: dust, sweat, and the faint metallic tang that comes before blood is spilled.

The governor of Rome had been found at daybreak in his bed slaughtered—throat cut, temples bruised, his hand hacked off at the wrist as though he had tried to ward the blow. The murderer, traced to his servant, was to pay in kind.

Italian executions were not always cruel; but the city had decided this one must be exact, as if pain could balance a scale.

They brought the criminal first to the murdered man’s house and fastened him for half an hour to the wall, a thing for eyes to gnaw upon. Then they struck off his left hand. A new-killed fowl was split and bound round the stump—some physic of the doctors, a foolish poultice of warm flesh against bleeding; it looked, to any honest observer, like kitchen-work turned grotesque. Then, mutilated and bandaged, he was hurried to the scaffold.

A young friar was beside him—Brother Clement—earnest, affectionate, pressing the crucifix close, his voice thick with pity as he prayed with the man and for him, trying to give the dying a last mouthful of mercy.

The executioner, impatient, hauled the friar aside as one pushes away a child from a fire. In a moment the mallet fell; the culprit dropped; the knife drew a line from ear to ear.

The crowd cried out—not in joy, but in a sudden sick recoil, as if a gust of foul air had struck them.

Clement swooned.

A gigantic monk strode forward and carried him off like a child, his black sleeves swinging; and the crowd, denied its full meal of spectacle, began to buzz again, restless as flies.

Clement went back to the convent with his heart bruised. He confessed to the prior with tears he could not swallow.

“Courage, son Clement,” said Anselm. “A Dominican is not made in a day. Thou shalt have another trial. And I forbid thee to go to it fasting.”

Clement bowed, obedient. The prior spoke as a man who knows the body too has its law: a stomach empty makes the spirit more fragile, as a pot with a thin bottom cracks under heat.

He had not long to wait.

A robber was taken—no trembling servant, but a monster of cruelty who had killed for sport after robbing. Clement spent the last night in prison with him. The cell smelled of cold stone and old straw; outside, Rome’s sound ebbed and flowed like a sea against walls. Clement did not flinch from the man’s breath, nor from the stories that fell from his mouth, greasy with sin. He spoke to him as one speaks to a starving soul, not as a judge but as a cook might speak to a famished beggar—plainly, urgently, with the tender impatience of those who want to save what can still be saved.

In the morning he accompanied him to the scaffold. There, as rope and wood waited, Clement prayed so earnestly that the hardened ruffian wept—tears cutting tracks through grime. He embraced Clement. Clement embraced him too, though his flesh quivered with repugnance; he held the crucifix before the man’s eyes like a last light in a cellar.

They garotted the man. Clement, for a space, lost sight of the crowd entirely; he prayed aloud while that dark spirit struggled through its final choking. When the body sagged dead, the hangman raised a hatchet and began to quarter it on the spot.

Then—oh, the mystery of man’s heart!—the same people who had watched the taking of life with a kind of dull appetite cried out pitifully at each stroke upon the corpse that could feel nothing. Each chop drew a sound from the crowd as if the axe fell on their own bones. Clement shuddered too; but he stood firm, like a rock that vibrates yet will not be thrown down.

And at that moment Jerome’s voice cut in at his ear, sharp as a command in a kitchen when the fire is high.

“Brother Clement, get thee on that cart and preach to the people. Nay, quickly. Strike with all thy force on all this iron, while yet ’tis hot, and souls are to be saved.”

Clement’s colour came and went; his breath hurried. Yet he obeyed. With an ill-assured step he mounted the cart and looked out over that sea of heads. His throat felt parched as if he had swallowed ash; his heart hammered; his voice, when it came, trembled.

But as he spoke, the greatness of the occasion took him—this mingled smell of blood and sun, this crowd still raw with sensation, these faces turned up like bowls waiting to be filled. He told them the robber’s history—fresh from the man’s own lips in the prison—showing the slow steps by which folly becomes crime, the first small yielding that is like tasting a forbidden sweetness and then returning for more. He warned them not to set foot on the first rung of that ladder, because the last rung ends in rope and axe.

Then his voice strengthened. He thundered against shedders of blood; he pleaded for charity and pity; and he felt, to his own astonishment, the crowd’s pulse under his words, as a musician feels a lute answer his touch. He played on them sacredly: sobs, groans, the sudden hush—these were his proof. The air itself seemed to change; the street-noise, for once, became a kind of listening.

Jerome stared as one who goes to light a stick and fires a rocket.

After a time Clement saw Jerome’s astonishment and, finding no plain approval there, broke off abruptly and came down, humble as ever.

“It was my first endeavour,” he said, apologetic. “Your behest fell on me like a thunderbolt. Was I—did I—Oh, correct me, and aid me with your experience, Brother Jerome.”

“Humph!” said Jerome, doubtfully; and after long reflection he added, sullenly, “Give the glory to God, Brother Clement. My opinion is thou art an orator born.”

He reported as much at headquarters, half reluctantly—for Jerome, though disagreeable, was honest.

Not long after, another spectacle gave Jerome occasion to harden Clement further, though here cruelty wore the mask of law and ritual.

Julio Antonelli was accused of sacrilege: three witnesses swore they saw him come from the church at the very hour the candlesticks were stolen. Other witnesses proved an alibi as stoutly. Neither side could be shaken; so, in that doubt, Antonelli was permitted the ordeal by water, hot or cold.

The clergy who believed him innocent recommended the boiling water—an ordeal that, for those favoured, was not always as fierce as words made it. But Antonelli, poor wretch, had not the nerve for the steaming cauldron. He chose the cold.

So they brought him to the Tiber. The river’s voice was steady and indifferent, its surface catching the morning like a sheet of hammered metal. He took the sacrament, then they stripped him naked on the bank, where the crowd pressed close, their murmurs and cries swelling in the open air as if Rome itself were one great throat. They tied him hand and foot, to prevent those struggles by which a man, flinging his arms out of water, can sink his body.

Then they lowered him gently into the stream. For a moment he floated with just his hair above water.

A roar went up from both banks: guilty.

But the ropes were new; they drank the river, grew heavy, and he settled down.

Another roar: innocent.

They left him the appointed time, a little more than half a minute, then drew him up gurgling and gasping—his mouth working like a fish’s, his eyes wild. He screamed for mercy, though he had been granted it; the body, having tasted suffocation, does not reason. After the appointed prayers they dismissed him, cleared of the charge, trembling and alive.

During the whole Clement had stood on the bank and prayed, his lips moving with the river’s sound beneath them.

When it was over he thanked God aloud, his voice loud yet faintly quavering, as if the river had put its cold hand on his throat too.

And then, when the crowd began to drift away, that human tide receding with talk and laughter as if nothing had happened, Clement turned to Jerome.

“Brother,” he asked, “ought not the man to be compensated?”

“For what?”

“For the pain, the dread, the suffocation. Poor soul—he liveth, but hath tasted all the bitterness of death. Yet he had done no ill.”

Jerome’s eyes narrowed. “He is rewarded enough in that he is cleared of his fault.”

“But being innocent of that fault, yet hath he drunk Death’s cup, though not to the dregs; and his accusers, less innocent than he, do suffer nought.”

Jerome answered sternly, as if he would drive a nail into Clement’s soft places.

“It is not in this world men are really punished, Brother Clement. Unhappy they who sin yet suffer not. Happy they who suffer such ills as earth hath power to inflict; ’tis counted to them above, ay, and a hundred-fold.”

Clement bowed his head. “May thy good words not fall to the ground, but take root in my heart, Brother Jerome.”

Yet the severest trial Jerome gave him was not planned. It sprang, as the worst quarrels do, from an indulgent moment and a table where a thing lay open that ought perhaps to have stayed shut.

Jerome, softened for once, went with Clement to the lodgings of Fra Colonna. There upon the table lay a fair copy of “The Dream of Polifilo,” newly written out, the ink still rich and black, the letters standing up like raised crust on fresh bread. Colonna, poor man, was in the pride of his labour, like a chef who has perfected a sauce and cannot wait to have it tasted.

He pointed out what he called a master-stroke.

“For ages,” said he, “fools have been lavishing poetic praise on mortal women—mere creatures of earth, smacking palpably of their origin; sirens at the windows, where our Roman women in particular have by lifelong study learned the wily art to show their one good feature—be it but an ear or an eyelash—at a jalosy, and hide all the rest. Magpies at the door—Capre n’ i giardini, Angeli in strada, Sante in chiesa, Diavoli in casa. Then come I, and ransack the minstrels’ lines for amorous turns, not forgetting those Petrarch wasted on that French jilt Laura; and I lay you the whole bundle of spice at the feet of the only females worthy amorous incense—to wit, the Nine Muses.”

Jerome had been turning pages while he talked. He shut the book with a slap that sounded like a lid on a pot.

“By which goodly stratagem,” said Jerome, “you, a friar of St. Dominic, have produced an obscene book.” He dashed Polifilo down upon the table.

“Obscene? thou discourteous monk!” Colonna flushed as if scalded. He ran round, snatched the manuscript away as a housewife snatches bread from a dog, locked it up, and, trembling with mortification, tried to laugh it off. “My Gerard—pshaw! Brother What’s-his-name had not found Polifilo obscene. Puris omnia pura.”

“Such as read your Polifilo,” said Jerome, “—Heaven grant they may be few—will find him what I find him.”

Colonna swallowed the insult as one swallows a bitter herb—because to spit it out would be to admit its taste. Had he not been in his own lodgings, and a gentleman by birth as well as a scholar, there might have been a vulgar quarrel then and there. As it was he forced the talk into another channel, and brought forth a chrysolite the Cardinal Colonna had lent him. He put it into Clement’s hand, and Clement, who had the trained senses of one who has lived by touch and smell and sight, turned it to the light, watching its green-gold heart kindle.

Colonna began to speak, with the eager exactness of his kind, of the jewel’s virtues—how this stone could strengthen courage, that could preserve chastity, another guard from poison, another from drunkenness. He went the whole length of his age as a worshipper of jewels, believing in the moral flavours of dead stones as some believe certain herbs can cool anger or quicken love.

Jerome would not have it. He expostulated, contempt in every syllable, at the thought that a dead stone could confer valour, chastity, safety, temperance.

“The experience of ages proves they do,” said Colonna. “As to the last virtue you have named, there sits a living proof. This Gerard—pardon, Brother Thingemy—comes from the north, where men drink like fishes; yet was he ever most abstemious. And why? He carried an amethyst, the clearest and fullest-coloured e’er I saw on any but a noble finger. Where, in Heaven’s name, is thine amethyst? Show it this unbeliever!”

“And ’twas that amethyst made the boy temperate?” Jerome asked, with a thin smile.

“Certainly. Why, what is the derivation and meaning of amethyst? a negative, and methua—to tipple. Go to; names are but the signs of things. A stone is not called amethustos for two thousand years out of mere sport, and abuse of language.”

He went through the chief jewels—ruby, sapphire, emerald, opal—spicing each with anecdotes out of grave historians, as a cook seasons a dish with citations, certain that authority improves the flavour.

“These be old wives’ fables,” said Jerome. “Was ever such credulity as thine?”

It stung. Colonna, branded with that word—credulity—writhed; for nothing hurts a learned man more than to be told he is merely gullible. He fell silent. Jerome, mistaking silence for yielding, pressed on, urging him to blot out pagan lore, to study the lives of saints, to cleanse his mind as Christianity had cleansed the earth. In this zealous harangue he repeated, carelessly, some loose theological assertions that sat in the air like half-baked loaves.

Colonna’s pride, already sore from Polifilo, found its revenge. He burst out and flung at Jerome a mountain of crude, miscellaneous learning, sweeping from sculpture to sewers, from Doric columns to Roman roads, with that breathless momentum scholars use when they mean not to convince but to overwhelm.

“The heathen blotted out? Why, they hold four-fifths of the world. And what have we Christians invented without their aid? Painting? Sculpture? These are heathen arts, and we but pigmies at them. What modern mind can conceive and grave such god-like forms as did the chief Athenian sculptors—Dinocrates, Scopas, Timotheus, Leochares, Briaxis, Chares, Lysippus—and the immortal three of Rhodes that wrought Laocoon from a single block? What prince hath the genius to turn mountains into statues, as was done at Bagistan, and projected at Athos? What town the soul to plant a colossus of brass in the sea, for the tallest ships to sail in and out between his legs?

“Is it architecture we have invented? Here too we are but children. Can we match the Parthenon, and for grandeur and finish the theatres of Greece and Rome, or the prodigious temples of Egypt, where men walked awe-struck through avenues a mile long of sphinxes, each as big as a Venetian palace? Those columns of porphyry cut and polished like crystal—not rough-hewn like our puny work. Even now their broken pillars lie o’ergrown with acanthus and myrtle, sparkling still, flouting the slovenly art of modern workmen. Is it sewers, aqueducts, viaducts? Why, we have lost the art of making a road—lost it with the world’s greatest models under our very eye.

“Is it sepulchres? No Christian nation has erected a tomb the sight of which does not set a scholar laughing. Think of the Mausoleum, the Pyramids, the monstrous sepulchres of the Indus and Ganges—mountains without, mines of precious stones within. Ah, you have not seen the East, Jerome, or you could not decry the heathen.”

Jerome, who could endure a blow better than a lecture, cut in: these were material things; true greatness lay in the soul.

“Well then,” cried Colonna, “in the world of mind, what have we discovered? Geometry? Logic? We are all pupils of Euclid and Aristotle. Written characters—almost divine—we no more invented than Cadmus did. Poetry? Homer hath never been approached by us, nor Virgil, nor Horace. Tragedy or comedy? Poets, actors, theatres—all fell to dust at our touch. Have we revived them? Compare our miserable mysteries, frigid personification and dog Latin, with a Greek play—decoration costing a hundred thousand crowns—performed inside a marble miracle, the audience a seated city, and the poet a Sophocles.

“What then have we invented? Monotheism? The learned Greeks and Romans held it; even their poets were monotheists in their sleeves. Zeus estin ouranos, Zeus te gy, Zeus toi panta—saith the Greek; and Lucan echoes him: Jupiter est quodcunque vides, quocunque moveris.

“Their vulgar were polytheists; and what are ours? We have not invented invocation of saints. Our sancti answer to their Daemones and Divi; they prayed to deified mortals to intercede with higher divinity. The rude among them worshipped those they should have invoked. So do our mobs—by unbroken tradition. In holy writ is no polytheism of any sort.

“We have not invented so much as a variety of polytheism. The pagan vulgar worshipped deified mortals; each had his favourite, to whom he prayed ten times for once to the Omnipotent. Our vulgar worship canonized mortals; each has his favourite, to whom he prays ten times for once to God. Call you that invention? Invention is in the East.

“Among the ancient vulgar only mariners were monotheists; they worshipped Venus and called her Stella maris, Regina caelorum. Among our vulgar only mariners are monotheists; they worship the Virgin Mary and call her Star of the Sea, Queen of Heaven. Their new religion? An old doublet with a new button.

“Our vulgar make images and adore them—absurd; adoration is due from creature to creator; here man is creator, so statues ought to worship him, and would, had they brains enough to justify a rat in worshipping them. But even this abuse is ancient. The pagan vulgar made images, knelt before them, adorned them with flowers, offered incense, lighted tapers, carried them in procession, made pilgrimages—just to the smallest tittle as we do.”

Jerome, impatient, struck in: the most revered images in Christendom were made by no mortal hand, but had dropped from heaven.

“Ay,” cried Colonna, “such are the tutelary images of most great Italian towns. I have examined nineteen and made drafts. If they came from the sky, our worst sculptors are our angels. But my mind is easy. Ungainly statue or villainous daub fell never yet from heaven to smuggle bread out of capable workmen’s mouths.

“This is pagan, and arose thus: the Trojans feigned their Palladium fell from heaven, a wooden statue three cubits long. The Greeks carried the fib home, and soon it rained statues over all Greece and their Latin apes. One Palladium gave St. Paul trouble at Ephesus—Diana that fell from Jupiter: credat qui credere possit.”

Jerome demanded if he would cast profane doubts on the picture of Our Lady that, scarce a century gone, hung lustrous in the air over Rome and was taken down by the Pope and bestowed in St. Peter’s.

“I have no profane doubts,” said Colonna, and his voice turned sly with scholarship. “This is Numa’s shield revived by theologians with an itch for fiction but no talent—being not orientals. The ancile hung lustrous in the air over this very city till Numa took it down and hung it in Jupiter’s temple. Be just: swallow both stories or neither. The Bocca della Verità passes for a statue of the Virgin and convicted a woman of perjury the other day; it is in truth an image of Rhea, and the modern figment is but one of its ancient traditions. Swallow both or neither.

“Indeed we owe all our Palladiuncula, and all our speaking, nodding, winking, sweating, bleeding statues, to these abused heathens. Athenian statues sweated before Chaeronea; Roman statues in Tully’s day—Victory at Capua, Mars at Rome, Apollo outside the gates. Antony’s statue on Mount Alban bled from every vein before Actium. Others cured diseases. And all these marks and dents in stone made by soft substances—this saint’s knee, that saint’s finger—are heathen too. Hercules’ footprints were shown in Scythia. Castor and Pollux left hoof-prints at Regillum; a temple was built there, and the marks were seen in Tully’s day. Near Venice you may see a stone nearly cleft by St. George’s sword; yet he had but followed the old Roman who cut a whetstone with his razor.

“Kissing of images, and the Pope’s toe, is Eastern paganism. Egyptians had it of Assyrians; Greeks of Egyptians; Romans of Greeks; we of Romans—whose Pontifex Maximus had his toe kissed under the Empire. Druids kissed the High Priest’s toe a thousand years before Christ. Mussulmans, who profess to abhor heathenism, kiss the stone of the Caaba—pagan practice. Priests of Baal kissed their idols. Tully tells of a fair Hercules at Agrigentum whose chin was worn by kissing.

“The lower parts of the statue we call Peter are Jupiter. The toe is worn—not all by Christian mouths. Heathen lips laid there first, and ours have followed, as monkeys their masters. And that is why—down with the poor heathen!

“Pereant qui ante nos nostra fecerint.

“Our infant baptism is Persian, with the font and the signing of the child’s brow. Our three handfuls of earth on the coffin—dust to dust—is Egyptian. Our incense is Oriental, Roman, pagan; and the early Fathers died for refusing to touch it. Our holy water is pagan—see, here is a pagan aspersorium; could you tell it from ours? It stood in the same part of their temples, used as ours, in worship and purifications. They called it aqua lustralis. Their vulgar, like ours, thought a few drops could wash out sin; their men of sense smiled or sighed at such credulity. Ovid himself mocked it:

‘Ah nimium faciles, qui tristia crimina caedis
Fluminea tolli posse putetis aqua.’

“Thou seest the heathen were not all fools. No more are we. Not all.”

So the scholar’s torrent ran, filling the room with names and proofs, like a pantry flung open, every jar and sack emptied at once. Jerome stood stiff, Clement silent between them, hearing not only the words but the room’s changing sound—the sharp strike of pride against pride, the way Latin and Greek rang like hard coins on a table, the way the very air seemed to thicken with untranslatable meanings, each phrase carrying a world no other tongue could wholly hold.

And in that lodging, where a manuscript had been called obscene and a jewel made a battleground, Clement learned another lesson Jerome had not meant to teach: that languages themselves are power—tools that can feed or starve memory; that a dominant lexicon can bless or bruise; and that men, even vowed men, can turn learning into a cudgel as easily as a crowd can turn death into entertainment.

A Catherine is no simple blessing in a house that is not her own.

She had scarce set foot over Margaret’s threshold before the place began to look as if it had been awaiting her all along: pewter took a cleaner shine under her eye; the hearth seemed to sweep itself for shame; the window-lattices admitted a whiter day. The very sound of the dwelling altered. Where before there had been the soft, homely music of a Dutch room—milk in the pail, a sparrow’s skitter on the sill, the hush of a woman moving carefully for love of her burden—now came the brisk clack and scrape of governance: stool-legs shifted, pots set down with decision, lids lifted and replaced as if each had a proper note to strike in the kitchen’s rough orchestra.

But this hearth-cricket that animated the house was no singer of content; it was a busy-body. And a busy-body, once possessed, sets to rights not only things that want it, but things that ought to be left to their own familiar crookedness. Catherine altered the place of every chair and table; perhaps she bettered the air of the room, perhaps she merely made it hers. Yet she could not rest while the live furniture remained.

When Margaret’s time drew close, Catherine—under a show of motherly prudence—treacherously enlisted Denys and Martin. The poor simple fellows, earnest as dogs that long to be useful, asked what they might do. Catherine told them they could make themselves comparatively serviceable by taking a little walk.

So far, fair.

But then, with her chin lifted and the dish-clout snapping like a banner, she intimated that if their promenade should chance to extend into the middle of next week, why, so much the better.

This did not ingratiate.

After that, the bearing of strong men under a weak woman’s yoke might have softened a she-bear robbed of sleep. Denys and Martin slipped out at daybreak, and stole in like thieves at night; and if chance caught them within doors, they went about like cats on a wall strewn with broken glass—eyes wide, shoulders drawn in, every movement cautious, as if a tongue might lash them from behind the dresser. Yet even this humility did not buy peace. Their very presence jarred on Catherine’s nerves, like an ill-timed loud voice in a room where one listens for a baby’s breath. Perhaps instinct whispered that depopulators have no business where multipliers are at work. A breastplate is no armour against a woman’s words; and Catherine ran infinite pins and needles of speech into them.

In brief, when Margaret came downstairs at last, pale but smiling with that subdued radiance which seems to rise in a woman from the mere fact of having endured and been spared, she found the kitchen swept of heroes.

Martin, old and stiff, had retreated no farther than the street—yet with the honours of war; for he had carried off his baggage, a stool, and sat on it in the open air. The sun lay on his bent shoulders; he looked like a man planted there to dry, and had taken root in the light.

Margaret saw him, and was glad he was warm; but she did not guess he had become a fixture in that luminary. Her first thought went elsewhere.

“Denys?” said she. “Good, kind Denys; he will be right pleased to see me about again.”

Catherine stood wiping a bowl with a vigour now in excess of need, as if the pottery had offended her. Without looking up she answered, “Gone to his friends in Burgundy. And high time. Hasn’t been anigh them this three years, by all accounts.”

Margaret’s face changed as quickly as milk clouds when a hand’s shadow passes over the pail.

“What—gone without bidding me farewell?” she asked; and her eyes lifted, tender and full, like violets in bloom after rain.

Catherine reddened. This turn of the matter pricked her, and for a moment the kitchen clatter seemed to falter, as if even the ladle listened. But she gave her head a little toss, and hardened her voice into practicality.

“Oh, you were asleep at the time. And I would not have you wakened.”

“Poor Denys,” said Margaret; and the dew gathered visibly on the violets.

Catherine saw it out of the corner of her eye, and without openly owning it, slipped away—suddenly—and lavished hospitality and tenderness upon the surviving depopulator, as if kindness might mend what conscience had nicked.

She went to Martin in the street, and made her voice honey.

“Come in, Martin,” said she. “Why, you’ll take cold sitting there like a stone. There’s broth within, good broth, with a bit of onion sweated soft, and parsley chopped fine as green threads; and bread to it, not new so as to stick, but yesterday’s, that drinks kindly. Come, I’ll set it by the fire for you.”

But Martin—old and stiff in more ways than one—shook his head.

“No, thank you, dame. I’ve got used to out o’ doors. And I love not changing and changing. I meddle wi’ nobody here; and nobody meddles wi’ me.”

“Oh, you nasty, cross old wretch!” screamed Catherine; and in a moment treacle turned to the sharpest vinegar. She flounced back into the house, and the door shut with that particular thud that makes every pan and trencher in a kitchen answer it in little echoes.

On calmer reflection she had a little cry. The sound was small—more a catching of breath than any sob—yet in such a room, where one listens always for the slightest stir of a child, even that seemed loud. Then she half reconciled herself to her own conduct by vowing to be so kind that Margaret should never miss her plagues of soldiers.

But the uneasiness remained—a grain of grit under the tongue.

So she dispersed all regrets by a process at once simple and sovereign.

She took and washed the child.

From head to foot she washed him in tepid water; not hot—no, Catherine would have scalded her own hand sooner than a baby’s skin—and not cold to shock his tender bones, but a temperature judged by the back of her wrist, and by long practice with water and flesh. She made a mild lather with good soap, the kind that smells of clean fat and ash, and she turned the little limbs carefully, as if each joint were a delicate hinge in a costly casket. The room filled with that particular odour of a well-kept home: warm water, soap, linen, and the faint sweet steam that rises from a child’s head like blessing made visible.

Heroes, and their wrongs, sank like dust in an ocean of soap and water.

Margaret could not keep still. She hovered round the fortunate performer as if the basin were an altar and Catherine its priest. She must have an apparent hand in the rite, if not a real one. She slipped a finger into the water—to pave the way for her boy, perhaps; for she could not have deceived herself so far as to imagine Catherine would allow her to choose the heat.

During the ablution she kneeled opposite little Gerard and prattled to him with amazing fluency; taking care, however, not to articulate like grown-up people—for how could a cherub be expected to understand their ridiculous pronunciation? The very cadence of her baby-talk was different from her speech to women: it fell in coos and soft clicks, the domestic dialect of love, unrecorded and untranslatable, which no learned lexicon has ever mastered.

Then, as Catherine lifted the tiny hand and washed between the fingers with her thumb, Margaret’s eyes fixed on something.

“I wish you could wash out that,” said she.

“What?” asked Catherine, still intent on her work. “Where?”

“What—have you not noticed? On his little finger.”

Catherine looked, and there indeed was a little brown mole.

“Eh, but this is wonderful!” she cried. “Nature, my lass, you’re strong—and meddlesome to boot. Hast noticed such a mark on some one else? Tell the truth, girl!”

Margaret stared, and for a moment her mouth parted as if the thought were a taste she had not expected.

“What—on him? Nay, mother, not I.”

“Well then he has,” said Catherine, with the triumph of one who has stored a hundred homely observations and brings them forth in season. “And on the very spot. And you never noticed that much. But, dear heart, I forgot; you han’t known him from child to man as I have. I’ve had him hundreds o’ times on my knees, the same as this, and washed him from top to toe in lukewarm water.”

She swelled with conscious superiority, not cruelly, but as women do who have held another’s whole life in their hands by sheer daily labour. Margaret looked up meekly, as at a woman beyond competition.

Catherine, from her dizzy height, did what made her differ from many busy-bodies: she reflected—if not deep, at least real.

“It is strange,” said she, “how things come round and about. Life is but a whirligig. Leastways, we poor women, our lives are all cut upon one pattern. Wasn’t I for washing out my Gerard’s mole in his young days? ‘Oh, fie! here’s a foul blot,’ quoth I; and scrubbed away at it I did till the poor wight cried; so then I thought ’twas time to give over. And now says you to me, ‘Mother,’ says you, ‘do try and wash you out o’ my Gerard’s finger,’ says you. Think on’t!”

“Wash it out?” cried Margaret. “I wouldn’t for all the world. Why, it is the sweetest bit in his little darling body.” Her voice softened into that private dialect again, the one that belongs to cradles and hearths and cannot be carried, whole, into any other tongue. “I’ll kiss it morn and night till he that owned it first comes back to us three. Oh, bless you, my jewel of gold and silver, for being marked like your own daddy, to comfort me.”

And she kissed little Gerard’s little mole.

But she could not stop there. Presently she had him sprawling on her lap, warm and damp and clean, and she kissed his back all over again and again—those round baby-shoulders, the soft spine, the dimples where the skin gathers like dough under a gentle finger. She seemed to worry him as a wolf a lamb; and the child, half laughing and half protesting in that thin piping language of infancy, answered with small squeaks and gurgles that filled the kitchen with a music no minstrel ever sold in a market.

Catherine looked on and smiled. She had seen a good many of these savage onslaughts in her day.

And this little sketch shows the tenor of Margaret’s life for several months. One or two small things occurred in that time which must be told; but I reserve them, since one string will serve for many glass beads.

Meanwhile, while her boy’s father was passing through fearful tempests of the soul, ending in the dead monastic calm, her life might fairly be summed in one great blissful word—Maternity.

You who know what lies in that word, enlarge the sketch: see the young mother nursing and washing, and dressing and undressing; see her stir a little pot with one hand while the other rocks the cradle with a foot; see her taste a broth—salt, a pinch more—then listen, always listen, to the room: to the crackle of turf, the scold of a kettle, the far-off wheel on the street, the blessed quiet between cries. In such quiet, a woman can think. In such quiet, memory has room to live. And in the very syllables she croons—those intimate household sounds—her identity dwells, safe from the heavy foreign words of men and markets.

Then, swifter than lightning, dart your eye into Italy, and see the cold cloister; monks passing like ghosts, eyes down, hands meekly crossed over bosoms dead to earthly feelings. There the sound is different: not the genial clatter of pots and the little noises of a growing child, but measured footsteps, a murmured Latin that belongs to all and therefore to none, doors that shut softly on human speech. One of these cowled ghosts is he, whose return—full of love, and youth, and joy—that radiant young mother awaits.

In the valley of Grindelwald the traveller has on one side the perpendicular Alps, all rock, ice, and everlasting snow, towering above the clouds and piercing to the sky; on the other hand little every-day slopes, green as emeralds and studded with cows and pretty cots and life; whereas those lofty neighbours stand leafless, lifeless, inhuman, sublime. Elsewhere sweet commonplaces of nature pass unnoticed; but fronting the grim Alps they soothe, and gently strike, the mind by contrast with their tremendous opposites.

Such, in their way, are the two halves of this story, rightly looked at: on the Italian side rugged adventure, strong passion, blasphemy, vice, penitence—pure ice, holy snow, soaring direct at heaven; on the Dutch side, all on a humble scale and womanish, but ever green—hearth, basin, bread, and the unrecorded tongue of love spoken over a child.

And as a pathway parts the ice towers of Grindelwald, aspiring to the sky, from its little sunny braes, so here is but a page between the Cloister and the Hearth.

The new Pontiff, being of a mind to strengthen the brethren of Saint Dominic, sent word to the convent that a capable friar must be furnished for the University of Basle. The summons fell upon Clement as naturally as a hand finds the right tool in a darkened chest: he was read in languages; in his lay days he had sat at learned men’s feet; and now his obedience was a thing as plain as bread.

So the visit to England was delayed—not relinquished—and, because Basle would not need him for three months, he was bidden to take the road and preach as he went.

He passed out by the northern gate barefoot, his eyes lowered, the cord at his waist hanging quiet as a plumb-line, and the whole man wrapped in that inward labour men call contemplation.
