If a painter could lay on fresco the story of a mind, what colours had been ground and mixed upon this one robe within the compass of a single year—hope, the quick wine of love, bereavement like a knife in warm flesh, despair, impiety, vice, the black thought of self-slaughter, remorse, the long sour bread of penitence, death to the world, and at last a kind of resignation that was not joy, yet was not emptiness.

He was a traveller again, and on foot again; but now the road had lost its teeth. No perilous adventure sprang at him from hedge or hollow. The very thieves, seeing the white habit and the bare feet, bowed as if a power stood behind the man; and more than once, instead of stripping him, they thrust stolen coin upon him with rough, shamefaced fingers, and begged his prayers. Such passages make little show; yet there are days on a road when nothing happens outwardly, and the inward world changes its climate.

The first Sunday of his journey was such a day.

After preaching in a small Italian town—where the air, being Sunday-clean, held incense mingled with the faint sour of pressed olives and the human breath of a crowded nave—he found himself mightily carried onward, not by praise (he had learned to dread it), but by a soft persuasion, like warm broth slipping into an empty stomach. That day he prayed for Margaret’s soul.

He had never done so before.

Not because her eternal welfare was less dear to him than life itself, but because humility, taken in him to an extreme, had become a kind of scruple. Those terrible impieties that had broken from him when he first heard of her death had horrified others; but, when the first storm passed, they horrified no one as they horrified him who had uttered them. During many weeks of novitiate he had been oppressed by religious despair and believed he had committed that sin against the Holy Ghost which shuts the gate for ever. Anselmo—patient as an old ox in a stony field—had helped him through that blackness; yet deep self-abasement remained. His own salvation seemed insecure to him; and, more than that, he thought it a mockery of Heaven that he, so stained, should lift up prayer for a soul so innocent, comparatively, as Margaret’s. He had used to coax good Anselm and another kindly monk to pray for her; and they, like men who know what hunger is, had not prayed by halves.

But now, after that Sunday sermon, a balmy sense of God’s forgiveness and love descended on him; and with it came this new courage: he prayed for Margaret. From that hour it became his daily habit—the one purified tie that by memory bound his heart to earth. His family were to him as if they had never been. The Church would not share with earth; nor could even the Church cure the great love without annihilating the smaller ones.

On most days of that journey he felt little spring of life within him, save when he stood in the pulpit and words, like water from a hill, ran clear. The other times were when he could ease another creature’s pain.

Once, in a poor village where the hens scratched under carts and the dust tasted of sunburnt clay, he found a young man tarantula-bitten—or, as often happens, persuaded by terror and gossip that he was. For two days the youth had had no sleep and was in convulsions most extraordinary, leaping, twisting, striking the wall with his fists as if he would beat a door through it. The village musicians had tried their art—pipes and a shrill fiddle—and only whipped the frenzy higher; for there are sounds that heal and sounds that wound, and the difference is as subtle as the difference between salt that seasons and salt that scalds.

Exhaustion and death follow such a disorder when it mounts so far.

Clement, hearing the tale, sent for a psaltery. The instrument came, smelling of old wood and sweat from many hands, its strings dulled by dust. He tried the sufferer with soothing melodies such as had calmed novices in their first nights, and had made even an angry dog lay his head down; but if the village tunes had maddened the patient, Clement’s seemed to crush him. The youth groaned and moaned under them and fell grovelling on the floor as if the very harmony pressed him down.

Clement listened—listened not only with ear but with that inward attention a preacher learns from long silence. At intervals the young man’s lips moved. Clement bent; he caught it: the patient was whispering a tune, a strange crooked little air that had no existence in the world. It was born of fever, stitched together by a mind turned in upon itself—yet it had its own logic, its own small home of consonance.

Clement learned it, phrase by phrase, and played it back to him.

At once the young man’s face brightened, as if a window had been opened. He rose and marched about the room on the light fantastic toe, enjoying his own creation returned to him in sound. Clement played until his fingers ached as if pricked by needles; yet at last he had the satisfaction of seeing the youth sink, quiet and complacent, into sleep—lulled by the strange cradle-song his own mind had made. That sleep saved his life. Clement taught the tune to another in case it should be needed again, and went forward with his heart a little warmer, pondering how a man may be torn to pieces by noise, and yet gathered whole by the one sound that matches his inner weather.

On another day he came upon a mob dragging a decently dressed man along the street. The man struggled and shouted, but in a language none there understood; it rang sharp and island-hard among the Italian vowels, as a crow’s caw among doves. He had walked into their town erect and sprightly, waving a mulberry branch over his head to shade himself from the heat. The townsfolk had first stared as if their eyes lied to them; then, as if one mind had leapt from body to body, they pounced and hauled him before the podestà.

Clement went with them. On the way he edged near and spoke quietly to the prisoner in Italian. No answer. In French; in German; in Dutch. Still none. At last the man tried Clement in tolerable Latin, with a sharpish accent, as of a blade honed on stone.

He said he was an Englishman, oppressed by the Italian sun, and had taken a bough from the nearest tree to save his head.

“In my country,” he cried, “anybody is welcome to what grows on the highway. Confound the fools; I am ready to pay for it. But here is all Italy up in arms about a twig and a handful of leaves!”

The podestà, pig-headed as an ox and as proud, would have clapped the dogged islander into prison; but Clement mediated. With some difficulty he made the stranger understand that silkworms—and therefore mulberry leaves—were held sacred, being under the Sovereign’s protection and a source of revenue; and he urged upon the podestà that ignorance of such laws was natural in a far country where the tree itself might be unknown.

The islander, opinionated even in humility, tipped the trembling scale by drawing out a long purse and repeating his first theory, that the whole matter was mercantile.

“Quid damni?” he demanded. “Dic; et cito solvam.”

The podestà sniffed the gold as a dog sniffs meat: he fined him a ducat for the Duke—about the value of the whole tree—and quietly pocketed the coin.

The Englishman shook off his ire the instant he was free. He laughed heartily at the affair and was grateful to Clement with that open-handed gratitude which, like good ale, makes no secret of itself.

“You are too good for this hole of a country, father,” said he. “Come to England. That is the only place in the world. I was an uneasy fool to leave it and wander among mulberries and their idiots. I am a Kentish squire, educated at Cambridge. My name is Rolfe; my place Betshanger. The man and the house are both at your service. Come over and stay till Doomsday. We sit down forty to dinner every day at Betshanger. One more or one less at the board will not be seen. You shall end your days with me and my heirs if you will. What an Englishman says he means.”

And he gave Clement a hearty grip to seal it.

“I will visit thee some day, my son,” said Clement; “but not to weary thy hospitality.”

The Englishman then begged him to shrive him.

“I know not what will become of my soul,” said he; “I live like a heathen since I left England.”

Clement consented gladly, and soon the islander was on his knees by the roadside, confessing the last month’s sins with the same directness with which he had spoken of mulberries and money. When Clement found him, for all his bluster, a pious son of the Church, he let slip that he too was bound for England.

Then he asked, as men asked in every cloistered corridor, whether it was true that England was overrun with Lollards and Wickliffites.

The other coloured a little, as if the question had touched not the skin but something beneath.

“There be black sheep in every land,” said he; but after a moment he added gravely, “Holy father, hear the truth about these heretics. None are better disposed towards Holy Church than we English. But we are ourselves, and by ourselves. We love our own ways, and above all, our own tongue. The Norman could conquer our bill-hooks, but not our tongues; and hard they tried it for many a long year by law and proclamation. Our good foreign priests utter God to plain English folk in Latin, or in some French or Italian lingo—like the bleating of a sheep. Then come the fox Wickliff and his crew, and read Him out of His own book in plain English, that all men’s hearts warm to. Who can withstand this? God forgive me, I believe the English would turn deaf ears to Saint Peter himself, spoke he not to them in the tongue their mothers sowed in their ears and hearts along with mothers’ kisses.”

He broke off, then added, as if to save his own orthodoxy, “I say not this for myself. I am Cambridge-bred, and good words come not amiss to me in Latin; but for the people in general. Clavis ad corda Anglorum est lingua materna.”

Those words struck Clement with a force that had nothing of argument in it; it was like recognizing a scent long lost—the first loaf of one’s childhood, the smoke of one’s own hearth. He, who had suffered the tearing of his own speech in foreign lands and had clung to Latin as a plank in a flood, heard in this blunt squire’s saying the whole sorrow of tongues crushed under dominant tongues, and the hidden power that lies in the mother-syllables.

“My son,” said Clement, “blessed be the hour I met thee; for thy words are sober and wise. But alas! how shall I learn your English tongue? No book have I.”

“I would give you my book of hours, father,” cried Rolfe, quick as bargaining blood. “’Tis in English and Latin, cheek by jowl. But then—what would become of my poor soul, wanting my ‘hours’ in a strange land? Stay: you are a holy man, and I an honest one. Let us make a bargain. You to pray for me every day for two months, and I to give you my book of hours. Here it is. What say you to that?”

His eyes sparkled; he was all on fire with mercantility, even at the gate of confession.

Clement smiled gently, and from his girdle drew a manuscript of his own, written in Latin and Italian.

“See, my son,” said he, “Heaven hath foreseen our several needs and given us the means to satisfy them. Let us change books; and, my dear son, I will give thee my poor prayers and welcome, not sell them thee. I love not religious bargains.”

The islander was delighted.

“So shall I learn the Italian tongue without risk to my eternal weal. Near is my purse, but nearer is my soul.”

He forced money on Clement. In vain the friar told him it was contrary to his vow to carry more than was barely needful.

“Lay it out for the good of the Church and of my soul,” said Rolfe. “I ask you not to keep it, but take it you must and shall.”

He gripped Clement’s hand again; Clement kissed him on the brow and blessed him; and they went each his way, the one carrying away Italian words as if they were spices, the other carrying away English prayers as if they were stored grain.

A mile or so after they parted, Clement saw, in the deep shade of a great chestnut-tree at the edge of a grove, two tired wayfarers lying like men felled by heat. Beside them stood a little cart, and in it a printing-press—rude, clumsy, built almost like a vine-press, as if some peasant’s knowledge of crushing grapes had been turned to crushing ink upon paper. A jaded mule drooped in the shafts.

Clement stopped.

So he stood face to face with his old enemy.

As he looked on the press and on the honest blue-eyed faces of the wearied craftsmen, he looked back as upon a dream at the bitterness he had once felt against that machine—this contrivance that could set words free like swarming bees, sweet or stinging. Now his eyes softened.

“Sweynheim,” he said softly.

The men started up as if an arrow had struck the air.

“Pannartz!” he added.

They scuttled into the wood like startled deer and were seen no more.

Clement stood amazed, puzzling. Presently a face peeped from behind a tree, pale with superstition and fear.

“What fear ye?” Clement called.

A quavering voice answered, “Say rather, by what magic you—a stranger—can call us by our names! I never clapt eyes on you till now.”

“O superstition!” Clement sighed. “I know ye, as all good workmen are known—by your works. Come hither and I will tell ye.”

They advanced gingerly from different sides, each measuring his courage by the other’s step, until they stood within speaking distance.

“My children,” said Clement, “I saw a Lactantius in Rome, printed by Sweynheim and Pannartz, disciples of Fust.”

“D’ye hear that, Pannartz?” cried Sweynheim, his face lighting as a hearth does when a coal is roused. “Our work has gotten to Rome already.”

“And by your blue eyes and flaxen hair I wist ye were Germans,” Clement went on; “and the printing-press spoke for itself. Who then should ye be but Fust’s disciples, Pannartz and Sweynheim?”

The honest men were abashed that they had suspected magic in plain wit.

“The good father hath his wits about him, that is all,” said Pannartz.

“Ay,” said Sweynheim, rubbing his neck, “and with those wits would he could tell us how to get this tired beast to the next town.”

“Yea,” added Pannartz, “and where to find money to pay for his meat and ours when we get there.”

“I will try,” said Clement. “Free the mule of the cart, and of all harness but the bare halter.”

They did so; and the animal, feeling the sudden liberty, lay down at once and rolled on his back in the dust like a kitten, legs in the air, as if joy were nothing but soundless relief in the spine. Clement watched, and his mouth softened.

“I told ye,” said he, “I would rise up a new mule. His Creator hath taught him this art to refresh himself, which the nobler horse knoweth not.”

Then, as to money, he remembered Rolfe’s forced charity.

“Know,” said he, “that a worthy Englishman hath entrusted me with a certain sum to bestow in alms. To whom can I better give a stranger’s money than to strangers? Take it; and be kind to some Englishman—or other stranger—in his need. May all nations learn to love one another one day.”

Tears stood in the workmen’s eyes. They took the money with heartfelt thanks.

“It is your nation we are bound to thank and bless, good father—if we but knew it.”

“My nation is the Church,” said Clement simply.

He would have gone then; but the honest fellows would not let him depart empty-handed. They had no silver nor gold to offer, but they had their craft. They took the press out of the cart and, while Clement fed the mule and rubbed its ears until it stopped shivering at flies, they bustled about—now on the white-hot road, now in the deep green coolness under the chestnuts, now half in and half out like men at the door of a bakehouse on a cold day—setting, inking, adjusting. The smell of ink rose sharp as pitch, and the press’s wooden throat groaned in the heat as they worked its screw.

Presently they printed a quarto sheet of eight pages that was already set up; they had not type enough to print two sheets at once. After the slow preliminaries—letters arranged, ink spread, paper laid—came the marvel: the pull, all in a moment, like the swift closing of a lid.

Clement stared as if he had seen bread rise in a cold oven.

“What,” he cried, “are all these words really fast upon the paper? Is it verily certain they will not go as swiftly as they came? And you took me for a magician! ’Tis Augustine, De Civitate Dei. My sons, you carry here the very wings of knowledge. Oh, never abuse this great craft. Print no ill books. They would fly abroad countless as locusts, and lay waste men’s souls.”

The workmen swore, in the simple fierce sincerity of good craftsmen, that they would sooner put their hands under the screw than so abuse their goodly art.

So they parted. There is nothing but meeting and parting in this world; and the road, like a long table, seats companions for a moment, then shifts them away.

At a town in Tuscany the holy friar had a sudden and strange encounter with the past. He fell in with one of those motley companies of pilgrims—patricians and plebeians, piety and profligacy mingled like flour and grit in the same sack—who travel with prayers on their lips and gossip in their pockets. They lodged in an immense barn belonging to the inn. The place smelled of straw, old wine, damp cloaks, and the cook’s onions frying somewhere beyond a wall—homely scents, threaded with the sour breath of too many bodies. Above it all ran the soundscape of travel: coughing, rosaries clicking like dried seeds, boots scraped on boards, a distant mule braying in complaint, and a fife somewhere playing too sharply for the hour.

Clement, dusty and wearied and no lover of idle talk, sat in a corner with Rolfe’s book of hours, studying the English page and making it out as much by his own Dutch as by the Latin beside it. He tasted each foreign word as if it were a new herb—recognizable in family, yet strange on the tongue—and thought how little of a man’s soul can be carried over when the mother-speech is taken away.

Presently a servant brought a bucket half-full of water and set it at Clement’s feet. Another followed with two towels. Then a woman came forward. She crossed herself, knelt at the bucket without a word, pushed her sleeves up—nay, drew them wholly off—and motioned to him to put his feet into the water.

It was some lady of rank doing penance. She wore a mask scarce an inch broad, yet effectual. And she handled the friar’s feet more delicately than those do who are born to such offices, as if the very touch were part of her prayer. Such penances were not uncommon. Clement, though he had small faith in contrition that shows itself chiefly in spectacle, received her service as a matter of course.

But presently she sighed—deeply; and with that sigh, her head bowed low over her menial office, she seemed so broken with inward weight that he pitied her.

“Can I aught for your soul’s weal, my daughter?” he asked calmly.

She shook her head with a faint sob.

“Nought, holy father, nought—only to hear the sin of her who is most unworthy to touch thy holy feet. ’Tis part of my penance to tell sinless men how vile I am.”

“Speak, my daughter.”

“Father,” she whispered, bending lower and lower, “these hands of mine look white, but they are stained with blood—the blood of the man I loved.”

Clement’s foot drew back an instant, a movement not of doctrine but of flesh; and the lady, seeing it, gave a little moan as if struck.

“Ah me! What shall I do? All holy things shrink from me.”

“Culpa mea! culpa mea!” cried Clement eagerly. “My daughter, it was an unworthy movement of earthly weakness, for which I shall do penance. Judge not the Church by her feebler servants. Not her foot, but her bosom, is offered to thee, repenting truly. Take courage, then, and purge thy conscience of its load.”

Then the lady, in a trembling whisper, hurried and cringing, as if she feared the Church would strike her for what she had done, poured out her confession.

“He was a stranger, and base-born, but beautiful as Spring, and wise beyond his years. I loved him. I had not the prudence to conceal my love. Nobles courted me. I ne’er thought one of humble birth could reject me. I showed him my heart—oh, shame of my sex! He drew back; yet he admired me; but innocently. He loved another; and he was constant. I resorted to a woman’s wiles; they availed not. I borrowed the wickedness of men, and threatened his life, and to tell his true lover he died false to her.”

Clement’s toes curled in the water; not from the woman’s touch, but from the picture she painted.

“Ah! you shrink—your foot trembles. Am I not a monster? Then he wept and prayed to me for mercy; then my good angel helped me; I bade him leave Rome. Gerard, Gerard, why did you not obey me? I thought he was gone. But two months after this I met him. Never shall I forget it. I was descending the Tiber in my galley when he came up it with a gay company, and at his side a woman beautiful as an angel, but bold and bad. That woman claimed me aloud for her rival. Traitor and hypocrite, he had exposed me to her, and to all the loose tongues in Rome. In terror and revenge I hired a bravo.”

Her hands, so gentle upon his skin, trembled as she spoke, and the water in the bucket made faint rings.

“When he was gone on his bloody errand I wavered—too late. The dagger I had hired struck. He never came back to his lodgings. He was dead. Alas! perhaps he was not so much to blame; none have ever cast his name in my teeth. His poor body is not found—or I should kiss its wounds, and slay myself upon it. All around his very name seems silent as the grave to which this murderous hand hath sent him.”

As she moved, Clement’s eye was drawn to her arm—shapely, white, and familiar in its grace. A recognition, like a sudden taste of bitter almond, went through him.

“And oh! he was so young to die,” she whispered. “A poor thoughtless boy that had fallen a victim to that bad woman’s arts, and she had made him tell her everything. Monster of cruelty, what penance can avail me? Oh, holy father, what shall I do?”

Clement’s lips moved in prayer, but no words came. Duty lay before him, yet he could not see it clear. Then the woman took his feet and began to dry them. She rested his foot upon her soft arm and pressed it with the towel so gently she seemed incapable of hurting a fly. And yet her mouth had just spoken murder.

While Clement still prayed for wisdom, a tear fell upon his foot—hot as broth on cold skin.

It decided him.

“My daughter,” said he, “I myself have been a great sinner.”

“You, father?”

“I; quite as great a sinner as thou, though not in the same way. The devil hath gins and snares, as well as traps. But penitence softened my impious heart, and then gratitude remoulded it. Therefore, seeing you penitent, I hope you can be grateful to Him who hath been more merciful to you than you have to your fellow-creature. Daughter, the Church sends you comfort.”

“Comfort to me?” she breathed. “Ah, never—unless it can raise my victim from the dead.”

“Take this crucifix in thy hand, fix thine eyes on it, and listen to me.”

“Yes, father—but let me thoroughly dry your feet first; ’tis ill sitting in wet feet; and you are the holiest man of all whose feet I have washed. I know it by your voice.”

“Woman, I am not. As for my feet, they can wait their turn. Obey thou me.”

“Yes, father,” she said humbly; yet with a woman’s evasive pertinacity she wound one towel swiftly round the foot she was drying and placed his other upon the dry napkin; then took the crucifix and bowed over it.

The barn’s noises—snoring, murmured prayers, a cough that scraped like a file—fell away from Clement as if a door had been shut. In the low solemn tones of the friar, words dropped, one by one, like measured grains into a scale.

“My daughter, he you murdered—in intent—was one Gerard, a Hollander. He loved a creature as men should love none but their Redeemer and His Church. Heaven chastised him. A letter came to Rome. She was dead.”

“Poor Gerard! Poor Margaret!” moaned the penitent.

Clement’s voice faltered at the name, as if his throat had been touched by ash. But by a strong effort he recovered his calm.

“His feeble nature yielded, body and soul, to the blow. He was stricken down with fever. He revived only to rebel against Heaven. He said, ‘There is no God.’”

“Poor, poor Gerard!”

“Poor Gerard?” Clement’s tone sharpened, not with cruelty, but with truth. “Thou feeble, foolish woman! Nay—wicked, impious Gerard. He plunged into vice and soiled his eternal jewel. Those you met him with were his daily companions. But know, rash creature, that the seeming woman you took to be his leman was but a boy dressed in woman’s habits to flout the others—a fair boy called Andrea. What that Andrea said to thee I know not; but be sure neither he nor any layman knows thy folly. This Gerard, rebel against Heaven, was no traitor to thee—unworthy.”

The lady moaned as if in bodily pain. The crucifix trembled in her trembling hands, and the small sound of its quiver was louder to Clement than the whole barn.

“Courage,” he said. “Comfort is at hand.”

“From crime he fell into despair; and bent on destroying his soul, he stood one night by Tiber, resolved on suicide. He saw one watching him. It was a bravo.”

“Holy saints!”

“He begged the bravo to despatch him. He offered him all his money, to slay him body and soul. The bravo would not. Then this desperate sinner, not softened even by that refusal, flung himself into Tiber.”

“Ah!”

“And the assassin saved his life. Thou hadst chosen for the task Lodovico, husband of Teresa, whom this Gerard had saved at sea—her and her infant child.”

For a heartbeat the penitent could not breathe. Then the words burst from her like a bell’s release after a long held note.

“He lives! he lives! he lives! I am faint.”

Clement, fearing the crucifix might fall, took it from her hands. A shower of tears came, relieving her as rain relieves a parched garden. He gave her time; then continued, his voice even.

“Ay, he lives—thanks to thee and thy wickedness, guided to his eternal good by an almighty and all-merciful hand. Thou art his greatest earthly benefactor.”

“Where is he? Where? Where?”

“What is that to thee?”

“Only to see him alive. To beg him on my knees forgive me. I swear to you I will never presume again to—How could I? He knows all. Oh, shame! Father—does he know?”

“All.”

“Then never will I meet his eye; I should sink into the earth. But I would repair my crime. I would watch his life unseen. He shall rise in the world, whence I so nearly thrust him—poor soul. The Cæsare, my family, are all-powerful in Rome; and I am near their head.”

“My daughter,” said Clement coldly, “he you call Gerard needs nothing man can do for him. Saved by a miracle from double death, he hath left the world and taken refuge from sin and folly in the bosom of the Church.”

“A priest?”

“A priest, and a friar.”

“A friar?” Her breath caught. “Then you are not his confessor? Yet you know all. That gentle voice—”

She raised her head slowly and peered at him through her narrow mask, as one might peer through a slit into a bright kitchen where familiar labour goes on. The next moment she uttered a faint shriek and fell forward, laying her brow upon his bare feet.

Clement heaved a quiet sigh, the sort a man draws when he feels the ground shift beneath rules he has trusted. He began to doubt whether he had chosen the wisest course with a creature so vehement, so swift in feeling that her very body seemed to leap before her judgment. Yet young as he was, he had already learned one craft of the cloistered mind: to pause—there are storms in which the safest pilot neither rows nor speaks until the water shows its own channel.

So he held his peace and prayed for wisdom. He did nothing but gently draw back his foot.

But his penitent, with a cry that went through the chamber like a knife on stone, flung both arms about it and clung as if it were a plank in deep water. Her tears ran hot over his instep; her whole frame shook. Shame, not less than penitence, broke over her like a sudden flush of wine: the red rose up past her cheeks and crept down even to her throat as she lay quivering at his feet. The small sounds—the hitching breath, the wet fall of tears on leather, the rustle of her gown against the floor—filled the room more than any sermon could have done. Even the house noises beyond, muffled as they were, seemed to hush, as if the air itself had learned reverence.

“My daughter,” said Clement at last, very gently, “take courage. Torment thyself no more about this Gerard, who is not. As for me, I am Brother Clement, whom Heaven hath sent to thee this day to comfort thee, and help thee save thy soul. Thou last made me thy confessor; I claim, then, thine obedience.”

“Oh, yes,” sobbed she, her voice breaking upon the word like bread pulled too fast from the loaf.

“Leave this pilgrimage, and instant return to Rome. Penitence abroad is little worth. There where we live lie the temptations we must defeat, or perish; not fly in search of others more showy, but less lethal. Easy to wash the feet of strangers, masked ourselves; hard to be merely meek and charitable with those about us.”

“I’ll never—never lay finger on her again,” she gasped, as if that one promise were the last rung of a ladder.

“Nay,” said he, “I speak not of servants only, but of dependents, kinsmen, friends. This be thy penance: the last thing at night, and the first thing after matins, call to mind thy sin, and God His goodness; and so be humble and gentle to the faults of those around thee. The world it courts the rich; but seek thou the poor: not beggars; these for the most are neither honest nor truly poor. But rather find out those who blush to seek thee, yet need thee sore. Giving to them shalt lend to Heaven. Marry a good son of the Church.”

“Me? I will never marry.”

“Thou wilt marry within the year. I do entreat and command thee to marry one that feareth God. For thou art very clay. Mated ill thou shalt be naught. But wedding a worthy husband thou mayest, Dei gratia, live a pious princess; ay, and die a saint.”

“I?” She said it as if the syllable were a strange tongue in her mouth—untranslatable to the life she had imagined for herself.

“Thou.”

He bade her rise and go about the good work he had set her. She lifted herself to her knees; then, with a motion at once timid and resolute, she took off her mask. Her face, freed from that dumb covering, spoke more than any courtly rhetoric: she cast on him one long, eloquent look—such a look as women give when they would pour out a whole life and are forbidden speech—then lowered her eyes, obedient, meek.

“I will obey you as I would an angel. How happy I am, yet unhappy; for oh, my heart tells me I shall never look on you again. I will not go till I have dried your feet.”

“It needs not,” said Clement. “I have excused thee this bootless penance.”

“’Tis no penance to me.” She leaned nearer, and her voice, still wet with tears, softened to a pleading that had almost the warmth of a hearth. “Ah! you do not forgive me, if you will not let me dry your poor feet.”

“So be it then,” said Clement, resigned; and in his heart, with that half-humorous weariness monks allow themselves in secret, he thought, Levius quid foemina.

Yet these weak creatures, that gravitate towards the small as heavenly bodies towards the great, have their own sudden illuminations—swift as the flash of a knife in lamplight. She fetched the linen and did her office with a care that was almost ceremonial. The cloth, clean and faintly scented, drew the damp from his skin and the road-dust from the seams; her hands, though trembling, moved with the steadiness of one who has watched kitchens and chambermaids and knows how stubborn grime sits in the creases. The little rasp of fabric on leather, the gentle tap as she set his boot aside, were homely sounds—and in that homeliness, strangely, the act grew more human than any pageant of penitence abroad. It was as if she were being taught, by touch and smell and sound, that holiness must live in rooms where people eat and sleep and weep.

When she had done, she looked up. Tears stood in her beautiful eyes, and she murmured—so tenderly, so simply, that the words seemed to come not from pride abased but from pity awakened:

“I will have masses said for her soul. May I?” she added, timid as a child asking leave to give bread away.

A faint blush rose in the monk’s cheek; the cold blue of his eye moistened. It came so suddenly from one he had been ready to rate so low, and the thought carried with it the weight of names—how a soul may be remembered or forgotten, how prayer keeps a person’s story from being swallowed by silence.

“It is a gracious thought,” said he. “Do as thou wilt: often such acts fall back on the doer like blessed dew. I am thy confessor, not hers; thine is the soul I must now do my all to save, or woe be to my own. My daughter, my dear daughter, I see good and ill angels fighting for thy soul this day—ay, this moment; oh, fight thou on thine own side. Dost thou remember all I bade thee?”

“Remember!” said she, and the word came out with a fervour that was almost fierce. “Sweet saint, each syllable of thine is graved in my heart.”

“But one word more, then. Pray much to Christ, and little to his saints.”

“I will.”

“And that is the best word I have light to say to thee. So part we on it. Thou to the place becomes thee best, thy father’s house; I to my holy mother’s work.”

“Adieu,” faltered the princess. “Adieu, thou that I have loved too well, hated too ill, known and revered too late; forgiving angel, adieu—for ever.”

He caught her words, though they were breathed rather than spoken, like a sigh lost in a chapel.

“For ever?” he cried aloud, and the ardour in him sprang up like fire taking dry flax. “Christians live ‘for ever,’ and love ‘for ever,’ but they never part ‘for ever.’ They part, as part the earth and sun, to meet more brightly in a little while. You and I part here for life. And what is our life? One line in the great story of the Church, whose son and daughter we are; one handful in the sand of time, one drop in the ocean of ‘For ever.’ Adieu—for the little moment called ‘a life!’ We part in trouble, we shall meet in peace: we part creatures of clay, we shall meet immortal spirits: we part in a world of sin and sorrow, we shall meet where all is purity and love divine; where no ill passions are, but Christ is, and His saints around Him clad in white. There, in the turning of an hour-glass, in the breaking of a bubble, in the passing of a cloud, she, and thou, and I, shall meet again; and sit at the feet of angels and archangels, apostles and saints, and beam like them with joy unspeakable, in the light of the shadow of God upon His throne, FOR EVER—AND EVER—AND EVER.”

The words rang through the room; even after his voice ceased, it seemed the air kept the echo, as a cloister keeps the last note of a chant. Outside, some distant sound—a footfall, a door settling, a muted call—came back into hearing, and with it the world’s ordinary life resumed, as if the great and the daily were stitched together without seam.

And so they parted: the monk erect, his eyes turned heavenwards and glowing with the sacred fire of zeal; the princess slowly retiring, turning more than once to cast a lingering glance of awe and tender regret upon that inspired figure.

She went home subdued, and purified.

Clement, in due course, reached Basle and entered on his duties—teaching in the University, and preaching in the town and neighbourhood. He led a life that can be comprised in two words: deep study, and mortification. My reader has already a peep into his soul. At Basle he advanced in holy zeal and knowledge, and the brethren of his order began to see in him a descendant of the saints and martyrs.

Little Gerard was not yet three months old when a messenger, dust in his hair and haste in his limbs, clattered up from Tergou with a summons for Catherine.

“Get thee back,” Catherine cried from the threshold, wiping her hands on her apron as if she could wipe away their need with the same brisk motion. “Tell them I can’t come, and I won’t. They have got Kate.”

The fellow stared—he had ridden for obedience, not argument—and so, with a shrug, went down the stair.

Catherine turned, and the hard words fell from her mouth like a pot set too sharply on a hearthstone. Yet her eyes had already softened as they found the cradle. “There, child, I must go. They are all at sixes and sevens. This is the third time of asking; and to-morrow my man would come himself and take me home by the ear, with a flea in’t.”

Then, as if she were laying by winter stores, she began to lay up counsel in Margaret: how to swaddle and how to loosen; what a fretful cry might mean; what to do if the belly gripped, or if the gums rose; how to warm a cloth without scorching it; how to test milk by smell before offering it, lest sourness creep in unseen. She made domestic science of motherhood, and spoke of it with the authority of a woman who had heard too many midnight whimpers under too many roofs.

And then, because advice is easier given than parting, she pressed money into Margaret’s palm.

Margaret drew her hand back. “Nay, mother. I thank you kindly; but I cannot.”

Catherine thrust it forward again, with that impatient generosity that is half love and half temper. “Take it.”

“I cannot,” Margaret said, and held her hands together as if she were praying them steady.

Catherine’s face tightened; then, oddly, grew calm with contempt—contempt, not for the girl, but for a kind of girlishness she could not endure. “You make excuses like a man draws up reasons. Come—out with your heart. You and me parting; and mayhap shall never see one another’s face again.”

“Oh, mother, say not so.”

“Alack, girl, I have seen it so often; ’twill come into my mind now at each parting. When I was your age I never had such a thought. Nay, we were all to live for ever then. So—out wi’ it.”

Margaret’s eyes went down to the child, as if she would borrow courage from his small breathing. “Well, then, mother—I would rather not have told you—your Cornelis must say to me, ‘So you are come to share with us, eh, mistress?’ Those were his words. I told him I would be very sorry.”

“Beshrew his ill tongue!” Catherine snapped, and her voice was like a spoon rapping a pot. “What signifies it? He will never know.”

“Most like he would sooner or later. But whether or no, I will take no grudged bounty from any family; unless I saw my child starving, and—Heaven only knows what I might do. Nay, mother—give me but thy love. I do prize that above silver; and they grudge me not that, by all I can find. For not a stiver of money will I take out of your house.”

“You are a foolish lass.”

“Why, were it me,” Catherine retorted, and the old spirit in her flashed, “I’d take it just to spite him.”

“No,” said Margaret quietly. “You would not. You and I are apples off one tree.”

Catherine yielded at last, though she did it with a sort of reluctant grace, as one sets down a jug because another hand is steadier. Yet when the actual parting came, both women broke, and clung, and wept; tears running warm as broth down cheeks that had known rough wind and harsher words.

After Catherine was gone, the baby cried and cried: a thin, persistent wail that filled the room, climbed the rafters, and made the hearth’s small cracklings seem to hush in listening. Margaret tried her breast; she walked him; she sang him a fragment of an old Dutch lullaby, the words broken in her mouth as if they had travelled too far from their home. Nothing quieted him.

Then she thought, practical even through sorrow, There is a pin.

She undid him, searching between cloth and skin with careful fingers, and found—no pin—but a gold angel pressing against his little backbone.

“There, now, Gerard,” she whispered, half laughing and half choked, “I thought granny gave in rather sudden.”

She wrapped the coin in linen and laid it deep in her box, under folded cloths that smelled of lye and sun. And she told the baby, with a stern tenderness, that she could be resolute too—at times as resolute as granny herself.

Catherine, once home, poured out the tale to Eli—how Margaret’s foolish pride had stood in the way, and how she had outwitted it. Eli, who had a gentler justice than Catherine’s, said Margaret was right, and she was wrong.

Catherine tossed her head. Eli pondered.

Margaret’s days were a wheel that turned without rest. Two men still sat at her table, and she must feed them as well as the child. She could not work so hard as she had done—her arms were full, her nights broken, her strength spent in little portions like flour measured out too thinly. Yet she swept, and scoured, and made the pot sing; she watched the bread, and knew by smell when it was near ready, and by sound when the crust began to firm. She listened always—listened not only for the baby’s smallest change of cry, but for the stair’s complaint under a familiar footstep.

She had a little money laid by. Often, as she rocked the cradle, she told the child his father would be home to help them before it was spent, as if her words could keep the coins from dwindling. With these bright hopes—and that treasury of bliss, her boy—she lived some happy months.

Time wore on; and no Gerard came. Stranger still—no news.

Then her mind, so used to tasks and tangible things, began to wander into places where there was nothing to grasp. She would stand over her pail, hearing only the drip, drip, drip from a cloth she wrung, and feel the drip inside her heart answering it. She would stir a thin broth and taste it, and it seemed to have lost its savour because it had lost the sound of his voice to season it. Her silence grew heavy. She sighed, not for show, but because the breath must go somewhere.

And while her heart was troubled, her money melted.

One day she opened the cupboard and found it bare. The emptiness stared back—wood and shadow where bread should have been, where a bit of cheese, a heel of meat, even a clove of onion might have waited. She looked into the faces of her dependents, and pity rose in her like hot water. She turned to the baby as if he could judge her. Could she let grandfather and poor old Martin want a meal?

She went to her box and took out Catherine’s angel.

As she unfolded the linen, a tear dropped on it—gentle mortification, not anger: the shame of a proud heart forced to eat its own words. She sent Martin out to change the coin.

While he was gone, a Frenchman came with one of the dealers in illuminated work—the man who once had offered her so poor a price that she had nearly bitten her lip through to keep from crying. The Frenchman spoke with the measured courtesy of one who traffics in beauty for a powerful table. He said he was employed by his sovereign to collect masterpieces for her book of hours.

Margaret brought forth her two best works—those sheets she had guarded as if they were her own memories pressed into pigment. The Frenchman bent close. He breathed in, not scent but colour. And he was charmed most by the page where flowers and raspberries and little creeping things had been shaded by Margaret Van Eyck’s hand: the berries like beads of dark wine, the leaves veined fine as fishbone, the small creatures set among them as naturally as crumbs invite sparrows. It was a garden one could almost smell—sweetness and green bruised stalk—though it lay flat and silent.

He named a price so high it made Margaret blink, as if someone had opened a shutter on full noon.

“Nay,” said she, drawing back, “flout not my need, good stranger. Three mouths there be in this house, and none to fill them but me.”

Curious arithmetic—she had left herself out, as women do when they have grown used to counting others first.

“I’d flout thee not,” he answered quickly. “My princess charged me strictly, ‘Seek the best craftsmen’; but I will no hard bargains. Make them content with me, and me with them.”

The next moment Margaret was on her knees by the cradle, kissing little Gerard, sobbing into his warm baby smell of milk and clean linen, and showering four gold pieces upon him again and again, as if coins could be blessings made visible.

“And oh—what a good princess,” she told him in very broken Dutch, the words coming haltingly, like a woman trying to speak her childhood tongue after living too long among other sounds. “Wasn’t she? We will pray for her, won’t we, my lambkin—when we are old enough?”

Martin burst in then, his face red with wrath, his old pride stung raw. “They will not change it. I trow they think I stole it.”

“I am beholden to thee,” Margaret said hastily, and almost snatched the angel from him. She wrapped it up again, and put it back in its hiding-place, as if shame itself might hear and come peering.

Before those unexpected funds were spent she took to her ironing and starching again. The house filled with the clean steam of boiled linen; the sharp, comforting scent of starch rose like a promise. The iron’s hiss on damp cloth was a small, steady music—work made audible—so different from the mind’s inward roar when it has nothing solid to do. She learned to judge the heat by ear and smell, to cool it by touching it to a wet rag till it gave the right sigh.

In the midst of this, Martin sickened.

He lay nine days, and the hearth seemed to burn lower, as if it grudged warmth to a room where an old man moaned. Margaret made him broths—thin at first, then richened with what she could spare: a bone begged from a neighbour, a pinch of herbs, a crust softened and strained. She listened to his breathing at night; each rattle was a sound that lodged in her chest.

Then he died.

Nearly all her money went to bury him decently. She saw to it herself; she would not let him go out of the world like refuse. Afterward there was an empty chair by her fireside. For Martin had preferred the hearth to the sun as soon as the Busy Body was gone; he had sat there, nodding, hearing the kettle’s murmur and the street’s distant life, content with that small kingdom of warmth.

Margaret would not allow anybody to sit in this chair now. And whenever her eye rested too long on it vacant, it cost her a tear—quick, involuntary, like salt flung on food.

Now there was nobody to carry her linen home. To do it herself she must leave little Gerard in charge of a neighbour. But she dared not trust such a treasure to mortal; besides, she could not bear him out of her sight for hours and hours. So she set inquiries on foot for a boy to carry her basket on Saturday and Monday.

A plump, fresh-coloured youth came in, cap in hand, cheeks pink as if from the cooper’s yard heat. He was called Luke Peterson; he looked fifteen, but was eighteen. He blushed, twiddled his bonnet, and asked, with a shy boldness, whether a man would not serve her turn as well as a boy.

Before he spoke, Margaret had been thinking, This boy will just do. But she took his cue. “Nay; but a man will maybe seek more than I can well pay.”

“Not I,” Luke said warmly. “Why, Mistress Margaret, I am your neighbour, and I do very well at the coopering. I can carry your basket for you before or after my day’s work, and welcome. You have no need to pay me anything. ’Tisn’t as if we were strangers, ye know.”

“Why, Master Luke, I know your face, for that matter; but I cannot call to mind that ever a word passed between us.”

“Oh yes, you did, Mistress Margaret. What, have you forgotten? One day you were trying to carry your baby and eke your pitcher full o’ water; and quo’ I, ‘Give me the baby to carry.’ ‘Nay,’ says you, ‘I’ll give you the pitcher, and keep the bairn myself;’ and I carried the pitcher home, and you took it from me at this door, and you said to me, ‘I am muckle obliged to you, young man,’ with such a sweet voice—not like the folk in this street speak to a body.”

“I do mind now, Master Luke,” said Margaret; and her voice softened, as it always did when remembering kindness. “And methinks it was the least I could say.”

“Well, Mistress Margaret, if you will say as much every time I carry your basket, I care not how often I bear it, nor how far.”

“Nay, nay,” said Margaret, colouring faintly. “I would not put upon good nature. You are young, Master Luke, and kindly. Say I give you your supper on Saturday night, when you bring the linen home, and your dawn-mete o’ Monday; would that make us anywise even?”

“As you please,” Luke answered, but he looked wounded at the thought of being thought greedy. “Only say not I sought a couple o’ diets! for such a trifle as yon.”

So Luke came and went with the basket. Sometimes his feet on the stair were light, a young man’s rhythm; sometimes the basket made its own music, cloth shifting and buckles clinking. The house, for a while, went pretty smoothly. Heaven gave the poor young woman health and strength to balance her many ills; she set her days in order like loaves on a board.

But the heart grew more and more troubled by Gerard’s long, and now most mysterious silence. Work could not drown it. The ear, trained to catch a child’s smallest whimper, could not help catching the absence of another sound: no knock, no tread, no messenger calling his name. The street noises—vendors crying, children shrieking, the hammering from a distant yard—seemed louder when they brought her no meaning. Suspense, that mental torturer, began to tear her heavy heart with hot pincers, till she cried often and vehemently, “Oh, that I could know the worst.”

One day, while she was in this state, she heard a heavy step mount the stair.

She started and trembled. That is no step that I know. Ill tidings?

The door opened, and Eli came in—unexpected—grave and kind. He filled the little room with his presence, as if age itself had entered, bringing the chill of far journeys and the weight of news.

Margaret eyed him in silence, and her agitation grew, as broth grows to a boil when one forgets it for a moment.

“Girl,” said he, and his voice was low, “the skipper is come back.”

“One word,” gasped Margaret, and all the blood in her seemed to rush to her ears. “Is he alive?”

“Surely I hope so. No one has seen him dead.”

“Then they must have seen him alive.”

“No, girl; neither dead nor alive hath he been seen this many months in Rome. My daughter Kate thinks he is gone to some other city. She bade me tell you her thought.”

“Ay,” said Margaret, and her tone fell dark, as if the hearth had suddenly gone out. “Like enough. Like enough. My poor babe!”

Eli’s mouth trembled; then, as if the body will still ask its plain needs even when the soul is shaken, the old man said in a faintish voice that he had come fasting, and asked her for a morsel to eat.

The surface of Margaret’s agitated mind took pity. Her hands moved of themselves—hands trained to feed grief as well as hunger. She set water to heat; she cut what little she had; she fried, she warmed, she poured. She scarcely knew what she did, only that the sound of a knife on board, the simmer of a pot, the small crackle of fire were things she could command when nothing else would obey. The smells rose—salt, fat, warmed bread—and for a moment the room was domestic again, as if the world were not falling through her fingers.

When Eli had eaten, and was ready to go, he laid his hand upon her head—heavy, blessing-like—and said, “Be he alive, or be he dead, I look on thee as my daughter. Can I do nought for thee this day? Bethink thee now.”

“Ay, old man,” she whispered. “Pray for him; and for me!”

Eli sighed, and went sadly and heavily down the stairs. Margaret listened half stupidly to his retiring footsteps until they ceased. The street took him, and the house was hers again—hers and the child’s and the empty chair’s.

Then she sank down by the cradle, moaning, and drew little Gerard tight to her bosom, as if she could make a father out of her own arms.

“Oh, my poor fatherless boy,” she sobbed into his hair. “My fatherless boy!”

They were midway through their pot of pottage at Tergou—barley gone soft as old linen, onions melted sweet, a heel of smoked bacon lending the whole dish its quiet salt—when the latch flew up, and Luke Peterson blundered in as if the very wind had chased him. Dust lay on him like flour on a baker, and his breath came in ragged spurts that filled the low room with a harsh, panting music; outside, the evening crows and the far creak of a cart-wheel kept their steadier measures.

“Good people,” he burst out, “Mistress Catherine is wanted instantly at Rotterdam.”

Catherine’s spoon halted. “My name is Catherine, young man. Kate, it will be Margaret.”

“Ay, dame,” said he, swallowing air and words together. “She said to me, ‘Good Luke, hie thee to Tergou, and ask for Eli the hosier, and pray his wife Catherine to come to me, for God His love.’ I didn’t wait for daylight.”

“Holy saints!” Catherine cried. The sound of her voice struck the wooden walls and came back sharper. “He has come home, Kate. Nay—she would sure have said so. What on earth can it be?” And as steam from the pot rose, so did her fears—each one swelling upon the last, until the very smell of their dinner turned thin and far away.

“Mayhap the young man can tell us,” Kate ventured, timid as one tasting a strange broth.

“That I can,” said Luke. “Why—her babe is a-dying. And she was so wrapped up in it!”

Catherine sprang to her feet as if scalded. “What is his trouble?”

“Nay, I know not. But it has been peaking and pining worse and worse this while.”

Across the table, Cornelis and Sybrandt exchanged a glance—quick as a knife-flash, and satisfied. Catherine did not see it; she was already turned to her husband, her whole face a command.

“Now, Eli,” she cried, fierce as a housewife defending her hearth, “if you say a word against it, you and I shall quarrel, after all these years.”

“Who gainsays thee, foolish woman?” Eli answered, without heat. “Quarrel with your own shadow, while I go borrow Peter’s mule for ye.”

“Bless thee, my good man! Bless thee!” She pressed her hands together once, as if prayer were a thing to be kneaded into deeds. “Didst never yet fail me at a pinch. Now eat your dinners who can, while I go and make ready.”

She took Luke back with her in the cart; the wheels sang over the hard ruts, and the hedgerows whispered in the mild night wind. All the way she questioned and cross-questioned him—now coaxing like a woman seasoning a reluctant stew with honey, now sharp as vinegar—until she had turned his mind inside out, what there was of it.

At Rotterdam Margaret met her at the door, pale and shaken, and flung her arms about Catherine’s neck; her hair smelt of sour sweat and milk, the smell of a mother who has sat too long above a failing child, listening for breath.

Catherine held her at arm’s length and scanned her. “Come,” she said briskly, catching Margaret’s pulse with her eye as another woman would catch it with her fingers. “He is alive, thank God.”

Inside, the room was close; the fire snapped now and then, and the kettle’s low simmer made a comfort that did not reach the bed. The child lay there like a little candle guttering in its own grease. Catherine bent, looked at the faint mouth, the dull skin, the slack hands; then she looked at the poor hollow-eyed mother, and back again, measuring with the certainty of long kitchens and many cradles.

“Lucky you sent for me,” said she. “The child is poisoned.”

“Poisoned!” Margaret gasped. “By whom?”

“By you.”

Margaret staggered as if struck. “By me? Nay, indeed, mother. How can I help fretting?”

“Don’t tell me, Margaret.” Catherine’s voice had the hard ring of a wooden spoon on an iron pot. “A nursing mother has no business to fret. She must turn her mind away from her grief to the comfort that lies in her lap. Know you not that the child pines if the mother vexes herself? This comes of your reading and writing. Those idle crafts befit a man; but they keep all useful knowledge out of a woman. The child must be weaned.”

Margaret’s face flamed. “Oh, you cruel woman! I am sorry I sent for you. Would you rob me of the only bit of comfort I have in the world? A-nursing my Gerard, I forget I am the most unhappy creature beneath the sun.”

“That you do not,” Catherine snapped, “or he would not be the way he is.”

“Mother!” Margaret pleaded, broken between anger and fear.

“’Tis hard,” Catherine said at last, and the edge of her tone dulled a little, like steel warmed by the hearth. “But bethink thee; would it not be harder to look down and see his lovely wee face a-looking up at you out of a little coffin?”

“Oh, Jesu!”

“And how could you face your other troubles with your heart aye full, and your lap empty?”

Margaret’s hands clutched the bedclothes as if they were the last plank on the sea. “Oh, mother, I consent to anything. Only save my boy.”

“That is a good lass. Trust to me! I do stand by, and see clearer than thou.”

Yet there was another consent to be gained: the babe’s. And he, when Catherine tried the first shift, turned away, wailing thinly, as if the world itself had changed its taste.

“There,” said Margaret, trying for a smile through her misery, “he loves me too well.”

Catherine had not lived through harvests and hunger to be beaten by a sucking child. On the road she had marked a healthy young woman sitting outside her own door with an infant, her breast full and her face calm. Catherine went to her at once, told her the case plain as a recipe, and asked would she nurse the pining child for the nonce, till matters were ready to wean him.

The young woman consented with a smile, set her own child into the cradle, and came in. She dropped a curtsey. Catherine placed little Gerard in her hands. The woman’s touch was sure and warm; she examined him, pitied him softly, and then, with a little crooning sound that rose and fell like the doves under the eaves, she set him to her breast as naturally as if he had been born of her. The room changed in an instant: the sharp, desperate crying gave way to the thick, greedy pull of a child drinking life; and that simple, domestic sound—milk drawn, breath steadied—was like rain on a roof after drought.

Margaret, paralyzed by the sight, cast one wild, reproachful look at Catherine and burst into tears. The visitor looked up, startled.

“What is to do?” said she. “Wife, ye told me not the mother was unwilling.”

“She is not,” Catherine returned. “She is only a fool. Never heed her; and you, Margaret, I am ashamed of you.”

“You are a cruel, hard-hearted woman,” Margaret sobbed, the words tasting bitter on her tongue.

“Them as take in hand to guide the weak need be hardish. And you will excuse me; but you are not my flesh and blood; and your boy is.”

She let that lie a moment, heavy as a stone in a bowl. Then she added, “Come now, she is robbing her own to save yours, and you can think of nothing better than bursting out a-blubbering in the woman’s face. Out fie, for shame!”

“Nay, wife,” said the nurse gently, her voice like warm milk itself. “Thank Heaven, I have enough for my own and for hers to boot. And prithee wyte not on her! Maybe the troubles o’ life ha’ soured her own milk.”

“And her heart into the bargain,” Catherine said, remorseless as ever.

Margaret looked full at her; then her eyes dropped. “I know I ought to be very grateful to you,” she sobbed to the nurse. But she turned her head away and leaned over the chair, unable to endure the intolerable spectacle of another nursing her Gerard—and Gerard, with the innocent tyranny of hunger, drawing no distinction between the new breast and the old, only between plenty and pain.

“You are very welcome, my poor woman,” said the nurse. “And so are you, Mistress Catherine, which are my townswoman, and know it not.”

“What, are ye from Tergou?” Catherine said, quickening. “All the better. But I cannot call your face to mind.”

“Oh, you know not me,” the woman replied. “My husband and me, we are very humble folk by you. But true Eli and his wife are known of all the town; and respected. So, I am at your call, dame; and at yours, wife; and yours, my pretty poppet; night or day.”

When she had gone, the door closing on her quiet step, Catherine nodded. “There’s a woman of the right old sort.”

“I HATE her. I HATE her. I HATE her,” Margaret cried, with a fervour that surprised even herself; and the words seemed to scrape out of her like a pot scoured raw.

Catherine only laughed, and the laugh was the clack of a knife on a board—practical, almost cheerful. “That is right; better say it, as set sly and think it. It is very natural after all. Come, here is your bundle o’ comfort. Take and hate that, if ye can;” and she put the child into Margaret’s lap.

“No, no,” Margaret said, turning half away; she could not for her life turn the other half. “He is not my child now; he is hers. I know not why she left him here, for my part. It was very good of her not to take him to her house, cradle and all; oh! oh! oh! oh! oh! oh! oh!”

“Ah! well,” said Catherine, softer now, “one comfort, he is not dead.”

But Margaret’s grief, finding an old channel, ran into a bitter jest. “This gives me light: some other woman has got him away from me; like father, like son; oh! oh! oh! oh! oh!”

Catherine was sorry for her, and let her cry in peace. After that, when she needed Joan’s aid, she would take Gerard out “for a little fresh air.” The street’s small sounds—children’s feet on the stones, a fishwife’s call, the faint tapping of a cooper’s hammer—seemed meant to soothe; yet to Margaret they were only the world going on while her own life stood arrested. She never objected, nor challenged the excuse; but when Catherine returned with the child, Margaret was always in tears, as if each coming-back were a reminder that some going had not been undone.

This connivance did not last. Margaret grew as eager to wean little Gerard as she had once been frantic to keep him. It was done—by methods Catherine knew as well as she knew the right moment to lift a loaf from the oven—and the child’s health returned, colour creeping back like sunrise into his cheeks. Another trouble fell on him directly: teething. But here Catherine’s experience was a storehouse; she knew what cooled and what inflamed, what to rub and what to withhold, how to keep the little gums from swelling into fever. In the midst of her grief and her gnawing dread for the father, Margaret found sudden, piercing moments of bliss watching the tiny teeth press and show.

“Teeth, mother?” she would cry, laughing through tears. “I call them not teeth, but pearls of pearls.”

And each pearl that peeped and sparkled on his red gums was, to her, the greatest feat Nature had ever achieved. Catherine caught the same fancy. Had any man dared tell them standing corn was equally admirable, Margaret would have looked at him like a reproachful gazelle, and Catherine would have turned him out of doors. So each pearl’s arrival was announced with a shriek of triumph by whichever of them discovered it first, and the whole house would ring with that bright, foolish sound—life insisting on its own small ceremonies.

During these days Catherine gossiped with Joan, and learned she was wife to Jorian Ketel of Tergou, once servant to Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, but fallen out of favour and returned to Rotterdam, his native place. His friends had gotten him the place of sexton to the parish; and with that and carpentering besides, he did pretty well. Catherine, in turn, told Joan whose child it was she had nursed, and all about Margaret and Gerard, and how his silence had plunged them into deep anxiety.

“Ay,” said Joan, rocking her own child and listening to the room’s noises as if they were part of the tale, “the world is full of trouble.”

One day she said to Catherine, low, “It’s my belief my man knows more about your Gerard than anybody in these parts; but he has got to be closer than ever of late. Drop in some day just afore sunset, and set him talking. And for our Lady’s sake say not I set you on. The only hiding he ever gave me was for babbling his business; and I do not want another. Gramercy! I married a man for the comfort of the thing, not to be hided.”

So Catherine dropped in before sunset, when the day’s work slackens and tongues, like fires, are easiest stirred. Jorian sat by the fireside; the flames licked the pot-hook and made a faint singing that filled the pauses. He was ready enough to tell her, with a rough pride, how he had once befriended her son, and perhaps saved his life. But this was no news to Catherine; she had gratitude enough for that already, salted and stored away. The moment she began to cross-question him—why Gerard neither came nor wrote, what held him silent—Jorian threw a grim look at his wife. Joan met it with an air of stolid candour and innocent unconsciousness; but Catherine heard the change as one hears a bird cease singing when a hawk passes.

His answers grew short and sullen. “What should he know more than another?” and the like.

After a pause he added, grudgingly, “Think you the burgomaster takes such as me into his secrets?”

“Oh, then the burgomaster knows something?” Catherine’s voice sharpened at once.

“Likely. Who else should?”

“I’ll ask him,” she said.

“I would.”

“And tell him you say he knows.”

“That is right, dame. Go make him mine enemy. That is what a poor fellow always gets if he says a word to you women.”

From that moment Jorian shrank in and became impenetrable as a hedgehog—and almost as prickly. His very silence had a sound to it, a bristling hush that made the room feel smaller. To Catherine and Margaret it was torment: Ghysbrecht had for some cause been Gerard’s mortal enemy—had stopped his marriage, imprisoned him, hunted him. And here was the late servant, who, when off his guard, had hinted that this enemy held the clue to Gerard’s silence. They sifted Jorian’s every word and look as carefully as flour through a cloth; all remained dark.

At last Catherine said to Margaret, “Go thyself to him. You are young, you are fair. You will maybe get more out of him than I could.”

The guess was reasonable. Margaret went with her child in her arms and tapped timidly at Jorian’s door just before sunset, when the street noises thin and each step seems louder.

“Come in,” said a sturdy voice.

She entered; Jorian sat by the fire. At sight of her he rose, snorted, and burst out of the house as if the devil had crossed his threshold.

“Is that for me, wife?” Margaret asked, cheeks burning.

“You must excuse him,” Joan replied, rather coldly, and her coldness was like skim-milk after cream. “He lays it to your door that he is a poor man instead of a rich one. It is something about a piece of parchment. There was one amissing, and he got nought from the burgomaster all along of that one.”

Margaret’s arms tightened round her boy. “Alas! Gerard took it.”

“Likely. But my man says you should not have let him: you were pledged to him to keep them all safe. And sooth to say, I blame not my Jorian for being wroth. ’Tis hard for a poor man to be so near fortune and lose it by those he has befriended. However, I tell him another story. Says I, ‘Folk that are out o’ trouble like you and me didn’t ought to be too hard on folk that are in trouble; and she has plenty.’ Going already? What is all your hurry, mistress?”

“Oh, it is not for me to drive the goodman out of his own house.”

“Well, let me kiss the bairn afore ye go. He is not in fault anyway, poor innocent.”

Margaret bent her head, received that kiss like a blessing she did not deserve, and went away with her heart bruised. On that rebuff she made a resolution, and she told it to no one—not even to Catherine.

After six weeks’ stay the good Catherine returned to Tergou. The house there, with its familiar smells of wool and soap and smoked meat, took her back into its old rhythm as if she had never left; and yet something had shifted, as if a beam had been moved and the whole roof now bore weight differently.

Soon after came the child’s birthday. Margaret did no work that day. She put on her Sunday clothes, clean linen that smelt of sun and lye, and took her boy in her arms. She went to the church and prayed long and fervently for Gerard’s safe return. The church had its own sound-world: the hush that holds even footsteps to gentleness, the small coughs swallowed, the murmur of distant beads, the faint wheeze of the bell-rope. Her words, formed in her own tongue, seemed to cling to the stone and the timber; she felt, with a kind of despair, how no prayer—however honest—can be translated into certainty.

That same day and hour, far away, Father Clement celebrated a mass and prayed for Margaret’s departed soul in the minster church at Basle.

Sybrandt—or some other rakehell of that stamp—had once flung out, with a laugh, that a lie is not like a blow from a curtal axe. True enough. A steel edge has its measure: you may guess where it will bite, how deep, and what it will hew. But a lie is a seed you cannot see sprout; it runs under doors, it creeps into beds, it takes root in wills and wedding-lines, and it bears a harvest no man can count.

Here, too, one heartless falsehood—minted lightly between brothers who only wished, as they told themselves, to lessen the number of hands that might dip into their father’s substance—spread farther than their malice had meant. They gained little. Instead they saw their mother’s heart, emptied of one son, fill itself the more fiercely with the name and face of little Gerard. And then, like salt cast upon their secret, there came a day when Eli, before them all, spoke plain as a bell: Gerard being lost, and like dead, he had set it down in his will that the child should be provided for, and Margaret too—Margaret, his poor son’s widow.

At that, a look went like lightning between the black sheep of the house: not triumph, but warning—such as thieves give one another when a door has creaked. Cornelis had the words on his tongue—Gerard is like to be alive—yet he saw his mother’s eyes on him, steady and searching, and he swallowed his speech as a man gulps down something that chokes.

But the other partner in the lie, Ghysbrecht van Swieten, had no such easy swallowing. He was failing; his breath grew short on stairs, his hands trembled at the clasps of his purse. He felt, with a chill that was not of weather, how near the hour came when all his goods would fall from him like clothes, and only the naked weight of his deeds cling fast to his soul.

He had never been able to blind himself altogether; he was too shrewd, too taught by years of reckonings. Remorse came upon him by fits, like a gust through a chink. And so, when Gerard’s letter had reached his hands—the letter meant for Margaret—he had compounded with himself, as men do who would be thought honest and yet mean to keep their hold on earth.

“I cannot give up land and money,” said his giant Avarice, squatting broad across his heart.

“I will cause her no needless pain,” piped his dwarf Conscience, thin-voiced, but not quite dead.

So he tampered with the seal, finger and nail worrying the wax; and, finding no syllable there of deed or property, he carried the letter himself to Margaret, and—strange jugglery of the human mind—took merit to himself for that crumb of right. He set it like a counter on the scale against all he withheld; and because he was both judge and prisoner, he found the weight convenient.

Then Margaret’s child was born; and that small wail in the world shifted the whole matter into another light. If Gerard’s letter should work as Gerard meant—if it should bring him back, or even bring the truth—then Ghysbrecht’s trick would not merely rob her of acres; it would stain her name. Dishonour would touch the daughter of Peter Brandt, the granddaughter of Floris: the child of two old friends that had once succoured Ghysbrecht in his plague-time and his poverty. These thoughts, coming at that season of life when a man’s body wanes and old faces rise up clearer than yesterday’s, filled him with dark horrors. He would start at night as if some dead hand had shaken him; the silence of his chamber seemed full of whispers.

Yet he dared not confess. The cure was an honest man; he would have made Ghysbrecht disgorge, not sentiments, but coin and land. And with Ghysbrecht, Avarice had hardened into habit—like salt meat long kept, tough and stubborn; penitence was but a taste on the tongue, gone as soon as swallowed.

Matters stood thus when one day, coming back from the town-hall to his own house, he found a woman waiting in his vestibule with a child on her arm. She was veiled; and, thinking her one of those who come by stealth to bargain with shame, he addressed her in a magisterial tone, as if he were already her judge.

At that she let fall the veil and looked him full in the face.

It was Margaret Brandt.

Her sudden presence—her pallor, her bright, fevered eyes—struck him like a clap; he could not hide the start nor the quick confusion that ran over him.

“Where is my Gerard?” she cried; and her breast rose and fell as if the words had been torn up from deep water. “Is he alive?”

“For aught I know,” stammered Ghysbrecht. “I— I hope so, for your sake. Prithee come into this room. The servants—”

“Not a step,” said Margaret. Her voice was low, but it had iron in it. She set her hand on his shoulder and held him, not with violence only, but with the sheer strength of a woman driven past fear. “You know the secret of that which is breaking my heart. Why does not my Gerard come, nor send a line this many months? Answer me, or all the town is like to hear me—ay, and thy servants too. My misery is too great to be sported with.”

He persisted, trembling, that he knew nothing; that he had no more knowledge than she.

She told him those who had sent her to him told her another tale. “You do know,” said she, with a dreadful quietness, “why he neither comes nor sends.”

Ghysbrecht turned paler and paler; but he gathered his dignity about him like a cloak, and tried to stand upon it.

“Would you believe,” said he, “those two knaves against a man of worship?”

“What two knaves?” said Margaret sharply; for she caught at every word as a hungry child snatches crust.

He stammered, snared by his own slip. “Said ye not—? There, I am a poor old broken man, whose memory is shaken. And you come here and confuse me so, I know not what I say.”

“Ah, sir,” said Margaret, and now her tone changed; grief and a strange tenderness made it deep, “your memory is shaken—or sure you would not be my enemy. My father saved you from the plague, when none other would come anigh you; and was ever your friend. My grandfather Floris helped you in your early poverty, and loved you, man and boy. Three generations of us you have seen; and here is the fourth of us.”

She shifted the child—little Gerard—so his face came into the light that fell from the vestibule window. He had been fretful, and now, feeling the mother’s quickened pulse, he hushed, staring with the grave wonder of infants; his mouth still shone with milk. The very smell of him—warm skin, clean linen, and that faint sour-sweet breath that clings to babes—went up like an appeal.

“This,” she said, “is your old friend Peter’s grandchild, and your old friend Floris his great-grandchild. Look down on his innocent face, and think of theirs!”

“Woman, you torture me,” sighed Ghysbrecht; and he sank upon a bench as if his knees had been cut.

But she saw her advantage, and she took it—not cruelly, but as drowning folk clutch. She kneeled before him and set the boy on his knees, steadying him with her hands. The child’s small fingers, exploring, caught at Ghysbrecht’s sleeve and the roughness of his furred gown; he made a soft sound in his throat, half coo, half question.

“This fatherless babe,” said Margaret, “is poor Margaret Brandt’s, that never did you ill, and comes of a race that loved you. Nay, look at his face; ’twill melt thee more than any word of mine. Saints of heaven, what can a poor desolate girl and her babe have done, to wipe out all memory of thine own young days—when thou wert guiltless as he is—that now looks up in thy face and implores thee to give him back his father?”

And with her arms under the child she held him up higher and higher, so the little one’s eyes were level with the old man’s. The baby smiled—one of those sudden, careless smiles that are like sunlight slipping through cloud, unbought and undeserved.

Ghysbrecht cast a wild look of anguish on the child, and another on the kneeling mother; and then something in him—wounded and venomous—sprang up. He started to his feet, shrieking:

“Avaunt, ye pair of adders!”

For a moment the stung soul lent the old limbs a cruel vigour. He walked rapidly to and fro, wringing his hands and clutching at his white hair, as if he would tear the thoughts out by the roots.

“Forget those days?” he cried. “I forget all else. Oh, woman, woman—sleeping or waking I see but the faces of the dead. I hear but the voices of the dead. And I shall soon be among the dead. There—there—what is done is done. I am in hell. I am in hell.”

The unnatural force fled as it had come. He staggered; and but for Margaret—who, in spite of her own shaking, flung an arm about him—he would have fallen full length. She cried out for help.

Two servants ran in. They took him, helpless now as an unbaked loaf that collapses when the oven’s heat fails, and carried him away in a swoon, his old furrowed face white and slack, his hair hanging down over a servant’s elbow like spilled flax.

“Heaven forgive me,” Margaret whispered, standing where they left her. “I doubt I have killed the poor old man.”

Yet the visit, meant to pierce the mystery, left it darker. When she turned over each word he had let slip, her suspicion grew teeth. He did know something. And that cry of “two knaves”—who were they? Who had told her, or seemed to tell her, a tale that made him betray himself?

“Oh, my Gerard,” she said, drawing her child close as if the babe were the only warm certainty left, “my poor deserted babe—thou and I are wading in deep waters.”

The journey to Tergou had eaten money like a hungry fire, and she could ill spare it; and then, as if the world watched for the instant her purse was thinnest, a customer ran away owing her. Bread had to be kneaded with less wheat; broth stretched with more water; the little household sounds—the scrape of a spoon in a pot, the clink of a farthing on wood—took on a sharpness that seemed to mock her.

Once more she was driven to unfold Catherine’s angel, that precious piece of gold, and feel its cold weight in her palm. She had it in her hand as she came down-stairs—already tasting in her mouth the shame of parting with it, as if she were selling a memory. And then she stopped.

Loose silver lay on the table, and beside it a written line.

For Gerard his wife.

She fell upon the writing with a little cry, not of pain but of astonished life; and soon it broke into a cry of joy that filled the small room like a sudden song.

“He is alive,” she whispered, and her lips trembled upon the letters. “He sends me this by some friendly hand.”

She kissed the writing again and again, as if she could drink comfort through ink. Then she hid it in her bosom, close to the heat of her heart.

Time rolled on. No news came—no word, no sure sign, no voice calling in the street, no footstep on the stair that made her certain. Yet about every two months a small sum in silver found its way into the house.
