Sometimes it lay quietly on the table, as if it had always belonged there. Once it was flung in through the bedroom window in a purse, the leather striking the floor with a dull thud that made her start from sleep. Once she found it at the bottom of Luke’s basket; he had stopped at the public-house to talk to a friend, and swore he knew nothing of it. The giver—or his agent—was never caught. Catherine disowned it with honest surprise. Margaret van Eyck swore she had no hand in it. So did Eli.

And Margaret, whenever it came, would look down at little Gerard—now sturdier, with bread-crumbs on his lips and a way of drumming his heels against her hip when he wanted to be let down—and say, half to him and half to the empty air:

“Oh, my poor deserted child, you and I are wading in deep waters.”

At least half of this modest, useful supply she spent—against prudence, and in defiance of her own station—on clothing the boy beyond what folk deemed fit. She scoured for decent cloth, chose seams that would hold, washed and aired the little garments till they smelled of soap and sun, not of sour damp. If there was to be hunger, let there not be slovenliness; if there was to be loss, let there not be shame upon the child’s body.

“If it does come from Gerard,” she told herself, tightening a stitch, “he shall see his boy neat.”

The mothers in the street began to sneer—especially those whose own brats went with elbows out, and whose envy made a harsher music than their tongues. Their voices, sharp as crows, followed her sometimes; but the sounds that ruled Margaret were other: the hush of her child asleep, the small steady chewing of crust, the crackle of kindling, the distant bell that marked the hours whether they were joyful or not.

Months rolled on; and the keener torments—those that sting and keep you moving—gave way to a dead sickness of heart, heavy as sodden bread. She went back to her first thought, the thought that had never truly left:

“Gerard must be dead.”

She should never see her boy’s father again; never see the marriage lines that would make the world shut its mouth. That last grief—her lack of proof—had been somewhat eased by Eli and Catherine, who, in their own way, had recognized the betrothal. But now it revived in full force; others would not be so gentle, nor would their tongues be bridled by family affection.

Often she moaned over the child’s illegitimacy, the word itself like a stone in her throat.

“Is it not enough for us to be bereaved?” she would whisper in the dimness, rocking the boy when he fretted. “Must we be dishonoured too? Oh, that we had ne’er been born.”

Then a change came over Peter Brandt.

For nearly two years his mind had been clouded since the paralytic stroke; he had lived as if behind a misted window, sometimes smiling at shadows, sometimes staring without seeing. Now the cloud began, by fits, to lift. He had intervals of clear intelligence; and in those hours he and Margaret would speak of Gerard, touching the name softly, as one touches a sore place to see if it still hurts—until his mind wandered again and the door shut.

One day Margaret, returning after some hours abroad, found him conversing with Catherine in a manner he had not done since the stroke—words linked, sense steady, his voice more like the old physician’s than she had heard in long.

“Eh, girl,” said Catherine, “why must you be out? But indeed I have told him all; and we have been a-crying together over thy troubles.”

Margaret stood silent, joy rising in her like leaven. She looked from one to the other, hardly daring to breathe lest the moment should crumble.

Peter smiled on her—a true smile, not the wandering one. “Come,” said he, “let me bless thee.”

She kneeled at his feet. His hand, though weakened, rested upon her head with a gravity that seemed to steady the whole house. He blessed her most eloquently, with the old cadence that had comforted sick-beds and frightened death away for many.

He told her she had been, all her life, the lovingest, truest, and most obedient daughter Heaven ever sent to a poor old widowed man.

“May thy son be to thee,” he said, “what thou hast been to me!”

After that his lids drooped and he dozed, the blessing still warm on her crown like fresh bread from an oven.

Then Catherine and Margaret whispered together, careful of the old man’s sleep; the house itself seemed to listen, the faint creak of timber and distant street-sounds softened, as if the world had stepped on tiptoe.

“All our talk e’en now,” Catherine breathed, “was of Gerard. It lies heavy on his mind. His poor head must often have listened to us when it seemed quite dark. Margaret, he is a very understanding man; he thought of many things. ‘He may be in prison,’ says he; ‘or forced to go fighting for some king; or sent to Constantinople to copy books there; or gone into the Church after all.’ He had a bent that way.”

“Ah, mother,” whispered Margaret back, “he doth but deceive himself as we do.”

She had scarce finished when a strange interruption broke in, as sudden as a shout in a still field.

A loud voice cried out, “I SEE HIM, I SEE HIM!”

Peter Brandt’s eyes flew wide, dilating; he seemed to look not at the wall, but through it—through brick, through distance, through time itself.

“IN A BOAT; ON A GREAT RIVER; COMING THIS WAY,” he cried. “Sore disfigured; but I knew him. Gone! gone! all dark.”

His head sank back; the fire that had flared in him died as quickly as it had blazed.

He asked feebly, “Where is Margaret?”

“Dear father, I am by thy side.” Her hand found his, and held it fast. “Oh, mother—mother—what is this?”

“I cannot see thee,” he murmured, “and but a moment agone I saw all round the world. Ay—ay. Well, I am ready. Is this thy hand? Bless thee, my child, bless thee! Weep not! The tree is ripe.”

The old physician’s own body read the signs aright. These calm words were his last. The next moment he drooped his head, and gently—placidly—drifted away from earth, like an infant sinking into rest.

The torch had flashed up before going out.

Margaret had wept for old Martin as one weeps for a tree that has stood long in the yard and made a kindly shadow; but this new felling smote her nearer, for it fell across the very hearth. Catherine, bustling with the good-will that loves to mend sorrow by handling it, tried her homely cordials.

“He is at rest,” she said; “he himself called it a ripe tree. And see now—there be but two mouths to feed, child; one pot the lighter.”

Margaret turned on her with wet eyes that had no anger in them, only a deep amaze, as if Catherine had spoken in some foreign tongue and mistaken the meaning of her own words.

“Such cares are all the joys I have,” she answered. “They fill my desolate heart; and now my heart seems void as well as waste. Oh, empty chair—my bosom it aches to see thee. Poor old man! how could I love him by halves? I that did use to sit and look at him and think, ‘But for me thou wouldst die of hunger.’ He—so wise, so learned erst—was got to be helpless as my own sweet babe; and I loved him as if he had been my child instead of my father. Oh, empty chair! Oh, empty heart! Well-a-day! well-a-day!”

Her tears fell as naturally as broth into a bowl, and would not be denied. The room itself seemed to listen: the small hush between the tick of the clock and the soft crack of settling wood; the far-off street noises dulled by the thick walls—sounds that had once been a comfort, because Martin’s breath had made a third, familiar sound among them. Now there was a gap in the household’s music; and the very silence had a sharpness, like a knife laid down on the table.

Catherine stood abashed. Her ready sayings, that were meant to serve for all griefs as salt serves for all meats, lay flat and tasteless here. At last she dropped her eyes, and, after a day in which she had watched Margaret move about the house like one who lays trenchers for a ghost, she came to her with a simpler voice.

“I speak to thee out o’ my head, and not out o’ my bosom,” said she. “Thou dost well to be deaf to me. Were I in thy place, I should mourn the old man all one as thou dost.”

Then Margaret caught at her as drowning folk catch a plank, and kissed her; and that one bit of true sympathy did her more good than all the earlier comfort. The commonplaces did none.

After this, Catherine’s heart—being soft under its meddlesomeness—yearned over the young wife. She watched her eat little, and yet still set food out as if three must dine; watched her ladle soup into an extra porringer by sheer habit, and then, remembering, stop short with the spoon trembling above the pot. Margaret’s grief took the form of household work; she clung to it as to a native tongue in a strange country, because it was something she could still speak without thinking.

One evening Catherine found her in the act of laying the board. She had taken down a platter that Martin had liked, and stood with it in her hands as if it were heavier than baked clay ought to be. Catherine came close and spoke low, as women do when they would put hard counsel into kindly words.

“My poor girl,” said she, “you were not born to live alone. I have got to look on you as my own daughter. Waste not thine youth upon my son Gerard. Either he is dead—or he is a traitor. It cuts my heart to say it; but who can help seeing it? Thy father is gone, and I cannot always be aside thee. And here is an honest lad that loves thee well this many a day. I’d take him and Comfort together. Heaven hath sent us these creatures to torment us and comfort us and all; we are just nothing in the world without ’em.”

Margaret stared, as if Catherine had slipped from plain Dutch into Latin.

Then Catherine, taking her perplexity for blindness, pushed on in her practical fashion.

“Why, sure you are not so blind as not to see it?”

“What? Who?” Margaret’s voice was small, like one that has been called out of sleep.

“Who but this Luke Peterson.”

“What—our Luke? The boy that carries my basket?”

“Nay, he is over nineteen, and a fine healthy lad. And I have made inquiries for you; and they all do say he is a capable workman, and never touches a drop; and that is much in a Rotterdam lad, which they are mostly half man, half sponge.”

The first smile that had visited Margaret in many days came and went, faint as the smell of cinnamon when the lid is lifted and clapped down again.

“Luke loves dried puddings dearly,” said she, and the kitchen seemed for a moment to warm with the memory of nutmeg and currants, of bread soaked and sweetened, pressed, steamed, and sliced. “And I make them to his mind. ’Tis them he comes a-courting here.”

She stopped, colouring suddenly to the roots of her hair, as if her own tongue had betrayed her into another dialect than she meant to speak.

“But if I thought he came after your son’s wife—that is, or ought to be—I’d soon put him to the door.”

“Nay, nay,” cried Catherine, frightened at the mischief her own hands had raised. “For Heaven’s sake let me not make mischief. Poor lad! Why, girl, Fancy will not be bridled. Bless you, I wormed it out of him near a twelvemonth agone.”

“Oh, mother—and you let him?”

“Well,” said Catherine, half ashamed and half stubborn, “I thought of you. I said to myself, ‘If he is fool enough to be her slave for nothing, all the better for her. A lone woman is lost without a man about her to fetch and carry her little matters.’ But now my mind is changed, and I think the best use you can put him to is to marry him.”

Margaret drew herself up, not in pride so much as in loyalty that had become the last structure standing in her desolation.

“So then,” said she bitterly, “his own mother is against him, and would wed me to the first comer. An, Gerard, thou hast but me. I will not believe thee dead till I see thy tomb, nor false till I see thee with another lover in thine hand. Foolish boy—I shall ne’er be civil to him again.”

Thus Luke Peterson, who had been coming and going with the basket like a tame creature of the house, met now a cold look where he had found gentle speech. At first he took it for some chance weather of the women’s minds; but coldness that lasts turns the stoutest heart into pulp. By-and-by, when Margaret spoke little, and then spoke short and sharp, the great soft fellow fell to whimpering, and at last asked her plump, with that blunt honesty that is a child’s weapon in a man’s hand, whether he had done aught to offend her.

“Nothing,” said Margaret, though her tone cut. “I am to blame. I am curst. If you will take my counsel you will keep out of my way awhile.”

“It is all along of me, Luke,” put in Catherine quickly, not able to bear the sight of his hurt.

“You, Mistress Catherine?” Luke gaped as if struck. “Why, what have I done for you to set her against me?”

“Nay,” said Catherine, half coaxing, half scolding, “I meant all for the best. I told her I saw you were looking towards her through a wedding ring. But she won’t hear of it.”

“There was no need to tell her that, wife,” Luke cried, with a sudden flare of misery. “She knows I am courting her this twelvemonth.”

“Not I,” said Margaret hotly; “or I should never have opened the street door to you.”

“Why, I come here every Saturday night,” said Luke, amazed. “And that is how the lads in Rotterdam do court. If we sup with a lass o’ Saturdays, that wooing.”

“Oh—that is Rotterdam, is it?” Margaret’s mouth tightened; the words were Dutch, but the meaning was not hers at all. “Then next time you come, let it be Thursday or Friday. For my part, I thought you came after my puddings, boy.”

“I like your puddings well enough,” said Luke, swallowing. “You make them better than mother does. But I like you still better than the puddings.”

The very mention of puddings—of the raisins she had picked over, the suet she had chopped fine, the spice she had grated till the air was full of warm sweetness—might once have softened her; food had always been her way of giving love a body. But now the words struck her as an invasion of the one sacred thing she had left: her name as Gerard’s wife.

“Then you have seen the last of them,” said she. And then, not loudly, but with a firmness that shut a door, “How dare you talk so to another man’s wife, and him far away? You need not trouble yourself to come here any more, Luke; I can carry my basket myself.”

“Oh—very well,” said Luke.

He sat a little while, silent and stupid, as if his thoughts were heavy as wet wool. Then he rose, looked once at Catherine with the face of a chastised dog, and said sadly, “Dame, I daresay I have got the sack,” and went out.

Yet habit is a chain that holds even when it galls. The next Saturday, as evening settled and the street’s noises thinned to the occasional footfall and a distant call, Catherine, opening the door, found him on the step, his great shoulders shaking, blubbering outright. He told her, between sobs, that he had got used to come there; and every other place seemed strange.

Catherine went in and told Margaret. Margaret listened, and her mouth softened against her will. She sighed.

“Poor Luke,” said she. “He might come in for her—if he could know his place, and treat her like a married wife.”

When Catherine carried back this message, Luke’s face brightened, then fell into doubt. He hesitated, as if the terms were a riddle spoken in a language he had not learnt.

“Pshaw!” cried Catherine, impatient with nicety. “Promises are pie-crusts. Promise her all the world, sooner than sit outside like a fool, when a word will carry you inside. Now you humour her in everything; and then, if poor Gerard come not home and claim her, you will be sure to have her—in time. A lone woman is aye to be tired out, thou foolish boy.”

Brother Clement had taught and preached in Basle more than a twelvemonth, when, one raw morning, the door of the schoolroom opened and in came Brother Jerome—powdered with road-dust as with flour, his cloak grey at hem and shoulder, and yet with a light in his eye as though he carried a banner under his ribs.

“Give the glory to God, Brother Clement,” said he; “thou canst now wend to England with me.”

Clement’s face, that could be tender as warmed wine and keen as vinegar, brightened at once. “I am ready, Brother Jerome; and expecting thee these many months, have in the intervals of teaching and devotion studied the English tongue somewhat closely.”

“’Twas well thought of,” Jerome replied; and, as they broke their fast—black bread, a scrap of cheese sharp with age, and the thin beer of the house—he told him why the delay had been so long. He had waited until he could win from Rome extraordinary powers: to collect moneys for the Church’s need in England, and to hear confession in the secular monasteries.

“So now,” said Jerome, setting down his cup as if it were a seal upon the table, “gird up thy loins, and let us go forth and deal a good blow for the Church, and against the Franciscans.”

They went out together, two black figures on the long river-road; and the Rhine went beside them with its own perpetual sermon—now a lap and suck at stones, now a broad hush like a held breath, now the slap of oar-blades under a ferry, and, in the towns, the clang of smiths and the crying of women in markets. Clement, who had a quick ear for a place, would listen to its sound as other men read a book: if the alehouse door clacked all day, if the street-song was coarse, if at vesper-time the bell was drowned by shouting, he knew something of the town before he ever saw its faces.

Down the Rhine they preached for England. In the larger places they mounted the same pulpit in turn; in the smaller they often divided, taking different sides of the river, and meeting again at some appointed stone-cross or ferry. Both were able orators, yet of unlike craft.

Jerome’s preaching was noble, grave, and impressive; it marched like a file of armed men—step after step the same, and each step sure. His voice, too, held one note longer than most men would dare; it made a roof over the hearers’ heads, and under that roof they sat still. Clement’s was another manner: full of turn and variety, sometimes homely as talk in a bakehouse, and then suddenly lifting, as a wind lifts smoke straight up from a chimney. In its common flow it was gentle and winning; it curled round the understanding and the heart as the smell of good broth steals into a house and makes even the sour-tempered child think of sitting down. Yet when the thought rose, he rose with it; and then, for moments, he thundered and flashed and swept men off their feet as a torrent in spring.

Clement had also a habit—quiet as the salting of meat—that Jerome scorned. Before he preached he would contrive, without seeming to do so, to learn what had lately befallen a town, and what sin lay nearest its daily hand. He would question a lay-brother at the convent gate, a woman drawing water, a boy selling eels, a host in an inn; and, like a careful cook who tastes the pot before he adds pepper, he would know what spice the souls before him required. Jerome, unbending, would go straight to his chosen theme as a plough to its furrow, and thought it beneath him to bend aside to men’s particular mire.

Once, at a great town some leagues from the Rhine, they mounted the same pulpit in turn. The church was full—oil lamps staling the air, wet cloaks steaming, and the breath of a hundred bodies mixed with the faint sweet rot of rushes on the floor. Outside, through a door left ajar, came the market’s life in scraps: a donkey braying, a knife hammered on a stall, the far-off singing of a drinker already rehearsing the night.

Jerome preached against vanity in dress, a favourite quarry of his. He was eloquent and satirical; he pricked the pride of ribbons and sleeves and painted faces, and the people listened with complacency, for the barbs flew over them. It was a vice they were little given to; they could enjoy the lash when it fell on another’s back.

Then Clement rose, and the very shifting of the crowd told Jerome that the key had turned in another lock. Clement preached against drunkenness.

Here the air changed. The sin was a besetting one and, in those parts, almost fenced round from rebuke by custom; for the clergy themselves were infected, and a broad popular indulgence stood guard like a brawny porter at a tavern door. Clement struck at it without mercy, with blows taken from Holy Writ and from the plain records of village talk. A crime in itself, he called it the nursing mother of crimes—especially theft and murder. He named, without flinching, a parricide lately committed in that very town by an honest man in liquor; he told how a band of drunkards had roasted one of their comrades alive in a neighbouring village, as if man were pig at a feast and the devil the cook.

“Your last prince,” cried he, “is reported to have died of apoplexy; but well you know he died of drink. And of your aldermen, one perished miserably last month—dead drunk, suffocated in a puddle. Your children’s backs go bare that ye may fill your bellies with that which makes you the worst of beasts—silly as calves, yet fierce as boars—and drives your families to need and your souls to hell.”

The church muttered like a pot beginning to simmer.

“I tell ye,” he went on, and his voice took that strange mingling of pity and scourge which made women press their hands to their mouths, “your town—ay, and your very nation—would sink to the bottom of mankind, did your women drink as you do. And how long will they be temperate, and, contrary to nature, resist the example of their husbands and fathers? Vice ne’er yet stood still. Ye must amend yourselves, or see them come down to your mark. Already in Bohemia they drink along with the men.”

The whispering rose; the men scowled; the women’s eyes widened, not at the men’s guilt, but at the picture he painted.

“How shows a drunken woman?” he demanded. “Would you love to see your wives drunken, your mothers drunken?”

At this there broke forth a shout of horror; for those audiences had not learned to sit mute when the preacher drove a nail home. Clement caught the sound as a man catches the crackle of kindling.

“Ah, that comes home to you!” he cried. “What madmen! Think you it doth not more shock the all-pure God to see a man—His noblest work—turned to a drunken beast, than it can shock you creatures of sin and unreason to see a woman turned into a thing no better nor worse than yourselves?”

Then, with a skill that was almost household-craft, he set before them two pictures as plainly as a table laid: a drunkard’s house, and a sober man’s.

He made them smell the sour ale that had spilled and dried on boards; see the bread so thinly cut it was shame; hear the child’s thin crying at night because there was no milk, no pottage, no peace; see the wife’s face, once fresh as new churned butter, now pinched and grey; and, above all, hear the house’s sound—the drunken foot against the bench, the quarrel like a dog-fight, the sudden dead hush after a blow. Then he turned, and made them taste the other dwelling: the clean smell of wood-smoke; the pot that had something in it besides water; the loaf baked honest and shared; the ale taken in measure, as a seasoning not a flood; the children’s laughter, the wife’s voice not trembling, the husband’s steps steady; and in that house, even the silence was a good silence—the kind that lets a man sleep and a woman breathe.

He spoke so truly, with such domestic exactness, that the wives fell all to “ohing” and “ahing,” and “Eh, but that is a true word,” as if he were recounting their own pantries and bedsides.

The discourse made uproar. When they poured out, the crowd did not break cleanly like water; it clotted into knots. The men were indignant, their pride stung where it was tenderest; and then—strange commerce of household power—the women, who had cried out at his pictures, flattered their men and took their part openly against the preacher. A married man had a right to a drop; he needed it, working for all the family. And for their part, they said, they did not care to change their men for milksops. Thus did they defend with their tongues what their eyes had condemned.

Yet the very evening gave Clement his answer. A band of women—near a hundred—found him, crowded round him, and with a kind of hungry gratitude poured gifts into his wallet: the best they had, as if they were laying up provision against a famine of the soul. One pressed on him a little loaf, another a lump of butter wrapped in leaf, another a string of dried apples; some offered him the roses off their heads as though giving up an ornament for a remedy. They kissed his frock, blessed him “for taking in hand to mend their sots,” and spoke low and fast, like people afraid the men might hear and forbid their hope.

Jerome, watching, felt a chill disapproval, as of a monk tasting spice and calling it worldly. “Drunkenness is not heresy, Clement,” said he; “that a whole sermon should be preached against it.”

But as they went on down the river-road, town after town, Jerome found—much to his surprise—that Clement’s words sank deeper than his own. Men listened, thought, cried; sometimes they even amended their ways. Clement, in confession, would draw out a man’s shame as patiently as bones are picked from a fish; he would name the sin in the sinner’s own dialect and cadence, so that it was no Latin ghost but the very thing that stank on the man’s breath. Jerome saw it, and could not deny it.

“He hath the art of sinking to their peg,” thought Jerome. “Yet he can soar high enough at times.”

Upon the whole it puzzled him. He had a secret sense of superiority to his tenderer brother; and after about two hundred miles of such travelling, that puzzle began to displease him as well. He checked the feeling as petty and unworthy; for he was stern first with himself.

“Souls differ like locks,” said he within, “and preachers must differ like keys, or the fewer should the Church open for God to pass in. And certes, this novice hath the key to these northern souls, being himself a northern man.”

So they came slowly down the Rhine—sometimes drifting a few miles by boat, the water slapping the timbers and the oars creaking like old doors; but in general walking the banks, barefoot, preaching and teaching and confessing, the soundscape of each place entering their bodies as surely as its bread and air.

At length they reached the town of Düsseldorf.

There was the little quay. There were the same waters licking the posts. There were the streets, the familiar angles of houses, the smell of river-mud and tarred rope, the calls of boatmen that a man might recognise blindfold. There stood “The Silver Lion.”

Nothing had changed—save he who looked on it.

Brother Clement landed and walked through it barefoot, his heart calm and cold, his hands crossed on his breast, his eyes bent meekly on the ground: a true son of Dominic and of Holy Church, passing through the world like a shadow that had once been flesh.

“Eli,” said Catherine, laying down her distaff as if it were a ladle and she were about to season a pot, “answer me one question like a man, and I’ll ask no more to-day. What is wormwood?”

Eli, caught as a cook is caught when asked the name of a spice he has only ever tasted in another man’s broth, stared a moment, his honest face blank with the effort. Then he rallied.

“It is summat as tasteth main bitter.”

“That is a fair answer, my man,” said Catherine, “but not the one I look for.”

“Then answer it thyself,” said Eli, a little nettled.

“And shall,” replied she; and her voice, for all its homeliness, had the sharp clean ring of a knife on a board. “Wormwood is—to have two in the house a-doing nought, but waiting for thy shoes and mine.”

Eli groaned, as if she had thrust the bitter herb beneath his tongue.

The hearth snapped softly; the kettle sang in its thin, patient way; outside, the town had its own tide of sound—wooden soles on stone, a far cry from the quay, the clink of harness. Yet within, the quiet had grown heavy, a silence that was not peace but stoppage, like dough left too long without kneading. Catherine had heard it for days: the idle cough, the restless shifting, the long stretches where no work’s rhythm saved a man from his own thoughts.

“Methinks,” she went on, not cruelly, but with that practical pity that turns to action, “waiting for their best friend’s coffin, that and nothing to do, are enow to make them worse than Nature meant. Why not set them up somewhere, to give ’em a chance?”

Eli was willing—he always was, when Catherine’s mind was made up—but fear clung to him.

“They’ll drink and gamble their very shelves away,” said he, imagining barrels tapped and coins rattled away, the shop stripped bare as a larder after a feast-day.

“Nay,” said Catherine, “dost take me for a simpleton? Of course I mean to watch them at starting, and drive them wi’ a loose rein, as the saying is.”

“Where didst think of?” asked Eli. “Not here; to divide our own custom.”

“Not likely.” Catherine’s eyes brightened, quick as flame takes a new brand. “I say Rotterdam against the world. Then I could start them.”

She spoke it as if the word itself—Rotterdam—had a taste: salt air, tar, fish-skins, rye-bread, foreign tongues in the market, and money changing hands with a sound like dry beans poured from a sack. She called it prudence; and perhaps it was. Yet somewhere beneath, like a bay-leaf hidden in stew, lay the truer savor of her resolve: to be nearer little Gerard.

So there were many talks, and many promises. Cornelis and Sybrandt—men with hands made for work and mouths too easily tempted—vowed amendment upon these terms, swearing it with more heat than steadiness. Catherine listened as she might listen to a cook promising cleanliness: approving, but already planning how often she must look in on him, how sharply she must smell his pans.

At last she went to Rotterdam shop-hunting, and took Kate with her for a change. The journey had its own music: wheels grumbling over ruts, the whisper of skirts, the occasional bell, and then, nearer the city, the thicker chorus—water lapping against timber, rope squealing through pulleys, gulls crying, and every voice wearing its own dialect like a cap. To Catherine, tongues were not mere words; they were a people’s memory in the mouth. In Rotterdam, the speech ran faster, clipped and traded like herring; at times Kate had to lean close, catching meaning by tone when the vowels would not sit still. There are things one cannot translate—grief, longing, the exact comfort of one’s mother-sounds—and Kate, weary and pale, felt that keenly.

They soon found a shop in a good street; but it was sadly out of order. The place smelt of old dust and damp wood, as if it had once held spices and now held only their ghosts. Shelves sagged; corners were grey with neglect; the back room had the sour breath of a house where fires have gone out too often.

However, they got it cheaper for that, and Catherine, who could not abide a disorderly kitchen nor a disorderly shop, set to work at once. Brush in hand, she raised little storms of dust; she sent for boards and had proper shelves fitted, stout and square, to bear honest wares; she aired the dwelling-house until the stale air fled and the rooms began to smell again like sun on wood. Kate, though frail, sat where she could, sewing, sorting, making small things tidy—those quiet labors that are half housekeeping, half prayer.

Meanwhile Luke Peterson was always asking Margaret what he could do for her. He had the look of a man who would gladly fetch water till his back broke, if only it might be for the one face he watched.

The answer used to come, ever in the same sad tone, as if nothing in the world were worth the asking: “Nothing, Luke, nothing.”

“What,” said he, amazed and wounded by emptiness, “you that are so clever, can you think of nothing for me to do for you?”

“Nothing, Luke, nothing.”

But at last—whether the sight of Kate’s weakness pricked her, or whether Margaret’s own heart, tired of being entreated, sought any outlet—she changed her reply.

“If you could make something to help my sweet sister Kate about.”

The slave of love consented as joyfully as if she had bid him build a chapel. He went to it with hands and mind both eager. He chose wood that would not splinter, planed it smooth, fitted the joints close, and made Kate a little cart; then he cushioned it so that her bones should not ache the more for going abroad. And when it was done, he yoked himself into it as a horse is yoked, and at eventide drew her out of the town and along the pleasant boulevard, with Margaret and Catherine walking beside.

Evening had its own solace: wind moving through leaves like a soft broom, distant church-bells rounding the air, and the fading clatter of trade as stalls were shut and pots began to simmer in their homes. It looked a happier party than it was, because grief can walk out in fresh air and still keep step with you.

Kate, for one, enjoyed it keenly; for little Gerard was put in her lap, and she doted on him. His breath had the warm sweet-milk smell of infants; his fingers grasped at her sleeve; his small noises were like birds trying their first notes. In that cart, he seemed a cherub carried by a little angel, or a rosebud lying in the cup of a lily.

So the vulgar jeered; for there are always men who must spoil music with a coarse shout. They called after Luke, asking him how a thistle tasted, and whether his mistress could not afford one with four legs, and other such sour wit. Their laughter rang harsh, a cheap noise that scraped the ear and left a grime behind, like smoke from bad fuel.

Luke did not mind these jeers; they struck his back and slid off, for his mind was fixed on Margaret’s smallest wish as on a star. But Kate minded them for him; she heard every barbed syllable, and each one hurt her as if it had been flung at the child in her arms.

“Thou hast made the cart for me, good Luke,” said she gently, “’twas much. I did ill to let thee draw me too; we can afford to pay some poor soul for that. I love my rides, and to carry little Gerard; but I’d liever ride no more than thou be mocked for’t.”

“Much I care for their tongues,” said Luke, his jaw set. “If I did care I’d knock their heads together. I shall draw you till my mistress says give over.”

“Luke,” said Margaret, and there was quiet authority in her voice, “if you obey Kate, you will oblige me.”

“Then I will obey Kate,” said he at once; for her word was law to him, and Kate’s mercy became his obedience.

An honorable exception to the street’s cruelty was Jorian Ketel’s wife, Joan. She spoke not loudly, but with that steadiness that can change the whole sound of a moment. Watching Luke’s straining shoulders and Kate’s white face, she said, “That is strength well laid out, to draw the weak. And her prayers will be your guerdon; she is not long for this world; she smileth in pain.”

Luke, simple-hearted as bread, answered bluntly that he did not want the poor lass’s prayers; he did it to please his mistress, Margaret. In his mouth the word mistress carried no gaudy savor of power, but something quieter and more binding: the one voice he lived to hear approve him.

After that Luke often pressed Margaret to give him something to do—without success. Day by day he asked; day by day she fenced him off with “Nothing,” as if work were scarce as saffron and she dared not waste a thread of it.

But one day, as if tired of his importuning, she turned on him; and in her face there was a look, and in her voice an accent, that no plain telling can fully carry—like the difference between reading a recipe and tasting the dish.

“Find me,” said she, each word falling as if it had been weighed like spice, “my boy’s father.”

“Mistress, they all say he is dead.”

“Not so,” Margaret answered, though the words scraped her throat as if they were dry crusts. “They feed me still with hopes.”

“Ay—before thy face.” Luke’s mouth twisted; his honest bluntness had no salve on it. “But behind thy back they all say he is dead.”

At that, the tears she had held like water behind a dam broke through. They ran hot over her cheeks and dropped on her hands, which smelt faintly of bread and baby—of flour dust rubbed into skin, and the warm sour-sweetness that clung to linen after a child had lain there. Luke, who had the shoulders of a man and the soft heart of a maid, began to whimper too, as if sorrow were a tune and he could not keep from joining the chorus.

“Prithee, weep not so, sweet mistress,” he pleaded. “I’d bring him back to life an I could, rather than see thee weed so sore.”

“I think I weep,” said Margaret, swallowing, “because they are double-tongued with me.” And then, as if shame at crying before him stiffened her spine, she wiped her face with the back of her hand and laid that hand—light, grave—on Luke’s shoulder. “Luke, he is not dead.”

“Who can tell?” he whispered.

“Dying men,” she said, and her voice changed, as if she were speaking not from the kitchen, but from some place where the air ran colder, “are known to have a strange sight. Listen, Luke. My poor father—when he was a-dying—and I, simple fool, so happy, thinking he was to get well altogether—he said to mother and me—he was sitting in that very chair where thou art now, and mother was as might be here, and I was yonder making a sleeve—said he: ‘I see him! I see him!’ Just so—clear—none of thy failing mutter. All o’ fire. ‘Sore disfigured—on a great river—coming this way.’”

Luke sat still, as if her words had set a weight on him. Outside, the town had its daily sounds—the distant clack of a cartwheel on cobbles, the cry of a vendor, the thin hammering of a cooper’s mallet like a heart trying to keep time. Inside, Luke’s breath and Margaret’s grief filled the room.

“Ah, Luke,” she went on, and now the plea came naked, without pride, “if thou wert a woman, and had the feeling for me thou thinkest thou hast, thou wouldst pity me, and find him for me. Take a thought! The father of my child!”

“Alack, I would if I knew how,” Luke said helplessly. “But how can I?”

“Nay, of course thou canst not,” she answered quickly, the old humility snapping into place like a lid. “I am mad to think it.” Then the lid slipped. “But oh, if any one really cared for me, they would; that is all I know.”

Luke’s brow furrowed. He was slow—she knew it; he knew it too—and his slowness was a kind of honesty. He chewed the matter like tough meat, unwilling to swallow a lie merely because it was easier.

“The old folk all say dying men can see more than living wights,” he said at last. “Let me think: for my mind cannot gallop like thine. On a great river… Well, the Maas is a great river.”

Margaret’s eyes clung to his face, hungry as a starving mouth.

He pondered on, lips moving soundlessly. “Coming this way? Then if ’twas the Maas, he would have been here by this time—so ’tis not the Maas. The Rhine is a great river, greater than the Maas; and very long. I think it will be the Rhine.”

“And so do I, Luke,” she breathed, eager despite herself; hope, when it came, came like the first scent of yeast in a cold house. “For Denys bade him come down the Rhine. But even if it is, he may turn off before he comes anigh his birthplace.” Her face tightened. “He does not pine for me as I for him; that is clear. Luke—do you not think he has deserted me?”

She asked it as if she begged for contradiction, for some spoonful of comfort to be pressed into her mouth. Luke, however, had never learnt to sweeten truth.

“It looks very like it,” he said, and then, in sudden indignation on her behalf, “what a fool he must be!”

“What do we know?” she pleaded, clutching at uncertainty as if it were a handhold on a slippery bank.

“Let me think again,” Luke muttered. “I cannot gallop.”

Out of that slow grinding of thought came his plan. He knew a station some sixty miles up the Rhine where all the public boats put in. He would go there—stand among the coming and going, under the cries of boatmen and the slap of water on timber—and try to cut the truant off. He did not know Gerard by sight; but as each boat landed, he would slip among the passengers and ask if one Gerard was there.

“And, mistress,” he added, “if you were to give me a bit of a letter to him; for, with us being strangers, mayhap he won’t believe a word I say.”

“Good, kind, thoughtful Luke,” she said, and a blush rose—shame and gratitude mingled, like wine poured into milk. “I will. How I have undervalued thee! But give me till supper-time to get it writ.”

All that afternoon she moved about her small tasks with the letter burning in her mind like a coal in a palm. There was broth to mind and bread to cut; the child to hush; the little domestic world to keep from falling into ruin. Even so, her senses would not leave her: the smell of onions softening, the scrape of a ladle, the familiar hush-and-sigh of the hearth. Grief did not stop the pot from boiling; it only made the steam taste salt.

At supper she put the letter into Luke’s hand. It was long, tied round with silk after the fashion of the day, and sealed over the knot. Luke weighed it, and a shadow crossed his face—discontent, not with her, but with the fate he was helping to knead.

“Say your father was not dreaming,” he said very gravely, “and say I have the luck to fall in with this man, and say he should turn out a better bit o’ stuff than I think him, and come home to you then and there—what is to become o’ me?”

Margaret coloured to the very brow.

“Oh, Luke,” she whispered, “Heaven will reward thee. And I shall fall on my knees and bless thee; and I shall love thee all my days, sweet Luke, as a mother does her son. I am so old by thee: trouble ages the heart. Thou shalt not go—’tis not fair of me. Love maketh us to be all self.”

“Humph!” said Luke, and there was a hurt boy in the sound.

“And if,” he went on, still in that same plain, deadly sense, “yon scapegrace shall read thy letter, and hear me tell him how thou pinest for him, and yet, being a traitor, or a mere idiot, will not turn to thee—what shall become o’ me then? Must I die a bachelor, and thou fare lonely to thy grave, neither maid, wife, nor widow?”

The question struck her like the sudden clang of an iron pot dropped on stone: it rang, it stunned, it could not be ignored. Her breath came quick; fear made her taste metal.

“If—” she began, and stopped, and started again, “which our Lady be merciful to me, and forbid—Oh!”

“Well, mistress?”

“If he should read my letter, and hear thy words—” Her voice broke and recovered. “And, sweet Luke, be just, and tell him what a lovely babe he hath—fatherless, fatherless. Oh, Luke, can he be so cruel?”

“I trow not—but if?”

“Then,” she said, and each word came like a pin drawn from flesh, “he will give thee up my marriage lines, and I shall be an honest woman, and a wretched one, and my boy will not be a bastard. And of course, then, we could both go into any honest man’s house that would be troubled with us; and even for thy goodness this day, I will—I will—ne’er be so ungrateful as go past thy door to another man’s.”

“Ay, but will you come in at mine?” Luke demanded. “Answer me that!”

“Oh, ask me not!” she cried. “Some day, perhaps, when my wounds leave bleeding. Alas, I’ll try. If I don’t fling myself and my child into the Maas. Do not go, Luke! do not think of going! ’Tis all madness from first to last.”

But Luke was as slow to forego an idea as to form one; and love, working in him like yeast, had begun to lift him from soft boy into stubborn man.

“Well,” he said, wiping his eyes with his sleeve as if ashamed of them, “madness is something, anyway; and I am tired o’ doing nothing for thee; and I am no great talker. To-morrow, at peep o’ day, I start. But hold—I have no money. My mother, she takes care of all mine; and I ne’er see it again.”

Margaret went to the little hoard of her hardships and hopes and drew out Catherine’s gold angel—the coin that had escaped so often, like a blessed thing that refused to be spent on folly. She pressed it into Luke’s hand. The gold lay heavy there, as if it carried not only value, but all the prayers that had touched it.

So, at dawn, Luke set out on his mad errand.

It did not seem so mad to him as it would to those who lived by colder measures. It was a superstitious age, and men acted upon a dying man’s vision much as later folk act upon respectable tidings. But when Catherine heard of it, she flamed like a pan when fat catches.

“To send the poor lad on such a wild-goose chase!” she cried. “But you are like a many more girls; and mark my words: by the time you have worn that Luke fairly out, and made him as sick of you as a dog, you will turn as fond on him as a cow on a calf, and ‘Too late’ will be the cry.”

*

Twelve hours after Luke started up the Rhine, two friars reached Holland from the south. Thus, wild-goose chase or no, the parties were nearing each other—quickly, too. Jerome, unable to preach in low Dutch, now pushed on towards the coast, anxious to win to England as soon as might be; and having the stream with them, the friars would, in truth, have missed Luke by passing him in full current below his station, but for an incident that turned their course like a hand on a tiller.

About twenty miles above the station Luke was making for, Clement landed to preach in a large village. The place had the ordinary noises of rural life—hens fussing, children calling, the steady creak of a well-rope—but over it lay the hush that gathers when a voice speaks in earnest to many souls. Towards the end of his sermon Clement noticed a grey nun weeping. Her sobs were small sounds swallowed by the crowd, but he saw them as one sees a candle in daylight.

When the people broke up, he spoke to her gently and asked her grief.

“Nay,” said she, “’tis not for myself flow these tears; ’tis for my lost friend. Thy words reminded me of what she was, and what she is, poor wretch. But you are a Dominican, and I am a Franciscan nun.”

“It matters little, my sister,” said Clement, “if we are both Christians, and if I can aid thee in aught.”

She searched his face, as if weighing whether charity could indeed wear another order’s hood. “These are strange words,” she murmured, “but methinks they are good; and thy lips are—oh, most eloquent. I will tell thee our grief.”

Then she told him: a young nun, the darling of their convent, had been lured away from her vows. Sin had led to sin, as one bad dish spoils the next; and now the girl lived in a small inn as chambermaid, in truth as decoy, selling her favours to wealthier customers.

“Anywhere else,” the nun said, “we might, by kindly violence, force her away from perdition. But this innkeeper is servant to the fierce baron on the height there, and hath his ear still; he would burn our convent to the ground, were we to take her by force.”

“Moreover,” Clement answered, “souls will not be saved by brute force.”

As they spoke, Jerome came up; Clement persuaded him to lie at the convent that night. But in the morning, when Clement told Jerome he had talked long with the abbess and had promised to try to win back the wandering nun, Jerome frowned.

“It is not our business,” he said. “It is a waste of time.”

Clement, however, was no longer a mere pupil. He stood firm; and at last they agreed: Jerome should go forward and secure their passage in the next ship for England, and Clement should be allowed time for his well-meant, perhaps idle, experiment.

About ten o’clock that day, a figure in a horseman’s cloak, great boots, and a large flapping felt hat stood near the auberge where the apostate nun lived. Disguised thus, Clement was in that moment truly wretched. Such ardent natures undertake wonders; but when they come hand to hand with the sickening difficulties, their nerves shake. Yet their hearts are steel; panting and dispirited, they struggle on.

He hesitated long at the door, prayed for help and wisdom, and at last entered. He sat down faint at heart, his body in cold perspiration. Then, as if he had stepped over a threshold within himself, he became another man.

He called lustily for a cup of wine. The landlord brought it. Clement paid for it with money the convent had supplied him, and made show of drinking.

“Landlord,” said he, “I hear there is a fair chambermaid in thine house.”

“Ay, stranger,” chuckled the man, “the buxomest in Holland. But she gives not her company to all comers—only to good customers.”

Clement dangled a massive gold chain in the landlord’s sight. The metal caught the light as if it had stolen it.

The landlord laughed and shouted, “Here, Janet! here is a lover for thee would bind thee in chains of gold; and a tall lad into the bargain, I promise thee.”

“Then I am in double luck,” came a woman’s voice, careless and used to being summoned. “Send him hither.”

Clement rose, shuddering, and passed into the room where Janet sat with a piece of work. She laid it down every minute to sing a broken scrap of a song; in her life she had not the patience to carry anything out—not stitch, not tune, not virtue.

After a few words of greeting, the disguised visitor asked if they might be more private.

“Why not?” she said, rising with a smile that had been practised until it seemed natural. She tripped before him. He followed, groaning inwardly, sore perplexed.

“There,” she said, leading him to an upper room. “Have no fear! Nobody ever comes here but such as pay for the privilege.”

Clement looked round and prayed silently for wisdom. Then he went softly and closed the window-shutters with care, one after another, until the room dimmed like a conscience.

“What on earth is that for?” Janet asked, uneasiness pricking through her boldness.

“Sweetheart,” he whispered, putting a mystery into his voice, “it is that God may not see us.”

“Madman,” she snapped. “Think you a wooden shutter can keep out His eye?”

“Nay, I know not,” he said, as if wavering. “Perchance He has too much on hand to notice us. But I would not the saints and angels should see us. Would you?”

“My poor soul,” she retorted, “hope not to escape their sight! The only way is not to think of them; for if you do, it poisons your cup. For two pins I’d run and leave thee. Art pleasant company in sooth.”

“After all, girl,” he said, “so that men see us not, what signify God and the saints seeing us? Feel this chain! ’Tis virgin gold. I shall cut two of these heavy links off for thee.”

“Ah! now thy discourse is to the point.” She handled the chain greedily, and in that touch her past brushed against her present like cloth against a sore. “Why, ’tis as massy as the chain round the Virgin’s neck at the conv—”

She did not finish the word.

“Whisht! whisht! whisht!” Clement hissed. “’Tis it. And thou shalt have thy share. But betray me not.”

“Monster!” cried Janet, drawing back, repugnance sharpening her face. “What—rob the blessed Virgin of her chain, and give it to an—”

“You are none!” Clement cried exultingly, and the trap sprang shut. “Or you had not recked for that—Mary!”

“Ah! ah! ah!”

“Thy patron saint, whose chain this is, sends me to greet thee.”

She ran screaming to the window and began to undo the shutters. Her fingers trembled. In those instants Clement had time to rid himself of his boots and hat; then he let the cloak fall. When light streamed in, he stood revealed: a Dominican friar, calm and majestic as a statue, holding his crucifix aloft over her—his look loving, sad, and solemn. It relieved her of mere bodily fear and crushed her with religious terror and remorse. She crouched against the wall as if it were a cliff over a pit.

“Mary,” he said gently, “one word. Are you happy?”

“As happy,” she whispered through clenched teeth, “as I shall be in hell.”

“And they are not happy at the convent; they weep for you.”

“For me?” Her voice cracked.

“Day and night. Above all, Sister Ursula.”

“Poor Ursula!” The name, spoken aloud, opened a seam in her, and she began to weep too, not for herself, but for the friend whose grief she had earned.

“The angels weep still more,” Clement said. “Wilt not dry all their tears, in earth and heaven, and save thyself?”

“Ay! would I could,” Mary sobbed. “But it is too late.”

“Satan, avaunt!” cried the monk sternly. “’Tis thy favourite temptation; and thou, Mary, listen not to the enemy of man, belying God and whispering despair. I who come to save thee have been a far greater sinner than thou. Come. Sin, thou seest, is not so sweet, e’en in this world, as holiness; and eternity is at the door.”

She stared at him through tears, as if he had spoken a word she thought dead.

“How can they ever receive me again?”

“’Tis their worthiness thou doubtest now. But in truth they pine for thee. ’Twas in pity of their tears that I, a Dominican, undertook this task; and broke the rule of my order by entering an inn; and broke it again by donning these lay vestments. But all is well done, and quit for a light penance, if thou wilt let us rescue thy soul from this den of wolves, and bring thee back to thy vows.”

She gazed, shaken. “And thou—a Dominican—hast done this for a daughter of St. Francis! Why, the Franciscans and Dominicans hate one another.”

“Ay, my daughter,” Clement said quietly; “but Francis and Dominic love one another.”

The answer struck her with a simplicity she could not argue with. He reminded her then of how she had recoiled at the thought of robbing the Virgin.

“But see now,” he said, “the convent, and the Virgin too, think ten times more of their poor nun than of golden chains; for they freely trusted their chain to me, a stranger, that peradventure the sight of it might touch their lost Mary and remind her of their love.”

He showed her—plainly, terribly—the end of her present course; and on the other side he revived her dormant memories and better feelings, like embers coaxed back into flame. She sank to her knees at his feet, sobbing, confessing she had known no happiness nor peace since she betrayed her vows. She would go back—if he would go with her. Alone she dared not; could not. Even if she reached the gate she could never enter. How could she face the abbess and the sisters?

“I will go with thee,” Clement said, “as joyfully as the shepherd bears a strayed lamb to the fold.”

But when he urged her to go at once, there sprang up those prodigiously petty difficulties that entangle like silken nets and hold like iron cobwebs.

“How can I walk beside thee in this habit?” she faltered.

“I have brought the gown and cowl of thy holy order,” he answered. “Hide thy bravery with them. And leave thy shoes as I leave these.” He pointed to his horseman’s boots cast aside.

She gathered her jewels and ornaments, hands shaking.

“What are these for?” Clement asked.

“To present to the convent, father.”

“Their source is too impure.”

“But,” she pleaded, “it would be a sin to leave them here. They can be sold to feed the poor.”

“Mary,” he said, lifting the crucifix nearer, “fix thine eye on this, and trample those devilish baubles beneath thy feet.”

She hesitated; then with a sharp sob she flung them down and stamped on them, as if stamping on the life she had lived.

“Now open the window,” Clement commanded, “and fling them out on that dunghill.”

She did so. The jewels tumbled into filth with a sound oddly small, and the act itself seemed to crack a chain about her heart.

“’Tis well done,” he said. “So pass the wages of sin from thy hands, its glittering yoke from thy neck, its pollution from thy soul. Away, daughter of St. Francis; we tarry in this vile place too long.”

She followed him out.

Yet they were not clear. In the kitchen, the landlord, seeing a black friar and a grey nun come through from within, gaped and muttered, “Why, what mummery is this?” Then comprehension struck him, and he sprang between them and the door.

“What ho! Reuben! Carl! Gavin!” he yelled. “Here is a false friar spiriting away our Janet!”

Men came running in, faces hard, hands ready. Clement rushed at them with crucifix in hand.

“Forbear!” he cried, voice like a bell over a marsh. “She is a holy nun returning to her vows. The hand that touches her cowl or her robe to stay her—it shall wither; his body shall lie unburied, cursed by Rome, and his soul shall roast in eternal fire.”

They shrank back as if they had felt heat.

“And thou—miserable panderer!” Clement’s sentence ended not in words but in action. He seized the man by the neck, and strong as a lion in his hot excitement, hurled him from the door. The landlord flew across the room and pitched head foremost upon the stone floor, bleeding, half stunned.

Clement tore the door open and carried the screaming nun out into the road.

“Hush, poor trembler,” he gasped. “They dare not molest thee on the highroad. Away!”

Mary, though she looked back again and again, saw no more of them. The landlord lay terrified, blood on stone; his men, cowed by fear of curse and of the strange authority in a friar’s voice, did not follow.

On the road Clement spoke to her of his own fault, as if confession were the only fair payment for hers.

“Hitherto,” said he, “we have spoken of thy faults: now for mine. My choler is ungovernable—furious. It is by the grace of God I am not a murderer. I repent the next moment; but a moment too late is all too late. Mary—had the churls laid finger on thee, I should have scattered their brains with my crucifix. Oh, I know myself. Go to; and tremble at myself. There lurketh a wild beast beneath this black gown of mine.”

“Alas, father,” Mary said, and in it was a strange gratitude, “were you other than you are I had been lost. To take me from that place needed a man wary as a fox; yet bold as a lion.”

Clement reflected, and the fierce energy in him settled into humility. “This much is certain: God chooseth well His fleshly instruments; and with imperfect hearts doeth His perfect work. Glory be to God!”

When they were near the convent, Mary stopped suddenly, seized his arm, and began to cry—not loud, but deep, like a spring under stone.

He looked at her kindly. “Thou hast nothing to fear,” he told her. “It will be the happiest day thou hast ever spent.”

Then he made her sit down and compose herself while he went within. He entered the convent and desired to see the abbess.

“My sister,” he said when she came, “give the glory to God: Mary is at the gate.”

The abbess’s astonishment and delight were unbounded. She yielded at once to Clement’s earnest request that the road of penitence should, at first, be smoothed for this unstable wanderer; and after some opposition she entered heartily into his counsel as to Mary’s reception.

To give time for their small preparations, Clement went slowly back. He sat by Mary, soothed her, and heard her confession, letting her words fall as quietly as drops into earth.

“The abbess has granted me,” he told her, “that you shall propose your own penance.”

“It shall be none the lighter,” Mary said, as if she feared mercy more than punishment.

“I trow not,” Clement answered; “but that is future. To-day is given to joy alone.”

He led her round the building to the abbess’s postern. As they went they heard musical instruments and singing within—voices rising and falling like birds in a sheltered orchard.

“’Tis a feastday,” Mary whispered. “And I come to mar it.”

“Hardly,” said Clement, smiling, “seeing that you are the queen of the fête.”

“I, father? what mean you?”

“What, Mary—have you never heard there is more joy in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, than over ninety-nine just persons which need no repentance? Now this convent is not heaven; nor the nuns angels; yet are there among them some angelic spirits; and these sing and exult at thy return. But here methinks comes one of them; for I see her hand trembles at the keyhole.”

The postern was flung open. In a moment Sister Ursula clung to Mary, sobbing and kissing her round the neck, as if she would fasten her back to life with embraces. The abbess followed more sedately, but little less moved.

Clement bade them farewell.

They entreated him to stay, but he refused, regretful. He had already tried Brother Jerome’s patience and must hasten to the river; perhaps sail for England on the morrow.

So Mary returned to the fold, and Clement strode briskly on towards the Rhine—and England.

This was the man for whom Margaret’s boy lay in wait with her letter.

*

That letter was one of those simple, piercing appeals only a woman can write to the man who has used her cruelly and is still, against all reason, beloved. Margaret began with the birth of the little boy, and the comfort he had been to her through the long distress of mind Gerard’s strange silence had brewed in her—like a pot left on the edge of the hearth, never boiling clean, never cooling.

She described little Gerard minutely, as if words could carry flesh across water; she did not forget the mole on his little finger.

“Know you any one that hath the like on his?” she wrote. “If you only saw him you could not choose but be proud of him; all the mothers in the street do envy me; but I the wives; for thou comest not to us. My own Gerard, some say thou art dead. But if thou wert dead, how could I be alive? Others say that thou, whom I love so truly, art false. But this will I believe from no lips but thine. My father loved thee well; and as he lay a-dying he thought he saw thee on a great river, with thy face turned towards thy Margaret, but sore disfigured. Is’t so, perchance? Have cruel men scarred thy sweet face? or hast thou lost one of thy precious limbs? Why, then thou hast the more need of me, and I shall love thee not worse, alas! thinkest thou a woman’s love is light as a man’s? but better, than I did when I shed those few drops from my arm, not worth the tears, thou didst shed for them; mindest thou? ’tis not so very long agone, dear Gerard.”

So the letter ran—tender, yearning, without a word of reproach at the end, for she dared not set a scolding tone upon it; doubt might frighten him away, and she needed him near enough even to blame.

Soft Luke was made the bearer of that sealed silk-tied hope.

At the station on the Rhine, Luke mingled with the passengers of two boats and heard nothing of Gerard Eliassoen. That did not surprise him. He had half expected the river to mock him. But at the third boat, a black friar spoke to him, somewhat severely.

“And what would you with him you call Gerard Eliassoen?”

Luke stared. “Why, father, if he is alive I have got a letter for him.”

“Humph!” said Jerome. “I am sorry for it. However, the flesh is weak. Well, my son, he you seek will be here by the next boat, or the next boat after. And if he chooses to answer to that name—after all, I am not the keeper of his conscience.”

“Good father,” Luke burst out, “one plain word, for Heaven’s sake. This Gerard Eliassoen of Tergou—is he alive?”

“Humph! Why, certes, he that went by that name is alive.”

“Well, then, that is settled,” Luke said drily; and then, in the next breath, the dryness broke. He turned, ran out of sight, and blubbered like a child.

“Oh, why did the Lord make any women?” he sobbed to himself. “I was content with the world till I fell in love. Here his little finger is more to her than my whole body, and he is not dead. And here I have got to give him this.”

He looked at the letter as if it were a coal meant to burn him. He dashed it on the ground—then snatched it up again in spiteful loyalty, as if he could not bear to see even paper wronged for her sake.

He went to the landlord with tears still on his face and begged for work.

The landlord declined at first. He had his own people.

“Oh, I seek not your money,” Luke said hoarsely. “I only want some work to keep me from breaking my heart about another man’s lass.”

“Good lad! good lad!” the landlord cried, struck with rough pity, and found him barrels to mend—on terms agreed.

So Luke coopered with fury between the boats coming down the Rhine, hammering staves into place while the river ran on, bearing toward him the man who might mend Margaret’s life—or split it wider.

An earnest letter, once loosed from the hand, would not lie quietly in the mind of her that wrote it. Margaret had poured her whole strength into Luke’s charge—her father’s dying sight, whether vision or sweet delusion, and her own faith harnessed to it like a cart-horse to a heavy wain. But when the words were gone and Luke with them, the heat ran out of her as from an oven when the door is left ajar. Doubt blew in cold. She began to marvel at her own credulity; then her conscience, sharp as vinegar on a raw tongue, stung her about Luke—of all men, Luke, whom she had sent on a road of danger for a hope that might be no more than smoke.

Catherine came and rated her soundly, and Margaret paid, as folk do, for that sudden lifting of spirits—by a deeper sinking after. She sat in a stupor that was not rest, hearing too much and too little at once: the thin domestic sounds that should have steadied her—the scrape of a chair-leg, the creak of a latch, the soft patter of the babe’s little breath—seemed to fall away behind a louder inward noise, a roaring as of a mill-wheel in flood. It made her long for one true, wholesome sound to lay upon her heart like a warm cloth: a fire crackling, a kettle singing, the firm rhythm of work done at the hearth.

In that ebb of spirit Joan Ketel found her.

Joan came in as if she brought summer with her, cheeks bright from walking, eyes alight with an idea. She was one of those women whose very step makes a room sound fuller of life: her skirts brushed, her shoes tapped briskly, and she spoke in a voice that had never learned to whisper despair.

“Margaret,” she cried, “I know the cure for thine ill. The hermit of Gouda—a wondrous holy man. Why, he can tell what is coming, when he is in the mood.”

“Ay, I have heard of him,” said Margaret, not lifting her eyes. Hope, to her, was like a dish she had once loved and now could not bear the smell of.

But Joan, who had learnt what kind of physic Margaret could give, had the courage to press. She coaxed and urged with that obstinate tenderness which is half mothering, half command, until at last Margaret let herself be led, as a sick body lets itself be carried into air.

They made ready as for a little errand of housewifery—because women’s lives, even at the edge of tragedy, must be tied down with baskets and bread. Joan brought butter and eggs, the best they had, laid in a basket with a clean cloth over them, as if the very gift must be wholesome, yellow, and sound. The butter was firm and sweet, smelling of churn and cool dairy; the eggs warm from the nest. Margaret’s fingers, handling them, remembered for a moment that the world was still made of tangible things.

What had made the pair such fast friends, these last weeks, was itself a story of the hearth—the kind of miracle that hides in a kitchen garden.

Some six weeks ago Jorian Ketel had fallen ill of a bowel disease. It began with raging pain; and when that went off, leaving him like a wrung rag, an awkward symptom came after—nothing, either liquid or solid, would stay in his stomach a minute. Bread, broth, even water, all returned as fast as fear. The doctor had come in his great importance and had said, as if death were a matter of recipe, “He must die if this goes on many hours; therefore boil thou now a chicken with a golden angel in the water, and let him sup that!”

So they had fetched a chicken and killed it. The scalding water steamed; the feathers came away; the bird went into the pot. A gold coin—holy money, they said, for its stamping—clinked in the simmer. The broth rose and fell, slick with fat, smelling rich and promising. Joan had ladled it out with trembling hands.

Alas! Gilt chicken broth shared the fate of the humbler viands that had gone before it. It stayed with him no more than the rest.

Then, because men love far-fetched marvels, the cure was changed: they steeped the thumb of St. Sergius in beef broth, as if sainthood could be boiled into a pan and swallowed. The beef had its deep, brown savor; the relic lay in it like a pale root. Same result.

Then Joan, spent and weeping, ran to Margaret to borrow linen to make his shroud.

“Let me see him,” said Margaret.

She went in, and the room struck her first by its staleness: a sick-sweet heat, close as a shut cupboard. The air had no honest sound in it either—no breeze at the casement, only the wet swallow and retch of the man fighting his own body.

She took his wrist and felt his pulse under her fingers; her face did not change much, but there was a certain quickening in her eye, as when a cook tastes a pot and knows at once what is missing.

“Ah!” said she. “I doubt they have not gone to the root. Open the window! Art stifling him; now change all his linen.”

“Alack, woman, what for?” Joan had cried, half in despair, half in household thrift. “Why foul more linen for a dying man?”

“Do as thou art bid,” said Margaret, dully; and she left the room as if to fetch something common, not a marvel.

Joan, whose hands were used to kneading dough and wringing cloth, found herself obeying like a child under a schoolmistress’s eye. The casement was thrown wide; new air came in with a rush and a whole choir of outside sounds—the distant clop of a hoof, the chirr of sparrows in the eaves, a cart somewhere on the road. The room seemed to sigh.

Margaret returned with her apron full of a flowering herb, freshly gathered, still damp at the stalk, smelling green and faintly sweet when bruised. Her eyes had seen it from the window—the very kind of seeing that marks a housewife and an herb-wife both: the knowledge that remedies may grow under one’s nose while folk send to saints and cities.

She set water to heat and made a decoction, stirring as if she had done it all her life—watching the first shiver, then the steady simmer, not letting it boil too hard lest the virtue be driven off in steam. The scent came up: sweet at first, then with a bitterness that tightened the back of the throat like good ale. She strained it, careful as a cook skimming a sauce, and carried it to the bed.

Before giving it, she took a spoonful herself and smacked her lips—too openly pleased for sincerity.

“That is fair,” said Jorian, with a feeble attempt at mirth. “Why, ’tis sweet, and now ’tis bitter.”

She drew him into talk as soon as he had swallowed it—because the mind, held in company, helps the body keep its hold. And lo, this bitter-sweet stayed by him. Seeing which, she built on it as cards are built: the third spoonful she strengthened with a very little schiedam, just enough spirit to warm the stomach without whipping it; in the seventh she slipped a little beaten yolk of egg, as gently as one enriches a thin broth, to give it body and gentleness. So, with the patience of her sex and the cunning of a good cook who will not spoil a dish by haste, she coaxed his body out of Death’s grasp; and finally Nature—being patted on the back instead of kicked under the bed—set Jorian Ketel on his legs again.

But the doctress made them both swear never to tell a soul her guilty deed.

“They would put me in prison, away from my child.”

The simple that saved him was called sweet feverfew. She had gathered it in his own garden.

That was the root of Joan’s devotion. Gratitude, when it is true, is like a loaf baked in a poor oven: small maybe, but it feeds.

So now Joan and Margaret went on toward Gouda, the basket on Joan’s arm, their steps making two different musics on the road—Joan’s brisk certainty, Margaret’s slower tread, as if her thoughts weighed at her ankles. The land lay domestic around them: hedges, ditches, flat fields, the smell of wet earth and cow-breath, and now and then the clean cry of a bird cutting the air like a knife. Even sorrow walked among these ordinary things.

They reached the hermit’s cave and found the little platform where folk set their offerings. They placed the butter and eggs there with a kind of reverence—food, the honest tribute of women.

Margaret then stooped, and put her mouth to the aperture made for that purpose, and spoke into the darkness:

“Holy hermit, we bring thee butter and eggs of the best; and I, a poor deserted girl—wife, yet no wife—and mother of the sweetest babe, come to pray thee tell me whether he is quick or dead, true to his vows or false.”

For a moment there was only the damp silence of stone. Then a faint voice issued from within, thin as breath through reeds:

“Trouble me not with the things of earth, but send me a holy friar; I am dying.”

“Alas!” cried Margaret, and the cry was not for herself alone. “Is it e’en so, poor soul? Then let us in to help thee.”

“Saints forbid! Thine is a woman’s voice. Send me a holy friar.”

So ended the errand, like a pot that will not come to boil no matter how long it sits on the fire.

They went back as they came. Joan could not help saying, with rough justice, “Are women imps o’ darkness then, that they must not come anigh a dying bed?”

But Margaret was too deeply dejected to answer. The refusal had struck her like a slap—another door shut in her face, another tongue saying in effect: you are earth, you are unclean, you are not fit. Words have their power; they set ranks in the world. Friar, hermit, woman: three names, and in them a whole order of who may speak and who must be silent. Margaret, who had lived between tongues and stations, felt again how a dominant lexicon can bruise the soul without drawing blood.

Joan tried her homely consolations, as one tries to cheer a sick child with broth and warm covering; but Margaret did not seem to hear until Joan spoke of Jorian.

“And Jorian will speak out ere long,” Joan said. “He is just on the boil. He is very grateful to thee, believe it.”

“Seeing is believing,” replied Margaret, quietly bitter; for she had been fed on assurances and found them thin.

“Not but what he thinks you might have saved him with something more out o’ the common than yon. ‘A man of my inches to be cured wi’ feverfew,’ says he. ‘Why, if there is a sorry herb,’ says he. ‘Why, I was thinking o’ pulling all mine up,’ says he.”

Joan’s voice took on the relish of repeating a husband’s foolishness, the way women season their talk with what makes it go down.

“I up and told him remedies were none the better for being far-fetched; you and feverfew cured him, when the grand medicines came up faster than they went down. So says I, ‘You may go down on your four bones to feverfew.’ But indeed, he is grateful at bottom; you are all his thought and all his chat. But he sees Gerard’s folk coming around ye, and good friends, and he said only last night—”

“Well?” Margaret’s head lifted a little at that name, as a starving person lifts at the word bread.

“He made me vow not to tell ye.”

“Prithee, tell me.”

“Well,” said Joan, wrestling between oath and pity, “he said: ‘An’ if I tell what little I know, it won’t bring him back, and it will set them all by the ears. I wish I had more headpiece,’ said he; ‘I am sore perplexed. But least said is soonest mended.’ Yon is his favourite word; he comes back to’t from a mile off.”

Margaret shook her head. The road seemed to widen into dark water under her feet.

“Ay,” said she low, “we are wading in deep waters, my poor babe and me.”

It was Saturday night, and no Luke.

“Poor Luke!” said Margaret at last, with a tenderness that was almost pain. “It was very good of him to go on such an errand.”

“He is one out of a hundred,” replied Catherine warmly.

Margaret’s hand went, almost without her knowing, as if to the place where her child lay, to that little warm weight that was both comfort and fear.

“Mother,” she said, “do you think he would be kind to little Gerard?”

“I am sure he would,” Catherine answered. “So do you be kinder to him when he comes back! Will ye now?”

“Ay,” said Margaret.

And the house settled again into its small sounds—the soft stir of bedding, the faint creak of a board—domestic noises that tried to hold together a life being pulled apart.

*

Brother Clement, directed by the nuns, had avoided a bend in the river and strode lustily forward, his sandals beating a steady monk’s rhythm on the road. He reached a station some miles nearer the coast than that where Luke lay in wait for Gerard Eliassoen. The next morning he started early and was in Rotterdam at noon.

He made at once for the port, not to keep Jerome waiting. The air there was full of salt and tar, and the clang of work—ropes slapping, men shouting, gulls crying overhead with their harsh laughter. A port is a place where sound rules: every call is command, every creak and groan of timber a warning. Clement felt it in his bones; it set the nerves on edge, and he longed for the cloister’s measured chant, where each syllable has its appointed place and silence is not emptiness but peace.

He observed several monks of his order on the quay and went to them; but Jerome was not amongst them. He asked one whether Jerome had arrived.

“Surely, brother,” was the reply.

“Prithee, where is he?”

“Where? Why, there!” said the monk, pointing to a ship in full sail.

Clement now noticed that all the monks were looking seaward. The ship was already drawing away, its canvas belly full, its ropes singing in the wind. It was as if the sea itself had swallowed Jerome up between one heartbeat and the next.

“What, gone without me! Oh, Jerome! Jerome!” cried Clement, and his cry was torn by the wind and scattered among the port’s other noises, a small human anguish lost under commerce.

Several friars turned and stared.

“You must be brother Clement,” said one at length; and then they kissed him and greeted him with brotherly warmth, and gave him a letter Jerome had charged them with.

It was a hasty scrawl. The writer told him coldly that a ship was about to sail for England and he was loth to lose time. Clement might follow if he pleased, but would do much better to stay behind and preach to his own country folk.

“Give the glory to God, brother; you have a wonderful power over Dutch hearts; but you are no match for those haughty islanders: you are too tender.

“Know thou that on the way I met one, who asked me for thee under the name thou didst bear in the world. Be on thy guard! Let not the world catch thee again by any silken net. And remember, Solitude, Fasting, and Prayer are the sword, spear, and shield of the soul. Farewell.”

Clement stood with the salt wind worrying the paper, and felt as if he had been struck across the face. Deserted; not only left behind, but measured and found wanting—too tender—as if tenderness were a fault in Christ’s service. The letter’s tone was like a knife wiped clean: no warmth, no fellowship, only counsel and dismissal.

He promised the good monks to sleep at the convent and to preach wherever the prior should appoint—for Jerome had raised him to the skies as a preacher—and then withdrew abruptly, for he was cut to the quick and wanted to be alone.

Walking, he questioned himself as a penitent questions his soul in the dark: Was there some incurable fault in him, repulsive to so true a son of Dominic? Or was Jerome himself devoid of that Christian Love which St. Paul had placed above Faith itself? They had been shipwrecked together, saved on the same fragment of the wreck; Jerome had been his pupil, his penitent, his son in the Church; for four hundred miles they had travelled as fellow-servants in Christ—and now he was shaken off like dirt at the first opportunity, with harsh and cold disdain.
