“Why, worldly hearts are no colder nor less trusty than this,” Clement said aloud, and the port’s racket answered him without pity. “The only one that ever really loved me lies in a grave hard by. Fly me, fly to England, man born without a heart; I will go and pray over a grave at Sevenbergen.”

Three hours later he passed Peter’s cottage. A troop of noisy children were playing about the door—shouting, clapping, chasing one another, their cries bright as sparrows. The house had been repaired, and a new outhouse added; prosperity had laid new boards where misery had once creaked. That quick, careless music of children, so like laughter and so unlike prayer, struck him with a pain he could not bear. He turned his head hastily away, not to disturb a picture his memory treasured, and went on to the churchyard.

There the air changed: fewer voices, more wind, the thin rustle of grass. He sought among the tombstones for Margaret’s. He could not find it. He could not believe they had grudged her even a stone, so he searched the churchyard all over again, counting names and reading them as if the dead could answer in their carved letters.

“Oh poverty! stern poverty!” he murmured. “Poor soul, thou wert like me: no one was left that loved thee when Gerard was gone.”

He went into the church; the hush there folded round him like a cloak. After kissing the steps, he prayed long and earnestly for the soul of her whose resting-place he could not find. In the stillness he could hear the faintest sounds—his own breath, the little tick of cooling stone, the distant cough of a sparrow in the rafters. Such quiet is a balm, and yet it made his loneliness ring louder inside him, as if the absence of human voice were itself an accusation.

Coming out he saw a very old man looking over the little churchyard gate. Clement went to him and asked did he live in the place.

“Four score and twelve years, man and boy,” the old fellow answered. “And I come here every day of late, holy father, to take a peep. This is where I look to bide ere long.”

“My son,” said Clement, “can you tell me where Margaret lies?”

“Margaret? There’s a many Margarets here.”

“Margaret Brandt. She was daughter to a learned physician.”

“As if I didn’t know that,” said the old man pettishly. “But she doesn’t lie here. Bless you, they left this a longful while ago. Gone in a moment, and the house empty. What, is she dead? Margaret a’ Peter dead? Now only think on’t. Like enow; like enow. They great towns do terribly disagree wi’ country folk.”

“What great towns, my son?”

“Well, ’twas Rotterdam they went to from here, so I heard tell; or was it Amsterdam? Nay, I trow ’twas Rotterdam. And gone there to die!”

Clement sighed; the sound seemed to sink into the earth between the graves.

“’Twas not in her face now, that I saw,” the old man went on, softer now, as if memory had taken the edge off his fret. “And I can mostly tell. Alack, there was a blooming young flower to be cut off so soon, and all old weed like me left standing still. Well, well, she was a May rose yon; dear heart, what a winsome smile she had, and—”

“God bless thee, my son,” said Clement; “farewell!” And he hurried away, because the man’s country words—so plain, so rooted—had made Margaret too alive again, and grief too sharp.

He reached the convent at sunset. The bell sounded, deep and measured, gathering the day into prayer; the chant rose, ordered and familiar, as if the very air of the chapel had been trained to carry holy syllables without waste. Clement watched and prayed there for Jerome and for Margaret until it was long past midnight, and his soul, after much beating, recovered its cold calm.

Sunday, after mass, Catherine’s house in the Hoog Straet seemed to breathe like a great kitchen at festival-time—every corner alive, every board in use, every sound answering another. The shop below had at last the look of a settled thing: planks scrubbed pale, shelves set straight as psalm-lines, and above the door the new names, Cornelis and Sybrandt, painted bold for all the street to read. Their sign swung in the soft air—a white lamb, lips at a gilt ewe—creaking gently on its iron, as if even the wood wished them profit.

Eli had come early, bringing from his own store more wares to give them their first good start: bundles and packets that smelt of dye and new cloth, and the faint peppery bite of imported things. He laid them down with the calm of a man who knew the weight of goods and the weight of beginnings. Catherine’s eyes shone at each piece, not for greed, but for the comfort of order—bread on the table to-morrow because cloth lay ready to-day.

In the little garden behind, Cornelis and Sybrandt walked together between the cabbages and the last of the herbs, speaking low. They had been wild enough in their season—“agriculture” in that unremunerative form that meant oats sown for folly rather than for bread. But the smell of clean timber, the sight of their own names above a door, had sobered them more than sermon. They agreed they were sick of the old waste; it was better to make money than throw it after sport. They vowed, with the vehemence of the newly converted, to stick to business like wax to a seal.

Catherine, at an open window, heard them as one hears a mouse behind the flour-sack: her quick, ever-watchful ear caught the very turn of their words. She did not call out—she only stored the sound away, as she stored spice, to use when it should season something else. She went to Eli with the look of a woman whose hearth was as much her throne as any duke’s chair.

The supper planned for that night was to be a kind of inaugural feast: Margaret and her boy were to come, and the elders would pour out trade counsel as freely as the wine. It was to be a warm blessing on the young men’s new life—Commerce instead of the wild-oats husbandry that had cost Catherine more sighs than any boiling pot.

So Margaret came over to help her mother-in-law, and perhaps, too, to shake off the heavy languor that had lain upon her like damp linen. Catherine put her straight to work—not cruelly, but as one sets a log on the fire. The kitchen soon grew red with heat and faces. A pot sang on the trivet; fat hissed where it met hot iron; onions split and softened under the knife, their sharpness rising and sweetening as they surrendered. Catherine’s hands moved in their old dominion—measuring by feel, tasting by instinct, hearing the very point at which a simmer would turn to a boil. Even the house sounded wholesome: the scrape of a peel on carrots, the steady thud of a pestle, the small clink of crockery—sounds that made a human peace, unlike the harsh racket of carts and hammers that sometimes bruised a street into bad temper.

Presently in came Joan with a salad from Jorian’s garden, the leaves still holding a cool, wet scent as if morning had not quite let them go. She had wrapped it in cloth, and when she opened it the green smelled like earth after rain.

“He cut it for you, Margaret,” she said, setting it down. “You are all his chat; I shall be jealous. I told him you were to feast to-day. But oh, lass—what a sermon in the new kerk! Preaching? I never heard it till this day.”

“Would I had been there then,” said Margaret, and her voice had in it the thirst of a dry mouth. “For I am dried up for want of dew from heaven.”

“Why, he preacheth again this afternoon. But mayhap you are wanted here.”

“Not she,” said Catherine briskly, without lifting her eyes from the pan. “Come, away ye go, if y’are minded.”

“Indeed,” said Margaret, “methinks I should not be such a damper at table if I could come to ’t warm from a good sermon.”

“Then you must be brisk,” observed Joan, always counting time by other folk’s feet. “See the folk are wending that way, and—as I live—there goes the holy friar. Oh, bless us and save us, Margaret; the hermit! We forgot.”

And away she went—out of the house like a gust through a doorway, across the road, stopping the friar as lightly as she would stop a child that ran too near the canal. She returned almost as soon, breath warm, eyes bright with the pleasure of having looked close at something talked of.

“There,” she cried, “I was bent on seeing him nigh hand.”

“What said he to thee?” asked Catherine, not unkindly, but with the impatience of a woman whose broth must not be forgotten for sermons.

“Says he, ‘My daughter, I will go to him ere sunset, God willing.’ The sweetest voice. But oh, my mistresses, what thin cheeks for a young man, and great eyes—not far from your colour, Margaret.”

Margaret’s mouth trembled as if she had tasted something bitter and necessary. “I have a great mind to go hear him,” she said. “But my cap is not very clean, and they will all be there in their snow-white mutches.”

“There, take my handkerchief out of the basket,” said Catherine, practical as salt. “You cannot have the child; I want him for my poor Kate. It is one of her ill days.”

Margaret answered by taking the boy upstairs.

The air changed on the stair—cooler, stiller. In Kate’s chamber the sounds of the kitchen fell away until they were only a distant murmur, like a river heard through closed shutters. Kate lay in bed; her face was drawn fine, and yet when she saw Margaret she smiled with that strange, unearthly sweetness pain sometimes cannot steal.

“How art thou, sweetheart?” said Margaret; then stopped, for the answer was written plain. “Nay, I need not ask. Thou art in sore pain; thou smilest so. See, I have brought thee one thou lovest.”

“Two, by my way of counting,” said Kate, and her smile did not falter.

At that very moment a spasm seized her that would have wrung a cry from a stronger body and a less patient soul; it passed, leaving her breath short, her brow damp. Margaret stood with hands helpless for an instant—she who could chop and stir and mend, and yet could not mend this.

“What, in your lap?” said Margaret, following a gesture of the suffering girl. “Nay, he is too heavy, and thou in such pain.”

“I love him too dear to feel his weight,” Kate replied simply, as if love were a cushion the body could lean on.

Margaret laid the boy where Kate wished, and while Kate’s thin fingers found his sleeve and held it as if it were a cord to the living world, Margaret took the chance to make herself fit for kirk. She washed her face quickly, turned her hair, smoothed what could be smoothed. It was a poor toilet beside those rich white mutches she feared; yet the clean water and the small act of care steadied her.

“I am for the kerk,” said she at last, “to hear a beautiful preacher.”

Kate sighed, and the sigh seemed older than her years. “And a minute ago, Kate, I was all agog to go; that is the way with me this month past—up and down, up and down, like the waves of the Zuyder Zee. I’d as lieve stay aside thee; say the word!”

“Nay,” said Kate, and there was command in her gentleness. “Prithee go; and bring me back every word. Well-a-day that I cannot go myself.”

Tears stood in her eyes—not loud tears, but quiet, like dew on a bruised leaf. That decided Margaret more than any urging. She kissed Kate; then, looking under her lashes at the boy, she heaved a little sigh.

“I trow I must not,” she whispered. “I never could kiss him a little; and my father was dead against waking a child by day or night. When ’tis thy pleasure to wake, speak thy aunt Kate the two new words thou hast gotten.”

Then she went out, looking back with love that was also pain, and shut the door so softly that even the house’s hush did not notice.

Below, Catherine had not wasted the time. She had the vegetables ready—roots pared, greens washed, the salad awaiting its dressing. The kitchen smelled of thrift and good intention: vinegar sharp in a small jug, herbs bruised between fingers to wake their oils, bread warming near the fire so that its crust gave out a nutty scent. A house’s memory lives in such smells; long after names fade from signs, the nose can summon back a Sunday like this.

“Joan, you will lend me a hand, and peel these?” said Catherine, turning a heap of pears or apples in the basket so that the sound of them—a soft knocking—mixed with the pot’s steady song.

“That I will, dame,” said Joan, and set to with a will.

They worked with silent vigour for a while, the knives whispering, the peel falling in curls. Outside, the street carried its own Sabbath noises—footsteps in clusters toward the new kerk, a distant child’s call, the brief hush when a group passed as if the houses themselves listened. Catherine valued that Sabbath sound: it was human, it had room for breath. Not the clang and roar that merchants sometimes praised as “progress,” as if noise itself were coin. A town that cannot hear its own prayers, she thought, is a town that will soon forget its own tongue.

“Now, Joan,” said she at last, “them which help me cook and serve the meat, they help me eat it; that’s a rule.”

“There’s worse laws in Holland than that,” said Joan, pleased. “Your will is my pleasure, mistress; for my Luke hath got his supper i’ the air. He is digging to-day by good luck.”

Margaret came down then, the borrowed handkerchief fresh about her, her face brightened by washing, her hair obedient. For an instant even Catherine, who could be sharp as mustard, softened at the sight; it was as if the hearth’s glow had risen into Margaret’s cheeks.

“Eh, woman,” Catherine exclaimed, half laughing, “yon is an ugly trade. There she has just washed her face and gi’en her hair a turn, and now who is like her? Rotterdam, that for you!” and she snapped her fingers at the capital, as if to say the great city could not outdo this small domestic miracle.

“Give us a buss, hussy!” she added, and kissed her. “Now mind, Eli won’t wait supper for the duke. Wherefore, loiter not after your kerk is over.”

Joan and Catherine both followed Margaret to the door and stood there, watching her go a good way down the street. Among homely housewives, the going-out is half an incident; it alters the sound of the house, like lifting a lid off a pot. Margaret’s steps joined the stream of others toward the church, and for a moment the street’s cadence was like a psalm: many feet, one purpose.

Catherine watched until Margaret was a smaller figure among larger ones, then spoke, not loudly, but with that confidential tone women use when they speak of what troubles them most.

“There, Joan,” said she, “it is almost to me as if I had just started my own daughter for kerk, and stood a-looking after: the which I’ve done it manys and manys the times. Joan, lass, she won’t hear a word against our Gerard; and he be alive, he has used her cruel; that is why my bowels yearn for the poor wench. I’m older and wiser than she; and so I’ll wed her to yon simple Luke, and there an end. What’s one grandchild?”

The sermon was already afoot when Margaret crossed the threshold of Saint Laurens.

The great church was more promise than completion: side aisles roofed and cool as cellars, but the broad middle still open to the sky, the chancel raw, the very ribs of arches standing up like bones with here and there a smear of whitewash. Only one window wore glass; the rest were jagged mouths bitten out of the walls. Yet on that summer afternoon the unfinished work had a kind of homely grandeur, as if the building, like a loaf not yet cooled, still gave off its own warmth.

Sunlight came in not as a single clean beam, but broken and sifted through those rough openings, falling in slanted sheets that turned dust into gold. It split the dim aisles with bright rivers, flashed on the pale pillars, and laid the central space with a patchwork of light and shadow—cool shade like water in a stone trough, hot light like amber held up to a flame. Overhead, from west to east, the blue sky vaulted the nave so near it seemed you could almost hear it, an airy bowl set above the crowd. Beneath, the women’s white caps spread like a field of linen in harvest-time; and though the mid-aisle was crammed, the multitude kept still, held as if by a hand upon the shoulder.

It was not the sight alone that stilled them. The preacher’s voice—mellow, gentle, earnest—moved through the half-built space and made it whole. In that mingled hush, Margaret became aware of every thread in the church’s sound: the soft breath of many bodies, the faint creak of timber somewhere aloft, a far pigeon’s coo swallowed by stone. The voice rode above it all like a steady chant above a hearth-fire, soothing without asking leave.

She slipped behind a pillar in the north aisle. There she could hardly seize a word, yet the cadence itself was enough; a devotional languor stole over her, as if warm oil were poured on the troubled water in her heart and smoothed it. Her eyelids drooped; her cheek leaned to the cool lime of the pillar; all things grew soft and dreamlike. It felt good—simply good—to be there where sound was ordered and gentle, not jangled and shouted as in streets and markets.

Presently she saw a lady forsake an excellent place opposite, fleeing the sun that poured straight upon her cap from the one glazed window. Margaret moved, softly but swiftly, and took the place. Now she stood by a pillar of the south aisle, no more than fifty feet from the pulpit, a little behind the preacher’s flank. Here the words came clear.

And then her attention was snared by something absurdly lively upon the wall: the shadow of a man’s head and shoulders bobbing up and down with such busy persistence that she had ado not to smile. It was no buffoonery; it was labour. She looked behind her, through the window, and saw Jorian Ketel the sexton digging in the churchyard, lifting and driving his spade with the patient rhythm of one who knows the weight of earth. Each thrust made its own dull thud, muffled by stone and sermon, like a potter’s hand tamping clay.

As she watched that honest motion, a certain tone in the preacher’s voice dropped upon her ear—and her very body answered it. It struck her so distinctly she felt it, as one feels the sudden sharpness of salt on the tongue or the first bite of hot spice; her hand flew to her bosom at the shock of the thrill.

She turned at once and looked toward the pulpit.

But his back was to her; nothing of him visible but the tonsure, pale as a shorn field. She sighed. The bare crown contradicted the voice in a way she could not name. Yet she leaned forward a little, eyes downcast, unwilling to lose that accent that had touched some hidden place in her like a remembered lullaby.

It did not come again—not in that same single unmistakable note. Still the voice grew strangely upon her. As the friar warmed, it rose and fell; it gathered and flowed; and in its turns it woke faint echoes of a thousand small memories—days when the world had seemed secure, and evenings when familiar speech had held its own flavour on the air. She would not look up, fearing to break the spell, as one might spoil a broth by lifting the lid too often, letting all its goodness fly.

Then, in the midst of an eloquent period, the preacher stopped.

The sudden absence of sound was like a snapped string. Margaret almost sighed aloud, as if music had been cut off mid-note. Was the sermon ended? She glanced about: no one stirred. But faces began to turn—many faces—toward her. She felt their attention like heat upon skin.

She looked sharply behind her. There was nothing—only the pillar, only the crowded stillness.

Startled countenances near her fixed on the pulpit. She followed their gaze; and there, above, was a face like a staring corpse. The friar’s eyes—naturally large and made larger by the hollows of his cheeks—stood out dilated beyond nature, glaring her way from a bloodless visage.

Margaret shrank and whipped her head about in terror, persuaded there must be some dreadful thing beside or behind her that drew such a look. There was nothing. She was but the outermost figure of the listening crowd, with bare stone at her back.

At once the church broke into commotion. People rose all over the building and craned forward. Hundreds of eyes flashed from the friar to Margaret, from Margaret back to the friar. The turning to and fro of so many white caps made a broad rustle, like wind worrying a field of dry grain. Then nervous women shrieked; men began to buzz; the ordered soundscape—the very calm that had been like balm—was torn and ragged in an instant.

Seeing herself so marked, Margaret slid behind the pillar, terrified, and stole one hurried glance at the preacher. Brief as it was, it caught something in that stricken face that made her shiver.

She went faint. She sank upon a heap of chips the workmen had left, and hid her face in her hands.

The sermon began again. She heard the sound of it, the lift and fall, but the meaning would not enter. Her thoughts whirled like flour in a draught; nothing would settle. Only one thing fixed itself, hard and sharp: that she had seen, stamped upon that prodigy-struck face, a look whose name she could not escape.

Recognition.

The friar’s discourse, after wavering, ended in a strain of exalted—almost feverish—eloquence, that carried the crowd with it and blurred, for many, the memory of that ghastly pause and stare. When at last they poured out, she mingled hastily with them, keeping her head down, and passed through the door into the common daylight.

Most went homeward in groups, their talk already turning to supper and the day’s close. Margaret did not follow. At the threshold she turned aside into the churchyard, where the air was warmer, and the earth smell rose clean and plain, as it does where spades have been at work.

She went to Peter’s grave.

Poor as she was, she had given him a slab and a headstone. She sat down upon the slab and kissed it, the stone tasting of sun and grit. Then she drew her apron over her head so none might know her by her hair.

“Father,” she whispered, “thou hast often heard me say I am wading in deep waters; but now I begin to think God only knows the bottom of them. I’ll follow that friar round the world, but I’ll see him at arm’s length. And he shall tell me why he looked toward me like a dead man wakened—and not a soul behind me. Oh, father; you often praised me here: speak a word for me there. For I am wading in deep waters.”

Her father’s tomb commanded a side view of the church door. Upon that tomb she sat, face hidden, listening to the yard’s small honest noises—the distant tap of tool on soil, a bird’s quick note, the low murmur of dispersing feet—lying in wait for the holy preacher.

The church held its coolness like water in a stone jar. Sunlight fell in long, slanted bars through the painted glass, laying bright lozenges on flagstones worn to a polish by generations of knees. High above, the purple in the window’s saints seemed not glass at all, but a bruise of heaven, softening the air with color. It soothed Margaret where she stood, and it soothed Father Clement too; more than soothed—set his mind, as a hand sets a bowl on a table, straight before the Maker of all clean joys.

Yet it was not only the light that governed the place. The church had its own living sound: the hush that gathers when a thousand bodies breathe at once; the minute rustle of linen caps as women inclined their heads; the faint creak of a pew under an old man shifting a stiff hip; a child checked with a finger to the lips. Even the swallows outside stitched the silence with their quick, bright cries. Clement heard it all as if it were the church’s second scripture, an acoustic shelter against the world’s harsher clamor—a world where hammers and carts and bargaining tongues could make a man’s thoughts as ragged as a torn sleeve.

He looked down the great aisle, crammed with his country folk: a sea of snowy caps, many of them edged and fretted with gold thread as fine as spider-work. He had traveled many a hundred leagues and seen nothing like that pale multitude, save snowfields under winter sun. In the morning he had thundered at them; the hour had demanded it, and his own zeal had driven him. But this sweet afternoon, this tempered light and the soft, communal breathing, made threats sound out of tune. His belly—his very bowels—yearned toward them. Poor souls; they heard almost as little of God’s love from pulpits in those days as the heathen were said to hear. So he changed the dish he served them. He set down, not the bitter herbs of warning, but the warm bread of glad tidings.

He spoke of salvation as of a table spread for the hungry: not for the proud alone, nor for the well-shod, but for those whose hands were chapped with digging and whose mouths knew mostly coarse rye and onions. He did not whirl about like a weathercock, chasing his own wind. He hardly moved; he let the words do the walking. The people leaned toward his gentle earnestness. Even those in the bad places—those with consciences like smoky chimneys—he did not quite neglect. He touched them too, as a careful cook will scrape the bottom of the pot where the last sweetness sticks, so none be wasted.

And then, warmed by that mercy, eager that no soul in all that crowd should miss the good news, he turned his face toward the south aisle.

There, caught full in a stream of sunshine, was a face that stopped his breath as surely as if a hand had closed his throat.

Margaret Brandt.

At first he only stared. There was no feeling, no thought, no prayer—only a benumbing, soul and body, as if he had stepped barefoot onto sudden ice. Her auburn hair was bathed in the sun and glittered, not like common hair, but like a saint’s ring of light painted in gold leaf. Her face glowed doubly: with its own bloom, and with the light that framed it. She leaned very lightly against a white pillar, as if the stone were a friend. Her lashes lay downcast; she listened with that tender stillness he had seen a hundred times—her whole attention like a bowl held steady to catch every drop.

There was no change in her. This was the blooming Margaret he had left, only riper by a shade, more lovely for it, like fruit that has taken one more day of sun. Clement’s cheeks went bloodless. His eyes grew monstrous. The people died out of his sight. The church’s sounds warped, as in a dream: a rising rustle ran over the nave—folk standing, shifting, crossing themselves—but he could not turn from that face, all life and color and beauty, and that hair glistening in the sun like flame tamed into silk.

He gazed, waiting for her to vanish. She did not.

Then, in a blink as simple as swallowing, she lifted her eyes and looked full at him.

Her own violet eyes.

His lips parted to cry out her name. The name was already in his mouth like a sob. But she turned her head swiftly away; and soon after she vanished from his sight, slipping behind the pillar and out of the sun. Yet not without one more glance—rapid as lightning—that met his and left her crouching inward, mind all whirl and startled questioning, and him panting, hands gripping the pulpit’s edge as if it were the only solid thing in a world gone fluid. For that glance was not recognition. It was the look that comes before recognition: startled, inquiring, nameless, indescribable, as when a tongue tastes a spice it cannot place and yet knows it has been eaten before.

He made a mighty effort and muttered words nobody could understand. His voice had gone thin and far. He resumed his discourse feebly, stammering, babbling, casting about for the thread he had dropped. Bit by bit—forcing himself, now she was out of sight, to treat the thing as a vision permitted from another world—he rose into an unnatural excitement. His closing words spilled out in a torrent that bordered on rhapsody. The simple folk, who could not have told you why, felt the hair rise on their arms. The air itself seemed charged, as if a storm had passed close without rain.

When at last it ended, he sat down on the pulpit stool shaken through and through, as if his bones were reeds.

And then an idea, very much of that age, took him as firmly as a hand takes a shoulder. He had sought her grave at Sevenbergen and found nothing. She had been permitted to appear to him—so the thought went—and show him she was buried here, probably hard by that very pillar where her spirit had shown itself. Once the notion entered, it settled with the certainty of a fact. In his mind it was as plain as a name on a wooden trencher: Margaret lay here.

He had only to ask the sexton—whom, to his great disgust, he had seen working during the sermon, shovel and all, as if holy words were no more than wind—to learn the spot.

By now the church was empty. The last footfalls had faded; the last whisper had died. The soundscape changed: no longer the soft massed breathing, only the clean echo of his own steps and the distant birds outside. He came down from the pulpit, passed through a small aperture in the south wall, and stepped onto the grass.

The smell of earth met him at once—damp, iron-dark, threaded with the sharpness of newly cut sod. A man was there with a spade: Jorian, digging with the steady rhythm of one used to opening the ground for the dead as another man opens a sack of grain for the living. Clement knew him in a moment. But Jorian never suspected the poor lad whose life he had once saved in this holy friar. The loss of Clement’s shapely beard had altered the very outline of his face; more than tonsure or close-cropped hair dusted with premature grey, more than cheeks thinned and paled by fasts and vigils. A beard that has never known a razor grows into a man’s features like an old habit; take it away, and the face is a stranger.

“My son,” said Friar Clement softly, “if you keep any memory of those whom you lay in the earth, prithee tell me—is any Christian buried inside the church, near one of the pillars?”

“Nay, father,” said Jorian, pausing only long enough to look up. “Here in the churchyard lie buried all that buried be. Why?”

“No matter,” Clement answered; and his voice, though steady, had the hollow note of a man speaking across water. “Prithee tell me then, where lieth Margaret Brandt.”

“Margaret Brandt?” Jorian stared stupidly, as if the name were a coin worn smooth. “She died about three years ago, and was buried here.”

“Oh, that is another matter,” he added after a moment, scratching at the thought like a dog at a flea. “That was before my time. The vicar could tell you, likely—if so be she was a gentlewoman, or at the least rich enough to pay him his fee.”

“Alas, my son,” Clement said, and the word had the weight of stone, “she was poor—and paid a heavy penalty for it—but born of decent folk. Her father, Peter, was a learned physician. She came hither from Sevenbergen—to die.”

When he had uttered it, his head sank upon his breast. It was as if speech had spent him. The present—the grass, the spade, the open sky—fell away. He was lost in the past, where voices spoke in dialects that warmed the blood, where a familiar name carried more than meaning: carried a whole life no other tongue could translate.

Jorian, in the grave, put down his spade with a thud that sounded too loud in the afternoon quiet. He stood upright, set his arms akimbo, and said sulkily, “Are you making a fool of me, holy sir, or has some wag been making a fool of you!”

And having flung out his irritation, he took up the spade again and dug with a vigor that showed his temper ruffled—metal biting earth with a blunt, offended rhythm. Clement gazed at him with a puzzled, gently reproachful eye; the tone was rude, and the words, in their sharpness, almost unintelligible to a man who had been living more with prayers than quarrels.

Good-natured though crusty, Jorian had not thrown up three spadefuls before shame cooled him. The churchyard’s quiet—broken only by spade and breathing—seemed to rebuke him better than any sermon.

“Why, what a base churl am I,” he said, “to speak thus to thee, holy father; and thou standing there, looking at me like a lamb.” He paused, then his face cleared as if a shutter had been opened. “Aha! I have it. ’Tis Peter Brandt’s grave you would fain see, not Margaret’s. He does lie here—hard by the west door. There; I’ll show you.”

He laid down his spade, climbed out, and pulled on his doublet and jerkin to go with the friar.

He did not know there was anybody sitting on Peter’s tomb. Still less that she was watching for this holy friar.

Pietro Vanucci and Andrea, too, did not recognize him without his beard.

Jorian, with his doublet half-laced and his jerkin hanging open, stood in the churchyard as if the very act of clothing himself were a sort of oath to the dead. He had been talking all the while—talking as men talk when their hands are busy and their minds refuse to be still—his breath sending little clouds into the cold air that smelled of wet earth and old stone.

“They used to call him a magician out Sevenbergen way,” he said, tightening a strap, his tongue running on as steadily as his fingers. “And they do say he gave ’em a touch o’ his trade at parting; told ’em he saw Margaret’s lad a-coming down Rhine in brave clothes and store o’ money, but his face scarred by foreign glaive, and not altogether so many arms and legs as a went away wi’. But, dear heart, nought came on’t. Margaret is still wearying for her lad; and Peter, he lies as quiet as his neighbours; not but what she hath put a stone slab over him, to keep him where he is: as you shall see.”

He braced both hands upon the edge of the open grave, palms damp with the clay that clung like dough, and began to heave himself up; the spade lay beside him, its blade dark and shining as if oiled by the grave-mould.

A hand—light, trembling, yet urgent—settled on his shoulder.

“How long since died Peter Brandt?” The voice was a whisper, but a whisper with the rasp of thirst and fasting in it.

“About two months. Why?” Jorian answered, looking up; and as he looked he saw the friar’s face drawn thin, as if the bells of the town had been ringing inside his skull all night.

“And his daughter buried him, say you?”

“Nay, I buried him; but she paid the fee and reared the stone.”

“Then—” The friar’s lips worked. “But he had just one daughter; Margaret?”

“No more leastways, that he owned to.”

“Then you think Margaret is—is alive?”

Jorian’s brows lifted, honest wonder at the question. “Think? Why, I should be dead else. Riddle me that.”

The friar swayed, the colour rushing to his cheeks and then draining away, as if some unseen choir were singing him from earth to heaven and back again.

“Alas, how can I?” he breathed. “You love her.”

Jorian gave a short, incredulous laugh. “No more than reason, being a married man, and father of four more sturdy knaves like myself. Nay, the answer is, she saved my life scarce six weeks agone. Now had she been dead she couldn’t ha’ kept me alive. Bless your heart, I couldn’t keep a thing on my stomach; nor doctors couldn’t make me. My Joan says, ‘’Tis time to buy thee a shroud.’ ‘I dare say, so ’tis,’ says I; ‘but try and borrow one first.’ In comes my lady, this Margaret— which she died three years ago, by your way on’t—opens the windows, makes ’em shift me where I lay, and cures me in the twinkling of a bedpost; but wi’ what? there pinches the shoe; with the scurviest herb, and out o’ my own garden, too; with sweet feverfew. A herb, quotha—’tis a weed; leastways it was a weed till it cured me, but now whene’er I pass my hunch I doff bonnet, and says I, ‘fly service t’ye.’ Why, how now, father, you look wondrous pale, and now you are red, and now you are white? Why, what is the matter? What, in Heaven’s name, is the matter?”

“The surprise—the joy—the wonder—the fear,” the friar gasped, as if each word were wrestled out of him. The yard seemed to sharpen around them: the caw of a distant crow, the thin scrape of twig against stone, the faint drip from a yew. “Why, what is it to thee? Art thou of kin to Margaret Brandt?”

“Nay; but I knew one that loved her well, so well her death nigh killed him, body and soul. And yet thou sayest she lives. And I believe thee.”

Jorian stared, silence settling on him like dust. Then he said slowly, very gravely, as a man who begins to fear he has been standing all his life upon a trapdoor.

“Father, you have asked me many questions, and I have answered them truly; now for our Lady’s sake answer me but two. Did you in very sooth know one who loved this poor lass? Where?”

The friar’s face tightened. He stood on the brink of some confession, but whatever name rose in him he smothered it, as if it burned.

“I knew him in Italy,” he said at last.

“If you knew him you can tell me his name,” said Jorian, cautious now.

“His name was Gerard Eliassoen.”

Jorian drew breath as if struck. “Oh, but this is strange. Stay—what made thee say Margaret Brandt was dead?”

“I was with Gerard when a letter came from Margaret Van Eyck. The letter told him she he loved was dead and buried.” The friar’s knees gave. “Let me sit down, for my strength fails me. Foul play! Foul play!”

“Father,” said Jorian, and there was a rough kindness in him, like coarse salt rubbed into a wound to keep it clean, “I thank Heaven for sending thee to me. Ay, sit ye down; ye do look like a ghost; ye fast overmuch to be strong. My mind misgives me; methinks I hold the clue to this riddle, and if I do, there be two knaves in this town whose heads I would fain batter to pieces as I do this mould.”

He seized the long spade and, with his teeth set, brought it down again and again upon the heap of loose earth; each blow made a dull, hungry sound, the sound of ground broken for sowing—only this was ground broken for vengeance.

“Foul play?” he went on. “You never said a truer word i’ your life; and if you know where Gerard is now, lose no time, but show him the trap they have laid for him. Mine is but a dull head, but whiles the slow hound puzzles out the scent—go to. And I do think you and I ha’ got hold of two ends o’ one stick, and a main foul one.”

Then, after those useless fore-ramblings by which plain folk edge toward what bites them hardest, he told his tale.

He had been hired by the burgomaster of Tergou to mend the floor of an upper room; and when the planks were near laid, he had come suddenly at an odd hour to fetch his tools. Below, voices rose sharp enough to pierce oak. Curiosity pricked him; he lay down flat, belly to the boards, and listened through a crack that tasted of dust and old pitch.

He heard the burgomaster speaking of a letter. Cornelis and Sybrandt—those names came like rancid smoke through the chink—were minded to slip their own letter into the place of one that a certain Hans Memling was taking to Gerard. They lacked courage; the burgomaster’s voice, thick with contempt and temptation, answered that.

“And to give them courage,” Jorian said, “the old man showed them a drawer full o’ silver; and if they did the trick they should each put a hand in, and have all the silver they could hold in’t.”

At that, Jorian confessed, he had slept badly: not for pity, not yet, but for the glitter of it. “Think on’t,” he muttered, as if the very thought still hurt his gums.

“Next morning at peep o’ day who should I see but my masters Cornelis and Sybrandt come out o’ their house each with a black eye. ‘Oho,’ says I, ‘what yon Hans hath put his mark on ye; well now I hope that is all you have got for your pains.’ Didn’t they make for the burgomaster’s house? I to my hiding-place.”

The friar’s nostrils flared; his eyes, restless as a hunted thing’s, fixed on Jorian’s mouth as if to drag each syllable out faster.

“Well,” said Jorian, “the burgomaster brought them into that same room. He had a letter in his hand; but I am no scholar; however, I have got as many eyes in my head as the Pope hath, and I saw the drawer opened, and those two knaves put in each a hand and draw it out full. And, saints in glory, how they tried to hold more, and more, and more o’ yon stuff!”

His voice, despite himself, took on the relish of the moment: the soft clink and slide of coins, the greedy rustle of sleeves, the breath held as fingers groped like thieves in a pantry.

“And Sybrandt,” Jorian added, his mouth twitching, “he had daubed his hand in something sticky— I think ’twas glue— and he made shift to carry one or two pieces away a sticking to the back o’ his hand, he! he! he! ’Tis a sin to laugh.”

Then his face hardened. “So you see luck was on the wrong side as usual; they had done the trick; but how they did it, that, methinks, will never be known till doomsday. Go to, they left their immortal jewels in yon drawer. Well, they got a handful o’ silver for them; the devil had the worst o’ yon bargain.”

He exhaled as if he had been holding this story in his ribs for years. “There, father, that is off my mind. Often I longed to tell it some one, but I durst not to the women; or Margaret would not have had a friend left in the world; for those two black-hearted villains are the favourites, ’Tis always so. Have not the old folk just taken a brave new shop for them in this very town, in the Hoog Straet? There may you see their sign, a gilt sheep and a lambkin; a brace of wolves sucking their dam would be nigher the mark. And there the whole family feast this day; oh, ’tis a fine world.”

He waited for the friar’s curse, for some holy thunder to answer his own earthy rage; but the friar sat rigid, as if turned to carved wood on a tomb.

“What, not a word, holy father?” Jorian burst out. “You sit there like stone, and have not even a curse to bestow on them, the stony-hearted miscreants. What, was it not enough the poor lad was all alone in a strange land; must his own flesh and blood go and lie away the one blessing his enemies had left him? And then think of her pining and pining all these years, and sitting at the window looking adown the street for Gerard! and so constant, so tender, and true—my wife says she is sure no woman ever loved a man truer than she loves the lad those villains have parted from her; and the day never passes but she weeps salt tears for him.”

His voice rose, filling the yard; even the small sounds seemed to shrink back—the finches went quiet, and the thin wind in the bare branches turned aside as if unwilling to be witness.

“And when I think,” he went on, “that, but for those two greedy lying knaves, yon winsome lad, whose life I saved, might be by her side this day the happiest he in Holland; and the sweet lass, that saved my life, might be sitting with her cheek upon her sweetheart’s shoulder, the happiest she in Holland in place of the saddest—oh, I thirst for their blood, the nasty, sneaking, lying, cogging, cowardly, heartless, bowelless—how now?”

The friar sprang up like a man who has been struck in the breast by a mace. His face went livid; his hands clenched and lifted, not in prayer, but in some terrible, wordless summoning. He rushed from the place, a black storm loosed among gravestones.

So fierce was that inarticulate fury that Jorian’s own anger fell away like a broken tool. He stood staring after the human tempest he had unchained.

Then fingers—small, cold, trembling—closed round his arm.

It was Margaret Brandt.

He started; her coming at that instant was as uncanny as the sudden chill that steals through a room when a door opens on an empty passage. She had waited long by Peter’s stone, listening to the yard’s ordinary life: the soft scuff of shoes, the cough of an old man inside the church, the distant market-hum that carried faintly even here. The friar did not return. So she had gone into the church to seek him; could not find him. Then, in the south aisle, the giant shadow of a friar had come swiftly along the flags and climbed a pillar like a living thing, seeming to pass through her.

She had nearly screamed—until memory, quick as instinct, told her how Jorian’s shadow had done the like coming from the churchyard. She scrambled out the nearest way, catching her skirt, breath snagged in her throat. By the time she gained the street, Clement was already tearing away; yet even at a distance his very body cried agitation.

Margaret and Jorian looked from one another to the wild figure diminishing down the road.

“Well?” she asked, and her voice shook as a spoon shakes in an empty pot.

“Well,” said Jorian, thickly, “you startled me. How come you here of all people?”

“Is this a time for idle chat? What said he to you? He has been speaking to you; deny it not.”

“Girl,” said Jorian, “as I stand here, he asked me whereabout you were buried in this churchyard.”

“Ah!”

“I told him, nowhere, thank Heaven: you were alive and saving other folk from the churchyard.”

“Well?”

“Well, the long and the short is, he knew thy Gerard in Italy; and a letter came saying you were dead; and it broke thy poor lad’s heart. Let me see; who was the letter written by? Oh, by the demoiselle van Eyck. That was his way of it. But I up and told him nay; ’twas neither demoiselle nor dame that penned yon lie, but Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, and those foul knaves, Cornelis and Sybrandt; these changed the true letter for one of their own; I told him as how I saw the whole villainy done through a chink; and now, if I have not been and told you!”

Margaret’s hand flew to her mouth. Her eyes shone wet, but in the wet there was sudden light, as when a hearth catches after long coaxing.

“Oh, cruel! cruel! But he lives. The fear of fears is gone. Thank God!”

“Ay, lass,” said Jorian. “And as for thine enemies, I have given them a dig. For yon friar is friendly to Gerard, and he is gone to Eli’s house, methinks. For I told him where to find Gerard’s enemies and thine, and wow but he will give them their lesson. If ever a man was mad with rage, its yon. He turned black and white, and parted like a stone from a sling. Girl, there was thunder in his eye and silence on his lips. Made me cold a did.”

“Oh, Jorian, what have you done?” Margaret cried. “Quick! quick! help me thither, for the power is gone all out of my body. You know him not as I do. Oh, if you had seen the blow he gave Ghysbrecht; and heard the frightful crash! Come, save him from worse mischief. The water is deep enow; but not bloody yet, come!”

The anguish in her voice did what no command could. Jorian sprang up out of the grave as if it had become suddenly unclean to him, and as he ran he dragged his jerkin on, half-wearing it, half-wrestling it, the leather creaking and his breath loud in his ears.

As they hurried, he tried to make sense of her words. “I talk of this friar,” he panted, “and you answer me of Gerard.”

“Man, see you not? this is Gerard!”

“This—Gerard? what mean ye?”

“I mean,” she said, and her voice broke and steadied in the same breath, “yon friar is my boy’s father. I have waited for him long, Jorian. Well, he is come to me at last. And thank God for it. Oh, my poor child! Quicker, Jorian, quicker!”

Jorian’s eyes widened, as if his mind were tasting some impossible flavour and could not name it. “Why, thou art mad as he. Stay! By St. Bavon, yon was Gerard’s face; ’twas nought like it; yet somehow—’twas it. Come on! come on! let me see the end of this.”

“The end?” Margaret whispered. “How many of us will live to see that?”

They went in breathless silence, their footfalls and the town’s living noises braiding together: a cart’s iron rim singing on cobbles, a woman calling from a doorway, a hammer somewhere ringing like a heart in a forge. Hoog Straet drew near; the smells changed—less damp stone, more yeast and tallow, more frying fat from some kitchen where even grief had to be fed.

Then Jorian, trying clumsily to comfort, said, “You are making your own trouble. Who says he has gone thither? More likely to the convent to weep and pray, poor soul. Oh, cursed, cursed villains!”

“Did not you tell him where those villains bide?”

“Ay, that I did.”

“Then quicker, oh, Jorian, quicker. I see the house. Thank God and all the saints, I shall be in time to calm him. I know what I’ll say to him; Heaven forgive me!” Her eyes darted, as if she saw not only the street before her but years behind it. “Poor Catherine; ’tis of her I think: she has been a mother to me.”

The shop stood on a corner, two doors like two mouths: one opening to the main street for customers and coin, the other round the corner, the private door where secrets entered and did not always come out again. Above hung the sign—gilt sheep and lambkin shining complacently in the pale daylight, as if innocence could be bought and sold with wool.

Margaret and Jorian were within twenty yards when a roar tore out from within, raw as a beast’s, making the very air tremble. In the next instant the friar burst out—white, raging, his habit flung wide as if the wind itself were trying to rip him free of it—and went tearing down the street.

Margaret screamed and sagged, fainting against Jorian’s arm.

Jorian bellowed after the flying figure, “Stay, madman, know thy friends!”

But the friar did not so much as turn his head. He went headlong, shaking his clenched fists high, high in the air, as if he would strike the sky for permitting the world’s lies.

“Help me in, good Jorian,” Margaret moaned; and then, sudden as a candle steadies when the draft is shut out, she grew eerily calm. “Let me know the worst; and die.”

He half carried her into the house. The stillness inside was unnatural, as if all the household sounds—laughter, plates, the gossiping clatter of a feast—had been swallowed at one gulp. Not a voice, not a step, not even the small domestic music of spoon against bowl.

Jorian’s heart thudded loud enough to seem an intruder. A door stood before him, unlatched. He set his left hand to it and pushed softly.

Margaret and he stood upon the threshold.

What they saw there you shall soon know.

Supper-time came, and with it the small, homely ceremony that in that house stood for law: the board drawn close, the trenchers set, the knives laid where each hand expected them, and the steam of good fare rising like a benediction to the rafters.

All were gathered—Eli at the head, Catherine fluttering and fussy with her household dignity, Joan in the place of an honored helper more than a guest, and Jorian, still pale from his late sickness, watching the dishes with that sharpened hunger illness leaves behind. Only Margaret was away.

To Catherine’s surprise, Eli did not give the word to begin.

“We’ll bide a bit for her,” said he.

“Why, I told her you would not wait for the duke,” Catherine returned, half reproach, half pride.

“She is not the duke,” said Eli. “She is a poor, good lass that hath waited—not minutes—but years—for a graceless son of mine. Put the meat on the board all the same. When she comes, we’ll lose no more time.”

So the dishes came in: brown bread with its cracked crust still sighing warmth when the knife went near; a joint that had been turned and basted till the fat ran clear and sweet, and the outside held that deep, savory skin a careful hand coaxes from fire; and a mess of herbs and roots, garden-things lifted from honest earth and stewed till their smell filled the room—leek and onion, maybe, and the green sharpness of parsley crushed between fingers, mellowed now into comfort. The very air was thick with supper; it clung to the tongue before a morsel was swallowed. Beyond the shutters lay the village’s evening sound—distant talk, a dog’s short bark, the soft scuff of feet in the street—acoustic small-wares that make a home feel held in the world.

Eli held out against it as long as he could, then his face softened—hunger and habit conspiring with hope.

“She will come if we begin,” said he; “they always do. Come, sit ye down, Mistress Joan; y’are not here for a slave, I trow, but a guest. There—” He lifted a hand, listening. “I hear a quick step off covers. Withdraw the covers, and fall to.”

Covers were whipped away; steel flashed; the first bread was broken. And then the expected light step did come—quick, urgent—only it was followed by a heavier, harsher tread, and a breathing like bellows. The door flew wide.

Not Margaret.

A Dominican friar burst in, his face grey with fury as if rage had drained it of blood. The whole room, full a moment before of warm smells and neighborly clatter, seemed suddenly to lose its ordinary sounds; the hush fell like a cloth thrown over a dish. He crossed the floor at a bound and was at the table in an instant, in front of Cornelis and Sybrandt.

He flung his long body over the narrow board, and spread his hands above their shrinking heads—hovering, rigid, like talons poised. Then, with a voice that struck the ear like iron on stone, he cursed them.

He cursed them by name; cursed their souls and bodies in this world and the next. The age had a terrible fluency for malediction, and he poured it out with a minute and dreadful craft, each clause fitted like a nail driven home.

“Cursed be the lips,” he shrieked, “which spoke the lie that Margaret was dead; may they rot before the grave, and kiss white-hot iron in hell thereafter! Doubly cursed be the hands that changed those letters—be they struck off by the hangman’s knife, and handle hell fire for ever! Thrice accursed be the cruel hearts that did conceive that damned lie, to part true love for ever! May they sicken and wither on earth, joyless, loveless, hopeless; wither to dust before their time; and burn in eternal fire!”

He cursed the meat at their mouths, and every atom of their bodies, from hair to sole; and while he did it the supper-smell itself seemed to turn strange—good food made suddenly hateful by a word that claimed Heaven for its warrant. Joan’s fingers tightened on her lap; Jorian’s swallow stuck. Catherine made a sound in her throat and could not shape it into speech. Cornelis and Sybrandt bent and cringed, as if the curses were stones hurled at them.

Then the friar tore a letter from his bosom and flung it down before Eli as one flings down a gauntlet.

“Read that, thou hard old man that didst imprison thy son,” he cried. “Read, and see what monsters thou hast brought into the world. The memory of my wrongs and hers dwell with you all for ever! I will meet you again at the Judgment Day; on earth ye will never see me more.”

And as he had come, so he was gone—gone like a gust that slams a door and leaves a house stunned in its wake. The room sat frozen around the steaming dishes, white-faced and rigid as if some Eastern tale had come true and turned living folk to images before untasted food.

That was the sight that met Margaret’s eyes—and Jorian’s—when, the next moment, they entered.

The change was so sharp that Margaret stopped on the threshold as though she had stepped into a chapel after market-noise. Her gaze ran from face to face—Eli standing half risen, Catherine drawn tight with fear and shame, Joan startled and still, the two lads sunk low as if hoping the table itself might hide them—then she caught her breath and cried out, brokenly:

“Oh, joy! all here—no blood hath been shed. Oh, you cruel, cruel men! I thank God he hath not slain you.”

At the sight of her Catherine gave a scream that was all mother and all dread; then turned her head away, as if the very look of Margaret were a judgment.

But Eli had snatched up the letter and cast an eye along it, and the sense of it struck him like a club. He began to understand—began to see the long, filthy work and the pain it had cost. When he looked up and beheld Margaret at that very instant, with her wrongs written in the pallor of her sweet face, his old blood leapt. He sprang to his feet in a transport of rage.

“Stand clear!” he shouted. “Stand clear, and let me get at the traitors. I’ll hang for them!”

In a flash his short sword was out. Steel sang—thin, sharp—a cruelly bright sound in a room that had been meant for bread and peace. He fell upon Cornelis and Sybrandt.

“Fly!” screamed Margaret. “Fly!”

They slipped, howling, under the table and crawled out the far side, knocking trenchers and scraping knees, their terror a clumsy, scrambling thing. But before they could reach the door Eli ran round and barred them, blade lifted. Catherine only screamed and wrung her hands—the great ones of the household, who manage servants and reckon stores and set the table straight, are often the helplessest when the blood rises.

There would have been blood—certainly—had not Margaret and Jorian, with one impulse, seized Eli’s arms and held them with all their strength. Jorian, though not yet fully recovered, set his shoulder and braced as if he had been born for such a moment; Margaret clung like a child to a father who would not listen, her voice breaking on his name.

The pair got clear of the house. Then Margaret and Jorian loosed Eli. He went raging out into the street after the fugitives; but they were already a furlong away, running like hares.

He came back with his breath heaving, and with a single savage stroke hacked down the board on which their names were written—one of those household tablets that keeps the memory of kin and work—and he flung it into the chimney-place as though he would burn the very notion of them out of his hearth.

Catherine sat rocking herself, her apron over her head, as if she could hide from what had been spoken. Joan ran to her husband and caught his hand. Margaret put her arms round Catherine’s neck; she was pale, panting, and yet tried, with a tenderness that had been taught by sorrow, to comfort the woman who had helped wrong her.

But it would not be done. Catherine’s grief burst out in sobs that were more fear than penitence.

“Oh, my poor children!” she cried. “Oh, miserable mother! ’Tis a mercy Kate was ill upstairs. There—I have lived to thank God for that!” And then, with a fresh storm: “It would have killed her. He had better have stayed in Italy than come home to curse his own flesh and blood, and set us all by the ears.”

“Hold your chat, woman,” Eli broke in, anger stiff with pain. “You are still on the side of the ill-doer. You are cheap served. Your weakness made the rogues what they are. I was for correcting them in their youth—for sore ills, sharp remedies; but you still sided with their faults, and undermined me, and baffled wise severity. And you, Margaret—leave comforting her that ought rather to comfort you; for what is her hurt to yours? She never had a grain of justice under her skin; and never will.”

He turned then, with a rough tenderness that was command as much as love.

“So come thou to me, that am thy father from this hour.”

She obeyed, because the voice allowed no choice. She kissed Catherine—softly, as one who parts from the past—and went tottering to Eli. He set her on a chair beside him, and she laid her weak head on his honest breast. No tears came; the ache was too deep for that, like hunger that has gone beyond craving into numbness.

“Poor lamb,” he said, and his voice broke on the words.

Time went on. The supper stood there still, sending up its honest steam into a room where no one could taste it. The smell of roasted fat, which a minute before had promised comfort, now felt like insult—goodness spoiled by human bitterness and by a curse spoken in the Church’s name. It was as though the very language that should guard memory and mercy had been used to strike them deaf.

At last Eli lifted his head and looked across at Jorian and Joan with a kind of shame-faced hospitality.

“Come, good folks,” said he, in a broken voice. “We are in a little trouble, as you see; but that is no reason you should starve. For our Lady’s sake, fall to; and add not to my grief the reputation of a churl. What the dickens!”—and he made a ghastly, brave attempt at heartiness—“the more knaves I have the luck to get shut of, the more my need of true men and women to help me clear the dish, and cheer mine eye with honest faces about me where else were gaps. Fall to, I do entreat ye.”

Catherine, sobbing under her apron, backed his request with a broken “Ay—do, do.”

Poor, simple, antique, hospitable souls—trained from childhood to believe a table was a kind of altar, and that to send a guest away unfed was a sin the house would remember.

Jorian’s appetite, especially since his illness, was keen; the smell of meat and herbs pulled at him like a hand. He moved as if to obey, but Joan leaned close and whispered in his ear—one quick sentence, low as a mouse in the thatch. He drew back at once.

“Nay,” said he. “I’ll touch no meat that Holy Church hath cursed.”

“In sooth, I forgot,” Eli answered, and his plain face took on a dumb wonder. “My son, who was reared at my table, hath cursed my victuals. That seems strange. Well—what God wills, man must bow to.”

So the supper—bread, meat, all that careful turning and basting, all that garden labor and hearth-skill—was flung out into the yard as if it were carrion. The sound of it hitting the wet earth was small, yet it jarred the ear, a wasteful thud that seemed to carry farther than it should into the night.

Jorian took Joan home; heavy sadness reigned in Eli’s house.

Meanwhile, where was Clement?

He lay at full length upon the cold floor of the convent church, his lips pressed to the lowest step of the altar. Terror and misery had him by the throat; penitence crushed him; self-abasement ground him into the stone. And through all that anguish there struggled, like a thin thread of dawn in cloud, gleams of joy—Margaret was alive.

Night fell and found him still there, weeping and praying. The church had its own sound-world: the drip of damp in some unseen corner, the hollow breath of the building, the far footfall of a monk passing like a shadow, and, under all, the pounding within his own ears, the loudest noise of all because it could not be escaped.

Morning would have found him there too, but suddenly another memory rose up, sharper than any curse: in his rage for his own wrongs and Margaret’s, he had committed yet another sin.

He had neglected a dying man.

He sprang up at once, groaning at his accumulated wickedness, and went out to repair the omission. The weather had changed. Rain fell hard, drumming on roof and road, turning earth to black paste; and when he got clear of the town, he heard wolves baying—on the foot, hunting by sound more than sight, their voices travelling through wet air and leafless spaces like a warning.

But Clement was himself again—or nearly. Danger and discomfort were little to him beside the shame of a duty left undone. He went stoutly forward through rain and darkness; and as he went he beat his breast, and cried into the storm, words that were Latin and therefore heavy with the Church’s authority, yet no tongue could fully translate what he felt within them:

“MEA CULPA! MEA CULPA!”

What passed through that keen, scrupulous spirit in those few hours—after a night spent beside a dying hermit, trading prayers like bread broken in the dark—cannot be carried whole into another man’s mouth. Some hungers are not spoken; they are heard: the rasp of a breath, the soft click of beads, the thin water-sound in a stone basin when dawn comes and the world pretends it is ordinary again.

At daybreak he set out—yet not toward Rotterdam. He turned his feet toward Tergou.

There was a reason as plain as salt: to face Ghysbrecht the burgomaster, the man who had sat warm in another household’s inheritance as if it were his own hearth-stool; and to make him, by the force of conscience and of Holy Church, bring up again what he had swallowed. Clement carried with him a parchment whose own story would have filled a winter’s evening by a peat-fire; but he did not finger it, nor take comfort from its crackle. He let it lie hidden, as one keeps a knife sheathed until it must be used, and prayed rather to win with words.

He walked hard. Dust clung to his sandals and rose at each step in little puffs that tasted of dry road and horse-dung and last year’s chaff. The country lay about him in its plain, domestic labor: ditches shining, alder-tops murmuring, a cart somewhere groaning on its axle, and far off a bell that did not ring for him and yet seemed to touch his ribs as if it knew his business.

By the time he reached the town his throat was parched. He stopped at the fountain, where the water ran with that cool, clean voice that can quiet a man’s inward tumult for the length of a swallow. He drew from his wallet a piece of black bread—coarse, sour with rye, the crust gritty where flour and bran had baked into one—and began to eat, letting the fountain-water wash it down. It was a poor meal; yet even poor bread has its comfort when a body is weary, and the mouth remembers the simple honesty of grain.

He had taken but a few bites when a woman came running—servant by her cap and apron, fear by her breath. Her words tumbled over each other like beans spilled on a board.

“Father—come—my master is dying. Shrieve him. Quick, for the love of God!”

Clement looked once at the bread in his hand as if it belonged to another life, then put it back into his wallet. He rose without a question and followed her.

Her haste led him not to a merchant’s house, nor to a craftsman’s low door smelling of pitch and onions, but straight to the Stadthouse.

At the threshold something went cold along his skin. He drew back—a small shudder, quick as a startled bird—seeing where she was taking him. The very boards seemed to remember: a stair creaking like accusation, voices once lifted in judgment, the weight of official words spoken in a tongue that could make theft sound like law. Yet he mastered himself almost at once; he would not be governed by the body’s recoil. He followed her in, and up, and up, while the building’s hush pressed on his ears, broken only by the servant’s sobbing and the faint, relentless tick of a clock that counted out the burgomaster’s remaining breaths.

In a chamber where the air was close with old linen and bitter herbs, propped high on pillows, lay Ghysbrecht. The man’s face was already half withdrawn from life—yellowed, slack, the lips thinned as if the mouth had at last learned what it would not say. Clement paused at the door and looked at him; and in that one look there rose like a tower in his mind the memory of wrongs—the tower, the wood, the letter—each a stone laid on another’s heart.

He spoke, low, and his voice trembled in spite of him.

“Pax vobiscum.”

Ghysbrecht’s eyes opened wider, eager in their weakness; even fear can be hungry.

“Thank Heaven,” he whispered, “thou art come in time. Absolve me, father, and pray for my soul—thou and thy brethren.”

“My son,” said Clement, and the old formal words came to him like a well-known knife-handle finding the hand, “before absolution cometh confession. In which act there must be no reservation, as thou valuest thy soul’s weal. Bethink thee, therefore, wherein thou hast most offended God and the Church, while I offer up a prayer for wisdom to direct thee.”

He knelt. The floor was hard, and he felt through his knees the solid, indifferent timbers; but the sound in the room changed as he prayed—the servant’s weeping softened, the sick man’s breath caught and let go, and beyond the shutter a sparrow called, careless of human accounts. When Clement rose, his face was composed, as if he had put his own anger—like a pot set too near the flame—further from the heat.

“My son,” he said, “confess thy sins.”

“Ah, father,” whispered Ghysbrecht, “they are many and great.”

“Great, then, be thy penitence, my son; so shalt thou find God’s mercy great.”

Ghysbrecht joined his hands. He began, with the exactness of a man reciting market-weights: he had eaten meat in mid-Lent; he had been absent from mass on the Lord’s day and on saints’ days; he had trifled with fasts and prayers and other observances, naming each omission as if each were a coin laid down on a table.

When he had ended, Clement said very quietly, “’Tis well, my son. These be faults. Now to thy crimes. Thou hadst done better to begin with them.”

The sick man’s eyes blinked, baffled.

“Why, father—what crimes lie to my account if these be none?”

“Am I confessing to thee,” said Clement, and there was steel under the softness, “or thou to me?”

Ghysbrecht swallowed, his throat moving like a bird’s. “Forgive me, father! Surely I to you. But I know not what you call crimes.”

“The seven deadly sins—art thou clear of them?”

“Heaven forefend I should be guilty of them. I know them not by name.”

“Many do them all that cannot name them,” said Clement. “Begin with that one which leads to lying, theft, and murder.”

“I am quit of that one, any way. How call you it?”

“Avarice,” said Clement. “Avarice, my son.”

“Avarice?” Ghysbrecht’s voice rose, thin and plaintive. “Oh, as to that—I have been a saving man all my day; but I have kept a good table, and not altogether forgotten the poor. Alas, I am a great sinner. Mayhap the next will catch me. What is the next?”

“We have not yet done with this one,” said Clement, and the air seemed to tighten, as if the room itself listened. “Bethink thee. The Church is not to be trifled with.”

“Alas! am I in a condition to trifle with her now?” The dying man’s fingers worried the coverlet. “Avarice? Avarice?”

He looked, for a moment, almost like a child who cannot understand why a grown man is angry.

“Hast thou ever robbed the fatherless?” Clement asked.

“Me? robbed the fatherless?” Ghysbrecht gasped. “Not that I mind.”

Clement’s patience had depth, but it had a bottom. “Once more, my son, I am forced to tell thee thou art trifling with the Church. Miserable man! another evasion, and I leave thee; and fiends will straightway gather round thy bed and tear thee down to the bottomless pit.”

At that the dying man’s courage broke like a crust under a knife.

“Oh, leave me not! leave me not!” he cried, clutching at Clement’s sleeve with a strength that startled in so wasted a body. “The Church knows all. I must have robbed the fatherless. I will confess. Who shall I begin with? My memory for names is shaken.”

It was a cunning shelter—fog thrown on a narrow road—yet Clement cut through it with a word, and that word was a name spoken as if it had weight and history and blood.

“Hast thou forgotten Floris Brandt?”

Ghysbrecht reared up among his pillows, eyes bulging, the skin about his mouth drawn tight with terror.

“How knew you that?” he panted.

“The Church knows many things,” said Clement coldly, “and by many ways that are dark to thee. Miserable impenitent, thou calledst her to thy side hoping to deceive her. Thou saidst, ‘I will not confess to the curé, but to some friar who knows not my misdeeds. So will I cheat the Church on my deathbed, and die as I have lived.’ But God, kinder to thee than thou art to thyself, sent to thee one whom thou couldst not deceive.

“He has tried thee. He was patient with thee, and warned thee not to trifle with Holy Church; but all is in vain: thou canst not confess, for thou art impenitent as a stone. Die, then, as thou hast lived. Methinks I see the fiends crowding round the bed for their prey. They wait but for me to go. And I go.”

He turned his back.

There is a sound a man makes when the world is dropping away: not speech, not sobbing, but a raw, animal crack in the breath. Ghysbrecht made it. In extremity he caught Clement by the frock, clutching as if cloth were salvation.

“Oh, holy man—mercy! stay. I will confess all, all.” His voice shook and scraped. “I robbed my friend Floris. Alas! would it had ended there; for he lost little by me; but I kept the land from Peter his son, and from Margaret, Peter’s daughter. Yet I was always going to give it back—but I couldn’t, I couldn’t.”

“Avarice, my son,” said Clement, and the severity in him was not hatred now, but the surgeon’s steadiness. “Avarice. Happy for thee ’tis not too late.”

“No—no; I will leave it her by will.” Ghysbrecht’s eyes darted as if seeking an escape even from repentance. “She will not have long to wait for it now—not above a month or two at farthest.”

“For which month’s possession,” said Clement, and his voice cut clean, “thou wouldst damn thy soul for ever. Thou fool!”

Ghysbrecht groaned, and pleaded weakly for reason, for time, for the small comfort of dying with his fingers still closed on what was not his. Clement held firm; but he did not rage. He spoke with a gentleness that did not yield, persuading and pressing as one kneads stubborn dough—patient, rhythmic, unwilling to be cheated by softness on the surface while the lump remains hard within.

More than once his own blood leaped, and his hand was tempted toward his bosom where the parchment lay: the swift, simple ending; the proof produced; the victory taken. Yet he remembered the previous day’s storm within him, and feared the taste of his own anger as a man fears meat too rich for a fasting stomach. He would not let choler season the work of God.

So he endured. His flesh crept with repugnance to the man, with the stale smell of fear and sweat in the sickroom, with the thin, complaining whine of self-pity; but he mastered that too. Step by step he loosened the dying miser’s grip upon another’s property—upon another’s history, another’s hearth—and at last, without once naming the deed he carried, he won Ghysbrecht to full and prompt restitution.

How that restitution was made shall be told elsewhere; and likewise certain curious effects it wrought in Ghysbrecht, and when and on what terms the burgomaster and the friar parted.

This was Clement’s first overt act, and it showed the temper of his mind after the first fierce tempest had fallen.

The second is told in two words.

As soon as he was quite sure Margaret had her own, and was a rich woman—he disappeared.

The day after that dreadful outburst, the little house in the Hoog Straet lay under a hush like a churchyard after rain. Even the common street-sounds came softened, as if the very air had been taught to tread gently—no jolly clatter of trenchers, no brisk scold-and-laugh between hearth and table. Only a thin simmering in the pot at noon, a spoon set down too carefully, and then long silences that swallowed the faintest creak of the settle.

Catherine, whose hands were made for bustle and whose tongue was born to stitch neighbours together with talk, went about as if her limbs had forgotten their business. After dinner she wiped her eyes with the corner of her apron—eyes red and swollen, like onions had been peeled without end—and said she would go to the convent and speak with Gerard, if only to lay the first stone of peace.

The convent porter, thick of ear or thick of patience, made her say it twice, then again; and even then stared at her as though the name did not fit his world. At last she got it from him: Gerard had gone late the previous night, and was not looked for back.

Catherine came away with that news in her mouth like bitter herbs, and carried it, sighing, to Margaret.

She found Margaret sitting idle, as if life had lost all savour—like broth after the salt has been forgotten. The child was in her arms so tightly clasped that one might have thought she feared hands would snatch him out of her very lap. The room held its own small noises—the boy’s breathing, the faint tick of cooling cinders—but Margaret’s stillness made them loud, and made Catherine’s heart ache.

“Come to the Hoog Straet,” Catherine begged.

“What for?” Margaret answered, and the words fell without heat, only weary. “You cannot but say to yourselves, she is the cause of all.”

“Nay, nay,” said Catherine quickly, as if haste could mend what sorrow had torn. “We are not so ill-hearted; and Eli is so fond on you. You will maybe soften him.”

Margaret drew a long breath, as though air itself weighed. “Oh—if you think I can do any good, I’ll come.”

They went together, the child bundled close, and when they reached the house they found Eli in the doorway with a carpenter. Hammer and mallet were at their work, and every blow rang sharp in that stripped, unhappy place, each thud like a seal set on a sentence already passed.

They were putting up a name where Cornelis and Sybrandt’s had been.

And the name painted there, bold as a proclamation, was—Margaret Brandt’s.

Though Catherine loved Margaret, that sight went through her like a knife between rib and rib.

“The bane of one is another’s meat,” she whispered, not meaning to wound, and yet wounded herself.

“Can he make me spend the money unjustly?” Margaret replied, and her voice held no triumph. It was cold, as if spoken from a room where the fire has gone out.

“You are a good soul,” Catherine said, and then, with the sour wisdom of the weak, she added, “Ay, so best, sith he is the strongest.”

The next day Giles dropped in. He brought with him the outer world—street-dust on his shoes, a brisker step, and the livelier jangle of a man who has errands and influence. Catherine, eager as ever to patch what was torn, poured out the story, turning it as much as she could in favour of the black sheep—anathematized by their brother and thrust upon the wide world by their father.

But Giles’s prejudice ran the other way. He heard her through, then snapped out his judgment as one snaps a bone to get at the marrow.

“They’ve got off cheap,” he said bluntly. “They deserve to be hanged at Margaret’s door into the bargain.”

Then, dismissing them with contempt, he brightened at once—crowed, almost, at the thought of his favourite’s return.

“I’ll show him,” said he, “what ’tis to have a brother at court with a heart to serve a friend, and a head to point the way.”

“Bless thee, Giles,” Margaret murmured softly, as one might bless a loaf put quietly into a poor hand.

“Thou wast ever his stanch friend, dear Giles,” said little Kate; “but alack, I know not what thou canst do for him now.”

Giles was gone. The house sank again into its sad quiet, broken only by the small domestic sounds that, in happier days, would have been the music of plenty: a pot-lid set straight, a spoon rinsed, a crust folded away. Now each sound felt like a reminder of what could still be done for hunger, and what could not be done for grief.

Then the door opened softly, as if the visitor feared to disturb the air itself. A well-dressed man stood there and asked, cautious and formal, was Margaret Brandt here.

“D’ye hear, lass? You are wanted,” said Catherine briskly; in her, the gossiping nerve was indestructible, twitching even under mourning.

Margaret rose without haste. “Well, mother,” she said listlessly, “and here I am.”

There came a shuffling of feet, and a colourless, feeble old man was helped into the room, his weight borne by others. The sight of him struck the house like a draught that puts out a candle.

It was Ghysbrecht Van Swieten.

Catherine gave a shriek and flung her apron over her head, as if cloth could keep out memory. Margaret shuddered so violently her whole frame answered, and she turned her head away swiftly, as though her eyes would burn at the looking.

A thin voice, worn down as a candle-wick, came from the old man’s lips. “Good people, a dying man hath come to ask your forgiveness.”

“Come to look on your work, you mean,” sobbed Catherine, dropping the apron, the tears breaking free as if they had been dammed too long.

“There, there—she is fainting; look to her, Eli, quick.”

“Nay,” said Margaret, and though her voice was weak it was clear. “The sight of him gave me a turn, that is all. Prithee, let him say his say, and go; for he is the murderer of me and mine.”

“Alas,” said Ghysbrecht, and he seemed to gather breath with effort, like a man climbing a steep hill. “I am too feeble to say it standing—and no one biddeth me sit down.”

Eli, who had followed him in, moved uneasily—half sullen, half ashamed at his own harshness, for this was still his house and he was still a host in it.
