“Well, burgomaster,” said he, fighting the shake in his voice, “’tis not our wont to leave a visitor standing whiles we sit. But man, man—you have wrought us too much ill.”

And then the advocate rose—one who seldom spoke in vain in that family.

Little Kate.

“Father, mother,” she said, and the voice was soft, but it carried, like a clear bell heard across water. “My duty to you, but this is not well. Death squares all accounts. And see you not death in his face? I shall not live long, good friends; and his time is shorter than mine.”

At that, Eli hurried, and with his own hands set a chair. Ghysbrecht’s attendants settled him into it as tenderly as one props a failing plant.

“Go fetch the boxes,” said Ghysbrecht.

They brought in two boxes—plain enough without ostentation, yet made to hold weight—and withdrew, leaving their master alone among the people he had wronged.

Every eye was fixed upon him now, save Margaret’s, which kept its averted vigil as if looking elsewhere could undo the years.

Ghysbrecht’s fingers trembled over the fastenings. When he opened the first box, the smell of old parchment rose—dry, ink-bitten, faintly moulded, like the breath of a chest that has kept secrets too long. He drew out title-deeds, and spoke slowly, as though each word cost him.

“This land and these houses belonged to Floris Brandt, and do belong to thee of right, his granddaughter. These I did usurp for a debt long since defrayed with interest. These I now restore their rightful owner with penitent tears.”

From the second box he poured out gold—angels, bright and heavy, their edges catching light even in that dim room. The coins made a sound as they shifted: not the rich chime that makes the blood quicken in ordinary folk, but a colder clatter, like hail on a shutter—wealth falling where warmth could not follow it.

“In this other box are three hundred and forty golden angels,” said he, “being the rent and fines I have received from that land more than Floris Brandt’s debt to me. I have kept it compt, still meaning to be just one day; but Avarice withheld me—pray, good people, against temptation! I was not born dishonest: yet you see.”

“Well, to be sure!” cried Catherine, and the scandal in her voice wrestled with relief. “And you the burgomaster! Hast whipt good store of thieves in thy day. However—’tis better late than never. What, Margaret, art deaf? The good man hath brought thee back thine own. Art a rich woman. Alack, what a mountain o’ gold!”

Margaret did not turn.

“Bid him keep land and gold,” she said, and the words came out like something scraped raw, “and give me back my Gerard, that he stole from me with his treason.”

“Alas!” said Ghysbrecht, and for the first time his face seemed to hold something beyond sickness—something like fear, or sorrow, or the shadow of both. “Would I could. What I can I have done. Is it nought? It cost me a sore struggle; and I rose from my last bed to do it myself, lest some mischance should come between her and her rights.”

“Old man,” said Margaret, still turned away, “since thou, whose idol is pelf, hast done this, God and the saints will, as I hope, forgive thee. As for me, I am neither saint nor angel, but only a poor woman, whose heart thou hast broken. Speak to him, Kate—for I am like the dead.”

Kate waited a moment, as if listening—not only to the room, but to what lay behind it: the long echo of wrong, the deeper hum of pity. Then her silvery voice fell, and it did not argue so much as soothe, like music laid over a wound.

“My poor sister hath a sorrow that riches cannot heal. Give her time, Ghysbrecht; ’tis not in nature she should forgive thee all. Her boy is fatherless; and she is neither maid, wife, nor widow; and the blow fell but two days syne, that laid her heart a bleeding.”

Margaret’s answer was a single heavy sob, dragged up from somewhere deep and dark.

“Therefore,” Kate went on, “give her time! And ere thou diest, she will forgive thee all—ay, even to pleasure me, that haply shall not be long behind thee, Ghysbrecht. Meantime we, whose wounds be sore, but not so deep as hers, do pardon thee, a penitent and a dying man; and I, for one, will pray for thee from this hour. Go in peace!”

Their little oracle had spoken, and the room took it as final. Eli even offered him food and drink, as custom bids a householder do—invited him to break a manchet and take a stoup of wine, to give him heart for the journey.

But Ghysbrecht declined.

“What I have done is a cordial to me,” he said, and his voice, though weak, held a strange ease, as if a strap had been loosened from his chest. “Man seeth but a little way before him, neighbour. This land I clung so to—it was a bed of nettles to me all the time. ’Tis gone; and I feel happier and livelier like for the loss on’t.”

He called his men. They lifted him into the litter, and the soft shuffle of their feet faded down the street—an old man carried away with his repentance, leaving the sound of gold behind him.

When he was gone, Catherine hovered over the coins as if their shine could heat the room. She had never seen so much together. The angels lay in a small glittering heap like a harvest of metal, each stamped face turned up to the light, each worth a hundred dinners and a hundred nights under a whole roof.

Catherine was almost angry with Margaret for sitting apart “like an image.” She spoke of what money could do—how it could buy flour when mills were dear, and a side of bacon when winter pinched, and decent cloth for the child; how it could set a pot to boiling with good things and keep a house from going thin.

She teased and coaxed and pressed, until at last she drew Margaret toward the box.

“Better let her be, mother,” Kate said quietly. “How can she relish gold, with a heart in her bosom liker lead?”

But Catherine persisted.

Margaret looked down at her wealth with wide, wondering eyes, as if she had been shown a language she could not speak. For a breath, she only stared—at the yellow heap, at the deeds, at the neat accounting of restitution.

Then, as if something snapped inside her, she wrung her hands and cried out—not in anger, but in a piercing anguish that made the very air feel thin:

“TOO LATE! TOO LATE!”

And she shook off her leaden despondency only to fall into strong hysterics over the riches that had come too late to be warmed by the life she wanted to share them with. A little of this gold, a portion of this land, a year or two ago—when it had been as much her own as now—and Gerard would never have left her side for Italy, or any other place.

“Too late! Too late!”

News came on a thin, wind-scraped morning, when the street outside sounded like a broom dragged over cobbles and the canal carried its small, constant lapping: Margaret van Eyck was dead, and already laid in earth.

It did not arrive with ceremony—only with the plain, official voice of a messenger, and then, later, the rustle of paper: a will made the year before. After funeral charges, and certain keepsakes to Reicht Heynes, the whole of Margaret van Eyck’s property was left to her dear daughter, Margaret Brandt, with one request folded like a last stitch in a seam: keep Reicht in the house, so long as she remained unmarried.

So Margaret inherited a furnished house, and pictures and studies that would one day feed the hungers of collectors the way bread feeds a family. But there was one painting she prized above all the rest, as if it were a loaf still warm from the oven, as if it could be broken and shared.

It was a betrothal.

The man’s face held the grave, braced solemnity of a vow; the woman’s, a demure composure that seemed almost to listen. Margaret van Eyck had painted her almost wholly; the rest Jan had touched—his hand in the accessories, in the hard bright truth of a jewel, in the sheen of cloth, in the tiny, obedient reflections that make a room feel inhabited. It was finished with such patient cunning that you could nearly hear the hush of witnesses in it, the faint creak of a bench, the soft tick of a ring against a cup.

Margaret Brandt sent word to Reicht: stay in the house until she herself could bear to step across its threshold and not be met by the face and voice that used to meet her there. And—above all—take especial care of the picture “in the little cubboord”: the diptych.

Not many days after, Luke Peterson came home.

He came in as men come back from roads—boots loud on boards, skin wind-chapped, and the whole body carrying the remembered clatter of other towns’ bells. He heard, almost at once, that Gerard was a monk.

Joy cracked in him like a nut under a hammer. He hurried to Margaret as if the words burned his mouth.

“Heed, mistress,” he burst out. “If he cannot marry you, I can.”

“You?” said Margaret, staring. “Why, I have seen him.”

“But he is a friar.”

“He was my husband, and my boy’s father, long ere he was a friar. And I have seen him—I've seen him.”

Luke stood bewildered, as if she had spoken in a tongue he could not parse. Then, with the stubbornness of a man who trusts ink and seals more than a woman’s heart, he said, “I'll tell you what: I have got a cousin a lawyer. I'll go and ask him whether you are married or single.”

“Nay. I shall ask my own heart, not a lawyer. So that is your regard for me—to go making me the town talk, oh, fie!”

“That is done already without a word from me.”

“But not by such as seek my respect. And if you do it, never come nigh me again.”

“Ay,” said Luke, and the sound of his breath was like a bellows that has been pulled and let go, “you are like a dove to all the rest; but you are a hardhearted tyrant to me.”

“’Tis your own fault, dear Luke, for wooing me. That is what lets me from being as kind to you as I desire. Luke, my bonny lad, listen. I am rich now; I can make my friends happy, though not myself. Look round the street—look round the parish. There is many a quean in it fairer than I twice told, and not spoiled with weeping. Look high, and take your choice. Speak you to the lass herself, and I'll speak to the mother; they shall not say thee nay. Take my word for't.”

“I see what ye mean,” said Luke, flushing to the ears. He swallowed once, hard. “But if I can't have your liking, I will none o’ your money. I was your servant when you were poor as I; and poorer. No. If you would liever be a friar’s leman than an honest man’s wife, you are not the woman I took you for. So part we withouten malice. Seek you your comfort on yon road, where never a she did find it yet; and for me, I’ll live and die a bachelor. Good even, mistress.”

“Farewell, dear Luke; and God forgive you for saying that to me.”

After he was gone, the house seemed to listen, as if a pot left too long on the hearth still whispered from heat though the fire was out. For some days Margaret dreaded—almost as much as she desired—the coming interview with Gerard. She told herself he would hang back. So should she, had she been he. Yet he would hear he was a father; and the pull of their child would draw him, like the smell of new bread draws a hungry man along a street.

“And if so be that meeting does not kill me,” she said to herself, pressing her boy’s small warm head to her cheek, “I feel I shall be better after it than I am now.”

But day after day went by, and no word. No footfall. No shadow across her doorway.

A cold suspicion began to crawl toward her mind, slow as frost creeping along a windowpane. What if his absence were chosen? What if he had gone to his fellow monks—men with smooth rules and hard hands—and they had told him never to see her more? The convent had already shown itself as merciless to true lovers as the grave itself.

At that thought, something in her went numb, as if life had been steeped too long in winter water.

And indignation—hot, sudden—mingled with grief.

“Can he have ever loved me?” she whispered aloud once, in the kitchen where Reicht had been rubbing a pan with sand and ash until it shone. “To run from me and his boy without a word! Why, this poor Luke thinks more of me than he does.”

She was in that fevered state when Giles came roaring in, his voice filling the room the way a storm fills a sail.

“I’ve hit the clout,” he bellowed. “Our Gerard is vicar of Gouda.”

A very brief sketch of the dwarf’s rise will serve; for the thing that made him dangerous at court was the same thing that made him useful in a kitchen: a sharp eye, a sharper tongue, and hands that could do work quickly while other folk were still talking about it.

Some months before he went to court his wit had budded sudden, like yeast taking hold. He dated the change from a certain eighth of June, when he had been swinging by one hand along the week’s washing on a tight rope in the drying ground; something went crack inside his head, and—lo—his thoughts came loose as birds from a cage. At court, shrewdness and blunt speech, coupled with a voice that could drown a trumpet and a body small enough to slip away from consequences, made him a Power. Without the small body, his great voice and his impudence might have led him to the gallows.

The young Duchess of Burgundy, and Marie the heiress apparent, petted him as great ladies have petted dwarfs in all ages, feeding him sweetmeats and laughter and using him, too, as a kind of living bell to ring when their rooms grew dull. And the court poet—paid to turn common life into sugared paste—took Giles’s rough sayings and melted butter by the six-foot rule, pouring it over them until they ran long and soft and shining, fit to serve to fine mouths. A letter even went to Eli, grandly titled with the princess’s name and the dwarf’s complaint and the poet’s elaborate crawling.

But Giles’s true climax came by a mixture of mind and muscle.

The day before a great court joust, he challenged the Duke’s giant to a trial of strength. Even grave men smiled; expectation hummed like a lute string.

Giles had a lofty pole planted. At the hour, he went up it like a squirrel, and by strength of arm made his body into a right angle and held it there—stiff as a spit, steady as a pot-hook. Then he slid down so fast that the high and puissant princess squeaked and hid her face in her hands, fearing the end of her pocket-Hercules.

The giant managed perhaps ten feet, then looked ruefully up and down and climbed down sweating to argue.

“It was not the dwarf’s greater strength,” he panted, “but his smaller body.”

The company took that excuse with loud derision: in their eyes, the fact was what mattered. The dwarf mounted; the giant excused.

“Come,” said Giles, “an ye go to that, I’ll wrestle ye, my lad—if so be you will let me blindfold your eyne.”

The giant, smarting, agreed.

“Madam,” said Giles, “see you yon blind Samson? At a signal from me he shall make me a low obeisance, and unbonnet to me.”

“How may that be, being blinded?” asked a maid of honour.

“I’ll wager on Giles for one,” said the princess.

“That is my affair,” said Giles; and when wagers were laid, he stepped in and struck the giant clean in the bread-basket. The man doubled—obeisance made—and his bonnet tumbled off.

The room screamed with delight. Giles ran. The giant followed as soon as he could breathe and tear away the bandage, but Giles had prepared a little door in the wall—painted so cunningly it looked like solid stone—which would pass a dwarf and deny a giant. He flung it wide and shot through, leaving behind on the back of the trick door a posy written large:

Long limbs, big body, panting wit  
By wee and wise is bet and bit

After that, they could not ignore him.

Now he stood before Margaret, stout with triumph, and seeing she would not swallow the good news whole, he began to tell his tale.

“When the princess sent for me to her bedchamber as of custom, to keep her out of languor, I came not mirthful nor full of country dicts, as is my wont, but dull as lead.

“‘Why, what aileth thee?’ quo’ she. ‘Art sick?’

“‘At heart,’ quo’ I.

“‘Alas, he is in love,’ quo’ she; whereat five brazen hussies—maids of honour, they call them—did giggle loud.

“‘Not so mad as that,’ said I, ‘seeing what I see at court of women folk.’

“‘There, ladies,’ quo’ the princess, ‘best let him a be. ’Tis a liberal mannikin, and still giveth more than he taketh of saucy words.’

“‘In all sadness,’ quo’ she, ‘what is the matter?’

“I told her I was meditating, and what perplexed me was: other folk can now and then keep their word, but princes never.

“‘Heyday,’ says she, ‘thy shafts fly high this morn.’

“I told her, ‘Ay, for they hit the Truth.’

“She said I was as keen as keen; but it became not me to put riddles to her, nor her to answer them. ‘Stand aloof a bit, mesdames,’ said she, ‘and thou speak withouten fear.’ For she saw I was in sad earnest.

“I began to quake a bit; for mind ye, she can doff freedom and don dignity quicker than she can slip out of her dressing-gown into kirtle of state. But I made my voice soft as honey”—and here he shot Margaret a look, for he loved to be admired—“and I said, ‘Madam, one evening, a matter of five years agone, as ye sat with your mother, the Countess of Charolois, who is now in heaven, worse luck—you wi’ your lute, and she wi’ her tapestry—do ye mind there came into ye a fair youth with a letter from a painter body, one Margaret van Eyck?’

“She said she thought she did. ‘Was it not a tall youth, exceeding comely?’

“‘Ay, madam,’ said I. ‘He was my brother.’

“‘Your brother?’ says she, and did eye me all over.

“So I told her what passed between her and Gerard, and how she was for giving him a bishopric; but the good countess said, ‘Gently, Marie! he is too young;’ and with that they did both promise him a living. ‘Yet,’ said I, ‘he hath been a priest a long while, and no living. Hence my bile.’

“‘Alas!’ said she. ‘’Tis not by my good will; for all this thou hast said is sooth, and more. I do remember my dear mother said to me, “See thou to it if I be not here.”’ So she cried out, ‘Ay, dear mother, no word of thine shall ever fall to the ground.’

“I, seeing her so ripe, said quick, ‘Madam, the vicar of Gouda died last week.’ For when ye seek favours of the great, behoves ye know the very thing ye aim at.

“‘Then thy brother is vicar of Gouda,’ quo’ she, ‘so sure as I am heiress of Burgundy and the Netherlands. Nay, thank me not, good Giles, but my good mother. And I do thank thee for giving of me somewhat to do for her memory.’ And doesn’t she fall a-weeping for her mother? And doesn’t that set me off a-snivelling for my good brother that I love so dear—and to think that a poor little elf like me could yet speak in the ear of princes and make my beautiful brother vicar of Gouda.

“Eh, lass, it is a bonny place, and a bonny manse; hawthorn in every bush at spring-tide, and dog-roses and eglantine in every summer hedge. I know what the poor fool affects. Leave that to me.”

He had strutted at the beginning—parading his court triumph as if it were a roasted capon carried high through a hall. But he ended in Margaret’s arms. She could not contain herself; she caught the little body up and hugged him, and kissed him, blushing at her own abandon.

“Oh, Giles,” she cried, “I cannot keep my hands off thee, thy body it is so little, and thy heart so great. Thou art his true friend. Bless thee! bless thee! bless thee! Now we shall see him again. We have not set eyes on him since that terrible day.”

“Gramercy, but that is strange,” said Giles. “Maybe he is ashamed of having cursed those two vagabones, being our own flesh and blood—worse luck.”

“Think you that is why he hides?” said Margaret, clutching at the notion as if it were a handhold on a slippery bank.

“Ay—if he is hiding at all. However, I’ll cry him by bellman.”

“Nay, that might much offend him.”

“What care I?” cried Giles. “Is Gouda to go vicarless and the manse in nettles?”

And, to Margaret’s secret satisfaction, Giles had the new vicar cried in Rotterdam and in the neighbouring towns: the bellman’s call rolling out over markets and quays, mixing with the cries of fishwives, the clop of hooves, the slap of oars, and the tolling of church bells that shaped the day’s hours like a cook’s rhythm shapes a meal.

Giles persuaded her that in a day or two Gerard would hear, and come to his benefice.

Margaret went to look at the manse. She walked its rooms slowly, hearing how each wall returned her own breath. She imagined the place warmed: a pot set to simmer; herbs hung to dry; clean rushes underfoot; a loaf cooling; the small domestic sounds that are kinder than any sermon—the knife on board, the kettle’s first singing, the child’s patter. She thought how comfortable it might be made for him, and how dearly she should love to do it.

But the days rolled on, and Gerard came neither to Rotterdam nor to Gouda.

Giles grew mortified, as if he had promised a feast and served an empty dish. Margaret grew indignant—and then, beneath indignation, wretched with a wretchedness that made food tasteless and mornings heavy.

“Thinking me dead, he comes home,” she told herself, “and now, because I am alive, he goes back to Italy—for that is where he has gone.”

Joan advised her, as women do when they have no power but counsel, “Consult the hermit of Gouda.”

“Why, sure he is dead by this time.”

“Yon one, belike. But the cave is never long void; Gouda ne’er wants a hermit.”

Margaret would not go again on such an errand. “What can he know, shut up in a cave? Less than I, belike. Gerard hath gone back t’ Italy. He hates me for not being dead.”

Presently a man from Tergou came in with a word from Catherine: Ghysbrecht van Swieten had seen Gerard later than any one else.

On that, Margaret resolved to go to the house and goods left her, and to bring Reicht Heynes home to Rotterdam. And as might be guessed, her feet carried her first to Ghysbrecht’s.

She found him in his garden, seated in a chair with wheels, diminished by illness, yet still holding himself as a man used to rule. The garden was full of low sounds: bees in the herbs, a spade set down, a sparrow’s sharp note. He greeted her feebly but with cordiality. When she asked if it were true he had seen Gerard since the fifth of August, he said, “Gerard no more, but Friar Clement. Ay, I saw him; and blessed be the day he entered my house.”

And then, in his own words, he told her.

He told how the friar had come to Tergou with the missing deed in his bosom, meaning to make him disgorge her land by force of law. Yet finding him disposed toward penitence, the friar had turned aside from vengeance to mercy and worked upon his soul instead.

“Was not this a saint,” said the burgomaster hoarsely, “who came to right thee, but must needs save his enemy’s soul in the doing it?”

When Margaret asked if he had recognized him, he shook his head. “I ne’er suspected such a thing. ’Twas only when he had been three days with me that he revealed himself. Listen while I speak my shame and his praise.

“I said to him, ‘The land is gone home, and my stomach feels lighter; but there is another fault that clingeth to me still.’ Then told I him of the letter I had writ at request of his brethren—I whose place it was to check them. Said I, ‘Yon letter was writ to part two lovers, and the devil aiding, it hath done the foul work. Land and houses I can give back, but yon mischief is done for ever.’

“‘Nay,’ quoth he, ‘not for ever, but for life. Repent it then while thou livest.’

“‘I shall,’ said I, ‘but how can God forgive it? I would not, were I He.’

“‘Yet will He certainly forgive it,’ quoth he; ‘for He is ten times more forgiving than I am, and I forgive thee.’

“I stared at him; and then he said soft, but quavering like, ‘Ghysbrecht, look at me closer. I am Gerard, the son of Eli.’

“And I looked, and looked, and at last—lo—it was Gerard. Verily I had fallen at his feet with shame and contrition, but he would not suffer me. He said it became not mine years and his, for a particular fault. ‘I say not I forgive thee without a struggle,’ said he, ‘not being a saint. But these three days thou hast spent in penitence, I have worn under thy roof in prayer; and I do forgive thee.’ Those were his very words.”

Tears began to run down Margaret’s face as she heard it—tears hot with love and pain and pride. The old man’s voice broke as he continued.

“And even with that he bade me farewell. ‘My work here is done now,’ said he. I had not the heart to stay him; for let him forgive me ever so, the sight of me must be wormwood to him. He left me in peace, and may a dying man’s blessing wait on him, go where he will. Oh, girl, when I think of his wrongs, and thine, and how he hath avenged himself by saving this stained soul of mine—my heart is broken with remorse, and these old eyes shed tears by night and day.”

“Ghysbrecht,” said Margaret, weeping, “since he hath forgiven thee, I forgive thee too. What is done, is done; and thou hast let me know this day that which I had walked the world to hear. But oh, burgomaster, thou art an understanding man—now help a poor woman, which hath forgiven thee her misery.”

She told him all that had befallen: her sight of Gerard, her fear, her waiting, and how the living could not be held open for ever. “He bids fair to lose that,” she said, “as well as break all our hearts.”

“Call my servant,” cried the burgomaster, and for a moment vigour flared in him like a coal stirred under ash.

A table was brought, and writing tools. He dictated letters to burgomasters in all the chief towns of Holland, and one to a Prussian authority—his friend. His clerk wrote, and Margaret wrote too, her hand moving fast, ink scratching like mice in a wall. Ghysbrecht signed each with the steadiness of a man spending his last authority like coin.

“There,” said he. “The matter shall be despatched throughout Holland by trusty couriers, and as far as Basle in Switzerland; and fear not, but we will soon have the vicar of Gouda to his village.”

Margaret went home with fresh hope, and with a new shame at having accused Gerard in her heart.

“I value my wealth now,” she told Joan that night, measuring out flour for the morning loaf with hands that trembled less than they had. For money, used well, could buy messengers and time and chances. It could buy, perhaps, a path back to a man lost in the world’s wide din.

And she resolved—hard as it was—to blame his conduct no more until she should hear, from his own lips, his reason.

Not long after her return from Tergou, a fresh disaster fell—quiet at first, like a knife slid into a sheath, and then loud with consequence.

Catherine, it appeared, had secret meetings with the black sheep the very day after they were expelled. Cornelis followed her to Tergou and lived there on secret contributions; but Sybrandt chose to remain in Rotterdam.

Before Catherine left, she asked Margaret for the loan of two gold angels. “For,” said she, “all mine are spent.”

Margaret was glad to lend them, glad even to give. But the words were scarce out when she caught a look—regret and distress—crossing Catherine’s face, and she saw, in a flash, where the money would go. Still she gave it, and then shut herself up with her boy, holding him close, smelling the clean milk-breath of him and the faint sourness of flour on her own fingers, as if small, homely scents could keep sorrow from crossing the threshold.

The money was meant to last Sybrandt until his mother could contrive an excuse to visit Rotterdam again, and then bring him more from her industrious savings.

But Sybrandt, with gold in his pocket, believed it inexhaustible. Freed from restraint, he sank into the life of a sot, drinking like a man trying to drown a voice inside him. One afternoon, in a drunken frolic, he climbed onto the stable roof at the inn where he caroused, and began to walk along it—a trick he had done often sober.

Now his unsteady brain made his legs unsteady. He rolled, slid, and fell with a loud thwack onto a horizontal paling, where he hung a moment in a half-circle like a broken doll, then toppled and lay silent in the yard amid roars of laughter. When they went to pick him up he could not stand, but kept giggling as they hauled him.

So they staggered and shouted down the street with him, carrying him—at risk of another fall—to the shop in the Hoog Straet, for he had babbled out his own shame and his lodging-place to all.

As soon as he saw Margaret, he hiccupped, “Here is the doctor that cures all hurts—a bonny lass.” He said he bore her no malice, though he paid her a visit sore against his will. “Wherefore, prithee send away these drunkards, and let you and me have t’other glass, to drown all unkindness.”

Margaret went pale and then red, the way a hearth flares and dies when damp wood is thrown on. His insolence struck her like smoke in the eyes. But one of the men whispered what had happened, and she saw something streaky and strange in Sybrandt’s face that was not mere drink.

“And he cannot stand up, say you?”

“A couldn’t just now. Try, comrade! Be a man now!”

“I am a better man than thou,” roared Sybrandt. “I’ll stand up and fight ye all for a crown.”

He heaved himself upright—and instantly folded, rolling into his companion’s arms with a groan that emptied the laughter from the room like a bucket of water on fire. Then he began to curse them, declaring they had stolen his legs away.

“He can feel nothing below the waist,” said one, suddenly sobered.

“Alas, poor wretch,” said Margaret, and her voice changed, as if pity were a new language forcing itself through her mouth.

She turned on the men, grave as judgment. “Leave him here. And if you have brought him to this, go on your knees; for you have spoiled him for life. He will never walk again. His back is broken.”

Sybrandt heard. The foolish drunken look fled; anguish took its place, sharp and naked. “The curse,” he groaned. “The curse!”

Margaret and Reicht Heynes carried him carefully and laid him on the softest bed, moving him as gently as one lifts a scalded child from a pot too near the fire.

“I must do as he would do,” Margaret whispered to Reicht, her voice low. “He was kind to Ghysbrecht.”

Her opinion proved true. Sybrandt’s spine was fatally injured; he lay helpless, groaning, fed and tended by the very woman he had most wronged.

Word was sent to Tergou, and Catherine came over.

The blow shattered something in her. She accused herself as the cause, as if her own hands had pushed him from the roof.

“Oh, false wife; oh, weak mother,” she cried, “I am rightly punished for my treason to my poor Eli.”

She sat for hours by Sybrandt’s bedside rocking herself in silence, the way women rock cradles when there is nothing else to do; only now it was grief she rocked, not a child. She was never quite herself again. From that hour the first grey hairs showed in her head, thin as ash on a black pot.

Sybrandt’s cry became a constant moan for Gerard. He would whine to Margaret like a suffering hound, “Oh, sweet Margaret—oh, bonny Margaret—for our Lady’s sake find Gerard, and bid him take his curse off me. Thou art gentle, thou art good; thou wilt entreat for me, and he will refuse thee nought.”

Catherine shared the belief that Gerard could cure him; she added her entreaties, desperate as prayer whispered over a feverish child.

Margaret hardly needed urging. Ghysbrecht’s letters and agents had failed; now she employed her own, and spent money like water, buying questions, buying rides, buying ears in taverns and at ferry-steps, buying the chance that a name spoken in the right dialect might unlock another man’s memory.

Among these agents, poor Luke enrolled himself.

She met him one day looking very thin, as if love had eaten him as sickness eats. She spoke to him compassionately. At that he began to blubber, saying he was more miserable than ever; he would like to be good friends again upon almost any terms.

“Dear heart,” said Margaret sorrowfully, “why can you not say to yourself: now I am her little brother, and she is my old, married sister, worn down with care? Say so, and I will indulge thee, and pet thee, and make thee happier than a prince.”

“Well, I will,” said Luke savagely, wiping his nose on his sleeve, “sooner than keep away from you altogether. But above all, give me something to do. Perchance I may have better luck this time.”

“Get me my marriage lines,” said Margaret; and in a moment the light went out of her face, leaving it sad and set.

“That is as much as to say, get me him—for where they are, he is.”

“Not so. He may refuse to come nigh me; but certes he will not deny a poor woman, who loved him once, her lines of betrothal. How can she go without them into any honest man’s house?”

“I’ll get them you if they are in Holland,” said Luke.

“They are as like to be in Rome,” replied Margaret.

“Let us begin with Holland,” said Luke, prudent even in passion.

The slave of love took money from the soft tyrant he could not resist and wandered hither and thither, coopering and carpentering for his bread, listening for Gerard’s name in the music of marketplaces—where every town had its own cadence, its own vowels and clipped endings that carried old memory like salt carries meat.

“I can’t be worse if I find the vagabone,” he told himself, “and I may be a hantle better.”

Months rolled on.

Sybrandt improved in spirit but not in body; he became Margaret’s pensioner for life, lying like a living reproach and a living lesson under her roof. A long-expected sorrow fell upon poor Catherine, bowing her further: she lost her fine, hearty, bustling way and went no more about the house singing. Her nerves shook; she lived in dread that some terrible misfortune might fall on Cornelis too. The curse, she believed, lay on him as well as Sybrandt.

She begged Eli—sturdy but not unkind—that if she had been a faithful partner all these years he would take Cornelis back into his house again, and let her live awhile at Rotterdam.

“I have good daughters here,” she said. “But Margaret is so tender and thoughtful, and the little Gerard—he is my joy. He grows liker his father every day, and his prattle cheers my heavy heart. I do love children.”

And Eli consented, sorrowfully, as a man consents to a necessary loss.

Meanwhile the people of Gouda petitioned the duke for a vicar—a real vicar.

“Ours cometh never nigh us,” they complained. “This six months past. Our children die unchristened, and our folk unburied, except by some chance comer.”

Giles’s influence baffled this just complaint once; but a second petition was prepared. And now even Giles, for all his roaring voice and court cunning, could give Margaret little hope the present state could be held one day longer.

Yes: the hermit of Gouda had been the vicar of Gouda, and never knew it—so thick had he walled himself from tidings, so absolute his withdrawal.

When the blaze of Clement’s rage went out, it left him in a cold ash of remorse. Not the sort that pricks and passes, but the kind that makes a man afraid of his own hands, as if his very soul had slipped and only by miracle had not plunged. “Ah, good Jerome,” he cried into the dim of his cell, “how much better you knew me than I knew myself! How bitter—yet how wholesome—was your admonition!”

He did what he had been trained to do: he searched himself like a careful cook tasting a sauce after it has turned—probing for the one hidden bitterness that has soured the whole pot. He found it at once. Margaret.

“I love her then better than God,” he said, and the words were a choking mouthful. “Better than the Church. From such a love what can spring to me—or to her?” He shuddered, as at rich meat eaten on a day of fast. “Let the strong battle temptation; ’tis for the weak to flee. And who is weaker than I have shown myself? What is my penitence, my religion? A pack of cards built patiently into a fair-seeming house; and lo—one breath of earthly love, and it lies in the dust.”

So he resolved to begin again, and on a surer foundation: to leave Holland at once; to hide himself for years in some distant convent, where the very air would be strange to his desire. Time would blunt the edge of passion; and he, older and better disciplined, might come back with mastery. Meanwhile Margaret—abandoned—would marry, and love another. The anguish that thought cost him was the hard proof he trusted: it showed him where duty cut against nature. He clung to that pain as a penitent clings to nettles.

Yet even while he planned to turn his back on her without a kind word or look—lest pity undo resolve—he would not neglect her temporal welfare. The thought that he could make her comfortable for life, rich enough in the world’s goods she was not bound to despise, was like a small crust offered to a starving man: not feast, but endurance.

“Oh, what will she think of me?” he groaned. “Shall I not seem to her, of all creatures, the most heartless—inhuman? But so best. Ay, better she should hate me. Heaven is merciful, and giveth my broken heart this comfort: I can make that villain restore her own, and she shall never lose another true lover by poverty. Another? Ah me! God and the saints to mine aid!”

How he fared on that errand has been told elsewhere; but first—before all bargains and reckonings—he went by night to shrive the hermit of Gouda.

He found him dying and stayed, never quitting the low chamber until the breath had gone and the eyelids were gently closed. Then he buried him beneath the floor of the little oratory that clung to the cell like a swallow’s nest to a wall. It was the peaceful end of a stormy life. The man had been a soldier; even now, under his rough wool, he wore a steel corslet against his skin, saying that he was Christ’s soldier now as he had been Satan’s.

When Clement had shriven him and prayed by him, he in turn sought counsel of one who lay with death already in his mouth and yet spoke with a strange simplicity, as if the world had fallen silent at last. The hermit urged him to be his successor in that retreat.

“It was a hard fight,” the dying man told him, “against the world, the flesh, and the devil; and I never thoroughly baffled them till I retired into the citadel of Solitude.”

Those words, and the seal set upon them by the hermit’s pious, untroubled death, sank deep in Clement. In that age the solitary recluse was still revered: whether immured in a cell fastened to a monastery, or hidden in the harsher, freer seclusion of an independent hermitage. And Clement knew more of hermits than most divines so young. At Tergou he had read their lives; at Rome he had devoured manuscripts; he had questioned mendicant friars—those great carriers of local memory before print—until names and places clung in his mind like well-worn prayers.

Jerome himself had once been anchorite on the heights of Camaldoli, where the Thebaid had been revived for centuries; and Jerome—cold on many themes—warmed into a grim delight on this. He had told Clement of nobles and famous warriors who ended as hermits; of bishops and archbishops who passed from the see to the cell and sometimes back again; of an Archbishop of Ravenna among the former, and Pope Victor the Ninth among the latter. He had relished the austerities: how each solitary hunted out his own weakest part and set upon it without pity until weakness was turned, if not to strength, then at least to obedience. He had described the sevenfold rhythm of their days: matins, prime, tierce, sexte, nones, vespers, compline—no excuse of weather, no bargaining with the body. In thunder and snow, in moonlight and torchlight, they would converge from scattered caves to the convent church, and the very soundscape of that holy mountain was their discipline: wind in firs, bell-stroke, chant, and the crunch of sandals on rock.

Under Clement’s eager questioning, Jerome had even drawn the faces of men he had prayed beside—Moncata, Duke of Moncata and Cardova, who fled youth’s pomp and pleasure; Father John Baptist of Novara, once leader of armies and now private soldier of Christ; Cornelius, Samuel, Sylvanus. Of Sylvanus he told, with relish, how he met the great Duchess de’ Medici at the first wooden cross when at last she had wrung permission to visit Camaldoli; how he rebuked her, warned her, and persuaded her to retreat, though she stood surrounded by courtiers and captains—so that a whole glittering troop withdrew before one hoary hermit.

At Basle Clement had gathered more—German and English anchorites—and had even begun, as a scholar hoards spices, a “Catena Eremitarum” from the year of our Lord 250, when Paul of Thebes commenced his ninety years’ solitude, down to 1470. He called them Angelorum amici et animalium—Friends of Angels and Animals. So though he had never then thought to become one, the path had been laid, stone by stone, in his mind.

And now the dying hermit of Gouda blessed solitude as a citadel where a man might win at last; and invited Clement to take up, as it were, the breastplate of faith that fell from his own shrunken body. Clement felt an inward certainty: Heaven had led his foot to this place for that end. It struck him, too, as no small coincidence that his patron, St. Bavon, was himself a hermit—an austere one, a cuirassier of the solitary cell.

So, once reconciled with Ghysbrecht Van Swieten, Clement went eagerly to the hermit’s abode, praying it had not been taken in these three days. Such dens rarely stood long without a tenant.

He found the rude stone door ajar. His heart sank—then he entered softly.

The cell was empty, and its poor furnishings lay as if the dead man’s hands had only just left them: a great ivory crucifix; pens and ink; seeds; and, memento mori, a skull. A hair cilice and another of bristles; a well-worn sheepskin pelisse and hood; hammer, chisel, and psaltery. Men and women had passed that way, but none had dared intrude, far less steal. Faith and simplicity had guarded that keyless door more securely than the laity guarded their houses with iron and bars, and the rich their halls with moat, bastion, chevaux-de-frise, and portcullis—like modern gaols dressed up as homes.

No sooner was Clement fairly within than there came a loud flap and a rush of feathers: a great brown owl sprang from a corner and whirled out of the window, beating the air so that it drove cold on his face. He started and shuddered. Was this owl a warning—something diabolical, come to bar him from his soul’s good? Then he checked himself: perhaps it was a good spirit, set there to keep the cell; perhaps—so the fancy came, half tender and half fearful—it was the hermit himself, departing. At last he smiled bitterly at his own imagination and concluded it was merely an owl. He resolved to make friends with it, if it returned.

He knelt and inaugurated his new life with prayer.

He had two battles now: not only to quell an earthly passion whose strength had made him tremble for eternity, but to do penance for his besetting sin—Ire—which had betrayed him into cursing his own brethren. He looked about him. The cell was roomy; it had comforts: stone walls that kept out some weather, a narrow place to sleep, tools, a window’s light. In his mind rose other hermitages: the eremus in eremo where holy Jerome had wrestled with sickness and despair; the thorny niche where the boy Benedict hid, living three years on what monk Romanus could spare, and dividing even that mouthful with a raven; the hollow tree of St. Bavon; the cavern at Fribourg where a nameless saint lived with eyes chilled by perpetual gloom and ears stunned by an eternal waterfall; the pillar where Simeon Stylites endured forty-five years; the stone box of St. Dunstan where he could scarce sit, stand, or lie; the living tombs sealed with lead; the damp dungeon of St. Alred. Against those places, this retreat seemed gentle.

“This sweet retreat is for safety of the soul,” he said to himself. “But what for penance? Jesu aid me against faults to come; and for the fault I rue—face of man I will not see for a twelvemonth and a day.”

There were precedents even for that severity. The original hermit of this cell had plainly been under the same vow: hence the two apertures through which he might be spoken to and might reply without being seen.

In other respects Clement adopted the common rule. He divided his day by the seven offices, refusing to be ruled by mere light and dark—the petty accidents of creation—when his work was to pray to the Creator. He learned the psalter by heart, so that the words might rise in him even when his own heart was numb; and in the intervals of devotion, not occupied by broken slumbers, he laboured with his hands. No command was older among hermits than this: work, lest idleness breed devils.

Here, however, his vow embarrassed him. How could he work for his neighbours without being seen? A hermit might labour for himself when subsistence required it, but Clement’s modest needs were supplied by the villagers: bread, herbs, water. He could not openly take up some craft and sell it without breaking his seclusion.

So he became a thief of charity. On moonlit nights—when the village slept and the only witnesses were the slow clouds and the steady talk of crickets—he stole out and dug some poor man’s garden on the outskirts. The earth then had a smell like wet rye-meal; the spade’s bite made a dull sound that seemed, in the hush, as loud as a bell. He made baskets by day and, when night covered him, dropped them silently at humble doors like loaves left for a hungry family. And since he could do nothing for the bodies of those who passed his cell in daylight, he went out in the dead of night with hammer and chisel and carved sentences on the sandstone rocks that bordered the road.

“Who knows?” he said. “Often a chance shaft strikes home.”

He chose his words carefully, as a food-historian chooses the right old term for an herb that has lost its name in the mouths of the young. He would comfort the poor and bereaved with holy sentences in their native tongue; for, said he, “well—’tis clavis ad corda plebis: the key to the people’s hearts.” Latin might thunder in churches, but Dutch—plain, homely, salted with hearth-speech—entered where grief lived and where hunger lodged. He remembered, too, what the learned Colonna had told him of written mountains in the East, where kings inscribed victories to make a blood-bubble last as long as stone.

“What,” thought Clement, “are these Eastern monarchs so wise as to engrave their warlike glory upon the rock; and shall I leave the rocks about me silent on the King of Glory, at whose word they were, and at whose breath they shall be dust? Nay. These stones shall speak to weary wayfarers of eternal peace, and of the Lamb, whose frail and afflicted servant worketh them among.”

At that time the inspired words that have since consoled the poor for centuries were not yet printed in Dutch. So to those who could not read Latin, Clement’s carved sayings from the evangelists came like fresh oracles, like dew on parched flowers. A sentence would meet a man as unexpectedly as the smell of bread from an unseen oven—sudden comfort where none had been hoped for. More than one heavy-laden traveller went away softly singing.

These “oracles” that seemed to spring up around the hermitage as if by magic; his prudent answers, given through a window to those who sought ghostly counsel; and above all his invisibility—these soon won him a prodigious reputation.

It was not diminished by the medical advice the villagers sometimes extorted from him, sore against his will, by tears and entreaties; for if the sick recovered, all credit went to the holy hermit; if they died, all blame was laid on the devil. He himself thought he killed nobody, because his remedies were “womanish and weak”—sage and wormwood, sion, hyssop, borage, spikenard, dog’s-tongue, our Lady’s mantle, feverfew, and Faith; all in small quantities except the last. He would have the herbs gathered in their proper season, clean and unbruised, dried where smoke did not taint them, and infused rather than boiled to death; and he insisted the spoon be washed and the water not stinking—small household exactitudes that seemed to him part of reverence.

His abstinence, too, was taken for sure sign of sanctity. The eggs and milk they brought him at first he refused with horror. The hermit’s rule was bread, or herbs, and water. Eggs—birds in disguise; for when the bird dieth, the egg rotteth. Milk—little better than white blood. When they brought too much bread, he refused it; then they would press it on him.

“Nay, holy father,” they begged, “give the overplus to the poor.”

“You who go among the poor can do that better,” he answered. “Is bread a thing to fling haphazard from an hermit’s window?”

And to those who persisted after that, he spoke sharply, for he would not let their piety become vanity: “To live on charity, yet play Sir Bountiful, is to lie with the right hand. Giving another’s to the poor, I should beguile them of their thanks and cheat thee the true giver. Thus do thieves, whose boast it is they bleed the rich into the lap of the poor. Occasio avaritiae nomen pauperum.”

That Latin—like a pinch of bitter herb—ended the debate. So did a line of Virgil, when he chose to fling it like a stone. The villagers, awed by words they could not fully taste, yet felt their authority as one feels strong vinegar in the nose.

All this reputation was external. Within the cell lived a man who held the hermit of Gouda cheap as dirt.

“Ah!” he said to himself, with a sort of savage honesty, “I cannot deceive myself; I cannot deceive God’s animals. See the little birds, how coy they be. I feed and feed them, and long for their friendship; yet will they never come within, nor take my hand by lighting on’t. For why? No Paul, no Benedict, no Hugh of Lincoln, no Columba, no Guthlac bides in this cell. Hunted doe flieth not hither, for here is no Fructuosus, nor Aventine, nor Albert of Suabia; nor e’en a pretty squirrel cometh from the wood hard by for the acorns I have hoarded; for here abideth no Columban. The very owl that was here hath fled. They are not to be deceived; I have a Pope’s word for that; Heaven rest his soul.”

He had one advantage over Margaret—over the image of her he was determined to unmake. He had once suffered the pang of bereavement and survived it, and the mind cannot quite repeat such anguish. He had built, in time, a habit of looking on her as dead. That habit had been struck and splintered in the churchyard of St. Laurens like a wall hit by lightning; yet enough stones remained to found it again: dead to him.

By a severe subdivision of time and thoughts—by prayers that came at appointed hours like bells, by labour that made the body sweat and the hands ache—he did, in about three months, succeed in benumbing the earthly half of his heart. A dim peace began, very slowly, to creep back.

Then, within a day or two of that first return of quiet, a horror descended upon his mind—a despondency so black that language, made for barter and blessing, will not paint it. Voices seemed to whisper, close to his ear, as if in the very skin: “Kill thyself! kill! kill! kill!” And he longed to obey, because life became intolerable, like stale bread in a mouth that has lost its thirst.

He wrestled with the enemy with prayers and tears. He begged God only to vary the temptation.

“Oh, let mine enemy have power to scourge me with red-hot whips,” he cried, “to tear me leagues and leagues over rugged places by the hair of my head, as he hath served many a holy hermit that yet baffled him at last; to fly on me like a raging lion; to gnaw me with a serpent’s fangs—any pain, any terror, but this horrible gloom of the soul that shuts me from all light of Thee and of the saints.”

And then a freezing thought crossed him—cold as water drawn from a deep well in winter. What if the triumphs of darkness over Christian souls in desert places had been suppressed, and only the defeats recorded? Dark hints in antiquity—phrases he had read long ago as one reads a marginal note—now began to grin at him with terrible meaning.

“THEY WANDERED IN THE DESERT AND PERISHED BY SERPENTS,” said an ancient father of hermits of those who went into solitude “and were seen no more.”

And another, later, wrote: Vertuntur ad melancholiam—“they turn to gloomy madness.”

Were not these two sayings one and the same? The ancient fathers did not mourn the death of the body; so those “perished” were perished souls, and the “serpents” were diabolical thoughts—the natural brood of too much silence, when the ear, starved of wholesome human sound, begins to magnify every inward whisper until it roars. Clement, who had loved the ordered music of liturgy and the speech of men in their own tongue, found now that solitude could be not a sanctuary but a cavern where one’s own breath becomes an enemy.

St. Jerome went into the desert with three companions: one fled in the first year, two died—how? The chronicler made no wonder of it. What if that was the true proportion in every age: many lost for one gigantic soul with an iron body that survived?

The darkened recluse cast despairing eyes over the Christian arsenal, hunting for weapons as a starving man hunts crumbs. The greatest was prayer. Alas, it was part of his malady that he could not pray with true fervour. The very mechanical severity of his offices—the rule he had kept so strictly—had checked rather than fostered that inward spring. He prayed louder than ever, but the heart hung back, cold and heavy, and let the words go up alone.

“Poor wingless prayers,” he cried, “you will not get half-way to heaven.”

A fiend of this complexion had been driven out of King Saul by music. Clement took up the hermit’s psaltery and, with much trouble, mended the strings and tuned it, listening to each note as one listens to a kettle’s first tremor before it sings. But he could not play. His soul was so out of tune that the sounds jarred on it and made him almost mad.

“Ah, wretched me!” he cried. “Saul had a saint to play to him. He was not alone with the spirits of darkness; but here is no sweet bard of Israel to play to me. I—lonely, with crushed heart, on which a black fiend sitteth mountain-high—must make the music to uplift that heart to heaven. It may not be.”

And he fell upon the earth, weeping, tearing his hair.

Vertebatur ad melancholiam.

One day—after many such days—he lay upon his rude pallet and let the groans go out of him as if they were his only breath. No prayer rose with them, no psalm kept time, no hope leaned on them. The cave was a mouth of black stone that seemed to swallow all sound and give back only his own misery, thickened and made dull.

Then, sudden as a spark struck from flint, a thought came clean through the smoke of his mind: what he had done for the poor and the wayfarer, he would do for himself. He had fed other men’s bodies to keep their souls from fainting; he would feed his own soul to keep it from dying.

He reached, not for a sword—he had none—but for the humbler iron that honest labour wields: his chisel. His hand closed on it as if on a handle of life. He set its edge against the soft stone of his wall and began to work with a fury that was half craft and half combat. He drew no guiding lines; he did not pause to measure; he went straight to memory, to the storehouse of words that had once been the common bread of his days, and he drove them into the stone as if engraving them could nail them inside his heart.

He begged from any who came near—shepherds, women with baskets, children shy as hares—for candle-ends and rancid oil. “Anything is good enough for me,” he would say, with the plain humility of a man who has ceased to bargain with comfort, “if ’twill but burn.” By night the little cell shone through its window and the gaping seams of the door like a smithy at work; and the rustics, hearing the steady chip and seeing that unnatural glow, crossed themselves and whispered of devilry. Yet within, the only magic was the old Church’s spell of syllables, cut into rock with aching wrists while the body starved and the mind wrestled.

Kyrie Eleison. Christe Eleison. Sursum Corda. Deus Refugium nostrum et virtus. Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere mihi. Sancta Trinitas unus Deus, miserere nobis. Ab infestationibus Daemonum, a ventura ira, a damnatione perpetua. Libera nos Domine. And the long collect—Deus, qui miro ordine Angelorum ministeria—spilled from his recollection as naturally as water from a jar once filled.

Beneath the great crucifix, fixed against the stone like a judgment and a refuge, he graved Augustine’s counsel, word by word, as one sets loaves in an oven, trusting the heat will do what hands cannot: O anima Christiana, respice vulnera patientis… Look, Christian soul, on the wounds, on the blood, on the price; weigh it in the balance of the mind until He is nailed to the heart who for thee was nailed to the cross—so that, remembering Christ’s Passion, nothing on earth remains too hard to bear with a level spirit.

The sweet sentences, set up about him like a fence against darkness, soothed him—little, very little—but the labour and watching ground him down. One morning, his limbs gave way as if the bones had been unpegged; he fell full length and sleep poured over him, deep and heavy, for hours.

When he woke, it was quietly; the first thing that met him was not fear, but a small sound, a thin cheep, like a needle of music pricking through wool. He opened his eyes.

Upon his breviary, laid on a low stool near his feet, perched a robin redbreast. The bird fluffed its feathers with one brisk pull, smoothed them with the next, cocked its head this way and that in an elaborate pretence of slyness, and looked as if it had invented caution and was proud of it.

Clement held his breath. He narrowed his eyes lest even the shine of them should startle this bright scrap of life away. The robin dropped to the floor and performed its little comedy of craft, then—pim, pim, pim—hopped in three stiff jerks like a ball of worsted dancing on wires, and landed upon the hermit’s bare foot.

He shut his eyes altogether then; he was content to feel, scarcely feel, the minute claw—feel it only because he knew it was there. After a moment the busybody flicked its wings and was back upon the breviary.

Clement, who had fed many mouths in better days and knew how gentleness must be measured, resolved to offer this guest a crumb without frightening it. A piece of bread lay within reach. To reach it was a whole task: he crept his hand towards it inch by inch until his fingers touched the crust, and then he dared not move his arm. He pinched a morsel and shot it with thumb and finger as boys shoot marbles, keeping his hand as still as a stone.

The robin saw it fall near, did its pantomime of sagacity, and would not move. Another crumb followed, then another. At last the bird darted down, snatched one, and, not trusting the mystery, fled with it to a safer height—namely, the hermit’s knee. So the game went on, a quiet traffic between hunger and trust, until a larger fragment than usual rolled out and lay like a prize.

The robin pounced, lifted it, and fled so swiftly into the world that the cave rang with the beat of buffeted air.

“Now bless thee, sweet bird,” sighed the stricken solitary. “Thy wings are music, and thou, a feathered ray, camedst to light my darkened soul.”

The sound of that flight—so small, so certain—tuned him like a string. He turned back to his orisons and then to his tools with a morsel of courage, and this was the day’s carving:

Veni, Creator Spiritus,
Mentes tuorum visita,
Imple superna gratia
Quae tu creasti pectora…
and so onward, the prayer shaped like a chant, the chant like a hearth-fire’s steady breathing.

Thus the days rolled. The weather sharpened; the cold came with clear teeth. Yet, strangely, Clement’s heart warmed. Despondency, that had come upon him like a cloud that blots out all landmarks, began to thin. It had not been argued away; it was outlived. One morning he perceived it was gone, as a man notices the fever is broken because the room looks itself again.

Then all was reversed. The cell that had been a den seemed lit from within. His work pleased him; his prayers had unction; his psalms became praise instead of pleading. Birds—hosts of them—followed their crimson leader and, fleeing the snow and a parish full of Cains, made friends one by one with Abel, and then fast friends. The cave’s soundscape, once mere echo and groan, filled with the scratch of claws on stone, with quick chirrs and feather-rustlings—small domestic noises that were as homely as a pot simmering in a poor cottage, and as wholesome.

One keen frosty night, as he sang to his psaltery, the hollow cave flung back the holy psalmody upon the dark as if the stone itself were a great instrument’s shell. Then he heard, outside, a long clear whine—not unmelodious. It rose and fell, grew louder and less in tune. He peeped through the chinks of his rude door and saw a great red wolf sitting and moaning with its nose high in the air, as though the sky were a bowl and it drank the cold.

Clement’s heart leaped. “My sins are going,” he cried, “and the creatures of God are owning me, one after another.” In a burst of fervour he struck up: “Praise Him, all ye creatures of His! Let everything that hath breath praise the Lord.” And at intervals, between his lines, the wolf bayed—answering, it seemed, in the only liturgy it knew.

After this, he believed himself drawing nearer to that celestial intercourse which saints had promised and hermits sought. His dreams grew vivid, not like common dreams, but like visions. Bright figures, clad in woven snow, leaned over him; eyes lovelier than any antelope’s he had once seen at Rome looked down; broad wings hued like a rainbow fanned him; gentle voices bade him speed and endure. Sleep, which had been an abyss, became a chapel.

But he had not long enjoyed this felicity when the dreams changed, and their taste went strange.

He wandered again with Fra Colonna among the relics of antique nations. The friar was lame now and leaned upon a staff; and when he waved that staff over ruins—Egyptian, Greek, or Roman—temples and palaces rose at once from their wrecks like breath from warmed glass, complete and crowded with the famous dead. The air filled with music: songsters who seemed to eclipse Apollo himself poured out their lays; women, godlike and draped like Minerva, moved in voluptuous yet effortless dances through marble courts. Sculptors carved while pupils watched; and forms of supernatural beauty sprang from Parian marble in the time it takes to knead a loaf and set it near the coals. Philosophers, grave and subtle, conversed while youth listened reverently. It was like a whole world restored—and still, underneath that splendour, an unease lay coiled in Clement’s mind.

This is a prologue, he thought. There is something behind. Something that means me no good.

One night, when the wizard Colonna surpassed himself, he pointed with his stick, and many great ancient cities were swallowed up. They stood upon a vast sandy plain beneath a huge crimson sun sinking toward rest. Palm-trees stood in black shapes; and everywhere on the sand were low bulrush hives, scarcely a man’s height, dotted to the horizon.

“These are the anchorites of the Theban desert,” said Colonna calmly—“followers not of Christ and His apostles and the great fathers, but of the Greek pupils of the Egyptian pupils of the Brachmans and Gymnosophists.”

Clement burned to run and embrace those lonely men, to tell them his trouble and ask their counsel. Yet he found his feet held fast, tied by something he could not see. The crimson sun sank; dusk thickened; the hives faded. Colonna’s figure grew shadowy and shapeless, but his eyes shone tenfold brighter; and that thing—all eyes—spoke: “Nay, let them be. A pack of fools; I see how dismal it all is.”

Then, with sudden sprightliness: “But I hear one of them has a manuscript of Petronius, on papyrus. I go to buy it. Farewell for ever—for ever—for ever.”

It became pitch dark; and behind Clement there came a light, gentle as a hand laid warm upon the shoulder—a glorious roseate light that both brightened and heated. It loosened his feet. He turned.

There stood Margaret Brandt, her face irradiated with sunshine, her hair glittering like a saint’s gloriola. She blushed and smiled, and her look was tenderness itself, unbearable in its truth.

“Gerard,” she murmured, “be whose thou wilt by day, but at night be mine.”

The very shock of her presence awakened him. He lay trembling from head to foot, as if the dream had struck a tuning-fork in his nerves and left it humming.

Awake, he could pray, praise, and worship; he could marshal his thoughts and drive them where he willed. But let him close his eyes, and Margaret—or Satan wearing her likeness—came to beset him, a seeming angel of light. He might dream a thousand things, as wide apart as poles, yet before waking her image would blaze and extinguish all else in a moment, as the sun makes lesser stars vanish. She came with two beauties never joined in heaven: an angel’s radiance and a woman’s blush. Angels cannot blush; therefore he knew it was a fiend.

The discovery alarmed him; yet it did not astonish him as much as the artifice’s fineness. From Anthony to Nicholas of the Rock, what hermit had not been thus assaulted? Sometimes by gross voluptuousness, sometimes by tender phantoms warm and womanly without and demoniac within. The records of such wars were part of his meat and drink. With those records came also the victories, and the weapons.

Domandum est Corpus. The body must be tamed. For twelve hundred years that cry had rung through the caves and deserts. They had called even the heart’s earthly affections “body,” and crushed it through mortified flesh. Clement told himself the enemy had only withdrawn to strike more surely; had given him days of purity and joy to lull him, and now poured soft blandishments over the soul that had stood the buffeting of black wings.

So he set himself to tame the body. He shortened sleep, lengthened prayer, and pressed temperance into abstinence. Hitherto he had eaten only at sunset; now he ate but once in forty-eight hours, and drank a little water daily.

The visions grew more distinct.

Then he flew to the anchorites’ famous antidote, their grand febrifuge: cold water. A stream ran by his cell, rising not far away at a holy well. He found its deepest reach and cleared the bottom of stones, making a hole where he could stand with water to his chin. Fortified by the examples he had read till they seemed like family lore, he sprang from his rude bed upon the next diabolical assault and plunged in.

The icy water stole his breath. It made him gasp, almost shriek; it froze his marrow. “I shall die,” he cried through chattering teeth, “I shall die; but better this than fire eternal.”

Next day he was so stiff he could scarcely move. Every joint seemed a hinge ground with sand; he was one ache from crown to heel. Even in sleep he felt his bones like so many raging teeth—until the phantom he dreaded came, gave one pitying smile, and all pain was gone, as if her presence were a balm.

Then, fearing that to go again into the icy stream—enfeebled by fasting as he was—might carry the guilt of suicide, he scourged himself till blood ran; and he lay down smarting. When exhaustion dulled the sting to a throbbing, the present slipped away and the past came smiling back.

He sat with Margaret at the duke’s feast; minstrels played so divinely that their notes seemed to gild the air; purple fountains gushed. Youth and love reigned in every heart and perfumed the very breath. Then the scene shifted, and they stood at the altar together, man and wife. No interruption came this time. They wandered hand in hand, and told each other their horrible dreams. He confessed he had dreamed she was dead and he a monk—and the dream had been so vivid, so crowded with particulars, that only his waking sight could now persuade him it had been false, and that they were truly one.

Once that keynote was struck, every tune ran upon it. Awake he was Clement the hermit, risen from visions as dangerous as they were sweet; asleep he was Gerard Eliassoen, happy husband of the loveliest, best, and truest girl in Holland—happier still for having lately been tormented by hideous dreams in which he had lost her.

Austerity had reduced him nearly to a skeleton; yet still, on those aching bones, flesh seemed unsubdued, quivering with earthly passion—or why should ill spirits have such power? His fear was confirmed when one day he caught himself sinking toward sleep with a shameful complacency, because now Margaret would come and he should feel no more pain; the unreal would be real, and the real unreal, for an hour.

He sprang up with a cry of dismay. Stripping to the skin, he climbed to the brambles above his cave and flung himself upon them, rolling and writhing. The thorns bit like hooked knives. He came back a mass of gore and lay moaning for hours, until sheer exhaustion dropped him into deep, dreamless sleep.

He woke to bodily pain and mental exultation. He had broken the fatal spell. Another day passed, then another; her image molested him no more.

Yet he caught himself sighing at his victory.

The birds grew tamer and tamer. They perched upon his hand. Two of them even let him gild their little claws, holding still with the solemn patience of creatures that live by light and seed and do not invent torment. Eating but once in two days, he had more crumbs to give them; and the soft scratch of their feet on his palm was like a small domestic comfort, the way a familiar ladle’s tap against a pot can steady a weary mind.

His tranquillity did not last.

A woman’s voice came from outside and, in a very few words, told him his own story—told it as if it were already a tale traded in the market—and asked him where Gerard was to be found. The sound struck him harder than a blow, because it carried the world’s language into his hermitage and named him in the tongue of men.

So astonished was he that instinct, not reason, answered. “Pray for the soul of Gerard the son of Eli,” he said—meaning that Gerard was dead to the world. Then he sat, staring at stone, while his heart thumped like a mallet on wood.

When the woman was gone, he fought an inward battle and determined to risk being seen; he peeped out after her to discover who she could be. But he took so many precautions, and she ran so quickly back to her friend, that when at last he dared look, the road was empty and harmless as if no human voice had ever travelled it.

“Satan!” said he directly.

That night the visions returned with a vengeance. Earthly love and happiness flooded him so vividly he could count every auburn hair on Margaret’s head, see the very pupils of her eyes as though she were before him in daylight. Despair rose again, and with it a new fear of his own cell.

“I must leave this country,” he whispered. “Here I am bound fast in memory’s chain.” And then, with sudden loathing: “A breath from hell hath infected it, and robbed even these holy words of their virtue.”

Unconsciously imitating Jerome in his own warfare with hallucinations, he took his warmest covering out into the wood hard by and flung himself under a tree—torn, wrinkled, a leather bag of bones that not long ago might have served a sculptor for Apollo. Whether his imagination’s fever intermitted—since all things, they say, intermit—or whether the change of place broke some subtle link, he did not know; but his sleep was dreamless.

He woke nearly frozen, yet warm with joy within. “I shall yet be a true hermit, Dei gratia,” he said.

Next day some good soul left on his little platform a new lamb’s-wool pelisse and cape, warm, soft, ample. For a moment he misgave at its delicious softness—so like an invitation to the body. Then the scruple passed. It was the right skin, a token that Heaven approved his present course. When he came in from his short rest, it put warmth back into his bones as broth restores a fainting man: not luxurious, but sustaining.

Now he would see victory before him if he could but live to it; then again he would tell himself, trembling, “’Tis but another lull. Be on thy guard, Clement.” The thought kept his nerves in continual awe. He lived like a soldier within the enemy’s lines, listening to every sound as if sound itself might betray him.

One night—a beautiful, clear, frosty night—he returned to his cell after a short rest in the wood. The stars were wonderful. Heaven seemed a thousand times larger, and brighter too, than earth; and to look with a thousand eyes instead of one.

“Oh, wonderful,” he cried, “that there should be men who do crimes by night; and others scarce less mad, who live for this little world, and not for that great and glorious one, which nightly—if custom have not blinded—reveals its glowing glories. Thank God I am a hermit.”

In this mood he came to the door of his cave and paused. It was closed.

“Why, methought I left it open,” said he. “The wind? There is not a breath of wind. What means this?”

He laid his hand on the rugged door. Through one great chink—since the door in places was far smaller than the hole it pretended to stop—he saw his little oil wick burning exactly where he had left it.

“How is it with me,” he sighed, “when I start and tremble at nothing? Either I did shut it, or the fiend hath shut it after me to disturb my happy soul. Retro Sathanas!”

He entered rapidly and set about, with nervous haste, to light one of his largest tapers. As he kindled it, a soft sigh sounded within the cave.

He started and dropped the candle at the very instant it caught; it went out. He stooped, seized it, and lighted it again, listening so hard he seemed to listen with his skin. When it burned, he shaded it with his hand and threw the small light about the cell.

In the farthest corner the outline of the wall was broken.

He took a step toward it, his heart beating. Another step—his knees knocking together.

It was the figure of a woman.

IT WAS MARGARET BRANDT.

Her bearing would have moved any eyes not clogged with a tale already told. She stood as a creature startled in its own nest: breast fluttering like a trapped linnet, red and white chasing one another across her cheeks, one palm braced against the stone as though the wall alone could keep her from falling. Yet the look she lifted—those purple eyes, brimmed with love and reverent fear and the soft, domestic remembering of a thousand small kindnesses—was the strangest thing that had entered that cave of penance.

“Aha!” cried the hermit, and the cry rang thin and sharp in the hollow. “Thou art come at last in flesh and blood; come as thou camest to holy Anthony. But I am ware of thee. I am armed.”

He snatched up his little crucifix and thrust it towards her; in the other hand the candle shook so that the flame fretted and licked at the air. Both hands trembled—hunger, vigil, and that long, starved solitude that makes a sound of every breath. “Exorcizo te.”

“Ah, no!” Her hands flew up, two pretty, pleading palms, as if to ward off a blow. “Alas, work me no ill! It is Margaret.”

“Liar!” he shouted. The word cracked like dry wood. “Margaret was fair, but not so supernatural fair as thou. Thou didst shrink at that sacred name, thou subtle hypocrite. In Nomine Dei exorcizo vos.”

“Ah, Jesu!” Margaret gasped, the terror in her voice not feigned, but born of the old dread that still lived in stone and candle-smoke. “Curse me not! I will go home. I thought I might come. For very manhood be-Latin me not! Oh, Gerard—is it thus you and I meet after all, after all?”

She crouched as if the floor would take her into it, sobbing with that mingled fear of heaven and fear of man that the age breeds in women. He—so soaked in dread of Satan that every tenderness had begun to look like a snare—might still have doubted whether Nature itself could be an art of Hell. But her spontaneous cry of his name, the very sound of it as she had once spoken it at a hearth, broke the phantom as a hand breaks a cobweb. His face changed; the glare went out like a wick pinched.

He gave a cry that was half repentance, half pain, and bent to lift her. Yet fasts had made him weak, and emotion weaker still; he shook above her and could not draw her up.

“What,” he panted, “is it thou? And have I met thee with hard words? Alas!”

For a little while neither could speak. Their breaths were loud in the cave; outside, the small stream kept its cold whispering, and the night insects made their thin, tireless music, as if the world, untroubled, continued its kitchen-work of grinding and pouring.

“I heed it not much,” Margaret said at last, brave against her tears. “You took me for another—for a devil; oh! oh! oh!”

“Forgive me, sweet soul!” His voice broke upon the words. When he found speech again, it came in fragments. “I have been much beset by the evil one since I came here.”

Margaret shuddered and glanced round at the dank walls, the straw, the soot on stone. Even the air smelled of old tallow and wet earth—no clean bread-smell, no wood-smoke seasoned with herbs. “Like enow. Then, oh, take my hand and let me lead thee from this foul place.”

He stared at her as if she had offered him a knife by the handle. “What, desert my cell and go into the world again? Is it for that thou hast come to me?” There was sadness in it, and reproach.

“Ay, Gerard. I am come to take thee to thy pretty vicarage. Art vicar of Gouda, thanks to Heaven and thy good brother Giles; and mother and I have made it so neat for thee.” Her words hurried now, as if she could warm him by naming warmth. “’Tis well enow in winter, I promise thee. But bide a bit till the hawthorn bloom, and anon thy walls put on their kirtle of brave roses, and sweet woodbine. Have we forgotten thee, and the foolish things thou lovest? And, dear Gerard, thy mother is waiting; and ’tis late for her to be out of her bed. Prithee, prithee, come! And the moment we are out of this foul hole I’ll show thee a treasure thou hast gotten and knowest nought on’t—or sure hadst never fled from us so.”

She stopped short, stricken by the look that came into his face. He had drawn himself up into a knot of fear, his eyes wide, his mouth tense, suspicion and longing wrestling like two dogs in one leash.

“Alas! what is to do?” she cried. “What have I ignorantly said, to be regarded thus?”

“Unhappy girl,” he said solemnly, though his whole body quivered, “would you have me risk my soul and yours for a miserable vicarage and the flowers that grow on it? But this is not thy doing: the bowelless fiend sends thee, poor simple girl, to me with this bait. But, oh cunning fiend, I will unmask thee even to this thine instrument, and she shall see thee, and abhor thee as I do. Margaret, my lost love—why am I here? Because I love thee.”

“Oh! no, Gerard, you love me not—or you would not have hidden from me; there was no need.”

“Let there be no deceit between us twain that have loved so true; and after this night shall meet no more on earth.”

“Now God forbid!” she cried.

“I love thee, and thou hast not forgotten me—or thou hadst married ere this, and hadst not been the one to find me, buried here from sight of man.” He spoke as if each sentence cost him blood. “I am a priest, a monk. What but folly or sin can come of you and me living neighbours, and feeding a passion innocent once, but now—so Heaven wills it—impious and unholy?
