No. Though my heart break I must be firm. ’Tis I that am the man; ’tis I that am the priest. You and I must meet no more, till I am schooled by solitude, and thou art wedded to another.”

“I consent to my doom but not to thine. I would ten times liever die; yet I will marry—ay, wed misery itself—sooner than let thee lie in this foul dismal place, with yon sweet manse awaiting for thee.”

At each word she spoke, two things stood clearer to him than the candle’s jittering light: duty, and the agony it demanded.

“My beloved,” he said, with tenderness and a stubbornness that was like a tightened cord, “I bless thee for giving me one more sight of thy sweet face; and may God forgive thee and bless thee for destroying in a minute the holy peace it hath taken six months of solitude to build. No matter. A year of penance will, Dei gratia, restore me to my calm. My poor Margaret, I seem cruel: yet I am kind. ’Tis best we part—ay, this moment.”

“Part, Gerard? Never. We have seen what comes of parting.” She stepped closer, her voice thick with hurt, yet driven. “Part? Why, you have not heard half my story—no, nor the tithe. ’Tis not for thy mere comfort I take thee to Gouda manse. Hear me!”

“I may not. Thy very voice is a temptation with its music—memory’s delight.”

“But I say you shall hear me, Gerard, for forth this place I go not unheard.”

“Then must we part by other means,” he said sadly.

“Alack! what other means? Wouldst put me to thine own door, being the stronger?”

“Nay, Margaret. Well thou knowest I would suffer many deaths rather than put force on thee; thy sweet body is dearer to me than my own; but a million times dearer to me are our immortal souls, both thine and mine. I have withstood this direst temptation of all long enow. Now I must fly it. Farewell! farewell!”

He turned, made for the door, opened it, and had half gone out when she sprang and caught him by the arm.

“Nay, then another must speak for me. I thought to reward thee for yielding to me; but unkind that thou art, I need his help, I find. Turn then this way one moment.”

“Nay, nay.”

“But I say ay! And then turn thy back on us an thou canst.”

She loosened her grasp a little, thinking he would not refuse so small a boon. He saw the smallest space and took it as a drowning man takes air.

“Fly, Clement, fly!” he almost shrieked; and zeal, that terrible strength, lent him his old limbs for a breath. He tore himself away, ran a few steps, leaped the little stream, and went along it with the wildness of one pursued by invisible claws. Then, finding she did not follow, he stopped and looked back.

Margaret lay prone, hands flung out. Without meaning it, he had thrown her down upon stone. The sight wrung a groan from him; he took one step toward her—and then, as if punishment must be taken at once to keep his soul from turning, he flung himself into the icy water instead.

“There,” he cried, teeth chattering on the words, “kill my body—but save my soul!”

The cold rose like knives. It took his breath, seized his throat. He stood, up to the neck, as if the stream were liquid winter. Margaret, still on the ground, sent up one long moan and rose to her knees. In the candle’s distant glow and the moon’s pale help he saw her face, whitened now, her eyes shining like wet violets.

And in the still night, over the hush of water and the far, soft rustle of leaves, he heard her words clearly, as if each syllable were dropped into a bowl of metal.

“Oh, God! Thou that knowest all, Thou seest how I am used. Forgive me then! For I will not live another day.”

She sprang up and fled past his hiding-place, not like a woman but like some wounded creature that has no thought left but speed and pain; and she shrieked as she ran, each cry tearing the air:

“CRUEL!—CRUEL!—CRUEL!—CRUEL!”

What a world of anguish can be poured into one syllable. Wounded love, wounded pride, despair, and the first shadow of madness—all were in it. It froze his heart more than the stream froze his bones. He had won, in his own stern account, a victory; and it tasted like ashes. For a moment, in that bitter triumph, a savage thought rose—almost a curse against the Church, against religion itself, for exacting such brutality from flesh-and-blood man.

At last he crawled out, half dead, and staggered back to his den.

“I am safe here,” he groaned. “She will never come near me again—unmanly, ungrateful wretch that I am.”

He flung his wasted, shivering body down upon the floor, with a secret hope it might never rise. But presently the hour-glass, patient as ever, showed him midnight had gone. He rose, slow and shaking, stripped off his wet garments, and with every movement moaned—not at his own pain, but hers, because in hurting her he had bruised the very place he loved.

He took the old hermit’s cilice of bristles and drew it on. The sharp points bit and scored; the sting was clean, like nettles, and for a moment it helped—pain answering pain. Over that he buckled the breastplate he had never dared to wear, doubting himself worthy of a tried soldier’s armour. Now he must take every aid, even if the aid were only the hard reminder of vows.

He knelt and prayed—humbly, doggedly—for release that very night from the burden of the flesh. Then he lit all his candles, until the cave’s black corners drew back and the smoke-smell thickened. He began to recite his psalter. Each word seemed a lump of lead dragged up from a leaden heart and dropped with a dull weight to the ground; and between the verses he moaned, not loud, but from the marrow.

In the midst of this, he noticed a little bundle in the corner he had not seen before in the weaker light; and at one end of it something shone like gold spun into silk. He went nearer; and the instant he saw what lay there, he lifted both hands as if in rapture.

“It is a seraph,” he whispered. “A lovely seraph. Heaven hath witnessed my bitter trial, and approves my cruelty; and this flower of the skies is sent to cheer me, fainting under my burden.”

He fell on his knees and stared as a famished man stares at bread: at the golden hair, the tender skin, the cheeks like a ripe peach. “Let me feast my sad eyes on thee ere thou leavest me for thine ever-blessed abode, and my cell darkens again at thy parting, as it did at hers.”

The lovely visitor stirred. Two eyes opened, sky-coloured and astonished; and seeing a wild figure kneeling close, armour glinting in candlelight, the child’s mouth puckered and he cried out, piteously, with the whole hunger of a little life:

“MUMMA! MUM-MA!”

Tears ran down his cheeks. The spell of angel-vision broke at once, yet not unhappily. Clement—who had not looked on a human face for six months and more—was perhaps the more just in his estimate of childish beauty. In truth, this fair northern child, with long hair like flax in sun, looked more like any angel men have ever truly wanted than the painted cherubs of churches.

The innocent distress went through the hermit’s heart. He was fond of children, and the monastic life, for all its harshness, often keeps a soft place for them as a hedge keeps a quiet nest. He used all his gentleness, all his small art of coaxing and making peace. He spoke low—low enough that the cave itself seemed to listen rather than echo. The child, wonderfully quick for his years, gulped down his sobs; wonder slid in where fear had been. With great wet eyes he studied the strange man who looked savage and yet spoke kindly; who wore metal and yet did not strike, but soothed.

Clement himself was at a loss how this little human flower had come blooming into his stony dark. He remembered the door left wide. A shameful thought came: that some unhappy creature, high or low, had taken the open hermitage as a place to leave a child and never return. At that, his bowels yearned so over the poor abandoned cherub that tears of tenderness stood in his eyes.

Yet even in the mother’s crime he saw, with that monkish habit of reading Providence in all things, the strange divine goodness that had guided such heartlessness to comfort His servant’s breaking heart.

“Now bless thee, bless thee, bless thee, sweet innocent,” he murmured. “I would not change thee for e’en a cherub in heaven.”

“At’s pooty,” the child replied, as infants do, ignoring all that did not touch his curiosity.

“What is pretty here, my love, besides thee?”

“Ookum-gars,” said the boy, pointing to the breastplate.

Clement half smiled despite himself. The sound of metal had caught the child as surely as a bright trencher catches a hungry eye. Hector’s babe had screamed at a glittering helm; this medieval little one was charmed by a polished cuirass, and his griefs eased by its shine.

“There are prettier things here than that,” Clement said. “There are little birds; lovest thou birds?”

“Nay. Ay. En um ittle, ery ittle? Not ike torks. Hate torks—um bigger an baby.”

Between broken words he confided that storks, with their great flapping wings, frightened him—darkened his small world with their shadow and clatter.

“Ay, but my birds are very little, and good, and oh, so pretty!”

“Den I ikes ’m,” said the child, dictating terms like a prince. Then his face puckered again. “I ont my mammy.”

“Alas, sweet dove! I doubt I shall have to fill her place as best I may. Hast thou no daddy as well as mammy, sweet one?”

At or within a breath of that question, another presence—unseen—caught every word as if it were bread to the starving. For the night had not ended for Margaret.

When she fled past Gerard, she was near mad, in that bleak state where love turns on itself like milk gone sour, and the mind whispers of throwing away what it cannot bear. She ran to Reicht Heynes, pale and trembling, flung her arms round the girl’s neck, and could only moan, “Oh, Reicht! oh, Reicht!”

Reicht kissed her and began to whimper; and the great mastiff beside them gave one long, human-sounding whine. Even his blunt sense knew sorrow was abroad.

“Oh, Reicht,” Margaret got out at last, choking, “see how he has served me!” She showed her hands, scraped and bleeding where she had fallen. “He threw me down—he was so eager to fly from me. He took me for a devil; he said I came to tempt him. Am I the woman to tempt a man? you know me, Reicht.”

“Nay, in sooth, sweet Mistress Margaret—the last i’ the world.”

“And he would not look at my child. I’ll fling myself and him into the Rotter this night.”

“Oh, fie! fie! eh, my sweet woman, speak not so. Is any man that breathes worth your child’s life?”

“My child!” Margaret started as if struck. “Where is he? Why, Reicht, I have left him behind. Oh, shame! Is it possible I can love him to that degree as to forget my child? Ah, I am rightly served for it.”

She sat down, and faithful Reicht beside her, and they sobbed in one another’s arms. After a while the sobbing dried into something harder.

“Let us go home,” Margaret said, dogged.

“Ay, but the bairn?”

“Oh! he is well where he is.” Bitterness made her reckless. “My heart is turned against my very child. He cares nought for him; wouldn’t see him, nor hear speak of him. And I took him there so proud, and made his hair so nice—I did—and put his new frock and cowl on him. Nay, turn about: it’s his child as well as mine; let him keep it awhile. Mayhap that will learn him to think more of its mother—and his own.”

“High words off an empty stomach,” said Reicht, practical as bread. “Time will show. Come you home.”

They took two steps, and Time showed quicker than it levels abbeys. Margaret stopped. She could neither go nor turn, but stood like a post in the road.

“Reicht,” she said, her voice suddenly small, “what else have I on earth? I cannot.”

“Whoever said you could?” Reicht answered, with a tenderness hidden under plain speech. “Think you I paid attention? Words are woman’s breath. Come back for him without more ado; ’tis time we were in our beds—much more he.”

Reicht led, and Margaret followed readily enough in that direction. Yet as they drew near the hermitage she halted again, dread and pride tangled.

“Reicht, go you and ask him, will he give me back my boy—for I could not bear the sight of him.”

“Alas, mistress, this do seem a sorry ending after all that hath been betwixt you twain. Bethink thee now: doth thine heart whisper no excuse for him? Dost verily hate him for whom thou hast waited so long? Oh, weary world!”

“Hate him, Reicht?” Margaret’s bitterness cracked and showed the love beneath, raw and bleeding. “I would not harm a hair of his head for all that is in nature; but look on him I cannot. I have taken a horror of him. Oh! when I think of all I have suffered for him—and what I came here this night to do for him—and brought my own darling to kiss him and call him father…” Her voice broke, and her mind, in its pain, ran backward in a circle to another hurt. “Ah, Luke, my poor chap, my wound showeth me thine. I have thought too little of thy pangs, whose true affection I despised; and now my own is despised. Reicht, if the poor lad was here now, he would have a good chance.”

“Well, he is not far off,” said Reicht; but she said it without alacrity, as if that nearness was a danger.

“Speak not to me of any man,” Margaret said fiercely. “I hate them all.”

“For the sake of one?”

“Flout me not. But prithee go forward and get me what is my own—my sole joy in the world. Thou knowest I am on thorns till I have him to my bosom again.”

Reicht went forward. Margaret sat by the roadside, covered her face with her apron, and rocked herself as her people did when grief would not be still. She was so deep in that inward storm she did not hear Reicht running back; she started when the young woman laid a hand upon her shoulder.

“Mistress Margaret,” said Reicht quietly, “take a fool’s advice that loves ye. Go softly to yon cave, wi’ all the ears and eyes your mother ever gave you.”

“Why? Reicht?” Margaret stammered.

“I thought the cave was afire, ’twas so light inside; and there were voices.”

“Voices?”

“Ay, not one, but twain, and all unlike—a man’s and a little child’s—talking as pleasant as you and me. I am no great hand at a keyhole for my part; ’tis paltry work. But if so be voices were a-talking in yon cave, and them that owned those voices were so near to me as those are to thee, I’d go on all fours like a fox, and I’d crawl on my belly like a serpent, ere I’d lose one word that passes atwixt those twain.”

“Whisht, Reicht! Bless thee! Bide thou here. Buss me—pray for me!”

Almost ere the words were out, Margaret flew toward the hermitage as noiselessly as a lapwing. Near it she crouched, and the old instinct of hiding—learned in childhood games and in womanhood’s necessities—made her movements supple and silent. She reached the door, found a chink, and listened.

More than once it cost her a struggle not to burst in; but defeat had taught her caution. She held herself like a drawn bow, resolute to let the moment ripen. After a while, slowly, she lifted her head to the widest crack and looked, listening with her whole soul.

Inside, the child—asked whether he had no daddy—shook his head at first, refusing. Then, pressed gently, he seemed to remember what some foolish tongue had told him, and said, in his broken speech, “Dad-da ill man; run away and left poor mum-ma.”

Margaret, outside, winced as if the words had struck her cheek. It was new to her as to Clement.

Clement burst out, all heat and indignation, the kind that is as much tenderness as anger. “The villain! the monster! He must be born without bowels to desert thee, sweet one. Ah! he little knows the joy he has turned his back on. Well, my little dove, I must be father and mother to thee, since the one runs away and t’other abandons thee to my care. Now to-morrow I shall ask the good people that bring me my food to fetch some nice eggs and milk for thee as well; for bread is good enough for poor old good-for-nothing me, but not for thee. And I shall teach thee to read.”

“I can yead, I can yead.”

“Ay, verily—so young? All the better; we will read good books together, and I shall show thee the way to heaven.” His voice softened, as if he were stirring something gentle in a pot, careful not to scorch it. “Heaven is a beautiful place—a thousand times fairer and better than earth—and there be little cherubs like thyself in white, glad to welcome thee and love thee. Wouldst like to go to heaven one day?”

“Ay, along wi’-my-mammy.”

“What, not without her then?”

“Nay. I ont my mammy. Where is my mammy?”

Oh, what it cost poor Margaret not to fling the door wide and gather him up, to feel the weight of him, warm and living, and smell his hair that she had smoothed and kissed.

“Well, fret not, sweetheart,” Clement said. “Mayhap she will come when thou art asleep. Wilt thou be good now and sleep?”

“I not eepy. Ikes to talk.”

“Well, talk we then. Tell me thy pretty name.”

“Baby.” The child stared in amazement at Clement’s ignorance.

“Hast none other?”

“Nay.”

“What shall I do to pleasure thee, baby? Shall I tell thee a story?”

“I ikes tories,” said the boy, clapping his hands.

“Or sing thee a song?”

“I ikes tongs,” and excitement shook him.

“Choose then, a song or a story.”

“Ting I a tong. Nay, tell I a tory. Nay, ting I a tong. Nay—” The corners of his little mouth turned down; he had half a mind to cry at the injustice of choice. Then his face cleared with sudden invention. “Ting I a tory,” he pronounced.

“Sing thee a story?” Clement laughed softly—softly, as if laughter were a fragile vessel in that place. “Well, after all, why not? And wilt thou sit o’ my knee and hear it?”

“Yea.”

“Then I must e’en doff this breastplate; ’tis too hard for thy soft cheek.” He unbuckled it with care; the metal gave a small clink that the cave caught and held. “And now I must doff this bristly cilice; it would prick thy tender skin, perhaps make it bleed—as they have me, I see.” He drew it off and shivered, not only from cold but from the sudden absence of pain. “And now I put on my best pelisse, in honour of thy worshipful visit. See how soft and warm it is; bless the good soul that sent it. And now I sit me down; so. And I take thee on my left knee, and put my arm under thy little head; so. And then the psaltery, and play a little tune—so, not too loud.”

“I ikes dat.”

“I am right glad on’t. Now list the story.”

He began to chant—a child’s tale set to a kind of recitative, with a little moral refrain returning now and then like a familiar scent in a kitchen. The boy listened with rapture.

“I ikes oo,” he said. “Ot is oo? Is oo a man?”

“Ay, little heart—and a great sinner to boot.”

“I ikes great tingers. Ting one other tory.”

He chanted a second. The child’s gaze never left his face, as if the voice were food.

“I ubbs oo,” the boy cried suddenly, impetuous as a spark. “Ot caft is oo?”

“I am a hermit, love.”

“I ubbs vermins. Ting other one.”

During the third, Nature lifted her leaden sceptre over the youthful eyelids. “I is not eepy,” he whined faintly, and surrendered.

Clement laid down the psaltery as one lays down a knife beside sleeping bread, and began to rock his new treasure in his arms. He crooned over him a lullaby well known in Tergou, the very tune his own mother had used, as natural to him as kneading. The child sank deep into sleep upon his arm.

Clement stopped singing and gazed on him with infinite tenderness and a sadness that went behind words. For in that moment, as the boy’s breath made its little regular music, he could not help thinking what might have been—what family sounds might have filled a house—had there not been a piece of paper with a lie in it. He sighed, and the sigh was like wind through bare branches.

The next moment, moonlight burst into the cell, and with it, and in it, swift as it, Margaret Brandt was down at his knee, her hand timorous upon his shoulder.

“GERARD, YOU DO NOT REJECT US—you cannot.”

The hermit started as if the stone under him had cried out. His gaze flew from the sleeping child on his left arm to the woman at his right knee, and back again, and in that to-and-fro there was more terror than when he had first faced solitude.

An hour or two ago she had been pale, breathless, mastered. Now she shone. The blood had come back into her cheeks, her eyes were quick as fire on a hearth, and her mouth—half parted—had the look of victory in it; yet it was not the hard triumph of spite. It was something he had never seen there before, not even in the days when she laughed over her kneading-trough and sang. It was the grave pride of a mother.

He stared as a man stares at a miracle that has chosen to happen in his own poor room.

“Us?” he got out at last, hoarse, and still his eyes went between the child and her, as if he must be sure the two were not a trick of fasting.

Margaret, in her turn, was genuinely taken aback. In that age men read meanings in signs and feelings more readily than they counted facts; yet here was a fact with a warm weight and a pulse. She drew back a little, then leaned in, scandalised.

“What!” she cried. “Doth not a father know his own child? and a man of God, too? Fie, Gerard, to pretend! Nay, thou art too wise, too good, not to have—why, I watched thee; and e’en now look at you twain! ’Tis thine own flesh and blood thou holdest to thine heart.”

The hermit’s lips worked. His whole body shook, not with cold, though the cell was chill, but with the breaking of some inward frost.

“What words are these?” he stammered. “This angel mine?”

“Whose else?” said she, and her voice softened at once into possession and tenderness. “Since he is mine.”

He bent his eyes on the child as if to drink him in. His stare had no common seeing in it, but that desperate greed with which a starved man looks at bread. Margaret watched him greedily too, yet proudly, as if she had made this food and set it on the board.

“He is not a bit like me,” she said, pleased and fierce in the same breath; “but oh, at whiles he is thy very image in little. And see this golden hair. Thine was the very colour at his age; ask mother else. And see this mole on his little finger; now look at thine own—there! ’Twas thy mother let me weet thou wast marked so before him; and oh, Gerard, ’twas this our child found thee for me; for by that little mark on thy finger I knew thee for his father, when I watched above thy window and saw thee feed the birds.”

As she spoke she seized the child’s hand and kissed it with an eagerness that was almost hunger. She actually got half the tiny fingers into her mouth, Heaven knows how, as if the taste of him might steady her joy.

“Ah! bless thee,” she whispered to the sleeper, “thou didst find thy poor daddy for her; and now thou hast made us friends again after our little quarrel—the first, the last. Wast very cruel to me but now, my poor Gerard, and I forgive thee; for loving of thy child.”

At that the man broke.

A sound came from him—half sob, half laugh, half prayer—so wild that it startled even Margaret, who had seen men’s hearts crack in childbirth rooms and at graves. Lowered by fasts and unstrung by silence, the once strong Gerard was hysterical; his head swam, his breath came in snatches, and the child on his arm stirred faintly, feeling the tremor.

“Nay, take not on so,” Margaret murmured, and laid her hand on his brow as a mother lays it on fever. Her palm was warm; her touch had the homely certainty of someone used to quieting a fire that threatens to run up the chimney. “Be brave! So, so. Dear heart, thou art not the first man that hath gone abroad and come back richer by a lovely little self than he went forth. Being a man of God, take courage, and say He sends thee this to comfort thee for what thou hast lost in me; and that is not so very much, my lamb; for sure the better part of love shall ne’er cool here to thee; though it may in thine, and ought, being a priest, and parson of Gouda.”

“I?” he whispered, faint. “Priest of Gouda? Never. I am a friar of St. Dominic.” His eyelids fluttered; yet his voice, for all its weakness, clung to the one thing it dared ask. “Speak on—sweet music—tell me all that hath happened thee, before we are parted again.”

Some women would have seized that word—parted—and made it the battlefield. Margaret did not. She had learned how not to strike the same stone twice and call it wisdom. She accepted the word as if it were settled, turned her face from arguing about the manse as from a pot already set to boil, and poured out her tale.

She told him, above all, of the kindness of his parents; of bread given and doors opened; of hard words borne; of nights where the house sounded with nothing but the ticking of a poor clock and the wind worrying the shutters. She spoke with that gift she had—making the past live again in the mouth. As she talked, his hand stole to hers. Sometimes he squeezed it so hard she felt his nails; sometimes she felt him wince and tremble, anger flashing through him when she named injuries. At other moments he pressed her hand with a gentle sympathy that ran, like warm broth, into the marrow.

“Oh, piteous tale,” he said, “of a true heart battling alone against such bitter odds! It all seems small, when I see thee here again, nursing my boy. We have had a warning, Gerard. True friends like you and me are rare, and they are mad to part, ere death divideth them.”

“And that is true,” said he—off his guard, the old Gerard speaking before the hermit could stop him.

Then she would have him tell her what he had suffered for her. He begged to be spared; she agreed—then, by questions that sounded simple as a cook’s “How did the bread take?” drew it all out: the perils, the turns, the loneliness, the temptations that came like night-bats to a cell. More than once she hid her face in her hands at a peril past; and to comfort him, she slid her arms under the child, lifted him with a practised gentleness, and offered the small warm mouth like an answer to fear.

“Kiss him softly,” she whispered. “Again, again—kiss thy fill if thou canst. He is sound. ’Tis all I can do to comfort thee till thou art out of this foul den and in thy sweet manse yonder.”

He shook his head, stubborn as a man with a vow between his teeth.

“Well,” said she, letting it pass as if it were but a dish she would serve again in due course. “Know that I have been sore affronted for want of my lines.”

“Who hath dared affront thee?”

“No matter. Those that will do it again if thou hast lost them—which the saints forbid.”

“I lose them?” He dropped his eyes. “Nay—there they lie, close to thy hand.”

“Where, where, oh, where?”

He bowed his head still lower, ashamed, and pointed with a finger that trembled.

“Look in the Vulgate. Heaven forgive me: I thought thou wert dead, and a saint in heaven.”

She opened the poor book. There, on blank leaves, were her marriage lines. A cry broke from her like a kettle boiling over.

“Thank God! thank God! Oh, bless thee, Gerard, bless thee! Why—what is here, Gerard?”

For other leaves were thick with relics: every scrap she had ever sent him, pinned and guarded as if each were a wafer; their two names she had once written together in sport; the lock of her hair; half a silver coin broken between them; and—oddest and tenderest—one straw, browned and dried, from which she had sucked soup the first day he ever saw her. The very objects had an odour to her memory: broth and hearth-smoke, salt on the lip, the clean dryness of straw between teeth, the faint metallic tang of that coin.

At sight of these proofs of love, her exultation over the lines was drowned. She swayed; her hand went to her bosom as if to hold her heart in. She leaned her forehead against the stone and wept without sound—so silently he did not know. She would not let him. In this hour, to befriend him, she must be the stronger; tears, like spilled water, weaken the hands.

When she spoke, her voice was steady again, though it had a tremor like a lute-string after it is struck.

“Gerard,” said she, “I know you are wise and good. You must have a reason for what you are doing, let it seem ever so unreasonable. Talk we like old friends. Why are you buried alive?”

“To escape temptation,” he answered. The words came out as if he had rehearsed them in his prayers. “My impious ire against those two had its root in the heart; that heart then I must deaden, and, Dei gratia, I shall. Shall I, a servant of Christ and of the Church, court temptation? Shall I pray daily to be led out on’t, and walk into it with open eyes?”

“That is good sense anyway,” said Margaret, with such a plain look of candour that it might have deceived a saint.

“’Tis unanswerable,” said he, and sighed.

“We shall see.” She tilted her head a little, listening—not to him only, but to the place itself. The cell had its own sound: the damp drip in the corner, the small scratch of a mouse, the far sighing of wind through leafless boughs. “Tell me: have you escaped temptation here? Why I ask is, when I am alone, my thoughts are far more wild and foolish than in company. Nay, speak sooth; come!”

He hesitated; then humility, sore-earned, forced his confession.

“I must needs own I have been worse tempted here with evil imaginations than in the world.”

“There now.”

“Ay, but so were Anthony and Jerome, Macarius and Hilarion, Benedict, Bernard, and all the saints. ’Twill wear off.”

“How do you know?”

“I feel sure it will.”

“Guessing against knowledge,” said she, and there was the quick bite of her wit. “Here ’tis men folk are sillier than us that be but women. Wise in their own conceits, they will not let themselves see; their stomachs are too high to be taught by their eyes. A woman, if she went into a hole in a bank to escape temptation, and there found it, would just lift her farthingale and out on’t, and not e’en know how wise she was, till she watched a man in like plight.”

He half smiled, then sobered.

“Nay, I grant humility and a teachable spirit are the roads to wisdom; but when all is said, here I wrestle but with imagination. At Gouda she I love—as no priest or monk must love any but the angels—she will tempt a weak soul, unwilling, yet not loth to be tempted.”

“Ay, that is another matter. I should tempt thee then? to what, i’ God’s name?”

“Who knows? The flesh is weak.”

“Speak for yourself, my lad.” She drew herself up, and the pride in her was as frank as a trumpet-call. “Why, you are thinking of some other Margaret, not Margaret a Peter. Was ever my mind turned to folly and frailty? Stay—is it because you were my husband once, as these lines avouch? Think you the road to folly is beaten for you more than another? Oh! how shallow are the wise, and how little able are you to read me, who can read you so well from top to toe.

“Come, learn thine A B C. Were a stranger to proffer me unchaste love, I should shrink a bit, no doubt, and feel sore, but I should defend myself without making a coil; for men, I know, are so—the best of them sometimes. But if you, that have been my husband, and are my child’s father, were to offer to humble me so in mine own eyes, and thine, and his—either I should spit in thy face, Gerard, or, as I am not a downright vulgar woman, I should snatch the first weapon at hand and strike thee dead.”

Her eyes flashed; even her nostrils widened with indignation. In that moment she was terrible, and wholly sincere. The hermit’s fear—so long fed on shadows—fell back before that clear blaze of honour.

“I had not the sense to see that,” said Gerard quietly, and he sat pondering as if a door in his mind had opened.

Margaret watched him, then softened as quickly as she had flamed.

“Let not you and I dispute,” she said gently. “Speak we of other things. Ask me of thy folk.”

“My father?”

“Well—and warms to thee and me. Poor soul, he drew glaive on those twain that day; but Jorian Ketel and I we mastered him, and he drove them forth his house for ever.”

“That may not be,” said Gerard at once, the old dutiful son answering before priest or hermit. “He must take them back.”

“That he will never do for us. You know the man; he is dour as iron; yet would he do it for one word from one that will not speak it.”

“Who?”

“The vicar of Gouda. The old man will be at the manse to-morrow, I hear.”

“How you come back to that,” he said, but without anger.

“Forgive me: I am but a woman. It is us for nagging; shouldst keep me from it wi’ questioning of me.”

“My sister Kate?”

“Alas!”

“What, hath ill befallen e’en that sweet lily? Out and alas!”

“Be calm, sweetheart—no harm hath her befallen. Oh, nay, nay, far fro’ that.”

She made herself very composed. And in a voice low and sweet, as if she were singing a cradle-song to a grown man, she told him how Kate had died.

It was not told like a sermon; it was told like a memory of a room, and of the sounds in it: the quiet breathing, the soft murmur of gossips, the clink of a spoon against a cup, the ticking of a clock that seemed too loud because grief had hushed all else.

“My poor Gerard,” said she, “Kate hath left her trouble behind her. For the manner on’t, ’twas like the rest. Ah, such as she saw never thirty, nor ever shall while earth shall last. She smiled in pain too.

“A well, then, thus ’twas: she was took wi’ a languor and a loss of all her pains.”

“A loss of her pains? I understand you not.”

“Ay, you are not experienced. Indeed, e’en thy mother almost blinded herself and said, ‘’Tis maybe a change for the better.’ But Joan Ketel, which is an understanding woman, she looked at her and said, ‘Down sun, down wind!’ And the gossips sided and said, ‘Be brave, you that are her mother, for she is half way to the saints.’ And thy mother wept sore, but Kate would not let her.

“And one very ancient woman, she said to thy mother, ‘She will die as easy as she lived hard.’ And she lay painless best part of three days, a sipping of heaven afore-hand.

“And, my dear, when she was just parting, she asked for ‘Gerard’s little boy,’ and I brought him and set him on the bed, and the little thing behaved as peaceably as he does now. But by this time she was past speaking; but she pointed to a drawer, and her mother knew what to look for: it was two gold angels thou hadst given her years ago. Poor soul! she had kept them, till thou shouldst come home.

“And she nodded towards the little boy, and looked anxious; but we understood her, and put the pieces in his two hands; and when his little fingers closed on them, she smiled content. And so she gave her little earthly treasures to her favourite’s child—for you were her favourite—and her immortal jewel to God, and passed so sweetly we none of us knew justly when she left us. Well-a-day, well-a-day!”

Gerard wept outright now, not ashamed.

“She hath not left her like on earth,” he sobbed. “Oh, how the affections of earth curl softly round my heart! I cannot help it; God made them after all. Speak on, sweet Margaret; at thy voice the past rolls its tides back upon me; the loves and the hopes of youth come fair and gliding into my dark cell, and darker bosom, on waves of memory and music.”

“Gerard,” she said, and the tenderness in her had an edge like a knife in cloth, “I am loth to grieve you, but Kate cried a little when she first took ill at you not being there to close her eyes.”

His breath caught.

“You were within a league,” she went on, very quietly now, “but hid your face from her.”

He groaned as if struck.

“There, forgive me for nagging; I am but a woman. You would not have been so cruel to your own flesh and blood knowingly, would you?”

“Oh, no.”

“Well, then. Know that thy brother Sybrandt lies in my charge with a broken back—fruit of thy curse.”

“Mea culpa! mea culpa!” The words came from him like blows on the breast.

“He is very penitent. Be yourself and forgive him this night.”

“I have forgiven him long ago.”

“Think you he can believe that from any mouth but yours? Come! he is but about two butts’ length hence.”

“So near?” He started. “Why, where?”

“At Gouda manse. I took him there yestreen. For I know you: the curse was scarce cold on your lips when you repented it.” He nodded, stricken. “And I said to myself, Gerard will thank me for taking Sybrandt to die under his roof; he will not beat his breast and cry mea culpa, yet grudge three footsteps to quiet a withered brother on his last bed. He may have a bee in his bonnet, but he is not a hypocrite—a thing all pious words and uncharitable deeds.”

He staggered as if she had put her hand under his ribs and pressed. She had chosen her moment; she struck, not to hurt, but to drive the nail home.

“Forgive me for nagging,” she said, softer; and then, with the simplest sentence of all, she brought his mother into the cell as surely as if the door had opened on her.

“Thy mother too is waiting for thee. Is it well done to keep her on thorns so long? She will not sleep this night. Bethink thee, Gerard: she is all to thee that I am to this sweet child.”

As she spoke, the baby’s breath made its tiny sound—like milk simmering very low. The cell’s silence took it in and magnified it. Margaret looked down at the child as if she were reading a psalm in his face.

“Ah, I think so much more of mothers since I had my little Gerard. She suffered for thee, and nursed thee, and tended thee from boy to man. Priest, monk, hermit—call thyself what thou wilt—to her thou art but one thing: her child.”

“Where is she?” he asked, and his voice quavered like a bell in wind.

“At Gouda manse,” said Margaret, “wearing the night in prayer and care.”

Now she did the thing she had held back, like a cook who keeps the strongest spice for the end so it may carry through the whole dish. She spoke to his reason, in her own good straightforward Dutch, with no lace of Latin to hide the plainness.

She told him, without cruelty, that his cave-life was only a higher selfishness, spiritual egotism: caring for his own soul alone. A priest, she said, had no more right to think only of his own soul than only of his own body. His path to heaven lay through others.

“But,” she argued, “whoever yet lost his soul by saving the souls of others? The Almighty loves him who thinks of others; and when He shall see thee caring for the souls of the folk the duke hath put into thine hand, He will care ten times more for thy soul than He does now.”

Gerard looked up as if he had heard a new note in familiar chant.

“Art shrewd in dispute,” he said.

“Far from it,” said she. “Only my eyes are not bandaged with conceit.”

Then she flung her thought wider than the cell: she spoke of the world outside, of the way wickedness ran abroad and did not hide itself in caves; of how good men, by skulking, gave evil the odds. She brought in Denys, the duke’s soldier, and asked whether he had ever crept away from battle because battle was dangerous.

“And thy sole excuse is fear,” she said, and she did not soften that word. “Go to, no duke nor king hath such cowardly soldiers as Christ hath. What was that you said in the church at Rotterdam about the man in the parable that buried his talent in the earth, and so offended the giver? Thy wonderful gift for preaching—is it not a talent, and a gift from thy Creator?”

“Certes,” said he, subdued, “such as it is.”

“And hast thou laid it out? or buried it? To whom hast thou preached these seven months—to bats and owls? Hast buried it in one hole with thyself and thy once good wits?

“The Dominicans are the friars preachers. ’Tis for preaching they were founded. So thou art false to Dominic as well as to his Master.”

Then, with that gift she had for turning the grand into the homely, she carried him back to their youth.

“Do you remember, Gerard, when we were young together—which now are old before our time—as we walked handed in the fields, did you but see a sheep cast—ay, three fields off—you would leave your sweetheart (by her good will) and run and lift the sheep for charity?

“Well, then, at Gouda is not one sheep in evil plight, but a whole flock; some cast, some strayed, some sick, some tainted, some a being devoured—and all for the want of a shepherd. Where is their shepherd? Lurking in a den like a wolf—a den in his own parish. Out fie! out fie!

“I scented thee out, in part, by thy kindness to the little birds. Take note: you Gerard Eliassoen must love something. ’Tis in your blood; you were born to’t. Shunning man, you do but seek earthly affection a peg lower than man.”

He broke in, defensive for once with warmth.

“The birds are God’s creatures—His innocent creatures—and I do well to love them, being God’s creatures.”

“What,” said Margaret swiftly, “are they creatures of the same God that we are—that he is who lies upon thy knee?”

“You know they are.”

“Then what pretence for shunning us and being kind to them? Sith man is one of the animals, why pick him out to shun? Is’t because he is of animals the paragon?

“What, you court the young of birds, and abandon your own young? Birds need but bodily food; and having wings, deserve scant pity if they cannot fly and find it. But that sweet dove upon thy knee—he needeth not carnal only, but spiritual food. He is thine as well as mine; and I have done my share. He will soon be too much for me, and I look to Gouda’s parson to teach him true piety and useful lore. Is he not of more value than many sparrows?”

She waited. The silence was thick as dough before it rises. Gerard, cornered by truth, stammered an assent.

“You wonder,” she continued, “to hear me quote holy writ so glib. I have pored over it this four years, and why? Not because God wrote it, but because I saw it often in thy hands ere thou didst leave me. Heaven forgive me, I am but a woman.

“What thinkest thou of this sentence? ‘Let your work so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father which is in heaven!’ What is a saint in a sink better than a light under a bushel?”

Then she gathered all her reasons as one gathers sticks to make a fire that will not be put out.

“Therefore—since the sheep committed to thy charge bleat for thee and cry, ‘Oh desert us no longer, but come to Gouda manse;’ since I, who know thee ten times better than thou knowest thyself, do pledge my soul it is for thy soul’s weal to go to Gouda manse—since duty to thy child, too long abandoned, calls thee to Gouda manse—since thy sovereign, whom holy writ again bids thee honour, sends thee to Gouda manse—since the Pope, whom the Church teaches thee to revere, hath absolved thee of thy monkish vows, and orders thee to Gouda manse—”

“Ah!” He flinched, as if the Pope’s name had struck his vow like a hammer.

“Since thy grey-haired mother watches for thee in dole and care, and turneth oft the hour-glass and sigheth sore that thou comest so slow to her at Gouda manse—since thy brother, withered by thy curse, awaits thy forgiveness and thy prayers for his soul, now lingering in his body, at Gouda manse—take thou in thine arms the sweet bird wi’ crest of gold that nestles to thy bosom, and give me thy hand; thy sweetheart erst and wife, and now thy friend, the truest friend to thee this night that e’er man had—and come with me to Gouda manse!”

The hermit lifted his head. His eyes, hollowed by fasting, shone as if lit from behind.

“IT IS THE VOICE OF AN ANGEL!” he cried.

“Then hearken it,” said Margaret, and her practical courage rang like a ladle on a pot, “and come forth to Gouda manse!”

The battle was won.

She lingered one moment. Her eyes swept the cell: its poor hoard, the sad furniture of penance. She chose the Vulgate and the psaltery—bread for the mind, and music for the heart. The rest she left with a sigh, as one leaves broken crockery.

Then she caught sight of the breastplate and the cilice of bristles. Something in her—pity mixed with anger—rose up, and she dashed them down with feeble ferocity.

Gerard watched her from outside, surprised.

She coloured, half ashamed of her own little spite.

“I am but a woman,” said she; “’little’ will still be ‘spiteful.’”

“Why encumber thyself with those?” he asked. “They are safe.”

“Oh,” said she, “I had a reason.”

So they set their faces toward the parsonage.

The moon and stars were bright enough to make the snow glimmer like sifted flour. The world was hushed, and that hush, after the cell’s dripping and the heart’s tumult, felt like a great clean linen laid over noise. Even their steps had a different sound out here: a soft crunch, a small squeak—nature’s own music, not the harsh clatter of men. Gerard, who had lived on silence till it turned against him, drank in the gentler noises as if they were part of his absolution.

Suddenly he stopped.

“My poor little birds!”

“What of them?” Margaret asked, but not sharply.

“They will miss their food. I feed them every day.”

“The child hath a piece of bread in his cowl,” said she at once, ready as ever. “Take that, and feed them now against the morn.”

He looked down at the baby’s face—so unconscious, so trusting. His arms tightened.

“I will,” he began; then shook his head. “Nay, I will not. He is as innocent, and nearer to me and to thee.”

Margaret drew a long breath. Her jealousy—quick and honest—had been waiting like a knife under cloth.

“’Tis well,” she said low. “Hadst taken it, I might have hated thee. I am but a woman.”

They walked on. Before they had gone a quarter of a mile, Gerard’s breath grew short. The child, though small, weighed like a sack of grain to a man emptied by fasting.

“Margaret,” he said, and shame coloured his voice, “I must e’en rest; he is too heavy for me.”

“Then give him me, and take thou these,” said she briskly, and shifted the Vulgate and psaltery to him as if they were no heavier than a loaf. “Alas! alas! I mind when thou wouldst have run with the child on one shoulder, and the mother on t’other.”

She took the boy, and carried him with perfect ease, his head lying against her like a warm roll newly drawn from the oven. Gerard looked down at her, pondering what he had done to his body, and what he had called holiness.

“I trow,” he said at last, with a rueful simplicity, “overmuch fasting is not good for a man.”

“A many die of it each year,” she replied, “winter time.”

He glanced askant at her carrying the child, and those plain words sat in his mind like salt in a dish—bringing out the truth.

After they had gone near a mile, he said, surprised and a little reproachful, “You thought it was but two butts’ length.”

“Not I.”

“Why, you said so.”

“That is another matter.” She turned on him then the face of a Madonna—sweet, fearless, and entirely resolved. “I lied,” she said simply. “And to save your soul and body, I’d maybe tell a worse lie than that, at need. I am but a woman. Ah, well—it is but two butts’ length from here at any rate.”

“Without a lie?”

“Humph! Three, without a lie.”

And indeed, in a few minutes, the manse rose before them. A candle burned in the vicar’s parlour.

“She is waking still,” Margaret whispered.

Gerard stopped, arrested by the sight. Through the window the candle looked immense against the night, as if the darkness made it larger.

“Beautiful,” he murmured. “Beautiful.”

“What, in Heaven’s name?” Margaret whispered back, half impatient.

“That little candle, seen through the window at night,” he said, almost reverently. “Look an it be not like some fair star of size prodigious. It delighteth the eyes, and warmeth the heart of those outside.”

“Come,” said Margaret, and her voice softened; for she understood that he was learning again to love the world he had tried to unlearn. “And I’ll show thee something better.”

She led him on tiptoe to the window. They peeped in.

Catherine knelt on the hassock, her “hours” open before her. The room had that quiet sound a praying room has: the faint rustle of page, the whisper of breath, the soft creak of wood as a body shifts under devotion. Her shoulders moved with the last of recent sobbing.

“Folk can pray out of a cave,” whispered Margaret.

“Ay,” Gerard whispered, and his throat tightened, “and hit heaven with their prayers; for ’tis for a sight of thee she prayeth, and thou art here. Now—be prepared. She is not the woman you knew her; her children’s troubles have greatly broken the brisk, light-hearted soul. And I see she has been weeping e’en now. She will have given thee up, being so late.”

“Let me get to her,” he said hastily, trembling all over. “That door! I will bide here.”

When he went toward the door, Margaret, fearing the shock of sudden joy might strike the older woman down, rapped once, sharp, on the pane, and cried “Mother!” with such a tone that Catherine understood at once.

Catherine clasped her hands; she was half risen from her knees when the door burst open and Gerard flung himself down at her feet, arms out as if he would climb back into childhood.

A cry came from her—one of those cries that no other throat can make, because no other heart has had the same labour.

“Ah! my darling, my darling!”

She clung to his neck and sobbed, and in her embrace she did not hold a friar, a hermit, a priest, a famous preacher. She held her child—lost, despaired of, given back.

After a little while Margaret came in with wet eyes and cheeks, the baby heavy and warm on her arm. She stood a moment, letting the mother and son have their flood; then, by degrees, a holy calm of affection settled on them all, like a steadying hand on a boiling pot.

They sat together—three of them—hand in hand. They murmured their sweet and loving converse, with pauses in which the house spoke: the candle’s faint hiss, the wind outside, the muffled night sounds of Gouda that a man cannot hear from a cave. Gerard, seated between them, drank right and left of their true affection and their humble, genuine wisdom.

And because love is not all air and vow but also bread and warmth, they forced him to eat a good nourishing meal: food with substance in it, laid before him as a duty no less than prayer. The smell of it—simple, honest fare—rose into him like life returning. At daybreak they packed him off to a snowy bed.

He slept.

When he woke, it was as from a hideous dream—friar and hermit no more, Clement no more, but Gerard Eliassoen, parson of Gouda.

Margaret was back in Rotterdam long before Gerard opened his eyes; and—hardest stroke of all to her own breast—she left her boy behind her at Gouda.

She had done it with the same practical swiftness that made her knead dough while she reckoned accounts: no fuss, no flourish, only the quick hand and the set mouth. Reicht Heynes she despatched straightway to Gouda with a vicar’s grey frock and a broad felt hat, and such close, motherly instructions on the governing of her “new master” as if she were sending a seasoned cook into a strange kitchen with a list of what would scorch and what would curdle.

Then she went to Jorian Ketel; for she said in her heart, “He is the closest I ever met; so he is the man for me.” And there, between them, were done two sly things—mortal sly, as she counted it; yet not venomous, though she believed they were. What were they? She, being “but a woman,” carried them locked in her bosom to her dying day; and I, being a man—Verbum non amplius addam.

She kept away from Gouda parsonage.

In the heat of wrangle a word passes for wind; but after, it can sit like grit under the eyelid. When Margaret went over all that had been said, she smarted at Gerard’s thinking she could ever forget the priest in the sometime lover. “For what did he take me?” she cried to herself; and though she was downright innocent, pride took modesty by the hand and they walked together into shyness. “Go no more to Gouda parsonage,” whispered Pride; and Modesty, that had no cause to fear, yet feared.

She left little Gerard there to finish the conquest her maternal heart ascribed to him—not to her own wit and patient eloquence—and to anchor his father for ever to humanity.

But that generous stroke of policy cost her dear. She had never yet been parted from her boy an hour; and now the house in Rotterdam, though it smelled of clean rushes and good bread, seemed hollow as a scoured pot. The first day she bore it as women bear toothache—set teeth and silent. The second day it was a pain that ran into her very sleep. The third it grew intolerable.

So at dark, like one ashamed of her own tenderness, she crept up to Gouda parsonage and lurked about the premises like a thief. The night had that soft Dutch hush, broken only by the far slap of water against piling, a dog’s single bark, and the homely clink within of kitchen things. She waited till she saw Reicht Heynes alone by the hearth, and then tapped lightly at the window.

“Reicht,” she whispered, “for pity’s sake bring him out to me unbeknown.”

With Margaret, the person that filled her mind at that moment ceased to have a name, and sank to a pronoun.

Reicht found an excuse to take little Gerard out. There was a moment of rapture—mother’s arms, child’s warm face pressed into her neck, the familiar milk-sweet smell of him under the night air; and then, as if joy must always pay toll, a breaking into tears when they parted again.

They arranged thenceforward that Reicht should bring him half-way to Rotterdam daily at a set hour, and Margaret meet them. The place was by a hedge where the wind combed through reeds and made a sound like flour sifted in a sieve—soft, constant, comforting; and from beyond, the lowing of cattle, and sometimes the creak of a cart, and the far bell that kept the hours like a steady heart.

At these meetings, after the first tumults, and after mother and child had gambolled together like a young cat and her first kitten, the boy would sometimes busy himself alone at their feet with a twig, a pebble, a beetle; and the two women—standing close enough that one cap might have covered both heads—would seize the moment to speak very seriously of Luke Peterson. It began thus:

“Reicht,” said Margaret, “I as good as promised him to marry Luke Peterson. ‘Say you the word,’ quoth I, ‘and I’ll wed him.’”

“Poor Luke!”

“Prithee, why poor Luke?”

“To be bandied about so, atwixt yea and nay.”

“Why, Reicht, you have not been so simple as to cast an eye of affection on the boy, that you take his part?”

“Me?” said Reicht, with a toss of the head that might have shaken a whole pan of curds if she’d been carrying it.

“Oh, I ask your pardon. Well, then, you can do me a good turn.”

“Whisht! whisper! that little darling is listening to every word—eyes like saucers.”

On this both their heads would indeed have gone under one cap.

Two women plotting against one boy? Oh, you great cowardly serpents!

But when these stolen meetings had gone on for about five days, Margaret began to feel the injustice of them and to be irritated as well as unhappy. She cried, too—cried like a woman who can face a market full of hard bargainers, but cannot face an empty cradle.

Then, as if Providence had heard the thin, private sound of her weeping, a cart came to her door. In it, clean as a new penny, beard close shaved, hands white as snow, a little colour in his pale face, sat the Vicar of Gouda in the grey frock and large felt hat she had sent him.

She ran upstairs directly, washed away all trace of tears, put on a cap which—having just come out of the drawer—was theoretically cleaner than the one on her head, and came down to him.

He seized both her hands and kissed them. A tear fell upon them. She turned her head away to hide her own, which started up as if the sight had summoned it.

“My sweet Margaret,” he cried, “why is this? Why hold you aloof from your own good deed? We have been waiting for you every day, and no Margaret.”

“You said things.”

“What! when I was a hermit, and a donkey.”

“Ay! no matter—you said things. And you had no reason.”

“Forget all I said there. Who hearkens the ravings of a maniac? For I see now that in a few months more I should have been a gibbering idiot; yet no mortal could have persuaded me away but you. Oh what an outlay of wit and goodness was yours! But it is not here I can thank and bless you as I ought. No—it is in the home you have given me, among the sheep whose shepherd you have made me; already I love them dearly. There it is I must thank ‘the truest friend ever man had.’ So now I say to you as erst you said to me: come to Gouda manse.”

“Humph! we will see about that.”

“Why, Margaret, think you I had ever kept the dear child so long, but that I made sure you would be back to him from day to day? Oh he curls round my very heartstrings; but what is my title to him compared to thine? Confess now, thou hast had hard thoughts of me for this.”

“Nay, nay, not I. Ah! thou art thyself again; wast ever thoughtful of others. I have half a mind to go to Gouda manse for your saying that.”

“Come then, with half thy mind; ’tis worth the whole of other folk’s.”

“Well, I dare say I will; but there is no such mighty hurry,” said she coolly—though in truth she was burning to go. “Tell me first how you agree with your folk.”

“Why, already my poor have taken root in my heart.”

“I thought as much.”

“And there are such good creatures among them; simple and rough, and superstitious, but wonderfully good.”

“Oh I leave you alone for seeing a grain of good among a bushel of ill.”

“Whisht! whisht! And Margaret—two of them have been ill friends four years and came to the manse each to get on my blind side. But give the glory to God, I got on their bright side, and made them friends, and laugh at themselves for their folly.”

“But are you in very deed their vicar? Answer me that.”

“Certes; have I not been to the bishop and taken the oath, and rung the church bell, and touched the altar, the missal, and the holy cup before the church-wardens? And they have handed me the parish seal—see, here it is. Nay, ’tis a real vicar inviting a true friend to Gouda manse.”

“Then my mind is at ease. Tell me oceans more.”

“Well, sweet one, nearest to me of all my parish is a poor cripple that my guardian angel and his—(her name thou knowest even by this turning of thy head away)—hath placed beneath my roof. Sybrandt and I are that we never were till now—brothers. ’Twould gladden thee, yet sadden thee, to hear how we kissed and forgave one another. He is full of thy praises, and wholly in a pious mind; he says he is happier since his trouble than e’er he was in the days of his strength. Oh! out of my house he ne’er shall go to any place but heaven.”

“Tell me somewhat that happened thyself, poor soul! All this is good, but yet no tidings to me. Do I not know thee of old?”

“Well, let me see. At first I was much dazzled by the sun-light, and could not go abroad (owl!), but that is passed; and good Reicht Heynes—humph!”

“What of her?”

“This to thine ear only, for she is a diamond. Her voice goes through me like a knife, and all voices seem loud but thine, which is so mellow sweet. Stay—now I’ll fit ye with tidings. I spake yesterday with an old man that conceits he is ill-tempered, and sweats to pass for such with others; but oh! so threadbare, and the best good heart beneath.”

“Why, ’tis a parish of angels,” said Margaret, ironically.

“Then why dost thou keep out on’t?” retorted Gerard. “Well, he was telling me there was no parish in Holland where the devil hath such power as at Gouda; and among his instances, says he: ‘We had a hermit, the holiest in Holland; but being Gouda, the devil came for him this week, and took him, bag and baggage; not a ha’porth of him left but a goodish piece of his skin, just for all the world like a hedgehog’s, and a piece o’ old iron furbished up.’”

Margaret smiled.

“Ay, but,” continued Gerard, “the strange thing is, the cave has verily fallen in; and had I been so perverse as resist thee, it had assuredly buried me dead there where I had buried myself alive. Therefore in this I see the finger of Providence, condemning my late, approving my present, way of life. What sayest thou?”

“Nay, can I pierce the like mysteries? I am but a woman.”

“Somewhat more, methinks. This very tale proves thee my guardian angel, and all else avouches it—so come to Gouda manse.”

“Well, go you on, I’ll follow.”

“Nay, in the cart with me.”

“Not so.”

“Why?”

“Can I tell why and wherefore, being a woman? All I know is I seem—to feel—to wish—to come alone.”

“So be it then. I leave thee the cart, being, as thou sayest, a woman; and I’ll go a-foot, being a man again, with the joyful tidings of thy coming.”

When Margaret reached the manse, the first thing she saw was the two Gerards together: the son performing his capriccios upon the little plot, a whirl of sudden crouches and leaps and solemn stops; and the father slouched in a chair in his great hat, pencil and paper in hand, trying very patiently to sketch him.

The sounds of the place came to her like a remembered language: the rasp of pencil, the soft thud of the child’s feet on earth, the faint clack from the kitchen where Catherine moved among her pots, and the bell’s after-hum still lying in the air as smoke lies in a room after a lamp is quenched.

After a warm welcome Gerard showed her his attempts.

“But in vain I strive to fix him,” said he, “for he is incarnate quicksilver. Yet do but note his changes—infinite, but none ungracious; all is supple and easy; and how he melteth from one posture to another.”

He added presently, “Woe to illuminators! Looking on thee, sir baby, I see what awkward, lopsided, ungainly toads I and my fellows painted in missals with, and called them cherubs and seraphs.”

Finally he flung the paper away in despair; and Margaret, with the thrift of love, conveyed it secretly into her bosom, as if to keep there a relic of this hour.

At night they sat round the peat fire. The hearth breathed out a rich, sweet earth-smell; peat does not blaze like resinous wood, but it glows and murmurs, and the room fills with a steady warmth that seems to have a sound of its own. Gerard bade them mark how beautiful the brass candlesticks and other glittering metals were in the glow.

Catherine’s eyes sparkled at that.

“And oh the sheets I lie in here,” said Gerard, “often my conscience pricketh me, and saith, ‘Who art thou to lie in lint like web of snow?’ Dives was ne’er so flaxed as I. And to think there be folk in the world that have all the beautiful things which I have here, yet not content! Let them pass six months in a hermit’s cell, seeing no face of man, then will they find how lovely and pleasant this wicked world is, and eke that men and women are God’s fairest creatures. Margaret was always fair, but never to my eye so bright as now.”

Margaret shook her head incredulously; the warmth made her cheeks bloom, and her hair, loosening a little, caught the peat-light like brown sugar in a pan.

Gerard continued, “My mother was ever good and kind, but I noted not her exceeding comeliness till now.”

“Nor I neither,” said Catherine; “a score years ago I might pass in a crowd, but not now.”

Gerard declared each age had its beauty. “See this mild grey eye,” said he, “that hath looked motherly love upon so many of us—all that love hath left its shadow, and that shadow is a beauty which defieth Time. See this delicate lip, these pure white teeth. See this well-shaped brow, where comeliness just passeth into reverence. Art beautiful in my eyes, mother dear.”

“And that is enough for me, my darling. ’Tis time you were in bed, child. Ye have to preach the morn.”

And Reicht Heynes and Catherine interchanged a look that said, without words, We two have an amiable maniac to superintend; he calls everything beautiful.

The next day was Sunday; and they heard him preach in his own church. It was crammed with persons who came curious, but remained devout. Never was his gift displayed more powerfully. He was himself deeply moved by the first sight of all his people; and his bowels yearned over this flock he had so long neglected. In a single sermon—two hours long, and yet seeming but twenty minutes—he declared the whole scripture: terrified the impenitent and thoughtless, confirmed the wavering, consoled the bereaved and afflicted, uplifted the heart of the poor; and when he ended, left the multitude standing rapt, as if unwilling to believe the divine music of his voice and soul had ceased.

Need I say that two poor women in a corner sat entranced, with streaming eyes? In that packed church the air was thick with woollen breath and damp cloaks, and with it the soft symphony of a congregation—shuffles, sniffles, a child’s stifled cough—until his voice took the whole soundscape in hand and made even those little noises seem like a ground-bass under a great air.

“Wherever gat he it all?” whispered Catherine, with her apron to her eyes. “By our Lady—not from me.”

As soon as they were by themselves Margaret threw her arms round Catherine’s neck and kissed her.

“Mother, mother, I am not quite a happy woman, but oh I am a proud one.”

And she vowed on her knees never by word or deed to let her love come between this young saint and Heaven.

Reader, did you ever stand by the seashore after a storm, when the wind has gone down suddenly? The waves cannot cease with their cause; indeed they seem at first to lash the sounding shore more fiercely than while the wind blew. Still we are conscious that inevitable calm has begun, and is now but rocking them to sleep. So it was with those true and tempest-tossed lovers from that eventful night when they went hand in hand beneath the stars from Gouda hermitage to Gouda manse.

At times a loud wave would come roaring; but it was only memory’s echo of the tempest that had swept their lives. The storm itself was over; and the boiling waters began from that moment to go down—down—down—gently, but inevitably.

This image must serve for the place of details that would be tedious and tame. What best merits heed is the general situation, and the strange complication of feeling it bred. History itself, though a bolder storyteller than romance, shows few things stranger than the footing on which Gerard and Margaret now lived for many years: united by present affection, past familiarity, and a marriage irregular but legal; separated by Holy Church and by their own consciences, which sided unreservedly with Holy Church; separated by the Church, yet united by a living pledge of affection—lawful in every sense at its date.

Living but a few miles from one another, and she calling his mother “mother.” For some years she took her boy to Gouda every Sunday, returning home at dark. Go when she would, it was always fête at Gouda manse, and she was received like a little queen. Catherine in those days was nearly always with her, and Eli very often. Tergou had so little to tempt them compared to Rotterdam; and at last they left it altogether and set up in the capital.

Thus the years glided: so barren now of striking incidents, so void of great hopes, and free from great fears, and so like one another that without dates I could scarce show the march of time. Yet in their sameness were little rites that stitched the days together: Sunday journeys with a basket of baked things for the manse, the smell of butter and mace, the careful wrapping so the crust should not sweat; the evening return as the frogs began their chorus in the ditches and the wind made a low organ of the reeds. It was as if their life, cut off from one language of the heart, had made itself a dialect of gestures, meals, and tones of voice—intimate, exact, and impossible to translate.

Early next year, 1471, the Duchess of Burgundy, with open dissent but secret connivance of the Duke, raised forces to enable her dethroned brother Edward the Fourth of England to invade that kingdom. Our old friend Denys thus enlisted; and passing through Rotterdam to the ships, heard on his way that Gerard was a priest, and Margaret alone. On this he told Margaret that marriage was not a habit of his, but that as his comrade had put it out of his own power to keep troth, he felt bound to offer to keep it for him.

“For a comrade’s honour is dear to us as our own,” said he.

She stared, then smiled. “I choose rather to be still thy she-comrade,” said she; “closer acquainted, we might not agree so well.”

And in her character of she-comrade she equipped him with a new sword of Antwerp make and a double handful of silver. “I give thee no gold,” said she, “for ’tis thrown away as quick as silver, and harder to win back. Heaven send thee safe out of all thy perils; there be famous fair women yonder to beguile thee with their faces, as well as men to hash thee with their axes.”

He was hurried on board at La Vere, and never saw Gerard at that time.

In 1473 Sybrandt began to fail. His pitiable existence had been sweetened by his brother’s inventive tenderness and his own contented spirit, which, his antecedents considered, was truly remarkable. As for Gerard, the day never passed that he did not give two hours to him: reading or singing to him, praying with him, and drawing him about in a soft carriage Margaret and he had made between them—a thing that rolled with the gentlest sound over the floor, as if mercy itself had wheels.

When the poor soul found his end near, he begged Margaret might be sent for. She came at once; and almost with his last breath he sought once more that forgiveness she had long ago accorded. She remained by him till the last; and he died, blessing and blessed, in the arms of the two true lovers he had parted for life. Tantum religio scit suadere boni.

1474 there was a wedding in Margaret’s house: Luke Peterson and Reicht Heynes.

It may seem less strange if I give the purport of that dialogue broken off long before.

Margaret had gone on to say, “Then in that case you can easily make him fancy you; and for my sake you must, for my conscience it pricketh me, and I must needs fit him with a wife—the best I know.” Margaret then instructed Reicht to be always kind and good-humoured to Luke; and she herself would be a model of peevishness to him.

“But be not thou so simple as run me down,” said she. “Leave that to me. Make thou excuses for me; I will make myself black enow.”

Reicht received these orders like an order to sweep a room, and obeyed punctually. She sweetened her voice, softened her eyes, made Luke’s humble meals taste of approval; while Margaret, with a craft that would have served at any great market, contrived to sour his hopes of herself without wounding his pride too cruelly—turning a word, delaying an answer, putting him off with a look, as one might keep a sauce from boiling over by a finger on the pot-lid.

After they had played this double artillery upon poor Luke for a couple of years, he got to look upon Margaret as his fog and wind, and Reicht as his sunshine; and his affections transferred themselves, he scarce knew how or when.

On the wedding day Reicht embraced Margaret and thanked her almost with tears.

“He was always my fancy,” said Margaret, “from the first hour I clapped eyes on him.”

“Heyday, you never told me that. What, Reicht, are you as sly as the rest?”

“Nay, nay,” said Reicht eagerly; “but I never thought you would really part with him to me. In my country the mistress looks to be served before the maid.”

Margaret settled them in her shop, and gave them half the profits.

1476 and 1477 were years of great trouble to Gerard, whose conscience compelled him to oppose the Pope. His Holiness, siding with the Grey Friars in their determination to swamp every palpable distinction between the Virgin Mary and her Son, bribed the Christian world into his crotchet by proffering pardon of all sins to such as would add to the Ave Mary this clause: “and blessed be thy Mother Anna, from whom, without blot of sin, proceeded thy virgin flesh.”

Gerard, with many of the northern clergy, held this sentence flat heresy. He not only refused to utter it in his church, but warned his parishioners against using it in private; and he refused to celebrate the new feast the Pope invented at the same time, “the feast of the miraculous conception of the Virgin.”

This drew upon him the bitter enmity of the Franciscans, and they were strong enough to put him into more than one serious difficulty, and to inflict many a little mortification on him—those pin-pricks that smart more than a blow because they come daily, and often with a sanctimonious smile.

In emergencies he consulted Margaret; and she always did one of two things: either she said, “I do not see my way,” and refused to guess; or else she gave advice that proved wonderfully sagacious. He had genius, but she had marvellous tact—an instinct for the hidden seasoning in men’s words, the way a phrase could be salted to preserve peace or over-salted to spoil it. And she had, too, an ear for the noises that govern temper: when the monks’ chanting came like a net over the town, she heard in it not only devotion but power; and when their sharp Latin clipped the air, she felt how a dominant tongue can press down the homelier speech of hearts.

Where affection came in and annihilated the woman’s judgment, he in turn stepped to her aid. Thus, though she knew she was spoiling little Gerard, and Catherine was ruining him for life, she would not part with him, but kept him at home, his abilities uncultivated. There was a shrewd boy of nine, who instead of learning to work and obey played about learning selfishness from their infinite unselfishness, and tyrannised with a rod of iron over two women—both sagacious and spirited—yet reduced by fondness to the exact level of idiots.

Gerard saw this with pain, and interfered with mild but firm remonstrance. After a considerable struggle he prevailed, and got little Gerard sent to the best school in Europe, kept by one Haaghe at Deventer: this was in 1477. Many tears were shed; but the great progress the boy made at that famous school reconciled Margaret in some degree. And the fidelity of Reicht Heynes, now her partner in business, enabled Margaret to spend weeks at a time hovering over her boy at Deventer—bringing him little comforts, the kind that carry one’s native air and taste: a spiced cake wrapped in linen so it should not stale, a bit of cured eel, a small cheese pressed with her own mark, and always some word in the homely tongue that no school Latin could quite replace.

So the years glided; and these two persons, subjected to as strong and constant a temptation as can well be conceived, were each other’s guardian angels—and not each other’s tempters.

To be sure the well-greased morality of the next century, which taught that solemn vows to God are sacred in proportion as they are reasonable, had at that time entered no single mind; and the alternative to these two minds was self-denial or sacrilege.

It was strange to hear them talk with unrestrained tenderness of their boy, and yet feel an icy barrier between themselves all the time—like a warm kitchen where bread is rising, but a door stands shut on a winter room, and one must not cross the threshold.

Eight years had now passed thus; and Gerard, fairly compared with men in general, was happy.

But Margaret was not.

The habitual expression of her face was a sweet pensiveness; but sometimes she was irritable and a little petulant. She even snapped Gerard now and then. And when she went to see him, if a monk was with him she would turn her back and go home. She hated the monks for having parted Gerard and her; and she inoculated her boy with a contempt for them which lasted him to his dying day. It was not only their doctrine she hated, but their tone—the way their words claimed dominion, as if holiness were a language only they might speak, and all other speech mere chatter.

Gerard bore with her like an angel. He knew her heart of gold, and hoped the ill gust would blow over.

He himself, being now the right man in the right place these many years—loving his parishioners and beloved by them, and occupied from morn to night in good works—recovered the natural cheerfulness of his disposition. To tell the truth, a part of his jocoseness was a blind: he was the greatest peacemaker—except Mr. Harmony in the play—that ever was born. He reconciled more enemies in ten years than his predecessors had done in three hundred; and one manoeuvre in his art was to make the quarrellers laugh at the cause of quarrel, so undermining the demon of discord.

Independently of that, he truly loved a harmless joke. He was a wonderful tamer of animals—squirrels, hares, fawns, and the like. So half in jest a parishioner who had a mule supposed possessed with a devil gave it him, saying, “Tame this vagabone, parson, if ye can.” In about six months—Heaven knows how—he not only tamed Jack, but won his affections so that Jack would come running to his whistle like a dog.

One day, having taken shelter from a shower on the stone settle outside a certain public-house, he heard a toper within—a stranger—boasting he could take more at a draught than any man in Gouda. Gerard marched in at once.

“What, lads,” said he, “do none of ye take him up for the honour of Gouda? Shall it be said there came hither one from another parish a greater sot than any of us? Nay, then, I your parson do take him up. Go to, I’ll find thee a parishioner shall drink more at a draught than thou.”

A bet was made. Gerard whistled. In clattered Jack—for he was taught to come into a room with the utmost composure—and put his nose into his backer’s hand.

“A pair of buckets!” shouted Gerard. “And let us see which of these two sons of asses can drink most at a draught.”

On another occasion two farmers had a dispute whose hay was the best. Failing to convince each other, they said, “We’ll ask parson,” for by this time he was their referee in every mortal thing.

“How lucky you thought of me!” said Gerard. “Why, I have got one staying with me who is the best judge of hay in Holland. Bring me a double handful apiece.”

So when they came, he had them into the parlour and put each bundle on a chair. Then he whistled, and in walked Jack.

“Lord a mercy!” said one of the farmers.

“Jack,” said the parson, in the tone of conversation, “just tell us which is the best hay of these two.”

A priest is never so wholly priest as when the room is darkened, the candles burn low, and Death—patient, noiseless, and absolute—sits at the bedside like an old acquaintance. Gerard did the last offices as the Church had taught him, word following word, sign following sign, as steadily as he had done for the poorest hind that ever lay with clay on his boots. His hands moved; his voice obeyed; the rites went on with a terrible propriety, as if order itself could keep calamity at bay.

When all was finished, he sat down, stunned, his mind refusing the shape of what had happened. Grief had not yet found its teeth. The chamber had its own small sounds—the faint wick-sputter, the soft settling of linen, the far-off creak of timber in the house—each sound too clear, too near, because her breathing was no longer there to round them and make them homely.

Then, as though a spring within him leaped, he fell upon his knees and, in a sudden blaze of religious fervour, thanked Heaven—not for the stroke, but for her Christian end; for the seal of peace upon her; for the prayers said in time; for the merciful ordering of her last hour. He clung to that, because it was something he could name. And after that one fierce act of praise, thought narrowed to a single, burning duty: to take her away from strangers and lay her in his own earth, among the graves that knew his footstep and the psalms of his voice.

That very evening a covered cart, with one horse, set out for Gouda. In it lay a coffin; and beside it—so close that his breath seemed meant to warm the metal—lay a broken-hearted man with his arms and chin resting on the lead that held her.
