The haste and labour of making ready—ordering boards, seeing to the fitting, the decent covering, the necessary papers and words to men who did not understand—had spent the little force his soul could muster. Now he lay crushed, as if the cart-wheels ran over his very heart, and clung to the cold lid like a man clinging to a plank in black water.

The carter walked by the horse’s head and did not speak to him. There was a kind of reverence in his silence, as there is in a kitchen when a great pot has boiled over and scalded some one—no loud calls, no clatter, only the careful hush that says: pain is here, tread softly. When he baited the horse at a wayside, he spoke even then but in a whisper, out of respect to that dumb agony that lay inside the tilt. The world outside went on with its ordinary noises—wind in the hedges, a distant dog, the far ring of a smith’s hammer on iron—yet those sounds were muffled by the cart’s canvas and by Gerard’s own inward roar.

At the night stop the carter and the landlord made a well-meant attempt to coax him down, to get him into a room, to put food before him and make him sleep. The smell of bread and broth came to the doorway—honest, saving smells that had comforted men a thousand times—yet to him they were like a language he could not speak. He repulsed them; and when they persisted, he almost snarled, not as a priest, not as a reasoning man, but like a faithful dog guarding what has been given him to guard. He clung to the lead all night, refusing even the little mercy of a pillow, as if to move an inch away were to betray her.

So they drew a cloak over him and left him in peace.

At noon next day the sorrowful cart came up to the manse. There were full a score of parishioners gathered there already, each with his own poor grievance—a cow gone lame, a child feverish, a neighbour’s boundary disputed, a husband too fond of the alehouse. They had missed the parson and came, as folk do, for counsel and for comfort. But when they saw what the cart bore, and saw their healer stricken down like any other man, the crowd’s small murmurs broke into a loud wail of grief.

That human cry, rising all at once like a gust through trees, startled him from his lethargy. He lifted his head, and the familiar faces swam before him—faces he had known in sowing-time and harvest, in christening and confession. He tried to speak; and the words that came were not sermon, not rebuke, not doctrine, but sheer fatherhood. “Oh, my children! my children!” he cried. Then anguish closed his throat, and he could say no more.

Yet the next day, in spite of all remonstrance, he buried her himself. He would not be spared that final service, as if any other hand at the grave were an intrusion. He read the appointed words, and his voice only trembled now and then, like a bell that has a crack yet still gives a true note. Many tears fell upon the earth that received her—tears of women who had come to her for kindness, of men who had respected her, of children who had felt her hand upon their hair; and tears, too, of those who did not know her well but knew what it is for a household’s heart to be taken away.

When the service ended, Gerard stayed there in the churchyard, standing like a statue. The people withdrew, one by one, out of respect, leaving him alone with the new mound and the raw smell of turned soil—a smell that in other seasons meant potatoes planted, cabbages set, the promise of stew in winter; but now meant only that the ground had swallowed his life’s companion. The birds went on with their thin notes in the yews; somewhere beyond the wall a cart rumbled; the village breathed. He stood as one in a dream, hearing everything and understanding nothing.

The sexton, who was—as most men are—a fool, began to fill in the grave without giving due warning. The first patter of earth upon the coffin-lid came sharp and sudden, like hail on a roof. At that sound Gerard uttered a piercing scream, so wild that it made the very air shudder.

The sexton stopped short. Gerard staggered, and his hand flew to his breast as if something within had given way like a snapped cord. The sexton caught him, clumsy but frightened into gentleness, and called for help. Jorian Ketel, who had lingered near, mourning his benefactress, ran into the churchyard at once; and between them they supported Gerard to the manse.

“Ah, Jorian! good Jorian!” Gerard gasped, with a dreadful simplicity. “Something snapped within me; I felt it, and I heard it; here, Jorian, here;” and he pressed his hand hard upon his breast, as if to keep the broken place from widening.

A fortnight after, when the flat land about Gouda lay rinsed clean by a thin rain, a pale, bowed figure came up the causeway toward the Dominican house that stood beyond the town, where fields began again and the air changed its temper. The convent’s bell did not clang like a market bell; it spoke with a softer throat, and the sound went abroad over wet hedges and the breathing ditches, mingling with the plash of oars, the far cry of geese, the low, perpetual chew of wind in reeds. Even the gate—heavy oak, iron-scarred—made its own honest music when the porter drew it, not the brutal shriek of newfangled wheel and forge, but a deep complain that settled the mind instead of fretting it.

The man who entered had the look of one who had eaten little, and slept less. It was Gerard.

He came as men sometimes come home to a first hearth: not because it is grand, but because its smells and sounds are older than their grief. His own manse had become more than he could bear. Every board and ledge there remembered her; the very common noises were turned against him—footsteps that were not hers, a pot-lid that fell too sharply, a gust that rattled the shutters with an empty hand. Here, within these walls, the day was portioned by rule: not by appetite, nor by memory’s cruel caprice. The broth would be broth at noon, the bread would be bread at night; and the bell would tell him when to rise, when to kneel, when to sleep. He desired peace as a starving man desires a bowl held steady.

He asked speech with Brother Ambrose.

Ambrose governed the convent as deputy, the prior having lately died, and the new one, though appointed, not having yet arrived. Ambrose, kind by nature and made kinder by discipline, received Gerard as one receives a worn traveler: he did not begin with questions that bite, but with a chair, and a cup, and quiet.

They gave him the convent’s plain refreshment—dark bread that still held the scent of rye-fields, and a pottage of peas and herbs, not over-salted, warmed through with that slow, patient stirring that keeps the bottom from catching. The kitchen sounds came muffled through stone: the scrape of a ladle on the cauldron’s rim, the thud of a loaf on the board, the steady whisper of knife against onion. Such homely acoustics, ordered and unadvertised, can heal more than sermons; they are a language of care no proud tongue can translate.

Gerard entered as a novice, on probation; yet the truth was, he was a failing man and knew it, and came there to end life as he began it—under a rule, among brethren, near gentle Ambrose, his friend, and the other monks to whom his house and heart had always stood open. It was not that he sought to be remarkable in dying. He wanted the opposite: to slip into the convent’s rhythm as into a familiar tune, where the notes are known and there is no need to improvise pain into speech.

Ambrose, who knew his value and his sorrow, was not without a kindly hope of curing him and restoring him to his parish. With this view he lodged him in a comfortable cell over the gateway, where one could hear the gate-chain and the porter’s step, and, beyond, the low talk of travelers and the more distant hush of fields—a soundscape that keeps a man tethered to the world without dragging him into it. And Ambrose forbade him to fast or to practice any austerities.

“Eat,” Ambrose bade him, with that practical tenderness which understands that the soul rides the body like a rider on a horse. “Take the broth. Take the bread. You shall not scrape yourself to holiness. God is not fed by your hunger.”

So for some days Gerard obeyed. He drank what they set him—thin ale that smelt faintly of grain and smoke, water cool as a stone cup can keep it. He took the convent fare, small, regular, honest. Yet the food did not bloom in him; it only stayed him, as a little lamp stays the dark without conquering it. The past still pressed on him, but here it pressed more softly, as if the walls themselves remembered other sorrows and did not make a spectacle of his.

Then, in a few days, the new prior arrived.

He proved a very Tartar.

At first he was absorbed in curing abuses and tightening the general discipline. He strode through the house as if correction were a virtue in itself: ears pricked for laughter, eyes sharp for comfort, as though a man’s peace must always be purchased with a visible pinch. The convent’s sounds altered under him: the same bell now seemed to command more than to invite; the same footsteps in the cloister rang harder, for men walked as if on eggs for fear of being heard.

One day, hearing that the vicar of Gouda had entered the convent as a novice, the prior’s mouth tightened, and his words struck like a cleaver on a block.

“’Tis well,” said he. “Let him first give up his vicarage then, or go. I’ll no fat parsons in my house.”

So the prior sent for Gerard.

Gerard went.

He crossed the cloister, where the air smelt of damp stone and extinguished tallow, and of the kitchen’s distant steam. A sparrow chattered in the gutter, and the sound, small and innocent, seemed for a moment like a remembered word in a mother tongue—something one cannot quite carry into harsher speech. He mounted the stair, hearing his own breath in the hush, and came before the prior.

The moment they saw one another they both started, as if an old name, long buried, had been spoken aloud in the wrong language.

“Clement!”

“Jerome!”

Jerome was morose by nature—his brow seemed carved for disapproval—yet toward Gerard he had softened a little, as winter yields a finger’s breadth to sun. In England he had missed him more than pride would let him name; and afterward, at odd hours, he found himself listening for his brother’s step in the cloister passage, as if sound could undo distance.

What he heard at Gouda had raised Gerard in his esteem. Above all, men told how Clement—so they called him now—had stood firm against Pope and Minorites upon that “infernal heresy of the immaculate conception,” as Jerome named it, grinding the words between his teeth like hard grain. That was the sort of resistance Jerome could honour: not the soft rebellion of appetite, but the stern refusal that cost a man friends and favour.

Then a young monk, wet-faced, came to him with the cause of Gerard’s sickness. Jerome’s brief tenderness snapped back into its old disdain.

“Dying for a woman?”

He resolved to stop the scandal if he could, and if he could not, to fence it in with doctrine. Twice a day he went to Clement’s cell, where the air was thin with candle-smoke and old lime, and tried all his former influence—his iron logic, his stern exhortations—to make Gerard shake off what he called unspiritual despondency, and not rob the Church of piety and eloquence at so critical a season.

Gerard listened, approved the reasoning, admired Jerome’s strength, confessed his own weakness—and yet, before Jerome’s very eyes, continued to ebb. It was like watching a hearth-fire whose embers will not take, no matter how patiently you coax them: you add the kindling, you breathe, you shelter it from draft, and still it sinks to grey.

One day Jerome came with his argument sharpened to a point.

“I have heard thy story,” he said, “and heard it with pride. But now thou spoilest it all, Clement; for this is the triumph of earthly passion. Better thou hadst yielded and repented, than resist while she lived, and succumb under it now, body and soul.”

“Dear Jerome,” said Clement—so gently that the words ceased to be rebuke and became a plea—“here I think thou dost me some injustice. Passion there is none; but a deep affection, for which I will not blush here, since I shall not blush for it in heaven. Bethink thee: the poor dog that dies of grief upon his master’s grave—is he guilty of passion? Neither am I.

“Passion had saved my life and lost my soul. She was my good angel. She sustained me in duty and charity; her face encouraged me in the pulpit; her lips soothed me under ingratitude. She intertwined herself with all that was good in my life; and after leaning on her so long, I could not go on alone.

“And, dear Jerome, believe me, I am no rebel against Heaven. It is God’s will to release me. When they threw the earth upon her poor coffin, something snapped within my bosom here that mended may not be. I heard it, and I felt it. And from that time, Jerome, no food that I put in my mouth had any savour. With mine eyes bandaged now I could not tell thee which was bread and which was flesh, by eating of it.”

Jerome’s mouth fell open an instant, as if he had smelt something impossible—like honey turned to smoke.

“Holy saints!”

“And again,” Clement went on, as if reporting a change in the weather, not the sundering of a life, “from that same hour my deep dejection left me, and I smiled again. I often smile—why? I read it thus: He in whose hands are the issues of life and death gave me that minute the great summons. ’Twas some cord of life snapped in me. He is very pitiful. I should have lived unhappy; but He said, ‘No; enough is done, enough is suffered; poor feeble, loving servant, thy shortcomings are forgiven, thy sorrows touch their end; come thou to thy rest!’ I come, Lord, I come!”

Jerome groaned, not in argument now but in defeat.

“The Church had ever her holy but feeble servants,” he said. “Now would I give ten years of my life to save thine. But I see it may not be. Die in peace.”

And so it was. In a few days more Gerard lay a-dying in a mind so holy and happy that more than one aged saint came to gather his last sayings, as men go out at harvest to glean what the reapers miss.

In the evening he had seen Giles, and begged him—his voice already loosened from the world—to do small homely mercies, the sort that keep a life from falling utterly into neglect: not to let poor Jack starve; to see that little Gerard’s trustees did their duty; to kiss his parents for him; and to send Denys to his friends in Burgundy.

“Poor thing,” he murmured, “he will feel so strange here without his comrade.”

After that he had speech with Jerome alone. What passed between them was never clearly known; but it must have been something remarkable, for Jerome came from the door with his hands crossed upon his breast, his high head lowered, sighing as he went—as if some proud instrument in him had been re-tuned, and he did not yet know how to bear the new music.

Two monks watched with Clement till matins. They said that all through the night he broke out now and then into pious ejaculations and praises and thanksgivings; only once, they said, he wandered and thought he saw her walking in green meadows with other spirits clad in white, and beckoning him; and they all smiled and beckoned him. The watchers smiled too, half in awe, half in the tender foolishness that takes comfort from another’s comfort.

And both of them—though it might have been fancy born of candle-flame and vigil—declared that just before dawn there came three light taps against the wall, one after another, very slow. In that hush the monastery’s smallest sounds were magnified: the creak of timber settling, the far drip from a gutter, the faint brush of a mouse behind wainscot. Yet these taps were distinct, as measured as a knuckle upon a door.

The dying man heard them, and said, very clearly, “I come, love, I come.”

This at least is certain: he did utter those words, and having uttered them, prepared for departure as a man rises and sets his cloak when the time has come.

He sent for all the monks who at that hour were keeping vigil. They came and hovered about him like gentle spirits, their voices braided of prayer. Some prayed in silence with faces to the ground; others supported his head tenderly, as if afraid that the least roughness might bruise the soul on its way out.

When one said something of his life of self-denial and charity, Gerard stopped him. His voice—worn these days to a thread—suddenly cleared and rang with a force that seemed not his own.

“My dear brethren,” he said, “take note that he who here dies so happy holds not these new-fangled doctrines of man’s merit. Oh, what a miserable hour were this to me an I did! Nay, but I hold, with the Apostles and their pupils in the Church, the ancient fathers, that we are justified not by our own wisdom, or piety, or the works we have done in holiness of heart, but by faith.”

Silence fell. The monks glanced at one another, each hearing in those words not only comfort but a challenge, a shaping of memory, a refusal to let his last breath be translated into some other man’s triumph. In the cloister, language was power; the phrase that survived would govern how the dead were used by the living.

Then Gerard, still with that strange lucidity, said, “Please you sweep the floor.”

They obeyed at once, with awe and curiosity. The broom rasped over stone, raising a dry scent—dust, chalk, and the faint sharpness of old ash that had lodged in cracks. In that sound there was something domestic, almost kitchen-like, as if a hearth were being cleared for the next baking, and the act steadied them.

“Make me a great cross with wood ashes,” said Clement.

They fetched ashes—grey, light, and powder-fine, the residue of yesterday’s fire. They strewed them upon the floor in the form of a great Cross. The ash lay like flour on a board, dulling the stone’s cold shine, and the air took on that particular smell of extinguished warmth: char without flame, the ghost of fuel.

“Now lay me down on it,” he said, “for so will I die.”

They lifted him gently from the bed. He was so wasted that he seemed to weigh nothing, as if grief had consumed him the way a slow fire consumes wood from within. They laid him upon the cross of ashes.

“Shall we spread out thine arms, dear brother?” one asked, trembling.

“Now God forbid!” he answered. “Am I worthy of that?”

He lay silent, eyes raised, not staring but seeing. Presently he spoke, half to them and half to himself, with rapture gathered tight as a fist.

“Oh,” he said, “I feel it buoyant. It lifts me floating in the sky whence my merits had sunk me like lead.”

Day broke and showed his face cast upward in silent joy, hands together—like Margaret’s, they said afterward, remembering that other death as men remember the taste of a bread once eaten in hunger: never quite describable, never forgotten.

And just about the hour she died, he spoke his last word in this world.

“Jesu!”

And even with that word he fell asleep.

They laid him out for his rest. Under his linen they found a horse-hair shirt, rough as penance itself.

“Ah!” cried the young monks, “behold a saint!”

Under the hair-cloth they found a long thick tress of auburn hair.

They started back, horrified; and a babel of voices rose—some condemning, some excusing—each man trying to force the ungovernable fact into the lexicon he trusted. The lock, mute and fragrant with some ghost of the past, resisted them all.

In the midst of the dispute Jerome came in. He listened a moment, his face hardening at the sound of eager judgment. Then he turned to an ardent young monk called Basil, who was crying scandal the loudest.

“Basil,” said he, “is she alive or dead that owned this hair?”

“How may I know, father?”

“Then for aught thou knowest it may be the relic of a saint.”

“Certes it may be,” said Basil, sceptically.

“Thou hast then broken our rule,” Jerome replied, “which saith, ‘Put ill construction on no act done by a brother which can be construed innocently.’ Who art thou to judge such a man as this was? Go to thy cell, and stir not out for a week by way of penance.”

He carried off the lock of hair. And when the coffin was to be closed, he cleared the cell and, alone with the dead, put the tress upon Clement’s bosom.

“There, Clement,” he said to the still face.

Then, as if he feared even that mercy might be pride, he set himself a penance for doing it—and nailed the coffin up with his own hands.

The next day Gerard was buried in Gouda churchyard. The monks followed in procession from the convent, their footsteps and chant making a slow river of sound through streets that otherwise held their tongues. Jerome, evidently fulfilling the wishes of the deceased, read the service.

The grave was deep, and at the bottom of it lay a lead coffin already waiting. Poor Gerard’s—light as a feather, so had he wasted—was lowered and placed beside it.

After the service Jerome spoke a few words to the crowd of parishioners who had come to take the last look at their best friend. When he named the departed man’s virtues, loud wailing broke out, and tears fell upon the coffin like rain—salt upon wood, grief upon grief.

The monks went home. Jerome gathered them in the refectory, that room of daily bread and measured silence, and there spoke to them—not as one triumphing, but as one chastened.

“We have this day laid a saint in the earth,” he said. “The convent will keep his trentals, but will feast, not fast; for our good brother is freed from the burden of the flesh; his labours are over, and he hath entered into his joyful rest. I alone shall fast, and do penance; for to my shame I say it, I was unjust to him, and knew not his worth till it was too late.

“And you, young monks, be not curious to inquire whether a lock he bore upon his bosom was a token of pure affection or the relic of a saint; but remember the heart he wore beneath. Most of all, fix your eyes upon his life and conversation, and follow them an ye may: for he was a holy man.”

Thus, after life’s fitful fever, these true lovers were at peace. The grave—kinder to them than the Church—united them for ever; and now a man of another age and nation, touched with their fate, has laboured to build their tombstone and rescue them from long and unmerited oblivion. He asks for them your sympathy, but not your pity. No: put this story to a wholesome use.

Fiction must often give false views of life and death; here, as it happens—curbed by history—she gives you true ones. Let the barrier that kept these true lovers apart prepare you for this: that here on earth there will nearly always be some obstacle or other to your perfect happiness. To their early death apply your Reason and your Faith, by way of exercise and preparation. For if you cannot bear to be told that these died young—who, had they lived a hundred years, would still be dead—how shall you bear to see the gentle, the loving, and the true glide from your own bosom to the grave, and fly from your house to heaven?

Yet this is in store for you. In every age the Master of life and death, kinder as well as wiser than we are, has transplanted to heaven, young, earth’s sweetest flowers. I ask your sympathy, then, for their rare constancy and pure affection, and their cruel separation by a vile heresy in the bosom of the Church; but not your pity for their early yet happy end.

Beati sunt qui in Domino moriuntur.

In obedience to a custom I have always disliked, yet never quite had the stubbornness to refuse, I loiter a moment longer on the threshold and gather up the smaller lives I have dropped along the road—those crumbs of humanity that prove Gerard did not journey from Holland to Rome through a toy-world of carved dolls, but through breathing folk, each with a mouth to be fed, a tongue to speak, and a fate to taste.

Eli and Catherine lasted into a great age—so long that, in their dimming rooms, Gerard and Margaret became like old sayings: repeated less for exactness than for comfort. Their house kept its habits. The day still began with the small domestic music of it: a latch lifted, a pail set down, the soft chide of a hen, the scrape of a knife on a board. Bread still rose and browned; porridge still thickened with patient stirring; herbs still hung to dry where the air moved cleanly through them. If time thinned their sight, it sharpened, oddly, the other senses—Catherine could tell, by the first crackle in the hearth, whether the wood was too green; she could judge, by the sound of boiling, whether a pot wanted skimming. In such homely acoustics a life can root itself deeper than in any speech of pride.

Giles, too, was long-lived: he went to the court of Bavaria and was known there at ninety—yet by then had somehow turned into bones and leather, all angles and straps, his very voice grown trumpet-toned, as if it had been cured in smoke and hung in a draught. He was the sort of old man whose laugh startled birds from hedges, and whose step, though slow, still struck the floor like a signal.

Cornelis, rid at last of rivals and forgiven long since by his mother—who clung to him more and more now all her brood was scattered like seed—waited and waited and waited for his parents’ decease. He waited as some men watch a loaf in an oven, not with love but with appetite, counting minutes that belong to Heaven. Yet Catherine’s shrewd word came true: before she and her mate wore out, this worthy rusted away. At five-and-sixty he lay dying of mere old age in his mother’s arms—she a hale woman of six-and-eighty, with hands that had kneaded and scrubbed and tended and did not yet forget their work. He had lain unconscious awhile, but came to himself in articulo mortis; and seeing her close, he told her—there, on the edge of silence—how he would transform the shop and premises as soon as they should be his.

“Yes, my darling,” said the poor old woman, soothing him as one soothes a fevered child that begs for sweetmeats, and in another minute he was clay. And that clay was followed to the grave by all the feet whose shoes he had waited for—an odd procession, for in a town people remember a man not by his prayers but by what he measured and sold them, by the small tyrannies he practiced at the counter, by the way his words pinched like a tight welt. So the last sound he made in the world—the last breath leaving his throat—was answered by the common, indifferent sound of many soles on a road: life stepping over death, as it must.

Denys, broken-hearted at his comrade’s death, was glad to return to Burgundy. There, a small pension the court allowed him kept him until, quite unexpectedly, he inherited a considerable sum from a relation—fortune coming late, like a dish set down when appetite is already dulled. For many years he was known in his native place as a crusty old soldier, who could tell good stories of war when he chose: tales in which the clink of harness and the cough of powder still lived in his mouth, though the battlefields were far behind him. But he was also a bitter railer against women—his speech, once meant to command, curdled into complaint, as milk will if you leave it too long by the fire. Yet even he, in some winter evenings when the wind combed the eaves and the room held only the honest noises of a household—spoon against bowl, log settling, a child’s small breath—would grow quiet, and the very silence showed what no boasting could: that a man’s heart has its own language, and sometimes loses it.

Jerome, disgusted with northern laxity, retired to Italy; and having high connections became at seventy a mitred abbot. He put on the screw of discipline. His monks revered and hated him. Under his rule the cloister grew sharp-edged: days were divided by bells that cut the air cleanly, prayers marched in their appointed ranks, and every fault—whether of flesh, of tongue, or of mind—was hunted down like a rat in a granary. He ruled with iron rod ten years. And one night he died, alone; for he had never found the way to a single heart. The Vulgate was on his pillow, and the crucifix in his hand, and on his lips something more like a smile than was ever seen there while he lived; so that, at that awful hour, methinks he was not quite alone.

Requiescat in pace.

The Master he served has many servants, and they have many minds; and now and then a faithful one will be a surly one, as it is in these our mortal mansions. A rule may keep a house standing, yet it cannot make it warm; words may govern a tongue, yet they cannot always translate the secret hunger beneath it. There are dialects of tenderness that no dominant lexicon can compel, and silences that rise, like steam from a pot, when a soul has been too tightly covered.

The yellow-haired laddie, Gerard Gerardson, belongs not to Fiction but to History. She has recorded his birth in other terms than mine. Over the tailor’s house in the Brede Kirk Straet she has inscribed: “HAEC EST PARVA DOMUS NATUS QUA MAGNUS ERASMUS,” and she has written half-a-dozen lives of him. But there is something left for her yet to do. She has no more comprehended magnum Erasmum than any other pigmy comprehends a giant, or partisan a judge. First scholar and divine of his epoch, he was also the heaven-born dramatist of his century. Some of the best scenes in this new book are from his mediaeval pen, and illumine the pages where they come; for the words of a genius so high as his are not born to die. Their immediate work upon mankind fulfilled, they may seem to lie torpid; but at each fresh shower of intelligence Time pours upon their students, they prove their immortal race: they revive, they spring from the dust of great libraries; they bud, they flower, they fruit, they seed, from generation to generation, and from age to age.
